Extending the final sample to the window end requires an explicit sample-and-hold assumption. Uncovered time remains unknown. CPU-frequency intervals are also available from linux.cpu.frequency below; check the kHz unit.

Error 4: stdlib table name / column name pitfalls

Commit a262dadf1 added these two pitfalls to the methodology prompt template. It did not establish that runtime learning generated two error/fix pairs. The clue was the orphan stderr after a timeout: the analysis had already ended, but trace_processor was still spitting out errors. Following those logs led back to these SQL problems.

Filters are omitted above; first INCLUDE PERFETTO MODULE android.garbage_collection; for the GC query. gc_dur describes a GC interval, not a main-thread stop-the-world pause. Associate running, runnable, and pause intervals separately. Fields are checked against Perfetto v58.3 frequency and garbage_collection.

Stdlib view authors often use domain-prefixed column names to avoid ambiguous column issues during multi-table JOINs, but Claude defaults to assuming conventional names like ts/dur. This “stdlib’s own naming conventions vs. general SQL conventions” conflict can’t be fully solved automatically through schema introspection – the lookup_sql_schema tool can tell Claude the table exists and what columns it has, but it can’t predict “this time Claude will definitely assume ts.” Actual-schema context, column constraints, and result-semantic checks also help; error/fix pairs are supplementary.

The detection and learning mechanism for these errors works as follows: when SQL execution fails, the error message and SQL are temporarily stored; when a subsequent SQL execution succeeds, the system uses Jaccard similarity matching (excluding SQL structural keywords like SELECT/FROM/WHERE, and Perfetto common tokens like utid/dur/slice) to determine whether it’s a corrected version of the same query. The matching threshold is >30%, with a 60-second time window. A successful match generates an error->fix pair that is persisted to disk.

When a new analysis begins, up to 10 error-correction pairs are loaded, with up to 5 rendered into the System Prompt, so Claude can see these known pitfalls before writing SQL. Error-correction pairs have a 30-day TTL and are automatically cleaned up upon expiration – Perfetto’s SQL schema changes with version updates.

Successful execution means SQL was accepted, not that the fix preserved intent or produced correct values. Similarity/time-window matching can pair unrelated queries, and a 30-day TTL does not bind a pair to a schema version. Recheck learned fixes against the target trace and engine.

Part 6: The Evolution of the Development Process Itself

This final section steps slightly outside the product itself to discuss the development process. SmartPerfetto was built with AI-assisted development – from the first line of code to now, Claude Code has been the primary programming tool. Looking back over these three months, the way I use AI-assisted development has itself gone through several iterations, with logic similar to SmartPerfetto’s evolution from agentv2 to agentv3.

Stages of AI-Assisted Development

First, a brief explanation of the tools and concepts involved:

  • Claude Code: Anthropic’s CLI tool that enables terminal conversations with Claude, where Claude can directly read/write files and execute commands. Throughout development, I ran with --dangerously-skip-permissions (dangerous mode) and bypass permissions enabled, allowing Claude to autonomously execute file edits, command runs, Git operations, etc. without per-action confirmation. This dramatically improved iteration speed – Claude can continuously execute complete “modify code -> run tests -> check results -> fix -> re-run” cycles without being interrupted by permission dialogs, at the cost of requiring the developer to have sufficient trust in Claude’s operations and perform after-the-fact review.
  • Claude Agent SDK: Anthropic’s Agent development framework, on which SmartPerfetto’s agentv3 backend is built. The SDK encapsulates multi-turn conversation management, MCP tool-calling loops, automatic context compression (auto-compact), and other capabilities. Developers define the tool set and System Prompt, and the SDK drives Claude to autonomously complete multi-round analysis.
  • Plan Mode: Claude Code’s planning mode, where the AI first outputs a structured implementation plan (which files to modify, what to change, order and dependencies), the human reviews and confirms, then the AI executes the code changes.
  • Superpowers: A third-party development workflow/Skill collection, not the name of Claude Code’s entire plugin ecosystem or of Chrome DevTools/Playwright MCP. The personal narrative retains the original “SuperPower” wording. Plan Mode is a Claude Code feature.
  • Codex + Codex MCP: Codex is OpenAI’s coding-agent product/tool family, not one fixed model name. The historical workflow used a local MCP integration to request review from another Agent. codex mcp-server is a CLI integration entry point; read-only behavior depends on tools and sandbox configuration, not MCP itself. See the CLI reference.
  • Agent Team / Subagent: Subagents can have separate contexts and roles. Current Agent teams and subagents are distinct mechanisms; launching parallel subagents is not automatically the full team feature.
  • Skills / Hooks: Claude Code’s extension mechanisms. Skills are reusable task templates (e.g., /commit, /simplify), and Hooks are scripts that automatically execute on specific events (e.g., before/after tool calls).

My Actual Evolution

Stage 1: Direct Conversation

The earliest development approach was describing requirements directly in Claude Code and letting the AI modify code. Similar to pair programming where one person talks and the other writes. At this stage, every change needed line-by-line human review because the AI’s understanding of project context was limited, frequently making local modifications that didn’t align with the overall architecture.

Stage 2: Plan Mode (SuperPower)

After adopting Plan Mode, the workflow became: I describe the requirement -> AI outputs a structured implementation plan (which files to modify, what to change in each, modification order and dependencies) -> I review the plan -> AI executes after confirmation. This shifted the review focus from “examining code line by line” to “reviewing the architecture plan,” noticeably improving efficiency.

Stage 3: Plan Mode (SuperPower) + Peer Review (Codex)

Relying on a single AI to generate plans is prone to blind spots. I began sending the plan to Codex for independent review after the Plan Mode plan was finalized. Codex accesses the codebase in read-only mode and provides feedback from three angles: architectural soundness, edge cases, and missed risks. This effectively introduces a code review step into the AI development workflow.

Most of the 9 rounds of architecture review mentioned earlier in the article went through this process. Taking the Perfetto Stdlib integration as an example (Round 7, March 15), Codex reviewed 3 rounds, raising a cumulative 36 feedback points, including issues I had missed in the plan such as the stdlib module preloading strategy and the Schema Index cache invalidation mechanism.

Stage 4: Harness-ified Engineering Pipeline

By the later stages, the development workflow had become:

In this workflow, human involvement is concentrated at Step 1 (requirements and architectural decisions) and Step 4 (evaluating review feedback). Code details, test execution, and formatting cleanup are handled by the engineering pipeline.

This is the historical SmartPerfetto workflow, not a universal command list for every checkout. The article does not supply a complete terminal record of these runs. A script existing, an SSE stream ending, or a report being written does not establish correct attribution. Reproduction needs a pinned commit, trace, model/configuration, expected evidence, and terminal outcome, distinguishing deterministic checks, real-model E2E, failures, and skips.

Correspondence with SmartPerfetto’s Architecture

Looking back, my AI-assisted development workflow and SmartPerfetto’s Agent analysis workflow are structurally similar:

DimensionSmartPerfetto Agent AnalysisMy AI-Assisted Development
Intent UnderstandingScene Classifier identifies the sceneI determine the requirement direction
Strategy Injection.strategy.md injects analysis methodologyPlan Mode outputs implementation plan
ExecutionMCP tool calls for SQL/SkillsClaude Code executes code changes
Quality Verification3-layer Verifier (heuristic + Plan + Haiku)Regression tests + Codex review
Correction LoopCorrection Prompt has Claude reviseTest failure -> analyze -> fix -> re-run
Cross-session LearningPattern Memory + SQL error-correctionCLAUDE.md rule accumulation + memory system

Both systems evolved in the same direction: human involvement shifted from the execution layer up to the decision layer. SmartPerfetto went from a fixed pipeline (humans define every step) to autonomous reasoning (humans define goals and constraints); my development approach went from line-by-line review to reviewing architecture plans.

This is not coincidental – the core of Harness Engineering is building sufficient engineering infrastructure (tests, verification, review) so that humans can trust the AI’s execution results and focus their attention on higher-level decisions.

The diagram below summarizes SmartPerfetto’s complete Harness Engineering landscape – from input routing to cross-session learning:

The original diagram is retained for structure. “~30% false positives caught” is not supported by a detection-rate evaluation and cannot be inferred from the original observed ~30% error figure. An 80% cache-hit rate, 85% savings, and improving accuracy over time are not verified guarantees. The snapshot uses 60/90-day TTLs for positive/negative patterns respectively, not one universal 90-day TTL.

Conclusion

Looking back over three months of iteration, from agentv2’s 13-step fixed pipeline to agentv3’s autonomous reasoning, from observed misjudgments to three-layer verification, from a 15000-token System Prompt to 4500-token on-demand loading – every change was driven by a concrete failure experience.

After completing this project, I have two takeaways about AI Agent application development.

The first is: the bulk of the work is not in the LLM API calls themselves, but in the engineering infrastructure surrounding the LLM:

  • How should the System Prompt be organized so the LLM doesn’t confuse context? -> Scene classification + on-demand loading + token budget
  • How do you control the LLM’s execution order so it thinks before acting? -> Planning Gate + hypothesis submission
  • How much data should be returned to the LLM? -> Artifact Store: give summaries, not full data
  • How do you detect and intercept the LLM’s domain misjudgments? -> Three-layer verification + correction loop
  • How do you ensure data query precision? -> YAML Skills (declarative SQL) + SQL error-correction learning
  • How do you adapt to different rendering architectures and chip platforms? -> Architecture detection + vendor overrides

The second takeaway is: the Agent’s “environment” matters far more than prompt wording. In agentv3’s early days, I spent considerable time adjusting System Prompt wording and formatting. I later discovered that what truly affects Agent output quality is not how the prompt is written, but what tools it’s given, what data is returned, and what constraints are imposed. Three concrete examples:

  • After adding submit_plan gating, Claude stopped making directionless SQL queries (previously it would make purposeless queries like SELECT * FROM slice -> SELECT * FROM thread), and analysis paths became organized
  • After adding ArtifactStore, the data Claude received dropped from 200 rows to summary references, and reasoning focus noticeably improved
  • After adding the lookup_knowledge tool, root cause analysis depth progressed from “main thread blocked” to “Binder counterpart system_server had delayed response due to CPU being scheduled to a little core”

None of these improvements were achieved through adjusting prompt text – they were achieved by changing the Agent’s tool set and data environment. If I had one piece of advice for engineers building AI Agent applications, it would be to put more effort into tool design and data control, and rely less on prompt wording to solve these problems.

Future Directions

This is the April 2026 roadmap; the original “closed-source, not released” status is obsolete. At that point I was developing it individually, with the following directions:

  • Deep vendor integration – The current 8 vendors’ .override.yaml only covers core Skills. More vendor-specific metrics (Qualcomm Snapdragon Profiler data, MediaTek MAGT signals, Samsung GameOptimizing service) need to be integrated one by one.
  • CI integration + batch processing – Moving from interactive analysis to automatically analyzing performance regressions for each build in CI pipelines. Including unattended mode, result comparison against baselines, and automatic regression tagging.
  • E2E verification framework – The current 6-trace regression test verifies the correctness of Skill data output, but does not verify the quality of Agent conclusions. An E2E verification system is needed: given a trace + known root cause -> check whether the Agent correctly identified it.
  • Codebase integration – Mapping slices/functions in the trace back to source code locations, combined with git blame to locate the change that introduced the issue.

October 2026 update (v1.16.1): The project is now open source, with a Web UI, CLI, reports, and portable runtimes. Use the v1.16.1 README and release record for that version rather than the retrospective’s old tool list, model, or startup settings.

The release explicitly fixes retention of HTML-report rows, timelines, nested content, and comparison/batch data, plus offline interactions. Generating a report and preserving all evidence in it are separate acceptance criteria. Source, documentation, and release records are inspectable; this article review has not rerun every device, model, or trace scenario.

Historical source entry points: MCP registration, Artifact Store, and System Prompt. These pinned links explain the April design; newer behavior requires its corresponding tag.

SmartPerfetto Discussion Group

The original discussion-group QR code is retained as a historical image; its validity and available places are not verified. Current bug reports can use the project issue tracker.

For contact details, see About the author.

entry.title: OpenClaw FAQ: Token Costs, Use Cases, Local Models, Privacy, and Day-to-Day Experience
entry.content:
After publishing the previous OpenClaw hands-on review, the most common questions from comments and group chats fell into five buckets: token costs, what it can actually do, local models, privacy and security, and day-to-day experience. Today I am picking the five most frequently asked questions and answering each one in detail.

Historical and review note (October 2026): Personal experience and usage figures describe March 2026; the original includes no itemized bills or execution logs. The old price tables are obsolete and are not purchasing guidance. Billing boundaries below use current official documentation, while OpenClaw configuration is checked against v2026.10.3. Illustrations, including the token trend and status card, are conceptual rather than measured dashboard screenshots.

1. How Much Do Tokens Actually Cost? Is It Expensive?

Short answer: not as expensive as you think, but not free either. I have run two different setups—one based on a premium cloud provider, and one on a cost-effective domestic (Chinese) model plan. The difference in experience is noticeable.

Phase 1: ChatGPT Pro (Historical Choice)

I initially used the ChatGPT Pro plan described at the time as $200/month, sharing some usage with everyday coding. Not hitting a limit was my historical experience, not a guarantee of unlimited work or an OpenAI API balance included in that price.

OpenAI’s pricing documentation separates subscription usage from API token pricing. Sign in with ChatGPT also distinguishes sign-in from permission to use a plan. OpenClaw integrations must distinguish subscription sign-in and API-key routes. The original does not record complete authentication/billing details, so it cannot establish that arbitrary API calls were included or that its historical five-hour/weekly descriptions remain current.

Phase 2: Zhipu GLM Coding Plan (Historical Choice)

After Pro expired, I switched to Zhipu Coding Plan; the original records a promotional purchase at ¥980/year. That personal purchase history is retained. The former ¥1608/year figure, “roughly 30%” increase, and quarterly-price-times-four calculation are different pricing bases and cannot verify each other without matching orders or announcements. Historical notes and current plan rules are separated below.

March 2026 Plan Notes (Obsolete)

The old price table is obsolete and was not a verified annual checkout quote. Multiplying a quarterly price by four gives an arithmetic total for four quarters, not the provider’s annual, renewal, or promotional price. The old quotes and recommendation labels have been removed.

At the October 2026 review, Zhipu’s official overview lists GLM-5.3/GLM-5.3-Flash with weighted consumption for input, cached input, output, and tools. It supports OpenClaw with lower-priority, best-effort scheduling that can queue or rate-limit requests under load.

TierListed five-hour pointsWeekly points
Lite2,00010,000
Pro12,00060,000
Max28,000140,000

These are rules observed at review time, not token bundles or unlimited API access. Check the actual order for price, region, and renewal terms; the plan applies only through supported tools and the appropriate integration route.

GLM-5 API Pay-As-You-Go (If You Skip the Plan)

The original GLM-5/GLM-5-Code rate table has no reproducible historical quote and is not current pricing. Calculate pay-as-you-go cost using the actual model, endpoint, and billing rates, separating at least:

ComponentRequired data
Uncached inputUncached input tokens × applicable rate
Cached inputCache-hit tokens × cache rate
OutputBilled output tokens × output rate
Other usageApplicable tool, search, audio, or other charges

For rates per million tokens, divide each corresponding count by one million before multiplying. Do not count cache hits again as uncached input. A total of 240 million tokens without the input/output/cache split does not establish a ¥2400 bill. Subscription limits and API charges are not directly interchangeable allowances.

Domestic Plan Comparison (Reviewed October 2026)

The old prices, model list, and support ratings are obsolete. No common benchmark supported claims of “best” integration or equivalent performance. By the October 2026 review, the offerings had changed:

ProviderChange reflected in official documentationCheck before integration
ZhipuGLM-5.3 family, points, lower-priority OpenClaw schedulingSupported tools/endpoints and five-hour/weekly points
MiniMaxThe old entry now describes M Plan Go/Explore/Build and supports OpenClawPurchased benefits, models, and M Plan key; old Starter/Plus/Max prices do not apply automatically
KimiOld/new memberships coexist; new plans remove the weekly window but retain five-hour limits and a monthly allocationYour account’s plan; Kimi Code and the public API have distinct billing routes

Do not choose an annual plan from the obsolete price difference. Confirm that the workload is supported, try representative tasks, then compare completion, latency, limits, and actual cost.

Real Numbers: 240 Million Tokens in 7 Days

I checked the Zhipu dashboard at the time and saw roughly 240 million tokens in seven days. That number looked alarming: about 34.29 million per day. I did not include itemized billing, input/cache/output categories, or matching local counters in the article, so it cannot establish an API invoice, local-token share, or annual-plan savings.

The image shows conceptual Q1–Q4 trends, not that seven-day usage report. Cloud/local division remains my historical workflow choice; comparing cost requires cloud charges, local running costs, and task completion rates.

Mindset: Don’t Be Too Transactional

While we are on the topic of costs, let me share a bit about mindset. After running OpenClaw for this long—my kid calls it “Shrimp Bro” (虾哥)—my biggest takeaway is: don’t start out obsessing over monetization and ROI. The AI era is just getting started, and upfront investment is necessary. The time and money you put in now may not yield immediate returns, but they gradually build into something invaluable: an intuitive understanding of what AI can and cannot do, a feel for how agent collaboration works, and an instinct for which problems are solvable with AI. These things are hard to quantify in the short term, but their long-term value is enormous.

My approach has always been: think of running OpenClaw as buying yourself a great toy. The joy is worth the price. Watching it run tasks on its own, draft articles, and organize the knowledge base—that alone is deeply satisfying. If it pays for itself down the road, great. But whether it can pay for itself right now should never be the deciding factor for getting started. Just start building. That matters more than anything else.

2. What Can OpenClaw Actually Do? Give Me Real Examples

The previous hands-on review went into detail, but I know many people do not read start to finish. Here are the scenarios I find most valuable and most illustrative.

What I Am Currently Running

ScenarioDescriptionValue
Daily Paper DigestAuto-fetches Android/AI papers, translates, generates reading notes, saves to ObsidianReduce collection work; still verify sources and conclusions
GitHub Repo MonitoringWatches Issues/PRs for changes, proactively notifies on important updatesI monitor Perfetto—no more daily manual checking
Knowledge Base BuildingAuto-archives content from WeChat Official Accounts, X, blogs; structures it1,760 Markdown files and growing
Content ReviewDaily push of content worth re-readingSolves the “bookmarked and never read again” problem
Android News DigestAuto-summarizes domain news, extracts key topicsNo need to scroll through feeds

What I value most is turning the things you know are important but cannot sustain through willpower alone into background tasks that run automatically by default.

Advanced Case 1: Batch Import into NotebookLM for Deep Analysis

NotebookLM can answer questions and generate audio overviews from imported material; a two-host podcast is one presentation format. It already supports adding multiple sources: official help describes multiple web URLs and selecting several Drive files, rather than requiring every source to be added individually.

OpenClaw can collect, organize, and connect these steps when the required tools, login, and permissions are available. Google’s Enterprise source API provides sources.batchCreate within its Cloud product, project, and authorization scope. It is not a universal API automatically available to every personal NotebookLM account. Browser automation is a separate integration that also needs maintenance and verification.

In Practice

This is an example task request, not a built-in one-click command:

Verify collected sources, accessible content, successful/failed imports, and audio-generation status separately. Model filtering does not guarantee quality, and submitting generation does not mean playable audio is ready. Preserve missing sources, authentication failures, and quota errors in the result.

Why This Combination Works So Well

StageWork automation can reduceStill verify
CollectionTopic searches, deduplication, source listsAccessible originals and source reliability
ImportBatch submission through a supported API/UISuccess for each source
UpdatesPeriodic discovery and summariesMeaningful changes and obsolete conclusions

The value is less repetitive work, not treating automated filtering as proof of accuracy.

Advanced Case 2: Drop a Link, Auto-Fetch All Related Content and Save to Disk

This is one of my most-used scenarios—it triggers almost daily. While scrolling X or reading a WeChat Official Account, I come across a great article that references several papers, a few GitHub repos, some related links, and a couple of book recommendations. The old workflow is all too familiar: bookmark it, tell yourself you will read it later, forget, never look at it again. With OpenClaw, the process is different:

Handle each item according to access and authorization: download publicly available papers, extract readable content where saving is permitted, and record book metadata with purchase/borrowing links. Login requirements, paywalls, and dead links can prevent full retrieval; do not report that everything was captured.

This example explicitly requests stars and clones; execution still needs bounded repositories and counts, and cloning is not permission to run repository code. The final index should record successes, failures, original URLs, and save locations. Personal-Knowledge/source/ is a personal directory convention, not an OpenClaw default.

For Android Developers

These are directions I have not built yet but am actively planning. See if any resonate with your work:

Pain PointWhat OpenClaw Can DoAudience
High barrier to trace analysisUpload Perfetto/Systrace traces, AI-assisted interpretation, generate plain-language reportsApp perf optimization, system UX perf
Version compatibility checklistsAuto-fetch Android Release Notes, generate adaptation checklists, cross-reference code to flag check pointsApp developers (annual necessity)
Issue backlog overloadAuto-classify (bug/feature/question), priority scoring, key info extractionOpen source maintainers, team collaboration
Time-consuming code reviewDetect common patterns (null pointers, resource leaks, main-thread IO), generate review checklistsAll teams
Forgotten tech debtPeriodically scan TODO/FIXME comments, sort by priority, send reminders to “pay down the debt”All projects
Benchmarks nobody readsRun benchmarks on schedule, auto-compare against history, alert on anomalies (e.g., startup +500ms)Performance teams
Internal docs are unfindableAnswer questions like “have we seen this before?” or “where is the design doc?” based on the knowledge baseAll teams
Upstream change trackingMonitor AOSP/vendor code changes, flag items that need mergingSystem developers

None of these work out of the box—they require custom development for your specific scenarios. But OpenClaw’s architecture naturally supports extending in all of these directions. The key is to get the foundation running first, then iterate based on real needs.

One-Line Summary

Papers read daily, repos monitored daily, knowledge organized daily, reports written daily. What OpenClaw truly achieves is turning “things that require long-term consistency”—something that goes against human nature—into “tasks the system quietly handles in the background.”

3. What Can Local Models Do?

In my workflow at the time, local models mainly handled repetitive, high-frequency tasks. One line to describe the division of labor: the cloud “thinks deep,” local models “run hard.”

How Much Do Local Models Handle?

Here is the task distribution I recorded at the time; I did not include the time window, counting method, or raw logs:

Task TypeModelShare
Monitoring, inspection, batch processingLocal Qwen3.5-27B30%
Status checks, lightweight classificationLocal Qwen3.5-4B20%
Ultra-light tasksLocal Qwen3.5-2B10%
Cloud failure fallbackLocal Qwen3.5-9B5%
Long-form writing, polish, reviewsCloud GLM515%
Daily/weekly reports, auditingCloud GLM510%
Paper digest, ClawFeedCloud GLM510%

The listed shares add to 65% local tasks and 35% cloud tasks; this is table arithmetic, not a new runtime validation. Task share does not establish token share. The former “80%+ local tokens” claim lacks matching local counts and definitions and is not retained as a verified result.

My Setup

The hardware is a Mac Studio (M-series Apple Silicon) running multiple local models: Qwen3.5-2B/4B/9B using MLX 8-bit quantization for lightweight tasks and cloud-failure fallback; Qwen3.5-27B deployed via Ollama as the primary local workhorse for high-frequency structured tasks. MLX is a computation framework; Ollama is a model runtime/serving tool. Names alone do not establish a speed comparison. No matched model, quantization, context, and concurrency benchmark is provided here, so this does not prove MLX is always faster.

Division of Labor Principles

Local Models Excel AtCloud Models Excel At
High-frequency structured tasks (RSS, queue processing)Long-form writing and polishing
Monitoring and inspectionComplex reasoning and judgment
Data preprocessing (configured locally; verify outbound paths)High-quality translation and interpretation
Cloud failure fallbackPaper digest, deep analysis

I reused existing hardware, but electricity, capacity, maintenance, and depreciation still count. Without energy measurements, “no per-token invoice” is not a zero-cost result.

Token Burn Rate

I used GPT-5.4, GLM5, and Qwen3.5 together at the time. This describes my setup then, not a current default or ranking. Before choosing a Coding Plan, check supported tasks/tools, quota windows, concurrency, and queuing policy. There is no general “all-you-can-eat” guarantee. Budget ongoing automation from actual input, cached input, output, and retries before choosing subscription or pay-as-you-go billing.

Backup Channel

In the early days, OpenClaw (“Shrimp Bro”) occasionally ran into stability issues. When that happened, I would use Claude Code (Remote Control) to connect remotely and troubleshoot manually. This does not happen often, but having a backup channel gives real peace of mind.

The Analogy

Think of local models as “hardworking blue-collar workers” and cloud models as “brilliant senior consultants.” What OpenClaw does is fully automate the collaboration logic between them.

4. How Do You Protect Privacy and Security?

This question comes up constantly, and rightfully so—it is something everyone needs to think through carefully before getting started.

Core Principle

Keeping sensitive data on the machine is my operating goal, not an automatic property of installing a local model. The original principles still need end-to-end enforcement:

  1. Restrict sensitive files to authorized local inference and local tools; prevent fallbacks, summaries, or attachments from silently reaching a cloud model.
  2. Telegram, web tools, NotebookLM, and iCloud can all transmit data externally. “Local-first” does not remove those paths.
  3. Enforce access through effective tool policy, sandbox mounts, host permissions, and credentials. Workspace paths and Markdown instructions alone are not isolation mechanisms.

Technical Safeguards

Command execution: In the v2026.10.3 safe-bin guide, tools.exec.safeBins is a constrained stdin-filter fast path in allowlist mode, not a general read-only certification. Its built-in default list is cut, uniq, head, tail, tr, and wc. Commands such as git and find can write or execute work and are not wholly read-only by name.

deniedFlags constrains arguments in a particular safe-bin profile; it is not a global switch blocking every dangerous command. Execution also depends on host, security/ask policy, path allowlists, tool authorization, and sandboxing. These controls do not prove that prompt injection is impossible.

Sender and command authorization: In the command reference, commands.ownerAllowFrom applies to owner-only command surfaces, separately from commands.allowFrom, channel pairing, and ordinary messages. For Telegram, check channels.telegram.allowFrom, group policy/groupAllowFrom, and the documented account inheritance. The old generic channels.allowFrom is not a universal channel configuration. Permission to issue commands, reach the agent through messages, and invoke a tool are separate controls.

Custom checks: Daily configuration SHA256 comparisons and secret scans were part of the operational setup I configured at the time, not an automatically verified OpenClaw guarantee. Hash changes can be legitimate; protect the baseline and alert path, and confirm the job ran. Daily checks are not real-time detection, and secret scans can miss findings. No alert is not proof of no leak.

Runtime Isolation

  • OpenClaw runs on a dedicated Mac Studio, separate from my daily development machine
  • Sensitive accounts (company email, internal systems) are not connected to OpenClaw
  • External publishing channels like WeChat Official Accounts only have “save draft” permissions, not “publish directly”

These were the limits I set for my deployment. Draft-versus-publish restrictions need actual API, credential, and tool enforcement. If the same browser session can publish, a “draft only” instruction is not complete isolation.

Trust Boundary

I want OpenClaw to access only data I intend this system to process. That does not establish that it is inherently safer than another AI product. Cloud requests, Telegram messages, iCloud sync, and browser sessions can create separate copies. Local logs can themselves contain sensitive information, be incomplete, or be modified.

Audit destinations, readers, retention, and unrecorded operations. Owning the host does not prove that all data and a complete operation history stay exclusively on that host.

The Nature of Security

Default safeguards still need to be checked against your deployment and permissions; they do not automatically meet every security requirement. Build the cage before you raise the shrimp—never the other way around.

5. Day-to-Day Experience: Mobile Control and Data Retention

This one is not asked as often, but I personally think it is the key to OpenClaw feeling truly seamless. It deserves its own section.

Telegram: One Main Bot + Multiple Group Chats

Here is how I use it: the main bot handles everyday conversation, commands, and questions via private chat. Different daily tasks get forwarded to different groups—the Android group gets tech briefings, paper digests, and GitHub updates; the Daily group gets daily reports, weekly reports, and system notifications; other groups are split by topic as needed. Why separate groups? Three reasons:

  1. No information mixing: Technical content and operational logs are managed separately. Want a specific category? Just open that group.
  2. Controllable notifications: Important groups get notifications turned on, unimportant ones get muted. No notification overload.
  3. Easy collaboration: Some groups can include colleagues, sharing the same information sources.

Data Persisted to Obsidian

In my workflow, Telegram is the interaction/notification channel and important outputs are also written to the Obsidian Vault. This helps search, organization, and linking, but persistence is not a backup or a guarantee against loss. Deletion, overwrites, disk failure, and sync conflicts remain possible. Telegram messages being pushed up the chat history also does not mean they were deleted.

Verify the saved file and completeness, and keep a separate restorable backup. iCloud or another sync service can propagate deletions/conflicts; test recovery rather than relying only on a sync indicator.

Here is how I organized my directories at the time:

  • OpenClaw定时任务/: Scheduled outputs
  • 论文/: Original PDF, translation, and reading notes
  • Personal-Knowledge/source/: Knowledge base reported as 1,760 files at the time
  • X 文章/: Archived X content

These are personal paths; installing OpenClaw does not ensure every task writes to them.

Mobile Access Anytime

This matters more than I initially expected. When I am out, I pull out my phone, open Telegram, and send commands to Shrimp Bro (虾哥)—no different from sitting at my desk. Want to read today’s daily report? Open Obsidian on mobile—the files are already synced via iCloud. Need to adjust a task urgently? No need to fire up a computer; it is all doable from the phone. My daily routine now starts with checking Telegram in the morning to see what tasks ran overnight and whether anything went wrong. If there is an issue, I handle it right from my phone. When I am out, a quick glance at the running status keeps me informed.

That was my experience when the workflow was available; it still depends on the host, network, channel authorization, and completed synchronization. Tasks needing host interaction or approval may not be fully manageable by phone. The status card’s GPT-4 label, task counts, and health badge are illustrative, not evidence of a measured run. A sensitive Vault required to remain on one machine must not also be assumed safe to sync to iCloud.

Architecture Summary

Telegram handles interaction; the Obsidian Vault stores content. OpenClaw Gateway and related services perform persistent execution; the Vault is not the execution backend. The combination can make daily work convenient, but availability and recovery still depend on monitoring, permissions, sync, and backups—not a promise of uninterrupted 24/7 operation or permanent retention.

Related Posts

  1. After Running OpenClaw Locally for Three Weeks, I Realized It Is Not a Chatbot

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet — historical community introduction; closed in 2026.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: After Running OpenClaw Locally for Three Weeks, I Realized It's Not a Chatbot
entry.content:
I’ve been using OpenClaw heavily on my local machine for a while now. At first, I treated it like any other AI tool. But after wiring it into Telegram, Obsidian, scheduled tasks, local models, and my content workflow, I began to see it as a system that could keep working between conversations. It can receive messages, call tools, run scheduled tasks, dispatch to different models, build long-term memory, write results back to Obsidian, and delegate complex tasks to other agents. If you’re only using it as a chatbot, you’re using only part of its capabilities.

Historical and version note (reviewed October 2026): This post retains the personal experience, hardware, and file counts recorded on March 8, 2026. The original did not identify the exact OpenClaw version in use. Technical updates below reference OpenClaw v2026.10.3, without treating later behavior as a verified result from that earlier setup. Illustrations are conceptual, not product screenshots or execution logs.

I work on Android system performance, write, run communities, maintain a knowledge base, follow projects, and code. What stood out to me was that AI could keep moving this work forward between conversations.

1. When Did I Actually Start Using OpenClaw?

The initialization records in my local environment point to the evening of February 16, 2026, when I started running OpenClaw on my own machine. I kept adding it to my routine: messaging, scheduled tasks, Obsidian, daily and weekly reports, GitHub monitoring, paper reading, content collection, writing, and reviews. It became the place where I coordinated those tasks, kept memory, and handed coding work to Claude Code.

2. What Does OpenClaw Actually Do for an Android System Engineer?

For Android engineering, performance analysis, and stability work, I find it most useful for recurring tasks that span several tools and days. I use it in four areas.

Category 1: Information Flow Automation

Daily tech briefings, daily news digests, RSS scraping, high-value content filtering, GitHub issue/PR monitoring, daily paper reading – none of these are things I couldn’t do before. The problem was that they’re too fragmented, and I’d inevitably drop them. OpenClaw turns these from “powered by willpower” into “powered by system defaults.”

Category 2: Continuous Knowledge Base Maintenance

I consume a lot of content: technical articles, WeChat public accounts, long-form posts on X, RSS feeds, project materials, my own thoughts. The biggest problem used to be: I’d save things but never organize them, organize them but never find them again, find them but struggle to reuse them. After connecting OpenClaw, it continuously does incremental organization, structural repair, high-value archiving, content review, and memory maintenance. For me, the useful part is being able to find a piece of knowledge and use it again later.

Category 3: Daily Reports, Retrospectives, and Weekly Reviews

This is the part most people overlook, but it’s also the one with the most compounding returns. I now have OpenClaw running daily morning reminders, end-of-day reports, evening retrospectives, weekly distillations, project reviews, three-tier memory maintenance, and meditation/evolution logs. The thing that hooked me most about OpenClaw is this: It takes all those things I know are important but can never sustain as habits, and turns them into things the system does for me automatically.

Category 4: Engineering Collaboration

It can also participate in engineering work – tracking GitHub repo changes, patrolling issues and PRs, organizing code context, and calling other coding agents to do work. In my workflow, OpenClaw handles orchestration while Claude Code handles intensive terminal coding. Claude Code is more like a top-tier programmer sitting in your terminal. OpenClaw is more like an AI operations system.

3. Why Do I Always Keep Claude Code Nearby?

Because my early OpenClaw setup did break: upgrades caused errors, model configurations went wrong, scheduled tasks behaved unexpectedly, certain tool chains stopped working, certain file paths failed to write, and old sessions did not always sync with new configurations. If you only have OpenClaw itself, many of these problems are extremely frustrating. But if you have Claude Code on the side, things get much simpler.

My division of labor is clear: OpenClaw handles orchestration, memory, scheduling, archiving, messaging, and workflows. Claude Code handles bug fixes, log inspection, error diagnosis, complex code changes, and post-upgrade firefighting.

4. What’s My Local Setup?

My current machine is a Mac Studio M1 Ultra with 64GB of RAM and a 48-core GPU. This configuration is very comfortable for local agent workflows because it lets me run OpenClaw as a persistent service alongside Ollama local models, Obsidian, browser automation, and various scripts and knowledge base tasks. I run a cloud + local hybrid.

The Model Strategy Is Simple

High-quality tasks go to the cloud (long-form writing, weekly reports, complex summaries, critical decisions). High-frequency grunt work runs locally (structured tasks, patrols, batch processing, daily workers). My local model tiers look like this: 2B for status checks, 4B for lightweight patrols, 9B as the high-frequency workhorse, and 27B/35B for heavier local tasks. On my machine, 9B is the best value daily workhorse.

These parameter-count tiers describe my historical workload choices, not a reproducible benchmark. The original does not specify model identities, quantization, context length, or concurrency. Similar parameter counts do not guarantee similar tool use, writing, or reasoning. Test real task completion, latency, and memory use rather than only whether a model loads.

5. The Most Important Part of OpenClaw Isn’t the Models – It’s the Core Files

When people first encounter OpenClaw, they focus on models, tools, and the command line. But I’ve come to believe that its real power lies in its file-based rules. The files I care most about are:

  • SOUL.md: Defines its personality, style, and working posture
  • USER.md: Defines who it’s helping and what the goals are
  • AGENTS.md: Defines startup procedures, memory rules, safety boundaries, and group chat behavior
  • MEMORY.md + memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md: One stores long-term memory, the other stores what happened each day
  • TOOLS.md: Records environment-specific information unique to this machine

These files became an important part of keeping my setup consistent: personality, memory, and working rules that I could read and edit.

v2026.10.3 update: The versioned workspace guide places local tool conventions in AGENTS.md under ## Tools, rather than listing the older TOOLS.md convention as a required file. The list above preserves my earlier organization. These files guide behavior; they do not enable tools or enforce permissions. Memory must actually be written and retrievable, and a file’s existence does not mean it is fully loaded on every turn.

6. Why Does the Skill System Matter?

Many people think of Skills as “plugins,” but I think a more accurate framing is capability packages. A Skill usually isn’t just an extra button. It bundles together what scenarios it fits, how it calls tools, whether it depends on scripts, what the boundaries and caveats are, and when it should or shouldn’t be used. Capabilities like Obsidian integration, coding-agent, RSS, and skill auditing – once properly installed, OpenClaw stops just chatting and starts actually working. But my advice is also clear: Don’t install Skills just to show off. Start with core capabilities, run them for a couple of days to confirm they’re stable, then expand. For Skills involving elevated permissions or external connections, audit first, then decide whether to enable them.

In the v2026.10.3 skills guide, a skill centers on SKILL.md instructions with metadata and optional scripts/resources. Installing it does not by itself grant tools, credentials, or host permissions. Plugins, tool authorization, and skills are separate layers; required binaries, services, and credentials still need configuration. A skill allowlist does not replace constraints on exec.

7. Telegram: Single Agent with Multiple Group Chats Works, but Split by Role Later

Telegram gave me more ways to organize the work than a single private chat. The same system can serve several conversations, with different tasks assigned to them.

Option A: Single Agent, Multiple Group Chats

The upside is simplicity: fast setup, low initial cost, and an easy way to validate the workflow. But session isolation differs from shared configuration. In the v2026.10.3 session guide, groups default to separate sessions (session.groupScope: "per-group"); chat histories do not inherently merge. Explicit routing to main changes that behavior.

Groups handled by one agent may still share persona rules, workspace, accessible memory, and tool configuration. Those shared resources need attention when writing, reporting, and technical Q&A require different rules or data scopes.

Option B: Split Into Multiple Agents by Role

This is the approach I’ve come to prefer. For example, main handles the primary private chat, daily handles scheduled tasks, daily reports, patrols, and knowledge base work, writer handles writing and content refinement, and specialized agents handle specific groups, business lines, or projects. Separate agents can organize workspaces, sessions, and roles, but routing bindings, workspace paths, credential inheritance, and tool permissions must match that intent. Different names alone do not guarantee isolation. My recommendation: Start with a single agent and multiple group chats early on, but split by role as things mature.

The figure illustrates a workflow cycle, not Telegram routing configuration. Splitting by role is my workload preference, not a requirement for every deployment. The multi-agent guide states that a workspace is a default cwd, not a hard sandbox. The security model does not treat a shared Gateway as an isolation boundary between mutually untrusted users.

8. Security Is Not an Appendix – It’s a Prerequisite

I strongly recommend being upfront about this from the start. Once OpenClaw begins accessing the local file system, browser, command execution, external messaging, and a mix of local and cloud models, it’s no longer a “harmless chat box.” It becomes a system with real agency. At that point, security boundaries must be established first.

The principles I’ve come to follow are:

  • Layer your long-term memory: Something like MEMORY.md, which contains more personal and stable information, should ideally only be used in the main session – don’t let it be read freely in group chat contexts
  • Be cautious with outbound actions: Emails, public posts, social media publishing – these should require confirmation by default. Don’t let it automatically publish half-finished work
  • Don’t overstep in group chats: In a group, it’s a participant, not your spokesperson, and certainly not you
  • Don’t install Skills carelessly: Especially those involving network access, script execution, or local path reading – audit first, decide later
  • Don’t blindly give small local models broad permissions: Especially when accessing web pages, executing commands, or reading/writing paths, be clear about workspace and tool boundaries

If you plan to connect even more external capabilities, browser automation, or overseas models down the road, you’ll typically also need a stable network access setup. But the more capabilities you add, the more important it is to design the boundaries first.

These rules also need enforcement through tool policies, sandboxing, host permissions, and allowed destinations. Writing “do not read private memory” or “confirm before sending” in Markdown does not establish an enforced boundary. The v2026.10.3 sandbox guide says sandboxing is off by default in regular configuration. A local Gateway also does not mean all data stays local: cloud models, messaging platforms, and external tools have their own transmission boundaries.

9. The Really Critical Question: What Has It Actually Produced?

If this post only described what OpenClaw “can do,” readers might still see it as a conceptual system. What’s actually convincing is what this system has already deposited into Obsidian. As of the time I’m writing this, my Obsidian vault contains these tangible outputs:

  • Under OpenClaw定时任务/ there are 214 Markdown files, from the reporting, review, archiving, and patrol workflows described here
  • Under Personal-Knowlodge/source/ there are 1,760 Markdown files; the knowledge base was continuing to grow
  • Under X 文章/ there are 115 Markdown files – high-value external content has been consolidated into a long-term resource library
  • Under 论文/ there are 4 standardized paper directories, each organized as “original PDF + translation + deep reading”
  • Under 小说工坊/夜航之上（分章）/ there are 58 chapter-related files – it has entered a long-term creative workflow, not just technical tasks
  • Ebook/ already contains actual EPUB deliverables – not just notes, but distributable formats

To give a few concrete examples: OpenClaw定时任务/每日论文精读（Android+AI）/2026-03-08-每日论文精读（Android+AI）.md, Personal-Knowlodge/source/2026-03-08_wechat_Android_JNI原理分析.md, 论文/AI-2026-03-08-Agentic-Reasoning-Framework/01-paper.pdf + 02-翻译.md + 03-精读.md, 小说工坊/夜航之上（分章）/第018章-光标闪烁.md. This is what I value most about OpenClaw: the results stay in my library, where I can find them and use them in later work.

These counts remain the original writing-time record; the illustration depicts how outputs can be organized. Files on disk do not prove every scheduled run succeeded, every artifact is complete, or every message was delivered. Check execution records, artifacts, and delivery results separately.

10. What Pitfalls Did I Hit?

This section is critical, because it determines whether you’ll give up halfway.

Pitfall 1: It’s Genuinely Unstable Early On

You need to accept a reality: OpenClaw is powerful, but it is not “zero maintenance.” My pitfalls have included upgrade errors, misconfigured model allowlists, model switches that don’t take effect in old sessions, scheduled tasks that run but fail to write to disk, external path permission issues, and browser policy problems.

Pitfall 2: Don’t Mix Node Environments

I eventually unified my runtime environment under Homebrew Node and stopped mixing in nvm. That simplified my path management; it does not mean nvm is inherently unsupported.

Version update: The v2026.10.3 Node guide lists Node 24.16+ on 24.x or 26.1+, recommends Node 26, and requires compatible SQLite behavior. Its package.json declares >=24.16.0 <25 || >=26.1.0. During upgrades, verify the executable path/version used by both the CLI and persistent Gateway, not only node -v in an interactive terminal.

Pitfall 3: Don’t Get Sloppy with Obsidian External Paths

This one gave me a lot of trouble. Absolute paths and exec + python/pathlib helped me handle an external directory at the time. They are not universal OpenClaw requirements or a way around access controls.

  • Relative paths normally resolve against the configured workspace; an explicit absolute path makes an external Vault target easier to verify.
  • Write access depends on tool policy, sandbox mounts, and host permissions. write/edit is not inherently unreliable.
  • exec + Python is also subject to its effective permissions. Use an authorized method appropriate to the task rather than broadening host access to solve a path issue.
  • Append or update specific content according to the file’s purpose. Concurrent appends can still duplicate or conflict; verify the destination, content, and completeness afterward.

Pitfall 4: More Automation Isn’t Always Better

It’s easy to get carried away early on, wanting to automate everything. But eventually you’ll find that too many tasks lead to duplication, conflicts, noise, rising token costs, and outputs nobody actually reads. I would start with the few recurring tasks whose results I actually use.

11. Who Is OpenClaw Best Suited For?

I think there are three types of people it fits best. The first are people with continuous input and output needs – engineers, indie developers, technical bloggers, community managers, research-oriented creators. The second are people who enjoy tinkering with workflows – if you have a natural interest in automation, systematization, and structure, OpenClaw will feel more natural the more you use it. The third are people who want to actually integrate AI into their workflow – if you don’t just want to ask a few questions but genuinely want continuous monitoring, automated organization, proactive reminders, scheduled output, long-term memory, and cross-platform content coordination, OpenClaw will serve you well.

12. Who Might Not Be a Good Fit?

I should be honest here too. People who just want a ChatGPT replacement, people who don’t want to maintain environments or read logs, and people without a sustained workflow – these three groups won’t necessarily fail at it, but they probably won’t experience its real value.

13. Hardware Recommendations

If you ask me what machine to get, I’d break it into three tiers:

  • Entry tier: 16GB RAM, primarily running cloud models, with only light local assistance
  • Practical tier: 32GB RAM, can run some local models, handles light to medium workloads
  • Comfortable tier: 64GB and above, Mac Studio or high-end workstation class, cloud + local hybrid running persistently

If you truly want to run OpenClaw as a “long-term persistent, cloud + local hybrid, multi-task parallel” system, the 64GB tier is where the experience becomes noticeably more stable.

These tiers describe my experience running local models alongside other apps, not OpenClaw’s minimum RAM or a guarantee that a model fits. The v2026.10.3 local-model guide ties requirements to weights, runtime/quantization, context, and concurrent work. Cloud-model use does not itself require a 64GB machine. Measure the intended workload before choosing hardware.

14. My Final Take on OpenClaw

What keeps me using OpenClaw is the work it carries forward: collecting information, organizing it, filing it, following up, and preparing material for the next task. Getting there took maintenance. It crashed, produced errors, and needed fixes. Once it was running well, though, I no longer had to initiate every step myself. That is why the setup was worth the effort for me.

Closing Thoughts

My experience may be useful if you have recurring work like this and are willing to maintain the setup.

Related Posts

  1. OpenClaw FAQ: Token Usage, Capabilities, Local Models, Privacy, and User Experience

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet — historical community introduction; closed in 2026.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Android Perfetto Series 10: Binder Scheduling and Lock Contention
entry.content:
A long main-thread Binder call can include dispatch delay, server processing, scheduling, and lock waits. This article combines Binder events, thread states, and Java monitor contention to separate those intervals.

These signals must be recorded. Sleeping or a futex stack alone does not establish a Binder or Java-lock bottleneck.

Version note (reviewed October 2026): The original screenshots show different processes and captures, not one complete incident. Binder/ART behavior is checked against android-16.0.0_r1, and SQL/UI against Perfetto v58.3. Recording events, permissions, and vendor behavior remain device-specific. Freezer requirements are distinguished below.

Table of Contents

  • Perfetto Series Catalog
  • Binder Basics
  • Perfetto Setup and Data Sources
    • Other Binder Analysis Tools
  • Binder Analysis Workflow
    • Step 1: Identify Transaction Latency
    • Step 2: Evaluate Thread Pool and Oneway Queue
    • Step 3: Investigate Lock Contention
  • Case Studies
    • Case 1: Window Management Delay
    • Case 2: Binder Thread Pool Saturation
  • Platform Features and Best Practices
  • Summary
  • References
  • Attachments
  • About the Author & Blog

Perfetto Series Catalog

  1. Android Perfetto Series Catalog
  2. Android Perfetto Series 1: Introduction to Perfetto
  3. Android Perfetto Series 2: Capturing Perfetto Traces
  4. Android Perfetto Series 3: Familiarizing with the Perfetto View
  5. Android Perfetto Series 4: Opening Large Traces via Command Line
  6. Android Perfetto Series 5: Choreographer-based Rendering Flow
  7. Android Perfetto Series 6: Why 120Hz? Advantages and Challenges
  8. Android Perfetto Series 7: MainThread and RenderThread Deep Dive
  9. Android Perfetto Series 8: Understanding Vsync and Performance Analysis
  10. Android Perfetto Series 9: Interpreting CPU Information
  11. Android Perfetto Series 10: Binder Scheduling and Lock Contention (this article)
  12. Android Perfetto Series 11: PerfettoSQL, Trace Processor and Regression Detection
  13. Android Perfetto Series 12: Trace Dataflow and Data Loss
  14. Android Perfetto Series 13: Perfetto SDK, Track Event and App Field Traces
  15. Android Perfetto Series 14: heapprofd and Memory Profiling
  16. Android Perfetto Series 15: Boot Traces and Long-running Field Tracing
  17. Android Perfetto Series 16: GPU, Power Counters and Hardware Bottlenecks
  18. Android Perfetto Series 17: Scenario Automation and Platform Tracing
  19. Android Perfetto Series 18: Input Response Latency
  20. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto Basics and Case Studies
  21. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto: Trace Graph Types - AOSP, WebView, Flutter + OEM System Optimization

Binder Basics

Binder supports cross-process object calls on Android. This article primarily covers Java/AIDL remote calls through /dev/binder. A local interface in the same process may execute directly without the driver or a Binder worker.

  1. Client: A generated AIDL proxy serializes arguments into a Parcel and submits a transaction through paths such as IBinder.transact().
  2. Server: A Java Stub dispatches through onTransact() to the implementation. Native backends have their own paths, and services need not run in system_server.
  3. Driver: Manages transactions, target buffers, references, and scheduling-related behavior. Different Binder contexts/device nodes are not one communication domain.
  4. Thread pool: Receiving threads can be created on demand. Per-node Oneway serialization and nested synchronous reentrancy also affect dispatch; queuing is not limited to a completely full pool.

Why is Binder needed?

Android commonly isolates apps with processes and UIDs, and one app can use several processes. System capabilities often involve services, while an ordinary local Framework call need not cross a process boundary. Binder standardizes identity, object references, lifetime, and call protocols:

IPC methodDifference from Binder object calls
SocketCan communicate and expose peer credentials; interface and object lifetime need separate design
PipeProvides a byte stream; anonymous pipes often use inherited fds, while named pipes are not limited to parent/child processes
Shared memorySupports large data and access controls, but requires coordination of synchronization and lifetime

Binder supplies caller identity, but the service still enforces permissions. A caller PID is not always available for asynchronous transactions. Synchronous calls wait for a reply; remote Oneway calls do not wait for server completion, but still incur serialization, driver submission, and possible errors. Priority inheritance depends on the transaction, node, and scheduling policy and does not eliminate lock waits.

The official threading model also describes reentrancy: a thread waiting for a synchronous reply may execute a nested callback. Holding a lock across Binder calls can therefore create deadlocks or reentrant state changes.

Case from App Developer’s Perspective

The screenshot contains AIDL::java::IActivityManager::attachApplication::server. In Android 16, IActivityManager.attachApplication is synchronous. ActivityManager.getService() returns an AIDL proxy wrapping a remote BinderProxy; those are different types. After serialization and submission, the server Stub dispatches to AMS and returns a reply when handling finishes.

Here, app PID 8111 calls thread 2055 in system_server PID 1339. The client binder transaction lasts about 5.255ms, mostly Sleeping but also Running/Runnable. The server interval is not continuously Running either; inspect its thread states separately.

Thread-track binder transaction, binder reply, and flow events establish transaction relationships. AIDL server slices are separate user-space markers; method names may be absent without them. In Perfetto v58.3, aidl_name holds the full marker, while interface holds the interface component. It is not simply aidl_name=IActivityManager.

Synchronous waits often occur through Binder ioctl, but blocked_function reports a kernel blocking function only when the relevant event and symbols are available. It is not a complete Java/native stack, nor is it always epoll_wait or the text ioctl(...).

Perfetto Setup and Data Sources

To diagnose Binder in Perfetto, you need to prepare the data sources and Trace configuration in advance.

Data Sources and Track Overview

Correlate transaction events, scheduler state, and user-space markers:

  • linux.ftrace: binder_transaction and binder_transaction_received connect send/receive activity for synchronous requests, replies, and asynchronous paths. “Received” is not restricted to the server receiving a request. Sched events add execution and wakeups. binder_transaction_alloc_buf records a successful allocation, not an allocation-failure log.
  • Atrace categories and app scope: am, wm, and dalvik add Framework/ART markers. App-side markers also need the appropriate atrace_apps scope and device support. dalvik can enable monitor contention but does not guarantee every contention or a full lock-ownership history.
  • linux.process_stats: Adds process/thread names and mappings. It has recording overhead; a generic “negligible” rating is not a measurement for every device.

android.binder and android.monitor_contention are Trace Processor SQL modules, not additional recording sources. UI names and entry points vary; the v58.3 paths are described below.

Recommended Trace Config

Save this textproto as binder_config.pbtx. The 64MiB ring buffer and 15s duration are example settings; long or busy captures can overwrite early data, so inspect loss statistics. One config cannot guarantee coverage across Android 12–17 and OEM builds.

Configuration Item Description

SettingEvidenceLimit
Binder tracepointsTransactions and selected driver behaviorCheck kernel event availability; missing events do not mean no calls
Sched eventsRunning/Runnable/Sleep and wakeupsRequire sufficiently complete scheduling data; not a business call stack
Atrace am/wm/dalvikService semantics and ART contentionCategories, app scope, and build control visibility
Process statsPID/TID and process/thread mappingsStill distinguish trace-local upid/utid identities

For app markers, add atrace_apps: "actual.package.name" inside ftrace_config. "*" broadens scope and can increase overhead. symbolize_ksyms resolves recorded kernel symbol references; it does not collect a complete kernel call stack. Legacy binder_lock/locked/unlock events are absent from the referenced Linux v6.12 binder_trace.h, so they are omitted rather than assumed available by Android version.

Quick Start: 3 Steps to Capture and View Binder Trace

These paths apply to Android 12+ devices that expose the configuration directory. See Part 2 for permissions and config loading. The output filename is an example; do not overwrite a capture you need.

  1. Start recording with the commands below. The second command records in the foreground. Reproduce on the phone during its 15-second run, not after it returns.
  1. Wait for recording to finish, pull the file, and drag it into Perfetto UI:
  1. Inspect raw tracks and derived views: Find client-thread binder transaction or binder transaction async slices and follow flows to the peer. In v58.3, AndroidBinderViz creates a Binder group with Server Transaction Counts and Client Transaction Counts. The lock plugin registers Android Lock Contention: Toggle View. Names vary by plugin and version. If derived views are absent, use the SQL below to check data coverage.

Other Binder Analysis Tools

Besides Perfetto, two tools are often useful: am trace-ipc (built in) and binder-trace (open source, focused on message decoding).

am trace-ipc: Java Layer Binder Call Tracking

am trace-ipc tracks Java-layer Binder call stacks. In Android 16, AMS requires SET_ACTIVITY_WATCHER and checks eligible processes: either the OS build or the process must be debuggable. A normal user build does not expose arbitrary third-party apps through this command; shell authorization is device-dependent.

Basic usage is very simple, just three steps: “start → operate → stop and export”:

The output aggregates stack counts. This is an illustrative format, not captured output; interface membership and line numbers depend on the target version:

It groups recorded stacks by process and occurrence count. It does not report each call’s duration or cover all native/local Binder calls.

Using with Perfetto: Perfetto provides timing, scheduling, and flow context; trace-ipc adds Java caller stacks within its capture scope. Stack collection adds overhead, so distinguish it from normal execution.

Best for: validating frequent IPC as ANR/jank cause, and pinpointing Java-origin call sites.

binder-trace: Real-time Binder Message Parsing

binder-trace uses Frida interception and interface structure definitions to decode messages. The reviewed README at a8a9a06 specifies Python 3.9+, an instrumentation-capable device/emulator, and a matching frida-server. Its bundled Android structure choices are 9–14; -a 11 is not a recipe for Android 16/17.

-n selects a process name, which need not equal the package name. Consult the tool’s help for pid selection or a matching structure directory. Android/OEM interface differences can affect decoding. Instrumentation adds overhead, so use it for message semantics without treating its timing as an uninstrumented performance measurement.

Binder Analysis Workflow

Do not start by searching the whole trace for anything unusual. Find the transaction you care about, then check its duration, threads, and wait dependencies in that order.

Step 1: Identify Transaction Latency

Define the problem window and client thread, then find transaction slices and flows. Search interface/method names when AIDL markers exist. Sleeping alone is not Binder evidence; correlate it with a transaction or stack.

In Perfetto v58.3 android.binder, synchronous transactions use reconstructed Binder intervals:

  • client_dur: Wall duration of the client Binder slice, not the entire Java API including all serialization work, and not necessarily all Sleeping.
  • server_dur: Wall duration of the server binder reply interval, including execution, waits, and nested calls; not pure server CPU time.
  • dispatch_dur = server_ts - client_ts: Recorded send-to-receive interval, including transfer, queuing, wakeup, and scheduling; not pure thread-pool queue time.
  • return_dur = client_end - server_end: Remaining time after the server interval ends, including return-path and client scheduling delay.

The image retains an older query result; the updated query adds instance IDs and return time. Missing names mean no decoded marker, not a nonexistent interface. The module filters incomplete or uncorrelated transactions, so an empty result is not proof that no calls occurred.

When the server interval lies inside the client interval, the three components reconcile with client duration. Investigate negative dispatch/return values as correlation, clock, or data-loss issues rather than clamping them to zero. For dispatch delay examine scheduling, pool availability, and serialization; for server time inspect its work/waits; for return delay inspect client rescheduling.

Step 2: Evaluate Thread Pool and Oneway Queue

A long send-to-receive interval makes worker availability one investigation target. First, a few common questions: how many Binder threads does a process have? What about system_server? When can we call the pool exhausted? Use worker availability and transaction activity to distinguish pool capacity, scheduling, and per-node serialization.

SystemServer’s Binder Thread Pool Scale

In Android 16 ProcessState, mMaxThreads defaults to 15. SystemServer sets sMaxBinderThreads to 31. This configures driver-requested growth; it is not the final total thread count.

startThreadPool() starts an additional thread, and explicit joinThreadPool() callers can add more. That version’s getThreadPoolMaxTotalThreadCount() distinguishes these sources. Apps are not guaranteed exactly 15 workers, nor system_server exactly 31. Java and native Binder do not imply two independent pools of 15 each.

Pool threads normally grow on demand rather than shrinking with momentary load. Check the process instance, Binder context, names, and transaction activity. Counting visible Binder: tracks does not establish the configured cap or that every worker is busy.

Binder Thread Count, Buffer, and “Binder Exhaustion”

When someone says “we ran out of Binder,” do they mean threads, transaction buffers, or object references? Separate those resources before deciding what was exhausted:

  • Thread pool: Establish that available receiving workers are occupied with transactions/dependencies while new requests are delayed. Exclude Runnable scheduling delay, per-node serialization, and freezing. An S-state worker may be idle or waiting on downstream work; Running/D alone does not prove pool saturation. Synchronous reentrant paths may reuse a thread waiting for a reply.
  • Transaction buffers: The Android documentation describes about 1MB shared per process, not 1MB dedicated to every call. Android 16 libbinder subtracts two pages from its mapping request; usable space also depends on concurrency, asynchronous quotas, objects, and allocation layout. Allocation failures can return errors rather than merely lengthening a queue. Either request or reply can be too large, and the exception does not establish which business operations already completed.
  • Objects and references: Retained references consume memory and affect lifetime. There is no universal “Binder object count” equivalent to the 15/31 worker settings. Inspect actual driver/process data before drawing performance conclusions.

For large payloads, consider shared memory, files, or ParcelFileDescriptor with explicit ownership, permissions, and error handling. Bitmap parceling varies by representation and implementation; pixel size alone does not prove fully inline transport. More workers are not a general buffer fix.

Identifying Oneway: A remote call does not wait for a business reply, but the client still serializes, interacts with the driver, and receives submission completion. It is not guaranteed to return instantly without blocking. A local interface does not automatically move work off-thread because it is oneway. Check flags, binder transaction async/binder async rcv, and android_binder_txns.is_sync=0, not a required [oneway] name suffix.

The image shows SystemUI 4024 sending to SurfaceFlinger 1483 with flags 0x11. Duration=0s is an instant event and the flow delay is about 63µs; neither measures the entire Java call or proves all Oneway calls are wait-free. The v58.3 asynchronous table uses receive instants; an available aidl_dur can describe method work. Do not apply synchronous server_dur semantics to it.

Async transactions on one Binder node are serialized, while different nodes may run concurrently. Dense short slices show activity, not queue depth; correlate sends and receives by endpoint with adequate event coverage. Ordinary AMS-to-WMS calls are local, while services can make nested calls to other processes. Follow actual dependencies to determine which clients are affected.

Step 3: Investigate Lock Contention

Interpret S, D, and Runnable intervals separately. D means uninterruptible sleep, not specifically disk I/O. Futex waits can underlie Java monitors, native locks, or condition variables, so the symbol alone does not classify the lock.

Java monitor contention: Recorded ART monitor contention with owner ... slices can be parsed by the v58.3 monitor_contention module. blocked_* identifies the waiter; blocking_* describes the recorded owner. Owner/method data are a snapshot, not proof that one thread held the lock throughout the entire interval.

This image concerns SettingsProvider with PhotonicModulator as the recorded owner, not WindowManagerGlobalLock. Its 164µs contention interval includes roughly 105µs Sleeping, 41µs Running, and 18µs Runnable. Contention duration is neither pure sleep nor the owner’s complete lock-holding duration.

Native/kernel waits: pthread_mutex_lock is a user-space library path, while mutex/rwsem waits can involve kernel locks. sched_blocked_reason supplies a kernel blocking location, not a full native stack. Combine stacks, lock markers, scheduling, and I/O evidence. Native contention is not inherently rarer than Java contention.

SQL for Java Monitor Contention in system_server (Optional)

Use the standard library rather than manually splitting slice names. Keep upid/utid to distinguish same-named instances. This lists system_server processes by name while retaining their identities:

In Android 16 ART, waiters= records the count before this waiter increments it. Adding one can describe a count including itself at that observation, not a maximum over the interval or a live queue length at query time. The query retains raw waiter_count, leaving unknowns as NULL.

The image uses the older waiter_threads column; do not confuse it with the new raw field. For no results, check dalvik, app scope, build/symbols, event format, and loss. An empty result does not prove no contention.

Case Study: Window Management Delay

These two cases are hypothetical walkthroughs, not measured conclusions from the screenshots above. No matching raw trace is attached; the numbers illustrate accounting.

Suppose a doFrame lasts 30ms in a 60Hz scenario, with 18ms overlapping a synchronous IActivityTaskManager.startActivity transaction. The 16.67ms refresh interval is not automatically the app’s complete deadline; verify FrameTimeline and pipeline timing before inferring presentation from doFrame duration.

  1. Use flow to identify the server thread rather than guessing the interface from Sleeping.
  2. Suppose server duration is 15ms with 12ms of monitor contention. Confirm that contention lies on the transaction’s critical path and the owner is attributable; separate the remaining roughly 3ms of client-side dispatch/return time.
  3. If the owner snapshot points to android.anim, inspect its overlapping work. Name WindowManagerGlobalLock only with supporting stack/log/lock evidence; a method name or contention marker need not identify the lock object’s class.

Candidate improvements include removing redundant startup IPC and shortening confirmed lock-held work. Re-measure the same scenario before claiming a visible-jank improvement.

Case Study: Binder Thread Pool Saturation

Suppose several clients wait on system_server during a burst of IPackageManager queries. A busy-looking Binder track group alone does not establish thread-pool exhaustion:

  1. Confirm that those transactions account for the waits, keeping process instances, nodes, and windows separate.
  2. Check occupied receivers, available workers and growth capacity, plus Runnable delays, freezing, and serialization.
  3. Even if each server call takes about 5ms, whether hundreds of calls saturate the pool depends on arrival rate, concurrency, locks, and CPU load. A large dispatch interval remains a delay to explain.
  4. Attribute slow responsiveness to the burst only when the evidence supports that queue/dependency chain.

Use semantically appropriate batching, deduplication, or rate limits and measure the result. getPackagesForUid returns package names for one UID; it is not a general bulk replacement for PackageManager calls. Service-side rate limits or hotspot optimization may also help.

Platform Features and Best Practices

Cached apps freezer: The official guide dates framework support to Android 11 / API 30. Compatible cgroup/kernel support and device policy are also required; Android 12+ does not universally mean freezing is enabled. A frozen process cannot normally handle transactions. Synchronous calls to it fail and framework checks can terminate the target. Async transactions may be buffered, but capacity is finite and excess traffic can also trigger termination. Cached is not the same as frozen; inspect actual freeze events.

Frozen-callee policy (API 36): RemoteCallbackList.Builder offers DROP, ENQUEUE_MOST_RECENT, and ENQUEUE_ALL.
