entry.title: Android Perfetto Series 7: MainThread and RenderThread Deep Dive
entry.content:
During a scrolling slowdown, the main thread may be doing layout or may already have handed drawing work to RenderThread. This article follows their hand-off, buffer submission, and SurfaceFlinger activity in Perfetto screenshots to locate waits.

The focus is the hardware-accelerated View/HWUI path. Other engines and software drawing can use different threads. FrameTimeline and presentation-side evidence are needed to determine what reached the screen.

Table of Contents

  • Series Catalog
  • Rendering Flow Analysis Based on Perfetto
  • Evolution of Dual-Thread Rendering Architecture
  • Main Thread Creation Process
  • ActivityThread Functionality
  • RenderThread Creation and Development
  • Performance
  • Perfetto’s Unique FrameTimeline Feature
  • Vsync Signals in Perfetto
  • References
  • Attachments
  • About Me && Blog

Series Catalog

  1. Android Perfetto Series Catalog
  2. Android Perfetto Series 1: Introduction to Perfetto
  3. Android Perfetto Series 2: Capturing Perfetto Traces
  4. Android Perfetto Series 3: Familiarizing with Perfetto View
  5. Android Perfetto Series 4: Opening Large Traces via Command Line
  6. Android Perfetto Series 5: Android App Rendering Flow Based on Choreographer
  7. Android Perfetto Series 6: Why 120Hz? Advantages and Challenges of High Refresh Rates
  8. Android Perfetto Series 7: MainThread and RenderThread Deep Dive
  9. Android Perfetto Series 8: Understanding Vsync Mechanism and Performance Analysis
  10. Android Perfetto Series 9: CPU Information Interpretation
  11. Android Perfetto Series 10: Binder Scheduling and Lock Contention
  12. Android Perfetto Series 11: PerfettoSQL, Trace Processor and Regression Detection
  13. Android Perfetto Series 12: Trace Dataflow and Data Loss
  14. Android Perfetto Series 13: Perfetto SDK, Track Event and App Field Traces
  15. Android Perfetto Series 14: heapprofd and Memory Profiling
  16. Android Perfetto Series 15: Boot Traces and Long-running Field Tracing
  17. Android Perfetto Series 16: GPU, Power Counters and Hardware Bottlenecks
  18. Android Perfetto Series 17: Scenario Automation and Platform Tracing
  19. Android Perfetto Series 18: Input Response Latency
  20. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto Basics and Case Sharing
  21. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto: Trace Graph Types - AOSP, WebView, Flutter + OEM System Optimization

If you haven’t read the Systrace series yet, here are the links:

  1. Systrace Series Catalog: A systematic introduction to Systrace, Perfetto’s predecessor, and learning about Android performance optimization and Android system operation basics through Systrace.
  2. Personal Blog: My personal blog, mainly Android-related content, with some life and work-related content as well.

Find ways to get in touch on the About Me page to discuss your questions, what you’d most like to see about Perfetto, and all Android development-related topics with fellow group members.

I uploaded the trace used in this article to GitHub: https://github.com/Gracker/SystraceForBlog/blob/master/Android_Perfetto/demo_app_aosp_scroll.perfetto-trace
Feel free to download it.

Version note (reviewed October 2026): Java/HWUI excerpts are checked against android-16.0.0_r1, with BLAST counters explained using android-15.0.0_r1. Android 13 unsignaled latching and Android 17 MessageQueue changes are labeled separately. The attached trace’s SystemInfo reports OPPO PKH110, Android 15/API 35, and Perfetto v46.0; aosp in its filename does not mean stock AOSP firmware. Most newer images show the demo app, but a com.tencent.mm detail image and an older Systrace example come from other captures.

Rendering Flow Analysis Based on Perfetto

Using a scrolling list as an example, we’ll inspect main-thread and RenderThread activity near one frame in Perfetto. The phases vary by frame and rendering path, so check frame tokens before treating nearby slices as one frame.

Frame Concept and Basic Parameters

Before analyzing Perfetto traces, distinguish the display’s nominal interval in a fixed mode from the number of distinct app frames actually presented:

  • 60Hz mode: Nominal refresh interval about 16.67ms
  • 90Hz mode: Nominal refresh interval about 11.11ms
  • 120Hz mode: Nominal refresh interval about 8.33ms

The display can repeat the preceding frame; none of these modes proves that the app produced that many new frames per second.

When analyzing rendering performance in Perfetto, focus on these two threads:

  • UI Thread: The application main thread, handling user input, business logic, and layout calculations
  • RenderThread: The rendering thread, preparing and submitting GPU commands and interacting with the buffer submission path; the GPU executes those commands

Main Thread and RenderThread Workflow

The screenshot shows overlapping work for frames such as 82272289 and 82272296. Match doFrame/DrawFrames tokens before treating neighboring slices as the same frame. The arrows are a guide to dependencies, not a complete function trace.

Important Note: Not every frame executes all steps. Input, Animation, and Insets Animation are all on-demand. Traversal (measure, layout, draw) is also on-demand: requestLayout, invalidate, and window or visibility changes are common reasons for scheduleTraversals() to post CALLBACK_TRAVERSAL. In continuous scrolling/animation scenarios, it often looks like it runs every frame.

Follow the recorded stages below:

1. Main Thread Waits for Vsync Signal

  • Perfetto trace: The main thread may be Sleeping between two periods of work
  • Process description: With a pending frame, Choreographer requests a Vsync callback. Sleeping alone does not prove the thread is waiting specifically for Vsync.

2. Vsync-app Signal Delivery Process

SurfaceFlinger schedules notifications using display timing and software prediction. A VSYNC-app transition is not necessarily an immediate forwarding of a hardware interrupt. The app/EventThread service can have multiple connections, so the global counter cannot identify one app by itself.

Choreographer requests one-shot notifications as needed. Other subscriptions and rendering paths can differ; no request for this Choreographer cycle does not prove there are no other frames or buffer submissions.

3. SurfaceFlinger Wakes Up App Main Thread

DisplayEventReceiver delivers events through native FD handling and JNI to Java onVsync, which posts an asynchronous Message. Looper later dispatches the Receiver Runnable into doFrame. Delivery and frame processing are distinct times; visibility of their slices depends on instrumentation and capture settings. See part five.

4. Processing Input Events (Input)

  • Perfetto trace: Input block
  • Process description: Runs when the frame has a registered Input callback; not every system input event is handled in this callback
  • Trigger conditions:
    • May have an Input callback: Batched input work was registered for this frame
    • May have no Input callback: No corresponding batched work is due, including some inertial or static periods
  • Note: Check whether the callback was registered for this frame; finger state alone does not determine whether the slice appears

5. Processing Animations (Animation)

The animation phase executes due CALLBACK_ANIMATION work, including property animations, View.postOnAnimation, and app FrameCallbacks. Its presence does not prove visible animation, and item creation/input alone does not guarantee it. Callbacks may be posted earlier or during preceding phases of the current frame, not only the previous frame.

6. Processing Insets Animations

The insetsAnimation phase handles due window-insets animation callbacks, such as supported IME/system-bar transitions. Insets describe areas occupied by system UI, not newly inserted windows. A static inset change or keyboard appearance does not necessarily produce this slice.

7. Traversal (Measure, Layout, Draw Preparation)

  • Perfetto trace: performTraversals, measure, layout, draw
  • Process description: These are the three core UI rendering stages, but they do not run as a complete set on every Vsync. Execution depends on whether the current frame has layout/draw requests.

7.1 Measure Phase

  • Purpose: Determine the size of each View
  • Process: Parents measure children required by their layout policy; cached or skipped branches mean the entire tree need not be remeasured
  • Key concepts:
    • MeasureSpec: Encapsulates parent container’s size requirements for child Views (EXACTLY, AT_MOST, UNSPECIFIED)
    • onMeasure(): Custom Views can override this method for their measurement logic
  • Perfetto representation: measure event, duration depends on View hierarchy complexity

7.2 Layout Phase

  • Purpose: Determine each View’s position coordinates in the parent container
  • Process: Based on Measure phase results, assign actual display positions to each View
  • Key concepts:
    • layout(left, top, right, bottom): Set View’s four boundary coordinates
    • onLayout(): ViewGroup overrides this method to determine child View positions
  • Perfetto representation: layout event; cost depends on layout code and hierarchy, with no universal ranking against measure

7.3 Draw Phase

  • Purpose: Draw View content onto canvas
  • Hardware-accelerated View path: Records or updates display lists; software Canvas drawing can still rasterize pixels
  • Key process:
    • draw(Canvas): Draw View’s own content
    • onDraw(Canvas): Subclass overrides to implement specific drawing logic
    • dispatchDraw(Canvas): ViewGroup uses this to draw child Views
  • Perfetto representation: draw event, mainly builds DisplayList under hardware acceleration

ViewRootImpl.performTraversals Core Code

Android 16 relationship sketch, with surrounding locals and branches omitted; not a compilable method. Invisible windows, canceled draws, and rescheduling are distinct branches, and performDraw can return without drawing.

Execution conditions for the three phases:

  • Measure: Runs on first draw and when layout/configuration/insets/window changes require it, not fixed every frame
  • Layout: Runs when layoutRequested is true and the app is in a drawable state
  • Draw: Runs only when draw conditions are satisfied; canceled/pre-draw-blocked cases reschedule traversal

8. Sync DisplayList to Render Thread

  • Perfetto trace: syncAndDrawFrame, visible “sync” or “syncAndDrawFrame” event (usually shown as data transfer point from main thread to render thread)
  • Process description: Main thread syncs current-frame RenderNode/DisplayList state to RenderThread through syncAndDrawFrame. This is not pure fire-and-forget async: UI thread waits for a key sync point (DrawFrameTask::postAndWait) and is then unblocked as early as possible; it does not wait until the frame is actually presented.

9. Render Thread Acquires Buffer

  • Perfetto trace: Inspect recorded dequeueBuffer/queueBuffer slices when available. DequeueBufferDuration and QueueBufferDuration are HWUI frame-stat fields, not guaranteed slice names.
  • Process description: During draw submission, RenderThread goes through the ANativeWindow/RenderPipeline path for buffer acquire/swap. Whether it waits, and how long it waits, directly affects deadline miss risk.

10. Process Rendering Instructions and Flush to GPU

  • Perfetto trace: drawing related blocks
  • Process description: RenderThread (CPU side) processes the RenderNode tree synced from UI thread via HardwareRenderer/CanvasContext, builds GPU commands, and submits them. GPU work executes asynchronously; the associated fence signals completion for downstream synchronization.

11. Submit Buffer (Possibly Unsignaled)

queueBuffer can submit an acquire fence that has not signaled yet in an asynchronous GPU pipeline. Submission is distinct from SurfaceFlinger’s policy for latching an unsignaled buffer. The queueBuffer slice alone does not establish fence state; correlate relevant fence/graphics data.

12. Trigger Transaction to SurfaceFlinger

  • Perfetto trace: TransactionQueue or BLAST transaction events, generally after queueBuffer, some traces don’t have this tag
  • Process description: App side associates buffer and layer-property updates via BLAST/SurfaceControl transactions and submits them to SurfaceFlinger. SurfaceFlinger then decides latch timing based on LatchUnsignaledConfig and related policies, composes, and presents.

Identifying different rendering modes in Perfetto:

  • During finger sliding: Look for Input and Traversal, then confirm whether RenderThread submitted a frame
  • During inertial scrolling: Animation and Traversal are common; whether Input also appears depends on the captured callbacks
  • In static state: The app may submit no new frame; background animation or another update can still trigger work

Software Drawing vs Hardware Acceleration

Although hardware-accelerated rendering is now basically standard, understanding the differences between the two rendering modes still helps understand Perfetto traces:

AspectSoftware DrawingHardware Acceleration
Drawing ThreadUsually main thread for ordinary Views; other Canvas uses can differMain records, RenderThread submits, GPU executes
Drawing EngineSkia (CPU)Skia with an OpenGL/Vulkan GPU backend
Perfetto CharacteristicsMain-thread draw may include rasterization/waitsBoth main thread and RenderThread may do work or wait
Performance ImpactMay occupy the main threadSome work moves to RenderThread, but synchronization can still block the main thread

The above introduces the basic rendering process. For more detailed Choreographer principles, refer to Android Perfetto Series 5: Android App Rendering Flow Based on Choreographer.

Next, we’ll focus on in-depth content about the main thread and render thread:

  1. Main thread development
  2. Main thread creation
  3. Render thread creation
  4. Division of labor between main thread and render thread

Evolution of Dual-Thread Rendering Architecture

Android’s rendering system has undergone an important evolution from single-thread to dual-thread.

Earlier View Rendering (Before Android 5.0)

Hardware acceleration was supported from Android 3.0 (API 11), before the HWUI RenderThread introduced in Android 5.0. Pre-5.0 does not mean CPU-only rendering; this section concerns earlier ordinary View paths.

In early software-drawn View paths, the main thread handled more UI drawing work:

  • Processing user input events
  • Executing measure, layout, draw
  • Submitting software-drawn buffers; other graphics paths could use other threads

Problems with this design:

  1. Poor responsiveness: Main thread overloaded, prone to ANR
  2. Performance bottleneck: Drawing work competes with input and business messages on the main thread
  3. Unstable frame rate: Complex interfaces easily cause frame drops

Dual-Thread Era (Starting from Android 5.0 Lollipop)

Android 5.0 introduced RenderThread, implementing separation of rendering work:

Main Thread Responsibilities:

  • Processing user input and business logic
  • Executing View’s measure, layout, draw
  • Building DisplayList (drawing instruction list)
  • Synchronizing data with render thread

Render Thread Responsibilities:

  • Receiving and processing DisplayList
  • Generating and submitting OpenGL/Vulkan rendering commands for the GPU to execute
  • Managing textures and rendering resources
  • Interacting with SurfaceFlinger

Advantages of this architecture:

  1. Parallel opportunity: After the key sync point, the main thread can process other messages while RenderThread continues
  2. Sync boundary: The main thread can still block at syncAndDrawFrame; the two threads are not fully independent
  3. Performance depends on the workload: Scheduling, GPU work, buffers, and resource synchronization determine the actual benefit

Main Thread Creation Process

Ordinary Android app processes are typically forked and specialized from Zygote, with preparation differing for paths such as USAP. fork creates a child process retaining the calling thread; a process and its main thread are distinct.

The central operation in frameworks/base/core/jni/com_android_internal_os_Zygote.cpp is:

ActivityThread is a framework object running on the app’s main thread, not a Thread subclass or the creator of that Linux thread. Its entry prepares the main Looper, instance, and system connection. H dispatches lifecycle work; app Handlers, Choreographer’s Handler, and native FD events do not all pass through H.

ActivityThread Creation

The following is an Android 16 ordinary Zygote child path, omitting surrounding setup and special branches:
ZygoteConnection.handleChildProc → ZygoteInit.zygoteInit → RuntimeInit.applicationInit → ActivityThread.main

Android 16 ZygoteConnection.java

For regular app processes, this goes through zygoteInit and eventually reaches ActivityThread.main. childZygoteInit is for child-zygote flow, not the normal app path.

Android 16 ActivityThread.java

The comments are very clear, so I won’t elaborate here. Once Looper.loop() starts, the main thread begins dispatching messages; ActivityThread.main() does not normally return while the app is running.

ActivityThread Functionality

ActivityThread’s Handler dispatches many component lifecycle messages on the main thread. Subsequent work in a Service or Receiver can move to other threads, so this does not mean every operation of all four component types runs on the main thread.

H does not create the process. Activity lifecycle work also uses EXECUTE_TRANSACTION; Service/Receiver lifecycle callbacks commonly run on main, while remote Binder methods and Provider query/insert requests can execute in a pool. Not every component method passes through H. On Android 17, apps targeting API 37 or higher use a new lock-free MessageQueue implementation. Looper and Handler usage remains the same, but queue-internal lock analysis must account for targetSdkVersion, and tools reflecting on private MessageQueue internals may break.

RenderThread Creation and Development

HWUI RenderThread has carried part of the UI rendering work since Android 5.0. It is a CPU thread; GPU-accelerated View rendering existed earlier, so its introduction was not Android’s first use of the GPU.

Software Drawing

Hardware acceleration is enabled by default for target API 14+, with Application/Activity-level configuration. The following attribute belongs on an existing application tag; activity overrides and other graphics components may still use hardware paths:

It affects ordinary View drawing, not necessarily every graphics component or RenderThread in the process, and differs from a software layer on one View. The old image visibly contains RenderThread, DrawFrame, and dequeueBuffer. It is retained as a historical rendering-wait example, not proof of purely software drawing:

This Systrace image and the opening Perfetto capture are not a controlled comparison. Slices include waits, so their lengths do not establish an acceleration factor or pure CPU raster cost.

Hardware-Accelerated Drawing

The ordinary hardware-accelerated View path records or updates display lists in RenderNodes on the main thread before syncAndDrawFrame. The UI may be unblocked before subsequent drawing, or only after later draw/flush work. The wait is not guaranteed to be brief.

Render Thread Initialization

In Android 16, RenderProxy construction calls RenderThread::getInstance, which creates/starts the process’s HWUI thread on demand. initializeIfNeeded primarily handles renderer/Surface state and is not necessarily the thread-creation point. BLAST updates occur elsewhere in ViewRootImpl; the two excerpts below are not a consecutive call sequence.

android/view/ViewRootImpl.java

The BlastBufferQueue created here will play a key role in subsequent rendering processes:

  • Manages client-side BufferQueue endpoints and SurfaceControl transactions
  • Can associate buffer and property updates; reduced calls or waits require measurement
  • QueuedBuffer metric changes can be observed in Perfetto

When drawing is required, ThreadedRenderer.draw is used. The following method is from Android 16:

Android 16 ThreadedRenderer.java

The draw above updates DisplayList first, then calls syncAndDrawFrame for the key UI Thread to RenderThread sync stage.

UI Thread and RenderThread DisplayList Synchronization Mechanism

In the syncAndDrawFrame key function, the following important synchronization operations occur:

syncAndDrawFrame is not fully non-blocking. In Android 16, DrawFrameTask::drawFrame() calls postAndWait(): it posts work to RenderThread queue and then waits on a condition variable; RenderThread unblocks UI at an appropriate sync point. So this is a conditional early-unblock design, not “UI never waits”.

In run(), canUnblockUiThread selects release before later drawing or after the draw/flush/wait path. Queued work, resource synchronization, and fences can extend the UI wait. See Android 16 DrawFrameTask.

The specific synchronization process includes:

  1. RenderNode tree transfer: The RenderNode tree (containing DisplayList) built by the main thread during the draw process is passed to RenderThread
  2. Property synchronization: View’s transformation matrices, transparency, clipping regions, and other properties are synchronized together
  3. Resource sharing: HWUI manages staging/render state and resource lifetime; this does not make arbitrary concurrent mutation of app Paths/Paints safe
  4. Rendering state transfer: Rendering state information needed for the current frame is passed to RenderThread

This synchronization process is the core of Android hardware-accelerated rendering. It implements a division of labor where UI Thread focuses on logic processing and RenderThread focuses on rendering.

The core implementation of the render thread is in the libhwui library, with code located at frameworks/base/libs/hwui

RenderThread and BlastBufferQueue Interaction Flow

After RenderThread receives the synced DisplayList, it begins actual rendering work. During this process, it interacts closely with BlastBufferQueue:

Note: The old intuitive flow (dequeueBuffer/queueBuffer/flushTransaction) is still useful as a mental model, but in the Android 16 implementation checked here these details are handled through RenderPipeline/ANativeWindow path, and CanvasContext::draw() is no longer in the old shape.

Key Features of BlastBufferQueue:

  1. App-side management: In the window paths compared here, the client creates and manages BLASTBufferQueue
  2. Buffer acquisition: Producer and consumer are local to the app, but dequeueBuffer can still wait when no buffer is available
  3. Buffer rotation: Measure any waiting-time or high-refresh-rate benefit on the target device trace
  4. Asynchronous submission: Submits buffers and acquire fences through transactions; GPU work may still be pending
  5. Supports unsignaled buffer: Cooperating with SurfaceFlinger unsignaled-latch policies can reduce end-to-end latency in specific scenarios

In-depth Discussion on Latching Unsignaled Buffers

Modern Android systems can sometimes latch a Buffer before its acquire fence signals. This policy is called “Latching Unsignaled Buffers”. The present fence records a later presentation stage and must not be confused with the acquire fence.

  • Traditional mode: SurfaceFlinger checks the Buffer’s acquire fence before reading content that the GPU may still be writing.

  • Latch Unsignaled mode: Under the supported policy, SurfaceFlinger can latch a Buffer whose acquire fence has not yet signaled. It must still wait before actually reading unfinished content; whether this lowers latency depends on the device and scene.

Control Switch and Policy (Android 13+):

The Android 13 policy documentation describes boot-time LatchUnsignaledConfig selection and debug.sf.auto_latch_unsignaled. It is not a runtime switch guaranteed across all releases. AutoSingleLayer means:

  • In Android 13’s default AutoSingleLayer policy, early latch requires a single updated layer with a Buffer-only update and no synchronizing transaction or geometry change.
  • Multiple updated layers or other excluded transaction conditions do not take that early-latch path.

SurfaceFlinger therefore follows an acquire-fence and layer-update policy; the present fence is used later to assess when presentation completed.

Division of Labor Between Main Thread and Render Thread

For ordinary Views, main handles input, business logic, layout, and command recording; RenderThread organizes later GPU work and submission. Main can also update layer properties and transactions through ViewRootImpl/SurfaceControl, so SF interaction is not exclusive to RenderThread.

RenderNode combines drawing records with properties such as transforms and alpha. DisplayList is the recorded commands, not a synonym for RenderNode. Reuse and property-only updates can avoid another onDraw, while layout/content changes may require recording. Batching must preserve order, clipping, and blending; it cannot arbitrarily combine all text into one draw.

BlastBufferQueue Working Principle

This compares an older window BufferQueue consumed by SurfaceFlinger with client-side BLAST. BufferQueues also serve cameras/codecs and are not universally created by SF.

In the common Android 15 window path, ViewRootImpl manages BLASTBufferQueue. Its local consumer acquires a buffer and associates it with a SurfaceControl transaction. Synchronization/merging affect submission, while buffer/fence back-pressure can still block. The counters below use Android 15 BLASTBufferQueue, not a performance guarantee from BLAST alone.

App-side QueuedBuffer Metric

  • Perfetto display: QueuedBuffer value track
  • AOSP definition (BLASTBufferQueue): QueuedBuffer = mNumFrameAvailable + mNumAcquired - mPendingRelease.size()
  • How to read it: This is a composite state metric, not a fixed-offset formula
  • Practical use: Focus on trend and duration, not one instantaneous value

QueuedBuffer Value Change Timing

The rising example shows queueBuffer/onFrameAvailable near a counter update. Android 15 emits the combined state after updating available frames; synchronization, merging, and release paths can affect the result. Do not translate every function invocation into exactly +1.

The falling example shows an app Binder-thread release callback near the decrease. This does not prove the release fence has completed or the buffer is immediately safe to rewrite. BLAST can retain pending releases, which the counter subtracts; it is not a count of free buffers.

SurfaceFlinger-side BufferTX Metric

Android 15 Layer uses mPendingBufferTransactions, traced as BufferTX - plus the layer name. Valid buffer transactions increment it; latch/drop paths decrement it. Property-only transactions are not necessarily +1, and a decrease is not completed presentation.

The annotated 1 and 2 are observed values. The track’s vertical scale is not a universal capacity or fixed maximum of three.

Collaboration Flow Between App Side and SF Side

  1. BLAST receives/acquires app buffers according to queue and synchronization state.
  2. SurfaceControl transactions associate buffers, frameNumber, and layer properties; frameNumber is not a doFrame token without explicit correlation.
  3. SF updates pending counts; latch/drop and later composition/presentation are separate stages.
  4. Release callbacks/fences and BLAST pending-release management govern return. A counter decrease proves neither presentation nor immediate reuse.

Key Performance Observation Points

Counter trends suggest investigation, not a unique cause. High occupancy can involve intended pipelining, synchronization, GPU/fence waits, or delayed consumption; low occupancy can mean unchanged content. Correlate frameNumber/token/layer, doFrame/DrawFrames, scheduling, fences, and presentation before attributing a bottleneck to app, GPU, or SF.

Performance

Synchronous database access, locks, and other waits occupy main-thread dispatch time, delaying input and frame callbacks. Diagnose jank and ANRs separately:

  1. Jank: Use the frame deadline and presentation. UI, RenderThread, and GPU stages overlap; adding wall durations and comparing with a fixed 8.33 ms is misleading.
  2. ANR: Specific input/component timeout rules apply. Not every pause of a few seconds produces a dialog; foreground/background state, configuration, and failure type affect handling. No dialog does not imply a crash. See the ANR series.

Dumps may arrive after the failure, so a stack does not guarantee an easy diagnosis. Use Perfetto/System Trace for scheduling and waits, then Android Studio method sampling/instrumentation when needed, accounting for overhead. Jank and an unresponsive app are both frustrating for users. That is one reason I wrote this series: understand how the two threads hand work to each other, then find where progress stops.

Perfetto’s Unique FrameTimeline Feature

FrameTimeline supplies expected/actual app and SurfaceFlinger records for investigating lateness. Compared with the older Systrace workflow, it provides correlated frame records that Trace Processor can also query.

Android 12+ support and actual collection are required. Missing tracks can reflect coverage or configuration, not an absence of jank.

Core Concepts of FrameTimeline

According to Perfetto official documentation, classification uses expected/actual timing and can include prediction errors, not a uniform perceptual result for every mismatch. Supported captured frames have two timeline types:

1. Expected Timeline

  • Purpose: Shows the rendering time window allocated by the system to the application
  • Start time: Predicted callback start, not the time it actually obtained CPU
  • Meaning: To avoid system jank, the application needs to complete work within this time range

2. Actual Timeline

  • Purpose: Shows the actual time the application completed the frame (including GPU work)
  • Start time: When Choreographer#doFrame or AChoreographer_vsyncCallback starts running
  • End time: max(GPU time, Post time), where Post time is when the frame was submitted to SurfaceFlinger

The App Actual duration includes app/GPU completion and posting, not final presentation or pure CPU time. Follow the linked SurfaceFlinger frame and inspect present/prediction fields.

Color Coding System

FrameTimeline uses intuitive colors to identify different frame states:

ColorMeaningDescription
GreenNormal frameNo jank observed, ideal state
Light greenHigh latency stateStable frame rate but delayed frame presentation, causing increased input latency
RedJank frameJank caused by current process
YellowApp-blameless jankFrame has jank but app is not the cause, jank caused by SurfaceFlinger
BlueDropped frameOn the SF side a newer frame was chosen; on the app side, a UI state update may have missed RenderThread before it drew

Clicking different colored ActualTimeline slices shows classifications such as jank_type; inspect threads and fences to identify the underlying cause:

These are common UI classifications, not code-level root causes. The detail image above is com.tencent.mm, token 54160848, rather than the demo app’s 8227… tokens. App Deadline Missed and Buffer Stuffing appear together; labels can combine.

Jank Type Analysis

FrameTimeline can identify multiple jank types:

App-side jank:

  • AppDeadlineMissed: App runtime exceeded expectations
  • BufferStuffing: Sustained queued work adds presentation latency; merely preparing the next frame before the previous one presents is normal pipelining and is insufficient evidence

SurfaceFlinger jank:

  • SurfaceFlingerCpuDeadlineMissed: SF’s composition path misses its deadline, not an ANR timeout or pure Running time
  • SurfaceFlingerGpuDeadlineMissed: CPU work met its deadline, but GPU composition did not
  • DisplayHAL: Presentation was late after timely SF hand-off; inspect available HAL budget and work
  • PredictionError: Scheduler prediction deviation

Configuring FrameTimeline

Add this textproto data-source fragment to a complete TraceConfig. It is not YAML or a standalone configuration with buffers/duration. See the capture guide:

Vsync Signals in Perfetto

In this trace, VSYNC-app is displayed as a Counter, which differs from many people’s intuitive understanding:

  • 0 → 1 change: Represents a Vsync signal
  • 1 → 0 change: Also represents a Vsync signal
  • Incorrect understanding: Many people mistakenly think only becoming 1 is a Vsync signal

Correct Vsync Signal Identification

In the diagram below, time points 1, 2, 3, 4 are all Vsync signal arrivals

Key points:

  1. Each value change in this screenshot corresponds to a recorded Vsync marker: Whether 0→1 or 1→0; this is not a universal encoding for all Vsync tracks
  2. Signal frequency: Measure adjacent recorded transitions in this capture; 120 Hz support alone does not imply constant 8.33 ms delivery, especially across mode changes or ARR
  3. Multi-app scenario: Counter may remain active due to other apps’ requests

Analysis Techniques

The SF counter alone does not prove delivery to the target app. Correlate app-side onVsync instrumentation, PID, timing, and doFrame tokens when available. An absent FrameDisplayEventReceiver.onVsync slice can simply mean missing instrumentation or capture coverage. Distinguish notification, dispatch, callbacks, and presentation.

References

  1. https://juejin.im/post/5a9e01c3f265da239d48ce32
  2. http://www.cocoachina.com/articles/35302
  3. https://juejin.im/post/5b7767fef265da43803bdc65
  4. http://gityuan.com/2019/06/15/flutter_ui_draw/
  5. https://developer.android.google.cn/guide/components/processes-and-threads

Attachments

The Perfetto trace files involved in this article have also been uploaded. You can download and open them in Perfetto UI (https://ui.perfetto.dev/) for analysis

Click this link to download the Perfetto trace files involved in this article

Below is a personal introduction and related links. I look forward to communicating with you all. When three people walk together, one of them can be my teacher!

  2. Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.

entry.title: Android Perfetto Series 6: Why 120Hz? Advantages and Challenges
entry.content:
120 Hz reduces the nominal refresh interval from 60 Hz’s 16.67 ms to about 8.33 ms. Display refreshes, app-produced frames, and distinct frames presented are different counts. This article uses a historical Perfetto trace to explain their relationship and the rendering/power trade-offs.

Part five covered Choreographer callbacks; here the focus is the shorter display cycle. The screenshots describe that capture, not every 120 Hz device’s scheduling configuration.

Version note (reviewed October 2026): The 2025 screenshots are retained without their original trace or device-build details. Buffer counters are explained against android-15.0.0_r1; frame-rate hints start at API 30, while ARR is discussed separately from Android 15. 120 Hz is the mode examined here, not a universal device requirement.

Table of Contents

  • Perfetto Series Catalog
  • Basic Concepts
  • System Implementation and Principles
  • Advantages and Challenges of 120Hz
  • Thoughts and Future Outlook
  • Conclusion
  • About Me && Blog

Perfetto Series Catalog

  1. Android Perfetto Series Catalog
  2. Android Perfetto Series 1: Introduction to Perfetto
  3. Android Perfetto Series 2: Capturing Perfetto Traces
  4. Android Perfetto Series 3: Familiarizing with the Perfetto View
  5. Android Perfetto Series 4: Opening Large Traces via Command Line
  6. Android Perfetto Series 5: Choreographer-based Rendering Flow
  7. Android Perfetto Series 6: Why 120Hz? Advantages and Challenges
  8. Android Perfetto Series 7: MainThread and RenderThread Deep Dive
  9. Android Perfetto Series 8: Understanding Vsync and Performance Analysis
  10. Android Perfetto Series 9: Interpreting CPU Information
  11. Android Perfetto Series 10: Binder Scheduling and Lock Contention
  12. Android Perfetto Series 11: PerfettoSQL, Trace Processor and Regression Detection
  13. Android Perfetto Series 12: Trace Dataflow and Data Loss
  14. Android Perfetto Series 13: Perfetto SDK, Track Event and App Field Traces
  15. Android Perfetto Series 14: heapprofd and Memory Profiling
  16. Android Perfetto Series 15: Boot Traces and Long-running Field Tracing
  17. Android Perfetto Series 16: GPU, Power Counters and Hardware Bottlenecks
  18. Android Perfetto Series 17: Scenario Automation and Platform Tracing
  19. Android Perfetto Series 18: Input Response Latency
  20. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto Basics and Case Studies
  21. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto: Trace Graph Types - AOSP, WebView, Flutter + OEM System Optimization

If you haven’t seen the Systrace series yet, here is the portal:

  1. Systrace Series Catalog: Systematically introduced the use of Systrace, the predecessor of Perfetto, and used Systrace to learn and understand the basic rules of Android performance optimization and Android system operation.
  2. Personal Blog: Personal blog, mainly content related to Android, and also put some content related to life and work.

Find ways to get in touch on the About Me page to discuss your problems, the parts about Perfetto you most want to see, and discuss all Android development related content with group friends.

Basic Concepts

What is Screen Refresh Rate?

Screen refresh rate is a hardware concept, referring to the number of times the screen refreshes the display content per second, in Hertz (Hz).

  • 60Hz screen: Refresh 60 times per second, each refresh interval is about 16.67ms
  • 90Hz screen: Refresh 90 times per second, each refresh interval is about 11.11ms
  • 120Hz screen: Refresh 120 times per second, each refresh interval is about 8.33ms

The active screen mode limits how often a new frame can be displayed. A refresh can repeat the previous frame, and devices with adaptive refresh rates need not stay at one fixed frequency.

What is FPS?

FPS (Frames Per Second) needs a measurement target: it may count frames produced by an app or distinct new frames actually presented on screen.

The following assumes evenly paced frames; average FPS alone does not establish each interval or processing duration.

  • 60FPS: About 16.67ms between successive frames; this is not necessarily the time spent processing each frame
  • 90FPS: About 11.11ms between successive frames
  • 120FPS: About 8.33ms between successive frames

A lower app frame rate is not automatically jank. A 24 FPS video can legitimately repeat frames on a 120 Hz display; inspect expected/actual presentation and cadence for interactive content.

  1. Content Type Difference:

    • Video Content: 24 or 30 FPS video need not synthesize 120 distinct images. Smooth playback still depends on regular presentation cadence and the chosen display mode.
    • Interactive Interface: Scrolling and direct-manipulation animations need consistent response. An occasional long frame can be noticeable even when average FPS remains high.

  2. Frame Rate Stability: Irregular frame intervals can be noticeable even when average FPS is high; compare frame presentation times in the same scene.

  3. System Behavior:

    • When FPS is lower than the refresh rate, the display can repeat an earlier frame; a black frame is not the normal fallback.
    • When an app produces frames faster than the display can present them, some work may not become a distinct visible frame; check buffer and presentation records before calling it a dropped frame.

Different application scenarios have different smoothness standards, and developers need to choose appropriate optimization strategies according to the application type.

What is Vsync?

Vsync (Vertical Synchronization) provides display-related scheduling points for apps and SurfaceFlinger. Choreographer requests a callback when an app has pending frame work; not every display Vsync makes every app render a new frame.

Why 120Hz Became the New Standard?

120 Hz provides more update opportunities when the content and device can use them:

  1. Smoother motion: An app producing distinct frames steadily can show more intermediate states in scrolling and animation; static content has no equivalent gain.
  2. Less wait for a refresh opportunity: The nominal interval falls from 16.67 ms to 8.33 ms. Input dispatch, app/GPU work, and composition remain part of end-to-end latency.
  3. Device capability: Chip, panel, and thermal limits determine sustainable performance; a supported mode does not guarantee 120 FPS content.
  4. Power management: Content and interaction policies can avoid unnecessary high-refresh operation.
  5. Variable refresh: Supported rates and policies differ. Mode switching and ARR’s within-mode adjustment are separate mechanisms, and LTPO alone does not establish Android ARR support.

Apple’s ProMotion provides a useful comparison for content-aware pacing. Its animation guidance below is not an Android device configuration.

System Implementation and Principles

120Hz Rendering Process from Perfetto’s Perspective

A fixed 120 Hz mode has a nominal 8.33 ms interval. Main-thread, RenderThread, GPU, and SurfaceFlinger stages can overlap across frames rather than run serially in that window. This is the historical capture:

  1. Vsync cadence: The selected 8.326 ms interval approximates 120 Hz. VSYNC-app is a software timing counter; its high level is not execution duration or independent proof of the hardware mode.
  2. Callbacks and deadlines: Choreographer processes due Input, Animation, Insets Animation, Traversal, and Commit callbacks. The “8.33 ms available to the app” annotation illustrates an interval. Actual remaining time depends on callback start, deadline, and FrameTimeline prediction.
  3. GPU and submission: RenderThread is a CPU thread. Arrow 4 groups GPU work and buffer queueing schematically; queueBuffer establishes neither simultaneous GPU start nor completion.

Interpret the counters against the captured build. In Android 15 BLASTBufferQueue:

  • QueuedBuffer is emitted in the app process as mNumFrameAvailable + mNumAcquired - mPendingRelease.size(). It combines available and acquired states while subtracting pending releases; it is neither the raw BufferQueue length nor GPU completion.
  • BufferTX counts pending buffer transactions on SurfaceFlinger’s side. Android 15 Layer uses mPendingBufferTransactions, traced as BufferTX - plus the layer name. The field is not universally named mPendingBuffers.

A typical path is:

  1. App submission reaches BLAST’s onFrameAvailable, updating its counter. Acquisition and transaction construction depend on synchronization/queue state; the acquire fence may still be pending.
  2. SurfaceFlinger increments the layer’s pending count for a valid buffer transaction; latch or drop paths decrement it. A decrease is not presentation.
  3. Unneeded buffers return through release callbacks and fences. BLAST can retain some pending releases, and a callback or counter decrease does not guarantee immediate safe reuse: the release fence still matters. Merely displaying static content for a long time does not automatically release its buffer.

The next image associates app frame 54161669 with a SurfaceFlinger frame. App Actual Timeline ends at completion of app/GPU work and posting, not final presentation; SF Actual Timeline extends to presentation. The red “over 50 ms” label is not 50 ms of continuous SF computation or main-thread blocking. The separate 23.58 ms selection is not a substitute for that measurement. Without the trace, no precise end-to-end latency is recalculated here.

Check frame tokens, layer, linked DisplayFrame, Present Type, and Prediction Type. Light green can indicate high latency, so color alone does not prove prompt response. See FrameTimeline documentation and part one.

System Architecture Optimization Supporting 120Hz

Sustained high-refresh operation requires control of frame timing and power. Display-rate selection is one part of that work.

Adaptive Refresh Rate Technology

Distinguish panel capability, traditional mode switching, and Android ARR. An LTPO panel specification does not guarantee a particular rate range or AOSP ARR support.

AOSP introduced ARR in Android 15, requiring panel, kernel, system, and composer3 v3 support. Refresh cadence can change within one display mode. TE/Vsync may differ from refresh rate: the official example uses 240 Hz timing with a 120 Hz maximum refresh rate. The app guide specifies Android 15 QPR1+ with the required HAL. Neither an OS version nor “120 Hz/LTPO” alone establishes support.

Surface.setFrameRate(float, int) is available from Android 11 (API 30). It hints at a Surface’s intended content frame rate; it does not force a display mode or throttle rendering. This game-content example assumes an app-owned, valid display Surface and compile SDK 30+:

The example’s 60 FPS is a content target, not guaranteed 60 Hz display or automatic 60 FPS rendering. Android 16 (API 36) adds FRAME_RATE_COMPATIBILITY_AT_LEAST for UI/scrolling hints requesting at least a given rate. Games keep DEFAULT; fixed-rate video uses FRAME_RATE_COMPATIBILITY_FIXED_SOURCE. Use constants only on their supported API versions; set frameRate to 0 when the hint is no longer needed. See the Surface API.

Other surfaces, display capabilities, and power policy affect selection; a multiple of the requested rate may be chosen. Keep animation time-based and work correctly when the hint is not adopted. See the frame-rate guide.

Advantages and Challenges of 120Hz

Experience Improvements Brought by 120Hz

When I got my first 120 Hz phone, these were the changes I noticed:

  1. Everything becomes smoother: From desktop sliding, application switching to browsing Weibo, screen updates are more frequent, and content follows finger movement more accurately. That was my impression when scrolling Moments or Weibo. Attributing it to refresh rate alone would require controlling app frame rate, motion, and display mode on the same device.

  2. Game experience can improve: When playing Honor of Kings and 和平精英 at the time, I felt that the controls were easier to use. If a game produces frames steadily and the display uses a matching mode, there are more opportunities to show new actions. “Seeing an action 8ms earlier” is not a fixed gain; input, rendering, and display latency must be measured.

  3. Reading comfort is personal: I find 120 Hz more comfortable while reading and scrolling for long periods. This is an impression, not a controlled comparison or a visual-health conclusion.

  4. Touch and display are separate: A 120Hz display mode does not by itself show that the touch sampling rate increased; check the two specifications separately.

Practical Problems Faced by 120Hz

Of course, high refresh screens also bring a series of technical challenges:

  1. Power consumption problem: A higher refresh mode may increase display and rendering power. The effect needs a same-device test with brightness, app workload, duration, and measurement method held constant; there is no universal 15-20% increase.

  2. Tighter frame cadence: An app targeting stable 120FPS produces a frame about every 8.33ms, but its precise deadline depends on device scheduling, reflected in FrameTimeline predictions; the entire rendering pipeline is not one serial 8.33ms task.

  3. Temperature: Sustained high-frame-rate gaming can increase CPU/GPU/display work and lead to thermal throttling. Separate refresh-rate effects from game workload through same-device, same-scene measurements.

  4. Application target frame rate: A 60FPS app on a 120Hz display is not necessarily an adaptation failure; video, static content, or power policy may intentionally use a lower rate.

Thoughts and Future Outlook

On-Demand Adjustment: Intelligent Management of Refresh Rate from ProMotion

Do we need to stay at 120 Hz in every situation? Static pages and fast scrolling need different update rates. Apple’s ProMotion guide provides content-based animation hints:

  1. High-impact motion: fullscreen transitions may request CAFrameRateRange(minimum:80, maximum:120, preferred:120); use high rates selectively.
  2. Opacity/color changes and small movements: use CAFrameRateRange.default.
  3. Slow, small animations: examples span 8–15, 15–24, or 30–48, with preferred=0. These ranges do not guarantee every integer hardware rate.
  4. Other cases: use the default range.

These are iOS 15+ API suggestions, not fixed system rules or Android settings. Requests are not guaranteed; custom iPhone animations requesting above 60 Hz also need the documented CADisableMinimumFrameDurationOnPhone configuration. Lower update frequency can reduce rendering work, while display power still depends on hardware and actual refresh behavior.

Trade-off Between Power and Experience

Reducing refresh rate from 120Hz to 60Hz may save power, but the amount depends on the device, brightness, content, and actual app frame rate. A universal 10-15% saving cannot be inferred without a controlled measurement.

High refresh rates help most with scrolling, animation, and other interactions that need quick feedback. For static content, the system can choose a lower mode, provided the transition does not introduce visible judder.

Developer’s Adaptation Strategy

For surfaces your app manages, hint at the content rate and pace production accordingly. Ordinary View animations follow framework scheduling; this example is for an app-managed Surface. ARR device requirements are described above.

Record active mode/refresh cadence, produced and presented frame intervals, input-to-feedback latency, and power-test conditions. “Supports 120 Hz” alone does not establish an improvement.

Conclusion

When I wrote this in 2025, I felt that 120 Hz had noticeably improved phone interaction. My expectation was that it could remain common for a long time, with more effort going into choosing the right rate for each situation. That was a personal forecast, not a standard every device must meet.

For developers, tools like Perfetto help inspect performance problems under 120Hz. The nominal refresh interval changes from about 16.67ms to 8.33ms, but sustained 120FPS still depends on the app workload, device, thermal state, GPU, and presentation timing; avoiding main-thread blocking alone does not guarantee it.

In Perfetto, check the active display mode and compare the app and SurfaceFlinger timelines to distinguish late app work, late presentation, and intentionally lower-rate content. Power claims need separate measurements on the same device, at the same brightness, in the same scene.

About Me && Blog

Here is a personal introduction and related links. I hope to communicate more with my peers. When three people walk together, there must be one who can be my teacher!

  2. This Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.
  3. Personal Collection of Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Know: Welcome everyone to recommend themselves and others (WeChat private chat is fine)
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: Historical introduction; the community has closed.

entry.title: Android Perfetto Series 5: Choreographer-based Rendering Flow
entry.content:
This article introduces Choreographer, a class that App developers may not frequently encounter but is critically important in the Android Framework rendering pipeline. We will cover the background of its introduction, a brief overview, partial source code analysis, its interaction with MessageQueue, its application in APM (Application Performance Monitoring), and some optimization ideas for Choreographer by mobile phone manufacturers.

Choreographer coordinates pending frame callbacks with display timing; it does not itself set the screen refresh rate. At 120 Hz, the interval is about 8.33 ms. Meeting a frame deadline also depends on CPU scheduling, GPU work, buffers, and composition. Apps request callbacks as needed rather than redraw on every physical Vsync. This article also distinguishes what FrameCallback, FrameMetrics, gfxinfo, Looper, and Perfetto can observe.

Version note (reviewed October 2026): Historical MethodTrace/Systrace and newer Perfetto images are retained. Without their original traces, interpretation is limited to what is visible. Older code skeletons use android-10.0.0_r1; excerpts involving VsyncEventData, FrameInfo, and newer callbacks are labeled against android-16.0.0_r1. BLAST discussion uses Android 15 source. Excerpts omit surrounding fields, checks, and branches: they are not standalone app code or one complete mainline implementation.

Table of Contents

  • Perfetto Series Catalog
  • The Essence of Main Thread Execution
  • Introduction to Choreographer
  • Source Code Analysis
  • MessageQueue and Choreographer
  • APM and Choreographer
  • Manufacturer Optimizations
  • Reference Materials
  • Zhihu Address
  • About Me & Blog

This is the fifth article in the Perfetto series, mainly giving a brief introduction to Choreographer in Perfetto.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from another perspective through the Perfetto tool, and also to learn about the Framework from a different angle. Maybe you have read many articles about the Framework, but always can’t remember the code, or are not clear about its running process. Perhaps from the graphical perspective of Perfetto, you can understand it more deeply.

  21. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto: Trace Graph Types - AOSP, WebView, Flutter + OEM System Optimization

If you haven’t seen the Systrace series yet, here is the portal:

  1. Systrace Series Catalog: Systematically introduces the use of Systrace, the predecessor of Perfetto, and learns and understands the basic rules of Android performance optimization and Android system operation through Systrace.
  2. Systrace version of this article: Detailed Explanation of Android Choreographer-based Rendering Mechanism
  3. Personal Blog: Personal blog, mainly Android-related content, also contains some life and work-related content.

Everyone is welcome to find ways to get in touch on the About Me page to discuss your questions, the parts of Perfetto you most want to see, and discuss all Android development-related content with other group members.

The Essence of Main Thread Execution

Much Java work on the main thread is dispatched by Looper through Handlers. MessageQueue queues and retrieves messages rather than executing business logic. nativePollOnce also processes file-descriptor events, including Vsync reception; not every main-thread operation is a Java Message. These images show waiting and dispatch in the captured examples.

MethodTrace

Perfetto

Evolution

The original text described these as pre-Vsync rendering, but they already contain Choreographer.doFrame and RenderThread. They illustrate continuous work under an unspecified historical configuration, not Android before Choreographer.

A dequeueBuffer wait can involve available buffers, consumer release, or fences. The image does not establish a fixed SurfaceFlinger consumption rate for every app; a traditional framebuffer description is not universal to modern displays.

Choreographer is available from API 16. Vsync pacing and buffering help organize rendering without guaranteeing a stable frame rate. BLAST later changes the buffer/transaction path, discussed below.

For users, a stable frame rate is a good experience. For example, when playing Honor of Kings, compared to frequent fluctuations between 60 and 40 fps, users feel better when it is stable at 50 fps.

This is an intuitive description of experience. Presentation cadence matters too: a fixed 60 Hz display cannot present 50 fps at equal integer-refresh intervals, so it is not a universal ranking for every device.

Introducing Choreographer

Choreographer gives due animation and traversal callbacks an opportunity to run in relation to display timing. A software Vsync notification still depends on the owning Looper’s scheduling; a hardware interrupt does not directly execute Java drawing.

This older 60 Hz diagram uses 16.6 ms, not a universal end-to-end budget. Its RenderThread “GPU” label is inaccurate: RenderThread is a CPU thread organizing/submitting work, with asynchronous GPU execution. UI, RenderThread, GPU, and SurfaceFlinger stages can overlap.

At 120 Hz, adjacent refreshes are about 8.33 ms apart; scheduling determines the actual work deadlines. See the 90 Hz article for refresh-rate versus frame-rate context.

Introduction to Choreographer

Choreographer coordinates callbacks registered with it, not all Handler messages. Framework work is processed in Input, Animation, Insets Animation, Traversal, and Commit order when callbacks are due. These are execution phases, not Linux thread priorities.

DisplayEventReceiver provides requested software Vsync timing. Timely app, RenderThread, GPU, and SurfaceFlinger completion still needs separate observation; using Choreographer and BLAST does not guarantee stable 60/90/120 fps. Monitoring boundaries are discussed below.

Diagrams help explain the mechanism, but here I will mostly use Perfetto and MethodTrace. Placing CPU, SurfaceFlinger, SystemServer, and app activity on a timeline and following the code makes their interactions easier to see. I will use a few diagrams, then work through traces; what they show still depends on what was recorded.

Choreographer’s Workflow from the Perspective of Perfetto

These historical Perfetto images show scrolling Settings. Green Running segments are CPU scheduling states, not presented frames; slices can include waits.

  1. The VSYNC-app counter toggles to indicate software Vsync cadence, annotated around 8.33 ms here. High/low levels are not durations of “Vsync executing”; do not mistake a whole square-wave cycle for one refresh interval. Match the producer’s definition.
  2. Follow doFrame, DrawFrame, buffer submission, and SurfaceFlinger dependencies, while accounting for overlapping threads/frames. Adding UI and RenderThread wall durations does not yield final frame latency.
  3. BLAST submits buffers with transactions. Submission does not prove GPU completion or presentation; inspect fences, composition, and presentation evidence.

Now zoom in on one main-thread frame to see where Choreographer sits and how it organizes the callbacks. The arrows locate that work chain. The old “queueBuffer means GPU starts” annotation is not valid: GPU submission/execution has no such fixed one-to-one relationship with queueBuffer. The end of the main-thread slice is not final presentation time either.

Choreographer’s Workflow

  1. getInstance() obtains the default thread-local instance on a thread with a Looper, initializing its Handler, DisplayEventReceiver, and callback queues.
  2. Due work requests Vsync. A file-descriptor event reaches onVsync() through JNI, which posts an asynchronous Message.
  3. When Looper dispatches it, run() calls doFrame() to handle timing, due callbacks, and diagnostic markers.
  4. Input → Animation → Insets Animation → Traversal → Commit run in order. Traversal may measure/layout/draw and synchronize with RenderThread; not every frame repeats every operation.
  5. RenderThread/GPU work, BLAST submission, and SurfaceFlinger composition can overlap this sequence. Commit is not a GPU-completion or presentation callback.
  6. Remaining animation/scroll work registers another callback. A single FrameCallback is not an indefinitely repeating callback.

This older MethodTrace helps locate calls, not establish identical signatures or all phases on every frame.

Interaction between Choreographer, RenderThread and BlastBufferQueue

The following uses Android 15’s common ViewRootImpl window path. It is not a universal implementation for every release, Surface type, or vendor build.

BlastBufferQueue Working Principle

Android 15 BLASTBufferQueue maintains producer/consumer endpoints in the client and puts acquired buffers into SurfaceControl transactions. This changes buffer/window transaction coordination with SurfaceFlinger, without eliminating buffer availability, fence, or back-pressure waits.

ViewRootImpl creates and updates the queue; a changed SurfaceControl may require recreation. The retained skeleton below is not the complete relayout condition:

UI/RenderThread synchronization also depends on HWUI DrawFrameTask, uploads, and queued work. BLAST alone does not prove earlier UI return or fewer stalls; use a same-scenario trace or measurement. See ANR part three for a related wait-chain example.

Source Code Analysis

These are call relationships and selected excerpts. Older registration, animation, and traversal skeletons use Android 10 Choreographer; constructor, FrameHandler, VsyncEventData, and doFrame marker/phase examples are updated against Android 16. Omitted fields, checks, and locals mean the snippets cannot be assembled into a compilable class. Native registration is explained with Android 10 source.

Choreographer Initialization

Choreographer Singleton Initialization

Choreographer Constructor

Android 16 retains the two-argument constructor, delegating to the three-argument version with layerHandle. Partial initialization:

FrameHandler

In Android 16, MSG_DO_FRAME is the timer fallback without Vsync. Normal Vsync delivery uses the Receiver Runnable below.

Choreographer Initialization Chain

Adding an Activity window can construct ViewRootImpl, which obtains a Choreographer. This older call-chain illustration is not a promise of creation after every onResume, nor the only initialization path: animation code may call getInstance() earlier.

Introduction to FrameDisplayEventReceiver

In Android 16, onVsync() saves timing and copies event data before posting an asynchronous Message; run() later calls doFrame(). scheduleVsync() is inherited from DisplayEventReceiver, which owns the native pointer. Checks and surrounding fields are omitted below:

Vsync Registration in Choreographer

How does Vsync arrival lead to onVsync()? Follow initialization to see how the file descriptor is registered. These three registration skeletons are from Android 10, not signatures to combine with the Android 16 Receiver above. DisplayEventReceiver establishes a native connection through JNI and registers the receiving FD with the native Looper.

Vsync event data travels through BitTube (a socket pair), while requesting the next notification uses Binder IDisplayEventConnection.requestNextVsync(). The image separates nativePollOnce→onVsync enqueueing from later Message dispatch→run/doFrame.

DisplayEventReceiver Communication Details with SurfaceFlinger

In Android 10’s native DisplayEventReceiver, the client creates a connection and obtains the BitTube receiving endpoint through Binder stealReceiveChannel(). Control requests and event delivery are separate; the app is not directly requesting a hardware interrupt through the socket:

FD monitoring integrates with Looper, but scheduling and queued work still affect delivery. This is not a real-time execution guarantee.

Logic of Choreographer Processing a Frame

Normal Vsync delivery posts the Receiver Runnable from onVsync(); Looper later dispatches run()/doFrame(). This repeats the Android 16 core excerpt with timestamp and pending-state checks omitted:

doFrame() checks scheduled work, handles lateness relative to the supplied frame time, updates frame metadata, and executes due phase callbacks. Its skippedFrames value estimates start delay, not final display drops.

Recording Frame Drawing Info

android.graphics.FrameInfo is hidden internal Framework/HWUI data recording selected phase boundaries, not every function or callback duration. These Android 16 fields stop at FRAME_INTERVAL; surrounding declarations such as FLAGS and the later WORKLOAD_TARGET are omitted. The old gfxinfo CSV below has a different header—do not decode it with these newer indices.

Android 16’s six-argument setVsync() includes vsyncId, deadline, start time, and interval. Markers precede their corresponding callback phases, simplified here:

Executing Callbacks

The second doCallbacks() argument here is Android 16’s frameIntervalNanos, not the older frameTimeNanos. The Input/Animation/Traversal paths below are older skeletons and historical stacks; each phase extracts only due callbacks.

Input Callback Call Stack

input callback generally executes ViewRootImpl.ConsumeBatchedInputRunnable

android/view/ViewRootImpl.java

The image shows one batched touch-input path through ViewRootImpl to DecorView/Activity/Views. Keys and non-batched input need not wait for CALLBACK_INPUT, and not every input event calls dispatchTouchEvent.

Animation Callback Call Stack

View.postOnAnimation posts work to CALLBACK_ANIMATION.

Which code calls View.postOnAnimation? I captured the call hierarchy below; it includes operations such as startScroll and Fling.

The static hierarchy includes fling callers, but the following runtime stack shows AnimationHandler, ValueAnimator/AnimatorSet, and property updates. It does not identify a specific FlingRunnable by itself.

In addition, our Choreographer‘s FrameCallback also uses CALLBACK_ANIMATION.

Traversal Call Stack

The following omits surrounding locals and branches, illustrating schedule→doTraversal→performTraversals. Measure, layout, and draw are conditional. The barrier is removed before performTraversals, not after GPU or display completion.

TraceView Example of doTraversal

Next Frame Vsync Request

Due to the existence of operations such as animation, sliding, and Fling, we need a continuous and stable frame rate output mechanism. This involves the request logic of Vsync. In continuous operations, such as animation, sliding, and Fling, doFrame of each frame will trigger the application for the next Vsync according to the situation, so that we can obtain continuous Vsync signals.

See the call stack of scheduleTraversals below (scheduleTraversals will trigger Vsync request)

invalidate() and requestLayout() can schedule traversal, but visibility, an existing traversal, and mFrameScheduled coalesce work. One call does not imply one independent Vsync request.

Let’s take Animation as an example to see how Animation drives the next Vsync to continuously update the screen.

ObjectAnimator Animation Driving Logic

android/animation/ObjectAnimator.java

android/animation/ValueAnimator.java

android/animation/AnimationHandler.java

Calling postFrameCallback will go to mChoreographer.postFrameCallback, where the Vsync request logic of Choreographer will be triggered.

android/animation/AnimationHandler.java

android/view/Choreographer.java

AnimationHandler reposts while animation callbacks remain. FrameCallback itself is one-shot; delayed or absent work does not imply a callback on every Vsync.
TraceView Example of a Frame During Animation

Source Code Summary

  1. getInstance() returns the default instance for the current Looper thread. It is not process-global or a ban on other internal Choreographer instances on that thread.
  2. Binder control, BitTube events, native FD callbacks, and Java asynchronous Messages are distinct steps, not direct Java execution of a hardware interrupt.
  3. The five-phase order lets due input/animation changes precede traversal. COMMIT is not a GPU fence or presentation notification.
  4. ListView/RecyclerView layout, binding, scrolling, and prefetch can occur through different paths. ViewHolder reuse is not a separate Choreographer phase or proof that one component is always faster; inspect its library version and trace.
  5. FrameCallback is removed after one invocation. Re-registration sustains animation; scheduling coordination does not guarantee timely callbacks or presentation of every buffer.

APM and Choreographer

Distinguish callback cadence, Window/HWUI work, SurfaceFlinger presentation, and one Looper dispatch. They are different metrics. FrameInfo is hidden internal data, not a stable reflection-based app interface.

  • API 16 FrameCallback: observes callback cadence; a long interval suggests delay, not measured display fps.
  • API 24 FrameMetrics: delivers window frame reports. The listener’s dropCountSinceLastInvocation counts lost reports, not display drops. Copy the reused metrics object before deferred processing.
  • API 33 postVsyncCallback: supplies FrameData timelines, deadlines, and expected presentation information. It is one-shot and predictive, not proof of presentation. See Choreographer.
  • gfxinfo/FrameTimeline: read version-specific HWUI output; Android 12+ FrameTimeline relates expected/actual work and presentation for jank analysis when its data source is collected.
  • Looper/IdleHandler: dispatch wall time and queue idleness aid diagnosis, but do not cover GPU/presentation. IdleHandler is not an end-of-frame callback.

Historical examples below are retained with their limits.

Use Perfetto for Advanced Monitoring

Perfetto aligns enabled scheduling, CPU frequency, app trace sections, graphics, and service data. Categories, app tracing permissions, and device support determine coverage; slices require instrumentation. Sampling, stacks, and graphics sources have their own costs, so lower overhead cannot be guaranteed without a configuration comparison.

Use Perfetto to Track Choreographer

Replace com.example.app with the target package. Perform the interaction while the foreground command records for 15 seconds, then pull after it exits. The 32 MB ring buffer is an example, not guaranteed full-window coverage. Categories vary by device/version.

Search for Choreographer#doFrame (possibly with a frame ID). It measures Choreographer callback processing, not full GPU/presentation latency. Configure android.surfaceflinger.frametimeline separately when needed; the shorthand command does not guarantee it. See the capture article for a full configuration.

Use framestats (internally backed by FrameInfo) for Monitoring

Use adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo <packagename> framestats, replacing the package. This is the original historical StatusBar output, not a new capture:

Parse the CSV by its own header. Timestamp fields differ from durations such as DequeueBufferDuration/QueueBufferDuration; units are ns, with monotonic rather than calendar time. In this older format, OldestInputEvent=9223372036854775807 and NewestInputEvent=0 are unrecorded-input sentinels, not values for calculating input latency.

FrameCompleted marks completion in that HWUI path, not physical presentation. Summary categories such as Missed Vsync and Slow UI can overlap and must not be summed as independent frames. This sample is not Android 16’s FrameInfo layout.

Use SurfaceFlinger for Monitoring

On older implementations, find a layer with adb shell dumpsys SurfaceFlinger --list, then query its latency, for example adb shell 'dumpsys SurfaceFlinger --latency "actual layer name"'. Bare --latency does not select an app; implementation and permissions vary.

In Android 10 FrameTracker, the first line is refresh period and the columns are desired present, actual present, and frame ready times in ns. Its ring has 128 slots but the dump iterates 127, not 128 guaranteed new valid frames. Identify zero and pending-fence INT64_MAX records as invalid/incomplete.

The old ceil((C - A) / refresh_period) uses ready minus desired time without actual presentation. It is not a general dropped-frame formula; refresh changes, pipeline deadlines, and missing values also matter. Prefer FrameTimeline frame/presentation correlation for modern analysis.

Use SurfaceFlinger PageFlip Mechanism for Monitoring

Obsolete interface—historical explanation only. Android 10’s private transaction 1013 returned the default display’s page-flip count under system UID/HARDWARE_TEST checks, not app fps. Android 16 returns NAME_NOT_FOUND for the same code. The original transact-then-readInt snippet ignored failure and is no longer presented as a usable monitoring example.

These are separate version excerpts, not one switch. Use FrameMetrics or FrameTimeline for the intended measurement. Unsupported, denied, or missing data must not become 0 fps. See Android 16 SurfaceFlinger.

Choreographer’s Own Dropped Frame Calculation Logic

This is an older simplified excerpt. jitterNanos is start delay relative to the supplied frame time. Dividing by the interval estimates missed scheduling opportunities, not the current doFrame duration or final presentation drops. Android 16 uses the event interval and handles zero-interval cases.

SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT defaults to 30 and is read from the property at class initialization. No warning does not mean no jank, and changing its threshold does not fix jank.

BlockCanary

BlockCanary historically used Looper MessageLogging to observe dispatch boundaries. The older skeleton below illustrates their placement; newer implementations may use loopOnce. This is not an installation or maintenance recommendation for the library.

Dispatch wall time includes blocking and scheduling delay, not just CPU work. It does not cover all nativePollOnce FD handling, GPU work, or presentation. Many short messages can also delay a frame. Logging costs work and must be coordinated with other users of the same Looper logger.

MessageQueue and Choreographer

A synchronization barrier changes queue eligibility, not CPU priority. In Android 10 MessageQueue.next(), a barrier at the head (null target) causes a search for the next asynchronous message, whose due time is still checked. This does not preempt a running callback or create another thread.

Framework code uses the hidden postSyncBarrier()/removeSyncBarrier() methods. Message.setAsynchronous(boolean) is public from API 22, and Handler.createAsync() from API 28; the older hidden-API claim was wrong. Without an obstructing barrier, the asynchronous flag does not automatically move a message to the front, and cross-Handler ordering dependencies still matter.

An Example of SyncBarrier Used in Choreographer

scheduleTraversals calls postSyncBarrier.

doTraversal calls removeSyncBarrier.

These frame-scheduling Messages are asynchronous so they can pass an active barrier. This does not raise Linux scheduling priority or make them precede all other messages.

Manufacturer Optimizations

System manufacturers can change framework code and try optimizations at this level. I cannot share that code, but I can outline the ideas. If you are interested, we can discuss them privately.

These are ideas I was considering at the time, not default AOSP behavior or validated benefits on every build. Changes must preserve input/lifecycle order, animation timebases, and buffer/fence contracts, with latency, presentation, power, and compatibility measured.

Input Event Optimization

Choreographer already has CALLBACK_INPUT, used by ViewRootImpl for batched input. Vendors may use more input state to schedule earlier, but must distinguish reception, batching, and app callbacks, validating ordering, resampling, and input-to-presentation latency.

Background Animation Optimization

Stop animation updates when they are invisible and unnecessary for the product, using lifecycle/visibility information. Vendor throttling needs similar care: background does not automatically make every callback useless, especially with multi-window, picture-in-picture, or state progression. This historical image shows dense doFrame work that I labeled as a background case; it does not independently establish visibility, power cost, firmware configuration, or the app’s current behavior.

Frame Drawing Optimization

A vendor can explore earlier composition scheduling in selected scenarios. That does not let a display present at arbitrary times: buffer/fence dependencies, display deadlines, and power constraints still apply. Earlier composition alone is not proof of fewer missed frames.

App Launch Optimization

If queued work delays critical startup messages, first identify unrelated work and waits, then consider controlled scheduling. Arbitrary front-of-queue movement can break lifecycle/input order or starve work. Validate first-frame/interactivity and regressions, not just an earlier message timestamp.

Animation Callback Front-loading

There may be slack after main-thread work, but that does not prove CPU idleness; other messages, threads, and GPU work can continue. Earlier animation calculation must preserve frameTime, property-update, and input-sampling consistency. It is a specific framework strategy, not an automatic jank reduction.

Frame Interpolation

This is closer to vendor pre-rendering or prediction of later animation states than a universal definition of frame interpolation. doFrame has scheduled-state, monotonic-time, and callback-queue constraints. Calling it twice does not establish two generated, submitted, or presented frames, nor image-based motion interpolation.

OverScroller predicts from current velocity and bounds, but new input, boundaries, layout, or content changes can invalidate that prediction. Any advance work needs cancellation, correct timing, buffer/power accounting, and presentation validation. Touch-up does not fix all later frame content.

High Refresh Rate Optimization

When the active display mode is 120 Hz, refreshes are about 8.33 ms apart rather than 16.67 ms at 60 Hz; app frame rate may differ. Evaluate deadlines, presentation cadence, and energy instead of treating the whole pipeline as a fixed single-thread budget. Vendor priorities include:

  1. Performance analysis and optimization of large apps
  2. Game high frame rate cooperation
  3. Logic of mutual switching between 120 fps, 90 fps and 60 fps

Reference Materials

  1. https://www.jianshu.com/p/304f56f5d486
  2. http://gityuan.com/2017/02/25/choreographer/
  3. https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/Choreographer
  4. https://www.jishuwen.com/d/2Vcc
  5. https://juejin.im/entry/5c8772eee51d456cda2e8099
  6. Android Development Expert Class
  7. Perfetto - System profiling, app tracing, and trace analysis
  8. Official Perfetto UI guide
  9. BufferQueue and Gralloc
  10. Android 15 Official Features: Graphics

Zhihu Address

Since blog comments are inconvenient, if you want to like or communicate, please move to the Zhihu page of this article

Juejin - Detailed Explanation of Android Choreographer-based Rendering Mechanism - Perfetto Version

About Me & Blog

Below is a personal introduction and related links. I look forward to communicating with you all!

  1. Blogger Personal Introduction: Contains personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.
