One person can go faster, a group of people can go further

entry.title: Android Perfetto Series 4: Opening Large Traces via Command Line
entry.content:
This is the fourth article in the Perfetto series, explaining how to use trace_processor_shell to open large files exceeding 2GB locally. In actual problem analysis, we often encounter very large Trace files (greater than 2GB) that may fail to open in ui.perfetto.dev because of browser memory limits. The limit applies to memory used while parsing, not directly to the trace file’s size. In this case, we can use the official trace_processor_shell tool to open large files locally.

When I started this series, Perfetto had largely replaced Systrace in my daily work, and the OPPO and vivo teams I encountered were also migrating. Newcomers found the interface overwhelming and asked me to explain the subjects of my Systrace articles through Perfetto.

Version note (reviewed October 2026): The original screenshots use v49’s trace_processor_shell. The official trace_processor wrapper currently selects v58.2; commands are checked against that release, with UI behavior checked against v58.3 source. server http is the current subcommand form; legacy --httpd remains supported. A binary named trace_processor_shell is not inherently obsolete. See both forms below and series 11 for more SQL usage.

Table of Contents

  • Perfetto Series Catalog
  • 0. trace_processor_shell Tool Download
  • 1. Using trace_processor_shell to Open Large Trace Files
  • 2. Difference Between Command Line Startup and Direct UI Opening
  • 3. Mac Permission Issues
  • Reference Documents
  • About Me && Blog

Paul Graham said: “Either give a lot of people something they kind of want, or give a small number of people something they really want.“ Perfetto is actually something that a small number of people really want, so let’s start writing. Please join the discussion. If you spot an error or an unclear explanation, let me know so I can fix it before it misleads someone.

In this series, I want to use Perfetto to look at how apps, the Framework, and Linux work together. If you have read plenty of source code and performance articles but still find the flow hard to follow, try placing that code on a trace timeline.

Perfetto Series Catalog

  1. Android Perfetto Series Catalog
  2. Android Perfetto Series 1: Introduction to Perfetto
  3. Android Perfetto Series 2: Capturing Perfetto Traces
  4. Android Perfetto Series 3: Familiarizing with the Perfetto View
  5. Android Perfetto Series 4: Opening Large Traces via Command Line
  6. Android Perfetto Series 5: Choreographer-based Rendering Flow
  7. Android Perfetto Series 6: Why 120Hz? Advantages and Challenges
  8. Android Perfetto Series 7: MainThread and RenderThread Deep Dive
  9. Android Perfetto Series 8: Understanding Vsync and Performance Analysis
  10. Android Perfetto Series 9: Interpreting CPU Information
  11. Android Perfetto Series 10: Binder Scheduling and Lock Contention
  12. Android Perfetto Series 11: PerfettoSQL, Trace Processor and Regression Detection
  13. Android Perfetto Series 12: Trace Dataflow and Data Loss
  14. Android Perfetto Series 13: Perfetto SDK, Track Event and App Field Traces
  15. Android Perfetto Series 14: heapprofd and Memory Profiling
  16. Android Perfetto Series 15: Boot Traces and Long-running Field Tracing
  17. Android Perfetto Series 16: GPU, Power Counters and Hardware Bottlenecks
  18. Android Perfetto Series 17: Scenario Automation and Platform Tracing
  19. Android Perfetto Series 18: Input Response Latency
  20. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto Basics and Case Studies
  21. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto: Trace Graph Types - AOSP, WebView, Flutter + OEM System Optimization

If you haven’t seen the Systrace series yet, here is the portal:

  1. Systrace Series Catalog: Systematically introduced the use of Systrace, the predecessor of Perfetto, and used Systrace to learn and understand the basic rules of Android performance optimization and Android system operation.
  2. Personal Blog: Personal blog, mainly content related to Android, and also put some content related to life and work.

Welcome everyone to find ways to get in touch on the About Me page to discuss your problems, the parts about Perfetto you most want to see, and discuss all Android development related content with group friends.

0. trace_processor_shell Tool Download

Download a matching host OS/architecture package from official Releases, for example mac-arm64 on Apple Silicon. These are historical v49 screenshots; use the selected release’s actual assets. An Android device package is not a macOS/Linux host executable.

On macOS/Linux, the official Python 3 wrapper is another option and requires curl. It downloads and verifies the manifest-selected native binary on first use, then uses its cache. The wrapper pins a build rather than fetching an arbitrary new binary on every invocation; record --version. Run these commands in your tools directory:

The native Trace Processor parses the trace and the UI queries it over local RPC. This bypasses the browser engine’s memory ceiling, but not host RAM/address-space limits or query intermediates; streaming input does not make memory unlimited. Normal local opening does not upload the trace. Fully offline use also requires a prepared binary and an offline-ready or locally hosted UI.

Keep the v58.2 command forms separate:

PurposeSubcommand formLegacy flat flags
HTTP serviceserver http --port 9001 "trace.pftrace"--httpd --http-port 9001 "trace.pftrace"
SQL filequery -f query.sql "trace.pftrace"-q query.sql "trace.pftrace"
Full sortingGlobal --full-sort--full-sort

Prefix these with ./trace_processor or the native executable name. Do not copy legacy -q into query, which uses -f/--query-file. Full sorting may raise peak memory usage; it is not a general large-file acceleration switch. A custom port also requires matching UI rpc_port and connection policy. Default 9001 is the simplest path. See the large-trace guide and CLI reference.

1. Using trace_processor_shell to Open Large Trace Files

With the wrapper, use the current form below. Replace the quoted path with your trace and keep the server running while the browser queries it:

For the historical v49 package, use the legacy form below. Choose one invocation; do not start both on the default port:

The original terminal screenshot actually shows Address already in use for both IPv4 and IPv6 on port 9001. It does not prove that this process started successfully. If your existing processor is intentional, connect and verify its loaded trace; otherwise stop only your unneeded instance before retrying.

Once loading and listening succeed, open Perfetto UI. It probes local port 9001 and queries over WebSocket RPC. A version mismatch may first prompt a matching UI or a tool update. If detection fails, check server errors, port selection, and browser local-network access restrictions. The preloaded-trace dialog below is historical and will not appear in every situation:

Pop-up Options

1. YES, use loaded trace

Reuse the trace already parsed by the server, avoiding another file import. This does not restore all previous filters, selections, notes, or SQL objects. The v58.3 UI preload path calls restoreInitialTables() to restore the initial SQL environment before UI initialization. Parsed data is reused, not a complete prior analysis session.

2. YES, but reset state

Keep the local accelerator and open another trace through the UI; this does not automatically reload the original command-line file. In v58.3, choosing the button does not restart the process. Importing new data after the previous trace’s EOF resets the parser. A different trace does not inherently require a new process or port, but replaces the old parsed state.

Use one active trace/UI client per service to avoid another tab’s reset or queries interfering with your analysis.

3. NO, Use builtin WASM

This tab uses the built-in WASM engine and needs a file/source supplied through the UI. It neither transfers the server’s parsed state into the browser nor stops the server. Both engines support SQL.

The historical screenshot below shows download/conversion limits for a preloaded RPC trace. In v58.3, availability depends on whether the UI has a downloadable original source: pure HTTP_RPC preload has no file bytes, whereas a UI-opened file is a different source. The restriction is not universal to every native-engine use. Downloading the original trace also does not write filters or SQL results into a “modified trace.” Sharing depends on source/deployment and may upload data or state; choosing WASM does not guarantee every collaboration feature. See the loading implementation.

2. Difference Between Command Line Startup and Direct UI Opening

Startup via Command Line (trace_processor_shell --httpd)

The native process performs parsing and SQL, listening on localhost:9001 by default (the UI probes 127.0.0.1:9001). The browser still renders the interface and consumes memory. Native processing is often a better fit for large traces, but duration depends on the data, host resources, and queries.

Loaded data can be reused while the server lives. Process exit, another import, or UI SQL initialization changes what remains available. Save important SQL scripts and original files instead of relying on temporary tables surviving across pages. A preloaded RPC source has the download/conversion limits described above.

Directly Open UI Web Page (ui.perfetto.dev)

This means opening a file with the built-in WASM engine. The same webpage can connect to a native server, so webpage access and command-line startup are not separate, mutually exclusive UIs.

WASM needs no additional server process and also supports PerfettoSQL and visualization. Normal local opening does not require uploading. Download/sharing capabilities depend on source and deployment. Runtime memory differs from file size: 2 GB is a historical reference for common limits, not a universal browser file threshold. Parsed data, query results, and the UI all consume memory. Without a same-trace measurement, do not assume WASM is always slower.

Summary and Suggestions

Try native processing when browser-engine memory limits block a large import. WASM is convenient for routine analysis. If the native process also runs out of memory, investigate import/query costs or narrow future recording scope and duration; a different command does not make every trace fit.

3. Mac Permission Issues

A downloaded executable may trigger Gatekeeper. This is a historical v49-era alert, not an error every Mac must show. Distinguish unidentified/unnotarized software from damage/malware alerts, missing executable permission, and an architecture mismatch.

For a verified official file you trust, Apple’s instructions are to attempt opening it, then use System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway and confirm the next prompt. Older screenshots may use different wording. This is a per-file exception, not a requirement to disable system protection. Damage or malware alerts require checking the official source instead of applying this step indiscriminately.

Reference Documents

  1. Perfetto Github Repository
  2. Perfetto Official Documentation

About Me && Blog

Here is a personal introduction and related links. I hope to communicate more with my peers. When three people walk together, there must be one who can be my teacher!

  1. Blogger Personal Introduction: Contains personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. This Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.
  3. Personal Collection of Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Know: Welcome everyone to recommend themselves and others (WeChat private chat is fine)
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: Historical introduction; the community has closed.

One person can go faster, a group of people can go further

entry.title: Android ANR Series 3 - ANR Case Studies
entry.content:
This is the third article in the Android App ANR series, focusing on real-world ANR cases. The series includes:

  1. Android App ANR Series 1: Understanding Android ANR Design Philosophy
  2. Android App ANR Series 2: ANR Analysis Workflow and Key Logs
  3. Android App ANR Series 3: ANR Case Studies

Version note (reviewed October 2026): These historical cases include logs from 2020. The exact ROM/app versions and complete traces are unavailable. Rendering mechanisms are checked against android-10.0.0_r47; updates use android-15.0.0_r1 and current documentation. These source baselines do not identify the original devices’ builds. Some spacing, line endings, and timestamps are incomplete; missing values are not reconstructed.

Identify type and impact with Android Vitals or field monitoring, then align bugreports, EventLog, main/system logs, and Perfetto covering the timeout window. Direct /data/anr access requires permissions. API 30+ ApplicationExitInfo contains historical exits; traces may be missing, and exit time is not ANR start time. See part two.

The abridged 2015 quotation below is retained as historical context. Attribution to an app does not establish an app-side cause, and ANRs are not confined to the main thread. Low incidence alone does not justify ignoring a problem. Each case below distinguishes observed waits from causes that still need evidence.

ANR (Application Not Responding) is a simple definition that covers many Android system design philosophies.

First, ANR belongs to the application scope. This differs from SNR (System Not Responding), which reflects issues in the system process (system_server). SNR is managed by the Watchdog mechanism, while ANR is managed by the message handling mechanism at the system layer through message scheduling and timeout handling.

Second, the ANR mechanism is primarily implemented in the system layer. All ANR-related messages are scheduled by system_server and dispatched to the application process. The system uses various timeout limits to track message processing. If an app fails to respond within these limits, the system collects diagnostics (CPU/IO usage, thread stacks) and reports that the process is not responding.

Third, ANR is essentially a performance issue. The mechanism limits the app’s main thread, requiring it to handle common operations (starting services, processing broadcasts, input) within fixed timeframes. Time-consuming operations in the main thread (heavy calculations, heavy I/O, complex layouts) reduce responsiveness.

Finally, some ANR issues are very difficult to analyze. System-level issues like Linux kernel bugs, memory fragmentation, or hardware failures can cause message scheduling failures that are hard to reproduce and diagnose.

– From duanqz

Common Causes of ANR

For ANRs, the approach is bold hypotheses, careful checks. Pick an unusual event, suppose it caused the problem, and read the surrounding logs to test that idea. If the evidence does not support it, try another lead.

The lists below identify places to investigate. An operation is not itself an ANR: connect it to the timed-out contract. Slow Activity lifecycle work can block input and other progress; there is no single independent ANR timer for every Activity callback.

Issues Within the Current Process

  1. Deadlocks.
  2. Main thread calls thread.join(), sleep(), wait(), or waits for a thread lock.
  3. Main thread waits at nSyncAndDrawFrame for a RenderThread synchronization point.
  4. Time-consuming operations on the main thread, such as complex layouts, massive for loops, IO, etc.
  5. Main thread is blocked by a sub-thread’s synchronized lock.
  6. Main thread times out waiting for a sub-thread.
  7. Slow Activity lifecycle work delays input or the first frame.
  8. Main thread Service lifecycle method execution timeout.
  9. BroadcastReceiver.onReceive() does not return promptly, or goAsync() work does not finish its PendingResult in time.
  10. RenderThread is time-consuming.
  11. Time-consuming network access.
  12. Application reads and writes a large amount of data.
  13. Database operations.
  14. Hardware operations (such as Camera).
  15. A Binder service process’s thread pool is saturated, queuing a critical synchronous request; this is not a universal limit on Binder objects.
  16. A worker fails without completing a business-level wait condition. Ordinary Thread.join() returns when the target terminates; termination itself does not imply an indefinite join.
  17. Dump memory operations.
  18. SharedPreferences loading/writes or pending persistence work at lifecycle transitions delay a critical thread.

Issues in Remote Processes or the System

  1. Binder communication with SystemServer, and SystemServer execution is time-consuming.
    1. The method itself takes a long time to execute causing timeout.
    2. Too much lock contention in SystemServer, resulting in lock wait timeout.
  2. Timeout waiting for other processes to return, such as getting data from other processes’ ContentProvider.
  3. Window state confusion leading to Input dispatch timeout.
  4. A ContentProvider process death may fail dependent calls or affect client survival, depending on the dependency type. Process death and ANR are distinct outcomes.
  5. System-wide low memory.
  6. System-wide high CPU usage.
  7. System-wide high IO usage.
  8. SurfaceFlinger timeout.
  9. Bug in system freezing function.
  10. A system_server Watchdog timeout is a separate system-failure detector. It may coincide with app ANRs without being the same event.
  11. The device triggers thermal control frequency limitation.

ANR Case Studies

ANR Case: Toutiao - Deadlock

The reported steps were to repeatedly pull Toutiao out of the sidebar into split-screen mode. After several attempts, the app reported an ANR and its split-screen area briefly went black and stopped responding. It recovered after 4–5 seconds.

The historical heading is retained, but the excerpt establishes a main-thread wait on a LogReaper lock during exception handling, not a proven deadlock.

Waited-on lock:

held by thread 34 is an ART tid. Find tid=34 in the same dump, not Linux TID 34; its Linux TID here is 28274.

Next wait:

LogReaper holds 0x0d3fbd00 and a DBHelper monitor while calling Object.wait() on 0x00fc7065. Object.wait releases the waited-on object’s monitor, not other monitors already held. The object being an AtomicInteger does not make this a lock-free atomic operation.

Find who changes and signals the condition, whether that path needs the main thread or either held lock, and whether the timed wait can expire. A cycle or unfinishable condition is still needed to diagnose deadlock or a logical hang. The uncaughtException frames also require investigating the original exception; a blocked crash handler is not necessarily the initial fault. The reported recovery after 4–5 seconds does not prove a persistent deadlock.

ANR Case: ANR caused by Freezing

Start with the am_anr timestamp and reason. This older input dispatcher reports unfinished previously delivered input preventing further delivery. It is not NoFocusedWindow, nor proof that an app callback was actively executing.

Then inspect the CPU report:

The CPU interval, 00:51:44.177–51.637, is after the 00:51:39.594 am_anr. Only three processes are listed, while Load is around 30. This cannot establish an idle system or exclude system pressure. Inspect pre-timeout scheduling, I/O/memory pressure, and freezer state.

The unfreeze reason: Signal line after the ANR gives us a lead: if the app was being unfrozen then, could an earlier freeze explain why it had not responded to input? Searching backward finds the freeze at 00:51:04.000. Put the timestamps together before deciding whether that hypothesis holds:

TimeWhat the excerpt records
00:51:04.000Vendor Hans logs freeze for UID 10182 / weather2, reason LcdOff
00:51:04.471–04.477Input policy logs BACK DOWN before queueing/dispatch; this is not proof of app processing
00:51:34.478Policy logs BACK UP about 30 seconds later, with a different downTime; do not reconstruct a normal paired press
00:51:39.484 / 39.594Input dispatch timeout / am_anr
00:51:40.868–40.870Signal Catcher reacts, Hans logs unfreeze reason: Signal, and the app drops/cancels events and reports a long input duration

Explanatory annotations below are corrected; log values are retained.

The sequence supports investigating input remaining unfinished during freezing and progressing around unfreeze. Actual freezer state, complete input IDs, and vendor unfreeze logic are still missing. Nearby logs alone do not close the causal chain. ANR stack collection commonly uses SIGQUIT (3), but this incomplete Signal Catcher line omits the number; millisecond log order across threads is not execution causality.

36391.9 ms is the dispatcher’s duration. Wall-clock 04.471→40.869 is about 36398 ms, so these are not identical timing boundaries; 04.477 is closer, but monotonic event timing is still needed. Skipped 2212 frames does not prove continuous CPU work. Escalate with these limits to the freezer/input owners rather than generalizing this 2020 Hans sequence to modern AOSP freezing.

ANR Case: Broadcast Timeout causing ANR

In this case, the user was migrating data. The receiver had started a worker thread, yet an ANR still occurred. At first, I missed the issue because I thought moving the slow work to a worker would let the broadcast finish. Then I noticed the call to goAsync(). The full broadcast reason, worker stack, and finish timing are missing. These two lines only show a database-upgrade window gaining focus; they do not establish the broadcast timeout cause.

Mechanically, goAsync() keeps the current broadcast active after onReceive() returns. It is not restricted to ordered broadcasts and does not restart the deadline or allow unlimited time. Starting an untracked thread alone does not guarantee process survival. Investigate late/missing PendingResult completion and worker queue delay, rather than automatically calling this a slow onReceive() body.

The older comment’s “10 seconds/30 seconds or more” wording and JobIntentService reference are historical guidance. Current diagnosis distinguishes version and FLAG_RECEIVER_FOREGROUND: common limits are 10/60 seconds through Android 13, and 10–20/60–120 seconds from Android 14 depending on CPU starvation, with OEM variations. Startup/scheduling and asynchronous work consume the budget too. See broadcast ANR diagnosis.

This shortened goAsync() logic shows the transfer of mPendingResult. It corrects the old transcription and omits Android 15 tracing:

In Android 15 BroadcastReceiver, finish() may wait for component QueuedWork before notifying the system; the call itself is not proof of immediate server-side completion.

Complete the app-side cleanup paths as below. This retains the original initialized mAsyncHandler and business method onReceiveAsync. The Handler must use an app-managed worker Looper that stays alive through completion, not the main Looper. This snippet demonstrates broadcast cleanup, not a migration implementation:

finally covers business exceptions and posting failure, but cannot interrupt long work or prevent queue timeout. Successful post() only means enqueueing. A rejected task is not a successful migration; handle failure/retry explicitly. For lengthy migration, keep the receiver’s durable handoff short and use an appropriate mechanism such as WorkManager. Finishing early and continuing an unmanaged thread does not solve its lifecycle problem.

ANR Case: Launcher - Input ANR

The am_anr reason identifies an input dispatch timeout with previously delivered input still unfinished, rather than NoFocusedWindow:

The CPU report is written at 19:45:07.753 and samples roughly 10.9 seconds from around the ANR onward. Load: 0.02/0.01/0.0 cannot exclude a specific scheduling, lock, or driver wait; logd 97% is not 97% of total device capacity. This incomplete sample neither proves a logic bug nor rules out system pressure. Follow the wait chain instead.

First inspect the main thread:

The main thread waits on a condition variable in DrawFrameTask::postAndWait(). Next inspect that process’s RenderThread:

RenderThread is waiting for a synchronous Binder reply to BpGraphicBufferProducer::dequeueBuffer(). This connects the main thread’s rendering wait to a buffer request, but the two stacks alone do not identify it as the previous frame.

Android 10 DrawFrameTask can unblock the UI thread before or after drawing, depending on canUnblockUiThread; earlier RenderThread work can also delay synchronization. Use frame IDs and a trace rather than assuming the UI always unblocks before dequeue.

The following Binder data is the original teaching example, not a captured transaction from this incident. It shows Launcher PID 3365 / TID 3616 calling PID 956 / TID 1357. The comment’s 1356 typo is corrected to match both illustrative transaction lines.

The separately listed Binder:956_4 stack shows that thread waiting inside dequeueBuffer. Without the incident’s transaction mapping, it does not prove that this was the RenderThread’s server thread:

This thread is in waitForFreeSlotThenRelock(). In Android 10 BufferQueueProducer, no available slot or too many outstanding queued buffers can lead to waiting; allocation policy, blocking mode, and dequeue timeout also matter. BufferQueueCore derives limits from acquired/dequeued counts and mode. A layer does not universally have three or four permanently fixed buffers.

The later logs provide additional clues; their explanatory annotations are corrected:

acquireBuffer: ... 2 (max 1) reports two buffers already acquired by the consumer and a configured limit of one. The Android 10 consumer permits one extra temporarily and returns INVALID_OPERATION at this boundary. Function not implemented (-38) is the error-code text, not proof that acquireBuffer is wholly unimplemented. The later -110 indicates a dequeue timeout without identifying who failed to release a buffer.

Keep the times separate: acquire failure is at 19:44:42.371, ANR at 19:44:56.815, and dequeue failure plus the 4002 ms message at 19:45:45. Nor does Davey duration=4015ms equal the roughly 7161 ms between IntendedVsync and FrameCompleted in the excerpt. Without vendor timing code, retain the fields rather than merging them into one proven frame. Zero buffer-duration fields do not invalidate the observed wait stack.

Ask the graphics owners to correlate buffer acquisition/release, consumer state, fences, and composition progress; this evidence does not assign the root cause directly to SurfaceFlinger. Re-identify dependencies on modern builds: Android 15 ViewRootImpl creates BLASTBufferQueue, whose implementation creates a client-side queue and submits buffers through SurfaceControl transactions. The old cross-process dequeue path is not a universal rule.

Anomalous Log Examples

Main Thread Database Operation

This stack establishes main-thread database opening/journal-mode configuration through getWritableDatabase(), while holding Java monitors. It does not identify a slow business query. Native usleep/nanosleep may involve SQLite lock-retry behavior, but unresolved ??? frames do not identify the busy handler or owning connection. SQLite busy timeout supports sleep-and-retry on lock contention; that does not make every SQLite sleep the same cause.

Correlate database open, initialization/migration, transactions, and connection ownership. Move blocking opening/migration work off the main thread without making the UI synchronously wait for it. Increasing busy timeout lengthens waiting; it does not remove the ANR risk. Do not change WAL mode from this stack alone. Without an ANR reason and duration, this is a risky snapshot, not proof of a separate ANR.

Large Binder Payloads

These lines report large Binder replies. Values such as size388568 are Parcel data bytes, not transaction counts or durations. They do not by themselves prove transaction failure, process death, or ANR.

Version matters: AOSP Android 10 Binder.checkParcel uses an 800 * 1024 byte threshold behind the default-disabled CHECK_PARCEL_SIZE; Android 15 retains this check. The listed values are smaller, so this historical device output cannot be attributed directly to that default implementation. Inspect its device-branch logging policy.

The TransactionTooLargeException documentation describes a process buffer shared by in-flight transactions, currently documented as 1 MB—not 1 MB reserved for each call. Reduce/page responses, use an appropriate file-descriptor or shared-data channel for large data, and account for concurrency. Its relevance to an ANR still requires timing evidence.

Binder Communication Failure

Decode the device kernel’s format before attributing transaction failed to memory exhaustion. Using Linux v4.14 binder.c as a reference, 1698:2362 is the issuing PID:TID, 29189/-3 is the protocol return code/additional error, size100-0 gives data and offsets bytes, and line3042 locates a kernel error path. Source line numbers are not portable across builds.

In that UAPI, 29189 (0x7205) is BR_DEAD_REPLY, not BR_FAILED_REPLY; the errno definitions map -3 to ESRCH and -22 to EINVAL. This does not identify the device as v4.14. In particular, verify the final line’s return-code/error combination against its kernel and earlier driver logs.

Inspect target-process death, Binder node/mapping state, and the failing branch; then correlate client exceptions, retries, and waits. A transaction may fail promptly without causing ANR. These lines do not justify increasing the Binder thread pool or blaming oversized payloads.

ANR Related Information Sharing

  1. Xigua Video Stability Governance System Construction 1: Tailor Principle and Practice
  2. Xigua Video Stability Governance System Construction 2: Raphael Principle and Practice
  3. Xigua Video Stability Governance System Construction 3: Sliver Principle and Practice
  4. Xigua Freeze & ANR Optimization Governance and Monitoring System Construction
  5. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Design Principle and Influencing Factors
  6. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Monitoring Tools and Analysis Ideas
  7. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Example Analysis Collection
  8. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Barrier Causes Main Thread Deadlock
  9. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Goodbye, SharedPreference Waiting
  10. Android ANR | Principle Analysis and Common Cases

Reference

  1. https://duanqz.github.io/2015-10-12-ANR-Analysis#1-%E6%A6%82%E8%A7%88
  2. https://duanqz.github.io/2015-10-12-ANR-Analysis
  3. http://gityuan.com/2016/12/02/app-not-response/
  4. http://gityuan.com/2017/01/01/input-anr/
  5. https://xiaozhuanlan.com/topic/5097486132

About Me && Blog

Below is a personal introduction and related links. I look forward to communicating with you all!

  1. Blogger Personal Introduction: Contains personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.
  3. Excellent Blog Articles Collected and Organized by Individuals - Must-Know for Android Performance Optimization: Welcome everyone to recommend yourself and recommend (WeChat private chat is fine)
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: Historical introduction; the community has closed.

entry.title: Android ANR Series 2: ANR Analysis Methodology and Key Logs
entry.content:
This is the second article in the Android App ANR series, focusing on ANR analysis methodology and key logs. The series includes:

  1. Android App ANR Series 1: Understanding Android ANR Design Philosophy
  2. Android App ANR Series 2: ANR Analysis Methodology and Key Logs
  3. Android App ANR Series 3: ANR Case Studies

Version note (reviewed October 2026): Historical device logs and screenshots are retained. AOSP field explanations are checked against android-15.0.0_r1; the older ART enum is labeled Android 11. Vendor logs, thresholds, and field order must be matched to the device build. The quotation below dates from 2015: an ANR attributed to an app does not establish an app-side root cause, and ANRs are not limited to the main thread. A low occurrence rate alone does not justify ignoring an issue.

ANR (Application Not Responding) - a simple definition that encompasses much of Android’s system design philosophy.

First, ANR falls within the application domain. This differs from SNR (System Not Responding), which reflects issues where the system process (system_server) loses responsiveness, while ANR explicitly confines the problem to applications. SNR is ensured by the Watchdog mechanism (details can be found in Watchdog mechanism and problem analysis); ANR is ensured by the message handling mechanism. Android implements a sophisticated mechanism at the system layer to detect ANR, with the core principle being message scheduling and timeout handling.

Second, the ANR mechanism is primarily implemented at the system layer. All ANR-related messages are scheduled by the system process (system_server) and then dispatched to application processes for actual processing. Simultaneously, the system process designs different timeout limits to track message processing. Once an application mishandles a message, the timeout limit takes effect: it collects system states such as CPU/IO usage, process function call stacks, and reports to the user that a process is not responding (ANR dialog; some ROMs don’t display the ANR dialog but directly crash to the home screen).

Third, ANR issues are essentially performance problems. The ANR mechanism actually imposes restrictions on the application’s main thread, requiring it to complete the most common operations (starting services, processing broadcasts, handling input) within specified time limits. If processing times out, the main thread is considered to have lost the ability to respond to other operations. Time-consuming operations on the main thread, such as intensive CPU computations, heavy I/O, complex UI layouts, etc., all reduce the application’s responsiveness.

Finally, some ANR problems are very difficult to analyze. Sometimes due to underlying system influences, message scheduling fails, and the problematic scenario is hard to reproduce. Such ANR issues often require significant time to understand system behaviors, going beyond the scope of the ANR mechanism itself. Some ANR problems are hard to investigate because there are many factors causing system instability, such as memory fragmentation caused by Linux Kernel bugs, hardware damage, etc. Such low-level causes often leave ANR problems untraceable, and these aren’t application issues at all, wasting much time for application developers. If you’ve worked on entire system development and maintenance, you’ll deeply understand this. Therefore, I cannot guarantee that understanding all content in this chapter will solve every ANR problem. If you encounter very difficult ANR issues, I suggest talking to friends working on Framework, drivers, and kernel, or if the problem is just a one-in-a-hundred-thousand phenomenon that doesn’t affect normal program operation, I’d suggest ignoring it.

– From duanqz

ANR Analysis Methodology

Organize evidence by ANR type: use Android Vitals or your monitoring platform to identify Input dispatch, Service, Broadcast, JobScheduler, device versions, and impact. For a local incident, collect a bugreport, EventLog, and main/system logs promptly. Direct access to /data/anr/anr_* requires device permissions; adb pull is not universally available on production builds. Capture Perfetto/System Trace early enough to include the lead-up to the timeout when investigating scheduling, Binder, locks, I/O, or rendering.

Android 11 (API 30)+ provides ApplicationExitInfo, but these are historical exit records. The timestamp is the process exit time; traces may be overwritten, and an app that recovered from an ANR may attach its earlier trace to a later exit for another reason. See part one for these limits.

Check application logic and system dependencies, then trace the waits between them. System pressure can amplify an existing synchronous wait; high CPU usage in one process does not establish ownership of the fault.

General ANR Analysis Steps:

When you get an ANR trace, first ask: does it capture the original incident? Logs, CPU samples, and thread dumps may describe different moments. If those times do not line up, it is easy to follow the wrong clue.

  1. Match package, PID, user, device boot, and am_anr reason before using a trace. Distinguish operation start, timeout detection, CPU sampling, thread dumping, and log output. am_anr is not guaranteed to mark the beginning of the failure, and a dump may arrive after the blocking operation ended.
  2. Search for ANR in; record the affected process, reason, CPU sample interval, process/thread usage, Load, PSI, and page-fault counts. The log writer may be system_server, rather than the affected process.
  3. Align relevant launches, unlocks, process changes, slow messages, lock contention, and Binder events across the timeout window. Collect useful lines in one file and search them in VS Code or Notepad++: was this the first unlock after a reboot, or did several apps start in quick succession? Follow the critical thread to lock owners, Binder servers, scheduling delays, or I/O waits; check how much of the window the evidence covers.
  4. If evidence is insufficient, leave the cause unresolved and add focused logs and tracing in a reproducible environment. Account for collection overhead; a later stack snapshot cannot reconstruct an unobserved interval.

Distinguishing Between Application Problems and System Problems

First, Analyze Whether It’s an Application Problem

Start with what the user was doing and which part of that operation the app was handling. Then check:

  1. Slow work in component lifecycle callbacks that only becomes noticeable under system load. Logs in those callbacks can help.
  2. Unusual workloads, such as a large data import or too many concurrent threads. Check the app’s CPU and I/O activity.
  3. Possible deadlocks.
  4. Waits for Binder replies.
  5. Unexpected MainThread or RenderThread activity in the trace.
  6. Waits between the main thread and worker threads.

Analyze System State

  1. Check CPU usage, Load, and scheduling waits in relevant processes such as system_server, Audio, and SurfaceFlinger. HeapTaskDaemon is an ART GC-related thread inside an application process, not a separate system service.
  2. Check I/O latency and /proc/pressure/io. Minor/major faults count page faults, not memory accesses or I/O throughput; see below.
  3. Align dumpsys meminfo, memory PSI, reclaim/swap activity, kswapd, and process-kill records. Older devices may use the kernel lowmemorykiller; modern Android commonly uses userspace lmkd. Kernel OOM is another mechanism.
  4. For suspected freezing, inspect the device’s freezer state and unfreeze logs. D means an uninterruptible wait, not proof of freezing. An older kernel’s __refrigerator stack is a freezer clue, but still requires the trigger and timing. xxxHansManager is vendor-specific.
  5. Follow a suspected system-service dependency to its Binder server or lock owner and inspect its stack and scheduling. Explain how the observed pressure blocked this particular operation.

Continue Analysis: Can Application Resolve It or System Resolve It?

  1. When the wait leads into the system or another process, provide the build version, timeline, stacks, and trace to the team owning that dependency. Escalation does not mean the issue is unsolvable.
  2. Also assess whether the app can move work off the main thread, shorten lock scopes, or avoid synchronous waits. A possible app mitigation does not establish an app-side root cause.
  3. Attribute the incident only when evidence connects the timeout to a specific blocker. Missing system access or incident data means the cause remains unresolved.

ANR Log Content

Logs can be captured via test tools, obtained from online platforms, or captured manually:

ANR Trace Log contains the following content:

Thread Details

The image below explains some fields in the trace:

The image is an older field guide, with some values from a different example. Read the actual dump using its build’s format. In Android 15 ART:

  • tid=1 is an ART thread ID; sysTid=5991 is the Linux TID. prio, nice, and sched describe different scheduling layers.
  • sCount is the current ART suspend count, not a lifetime suspension counter or proof of app freezing. The image’s old dsCount explanation is not portable; Android 15 prints ucsCount instead. These values do not establish a history of debugger attachment.
  • schedstat contains cumulative CPU runtime (ns), run-queue wait time (ns), and timeslices run. These are not ANR-window totals. ART may print 0 0 0 when reading fails, so missing data must not be treated as measured zero.
  • utm/stm are user/kernel clock ticks, converted using the printed HZ (100 here). core is the last CPU used, not a permanent affinity.

Thread Stack

Below is the call stack corresponding to the thread:

The stack contains Native and Java frames. Here, nativePollOnce shows an event wait at dump time. It does not prove the thread was idle throughout the timeout, nor exclude an asynchronous broadcast or another thread involved in the ANR. Match the ANR type and dump timing first.

Thread State

Java Thread.State, ART state, and Linux scheduling state describe different layers. Java RUNNABLE or ART Native does not guarantee on-CPU execution; inspect state=S/R/D and scheduling tracks too. This older enum matches Android 11. Android 15 uses an enum class, with kRunnable=0; the older values and table are not a complete current-version contract.

Blocked beside the thread name is an ART state. Owner 89 in the image is an ART tid; find it in the same dump before mapping to a Linux TID. One wait edge does not prove deadlock: continue looking for a cycle.

Normal Main Thread Trace

This example shows an event wait at dump time; it does not rule out an earlier blocker.

Abnormal Main Thread Trace

Follow this monitor wait to its owner. Its duration and dependency chain determine whether it explains the ANR.

CPU Usage Analysis

After finding ANR in, read the CPU sample interval. It is not necessarily before the ANR. These historical 2020 logs include explanatory annotations; intervals marked later may include diagnostic work after detection. Do not add percentages from the two intervals. Page-fault annotations are corrected below; original measurements are retained.

In Android 15 ProcessCpuTracker, process/thread percentages use the sampled uptime interval as the denominator. Parallel threads can give a process 191% or 290% CPU usage. TOTAL uses aggregate CPU time and therefore a different denominator. Fault counts are sample deltas. Align these measurements with the critical thread rather than attributing the failure from process totals alone.

CPU Load

Load represents average active task counts over roughly 1, 5, and 15 minutes, including runnable tasks and uninterruptible waits. It is not CPU utilization, and can remain elevated after CPUs become idle. Values of 0.7, 1, or 5 are not universal phone alarm thresholds: account for online CPUs, scheduling restrictions, and I/O waits. Heterogeneous cores, frequency, and thermal limits also prevent treating eight cores as eight times one core’s capacity. See the Linux loadavg definition.

When available, /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu%d/cpufreq/stats/time_in_state records frequency residency, not CPU busy time or app runtime, since driver initialization or a statistics reset. Upstream documents 10 ms usertime units; check vendor extensions separately. See CPUFreq Stats. The standalone extract says 1.871, whereas the preceding full log says 1.87; their original precision is retained without deriving a new result.

Memory Load

This is PSI output from /proc/pressure/memory. The old transcription somavg10 is corrected to some avg10, without changing the values. avg10/60/300 are smoothed pressure percentages at those timescales. total is cumulative stall time in microseconds (µs), not milliseconds.

some covers periods when at least some tasks stall on the resource; full covers periods when all non-idle tasks stall on it simultaneously. These measure resource pressure, not CPU utilization. See Linux PSI.

The following two-task I/O illustration explains the distinction:

Red marks I/O stalls. In this idealized 60-second interval, both tasks stall for 16.66% and at least one stalls for 50%. These are interval ratios, not a direct calculation of the kernel’s smoothed avg60. Stalls may be spread across several periods, as below.

Historical illustration background: Kernel Craftsman (Chinese).

IO Load

  1. Minor fault: a page fault resolved without loading a page from storage, for example by mapping an already-resident page. It is not a CPU cache miss or a counter of every memory access.
  2. Major fault: a page fault requiring a page to be loaded from storage. It does not cover all I/O; ordinary file reads and writes need not generate major faults.

Thus 118172 minor / 2 major counts faults during the sample interval, not I/O operations or bandwidth. Many major faults warrant checking fault latency, I/O PSI, and critical-thread waits, but do not establish a storage-related ANR by themselves. See Linux /proc/pid/stat.

Process Load

23% user and 6.4% kernel describe user-mode and kernel-mode CPU time. The displayed total of 30% uses formatting precision; independently rounded fields need not add up digit for digit. See the CPU usage section for denominators and multicore behavior.

CPU Anomalous Process

These are investigation leads, not conclusions based on process names:

  1. High system_server usage: identify the thread and service/lock this operation depends on.
  2. Active kswapd: correlate reclaim and swap activity with critical-thread delays.
  3. High logd usage: inspect log volume and actual write latency; this does not prove all processes block synchronously on logging.
  4. High vold usage: follow storage operations and Binder dependencies.
  5. High app CPU: separate main-thread work, worker threads, and scheduling contention. Low app CPU can still accompany a lock- or Binder-related ANR.
  6. A thread in D: inspect its blocked stack; see the earlier freezer discussion rather than attributing it to power policy from state alone.
  7. +/- on CPU lines: these mark additions/removals in sample tracking, not exact process birth/death timestamps. Correlate lifecycle logs.

Key System Log Introduction

Application Freezing

This vendor log identifies a UID, package, and LcdOff reason. Correlate process state, unfreeze timing, and the timeout before blaming a freezer bug. The AOSP cached apps freezer, supported from Android 11, uses cgroup v2; it is not interchangeable with older __refrigerator stacks or vendor Hans logs.

ActivityManager : Slow operation

The old AMS checkTime example is retained below. For Android 15 process-start checks, see ProcessList.checkSlow: checkpoints report cumulative time since startTime once it exceeds 50 ms. This is not automatic instrumentation of every AMS operation.

Three lines saying 138ms so far can be consecutive checkpoints in one operation, not three steps each taking 138 ms. Correlate frequent reports with scheduling, locks, and I/O; they do not establish the ANR cause alone.

Looper : Slow dispatch

418ms is the uptime duration of dispatchMessage (end minus start), including execution, waits, and preemption—not CPU runtime. h/c/m identify the Handler, callback, and what code. Logging depends on configuration and thresholds; there is no universal 500 ms rule. See Android 15 Looper.

Looper : Slow delivery

361ms is dispatch start minus msg.when: lateness relative to the scheduled execution time, not total time since creation or enqueueing. A delayed message intentionally has a future due time. Investigate why it was not dispatched after becoming due.

Looper：Slow Looper

This is a vendor extension. The definitions of late/wall/running/runnable/io and message history depend on that ROM, not a stable AOSP Looper interface. Earlier messages are leads; without the full trace these fields do not establish a complete causal chain.

onTrimMemory

80 is the historical TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETE level, not 80 MB or 80%. The API documentation says this level is no longer delivered from Android 14 (API 34), and the constant was deprecated in API 35. It helps interpret older incidents, but is neither a guaranteed modern low-memory signal nor proof of an imminent kill.

dvm_lock_sample

This is an older nine-field sample: process, sensitive-thread flag, waiting thread, wait in ms, waiter file/line, owner file/line, and sample percentage. - means the same filename; it does not prove that the lock object is AMS itself. Locate both positions in the matching build. The final 0 does not match the usual nonzero sampling condition; the original device implementation is unknown, so the value is retained without inventing a policy.

This is not a live alert emitted whenever a wait crosses 500 ms. ART records completed contention after acquiring the lock, using runtime configuration and possible sampling below the threshold. Android 15 also includes method names; do not decode it with fixed positions from this older format. See Monitor and LogContentionEvent.

binder_sample

PID and TID are both 6628, identifying the main thread in this historical sample. EventLogTags defines the descriptor, transaction code, duration in ms, blocking package, and sample percentage: IAccessibilityManager, code 6, 2010 ms, com.xxx.community, and 100% here. A retained tag definition does not mean collection is enabled on every release, or that a universal 500 ms threshold exists.

Resolve the code against the same build’s generated Stub/Proxy or AIDL. The older API 30 source view below maps FIRST_CALL_TRANSACTION + 5 (6) to addAccessibilityInteractionConnection. That mapping is not portable across versions. The duration is not purely server CPU time.

Long monitor contention

art/runtime/monitor.cc

TID 14216 writes this line; the recorded owner is InputDispatcher (17039). 141ms is lock-wait duration, not the owner’s CPU time. waiters=0 is a count at the recording point, not proof that nobody waited. The older formatting code is retained; match the ART version. Android 15 Monitor records contention after the wait ends.

Binder Thread

This is a saturation signal for that process’s libbinder pool. The 31-thread value is configuration-specific, not a universal limit. In Android 15 IPCThreadState, timing starts when executing threads reach the limit; after the count falls below it, a duration over 100 ms is logged. It does not prove that all Binder communication stopped or that a deadlock exists. Inspect the pool threads’ locks, synchronous calls, and work.

am_kill

This older five-field sample contains user 0, PID 18555, process name, OomAdj 945, and reason remove task. A stray transcribed 1 after the closing bracket has been removed. Android 15 EventLogTags adds an RSS field; parsers must match the version. The following five images index historical kill paths/reasons, not every current process-kill path.

force-stop

Abnormal Process Kill

Active Process Kill

Schedueled Process Kill

Other Process Kill

An am_kill emitted by a framework kill path is not a record of every process death. Process.killProcess(pid), shell signals, or LMK/lmkd may bypass that path while producing other logs. Signal delivery is restricted by identity, permissions, and SELinux; neither command can kill arbitrary PIDs.

An absent am_kill can also reflect overwritten or incomplete logs. Correlate death, exit, and kernel records rather than inferring the kill mechanism from a missing tag.

am_proc_died

In Android 15 EventLogTags, the fields are user, PID, process name, OomAdj, and ProcState. 935/19 are not death reasons. This event records an observed process death; correlate it with am_kill, crash, lmkd, or exit records.

am_anr

The fields are user, PID, process name, ApplicationInfo flags, and reason. Here they identify user 0, PID 8769, com.android.updater, and a BOOT_COMPLETED broadcast. 952680005 is not a timeout duration. The Intent’s flg=0x9000010 is separate from the app flags and does not contain 0x10000000 (FLAG_RECEIVER_FOREGROUND). Determine the timeout from the build, broadcast flags, and receiver path, not the apparent size of a hexadecimal value. The log timestamp is not the broadcast start time.

Lowmemorykiller

This is an older kernel lowmemorykiller format, not a promise that modern lmkd reports in the kernel log. The first line names PID 15545, UID 10136, a value labeled oom_adj of 995, and an estimated reclaim amount of 105068 kB. Do not decode 995 using the old Linux -17–15 oom_adj range; check whether the vendor uses oom_score_adj units.

The second line has no PID. Adjacency alone does not identify the same victim or establish that 606 is min_adj. A logged estimate or reclaim amount is not necessarily net physical memory freed. See AOSP lmkd for modern low-memory handling.

Blocked msg

This is internal/vendor instrumentation. The historical 1.5 s threshold belongs to that slow-message logger, not a universal AOSP ANR timeout. cost=32436 ms is message-processing duration, not CPU time. Current msg List is a pending queue snapshot, not a list of completed messages. Negative when values are offsets from scheduled execution times, not CPU durations. Decode what=110/114/121 against that build’s ActivityThread.H.

Common Scenario Logs Introduction

Screen Off Log

The key is power_screen_broadcast_done, screen_toggled and power_screen_state.

These historical logs are retained. power_screen_broadcast_done contains on, broadcast duration in ms, and wakelockCount. The 611 ms value measures the broadcast flow, not panel power-off latency. In power_screen_broadcast_send: 1, 1 is wakelockCount, not the screen state. See Android 15 Notifier.

Screen On Log

The key is power_screen_broadcast_done, screen_toggled and power_screen_state.

Where power_screen_state:

  1. offOrOn|1|5
  2. becauseOfUser|1|5
  3. totalTouchDownTime|2|3
  4. touchCycles|1|1
  5. latency|1|3

Likewise, 633 ms is broadcast duration, not total button-to-visible-screen latency. Codes such as |1|5 above are EventLog type/unit metadata, not actual event values. Check the writer for vendor-specific power_screen_state reason/latency semantics; these logs are not guaranteed on every device.

Unlock Complete Log

Values of wm_set_keyguard_shown:

  1. (keyguardShowing|1): Whether Keyguard is showing
  2. (aodShowing|1): Whether aodShowing is showing
  3. (keyguardGoingAway|1): Keyguard disappearing
  4. (Reason|3): Reason

This uses an older four-field format. Android 15 has six: DisplayId, keyguardShowing, aodShowing, keyguardGoingAway, occluded, and Reason. Do not parse it with the old positions. setKeyguardShown is a call reason, not proof that the launcher is visible or interactive; correlate window, rendering, and input evidence. See WindowManager EventLogTags.

Notification Panel Pull Down Log

The numeric sysui_multi_action values are version-specific Metrics codes. notification_visibility contains key, visible, lifespan, freshness, exposure, and rank; its duration fields are not absolute incident timestamps. visible=1 indicates notification visibility, not a complete gesture history.

Notification Panel Collapse Log

Here the visibility field becomes 0. Logging configuration and platform version affect availability; missing lines do not prove that the panel was never opened or collapsed.

App Launch Log

The retained extract has apparent PID truncations such as 0615 20615 and 8803 18803. Without the original file, missing digits are not reconstructed; match am_proc_start and the complete incident. The 471 ms wm_activity_launch_time reports that build’s launch measurement, not necessarily full rendering or readiness for interaction.

Window Focus Related Flows

A brief Launcher → null → App transition can be normal. A NoFocusedWindow ANR requires examining pending focus-dependent input, the focused application, how long the window is missing, and the timeout policy. A null focus alone is insufficient; these logs also depend on debugging settings. See part one.

ANR Related Information Sharing

  1. Xigua Video Stability Governance System Construction 1: Tailor Principle and Practice
  2. Xigua Video Stability Governance System Construction 2: Raphael Principle and Practice
  3. Xigua Video Stability Governance System Construction 3: Sliver Principle and Practice
  4. Xigua Freeze & ANR Optimization Governance and Monitoring System Construction
  5. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Design Principle and Influencing Factors
  6. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Monitoring Tools and Analysis Ideas
  7. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Example Analysis Collection
  8. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Barrier Causes Main Thread Deadlock
  9. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Goodbye, SharedPreference Waiting
  10. Android ANR | Principle Analysis and Common Cases

Reference

  2. https://duanqz.github.io/2015-10-12-ANR-Analysis
  3. http://gityuan.com/2016/12/02/app-not-response/
  4. http://gityuan.com/2017/01/01/input-anr/

Below is a personal introduction and related links. I look forward to communicating with you all!

entry.title: Android ANR Series 1: Understanding Android ANR Design Philosophy
entry.content:
This is the first article in the Android App ANR series, mainly analyzing the design philosophy of Android ANR from a system perspective. The series directory is as follows:

  1. Android App ANR Series 1: Understanding Android ANR Design Philosophy
  2. Android App ANR Series 2: ANR Analysis Routines and Key Log Introduction
  3. Android App ANR Series 3: ANR Case Sharing

Technical review: 2026-10-14. The original section structure is retained. Implementation details use AOSP android-15.0.0_r1, with Android 11/14/15 API and behavior boundaries called out separately. Default timeouts are not fixed contracts across all OEM devices. This update adds no new device ANR reproductions.

Start by identifying which operation failed to complete, then investigate what delayed it. Android vitals or field monitoring can establish the type and impact. For test devices, combine bugreports, ANR stacks, EventLog, and system/main logs. Older releases commonly used traces.txt; newer reports often contain /data/anr/anr_*, but those directories are not necessarily readable directly on production devices. Perfetto helps only if recording covered the period leading up to the timeout.

1. Universality and Complexity of ANR

An ANR means that an application failed to meet a responsiveness requirement. Expensive main-thread work is one cause; the thread may instead be waiting for a lock or synchronous Binder reply, or remain runnable without enough CPU time. A worker handling a goAsync() broadcast can also fail to complete in time.

A report attributed to an application does not establish that the root cause is entirely in that application. Slow system services or resource pressure can delay it. Conversely, finding Binder or system_server in the evidence does not establish a system bug: follow the actual wait relationship.

  • Application ANR: detects missed completion conditions such as component callbacks or input acknowledgements.
  • System unresponsiveness: sometimes called SNR in engineering discussions. AOSP’s system_server Watchdog checks progress of selected Handler threads and Monitors, not merely whether the process exists. SNR is not a universal classification paired one-to-one with every ANR type. Watchdog source

Much of this monitoring runs outside the application, allowing detection when its main thread is blocked. The monitoring threads can still suffer scheduling delays or lock contention; their deadlines are not hard real-time guarantees.

Detection, diagnostics, a dialog, and process termination are separate stages. There is no universal sequence of killing the app, freezing a complete snapshot, and then asking the user what to do. Some background ANRs are handled silently, and foreground handling depends on recovery, debugging state, and policy. ANR traces primarily contain stacks, not full heap snapshots or an atomic freeze of every thread. Handling source

2. Core Design Philosophy of ANR

Essence of ANR: System-Level Monitoring and Mandatory Intervention

Many detectors can be understood as recording a start condition, awaiting completion, and checking state when a deadline expires. Awaiting completion normally means retaining state and scheduling a check, not blocking AMS’s main thread until the app responds.

Completion differs by operation. Services report completed lifecycle callbacks, broadcasts report finished delivery, and input connections acknowledge processed events. An arbitrary Binder call does not automatically receive a common ANR timer.

For example, Android 15’s IApplicationThread is a oneway interface. After dispatch, work still needs to reach the appropriate app thread. This cannot be explained as synchronous Binder guaranteeing business-operation atomicity. Timeout tracking and synchronous/asynchronous transaction semantics must be examined separately.

Component-Class ANR: Global Protection Logic for Asynchronous Tasks

In Android 15’s ActiveServices, service creation records execution with bumpServiceExecutingLocked() before calling scheduleCreateService(). In the app, ActivityThread.handleCreateService() invokes Service.onCreate() and subsequently reports completion through serviceDoneExecuting(). Creation, starting, and binding have distinct paths; timing only onCreate() is insufficient.

Initialization or earlier main-thread work can consume the execution budget before the service callback runs. Moving long business work to a worker does not justify blocking onCreate() or onStartCommand() while waiting for it. Framework acknowledgement of a lifecycle callback is distinct from completion of the service’s entire workload.

TypeCompletion being monitoredDefaults and version boundary
Execute serviceLifecycle callback completion reported by the frameworkAndroid 15 AOSP commonly uses short/long execution limits of 20/200 seconds, selected from service execution state; this is separate from promotion to a foreground service
Broadcast receiveronReceive() returns, or PendingResult.finish() completes goAsync() workThrough Android 13: normally 10 seconds for foreground-priority broadcasts and 60 otherwise; Android 14+ can extend these to 20/120 seconds under CPU starvation
JobService callbackTimely return from onStartJob() / onStopJob()On Android 14+, apps targeting API 34+ receive explicit ANRs for callback response timeouts; this is not the deadline for completing all background work
ContentProviderTimely response to a monitored remote requestStartup, Binder threads, or the query itself can be involved; inspect the actual detection configuration rather than applying the input timeout universally

Broadcast foreground priority depends on FLAG_RECEIVER_FOREGROUND and related delivery conditions, not simply on the app having a foreground Activity. goAsync() retains the completion deadline. See the type-specific diagnosis guide and Android 14 JobScheduler change.

ProcessStateRecord holds process-state and OOM-adjustment information and already exists in Android 13. It is not an Android 14 invention for real-time monitoring of every main-thread message. Priority adjustments likewise cannot guarantee that ANR detection and diagnostics execute promptly under all load conditions.

Foreground services have additional, distinct deadlines:

  1. Promotion to foreground: after startForegroundService(), call startForeground() promptly. The troubleshooting guide lists failure to promote as ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException. It is incorrect to describe a universal Android 15 three-second ANR rule or rely on an unverified persist.sys.fgs_timeout property.
  2. shortService runtime: this Android 14 service type has approximately three minutes of runtime; failing to stop after timeout notification can lead to an ANR. This is a runtime limit in minutes, not a three-second initialization deadline. Service type
  3. Android 15 time-limited services: for apps targeting API 35+, background dataSync and mediaProcessing services each share a per-type budget of six hours in a 24-hour period. Bringing the app to the foreground resets the corresponding timer. Failing to stop after onTimeout() is documented as an internal-exception crash. The crash path in this source baseline is feature-gated, so its presence alone does not prove that every device enables it. Distinguish this from shortService ANRs. Timeout rules

Diagnostics also have limits. Android 11 (API 30) introduced historical exit records through ApplicationExitInfo. This is not a live database of all ANRs: getTimestamp() reports process death time, and getTraceInputStream() can return null after retention buffers overwrite data. An app can recover from an ANR, later exit for another reason, and still have the earlier trace attached. Check the reason, timestamps, and trace contents together.

Input-Class ANR: Dynamic Circuit Breaker System for Event Distribution

EventHub reads device data, InputReader interprets it, and InputDispatcher routes events according to their type and window state. “Circuit breaker” here is a description of timeout handling, not a promise that each timeout immediately kills a process.

  • EventHub uses epoll_wait() to wait for device file-descriptor activity, then reads Linux input_event records with read(). inotify primarily reports device-node creation and removal; it does not carry raw touch data. Blocking waits reduce busy polling but do not guarantee zero CPU consumption. Source
  • InputReader uses InputMappers to interpret device events and generate notification arguments for dispatch. Separate reader and dispatcher threads do not imply lock-free queues. Android 15 exchanges pending data under a lock, then notifies the next listener outside that lock. Source
  • InputDispatcher communicates through InputChannel. Keys require a focused target, while touch normally involves hit testing; not every event is simply sent to the focused window.

InputDispatcher maintains incoming events and per-connection outboundQueue and waitQueue structures. The former holds events awaiting publication; the latter holds delivered events awaiting completion acknowledgement.

Publication records delivery time and a deadline. mAnrTracker tracks outstanding deadlines, and the dispatch loop schedules its next wake-up accordingly. Completion responses advance the queues and tracking state. This is not the generic MonitoredTimeout or fixed-heartbeat mechanism described in the original text. Five seconds is a common default for input response, with actual deadlines affected by window, application, and system configuration.

An app main-thread stall does not automatically stop the reader thread. System-side locks, scheduling delays, and Binder waits can nevertheless affect the overall path. Check receipt, handling, completion, and exactly which acknowledgement the system is waiting for.

No Focused Window Class ANR

No Focused Window is an input-dispatch ANR. In Android 15, an event requiring a focused window can start a wait when a focused application exists but its focused window does not. If neither a focused application nor a focused window exists, the event can instead be dropped; an ANR is not unconditional.

The common default is also five seconds. It is not a faster detector triggered by several consecutive failures to locate a window. The distinction is an unavailable receiving window versus an existing connection that fails to acknowledge an event.

Focus depends on visibility, focusability, display, and window-management state. A new Activity, Dialog, or PopupWindow does not necessarily acquire focus. There is no universal transition requiring an old-window relayoutWindow followed by a new-window addWindow.

Common app-side causes include excessive startup work, a delayed first frame, and FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE on the main window. Check Application/Activity initialization, window configuration, and first-frame timing, then investigate WMS, system-server load, and service delays. Official diagnosis

The ANR name alone cannot allocate responsibility to either the app or the system. Use window state and timing evidence to identify the unfinished step.

Unifying Principles of System Design

Four principles follow from these implementations:

  1. Explicit completion conditions: different operations require different acknowledgements; a single “main thread blocked too long” timer cannot describe them all.
  2. Separate detection and execution: the system can detect an app stall, while remaining subject to its own locks and resource constraints.
  3. Separate detection and response: diagnostics, silent handling, dialogs, and termination depend on context. Neither a dialog nor automatic restart is guaranteed.
  4. Asynchronous work retains obligations: worker threads can reduce main-thread load without removing component deadlines or resource contention.

These principles help identify the missing completion condition before assigning every ANR to one kind of stall.

Global Resolution and Active Defense of ANR Problems

Expand investigation from the app to the system when evidence warrants it. A single main-thread stack is a starting point, not a recording of the entire timeout interval.

From Phenomenon to Root Cause: Dissecting ANR Problems Layer by Layer

  1. Establish the event: record ANR type, subject, process, threads, OS version, and time. No dialog does not mean no ANR; ordinary crashes are not automatically ANRs.
  2. Establish the detector: for components, inspect dispatch, callback execution, and completion reporting; for input, inspect windows, connections, and acknowledgements. Both can use asynchronous detection. AMS is not universally a synchronous blocking detector.
  3. Follow waits: inspect the remote thread and reply for synchronous Binder waits, the holder for lock waits, and CPU availability and load for extended Runnable states. Binder pool size and occupancy must be checked for the actual process rather than assumed from one universal constant.
  4. Verify resource causes: CPU, I/O, memory reclamation, or GPU hypotheses need evidence in the relevant interval. CPU out-of-order execution alone does not explain lock contention, and memory-bandwidth pressure does not establish a Binder copy storm.

If the evidence only proves that a thread is waiting, continue investigating what it awaits and when the other side progresses. Keep missing evidence explicitly unknown.

From Passive Response to Active Defense: Three Steps for ANR Governance

  1. Stack analysis: align detection and stack-sampling times. nativePollOnce can reflect recovery, genuine idleness, or message-scheduling problems and must be interpreted by ANR type. Without earlier sampling, existing logs cannot reconstruct every stack from five seconds before and after the event.
  2. Dynamic tracing: record Perfetto ahead of a reproducible scenario and inspect scheduling, Binder, locks, and I/O around the relevant window. Verify enabled sources, coverage, and losses before correlating stack snapshots; nearby timestamps do not prove causality.
  3. Preventive design: shorten main-thread critical paths and avoid long synchronous IPC while holding locks. Bound worker concurrency and queue buildup, and ensure component completion. Executors, HandlerThreads, and coroutines still require protection against pool saturation, main-thread waits, and missing completion reports. Broadcasts or event buses are not universal substitutes for synchronous calls.

Android vitals clustering and ANR Insights can help identify common patterns. A team building rules or machine-learning classifiers should validate labels, false positives, and missed cases, using predictions as investigative leads. The existence of clustering does not establish that Google uses an unpublished “20-plus-indicator” prediction model.

ANR Related Material Sharing

These are historical Chinese-language case studies. Their implementation details should be read in the context of the versions they discuss.

  1. Reflection | Design and Implementation of Android Input System & ANR Mechanism
  2. Xigua Video Stability Governance System Construction 1: Tailor Principle and Practice
  3. Xigua Video Stability Governance System Construction 2: Raphael Principle and Practice
  4. Xigua Video Stability Governance System Construction 3: Sliver Principle and Practice
  5. Xigua Stutter & ANR Optimization Governance and Monitoring System Construction
  6. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Design Principle and Influencing Factors
  7. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Monitoring Tools and Analysis Ideas
  8. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Instance Analysis Collection
  9. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Barrier Causes Main Thread Deadlock
  10. Toutiao ANR Optimization Practice Series - Farewell to SharedPreference Waiting
  11. Android ANR | Principle Analysis and Common Cases

References

  1. https://duanqz.github.io/2015-10-12-ANR-Analysis#1-%E6%A6%82%E8%A7%88
  2. https://duanqz.github.io/2015-10-12-ANR-Analysis
  3. http://gityuan.com/2016/12/02/app-not-response/
  4. http://gityuan.com/2017/01/01/input-anr/

entry.title: Android Perfetto Series 3: Familiarizing with the Perfetto View
entry.content:
The first two articles covered what Perfetto is and how to capture a trace. This third article starts after you open that trace: with so much on the screen, where do you look?

Android documentation labels Systrace a legacy tool and recommends Perfetto on Android 10+. When I wrote this article, Perfetto had largely replaced Systrace in my daily work, and the OPPO and vivo teams I encountered were migrating. This series continues the earlier analysis methods with Perfetto.

Technical review: 2026-10-14. The 2024 interface and case screenshots are retained. Updates to shortcuts and analysis semantics use official documentation and v58.3 source (11fbaed83636). The original case traces are not provided here; their illustrated wake-up chains and measurements are not new-version test results.

Table of Contents

  • Perfetto Series Catalog
  • Perfetto View Interface
  • Perfetto Trace Interface
  • Basic Operations
  • Perfetto Usage Tips
  • Summary
  • About Me && Blog

Paul Graham said: “Either give a lot of people something they kind of want, or give a small number of people something they really want.“ Perfetto is actually something that a small number of people really want, so let’s start writing. Please join the discussion. If you spot an error or an unclear explanation, let me know so I can fix it before it misleads someone.

In this series, I want to use Perfetto to look at how apps, the Framework, and Linux work together. If you have read plenty of source code and performance articles but still find the flow hard to follow, try placing that code on a trace timeline.

Perfetto Series Catalog

  1. Android Perfetto Series Catalog
