If you haven’t seen the Systrace series yet, here is the portal:

  1. Systrace Series Catalog: Systematically introduced the use of Systrace, the predecessor of Perfetto, and used Systrace to learn and understand the basic rules of Android performance optimization and Android system operation.
  2. Personal Blog: Personal blog, mainly content related to Android, and also put some content related to life and work.

The About Me page has WeChat group information for discussing Perfetto and Android development.

Perfetto View Interface

Open a captured trace in Perfetto UI. The official record_android_trace helper normally pulls the file and opens the browser, unless --no-open is used. The screenshot below shows the 2024 home page; entries such as Legacy UI should not be assumed to remain available.

Use Open trace file or drag the trace into the page. Browser memory can limit large files; a local native Trace Processor can work with the UI.

Perfetto Trace Interface

The interface after opening Perfetto Trace is as follows:

The historical screenshot has four broad areas. Menu names and locations can change between versions:

  1. The leftmost operation area: The most important thing here is the few under the Current Trace column that will be used frequently.
    1. Show timeline: Display current Trace, after switching to other interfaces, click this again to return to the Trace View interface
    2. Query: Place to write SQL query statements and view execution results
    3. Metrics: predefined analysis, requiring the relevant data sources and compatible versions; not every trace produces a complete set of metrics.
    4. Info and stats: trace metadata, parsing statistics, and data-loss indicators. Check that the capture covers the problem interval before analyzing it.
  2. Information and operation area at the top: The most important thing is to look at the time.
  3. Trace content area in the middle: scheduling, frequency, thread instrumentation, and other tracks. Input, Binder, memory, and frame information depend on what was recorded. In this article’s older terminology, a Task generally means a thread state or execution interval. A Running interval differs from an instrumentation slice: the latter can include waits and is not necessarily CPU time.
  4. Information area at the bottom: details for the selected event, range statistics, or query results. Android Logs requires recorded log data; an app having printed a message does not mean the trace contains it. Ftrace events likewise depend on the recording configuration.

Perfetto can look cluttered and overwhelming at first. Once you get used to it, though, it is hard to go back.

Basic Operations

In my environment at the time, a roughly 500 MB trace felt smoother in Perfetto than in Systrace. Loading and interaction still depend on event count and types, queries, browser, and host memory. That file size is neither a performance guarantee nor a supported-size ceiling.

W/S zoom, A/D pan, and a click selects an event. Press ? for current hotkeys, or Ctrl+Shift+P (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS) for the command palette. Use timeline shortcuts while the timeline has focus, not while typing SQL. The following help screenshots are historical; check current prompts for query-page actions and key combinations. See the UI guide.

Some frequently used shortcuts are:

  1. f is to zoom in on the selection

  2. M creates a temporary span note from the selection. In v58.3 it reuses one temporary-note ID, replacing that note next time; selecting a single event also creates an area selection. Esc clears the selection, which is not the same as deleting a note. See the Notes implementation.

  3. Shift+M creates a new span note each time instead of replacing the previous temporary note. This is useful for marking several intervals. “Persistent” in this sense does not mean the annotation has been written back into the original trace file.

    Select the corresponding range to inspect statistics. The screenshot’s SUM(dur) aggregates slice durations, which can overlap between parents and children. A null thread_dur does not mean zero CPU time.

  4. Delete continuous Mark

    1. Click the span note’s edge marker to select the annotation.
    2. The older UI shows it in Current Selection.
    3. Click Remove. v58.3 also provides Remove selected note (Delete by default) and the Notes & markers management tab.

  5. q: Hide and show the information Tab. Screen space is precious in Perfetto. Open the panel when you need the details, then hide it when you are done.

  6. Flagging: Perfetto can also use the method of inserting flags to make marks on Trace. Perfetto supports you to put the mouse on the top of Trace, and a flag will appear. Click the left button to insert a flag on it, which is convenient for us to mark the occurrence of an event, or a certain time point

  1. Cancel the inserted flag: Same as exiting continuous selection, click the flag, there is a Remove in the lower right corner, click it to remove the flag. I’ll skip another screenshot here.

Perfetto Usage Tips

Check Wakeup Source

Here, a wake-up source is the recorded waker when a thread becomes runnable. It is not the device’s suspend wake-up reason and does not directly identify a lock owner or complete application dependency. Scheduling and wake-up events must be present; missing data, IRQ context, and trace boundaries can leave the chain incomplete.

In the article Android Systrace Response Speed Practice 3: Response Speed Extended Knowledge, I talked about how Systrace checks the wake-up source. In fact, it is still a bit troublesome. Checking the wake-up source in Perfetto is very convenient and the operation is very smooth:

The examples below show both the main thread and RenderThread. Check which thread is actually selected in each screenshot.

Click Runnable Status

Select a Runnable interval on the thread-state track to inspect Related thread states. The first screenshot selects the main thread, scrollingexample, whose waker is SurfaceFlinger’s app thread—not RenderThread. A Runnable interval can also follow preemption, so not every such interval has a new external wake-up.

  1. Waker: the recorded waking thread/state, providing a lead for further investigation.
  2. Previous state: The previous state of this Task
  3. Next state: The next state of this Task

Click the Running status above it to view continuous wake-up information:

Select a Running interval on the thread-state track and follow its CPU link to the scheduling slice, then inspect the preceding Runnable interval and wake-up event. Merely adjacent or overlapping activity in another thread does not establish a waker relationship.

Click the Running status above RenderThread to jump to the CPU Info area via the small arrow

This historical screenshot links one RenderThread activation to the main thread. It does not mean that every RenderThread wake-up has that source.

Here, the main thread’s recorded waker is SurfaceFlinger’s app thread. Scheduling latency measures the interval from becoming runnable to obtaining CPU time, not the duration of the operation that issued the wake-up.

Check Critical Path (Task)

This Critical Path is a blocking path reconstructed from thread states and wake-up relationships. It helps investigate activity associated with a thread’s waits. It is not the union of every dependency and does not automatically establish a business-level root cause. Uninstrumented asynchronous relationships, missing data, and IRQ context can affect the interpretation.

In the v58.3 plugin, Critical path lite primarily shows the state path; the full Critical path overlays associated slices. These nested slices are not automatically sampled function call stacks. The wake-up graph implementation also notes that missing IRQ-context information before Android 14 can affect accuracy.

The old UI offers Critical path after selecting a Running state. In v58.3, the selected thread state slice command uses that thread and the whole trace’s time bounds. For a specific window, select an area over a thread-state track and use the over area selection command instead.

Wait for a moment to see the Critical path corresponding to the MainThread we selected:

This historical screenshot associates the end of the main thread’s wait with SurfaceFlinger’s app thread. Its CPU numbers describe this instance, not a fixed scheduling rule.

Continue by checking the app thread’s own waker in the trace. The original text mentions TimerDispatch but does not show that step; it needs the original trace for verification and should not be treated as a fixed chain for every frame.

This view places related states and instrumentation together for further investigation. It does not by itself prove that speeding up any one displayed thread will reduce end-to-end latency.

Pin (Fix to Top)

Use the Pin icon beside a track’s title to keep it at the top. Newer workspaces also help organize tracks without pinning so many that little viewing space remains.

Here I have pinned the tracks from the app through to SurfaceFlinger. Seeing them together makes the frame flow much easier to follow when investigating dropped frames.

CPU Info Area Task Highlight

In the CPU Info area, if you put the mouse on a certain Task, other Tasks of the Thread corresponding to this Task will be highlighted.

We often use this for an initial look at which CPUs ran a thread. Highlighting shows scheduling results; it does not establish why migration occurred, a core’s capacity, or the complete scheduling policy.

Check Buffer Consumption Stats

For layers submitted to SurfaceFlinger for display composition, an App Actual Timeline slice can link to the corresponding display frame. Check the layer name and frame token when a process has several layers. A flow is not a BufferQueue-depth measurement or proof that a buffer was copied. FrameTimeline requires Android 12+ and the corresponding recorded data.

Quickly Check App Execution Timeout

Here, “timeout” means a frame missing its expected budget, not an ANR. Multiple buffers can keep older content on screen but do not rule out delayed updates or jank.

Expected Timeline represents a budget; Actual Timeline covers frame processing, including waiting and GPU work. Check Present Type, On time finish, Prediction Type, and Jank Type together instead of reading every long slice as a CPU overrun.

A red frame is a starting point, not a full explanation. The detail screenshot shows App Deadline Missed, Late Present, and Valid Prediction; investigate the main thread, RenderThread, and relevant GPU data before attributing the cause to a function. See the FrameTimeline documentation.

View Log on Perfetto

When android.log data was recorded, Android Logs can align messages with thread activity. The old screenshot’s hover line is a time reference, not proof that the logged operation caused a nearby stall.

Ftrace events shows retained raw events. Missing entries can mean an event was not enabled, was unsupported, or was lost; absence does not establish that it never happened.

Analyze Running Information of Thread

Drag to select a time window and include the target thread-state track to inspect time in each state. Selecting only an instrumentation track gives slice statistics, not scheduler states. A single thread’s Running share is not whole-device CPU utilization. This is often useful when analyzing app startup.

For precise statistics, clip state intervals to the window and state whether the denominator is the window length or valid covered time. Do not fill unknown coverage with Sleep or zero. In the historical screenshot, total Wall duration is about 865.44 ms while Selected range is 857.5 ms, so those table values should not be treated directly as exact percentages of the selected window.

Moving from UI Analysis to SQL Automation

The UI is useful for understanding a trace. Once the analysis is repeatable, translate it into SQL for comparisons and batch work:

  1. Identify the selected event’s table and SQL ID. slice contains instrumentation intervals; track, thread_track, and process_track describe tracks and ownership. They are not interchangeable slice tables.
  2. Use thread_state for scheduler states and sched / sched_slice for on-CPU intervals. Clip to the same window and distinguish wall time, CPU time, and uncovered intervals.
  3. Prefer FrameTimeline tables or standard-library modules for frame analysis, checking tokens, layers, prediction validity, and dropped frames instead of only counting red slices.
  4. track_id, utid, and upid associate tracks, threads, and processes. They do not prove causality across processes; Binder, buffer, camera, and audio chains also need their own transaction, flow, or frame-token evidence.

Article 11: PerfettoSQL, Trace Processor and Regression Detection develops this workflow further.

Summary

That covers the interface and the operations I use most often. Perfetto keeps changing; when a useful feature turns up, I will add it here.

The basic chapter of Perfetto ends here. The follow-up is to understand the basic process of Android system operation through the tool Perfetto, and use Perfetto and Perfetto SQL to analyze the problems encountered such as performance and power consumption.

About Me && Blog

Here is a personal introduction and related links. I hope to communicate more with my peers. When three people walk together, there must be one who can be my teacher!

  1. Blogger Personal Introduction: Contains personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. This Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.
  3. Personal Collection of Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Know: Welcome everyone to recommend themselves and others (WeChat private chat is fine)
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: Closed in 2026; the page remains as a historical introduction.

One person can go faster, a group of people can go further

entry.title: Android Perfetto Series 2: Capturing Perfetto Traces
entry.content:
The previous article Android Perfetto Series 1: Introduction to Perfetto introduced what Perfetto is. This article provides a brief introduction to Perfetto capture.

Android documentation labels Systrace a legacy tool and recommends Perfetto on Android 10+. When I wrote this article, Perfetto had largely replaced Systrace in my daily work, and the OPPO and vivo teams I encountered were also migrating. This series revisits the earlier analysis methods with Perfetto.

Technical review: 2026-10-14. The main examples target Android 12+. Original 2024 screenshots remain, with older-system and newer-UI differences explained below. Commands and configuration were checked against official documentation and script source; this update adds no new device-capture results.

Table of Contents

  • Perfetto Series Catalog
  • Main Content
  • 1. Using Command Line to Capture Perfetto (Recommended)
  • 2. Using Official Script to Capture
  • 3. Using On-Device Developer Tools to Capture
  • 4. Using Web Interface to Capture
  • Reference Documents
  • About Me && Blog

Paul Graham said: “Either give a lot of people something they kind of want, or give a small number of people something they really want.“ Perfetto is actually something that a small number of people really want, so let’s start writing. Please join the discussion. If you spot an error or an unclear explanation, let me know so I can fix it before it misleads someone.

In this series, I want to use Perfetto to look at how apps, the Framework, and Linux work together. If you have read plenty of source code and performance articles but still find the flow hard to follow, try placing that code on a trace timeline.

Perfetto Series Catalog

  1. Android Perfetto Series Catalog
  2. Android Perfetto Series 1: Introduction to Perfetto
  3. Android Perfetto Series 2: Capturing Perfetto Traces
  4. Android Perfetto Series 3: Familiarizing with the Perfetto View
  5. Android Perfetto Series 4: Opening Large Traces via Command Line
  6. Android Perfetto Series 5: Choreographer-based Rendering Flow
  7. Android Perfetto Series 6: Why 120Hz? Advantages and Challenges
  8. Android Perfetto Series 7: MainThread and RenderThread Deep Dive
  9. Android Perfetto Series 8: Understanding Vsync and Performance Analysis
  10. Android Perfetto Series 9: Interpreting CPU Information
  11. Android Perfetto Series 10: Binder Scheduling and Lock Contention
  12. Android Perfetto Series 11: PerfettoSQL, Trace Processor and Regression Detection
  13. Android Perfetto Series 12: Trace Dataflow and Data Loss
  14. Android Perfetto Series 13: Perfetto SDK, Track Event and App Field Traces
  15. Android Perfetto Series 14: heapprofd and Memory Profiling
  16. Android Perfetto Series 15: Boot Traces and Long-running Field Tracing
  17. Android Perfetto Series 16: GPU, Power Counters and Hardware Bottlenecks
  18. Android Perfetto Series 17: Scenario Automation and Platform Tracing
  19. Android Perfetto Series 18: Input Response Latency
  20. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto Basics and Case Studies
  21. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto: Trace Graph Types - AOSP, WebView, Flutter + OEM System Optimization

If you haven’t seen the Systrace series yet, here is the portal:

  1. Systrace Series Catalog: Systematically introduced the use of Systrace, the predecessor of Perfetto, and used Systrace to learn and understand the basic rules of Android performance optimization and Android system operation.
  2. Personal Blog: Personal blog, mainly content related to Android, and also put some content related to life and work.

The About Me page has WeChat group information for discussing Perfetto and Android development.

Main Content

The steps for using Perfetto to analyze problems are the same as using Systrace:

  1. First you need to capture the Perfetto file
  2. Open the Trace file in ui.perfetto.dev for analysis or use the command line for analysis

I prefer capturing traces from the command line, either with my own configuration or with the official helper script. Here are the available methods.

1. Using Command Line to Capture Perfetto (Recommended)

Basic Command - adb shell perfetto

After connecting an Android device with authorized USB debugging, use its /system/bin/perfetto binary to record. This lightweight example runs in the foreground: reproduce the scenario on the phone during those 20 seconds, then run adb pull after the command finishes.

This example records for 20 seconds with a 64 MB ring buffer. Older events are overwritten when it fills, so the file may not retain all 20 seconds. The remaining arguments select atrace categories; use adb shell atrace --list_categories to check device support. Lightweight mode mainly covers ftrace/atrace. The memory category is not a full heap dump, and this command does not automatically enable FrameTimeline or callstack sampling.

To include your app’s android.os.Trace / ATrace annotations, add --app com.example.app before the category list and replace the package name. System categories such as gfx and view do not replace app selection. After recording, check command success and the retained time range and events before opening the file in Perfetto UI. The output path is on the device; adb pull copies it to the host.

Advanced Command - adb shell perfetto with config file

With so many data sources and settings, putting everything into a command each time gets cumbersome. Save them in a configuration file (Config) and select that file when you record.

The following examples primarily target Android 12+. config.pbtx contains UTF-8 text-format TraceConfig and requires --txt; its filename extension does not determine whether its contents are text or binary.

On Android 12 and later devices

Starting from Android 12, you can directly use the /data/misc/perfetto-configs directory to store configuration files, so you don’t need to pass the configuration file through stdin. The specific command is as follows:

Save the pure configuration shown later as config.pbtx, then run the commands above. Reproduce the scenario while recording and pull the result after completion:

On Android 10/11 (with a compatible config, for example removing the Android 12+ FrameTimeline source), or to avoid device config-path differences, a macOS/Linux shell can pass the config through standard input:

The host shell performs this redirection, and -c - reads stdin. Android 9’s built-in Perfetto does not support --txt and needs a binary config. Some Android 9/10 devices also require tracing services to be enabled; consult the official version and service notes rather than copying Android 12+ commands unchanged.

Source of Config

For Config, I suggest using Record new trace on ui.perfetto.dev to select and customize, and then save it to a local file. Different scenarios just load different Configs. The last part of the article talks about this in detail, you can take a look if you are interested.

Exported configurations can be shared. Start with the official examples or the basic config below, then save versions for individual scenarios.

The official repository also provides configuration examples. Check their data sources, permissions, duration, and buffer sizes before reuse; they are not universal device presets.

Precautions

  • Connection and versions: adb devices should show the target as device, not unauthorized or offline. For multiple devices, add -s DEVICE_SERIAL to raw adb commands, or --serial DEVICE_SERIAL to the helper script. Record the system version, device Perfetto version, and final config.
  • Stopping early: Ctrl+C is not reliably forwarded by a direct adb shell perfetto invocation. Exiting the host command does not establish that the device trace stopped cleanly. Use the helper script’s stop handling, or enter an interactive adb shell before running Perfetto there. The timed example can simply finish normally.
  • SELinux restrictions: On Android 12 and later, place configuration files in /data/misc/perfetto-configs; do not assume that perfetto can read a config directly from /data/local/tmp.

2. Using Perfetto Official Script to Capture (Strongly Recommended)

The official tools/record_android_trace script requires Python 3 and adb on the host PATH. It invokes the recording tool, waits, pulls the file, and normally serves it locally for the browser to open. Add --no-open to skip opening and serving, including on headless hosts. These examples were checked against the official main script on 2026-10-14; save the script version used for repeatable experiments. Android 10+ normally uses the system binary; older devices may receive a downloaded tracebox binary, so the implementation is not identical on every release.

On Linux/macOS:

On Windows PowerShell (with Python 3 and the py launcher installed):

After downloading the script, use -c on Linux/macOS to select a config:

On Windows, use py -3 record_android_trace -c config.pbtx -o trace_file.perfetto-trace.

With -c, put duration, buffers, and data sources in the config; do not expect short options such as -t or -b to override it. The basic config below includes duration_ms. A config without a duration or another stopping condition may continue recording indefinitely.

Reproduce the scenario after the script reports that recording has started. The script can handle Ctrl+C to request a stop; wait for the pull to finish and check the file. The 2024 screenshot below uses a 30-second command, unlike the 10-second example here.

The script content can be viewed directly by visiting: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/perfetto/main/tools/record_android_trace

3. Using On-Device Developer Tools to Capture

When a computer or USB cable is unsuitable for the scenario, use System Tracing. It is available from Android 9 (API 28): Android 10+ records Perfetto format, while Android 9 records Systrace format. OEMs may change or hide this interface, so its settings are not identical on every phone.

Start System Tracing Application

  1. Enable Developer Options: First, make sure your device has enabled developer options. If there is no developer option in your settings, you need to find the Build number in About Phone, and then click 7 times continuously to open the developer options.

  2. Open Developer Options: Find and open developer options in the Settings menu.

  3. Start System Tracing: Scroll down in the developer options until you find “System Trace” or similar options. Click it and the system tracking application will open.

The screenshot shows the original device’s interface. Use it to recognize the feature, then check the settings available on your device.

Common settings include categories, per-CPU buffer size, debuggable applications, and a Quick Settings tile. Devices offering Long traces can also limit file size and duration. Ordinary recording uses a rolling buffer, rather than guaranteeing a complete fixed-duration recording. The app manages output files, which you export through its saved-trace notification, Files, or sharing interface; it generally does not offer an arbitrary output-path field.

Start and Stop Tracing

After configuring all the required parameters, you can start tracking by clicking the “Record trace” button. Click the “Record trace” button again to end the capture. After the capture is completed, there will usually be a prompt telling you that the capture has been completed and providing options to view or share the trace file. You can export the trace file to a computer and use the Perfetto web UI for deeper analysis.

4. Using Web Interface to Capture

When I wrote this in 2024, web recording felt finicky: sometimes it would not connect, and sometimes it complained that ADB was already using the device. I preferred recording from the command line and using the page to prepare a config. The historical screenshots remain below, with current connection options explained alongside them.

Version update: the official CHANGELOG records a rewritten recording page in v49.0 (2025-01-06). The stable UI inspected read-only for this update was v58.3-11fbaed83, with multiple transports. This is not a device-connection reliability test.

Open Record new trace, select Android, and choose a transport. WebUsb requires browser support and exclusive access to the device’s USB interface, which can conflict with a local adb server. ADB + WebSocket uses a local bridge and can coexist with other adb tools. Follow the connection instructions, authorize the phone, configure the trace, and start recording. Do not indiscriminately terminate existing ADB sessions because an old screenshot mentioned killing adb; generating a config for command-line capture is also an option.

The old entry was called Recording command. In the inspected v58.3 UI it is Cmdline instructions, with separate Shell and textproto sections. Copy or download the configuration for repeatable command-line capture.

Choose sources for the problem instead of following the old screenshot’s suggestion to select everything. UI jank often needs CPU scheduling, relevant atrace categories, and the target app. FrameTimeline additionally requires Android 12+ and the android.surfaceflinger.frametimeline source. Logcat is optional. More sources increase overhead, data volume, and the risk of losing events.

Enable Stack sampling when call stacks are needed. It depends on traced_perf, device support, and target-process permissions. User builds generally require profileable or debuggable targets; the screenshot does not grant access to arbitrary system processes. The current CPU profiling tutorial describes a newer Android 15+ workflow; older devices need configurations compatible with their recording components. Samples are discrete observations, not a record of every function call, and frequency, unwinding, and missing symbols affect the result.

Feel free to explore the other options. Later posts will cover those data sources and what they look like in a trace.

Extracting Parameters from Web Interface

Current Cmdline instructions can download textproto directly. When using an older page’s complete Shell snippet, retain only the configuration: remove the leading adb shell ..., the <<EOF wrapper, and the final standalone EOF, while keeping the config’s own braces. The old screenshot is followed by a copyable basic config below.

Save this as config.pbtx for a short UI scenario on Android 12+, replacing com.example.app with the target package. The 32 MB ring buffer is an example: old events are overwritten when it fills, so retaining all 10 seconds is not guaranteed under every workload.

This collects scheduling events, app/system annotations, initial process information, and FrameTimeline. It does not include logcat, heap profiling, or complete call stacks. After recording, confirm that the scenario lies in the retained window and the required sources produced events, then check trace-loss statistics. A file opening successfully does not prove complete recording. Long traces require separate file-streaming and capacity settings; see TraceConfig.

Reference Documents

  1. https://perfetto.dev/docs/getting-started/system-tracing
  2. https://perfetto.dev/docs/concepts/config
  3. https://developer.android.com/tools/releases/platform-tools
  4. https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/nsqc51L5T4mrTUVsPgkj6A
  5. https://juejin.cn/post/7344983784549400613
  6. https://cs.android.com/android/platform/superproject/main/+/main:external/perfetto/test/configs/

About Me && Blog

Here is a personal introduction and related links. I hope to communicate more with my peers. When three people walk together, there must be one who can be my teacher!

  1. Blogger Personal Introduction: Contains personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. This Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.
  3. Personal Collection of Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Know: Welcome everyone to recommend themselves and others (WeChat private chat is fine)
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: Closed in 2026; the page remains as a historical introduction.

One person can go faster, a group of people can go further

entry.title: Android Perfetto Series 1: Introduction to Perfetto
entry.content:
This is the first article in the Perfetto series. It mainly provides a brief introduction to the Perfetto tool, including its history, development, and what Perfetto can do.

Android documentation labels Systrace a legacy tool and recommends Perfetto on Android 10+. By the time I wrote this article, Perfetto had largely replaced Systrace in my daily work, and the OPPO and vivo teams I encountered were also migrating. Newcomers facing its complex interface asked me to revisit the Systrace articles using Perfetto.

Technical review: 2026-10-14. The original article and screenshots date from 2024. The updates below distinguish Android 10/11/12 data-source requirements and Perfetto v48.0/v49.0 UI changes from that earlier experience. Available data still depends on the device, recording configuration, and tool version.

Table of Contents

  • Perfetto Series Catalog
  • Main Content
  • Why Performance Analysis Needs a God’s View
  • Introduction to Perfetto
  • Where it’s not as good as Systrace
  • Reference Documents
  • About Me && Blog

Paul Graham said: “Either give a lot of people something they kind of want, or give a small number of people something they really want.“ Perfetto is actually something that a small number of people really want, so let’s start writing. Please join the discussion. If you spot an error or an unclear explanation, let me know so I can fix it before it misleads someone.

In this series, I want to use Perfetto to look at how apps, the Framework, and Linux work together. If you have read plenty of source code and performance articles but still find the flow hard to follow, try placing that code on a trace timeline.

If you haven’t seen the Systrace series yet, here is the portal:

  1. Systrace Series Catalog: Systematically introduced the use of Systrace, the predecessor of Perfetto, and used Systrace to learn and understand the basic rules of Android performance optimization and Android system operation.
  2. Personal Blog: Personal blog, mainly content related to Android, and also put some content related to life and work.

The About Me page has WeChat group information for discussing Perfetto and Android development.

Main Content

I started the Systrace series in 2019 and gradually wrote more than 20 posts: basic usage, how system modules appear in a trace, and practical cases involving startup speed and smoothness. Together, they covered the basic Systrace workflows for new app and system developers. I also met many people through the blog; by the time I wrote this, we had six discussion groups. Thank you for all that support.

Android documentation labels Systrace a legacy tool and recommends Perfetto on Android 10+. By the time I wrote this article, Perfetto had largely replaced Systrace in my daily work, and the OPPO and vivo teams I encountered were also migrating. Newcomers facing its complex interface asked me to revisit the Systrace articles using Perfetto.

I used to think the Systrace series was enough. Here are the reasons I later shared on Knowledge Planet for writing a Perfetto series:

  1. In the teams I encountered in 2024, many OPPO and vivo colleagues were already using Perfetto to record and analyze traces. New readers often started with Perfetto; if I kept writing only about Systrace, I would miss them.
  2. The source code referenced by the Systrace series is now old. Later articles will discuss newer versions, including Android 17 (API 37), but each article is bounded by its stated source tag, device, and trace. Historical cases are not automatically revalidated on a newer system. Practical capture and analysis start at Android 12; that is not Perfetto’s minimum supported version.
  3. I had only scratched the surface of some advanced Perfetto features. Writing the series would give me a reason to learn them properly.
  4. Perfetto is a very powerful tool. Behind it is the entire Android + Linux system. So when writing this series, the focus should be on the Android + Linux behind it, rather than just being limited to the Perfetto tool. Tools are just our way of observing Android + Linux. Understanding the laws of the entire Android system operation, thinking about its operating principles, discovering problems through tools, and thinking about the essence through problems are meaningful to developers.
  5. Perfetto’s official documentation still does not cover many contents related to Android system operation. I can supplement this part; in addition, the official documentation is in English, and Chinese blogs can supplement this aspect.
  6. If the series turns out well, I can also use it for a Google DevFest talk.

Paul Graham said: “Either give a lot of people something they kind of want, or give a small number of people something they really want.“ Perfetto is actually something that a small number of people really want, so let’s start writing. Please join the discussion. If you spot an error or an unclear explanation, let me know so I can fix it before it misleads someone.

Why Performance Analysis Needs a God’s View

Why do we need tools like Systrace and Perfetto? Android performance depends on the app, system services, Linux, hardware, vendor policies, and the conditions on the device. Load, memory pressure, heat, OS versions, and usage patterns all matter. Looking at one app or module may not explain the problem; we need to see how these parts interact.

Perfetto can place several data sources on a shared timeline, helping us investigate the following stages:

  1. How Input events flow
  2. How every frame of the App you are using goes from generation to screen display
  3. Real-time frequency, load, core placement, wake-up of cpu, etc.
  4. How various Apps in the system are running
  5. ….

App and platform developers can add trace points to important code paths. A system-wide view still depends on available data sources, TraceConfig settings, permissions, and data loss. Ordinary scheduling events show when a thread ran on a CPU; they do not necessarily expose the scheduler’s complete reason for choosing that CPU. An absent event does not prove that the activity never happened.

Also, to illustrate the complexity of performance optimization, you can look at the description of performance in the book Systems Performance, specifically the methodology, which fits the theme of this article very well. I also strongly recommend that all students engaged in performance optimization keep this book as a frequent reading methodology book: System performance engineering is a challenging field due to many reasons, including the fact that system performance is subjective, complex, and often multi-problem.

Performance is Subjective

  1. Software fault investigation often has a relatively clear correctness criterion: does the behavior meet expectations, and can the failure be reproduced? A bug does not always produce an error log, and an error message alone may not explain its cause.
  2. Unlike this, performance is often subjective. When starting to address performance issues, the judgment of whether the problem exists may be vague. The same is true when the problem is fixed. Performance considered “bad” by one user may be considered “good” by another user.

The System is Complex

  1. In addition to subjectivity, performance engineering, as a challenging discipline, is not only because of the complexity of the system, but also because we often lack a clear starting point for analysis regarding performance. Sometimes we just start with guessing, for example, blaming the network, and performance analysis must verify whether this is a correct direction.
  2. Performance problems may arise from complex interconnections between subsystems, even if these subsystems perform well in isolation. It may also be due to cascading failure, which refers to a faulty component causing performance problems in other components. To understand these problems, you must clarify the relationship between components and understand how they cooperate.
  3. Bottlenecks are often complex and interconnected in unexpected ways. Fixing a problem may just push the bottleneck to other places in the system, resulting in the overall performance of the system not improving as expected.
  4. In addition to the complexity of the system, the complex nature of the production environment load may also lead to performance problems. It is difficult to reproduce such situations in a laboratory environment, or they can only be reproduced intermittently.
  5. Solving complex performance problems often requires a holistic approach. The entire system—including its internal and external interactions—may need to be investigated. This work requires a very wide range of skills, which is generally unlikely to be concentrated in one person, which drives performance engineering to become a varied and intellectually challenging job.

Multiple Problems May Coexist

  1. Finding a performance problem point is often not the problem itself. In complex software, there are usually multiple problems.
  2. Another difficulty in performance analysis: the real task is not to find the problem, but to identify the problem or identify which problems are the most important.
  3. To do this, performance analysis must quantify the importance of the problem. Some performance problems may not apply to your workload or only apply to a very small extent. Ideally, you should not only quantify the problem, but also estimate the speed increase brought by each problem fix. This information is especially useful when management reviews the reasons for engineering or operation and maintenance resource overhead.
  4. There is an indicator that is very suitable for quantifying performance, that is, latency.

Introduction to Perfetto

Perfetto is an open-source suite for recording and analyzing performance data, with collection components, Trace Processor, and a web UI. It can correlate enabled system and application events and query them with SQL. Memory analysis includes heapprofd allocation sampling (Android 10+) and ART heap reference graphs (Android 11+). Allocation profiles attribute memory to call stacks; reference graphs describe object retention, without object contents or allocation call stacks. On production user builds, heapprofd requires a debuggable or profileable target app. Ordinary system traces do not automatically contain these data.

Recording, analysis, and visualization can be used separately. Cross-platform support is component-specific: Android/Linux system data sources are not available on every platform. Consult the official repository and releases for development activity. Android recommends Perfetto, but its display and analysis behavior is not identical to every legacy Systrace feature.

Existing Systrace files can be opened in Perfetto UI, which supports importing the ftrace/ATrace data embedded in Systrace HTML. This does not reproduce every legacy viewer feature or analysis result. The Legacy UI link in the old screenshots was part of that interface; do not depend on current versions always providing a one-click fallback.

The figure below is the architecture diagram of Perfetto. It can be seen that Perfetto contains three major blocks:

  1. Record traces: The data capture module. It can be seen that the captured content and sources are very rich, involving Java, Native, and Linux, which is much richer than Systrace.

  2. Analyze traces: Mainly the trace analysis module, including Trace parsing, SQL query, Metrics analysis, etc. This part has a dedicated command line tool provided, which is convenient for everyone to call directly or call in the tool chain.

  3. Visualize Traces: Trace presentation, capture, etc.

These modules will be introduced in detail in subsequent articles in the series.

Perfetto’s Core Advantages and Highlights:

Based on daily use and the documentation, the main capabilities fall into the following groups:

  1. Long-running recording: background services record Protobuf data. Configure buffer sizes, write periods, and file limits for the intended duration. A ring buffer overwrites older events; keeping a session alive does not preserve its entire history. See configuration and data-loss analysis.
  2. Multiple data sources: Linux ftrace is one system-tracing source. ATrace, SDK Track Event, and memory profiling have their own configuration and support requirements; Perfetto as a whole is not limited to ftrace.
  3. Recording and triggers: web, command-line, and Android developer-option workflows can start recording. Triggers control configured sessions; they are not an independent data source.
  4. Analysis and visualization:
    • Trace Processor exposes SQL tables and views after parsing a trace. Conversion to a SQLite file is not a prerequisite, and a raw Protobuf trace is not a SQLite database.
    • The Python API can turn query results into pandas DataFrames. Their validity still depends on recording completeness and query definitions.
    • Browser memory limits can prevent large traces from loading. Use a native local Trace Processor with the web UI when needed; host memory remains a constraint.
    • Pinned tracks, Binder flows, scheduler wake-up relationships, and critical-path analysis require the relevant events. A thread’s waker is not the same question as what woke the device from suspend.
    • Function call stacks require suitable profiling data and symbols. Nested trace slices are not a complete sampled call stack; allocation stacks and ART object reference graphs are also different views.
  5. Versioned components: the UI, Trace Processor, SDK, and device recording components may have different versions. Record the tool version, system version, and TraceConfig when comparing SQL results or reports.

SQL deserves a closer look. Trace Processor exposes tables and views for repeatable analysis. The historical screenshot below illustrates filtering by duration, process, and scheduling state (image from Kernel Artisan).

Limits of these historical queries: OPF: is a trace-specific name, not a standard system event. The lock query counts name-derived identifiers and temporal nesting; this does not establish the number of threads contending for one object. Check fields against the current schema (for example, slice.id), exclude unfinished slices with negative dur, and check scheduling coverage before reuse. Unknown Running time must not be filled with zero.

The documentation also provides SQL and result examples. The screenshot below shows an earlier FrameTimeline query.

When the boss asks for before-and-after numbers, SQL lets you run the same query on both traces and turn the results into a chart. That makes preparing a report much easier. A report still needs the device, scenario, sample count, time window, and recording completeness; one trace alone does not establish a repeatable improvement percentage.

Where it’s not as good as Systrace

Vsync-App is not so intuitive

In the 2024 screenshots below, Perfetto lacks the Vsync-App guide lines that span the Systrace view. Readers accustomed to that presentation may need time to adjust:

In Perfetto, you can Pin Vsync-App to the top to see Vsync information

In Systrace, Vsync runs through the entire Trace in the form of a vertical line, which is easy to identify:

Vsync-App is a useful timing reference, but it cannot by itself identify which frame or process caused jank. FrameTimeline provides additional frame-level evidence. On Android 12+, a trace containing FrameTimeline data can show Expected and Actual Timeline tracks. See the official documentation.

  1. Expected Timeline: the slice represents the app’s rendering budget for a frame. It begins when the Choreographer callback was expected to run, not when execution actually began.
  2. Actual Timeline: it starts when Choreographer#doFrame or AChoreographer_vsyncCallback actually runs and ends at the later of GPU completion and posting the frame to SurfaceFlinger. This interval includes waiting and GPU work; it is neither CPU running time nor the complete interval until the app’s frame reaches the display.

Compare these tracks to select frames for investigation, then inspect Jank Type, Present Type, and Prediction Type. Red attributes jank to that process; yellow marks an app frame affected by SurfaceFlinger jank, while light green indicates high latency. Do not count only red frames. Blue indicates a dropped frame: the old legend only describes SurfaceFlinger, while the app case can involve a UI state update not reaching RenderThread in time. Check prediction validity and the relevant surface as well; article 7 develops this further.

The diagram shows why both GPU completion and posting time affect Actual Timeline. Its duration is not the sum of CPU and GPU execution time.

SurfaceFlinger has corresponding tracks for composition and presentation. Their durations should not be read as app main-thread time.

Folding function is relatively bad, wasteful of screen

The following preserves my experience with the 2024 UI: pinning several threads on a widescreen monitor left little space below, and tracks with deeply nested slices made it painful. At the time I found folding less convenient than in Systrace. These nested slices are not necessarily sampled function call stacks.

Solution:

  1. Pin fewer key threads (where’s the fun in that?)
  2. Turn the monitor upright (and lose width instead)

We eventually found a setup I loved: LG’s 16:18 DualUp monitor. It felt made for reading Perfetto traces. I had already talked colleagues into getting three for the office.

  1. If the budget allows: LG 28MQ780 - 3599
  2. A cheaper alternative: Innocn 28C1Q - 2999

Version update: the official CHANGELOG records the workspace API with nested tracks and multiple workspaces in v48.0 (2024-10-11), followed by the workspace switcher and track-moving menu in v49.0 (2025-01-06). Grouping the tracks needed for a task into a workspace can reduce dependence on pinned tracks. The monitor experience and prices above are historical 2024 observations, not current pricing or purchasing advice.

Reference Documents

  1. Perfetto Github Repository
  2. Perfetto Official Documentation
  3. Kernel Artisan - Perfetto Advanced

About Me && Blog

Here is a personal introduction and related links. I hope to communicate more with my peers. When three people walk together, there must be one who can be my teacher!

  1. Blogger Personal Introduction: Contains personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. This Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.
  3. Personal Collection of Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Know: Welcome everyone to recommend themselves and others (WeChat private chat is fine)
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: Closed in 2026; the page remains as a historical introduction.

One person can go faster, a group of people can go further

entry.title: Android Perfetto Series Catalog
entry.content:
Perfetto has largely replaced the old Systrace workflow in my daily work. Android recommends Perfetto for Android 10 and later and describes the Systrace command-line tool as legacy. Developers new to Android performance analysis often find Perfetto’s interface and features complex, so this series revisits the subjects of my Systrace articles through Perfetto.

Technical review: 2026-10-14. The motivation below dates from the series launch in 2024; the catalog has since expanded. Practical examples mainly start with Android 12, which is not Perfetto’s minimum supported Android version. Check each article’s source tag, device version, and data-source requirements; historical examples are not all Android 17 measurements.

I used to think the Systrace series was enough. Here are the reasons I later shared on Knowledge Planet for writing a Perfetto series:

  1. In my work around 2024, I saw teams at OPPO and vivo using Perfetto to capture and analyze traces, with many newcomers starting there. If I kept writing only about Systrace, I would miss those readers. This is a personal observation, not a survey of every team or its current tooling.
  2. The Systrace series references older code. This series continues to add newer behavior; Android 17 (API 37) releases and source tags are available references. Each analysis still depends on its stated AOSP tag, device implementation, and trace. New API documentation is not proof of an older device’s implementation.
  3. I haven’t fully mastered all of Perfetto’s high-level features myself. Re-writing this series helps me reinforce my own understanding.
  4. I want to spend time on the Android and Linux behavior we can observe through Perfetto, not just on the tool’s buttons. What is the system doing, why is it doing that, and how does that explain the problem we are investigating?
  5. Official Perfetto documentation still misses many nuances of Android system operation. I can fill in some of those gaps and explain them in Chinese.
  6. If the series turns out well, I can also use it for a Google DevFest talk.

Paul Graham once said: “Either provide something most people want a little, or something a few people want a lot.“ Perfetto is exactly what a dedicated minority “wants a lot.” Let’s begin. Please feel free to share feedback or point out errors so I can keep this as accurate as possible.

In this series, I want to use Perfetto to look at how apps, the Framework, and Linux work together. If you have read plenty of source code and performance articles but still find the flow hard to follow, try placing that code on a trace timeline.

Perfetto Series Catalog

  1. Android Perfetto Series Catalog
  2. Android Perfetto Series 1: Introduction to Perfetto
  3. Android Perfetto Series 2: Capturing Perfetto Traces
  4. Android Perfetto Series 3: Familiarizing with the Perfetto View
  5. Android Perfetto Series 4: Opening Large Traces via Command Line
  6. Android Perfetto Series 5: Choreographer-based Rendering Flow
  7. Android Perfetto Series 6: Why 120Hz? Advantages and Challenges
  8. Android Perfetto Series 7: MainThread and RenderThread Deep Dive
  9. Android Perfetto Series 8: Understanding Vsync and Performance Analysis
  10. Android Perfetto Series 9: Interpreting CPU Information
  11. Android Perfetto Series 10: Binder Scheduling and Lock Contention
  12. Android Perfetto Series 11: PerfettoSQL, Trace Processor and Regression Detection
  13. Android Perfetto Series 12: Trace Dataflow and Data Loss
  14. Android Perfetto Series 13: Perfetto SDK, Track Event and App Field Traces
  15. Android Perfetto Series 14: heapprofd and Memory Profiling
  16. Android Perfetto Series 15: Boot Traces and Long-running Field Tracing
  17. Android Perfetto Series 16: GPU, Power Counters and Hardware Bottlenecks
  18. Android Perfetto Series 17: Scenario Automation and Platform Tracing
  19. Android Perfetto Series 18: Input Response Latency
  20. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto Basics and Case Studies
  21. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto: Trace Graph Types - AOSP, WebView, Flutter + OEM System Optimization

Systrace Series

Systrace is a legacy toolchain, but the old series’ Framework flows, thread states, Binder waits, Vsync, SurfaceFlinger, and CPU scheduling remain useful subjects, subject to each article’s version boundaries. From Android 10, the system tracing utility saves Perfetto-format traces. .perfetto-trace is a common extension for protobuf trace data; renaming a file does not convert its format. Perfetto UI and Trace Processor provide visualization, parsing, and SQL analysis. See the official system tracing overview for legacy HTML/ctrace support and conversion.

Perfetto continues to support android.os.Trace, NDK ATrace, and internal ATRACE instrumentation, while ftrace supplies kernel events. Data sources must be enabled in TraceConfig; visibility also depends on OS version, permissions, and device support. An absent event does not prove that the behavior never occurred: it may have been disabled, unsupported, or lost during recording.

If you are coming from the Systrace series, use this mapping:

Systrace topicPerfetto content to read first
Tool introduction, capture flow, UI operationsPerfetto 1: Introduction, Perfetto 2: Capturing traces, Perfetto 3: Perfetto View
Why 60 fps and high refresh ratePerfetto 6: Why 120Hz?
Choreographer, main thread, RenderThread, jank analysisPerfetto 5: Choreographer rendering flow, Perfetto 7: MainThread and RenderThread
Vsync, SurfaceFlinger, Triple BufferPerfetto 8: Vsync and performance analysis
CPU frequency and Running/Runnable/Sleep statesPerfetto 9: CPU information
Binder, lock contention, and SystemServer waitsPerfetto 10: Binder scheduling and lock contention
Trace Processor, SQL, and batch regressionPerfetto 11: PerfettoSQL, Trace Processor, and Regression Detection
App instrumentation, Track Event, and field tracesPerfetto 13: Perfetto SDK, Track Event, and App Field Tracing
Boot traces and long-running field capturesPerfetto 15: Boot and Long-running Field Tracing
Input response and first-frame feedbackPerfetto 18: Input Response Latency
  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics: Prerequisites
  3. Systrace Basics: Why 60 fps?
  4. Systrace Basics: Interpreting SystemServer
  5. Systrace Basics: Interpreting Input
  6. Systrace Basics: Vsync Generation and Mechanism
  7. Systrace Basics: Vsync-App - Choreographer Rendering Explained

  15. Systrace Smoothness in Practice 3: Common Questions
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Practice 1: Understanding Principles

  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Practice 3: Extended Knowledge
  19. CPU Thread State Analysis 1: Runnable
  20. CPU Thread State Analysis 2: Running
  21. CPU Thread State Analysis 3: Sleep & Uninterruptible Sleep

About Me & My Blog

Here is a quick introduction and relevant links. I welcome communication with fellow developers!

  1. Author Introduction: Includes my WeChat and community links.
  2. Blog Content Map: A navigation guide to this blog.
  3. Android Performance Optimization Skills and Tools: A curated collection of excellent articles.
  4. The Performance archive: The community closed in 2026 and no longer accepts new members.

“If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”

entry.title: Reflections on 2023: Health, Career, and the Future
entry.content:
I’m taking the easy way out this year and using a template to look back at the past year through several lenses: Health/Fitness, Work/Career, Friendship/Social, Personal Life/Family, Learning/Knowledge Management, Travel/Culture, Interests/Creativity, Emotions/Mental State, and Finances.

This post is more of a personal record for 2023 than a formal summary, and my writing isn’t anything special. But as I’ve realized, if you don’t record things, they slowly fade away. I hope that whenever I look back at this post, I’ll remember 2023 as a vibrant year—filled with unforgettable moments, low points, visits from distant friends, and journeys through mountains and rivers. I also want to remember the things I did poorly so I can do better next time, and to remind myself to fight the laziness that often prevents me from following through on what I know is right.

Feel free to read along and have a laugh at my expense.

Health / Fitness

This year was dominated by cycling, thanks to a company-wide competition and the completion of the Chengdu Green Belt last year. I bought a used Merida Reacto 4000 on Xianyu at the start of the year and committed to riding. My goal was to complete one loop (97km) in under 3 hours, with a stretch goal of 2 hours 50 minutes. I hadn’t expected to meet both goals, but I did: 35 loops in total, with a best time of 2h 47min, and first place in the company competition. I also got my wife into cycling, and we rode a few loops together.

My chronic issues—asthma and rhinitis—didn’t see much improvement. However, the best news came at the end of the year: after being hospitalized for 4 days due to pneumonia and the flu, the IV treatment actually cured the loss of taste caused by my rhinitis! My blood oxygen also returned to 96% (it was consistently below 94%, which was causing me significant anxiety). Chengdu’s air quality is… challenging, to say the least; even doctors at Huaxi Hospital shook their heads at it. Something to consider if you’re thinking of moving here.

For the new year, I’m targeting both cycling and running. I’ve signed up for a half-marathon in Dujiangyan and hope to finish. Weight loss remains a priority—watching what I eat and getting moving. Stay hungry before bed!

Work / Career

Work was a bit rocky this year. I was involved in many disparate things, and several projects never made it into use. Looking back, I think it was a lack of planning and execution on my part. Still, I gained a lot of knowledge, researched many technical solutions, and collaborated with customers on several projects. There are plenty of people at the company who know much more than I do. I need to stay humble and learn from them.

AI was obviously the big story this year. AI has integrated into both company and personal workflows—boosting productivity and creating new tools. While it hasn’t completely disrupted our industry yet, we all know that day is coming fast.

“Once a new technology rolls over you, if you’re not part of the steamroller, you’re part of the road.” —— Stewart Brand

Friendship / Social

The most significant social event was traveling from Chengdu to Shenzhen for the GDG DevFest. I caught up with old friends, met people from my online groups, and indulged in my favorite claypot porridge and beef hotpot. Hearing the keynote speeches from various GDEs was incredibly rewarding.

The rest of my social life was mostly cycling with colleagues. Nothing gets you pushing through the Green Belt at midnight on a Friday like the promise of hotpot or spicy skewers afterward. @James @Hanzo @天宇 @宣总 @王 @陈大 @祥大 @果哥 @鹏哥 — let’s keep pushing each other in the new year!

@福滕 and @小陈 had a baby. @周岩 got the keys to his new place ahead of schedule (still no girlfriend, though—just teasing!). @老崔 and @和泉 have both settled down in Shenzhen.

Most of my daily communication happens in my WeChat groups, mostly with Android App and System developers. We have about 2,000 members across 5 groups (though 90% are dedicated lurkers). I’ve met many industry experts through these groups. The phone industry is small; more friends means more places to stay—kidding! There’s always someone who knows more than I do. Less talking, more learning.

My biggest takeaway: communicating with people on the same “frequency” saves a lot of effort.

Personal Life / Family

Little Orange is almost three now, and her mom has moved to a new team doing the same work as me: system performance optimization. My biggest wish is for my family to stay happy, healthy, and safe. Due to various reasons, I didn’t spend as much time with my family as I wanted this year, and several travel plans were shelved. In the new year, I need to be more efficient so I can dedicate more time to them.

I read a blog post recently that really resonated with me regarding the ultimate goal of life:

I want to enrich my experiences, do things I’ve never done, and see sights I’ve never seen. I hope one day I can spend my time on myself, not on work, and not on unimportant people or things. More specifically, I hope my family is healthy and safe, with love and companionship. I hope to travel all of China and the world, eat food I’ve never tasted, and see scenes I’ve never envisioned.

Thinking about this brings me clarity. I know what I’m pursuing in this life; the rest isn’t that important. So, how do I get there? I need time, and I need money.

From now on, everything I do revolves around this goal. As long as something moves me toward my ultimate life goal, no matter how hard it is, I must do it. Yes, must. No room for negotiation.

Learning / Knowledge Management

Learning was a bit of a failure this year. My English studies stalled until I picked them up again this month. Technical learning was mostly passive reading without enough writing or deep reflection. I have many unread books on my shelf. I only posted a few blog articles. I know the Feynman technique—using output to drive input—but I haven’t overcome my procrastination yet.

I did develop a good habit at work: using Typora to record daily work, technical projects, research, and bugs. As I switch to Microsoft Loop, I plan to be even more detailed in my logs and reflections and share more with the team so we can learn together. (I talked big about this at the start of the year and still hadn’t followed through by December.)

From my own experience, there are three obstacles to learning:

  1. Finding High-Quality Input: In the age of information overload, finding good sources is key. You need to curate a list of great blogs, GitHub repos, newsletters, and tech teams. (My article Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows is my attempt at this; feel free to recommend others!)
  2. Focusing and Diving Deep: Short-form content is destroying our attention spans. Sitting down to read and think through a deep article or book is becoming harder. We have to train ourselves to step away from social media and regain our focus.
  3. Overcoming Procrastination: We often say we know the “how” but aren’t doing it. Procrastination is a major factor. I recently saw a tip on fighting procrastination: The key is that we procrastinate because something is unfamiliar and we want to avoid it, which creates fear and anxiety. The way to defeat it is to mentally walk through the task first—visualize the steps and details—to get your neurons firing, then act immediately.

I also want to share a few points from a video I saw early in the year called “Life is a Journey, and I too am a Traveler”:

  1. Don’t limit yourself; move quickly into industries with more potential.
  2. Learn aggressively from the best in the field.
  3. Expand your horizons and perspective.
  4. Embrace change, or even seek it out.
  5. Keep doing the work to build a long-term reputation.
  6. Improve your “fault tolerance.”

Travel / Culture

I visited four places this year: Siguniang Mountain, Xiamen, Yantai+Weihai, and Leshan.

  1. Xiamen: A team trip. We saw the sea, ate satay noodles, and ginger duck. The weather there really makes me jealous. You can cycle along the coastal road, and there are walking trails in the city too—unfortunately, I didn’t get to try them.
  2. Yantai + Weihai: Went to @小婉’s wedding, then back to my alma mater to see a few teachers and old classmates. We got our Korean food and seafood fix. The coastal road was as beautiful as ever, and so was the sunset on the beach behind campus.
  3. Siguniang Mountain: Drove all day to Western Sichuan. We crossed a pass at 4,800m. My wife and baby had altitude sickness, so we didn’t stay long. But the snow-covered scenery the next morning was breathtaking. I have a video of it here: https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1H84y1Q7oM. It’s definitely worth another visit.
  4. Leshan: Visited the Giant Buddha and enjoyed the local snacks (sweet-skinned duck and fried skewers are amazing).

Traveling with a baby is a lot of work but so worth it. They see new things, make new friends, and try new foods. We’ll keep doing it in 2024.

Interests / Creativity

Finally, something lighthearted! My main interest this year was cycling. I bought a DJI Action 4 to record my rides. I’m no pro—it’s mostly just continuous shots. Creativity is definitely a talent!

Emotions / Mental State

I’m doing well, though I have some minor anxiety. Much of my well-being comes from my family’s support—having my parents help with the baby and having a spouse who also works in IT and supports my decisions. Chengdu has all sorts of food, and plenty of places to go: western Sichuan, old towns, Dujiangyan, Qingcheng Mountain; Chongqing isn’t far either. Tianfu New Area and the High-Tech Zone don’t feel particularly unwelcoming to outsiders. I’m comfortable here—except for the smog, which gets a definite negative score.

I’ll keep this mindset in 2024: stay positive and get enough sleep.

Finances

We still have a significant mortgage, and most of our salary goes to the bank. We don’t have much income beyond our day jobs, which is a source of anxiety for me—any job loss would create immediate financial pressure. My goal is to manage our money better and control spending. I recently read a breakdown of the financial habits of the poor, the middle class, and the wealthy:

  • The poor struggle to make ends meet, with income consumed by basic needs.
  • The middle class are stuck in the “rat race,” working for decades to pay off bills and loans.
  • The wealthy acquire and hold onto quality assets, creating a “money → asset → money” cycle.

My takeaway was to hold quality assets. As I understand it, those could be property or knowledge. Given my situation, I’ve decided to restart my Knowledge Planet (intro here: The Performance Knowledge Planet Intro). I hadn’t promoted it elsewhere, only introduced it on the blog. I believe the Feynman and Public Learning techniques are the best ways to learn, and the Knowledge Planet lets me share my daily thoughts, cases, progress, and tools. If that knowledge helps someone else, it’s worth it.

The Final Three

Proudest Achievement

Probably the thing I’m proudest of this year is teaching graduate students for three days at the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC). I got the opportunity through a company partnership. Preparing meant studying the slides @鹏哥 had made the year before, then working through each topic before getting up to teach. It was my first time, and thankfully I didn’t make a mess of it.

It looks like I may be teaching again this year. I won’t be quite as nervous this time! I need to update the content and optimize the delivery. Explaining Android from top to bottom is never easy.

Greatest Challenge

Beyond work, my biggest challenge is English speaking. There were several times this year where I struggled, which has motivated me to double down on learning. This is a top priority for 2024.

Goals and Wishes for Next Year

  1. Spend more time with family, do new things, and visit new places.
  2. Do a public presentation at a Google DevFest-level event.
  3. Travel abroad once.
  4. Grow the Knowledge Planet community.
  5. Keep fit and complete a marathon.
  6. Read more books.
  7. Update the blog every 2 weeks and finish the Perfetto series.
  8. Record more videos.

My writing is limited, but I’ll close with a quote:

I hope you can figure out “what kind of life you want to live.” Once you have that standard, every decision you make will become incredibly easy.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Performance Considerations in Operating System Design
entry.content:
This article was originally written by Yingyun for my Knowledge Planet. Since the Planet has closed, I am publishing this series on OS performance design here.

Yingyun is a veteran performance optimization expert with deep insights into system-level tuning, having worked at several major smartphone manufacturers. He is currently active in our community. If you have any questions or feedback, feel free to join our WeChat group.

1. The Genesis

This starts a new series exploring the various considerations in OS architectural design. In reality, these principles apply to the design of any large-scale software.

My knowledge and experience have limits, and these views are subjective. There will be gaps. I would like to hear other views and see what I have missed.

Technical review: 2026-10-14. This article retains Yingyun’s 2023 views on architectural trade-offs and developer ecosystems. Technical sections clarify kernels, memory reclamation, and background execution with version-specific updates. Platform preferences and forecasts are historical opinions, not comparative measurements of current releases.

From an OS perspective, I believe the core differences between Android and iOS manifest in four areas:

  1. IPC Mechanisms between applications and core services.
  2. Platform Development Environment: programming languages, IDEs, and developer ecosystems.
  3. Application Lifecycle Management: mechanisms and strategies.
  4. Runtime Organization of the kernel and core services.

Why did they make such different strategic decisions? It comes down to the constraints and goals they faced when making those decisions. A software architecture is a collection of decisions made to be the most “correct” for the present and foreseeable future. There is no absolute right or wrong—only choices made under different pressures. If you swapped the contexts of two equally skilled architects, they would likely end up with very similar designs. Architecture is an engineering craft; it follows predictable patterns.

The challenge lies in accurately understanding the organization’s environment and anticipating which factors—testability, release efficiency, security, reliability, performance, or scalability—must be prioritized. An experienced architect knows when to be rigid and when to compromise. Because of the law of diminishing marginal utility, these trade-offs continue throughout the software’s entire lifecycle.

Key takeaways:

  1. Software architecture design varies across different projects based on phase and constraints.
  2. Design decisions are fluid and happen continuously throughout the product lifecycle.

Interestingly, optimization goals often conflict. For example, increasing developer efficiency often comes at the cost of runtime performance. What were the priorities for the original designers of Android and iOS? To answer that, we must first define the relationship between the OS, the application, and the kernel.

2. Mechanism vs. Strategy

The OS and applications form a software stack above the hardware. Kernel code normally runs in a privileged CPU mode for tasks such as scheduling, memory management, and interrupt handling. Many system services run in user space with particular permissions; the entire OS does not run in kernel mode. Apps access these capabilities through system calls, IPC, and framework APIs.

From a user experience (UX) perspective, the hardware, OS, and app are a single entity. If they fail to collaborate, the device feels broken. All three have an obligation to cooperate to satisfy the consumer.

Most modern OSs consist of a Kernel and System Services:

  • macOS/iOS use the XNU kernel, which combines Mach, BSD components, and IOKit. XNU is part of the Darwin operating-system foundation; Darwin is not a kernel formed by placing XNU beside Mach. User-space daemons and frameworks provide further services. See Apple’s XNU overview.
  • Android uses the Linux kernel. SurfaceFlinger is a native system-service process; system_server hosts many Java framework services and also uses native components. Neither is the kernel itself.

While many OSs use similar foundations, the way they are deployed matters. Running an OS is not the same as running it well.

The Art of Unix Programming describes separating policy from mechanism and interfaces from engines. Mechanism provides a capability; policy decides how to use it.

  • Mechanism: Provides the capability (the “How”).
  • Strategy: Decides how to use that capability (the “What”).

The boundary depends on the level of discussion; an entire scheduler or filesystem contains both mechanisms and policies. For example, the kernel provides scheduling and frequency-control facilities, while policy uses workload and foreground/background information to choose resource allocations. A governor selects performance targets and a driver performs supported transitions. DVFS describes voltage/frequency scaling; predicting demand and choosing targets are policy decisions. See Linux CPUFreq’s governor/driver separation.

These decisions can combine application hints, system state, and hardware constraints. A policy that works for a server may not suit a phone or watch, even when both use Linux.

Memory compression is used by many systems, but it is not a requirement for every modern OS. Apple’s WWDC 2018 memory discussion describes the page-based compressor introduced in iOS 7; this does not mean compressing an entire process into one object. Android commonly uses Linux zRAM as a compressed in-memory swap device. Compressed pages still occupy RAM, and compression/decompression costs CPU time. Policies and any additional backing storage depend on the device.

Mechanisms might be similar across OSs, but strategies vary wildly. This depends on the designer’s understanding of the target service. The original desktop analogy concerns background-execution freedom; it does not mean Android was originally a desktop OS. Whether a vendor policy better suits a mobile device depends on its version and workload. Kernel, IPC, runtime, and framework differences also matter; policy is not the only source of performance differences.

One policy can create a problem that needs another policy to address it. Eventually, several policies may depend on one another to work well. Copying just one visible feature from another OS can miss those dependencies and make things worse. That is the kind of “negative optimization” I worry about.

3. Perspective Decisions

Apple’s operating systems share parts of their foundations but differ in background-execution, interaction, and resource policies. Both iOS and macOS support multitasking. iOS places stricter limits on ordinary third-party apps in the background; it does not lack “real” multitasking. The comparison here concerns product policies.

AOSP is Android’s open-source foundation; shipped Android products may also include vendor components and separately licensed services. Manufacturers take AOSP, add hardware-specific code and their own services. Since manufacturers have different business models and user bases, they modify AOSP differently. The market ultimately judges which modification is superior.

So if a boss tells you, “Making a phone is easy—just combine open-source Android with a vendor platform,” my advice is to keep your distance. You could waste years working under that assumption.

AOSP already contains resource and lifecycle policies, including JobScheduler, Doze/App Standby from Android 6.0, lmkd, and the cached apps freezer from Android 11. These policies are not all implemented in GMS. GMS is a separately licensed collection of apps and cloud services outside AOSP. Vendors can further adapt the platform; comparisons need specific devices, versions, and workloads.

The Origin Story

The verifiable timeline is that Apple announced third-party Web apps in June 2007, then released a native iPhone SDK beta and introduced the App Store in March 2008. The SDK included Xcode, Interface Builder, and Instruments. The original article discussed motives through the Jobs biographies, but it supplied no performance evidence that XNU overhead made third-party applications impossible. That causal claim should not be treated as a technical finding.

Contrast this with Android. Andy Rubin’s goal was a truly open system to balance the interests of developers, manufacturers, and carriers. This required using off-the-shelf components to deploy quickly. There was no time for the same level of polishing because they were in a race for survival.

Java offered a mature ecosystem and portability; its exact market rank depends on the measure used. Early Android used Dalvik, while ART became the default in Android 5.0 (API 21). They were not one VM designed together in 2007. Chet Haase’s Androids: The Team That Built the Android Operating System covers the early team. Google’s December 2007 SDK update already describes an Eclipse plugin; public SDK tooling was not limited to command-line tools.

The Power of the IDE

I consider Apple’s developer tools one part of its ecosystem advantage. This is a 2023 assessment, not a current feature or performance ranking of Xcode and Android Studio. LLVM also needs distinct attribution: it originated in research at the University of Illinois, with Apple later contributing; it should not be grouped with Swift and SwiftUI as an entirely Apple-originated project. See the University of Illinois history.

My view when writing in 2023 was that the early Eclipse tools had been adequate, but comparison made their shortcomings harder to ignore. Android Studio was a big improvement, helped by IntelliJ. I still preferred Xcode for application development and performance debugging: finding slow code felt easier, and the process was more pleasant. That is my experience of those tools at the time.
