Designing an OS is a means to an end (profit). To achieve that, you must help developers write good code. Many OSs provide the capability but leave the quality to the developer. Apple’s approach is: “I’ll give you limits, but I’ll also give you the solution to work within them.”

4. Strategy: Overload Protection

Phones run on batteries and mostly rely on passive cooling, with gaming phones and attachable fans as exceptions. Actual heat depends on workload, voltage, frequency, process technology, and power management, so transistor count alone does not tell us how hot a phone will get. The design problem is balancing performance, battery life, and temperature.

More runnable threads can compete for CPU time, and frequent wake-ups can use more energy. Thread count, CPU time, and visible delay are different measures. Desktops and servers have resource controls too; mobile devices place more weight on battery life and heat.

Java OutOfMemoryError, lmkd under system memory pressure, and the Linux kernel OOM killer operate at different levels. A managed-heap allocation failure can throw OOME; an unhandled error can crash the app. This is not simply a system kill when the heap crosses a threshold. lmkd instead considers memory pressure and process importance. Android 10 supports PSI-based detection, and Android 11 revised the reclaim policy.

CPU accounting is not divided by Java versus native code. Android 13 AppProfiler accumulates process user and kernel CPU time; ActivityManagerService applies process-state, observation-window, and threshold checks when handling excessive CPU use. Accounting scope and termination policy are separate; native threads are not inherently excluded.

iOS diagnostics also need to be separated by mechanism rather than described as a list of guaranteed kills:

  • EXC_RESOURCE can concern CPU, wake-ups, memory, or disk writes. NON-FATAL CONDITION means the report did not terminate the process on that occasion.
  • Jetsam reports describe process reclamation under memory and related pressure. vnode-limit concerns system-wide vnode exhaustion; fc-thrashing concerns file-cache thrashing. A background app selected for reclamation need not have caused the pressure.
  • A watchdog termination concerns time limits for responsiveness or lifecycle operations, not the same threshold as a resource exception.
  • Background tasks have API-specific completion and expiration requirements. Thermal protection can also apply, but a warmer device does not mean every app is immediately terminated.

Use the actual diagnostic report, hardware, and OS version to identify a termination. Example limits are not universal quotas across iOS devices and releases.

Vendors add resource controls to protect the user experience. But if the rules are undocumented and developers cannot find out why their app was terminated, how are they supposed to fix it? That is the part I object to.

Android 11 (API 30) added ApplicationExitInfo for historical process-exit information. Coverage varies: not every device reports REASON_LOW_MEMORY, and a trace is not always available. Vendor details can still be incomplete, but it is inaccurate to say developers have no exit information at all.

When developers respond with more tricks to keep their apps alive, cooperation turns into an arms race. Users pay for it. What I would like to see is clear documentation of resource limits, accessible diagnostic information when those limits are enforced, and tools that help developers fix the problem locally. Vendors should set quality requirements and require fixes, with removal from the store as a last step if those requirements are not met.

Manufacturers and developers should be partners. Many of the tools and system capabilities are in the manufacturer’s hands. Blaming developers for everything is a poor starting point.

5. Strategy: Lifecycle Management

Device categories use different lifecycle policies. Desktop apps generally have more scope for continuous execution, but users, crashes, memory pressure, shutdown, and administrative policies can end them. Desktops, servers, and laptops also face power, thermal, and resource limits; an app does not wholly control its lifetime.

Smartwatches make the constraints particularly obvious. Nobody wants a watch that heats their wrist and cannot last a day. Shared system services can do work that would otherwise require many separate apps to remain active.

iOS normally suspends ordinary execution after an app moves to the background. A suspended process does not execute code, but suspension is not termination. The original “five seconds” refers to the applicationDidEnterBackground return deadline, not a universal allowance for every background API. Specific modes and task grants have their own rules.

The original vendor comparison reflects a 2023 observation, not evidence about the following two or three years. AOSP does support freezing: the cached apps freezer has existed since Android 11 (API 30), using a kernel cgroup freezer to stop eligible cached processes while retaining their memory. Android 14 revised related cached-process and broadcast behavior. Enablement, exemptions, and timing depend on the OS, kernel, and device configuration. A process doing supported background work or hosting a foreground service is not necessarily eligible for cached-process freezing.

If an app is suspended in the background, how can it do the work that still needs doing? iOS offers several mechanisms, not one BackgroundTask permission:

  • UIKit beginBackgroundTask requests limited finishing time for important work already started in the foreground. End it promptly and handle expiration; it is not a periodic scheduler.
  • BGAppRefreshTask, available from iOS 13, supports short refresh work scheduled by the system, with up to about 30 seconds of runtime.
  • BGProcessingTask, also from iOS 13, supports longer processing. It can run for minutes but can be interrupted; it has no universal fixed 30-second allowance.
  • iOS/iPadOS 26 adds BGContinuedProcessingTask for user-visible work that starts in the foreground and continues in the background. It must report progress; the user can cancel it, and resource constraints can end it.

See background strategy selection, BGProcessingTask, and BGContinuedProcessingTask. The system chooses scheduling and budgets. There is no fixed daily count for every app or guaranteed periodic interval. Handle expiration, preserve progress, and report completion.

Background work also includes playing music, tracking location, and transferring files. How are those handled? They have distinct capabilities, permissions, and APIs. App Store review governs distribution; on-device OS mechanisms decide execution, suspension, and reclamation. The store is not the runtime scheduler. Memory pressure can terminate suspended processes, but reclamation also includes discarding caches and compressing memory rather than only killing processes.

What if the process has been terminated altogether—how does it run tasks or receive messages then? After system termination, eligible tasks may launch an app in the background, but this is not unconditional. User force-quit also differs from system reclamation; see Apple’s background execution limits. Distinguish system-displayed visible notifications, silent background-update notifications, and VoIP pushes for real incoming calls.

Background notification delivery and wake-up are not guaranteed and can be throttled. Background work is not limited to a notification tap or VoIP. PushKit VoIP notifications serve incoming calls; apps built with the iOS 13 SDK or later must follow the documented CallKit integration, not use them as a general keep-alive channel.

Android background scheduling and push delivery are separate. JobScheduler has provided platform job scheduling since API 21, and WorkManager does not require Google Play services. Neither is simply a GMS feature or permission for permanent process residency.

The standard FCM Android client requires the corresponding Google-services environment. Vendors also offer channels such as HUAWEI Push Kit. Device coverage, delivery, and execution rules differ. Lack of GMS does not technically require permanent app processes, and adding RAM is not the only possible response. My argument remains that vendors and app developers need to build the ecosystem together, instead of each solving only their own part of the problem.

6. Designing for the Future

Specialized accelerators can improve efficiency for particular workloads, as seen in GPUs, media codecs, and machine-learning engines. They do not imply that general-purpose CPUs have stopped improving or that every program benefits equally. DSA (Domain-Specific Architecture) tailors hardware and software interfaces to a domain. The idea that DSA would dominate the next decade’s gains is retained as the author’s 2023 forecast, not a verified prediction.

The 2020 M1 combines CPU, GPU, Neural Engine, and media encode/decode engines. Accelerator benefits depend on the task, format, and software path. A blanket claim that it outperforms Intel chips ignores generations, power limits, and workloads. This article provides no controlled benchmark; the example illustrates architectural specialization rather than a platform ranking.

Improving performance still requires understanding the work, then looking at algorithms, compilers, hardware, and the OS when application-level changes stop being enough. Failures teach you where a design needs support. By an “optimization matrix,” I mean the related pieces that have to work together: the OS, developer tools, cloud services, and the decisions connecting them.

The more I learn, the more work I can see to do. I want to stay aware of what I do not know. That is also why I value Munger’s advice to learn across disciplines. I have not reached the breadth of understanding I am describing; studying outside my specialty and writing down what I learn are ways to work toward it.

About Me && Blog

  1. About the author
  2. Blog content navigation
  3. Android performance resources

entry.title: Can an App Really Do Whatever It Wants With System Permissions?
entry.content:
In 2023, public research described vulnerability exploitation code and dynamically delivered DEX files associated with an Android app. I wanted to see which system capabilities this code attempted to use. I put the original article together in a hurry and did not examine all the code closely. The walkthrough remains here, with corrections based on the screenshots and AOSP source. The original references follow:

  1. Deep Blue Insight: The Most “Unpardonable” Vulnerabilities of 2022
  2. XXX apk embedded privilege escalation code and dynamic delivery dex analysis
  3. History of Android Deserialization Vulnerability Attack and Defense

Security is not my specialty. For background, see History of Android Deserialization Vulnerability Attack and Defense. This article does not reproduce the exploit chain or treat an API call as proof of root access.

Historical case; technical review: 2026-10-14. This article examines material published in 2023, not the current app or every vendor device. The source repository uses APK version 6.49 as an example. This article does not establish each DEX file’s full delivery history, execution identity, device OS version, or security patch level. Screenshots show attempted operations; they do not by themselves prove successful execution, collection of particular user data, or transmission. Vendor interfaces remain historical observations with unverified current applicability.

“System permissions” is not a single switch. Preinstallation, privileged-app status, platform signing, system UID, and root are different conditions. AOSP defines system UID as 1000 and root UID as 0. Operations still depend on Binder/Provider checks, AppOps, file access controls, and SELinux. Reflection and @SystemApi do not grant authority. See AOSP Process (Android 13), privileged permission allowlists, SELinux, and non-SDK interface restrictions.

Serialization and deserialization refer to the process of converting memory data structures into byte streams for network transmission or saving to disk, and then restoring the byte streams to memory objects. In the field of Web security, there have been many deserialization vulnerabilities, such as PHP deserialization, Java deserialization, etc. Because unexpected program logic is triggered during the deserialization process, attackers can use carefully constructed byte streams to trigger and exploit vulnerabilities to ultimately achieve goals such as arbitrary code execution.

This walkthrough examines decompiled screenshots of DEX files from the public repository. Their visible calls and targets fall into the categories below. Some capabilities are available to ordinary apps with user authorization; others require system or vendor privileges. These categories do not establish that every operation succeeded after privilege escalation.

  1. Changes to auto-start and associated-start settings, trying to enable them quietly or by default: another round of outsmarting phone manufacturers.
  2. Enable notification permissions.
  3. Listen to notification content.
  4. Query usage events, configuration files, or identifier fields, with results depending on the interface, permissions, and input.
  5. Modify system settings.
  6. Make some system permission tools for its own use.

The vendor-specific code for Huawei, Oppo, Vivo, and Xiaomi shows how much attention went into their different implementations. Phone manufacturers could learn something by studying this code too, this time to defend against it.

Finally, I also added user comments after this article was published on the WeChat official account, as well as the comment section of the Zhihu answer (the question has been deleted, but I can see it: How to evaluate Pinduoduo suspected of using vulnerabilities to attack user mobile phones, steal competitor software data, and prevent itself from being uninstalled? - Gracker’s answer - Zhihu https://www.zhihu.com/question/587624599/answer/2927765317, 2,471 likes as recorded when writing in 2023) which can be said to be mind-opening (regarding how Apps can do evil).

0. Dex File Information

I collected 37 DEX files from that repository. There were not many, and they were small enough to work through at a steady pace. The repository author describes dynamic delivery and lists historical CDN addresses. This article contains no independent packet capture establishing that every file was delivered or executed at each launch. Android source helps explain system behavior, but actual execution still requires call-chain and runtime evidence.

I used TTDeDroid and its showjar command to inspect DEX files. The original command below records that workflow; the samples were not executed for this review.

showjar 95cd95ab4d694ad8bdf49f07e3599fb3.dex

TTDeDroid defaults to jadx for decompilation. Executor classes are useful entry points, but their helpers and system-service calls also matter.

Decompilation can rename symbols, omit method bodies, or reconstruct control flow incorrectly. The discussion below is limited to visible code. Class names and code paths that report success are not evidence of a successful run.

1. Notification Listening and Notification Permission Related

1.1 Obtain Xiaomi Mobile Phone Notification Content

  1. File: 95cd95ab4d694ad8bdf49f07e3599fb3.dex
  2. Function: Get the user’s Active notifications
  3. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.xm_ntf_info.XMGetNtfInfoExecutor

1. Reflectively get ServiceManager

The screenshot uses reflection to access ServiceManager.getService, then converts the Binder into a service-interface proxy. Obtaining a proxy does not mean the service will authorize subsequent calls.

2. Get detailed content of notifications through NotificationManagerService

The service name is notification, and the result is an INotificationManager proxy; the code does not pass the NotificationManagerService class to getService. It then attempts a hidden getActiveNotifications call, filters by a set of titles, and reads these fields:

  1. Title of the notification
  2. Package name of the App that generated the notification
  3. Notification sending time
  4. key
  5. channelID: the id of the channel this notification posts to.

Maybe some people don’t know what this thing is. The picture below shows a typical notification.

Its code is as follows

Distinguish the similarly named APIs. Public NotificationManager.getActiveNotifications() has returned the caller’s own active notifications since API 23; API 29 also includes notifications it posted as a delegate. The cross-app service interface shown here is different: Android 13’s implementation checks ACCESS_NOTIFICATIONS, AppOps, and user scope. The screenshot does not prove that the sample passed those checks.

Another path is a NotificationListenerService with notification access enabled by the user. This is distinct from an accessibility service. Using a system API does not establish that a plugin is compliant or safe, and an anti-revoke feature cannot necessarily recover every message. Android 15 (API 35) further restricts untrusted listeners’ access to unredacted notifications containing detected one-time passcodes; see Android 15 behavior changes. Old screenshots do not establish behavior on every newer system.

1.2. Open Notification Permissions on Xiaomi Phones (Push)

  1. File: 0fc0e98ac2e54bc29401efaddfc8ad7f.dex
  2. Function: Attempt to enable notifications for a specified package and query its package-level state.
  3. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.xm_permission.XMPermissionExecutor

Handy, from the app’s point of view: ‘Naughty user. These notifications are for your own good. How could you turn them off? Let me quietly switch them back on for you.’

The code attempts setNotificationsEnabledForPackage. The service-side screenshot starts by checking the caller; Android 13 source uses enforceSystemOrSystemUI. Reflection alone cannot force this operation to succeed.
frameworks/base/services/core/java/com/android/server/notification/NotificationManagerService.java

The following query is areNotificationsEnabledForPackage, not another setter call. Its result describes package-level notification state, not visibility of every notification channel or delivery of network push messages.
frameworks/base/services/core/java/com/android/server/notification/NotificationManagerService.java

The other branch is named lbe (previously mistyped as leb) and accesses a MIUI permission-management Provider. Its authorization rules depend on the vendor version. Even that gets its own branch. Thorough!

1.3. Open Notification Permissions on Vivo Phones (Push)

  1. File: 2eb20dc580aaa5186ee4a4ceb2374669.dex
  2. Function: Attempt to enable notifications for an app on Vivo devices. Disabling notification display does not necessarily stop its network push connection.
  3. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.vivo_open_push.VivoOpenPushExecutor

The screenshot attempts the notification-setting call discussed above. Android 13 (API 33) introduced the POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission for posting non-exempt notifications, not receiving network messages. Old vendor behavior is not a general rule for Android 13 and later.

1.4 Open Notification Permissions on Oppo Phones

  1. File: 67c9e686004f45158e94002e8e781192.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.oppo_notification_ut.OppoNotificationUTExecutor

The method did not decompile completely. The visible fragment looks up ColorOS/OPlus notification-management Providers. Enabling notifications remains an inferred target, not a confirmed operation or result.

1.5 Notification Listener

  1. File: ab8ed4c3482c42a1b8baef558ee79deb.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.ud_notification_listener.UdNotificationListenerExecutor

The screenshot has listen and collect branches; the latter sends a collection broadcast and waits for a response. Which notifications and fields it collects depends on helpers not shown here.

Below is the framework’s onNotificationPosted callback declaration. It illustrates the mechanism, not the sample’s complete listener implementation.

I don’t know this part well either. Time to ask my wife, who has spent years working on SystemUI and Launcher… @ShiGong

1.6 App Notification Listener

  1. File: 4f260398-e9d1-4390-bbb9-eeb49c07bf3c.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.notification_listener.NotificationListenerExecutor

The one above is UdNotificationListenerExecutor, this one is NotificationListenerExecutor. What is UD?

This attempts to invoke a notification-listener authorization interface through reflection. @SystemApi identifies an API intended for particular system clients; it does not grant authority. In the Android 13 service, checkNotificationListenerAccess() checks system/phone identity or MANAGE_NOTIFICATION_LISTENERS, followed by user-choice and component checks. The sample’s two-argument call also differs from the three-argument framework screenshot; compatibility depends on the target version.

1.7 Open Notification Listener permissions on Huawei Phones

  1. File: a3937709-b9cc-48fd-8918-163c9cb7c2df.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.hw_notification_listener.HWNotificationListenerExecutor

The screenshot attempts to change notification access through a Huawei Settings Provider. Without that Provider’s versioned implementation and runtime results, acceptance of the request remains unverified.

1.8 Open Notification permissions on Huawei Phones

  1. File: 257682c986ab449ab9e7c8ae7682fa61.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.hw_permission.HwPermissionExecutor

The screenshot attempts to write Huawei/Honor notification-management Provider configuration. A success branch is not runtime proof; Provider authorization and the resulting state still need checking.

2. Backup Status

2.1. App Backup Status Related on HarmonyOS, for keeping alive?

  1. File: 6932a923-9f13-4624-bfea-1249ddfd5505.dex
  2. Function: Backup Related

I spent quite a while looking at this one. The screenshot first passes an IBackupSessionCallback to PackageManagerEx.startBackupSession, then attempts a backup task using the returned session ID. It does not wait for the callback before starting the session. This is a Huawei extension, not evidence of support across all HarmonyOS versions.

Here is the interface description I found at the time. A keep-alive purpose is unconfirmed; backup sessions, file operations, and process-lifetime effects need separate evidence.

2.2. Backup Status Related on Vivo Phones

  1. File: 8c34f5dc-f04c-40ba-98d4-7aa7c364b65c.dex
  2. Function: Backup Related

This image only shows the Binder interface definition of a Vivo backup/restore observer, not a backup invocation or runtime result.

3. File Related

3.1 File and SharedPreferences Operations in the Huawei Sample

  1. File: da03be2689cc463f901806b5b417c9f5.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.hw_get_input.HwGetInputExecutor

The screenshot attempts to copy a file specified by an input parameter, read it as SharedPreferences, and construct a response. The actual path and results are absent, so it does not establish access to keyboard input or all user data. Other apps’ private files remain subject to the application sandbox and other access controls. What did it want these contents for—data analysis? I wondered about that too, but the screenshot does not answer it.

Get SharedPreferences

The code below only creates a temporary .client_slog_cache/temp directory under the app’s own files directory. Calling it “Get slog” was inaccurate: this fragment does not read system logs.

4. User Data

4.1 Obtain data of user using mobile phone

  1. File: 35604479f8854b5d90bc800e912034fc.dex
  2. Function: Query usage events within a time window, then filter and collect package names, class names, timestamps, and event types.
  3. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.usage_event_all.UsageEventAllExecutor

The service name is usagestats, not usagestates. The screenshot calls UsageStatsManager.queryEvents; its result is not a complete installed-app inventory or record of everything the user does. Ordinary apps can also query usage after a user grants usage access in Settings. The Android 13 service checks AppOps and, in its default mode, PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS. A client-side checkPermission call is not the service’s complete authorization decision.

The system defines Activity, foreground-service, screen-state, and other events, but the sample applies filters. An event’s presence in the enum does not establish that it was collected. Queries are limited by their time range and retention; the API documentation says events are kept for a few days and may return null while the user remains locked from Android 11 onward.

The mapping below is UserUsageStatsService.eventToString from Android 13 tag android-13.0.0_r1, previously mislabeled as UsageEvents.java. It is a server-side debugging helper that includes internal events, not a standalone public-SDK example.

4.2 Obtain User Usage Data

  1. File: b50477f70bd14479a50e6fa34e18b2a0.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.usage_event.UsageEventExecutor

This Executor accepts a time range, package names, event types, and a count limit, then packages the query result. Activity resumed/paused events do not mean process launch/exit. Estimating usage duration also requires handling missing events, window boundaries, and multi-window behavior.

4.3 Obtain User Usage Data

  1. File: 1a68d982e02fc22b464693a06f528fac.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.app_usage_observer.AppUsageObserver

This registers an app-usage observer, not a permission. The screenshot attempts the hidden registerAppUsageObserver method. In Android 13, hasObserverPermission() checks system identity, device/profile-owner status, or OBSERVE_APP_USAGE. The client’s API 23 guard does not establish that this hidden method exists on every API 23 device.

5. Widget and icon Related

A reader suggested that a widget resembling an app icon could confuse “remove from home screen” with “uninstall app.” These are different operations. The screenshots below do not show a complete deceptive-uninstallation flow, and I did not encounter the case myself, so this remains a hypothesis.

5.1. Add Widget on Vivo Phones

  1. File: f9b6b139-4516-4ac2-896d-8bc3eb1f2d03.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.vivo_widget.VivoAddWidgetExecutor

The screenshot constructs and attempts to launch a Vivo Launcher widget-adding Activity. Component access, any user confirmation, and the final result are not shown.

5.2 Obtain icon related information

  1. File: da60112a4b2848adba2ac11f412cccc7.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.get_icon_info.GetIconInfoExecutor

The visible fragment queries a Launcher Provider for folder-related state. Its right side is cropped, so this image alone cannot establish the full row/column query or the eventual use of the data. Why collect this home-screen information? I could not work that out either.

5.3 Add Widget on Oppo Phones

  1. File: 75dcc8ea-d0f9-4222-b8dd-2a83444f9cd6.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.oppoaddwidget.OppoAddWidgetExecutor

Only conditional dispatch to a proxy or widget executor is visible; the widget-adding flow is not shown.

5.4 Update icon on Xiaomi Phones?

  1. File: 5d372522-b6a4-4c1b-a0b4-8114d342e6c0.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.xm_akasha.XmAkashaExecutor

The screenshot dispatches requests to helpers for shortcut permission, icon queries/updates, and restarting the Launcher. It establishes the branch names, not successful execution of each helper. Perhaps someone familiar with the Xiaomi implementation can shed some light on it.

6. Auto-start, Associated Start, Keep Alive Related

6.1 Open Auto-start on Oppo Phones

  1. File: e723d560-c2ee-461e-b2a1-96f85b614f2b.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.oppo_boot_perm.OppoBootPermExecutor

The screenshot references a ColorOS/OPlus security-center Provider and startup-related parameters. Writes and their effects depend on the version’s Provider checks; they do not imply removal of every background-execution restriction.

6.2 Open Vivo Associated Start Permission

  1. File: 8b56d820-cac2-4ca0-8a3a-1083c5cca7ae.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.vivo_association_start.VivoAssociationStartExecutor

The screenshot targets a Vivo associated-start allowlist configuration, not a general Android permission interface.

The code below constructs an XML node. That shows the proposed data structure, not that the file was written or reloaded by the system.

6.3 Huawei Power-Management Configuration

  1. File: 7c6e6702-e461-4315-8631-eee246aeba95.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.hw_hide_power_window.HidePowerWindowExecutor

The screenshots show power-management database/table names and cache-file cleanup. The original heading overstates this as turning off the power manager: these fragments do not prove that the entire feature, let alone thermal controls, was disabled. Anyone who works on this part of the Huawei system is welcome to take a look.

6.4 Vivo AMS Configuration Recovery

  1. File: 7877ec6850344e7aad5fdd57f6abf238.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.vivo_get_loc.VivoGetLocExecutor

The screenshots show recovery logic for a Vivo AMS configuration file and calls to a vendor daemon. I wondered whether this was for keeping the app alive, but without the complete call chain and results I cannot confirm that. The class name’s get_loc also does not establish location collection. Perhaps someone familiar with Vivo can help here.

7. Installation and Uninstallation Related

7.1 VivoRollbackUninstallExecutor and Launcher Configuration

  1. File: d643e0f9a68342bc8403a69e7ee877a7.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.vivo_rollback_uninstall.VivoRollbackUninstallExecutor

The screenshot shows downloading and replacing a Launcher configuration file and checking its digest. It does not show installing an older APK after uninstallation. The original “rollback to the preinstalled version” explanation was unverified and should not be equated with ordinary removal of a system-app update.

7.2 Vivo Phone App Uninstallation

  1. File: be7a2b643d7e8543f49994ffeb0ee0b6.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.vivo_official_uninstall.OfficialUntiUninstallV3

This also shows Launcher configuration replacement. An Uninstall class name is insufficient to establish its effect on the uninstall flow.

7.3 Vivo Phone App Uninstallation Related

  1. File: 183bb87aa7d744a195741ce524577dd0.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.vivo_official_uninstall.VivoOfficialUninstallExecutor

Only package-dependent dispatch to different helpers is visible here; the complete uninstall-related behavior is not shown.

Others

SyncExecutor

  1. File: f4247da0-6274-44eb-859a-b4c35ec0dd71.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.sync.SyncExecutor

I could not tell what this was for. The screenshot reads sid from input, calls CmdHandler.setSid and Utils.updateSid, then constructs version, state, and process-ID response fields. Without updateSid, this sid cannot be identified as a user identity or system UID.

UdParseNotifyMessageExecutor

  1. File: f35735a5cbf445c785237797138d246a.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.ud_parse_nmessage.UdParseNotifyMessageExecutor

The screenshot parses a supplied Intent’s extras and processes Parcelable values. Its caller determines where the Intent came from and whether it represents a remote notification; the class name alone cannot establish that.

6.3 TDLogcatExecutor

  1. File
    1. 8aeb045fad9343acbbd1a26998b6485a.dex
    2. 2aa151e2cfa04acb8fb96e523807ca6b.dex
  2. Class Name
    1. com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.td.logcat.TDLogcatExecutor
    2. com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.td.logcat.TDLogcatExecutor

I was unsure about this one too: it looked a bit like keep-alive code, but not quite. The visible fragment mainly checks initialization state and whether the target package remains installed before calling another method. Logging, keep-alive behavior, or other purposes require that implementation to be examined.

6.4 QueryLBSInfoExecutor

  1. File: 74168acd-14b4-4ff8-842e-f92b794d7abf.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.query_lbs_info.QueryLBSInfoExecutor

The screenshot reads the current Wi-Fi SSID and BSSID, not GPS coordinates. These fields can inform location inference but are not a direct location result. The WifiInfo documentation also describes permission-based redaction and unknown values for location-sensitive fields.

6.5 WriteSettingsExecutor

  1. File: 6afc90e406bf46e4a29956aabcdfe004.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.write_settings.WriteSettingsExecutor

The screenshot selects a Settings namespace and a putInt, putString, or similar method from parameters; actual keys and values are absent. Writing Settings.System and modifying restricted Settings.Secure entries involve different authority. Finding a put method does not allow arbitrary settings changes. See System.canWrite (API 23) and Settings.Secure.

6.6 OppoSettingExecutor

  1. File: 61517b68-7c09-4021-9aaa-cdebeb9549f2.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.opposettingproxy.OppoSettingExecutor

After a service connection, the screenshot sends a Messenger message containing plugin configuration. Server-side loading, execution, and authorization are absent, so the resulting settings changes or keep-alive effects remain unknown. What does this proxy do on the other end? Someone familiar with Oppo may be able to explain it.

6.7 CheckAsterExecutor

  1. File: 561341f5f7976e13efce7491887f1306.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.check_aster.CheckAsterExecutor

Check aster—what exactly is it checking? I do not know either. The visible code places the input uuid into tracking fields and constructs a success response. It does not show a specific Aster check, so the name cannot supply a missing detection result.

6.8 OppoCommunityIdExecutor

  1. File: 538278f3-9f68-4fce-be10-12635b9640b2.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.oppo_community_id.OppoCommunityIdExecutor

The screenshot attempts a vendor backup call targeting a preferences file in the Oppo community app whose name refers to a logged-in user ID. Neither file contents nor a successful backup are shown; this is not evidence of obtaining the phone user’s system identity.

6.9 GetSettingsUsernameExecutor

  1. File: 4569a29c-b5a8-4dcf-a3a6-0a2f0bfdd493.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.oppo_get_settings_username.GetSettingsUsernameExecutor

The screenshot reads an input-specified file of at most 10 KiB, places it in an xml response field, and labels the package as Settings. Without its contents, username cannot be resolved to an account name, display name, or another field.

6.10 LogcatExecutor

  1. File: 218a37ea-710d-49cb-b872-2a47a1115c69.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.logcat.LogcatExecutor

The screenshot passes page, line-count, and timeout parameters to an asynchronous log-capture helper. It neither guarantees system-wide log access nor proves completion; the visible success response follows the asynchronous call.

6.11 VivoBrowserSettingsExecutor

  1. File: 136d4651-df47-41b4-bb80-2ec0ab1bc775.dex
  2. Class Name: com.google.android.sd.biz_dynamic_dex.vivo_browser_settings.VivoBrowserSettingsExecutor

The screenshot handles a vendor-specific Vivo settings field through work/recover branches. Its consumer and later effects are not shown; it does not establish browser-history access or changes to all browser settings.

Comments area is more exciting than the article

The following reader comments are retained from 2023 as opinions and discussion, not technical evidence of exploit reproduction, data collection, or platform security rankings.

WeChat Official Account Comment Area

Zhihu Comment Area

The Zhihu answer has been deleted. I can see it through the homepage, but clicking in shows it has been deleted: How to evaluate Pinduoduo suspected of using vulnerabilities to attack user mobile phones, steal competitor software data, and prevent itself from being uninstalled? - Gracker’s answer - Zhihu https://www.zhihu.com/question/587624599/answer/2927765317

Which is more secure, iOS or Android?

The original article referred to a comment by sunwear, but its image is missing from the archive and the original wording cannot be restored. A comment and this set of historical Android samples cannot establish which platform is “more secure.” A comparison needs defined devices, OS versions, security patches, attacker capabilities, and protected data. This article has no corresponding iOS samples or comparative experiment, so it makes no platform ranking.

About Me && Blog

Below are personal introduction and related links. I hope to communicate more with everyone in the industry. If three people walk together, there must be one who can be my teacher!

  1. Blogger Personal Introduction: There are personal WeChat and WeChat group links inside.
  2. This Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.
  3. Excellent blog articles organized and collected by individuals - A must-know for Android efficiency optimization: Everyone is welcome to recommend themselves and recommend others (WeChat private chat is fine)
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One person can go faster, a group of people can go further

entry.title: The Performance Community Tea Talk - Episode 1
entry.content:
On Friday, March 25, 2022, at 9 PM, “The Performance” Knowledge Planet held its first online “Tea Talk.” We were joined by 3 planet hosts, 5 guest experts, and over 50 members. Thank you all for coming!

We had no set topic and expected to finish in an hour. We ended up talking for two and a half hours; introductions alone took an hour! We had talked plenty in the group and on Knowledge Planet, but this was our first voice chat together. People worked across the Android ecosystem, from app companies and phone manufacturers to chip companies and EV startups. Someone would mention their work, someone else would ask a question, and off we went.

At the time, we planned to hold more sessions with clearer themes and more guests, on topics beyond technology too. We did not record this session to protect participants’ privacy. The notes below reconstruct part of the conversation without including private details.

Technical review — 2026-10-14: This is a historical record of the 2022 discussion. Career advice and personal experience are retained. Updates below address log sharing, GPU tools and APIs, resource versions, and broken links. Event plans and community invitations describe the period when this was written.

On Career Development

“I’m a new grad and the vastness of the performance field is overwhelming.”

  1. Shift Your Mindset: University and professional work are different. In school, you have a textbook and a final exam. In the field, the “curriculum” never ends.
  2. Learn from What’s at Hand: Master the problems on your desk first. Aim for 100% or even 110% proficiency in your daily tasks while building a foundation for broader knowledge. Doing your current job exceptionally well earns you the reputation and the opportunity to touch new, more complex things. Don’t jump to a new field until you’ve mastered (or explicitly rejected) your current one.
  3. Problem-Oriented Programming: Your boss pays you to solve problems. Put in enough work to solve them well, but also watch how much the next round of effort will buy you.
  4. Climbing the Mountain: If you only stare at the peak, you’ll feel defeated. Keep your head down, take one step at a time, and check your map (and current career path) occasionally.

“I just switched from App development to System Performance. Where do I start?”

  1. Follow Company Projects: If you have a mentor, follow them closely. This is the fastest way to learn.
  2. Self-Drive: Keep doing your current work well while learning things that help with it. As you become more capable, you can take more initiative; colleagues and managers are also more likely to support you and give you opportunities.
  3. Don’t Limit Yourself: Knowledge is interconnected. Don’t stay in your “one-acre plot.” Performance spans App, Framework, Kernel, and Hardware. Aim for a state of “knowing what you don’t know.” The worst state is “not knowing that you don’t know” and thinking there’s nothing left to optimize.
  4. Systematize Knowledge: Performance is a broad field. When analyzing problems, take notes, summarize, and categorize. Don’t expect instant mastery; it’s a marathon of accumulation.
  5. Leverage Resources: Use this community, engineering blogs from major tech companies, and technical papers. Ask questions, no matter how “basic” they seem.

On Asking Questions

  1. This community is a powerful platform, but its value depends on your ability to ask precise questions. Asking a good question is a technical skill in itself.
  2. Recommended Reading: How to Ask Questions?
    • “A well-put question is half the solution.”
    • Einstein once said: “If I had an hour to save the world, I would spend 55 minutes defining the problem and 5 minutes solving it.”
    • Great questions inspire masters to teach. It is a bridge to the best minds.
  3. Use Google: The quality difference between Google and local search engines can be vast for niche technical issues. Don’t discriminate between Chinese and English resources—if it solves your problem, it’s a gold mine.
  4. Log Sharing:
    • Minimize the capture and establish permission to share it. Package names are only one possible field; paths, URLs, application markers, log messages, and device identifiers may also matter. A private message does not authorize sharing unredacted data.
    • Text logs can be processed in a copy using known fields, but search-and-replace may miss compressed or embedded data in Systrace HTML. Native Perfetto traces use protobuf, so they must not be edited as plain text; see the data model. Use a format-aware approach that preserves required relationships, then reopen and inspect the result. Replacing package names alone is not complete redaction.
    • If permission or the shareable scope is unclear, describe a minimal reproduction and necessary aggregate information instead of sending confidential raw logs.
  5. The Perfect Feedback Loop: Ask a question -> Analyze together -> Try solutions -> Verify with data -> Share the result with the community.

On Interviews

It can be useful to talk to competitors or people in a new field from time to time, just to see what is happening outside your company. You do not have to be looking for another job, though if a good opportunity comes along, why not? The point is to stay competitive in the job market.

Distinguish between your profession and your job. “Software Engineer” is your profession; “Working on Module X at Company A” is your job. Recognizing this difference allows you to remain calm during corporate restructuring. Ideally, pursue a profession you find exciting, as you’ll spend most of your life doing it.

Finding a job that fits also takes luck. Many things affect an interview. If it goes badly, perhaps that particular job was not a match; it does not tell you everything about yourself.

On Corporate Environments

Different companies have different strategies based on their industry and competition. Your manager’s style and your colleagues’ expertise define your immediate environment.

Some organizations reward “top 5% technical excellence,” while others only care that “the bug is fixed” regardless of how. Understand the game you are playing. Either challenge the environment or adapt to it, but don’t fall into the trap of self-doubt.

On Learning New Tech

Different technology stacks can hide the same underlying performance problems. Try to understand what stays the same, then use that understanding to judge new techniques and find further improvements. Skimming the surface of every new technology is tiring, and you do not get much out of it.

Once you get far enough into optimization, you have to look below the application: compilers, hardware features, and how the hardware fits together. These directly affect how fast the program runs.

On GPU

  • GPU architectures: generations and vendors differ. These are historical learning materials, not current specifications for every desktop or mobile GPU.

    1. GPU Architectures: the old sharing page remains accessible, while full-file access depends on sharing permissions. It is not used here as a current hardware specification.
    2. Introduction to GPU Architecture: Caroline Collange’s course notes, whose title page says ADA 2019. Read hardware examples in that context.
    3. Introduction to Modern GPU Architecture: the old NVIDIA TDCI_Arch.pdf URL now returns 404. The NVIDIA Ampere Tuning Guide is an available supplementary reference explicitly scoped to Ampere / CUDA, not general Android GPU advice.
    4. Graphics and Computing GPUs: John Nickolls and David Kirk’s textbook appendix includes GeForce 8800-era examples.
    5. GPU Architecture and Function: the original RIT endpoint timed out during this review and is not presented as a working download. A timeout does not establish permanent closure.

  • Mobile graphics hardware book: Mobile 3D Graphics SoC: From Algorithm to Chip, by Jeong-Ho Woo, Ju-Ho Sohn, Byeong-Gyu Nam, and Hoi-Jun Yoo, was published by Wiley in 2010. Use publisher or library access. It describes historical algorithm-to-chip design, not current product specifications.

  • Implementations and articles: I could no longer find many of the GPU posts I remembered, so these are the ones I could track down:

    1. Historical article recommendations include a GPU architecture article series and tile-based performance notes. They are historical reading suggestions; check technical conclusions against the target GPU and driver.
    2. SwiftShader currently describes a CPU-based Vulkan 1.3 implementation. ANGLE can layer OpenGL ES 3.1 on it as SwANGLE. This is not a direct desktop OpenGL 3.0 implementation. Check the branch when reading AOSP’s historical external/swiftshader tree. Software rendering helps explain API implementation but does not reproduce a hardware GPU’s microarchitecture or performance.
    3. Mesa’s official source instructions point to freedesktop.org GitLab; the old github.com/mesa3d/mesa address returns 404. Read the specific driver, API, and hardware backend rather than treating one implementation as universal.

  • Starting with OpenGL or Vulkan: starting with OpenGL was my personal learning preference. Graphics fundamentals transfer, but resource, synchronization, and state-management models differ. OpenGL is not a mandatory prerequisite: the current Khronos tutorial expects graphics fundamentals without assuming prior OpenGL knowledge. If you already know some OpenGL, here is how I learned Vulkan. It may not be the best route; treat it as one person’s experience.

    1. I used the original Vulkan Tutorial to work through basic examples, such as drawing a triangle. It now warns that it was written for the early 2016 API and no longer represents current recommended practice. New learners can use the Khronos Vulkan Tutorial and Vulkan Guide. Check API, binding, and SDK versions before mixing examples.
    2. Vulkan Programming Guide, by Graham Sellers and John Kessenich, is an Addison-Wesley 2016 first edition. It is historical study material, not a replacement for the current specification. I read it to get familiar with the APIs. It felt like a bare API walkthrough, with little explanation of why things worked that way.
    3. Learning Vulkan, by Parminder Singh, is a Packt 2016 first edition. I read the Chinese translation on WeChat Read and did not think much of the translation. If you can, read the English edition. I found its explanations of rendering flow and principles useful, but for fuller API coverage I would read it alongside Vulkan Programming Guide.
    4. Wu Yafeng’s Vulkan开发实战详解, ISBN 9787115509390, is the book I used when I wanted to move from introductory reading to writing code. I did not think it was particularly good. I picked it up because I had read the author’s OpenGL book at university; this one felt like a direct adaptation, and the explanations were rather dry. These are my experiences with the books at the time, not new evaluations of their current usefulness.

  • Why Vulkan? Apple’s Bringing OpenGL Apps to Metal (WWDC 2019) illustrates reducing implicit driver work and managing resources explicitly. Metal and Vulkan are different APIs, however: do not substitute Metal examples for Vulkan or assume both share a Mantle origin. Their object models, synchronization, and shader toolchains need separate study. MoltenVK is a layered Vulkan-on-Metal implementation with capability and portability limits.

Final Tip: Learning graphics and GPU internal counters is a marathon. Be patient and keep practicing. The old DS-5 reference should now lead readers to Streamline in Arm Performance Studio; Snapdragon Profiler is another platform-specific tool. Counter availability depends on GPU, driver, OS, and permissions. Software-renderer measurements do not substitute for hardware GPU measurements.

Recommended Resources

Articles

  • “Ten-Year Founder Shares Thoughts on Hiring”: categorizes talent into S, A, B, and C tiers. Worth reflecting on which tier you occupy. The original document now requires sign-in and appropriate access.

Books

  • “The Self-Cultivation of a Programmer” (俞甲子 / 石凡 / 潘爱民): Deep dive into compilation, linking, and runtime mechanics.
  • “Software Debugging (2nd Ed)” (张银奎): The “Encyclopedia” of debugging.
    • Vol 1: Hardware Foundations (CPU/GPU/Debug infrastructure).
    • Vol 2: Windows Platform.
    • Vol 3: Linux Platform was a publication expectation mentioned in 2022. This review did not verify an author or publisher announcement that the volume has been published, so it is not presented as current “upcoming” news. The earlier book summaries describe the editions discussed at the time; consult version-matched documentation for actual tool use.

About The Performance Community

“The Performance” was a Knowledge Planet community run by three engineers working on performance at major phone manufacturers. We shared methods, tools, and case studies from Android performance work. The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this section records what it was like at the time.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep
entry.content:
This is the third article in the “Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips” series. It focuses on the Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep states in Systrace—their causes, troubleshooting, and optimization. These states often represent normal waiting; investigate their conditions and dependencies when they delay a critical path.

The goal of this series is to use Systrace to view the Android system from a different perspective and to learn the Framework through visualization. While reading Framework source code can be difficult to remember, seeing the flow in Systrace can lead to deeper understanding. You can find the complete Systrace Basics and Action Series here.

Technical review — 2026-10-14: This 2022 article retains historical screenshots with corrected signal, wakeup-attribution, and I/O-flag interpretation. Code examples are explicitly Linux v5.10; Android-specific events have separate sources. These references do not establish the screenshot device versions. Use Perfetto for new captures and treat missing fields as unknown.

Table of Contents

  • What are Sleep States in Linux?
  • Analyzing the Sleep State
  • Analyzing the Uninterruptible Sleep State
  • Appendix
  • About Me && Blog
  1. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  2. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  3. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

What are Sleep States in Linux?

TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE vs. TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE

A thread which is neither Running nor Runnable is not necessarily sleeping: it may be stopped, traced, or exiting. The following are three common waiting semantics, not an exhaustive list of Linux states:

  • TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE: the wait can be woken by its condition or an applicable pending signal.
  • TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE: ordinary signals or SIGKILL alone do not end the wait; a signal may remain pending until the wait returns.
  • TASK_KILLABLE: combines TASK_WAKEKILL | TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE and responds to signals the kernel classifies as fatal, notably SIGKILL. TASK_WAKEKILL is a flag, not a separate sleeping mechanism.

Figure 1 is a simplified model. Historical viewers commonly label interruptible waits Sleep and distinguish Uninterruptible Sleep, but colors vary by viewer and theme. A sleeping thread is not executing on a CPU; after wakeup it must be scheduled again.

“Uninterruptible” does not mean permanently unwakeable or hardware interrupts disabled. Completion, an explicit wakeup, or a timeout supported by the particular wait API can resume the task. For example, wait_event_timeout uses an uninterruptible wait with a timeout. See the Linux 6.12 wait APIs and Linux 5.10 state definitions.

Looper polling and userspace futex waits commonly appear as Sleep, but Java/native locks and network operations do not all imply one kernel state. Inspect the actual path and wait API. An idle main thread waiting for messages is normally healthy; replacing that wait with busy polling is not an optimization.

The Purpose of TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE

Interruptibility here concerns how a wait responds to signals. POSIX signals, softirqs, and hardware IRQs are different mechanisms with different execution contexts; a sleeping thread is not simultaneously executing hardware interrupt handlers.

A kernel operation may use an uninterruptible wait because it has no ordinary-signal cancellation semantics or must await an internal condition. This is distinct from disabling preemption or local CPU interrupts. TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE does not itself disable an interrupt controller.

I/O completion, some kernel locks, page waits, and driver synchronization can use such waits. Not every I/O operation, network access, or lock wait enters D. Inspect the target kernel’s actual wait function; Linux 5.10 is a versioned reference, while a changing “latest” page cannot establish the implementation behind an old screenshot.

Analysis Philosophy

TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE and TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE are normal. A high sleeping percentage can simply mean idle work. Investigate when waiting delays a required result or deadline. Master these two points:

  1. Troubleshooting Methodology
  2. Optimization Methodology

You must identify if a sleep is active or passive. If active, is the logic sound? If passive, what is the source? This requires deep system knowledge and experience.

Note: I’ll use “Sleep” for TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE and “UninterruptibleSleep” for TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE to match Systrace terminology.

It is easy to get lost when you first analyze Sleep and UninterruptibleSleep. Reading Framework and kernel code helps you make sense of the clues in a trace. The trace only covers the events that were captured, and Systrace’s wakeup_from does not by itself identify a lock owner or the complete business dependency. You need both an understanding of the system and the trace to explain the cause. Otherwise, you end up doing what I call ‘performance optimization by bluffing’: you assert a cause that nobody can check, send the testers through another round of retesting, and let the issue disappear when they cannot reproduce it.

This article covers common types and cases. Use these diagnostic methods and source code analysis to navigate unique problems.

Visualization in Trace

These are historical viewer palettes, not standardized kernel colors. Non-IO versus Block I/O classification also depends on the captured events. A missing I/O flag leaves I/O classification unknown, not automatically Non-IO. A missing blocked function leaves the wait location unknown without invalidating an I/O flag that was captured.

Analyzing the Sleep State

The crops show waiting around Choreographer#doFrame / DrawFrame and a binder transaction. They suggest hypotheses such as UI-to-render-thread synchronization or a synchronous Binder reply wait. They do not include enough stacks, transaction links, and timing context to establish the entire dependency or root cause.

Diagnostic Methods

Use wakeup from tid: *** to Find Waking Threads

As discussed in the Runnable article, waking up and actually executing are separate steps. Timers, device completion, and interrupt paths can wake tasks as well as other threads. Preemption, yielding, and newly enqueued tasks also contribute runnable work; the original two-case classification was incomplete.

wakeup from tid identifies the wakeup context recorded by scheduler events. It is not necessarily the business-level producer or the owner of a contested lock. Interrupt context, proxy wakeups, multiple waiters, and missing events can make a simple tid attribution misleading.

The red annotations are historical. In particular, “Running instead” does not prove the other task had higher priority or caused the delay; it helps identify other work running at that time. The shown wakeup from tid: 14116 is a lead to investigate.

Current Perfetto can correlate sched_switch, sched_waking, and thread-state details. Depending on the capture, tables may expose waker_utid and irq_context. Missing values do not establish that there was no waker. See scheduler events and the thread_state table.

Other Methods

  1. Stacks and off-CPU analysis: ordinary CPU sampling mainly observes stacks while the thread runs; it does not reconstruct a complete execution flow during sleep. With supported kernels, permissions, and versions, simpleperf’s --trace-offcpu combines scheduling information with stacks at descheduling. It still does not record every function entry and exit. See the official simpleperf reference.
  2. Event correlation: use timing to identify candidates, then confirm with Binder transactions, futex addresses, application identifiers, kernel stacks, or source. Simultaneous events alone do not establish causality.

Ask what condition is awaited, who advances it, when it becomes satisfied, and how long scheduling takes afterward, rather than merely matching colors on timelines.

Common Causes for Long Sleep

  • Binder: a synchronous call may wait for remote queueing, execution, and a reply. Follow transaction links and distinguish service-side execution, lock waits, and CPU waits. A oneway call does not wait for a synchronous reply in the same way.
  • Java/futex locks and conditions: contention may occur in apps or services, but a futex is a mechanism and does not always mean a mutex wait. Identify the actual condition, lock, and dependency.
  • Intentional waits: timers, semaphores, and message queues can provide necessary pacing. Establish whether the wait delays a required result before trying to remove it.
  • Graphics fences: a fence can track GPU, display, or buffer use; waiting does not prove the GPU is continuously busy. Identify the producer, submission, and signal times, then consider shader, resolution, or texture reductions where relevant. Increasing GPU frequency is not a general app-level fix. See the AOSP synchronization framework.

Analyzing the Uninterruptible Sleep State

Diagnostic Methods

First establish a D-class wait, then look for I/O classification and a blocked function. These are optional capture details, not properties that every UninterruptibleSleep interval necessarily exposes:

  1. The I/O-wait flag can be 0, 1, or absent.
  2. Block reason depends on kernel tracepoints, capture configuration, symbols, and parser support.

IOWait vs. Non-IOWait

Here I/O wait is a kernel flag recorded for the task, not a complete test for any I/O performed by an operation, nor the CPU-usage statistic called iowait. iowait=0 means this point was not marked as I/O waiting; it does not rule out I/O elsewhere in the operation. A missing field is not zero.

A page-cache miss may cause storage access, while a cache hit may still require page-lock, writeback, or other synchronization. One syscall may include several running and waiting intervals. Non-IO candidates include kernel locks, page waits, and driver conditions; Non-IO is not synonymous with a kernel-lock wait.

Block Reason

The historical sched_blocked_reason change is c9f00aa0, authored by Riley Andrews on 2015-10-02, with a committer date of 2016-04-20 in this repository. Its title is:

In the inspected Android Common android12-5.10 event definition, pid comes from the task ID, caller from get_wchan(tsk), and iowait from tsk->in_iowait. This is a wait-location clue, not a full stack, lock address, or owner. Availability is kernel-dependent, and the recording must enable sched/sched_blocked_reason; see the Perfetto analysis guide.

The original line is retained as a format example:

The event’s pid is a task ID (TID); 30120 in the image is the process PID. These are not directly comparable fields. Without the selected thread’s TID and raw records, do not automatically combine the example line and screenshot as one event. Resolve get_user_pages_fast+0x34/0x70 against the actual device’s kernel build and symbols. The Linux 5.10 example below explains a mechanism; it does not establish the screenshot’s kernel version.

Here is the complete wrapper from Linux v5.10:

This version adds page references with FOLL_GET; that differs from the FOLL_PIN semantics of pin_user_pages*() and is not a generic long-term DMA-pinning API. See GUP and pin_user_pages.

The internal implementation attempts a fast path and falls back for remaining pages when permitted. The slow path may acquire mmap_lock or encounter faults and other page waits; the wrapper’s name alone does not identify one lock as the cause. Interrupt protection within the fast path also does not mean the D state disables interrupts.

The later Runnable selection shows wakeup from tid: 30235. It identifies a related wakeup, not proof that 30235 owned the earlier lock. Correlate complete stacks, lock or mmap operations, and timing. The full trace is unavailable here, so these crops do not verify the root cause.

Common Causes for IOWait and Optimizations

1. Active IO Operations

Candidates include synchronous reads/writes, fsync, filesystem metadata, competing storage users, and the actual swap backend. Distinguish them using request sizes, access patterns, latency, queues, and errors. A D interval alone does not diagnose fragmentation, flash aging, or low free space.

Optimization methods:

  • Reduce critical-path synchronous I/O, combine unnecessary small requests, and batch appropriately. After making work asynchronous, check that the wait was not merely moved onto another critical dependency.
  • Readahead helps predictable locality; excessive prefetch consumes bandwidth and memory. Measure the target workload instead of always increasing it.
  • Page-cache reclaim, system-file residency, and storage-maintenance policies belong to platform configuration. PinFile or locking many pages is not a general app solution and can crowd out other work.
  • An I/O benchmark describes its own conditions, not the complete application workload, cache state, temperature, and filesystem behavior.

Swap-in need not read physical storage. Android commonly uses compressed RAM through zRAM, with CPU decompression cost. zRAM configured with a backing device/writeback may also use storage. Check the actual configuration; see Android memory management and zRAM.

2. High IO due to Low Memory

File-page caching reduces repeated reads. Memory pressure may cause more eviction, faults, reclaim, or writeback, but it does not mean almost every I/O bypasses memory and hits disk. Distinguish file-backed and anonymous pages, clean and dirty pages, and the swap backend.

Optimization methods:

  • Reduce synchronous I/O on critical paths and organize data/prefetch for the measured access pattern.
  • Avoid unbounded business caches, unnecessary residency, and excessive short-lived allocations.
  • At the platform level, correlate reclaim, faults, storage, and memory-pressure events. Distinguish useful cache occupancy from pressure delaying work rather than maximizing free RAM.

System memory is shared by all processes. An app that grabs resources without considering its neighbors can hurt them, then suffer itself when the system intervenes. Expecting every developer to account for all of this is unrealistic. I think clear, enforced platform rules may be the way out.

Common Causes for Non-IOWait

  • Reclaim or page waits: pressure can involve locks, page waits, and writeback, with either Non-IO or I/O-marked intervals. Inspect the actual stack and events.
  • Binder kernel paths: particular operations or locks can produce this state, but waiting for a synchronous Binder reply commonly appears as ordinary Sleep. Transaction volume alone is not a diagnosis.
  • Other kernel locks, drivers, and completion conditions: Non-IO is a starting classification, not the final cause.

System Scheduling and UninterruptibleSleep Coupling

If a verified lock owner spends a long time Runnable, its scheduling delay can extend another thread’s lock wait; priority inversion is one possible case. Establish ownership first instead of inferring it from Non-IO or wakeup from.

Shorten critical sections, avoid expensive work while holding locks, and investigate why the dependency is not running. Linux provides RT-mutex / PI-futex priority inheritance for applicable locks, but not every mutex, rwsem, or futex wait automatically has PI. It does not replace sound locking design, and scheduler modification is not the only possible remedy.

Appendix

Linux Thread State Definitions

These are common Trace display symbols, not an exact mapping of every kernel version’s /proc state characters. Parsers also support historical combinations; use the actual event and viewer version.

Display symbolMeaning and limits
SSleeping, typically an interruptible wait
RRunnable; raw Linux TASK_RUNNING also includes execution, which the viewer separates as Running
R+Runnable after preemption
DUninterruptible Sleep; alone it does not establish I/O or fatal-signal behavior
T / tStopped / traced
ZZombie
X / xHistorical exit/task-dead representations
KWake-kill flag, potentially combined with other states; not a synonym for D
WWaking, depending on kernel and parser reporting
I / P / NIdle / Parked / No-load markers, version-dependent
Unknown or absent fieldsInsufficient data, not automatically Sleep, Non-IO, or zero wait

See Perfetto scheduling states.

Case: Waiting for Swap Data

The selected entry shows Uninterruptible Sleep - Block I/O with do_swap_page+0x138/0xf34, supporting investigation of the swap-in path. It does not prove the backing data came from flash or that the entire 295.448 ms selection at the top belongs to this one wait. Check the backend, page/I/O events, selected state interval, and kernel version.

Case: mmap Contention Across Multiple Threads

The UI thread’s blocked location is vm_mmap_pgoff+0x74/0x108; “Running instead” shows RenderThread. This suggests investigating address-space mapping contention, but does not prove RenderThread owns the relevant lock.

Threads in one process normally share mm_struct. The complete Linux v5.10 vm_mmap_pgoff below is a versioned mechanism reference:

The write-protected region runs from mmap_write_lock_killable() to mmap_write_unlock(). Its lock wait can return -EINTR for a fatal signal, so a D display alone does not prove SIGKILL is ineffective. mm_populate() runs after unlock; the function name alone does not locate the wait at lock acquisition. Resolve the offset with matching build symbols and correlate lock and thread activity.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro: Includes personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Welcome to recommend projects/articles.
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
entry.content:
This is the second article in the “Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips” series. It analyzes the causes of the “Running” state in Systrace and provides optimization strategies for when Running segments are excessively long.

The goal of this series is to use Systrace to view the Android system from a different perspective and to learn the Framework through visualization. While reading Framework source code can be difficult to remember, seeing the flow in Systrace can lead to deeper understanding. You can find the complete Systrace Basics and Action Series here.

Technical review — 2026-10-14: This 2022 article retains its six investigation categories, with corrected Running, ART compilation, and CPU-frequency interpretation and current tooling references. Scheduling and compilation vary by Android version, kernel, and device; color or a keyword alone does not establish the cause.

Table of Contents

  • Causes for Long Running States
  • About Me && Blog
  1. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  2. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  3. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

Long Running Duration

Visualization

Historical Systrace usually shows a Running thread in green: it is scheduled on a logical CPU. For new recordings, use Perfetto scheduling tracks and inspect the state and events rather than color alone.

Distinguish an instrumented function’s elapsed time (wall time), the thread’s scheduled running time, and its Runnable wait for a CPU. A long function interval can include locks, Binder, I/O, or scheduling waits. Conversely, Running does not mean every cycle retires useful instructions: cache misses, memory stalls, and interrupts affect its interpretation.

Select the interval relevant to the user scenario, clip scheduling slices at its boundaries, and avoid adding nested function durations twice. This article includes no complete trace or test program; the six causes below need verification rather than describing a newly reproduced device issue.

Cause 1: High Code Complexity and Execution Time

Start with the amount of work: repeated calculations, algorithmic complexity, loop counts, allocations, and copying can all increase running time. Platform libraries and system calls may also be hotspots, but a function name alone does not implicate a vendor modification.

Use a release-like build and compare the same workload, inputs, and device conditions with Android Studio Profiler or simpleperf, alongside scheduling data. Sample weight is neither invocation count nor the exact duration of each call. Account for missing symbols, unwinding limitations, and capture overhead.

To instrument known code, use Trace.beginSection() / Trace.endSection(), available from API 18. Synchronous sections must be paired on the same thread and correctly nested; use try/finally so exceptions also end the section. These sections measure elapsed time. Do not span arbitrary cross-thread asynchronous work with a synchronous begin/end pair.

Cause 2: Interpreted Code Execution

A Compiling label does not establish that the business code is being interpreted. In the Android 12.0.0_r3 ART JIT compiler, JIT compiling, Compiling OSR, Compiling optimized, and Compiling baseline surround compilation work. That work can consume CPU, but inspect the owning thread, stack, and compilation state before attributing the application’s delay. JIT “baseline” here is also distinct from an app’s Baseline Profile file.

Since Android 7, ART combines AOT, JIT, and interpretation. A newly installed app may already benefit from installation-time compilation or profiles; it is not necessarily entirely interpreted. The result of dex2oat also depends on its filter and profile, rather than proving every method is AOT-compiled.

A current investigation can:

  1. Specify whether it measures first installation, cold startup, or warmed execution, and control the build, inputs, and thermal conditions.
  2. Generate and correctly deliver Baseline Profiles for critical paths to reduce interpretation/JIT costs on first use. Startup Profiles instead inform DEX layout at build time; the two serve different purposes.
  3. Explicitly compare Macrobenchmark CompilationMode settings. None skips precompilation but still permits JIT during execution. Full is not guaranteed to beat Partial, because code size and instruction-cache pressure can change the result. One faster run after manual compilation does not establish a production benefit.

Frequent JNI transitions, data conversion, or reflection can also cost time, but measure the actual hot path first. Follow the official JNI guidance to reduce unnecessary crossings and marshalling rather than treating the presence of a language feature as the diagnosis.

Cause 3: Thread Running on Small Cores

CPU-bound work may take longer on a lower-capacity core, but little cores are not reserved for non-UX work. Placement balances load, energy, allowed CPUs, and thermal policy. Memory- or I/O-bound work may not improve much after moving to a big core.

Correlate the real topology, scheduling tracks, and frequency over the same window before blaming placement. Ordinary apps should not treat affinity or SchedBoost as universally available guarantees. A narrow affinity mask can increase Runnable latency; see the Runnable article.

For sustained workloads with reportable target and actual durations, evaluate PerformanceHintManager, available from Android 12 / API 31. It supplies hints rather than directly selecting a core, and results depend on device support and policy.

Cause 4: Big Cores Running at Low Frequencies

Low frequency can reflect workload changes, energy policy, or thermal limits. One frequency value does not prove scaling is insufficiently aggressive. Align frequency events with the relevant CPU and running interval, and check what the signal represents: a requested frequency or sampled value need not equal the actual clock throughout the interval. A CPUFreq policy may also be shared by multiple cores. See the Linux CPUFreq documentation.

Optimization suggestions:

  1. Reduce unnecessary work and compare the same workload before and after placement or frequency changes.
  2. Use supported public performance-hint APIs where appropriate instead of depending on private frequency-locking controls.
  3. Governor, frequency-limit, and platform boost tuning belongs to system-level investigation. Controlled experiments can isolate a cause, but locked-frequency results do not represent ordinary user conditions. Platform changes also need power, temperature, and sustained-performance evaluation.

Cause 5: Thermal Throttling: Core Shutdown and Frequency Capping

Thermal management may limit frequency, power, or other resources; the mechanism varies by device and does not always involve taking cores offline. Establish whether thermal limiting occurred in the problem window before identifying its cause. A long Running interval or low frequency alone is insufficient.

External factors include ambient heat and sunlight. Internal sources may include CPU, GPU, modem, camera, or charging activity. Compare the same workload, starting temperature, charging state, and run duration rather than mixing cold-device and hot-device results. Remove unnecessary foreground or background work first; for necessary work, consider suitable changes to concurrency, resolution, or quality.

Apps can use PowerManager thermal status from API 29 and thermal headroom from API 30 to assist adaptation. Devices may incompletely support them or return unavailable results; these are not generic Celsius readings. See PowerManager and the Thermal API guide.

Platform tuning must respect the device’s own cooling, power, and temperature constraints. Competitor comparisons can suggest questions, but do not justify relaxing protection thresholds or treating a higher short benchmark score as better sustained experience.

Cause 6: Weak CPU Compute Power

At the same clock speed, different microarchitectures, caches, memory systems, and instruction paths can perform differently. MIPS (Million Instructions Per Second) is not a universal performance ranking across architectures or programs; a higher instruction rate can simply mean more work was executed. Compare task completion time, CPU time, energy, and correctness.

Two optimization paths:

  1. Build and compilation: app developers can inspect release/R8 settings, native compiler optimization, and profiles. Compare controlled changes using toolchain documentation rather than piling on flags. A vendor compiler’s claims do not replace measurements of this app.
  2. Code and data access: locate hotspots through sampling, then use hardware counters where device support and permissions allow, to investigate cycles, instructions, and cache behavior.

Check PMU event definitions, measurement scope, and denominators; account for counter multiplexing and comparability across core types. cache-misses need not denote the same cache level on every device, and a high miss rate alone does not prove the main bottleneck. See simpleperf events and statistics.

  • If locality is the bottleneck, reduce unnecessary copies or improve data layout and access order, then measure again.
  • “Too many complex instructions” is not a diagnosis: algorithms, branches, vectorization, dependencies, and memory stalls can all matter.
