Continuous file output supports longer recordings but adds I/O and storage costs. Alternatively, a ring buffer can retain recent data in memory until a trigger finalizes the capture. Its capacity and event rate limit how much history survives: old data is overwritten, and producer-side loss can occur independently.

Perfetto distinguishes overwrite and discard policies and can periodically drain buffers to a file. A trigger does not guarantee that the root cause remains in the buffer. Check capture duration, enabled sources, buffer sizing, and reported data loss before treating an absent event as evidence. See buffer behavior and trace configuration.

1.3 Analysis Methods

Data Visualization Analysis

A timeline places events on process, thread, or other tracks so that their timing and recorded relationships can be examined together. Systrace and Perfetto provide this view; KernelShark serves related Linux tracing workflows. Overlapping intervals are useful clues but do not by themselves prove that one caused another.

The historical Systrace viewer belongs to the Catapult project. Its Trace Event Format is a specific schema, not a promise that any JSON log will render as a trace. Modern Perfetto also imports supported formats; check the format list for the actual input.

Database Analysis

Turning captured data into tables makes repeatable queries and aggregation possible. Perfetto’s Trace Processor exposes trace data through SQL; Python can organize queries and results into an automated analysis. Search systems such as Elastic’s stack provide another way to explore structured logs, with their own query model.

Text inspection, visualization, and SQL complement each other. A quick text search may locate an event; a timeline may explain its context; SQL may compare many occurrences. None is mandatory merely because a problem involves several modules. Preserve units, time boundaries, and correlation identifiers when converting data so that the analysis still answers the original question.

2 Google-Provided Android Performance Analysis Tools

The three tools discussed here are Systrace, Perfetto, and Android Studio Profiler. These were common starting points in our workflow when this article was written. Choose tools according to the evidence needed: a heap problem, for example, may call for a memory tool first. The comparison below summarizes scope rather than prescribing a fixed sequence.

2.1 First-Generation System Performance Analysis Tool — Systrace

Systrace is a historical Android system-tracing workflow that visualizes selected app, framework, and kernel events. It was never the only performance tool. System tracing is often less intrusive than recording every method entry and exit, but its overhead is not zero and varies with enabled categories and event volume. For new investigations, start with Android system tracing and Perfetto.

Systrace’s Design Philosophy

Android instrumentation marks selected operations such as input dispatch, rendering, and inter-process communication. Userspace markers produced through android.os.Trace or native ATrace APIs are distinct from kernel events such as sched_switch and cpu_idle; the historical capture path can collect them together through ftrace.

The screenshot shows both tracing_mark_write markers and kernel events. Java framework code and application code can emit trace sections; native framework code has corresponding ATrace facilities. Categories, app selection, permissions, kernel support, and buffer loss determine what is actually captured. The result exposes useful parts of system activity, not every operation in Android.

Practical Application Scenarios

System traces help investigate startup, slow interactions, scrolling, window animations, and periods of apparent unresponsiveness. Scheduler and Binder events can distinguish execution from some forms of waiting when the relevant sources were captured.

An ANR investigation also needs its reason and thread stacks; a crash may require logcat, an exception stack, or a native tombstone. A timeline alone does not explain every failure. Old Systrace HTML files belong to the historical viewer workflow; for a new recording use the current system-tracing tools and open a supported trace in Perfetto UI.

2.2 New-Generation Performance Analysis Tool Stack — Perfetto

Perfetto provides recording, visualization, and analysis components for system and application tracing. It is the current Android system-tracing direction. Support for importing a format is also separate from having every historical viewer feature.

The service model separates producers, data sources, the tracing service, and consumers. This architecture supports sources beyond ftrace and allows several kinds of data to share a recording.

Highlighted Features

A producer supplies data for configured sources; the service manages sessions and buffers. Kernel ftrace events and Android userspace markers are important sources, but process statistics, heap profiling, and other sources have different collection paths. The native trace format uses protobuf messages; it is not a SQLite database.

Perfetto can capture into memory or stream to a file. Long recordings still depend on buffer capacity, source rate, storage, and overhead. The official Android log source is documented as userdebug-only: logcat is not guaranteed to be present in an ordinary user-build trace. Missing tracks or samples do not mean zero activity.

The UI, command-line tools, and Android’s System Tracing app provide different recording entry points. The trigger API activates names in a session configured in advance by an authorized consumer. START_TRACING begins recording after the trigger; STOP_TRACING can finalize an already recording session and retain bounded pre-trigger history. An app activating a trigger does not thereby gain permission to configure arbitrary system-wide tracing.

Trace Processor parses a trace and provides SQL tables through the UI, command line, and APIs. You do not have to export a SQLite file first. Python and DataFrames can help automate analysis. Large traces may benefit from a native Trace Processor, but memory and parsing limits remain; “300 MB” is not a universal failure threshold for either viewer.

For CPU totals, identify whether SurfaceFlinger means the process or one thread, then sum captured running intervals clipped to the chosen time window. Summing nested function wall times would double-count and include waiting. Likewise, map CPU IDs to the device’s actual topology before labeling a core as big or little.

Practical Application Scenarios

Perfetto is a useful first tool for many system timing questions. Its flexibility does not make it an arbitrary dynamic-probe framework like an eBPF-based tracing setup, and it cannot manufacture events that its sources did not record.

Do not infer a high or negligible runtime cost from protobuf encoding alone. Measure the selected sources, sampling, buffers, and file output under the intended workload. The command-line Trace Processor supports scripted SQL and text output as well as interactive investigation; analysis is not limited to the webpage.

2.3 Android Studio Profiler Tools

Android Studio integrates profiling with application development. Its current Profiler workflow is organized around tasks and recordings; the old “CPU, Memory, Network, Battery” list is not a reliable map of today’s UI.

Network Inspector is under View → Tool Windows → App Inspection, with support depending on the networking library. Power Profiler, introduced in Android Studio Hedgehog 2023.1.1, uses supported device data; ODPM power rails require supported Pixel hardware, rather than being a generic battery meter on every Android phone.

Use a release-like, profileable build where the chosen task supports it. Some tasks, including Java/Kotlin allocation recording and heap dumps, require a debuggable app. Record Studio, Android, app build, and capture settings when comparing results; changing debug mode or instrumentation changes the measurement conditions.

Highlighted Features

The historical CPU Profiler menu below offers several different kinds of evidence:

  1. System Trace records selected scheduling, rendering, and instrumented intervals. UI aggregation or filtering is not the same as a guarantee that all short events were discarded. Export a supported recording to Perfetto UI when broader system analysis is useful.
  2. Java/Kotlin sampling or method tracing: stack samples estimate where execution is observed; instrumented entry/exit records expose call boundaries with greater perturbation. They are not interchangeable measurements.
  3. Native sampling, backed by simpleperf in the historical workflow, identifies sampled native stacks. It is not a complete C/C++ entry/exit trace. Simpleperf supports hardware PMU events and software events; available events, stack unwinding, and symbols depend on the target. See the simpleperf documentation.

This is an old Studio menu, retained to explain the original example. Current task names and available recording options depend on the Studio and Android versions.

Practical Application Scenarios

Slow response and jank are common timing problems, alongside memory, power, and other performance concerns. For an unfamiliar rendering problem, a system trace can locate a long interval, then method or native profiling can provide more detail. Choose the next recording according to the unresolved question rather than always running all three tools.

Suppose you’re handed a badly performing app and don’t know its code. Where would you start? In this historical example, egl_core has a long onDrawFrame interval. The selected interval is about one second of elapsed time. Its name alone does not establish the underlying source method or the amount of CPU work; use source instrumentation and scheduler data to check those points.

The Java recording points toward Utils.onDraw. Its selected interval shows roughly 1 s wall time but only 402 μs CPU time, suggesting waiting in this recording rather than one second of computation. That distinction matters before deciding what to optimize.

The native view contains Java_com_gl_shader_Utils_onDraw → sleep → nanosleep. This makes sleeping a candidate explanation for the delay. The three screenshots come from separate recordings, and their displayed CPU-time fields cannot be combined into a single CPU accounting result. The original complete captures and example source are not available here. Confirm the sleep call in source, correlate scheduling in a new capture, and repeat the same scenario after removing it before claiming a verified fix.

Studio’s integration makes this drill-down convenient for application developers. System-wide analysis may still need additional tools and permissions.

2.4 Comprehensive Comparison

Capture triggers, buffering, and file output are separate choices. The following table describes capabilities, not a claim that every tool continuously writes every event to disk.

ToolMain useEvidence and limits
SystraceHistorical Android system tracingSelected kernel events and userspace markers; legacy viewer workflow
PerfettoSystem and app tracingEvents, counters, stacks, and other configured sources; memory/file and trigger modes; UI and SQL analysis
Android Studio ProfilerApp-focused profiling tasksSystem traces, samples, method records, heap or allocation data depending on the task and build
simpleperfCPU event counting and stack samplingHardware or software events; sampled weight is not invocation count; text and visual reports
Snapdragon ProfilerSupported Snapdragon platformsCPU, GPU, and some DSP analysis; DSP support is not universal
Historical Mali Graphics Debugger / Graphics AnalyzerGraphics API debugging on supported devicesArm says Graphics Analyzer was last included in Performance Studio 2024.2; consult current Arm tools for the applicable workflow
Android logcat / dumpsysEvent logs / service diagnosticsLog buffers and service-specific snapshots or reports are different data sources; collection and redirection determine persistence
Android GPU InspectorSupported Android GPU system/frame profilingDevice, driver, Android version, and graphics API requirements apply
eBPF-based toolsProgrammable tracing and aggregationEvents, statistics, and stacks depending on the program and attachment point; requires suitable privileges and kernel support
ftraceLinux tracing infrastructureKernel events, function tracing, and supported dynamic probes; buffer and output policies are configurable

Choose GPU tools by the actual GPU, driver, OS, and API support matrix. A SoC vendor name alone does not establish Mali/Adreno compatibility.

3 About “Techniques, Methods, and Tools”

At the tool level, Linux and Android tools keep gaining data sources and bringing more information into one place. Those changes have a pattern. Learn what a tool can show you and when it is useful; the point is to solve problems more efficiently, not to spend all your time learning the next tool.

The technique level depends on knowing the system you work on: how a frame is drawn, how the CPU schedules work, how I/O is submitted. That knowledge helps you choose a tool and interpret its output. After enough experience, you can sometimes spot a useful clue before digging through every detail. You start connecting what you see with problems you’ve encountered before.

At the level of judgment, ask what problem you actually need to solve. How far does the improvement need to go? What will it cost, and what will you get for that effort? Which path is worth taking? What needs to happen first, and what depends on it?

We’ll use these three perspectives in the articles that follow. We want you to leave with more than one technique to copy: when the tool or even the system changes, you should still be able to ask useful questions, choose the information you need, and judge where to spend your effort.

4 About “The Performance Knowledge Planet”

Historical note: The following is the community plan we described in this 2022 article. The community closed in 2026 and no longer accepts members; these are the ideas we had then, not current service offers.

We started The Performance to exchange ideas and write useful articles together. The three organizers worked on performance at major phone manufacturers. We wanted to bring together the basics, methods, tools, and the part we valued most: real cases.

Here is what we planned to cover. The labels between # marks were tags, so readers could jump to the topics they cared about.

  • #ThePerformance# — Early chapters of the book we were planning, Android Performance Optimization: A Systematic Course. There were already plenty of good articles and libraries, but we wanted a book that connected principles, tools, and practice for app and system developers. We had a draft outline and expected to spend about a year writing it, sharing finished chapters along the way.

  • Part 1: → Performance Engineering

  • Part 2: → Analyzing Android Interaction and Core Systems from a Performance Perspective

  • Part 3: → Analyzing Linux Kernel Core Subsystem Design and Implementation

  • Part 4: → Problem Scenario Analysis Approach

  • Part 5: → Analysis and Debugging Tools

  • Part 6: → Quality Guardianship — Performance Monitoring Methods and Tools

  • #PerformanceTools# — Tools we used and how to use them, including one-to-one video sessions for Systrace and Perfetto. A live demonstration can make things much clearer; some steps are hard to explain in a static article.

  • #CaseAnalysis# — Case studies and discussions, including cases shared by community members. Reading real cases helps when a similar problem lands on your desk. We also welcomed people’s own cases and solutions, with sensitive details masked.

  • #ClassicReinterpretation# — Revisiting useful libraries, approaches, and courses such as the Android developer masterclass: compare solutions, read them closely, and fill gaps in our understanding.

  • #KnowledgeShare# — Good articles, blogs, tools, and open-source work that had been used in real projects. We would find and share material worth spending time on.

  • #KnowledgeDeposition# — Highlights from WeChat discussions, questions people asked us, and answers left in blog comments.

  • #PerformanceInterview# — Android performance interview questions and answers. A practical need for quite a few of us, I’d say.

  • #ProgrammingLanguage# — Programming language usage technique sharing.

  • #EfficiencyImprovement# — Ways to work more effectively, from engineering processes to useful tools. Time spent sharpening your tools pays off when you get back to work.

  • #IndustryDynamics# — First-time interpretation reports of new performance-related technologies, including but not limited to the following content:

    • Industry summits, academic summit new concept interpretation reports
    • Papers, industry, books, video introductions
    • Android large version performance-related content introduction
    • Android new hardware performance-related content introduction
    • Android performance-related open source project interpretations

  • #BigNameSharing# — Monthly invitations to industry experts for experience sharing, case analyses

The community has closed. The QR image above is retained as part of the original article; please do not use it to make a payment.

5 Appendix

  • Perfetto Project Address

    • Official usage documentation: https://perfetto.dev/docs/
    • Github code library: https://github.com/google/perfetto, where you can report bugs or feature requests, and of course can submit PR contributions to contribute your strength.

  • Android GPU Inspector

    • Official usage documentation: https://developer.android.com/agi

  • Other Major Manufacturers’ Performance Analysis Tools

    • Windows Performance Toolkit

About Me && Blog

Below is a personal introduction and related links. I look forward to communicating with colleagues in the same field. When three walk together, there must be my teacher!

  1. Blogger Personal Introduction: Inside are personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.
  3. Personally Organized and Collected Excellent Blog Articles - Essential Skills and Tools for Android Performance Optimization: Everyone is welcome to self-recommend and recommend (private WeChat chat is fine).
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

“An individual can move faster, a group can go further.”

entry.title: 2021 Year in Review: Baby, Career, and Growth
entry.content:
2021 has passed. Taking advantage of the New Year holiday, I’d like to look back at the year. This will be a casual review—writing whatever comes to mind. 2021 for me was marked by becoming a father, changing jobs (including a long, boring spell at home in between), and making new friends. Overall, it was a pretty good year.

However, in terms of personal growth, I feel like I might have stagnated or even regressed, which is a bit alarming. Learning is like rowing upstream; if you don’t move forward, you fall back. In 2022, I need to spend more time working through things properly. I hope to progress together with everyone reading this.

I’ve also tallied some data related to my technical sharing, shared my income from these platforms, and listed some hardware and software I recommend. Feel free to take a look.

Historical record (reviewed October 2026): This post preserves my 2021 experiences, platform statistics, and personal reflections. The software and hardware lists describe what I used then; “latest” models and old shopping links are not current buying guidance.

2021’s Greatest Achievement: “Little Orange”

The highlight of my year was definitely the addition of “Little Orange” to our family. Experiencing fatherhood has been incredible—our duo became a trio. She’s almost ten months old now and is an absolute angel. We don’t ask for much; just that she grows up healthy and happy. Mom and Dad will always be your strongest support.

Technical Sharing Statistics

Blog Data

I added 8 new articles to the blog in 2021. The Systrace series is finally complete with 18 articles total! (Go ahead and read those while I prepare the Perfetto version…)

  1. Systrace Smoothness in Practice 1: Understanding Jank
  2. Systrace Smoothness in Practice 2: MIUI Desktop Scroll Analysis
  3. Systrace Smoothness in Practice 3: Common Questions
  4. Systrace Responsiveness in Practice 1: Understanding Principles
  5. Systrace Responsiveness in Practice 2: Case Study — App Launch
  6. Systrace Responsiveness in Practice 3: Extended Knowledge
  7. Android System Development (1): Downloading, Compiling, and Flashing Android 12
  8. What Should a Book on Android Smoothness Contain?

Writing only 8 articles is a far cry from my initial goal of one per week. That was a bit ridiculous in hindsight. I won’t set such a high bar for 2022—perhaps two per month is more realistic.

I also maintained an Android Weekly column on Zhihu. Feel free to subscribe: https://www.zhihu.com/column/c_1278963991947780096

The blog AndroidPerformance uses Google Analytics. Comparing 2021 to 2020, the numbers are looking good:

Active Users grew by 38.9% compared to 2020. (The obvious dips are the New Year, May Day, and National Day holidays—good to see people aren’t “grinding” during breaks!)

Most Visited Pages are still primarily from the Android Systrace series.

WeChat Official Account Data

Followers for the AndroidPerformance account currently stand at 7,364. Since I don’t post many original articles and have many reposts, growth is slow. Most active users are long-time followers. Data for individual posts doesn’t mean much in the closed WeChat environment, so I won’t list it. I hope to break 10,000 in 2022.

Writing on WeChat is convenient for readers but unfriendly for creators—mostly because you can’t include external links. It feels like turning the internet into a local area network.

Zhihu

I have over 20,000 followers on Zhihu, but the platform seems to care less about technical content these days, so I haven’t been very active. Most articles I see are just reposts. I find myself spending more time on Jike and Twitter, where real developer activity is higher.

Juejin

Juejin still has a strong technical atmosphere. I browse it often, although it feels like it’s missing “something.” I’ll continue syncing my articles there, otherwise, others will just do it for me (and change the author!).

Jike

Fellow “Jiyou” (Jike users) can add me:

Other Platforms

  1. CSDN: …can be ignored.
  2. Weibo: …can be ignored.
  3. Twitter: I follow many domestic and international tech gurus. The technical vibe is quite good.

Making Money? Just Making Friends

I listened to Happy Xiao’s podcast recently, where he shared that his technical sharing earned him about 2,500 RMB a month. Looking at my own 2021 income in this area… it’s quite humble.

  1. Blog Income: 0. Actually negative, if you count domain and server costs.
  2. WeChat Account: I don’t use mid-article ads, so ad revenue is negligible. It’s mostly donations from readers, which totaled 1,039 RMB.
  3. Xiaozhuanlan: Totaled 560 RMB.

So, total income was 1,039 + 560 = 1,599 RMB. That’s about 133 RMB per month. Clearly not a gold mine! As the saying goes, “just making friends.” But I truly appreciate the donations—they pay for the extra egg in my breakfast! (If you’d like to support, you can scan the code at the end of any of my original articles.)

Speaking of friends, I did add many new tech peers this year. We started four WeChat groups. My general feeling there is: “Everyone’s a master except me.” Sometimes I wonder how I ended up in the group. There’s so much I don’t know, or only half understand. My goal for 2022 is to solidify my foundations and systematize my knowledge to keep up with their discussions.

If you find my content helpful, you can “buy me a chicken leg” below:

2022 Plans

New Year goals are a cliché, but here they are anyway. I’ll set them first and then break them into weekly and daily actions. Who knows, maybe I’ll actually manage them:

  1. Fitness: Walking to work, basketball, running, rowing machine, and home gym equipment (holding “Little Orange” counts too!).
  2. Improve English Reading/Listening: Listening to English podcasts, watching tech videos, and reading English books/articles. Using iPad split-screen with Youdao Dictionary is a great workflow.
  3. Systematize Knowledge: Read and write more code, read more books, and write a performance-related ebook.
  4. Update the Blog More Frequently: Goal set above.
  5. Grow The Performance Knowledge Planet with the team (June 20, 2022 update: paid membership temporarily paused): I can only do so much on my own. A few of us started this paid community to help readers and put a little pressure on ourselves. (How else will I find out what I can squeeze out of myself?)
  6. Try New Content: Podcasts, video, Vlogs, photography.
  7. Efficient Work: More thinking, summarizing, and sharing. Use tools to boost productivity.

2021 Software Recommendations

The software that brought me the most joy in 2021:

  1. Notion: For notes and planning. https://www.notion.so/
  2. Typora: The tool I used to write this very blog. https://typora.io/
  3. GitHub Copilot: Your AI coding companion. https://copilot.github.com/
  4. flomo: For recording fleeting thoughts. https://flomoapp.com/
  5. DeepL: Marketed then as the world’s most accurate translator; that slogan is not a benchmark covering every language and text type. https://www.deepl.com/

2021 Hardware Recommendations

Hardware I’ve tinkered with and highly recommend:

  1. NAS (Personal Cloud): Essential for data management.
  2. Electrostatic Capacity Keyboard: A godsend for programmers and writers.
  3. Xiaomi 27-inch 4K Monitor: Great value for the price.
  4. Apple TV 4K: The new model in 2021 was the second-generation A2169. A NAS, software router, and iPhone were parts of my setup, not universal prerequisites. Basic setup needs internet, a display with HDMI, and a suitable HDMI cable; manual setup works without an iPhone. 4K/HDR playback needs the corresponding display capabilities. Check account-region and availability requirements for the services you use rather than assuming everyone needs a Hong Kong or US account. See Apple’s setup guide.
  5. JOY25 Electric Standing Desk: The 1.8m width feels great. I couldn’t find a Loctek that wide, and I reckon this desk could last me ten years. Tired of standing? Sit down. Tired of sitting? Stand up again.

What Do I Want Most in 2022?

I feel my M1 Mac Mini is already starting to feel slow compared to the M1 Max MacBook Pro… Cook must be practicing remote magic.

Wanting one and needing one are different things. I need to be sensible about spending. (If the Mini breaks, though, I can replace it.)

Also, this chair looks amazing! (https://item.taobao.com/item.htm?id=614505490996)

And of course, who would say no to the latest iPhone 13 Pro Max?

Conclusion

2021 was a bit underwhelming professionally, but family life with “Little Orange” brought a lot of joy. Personal growth felt stagnant, which comes down to my own lack of self-discipline.

I hope everyone reading this can make progress together in 2022. Let’s keep at it!

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: What Should Be in a Book About Android Smoothness?
entry.content:
Recently, I read a new book: Building Smooth Android Apps (JD link: https://item.jd.com/10035215362170.html). I bought it because of the title, and after reading it, I felt it was necessary to write an article so that colleagues who haven’t bought it yet can understand what it’s about.

My personal suggestion is: if you are an experienced developer, I don’t recommend buying it. This book doesn’t go into much depth on principles and doesn’t offer a comprehensive overview of Android smoothness. If you are a beginner, it’s decent for broadening your horizons and identifying gaps in your knowledge, but it’s still a bit lacking for a deep understanding of Android smoothness.

I say this because the book doesn’t focus much on performance or smoothness. It lacks deep theoretical parts. Instead, a large portion is dedicated to static code analysis, using Android Studio Profiler, App architecture, app stay-alive techniques, network performance optimization, APK size optimization, app power consumption, etc. These topics are covered briefly and at a shallow level.

Reading note (reviewed October 2026): This is a book review and proposed outline from 2021. The personal opinions remain unchanged. Book links and WeRead availability record that period, not current stock or access. The updates below clarify performance categories and tool/version boundaries.

Content Overview

Here is a brief introduction to the book’s content and chapters:

  1. Overview: Briefly introduces why performance optimization is needed and how to configure Android Studio.
  2. Static Code Analysis: Covers various static analysis tools in detail, such as Android Lint, CheckStyle, SpotBugs, PMD, etc. Except for Lint, I hadn’t used the others much, so this was a good refresher.
  3. Performance Optimization with Android Profiler: Focuses on the CPU, Memory, and Network Profilers within the AS Profiler tool. The emphasis is on tool usage, with high-level introductions.
  4. High-Quality Apps Start with Architecture: Discusses architectural principles like MVC, MVP, and MVVM.
  5. Elegant App Stay-Alive Techniques: A brief introduction to techniques for keeping apps running in the background.
  6. Network Performance Optimization: Covers network interaction, multi-threading, and large-scale data transfer optimization.
  7. Optimizing APK Size: The usual topics: multi-channel packaging, resource optimization, and code obfuscation.
  8. App Power Consumption and Crash Experience Optimization: A brief overview of these areas.

As you can see from the chapter titles, there is relatively little content specifically about “smoothness.” The topics are quite diverse. If you’re interested, you can buy a copy to take a look.

What Do I Think a Book on Smoothness Should Contain?

I couldn’t write such a book myself, and I have great respect for technical authors. But that doesn’t stop me offering my “armchair” opinions. I’m good at that part. If I were to write this book, I would include the following content to ensure readers gain a deep understanding of Android smoothness principles and become proficient in using various tools to analyze issues.

In Android performance discussions, jank, responsiveness, and ANR often appear together, but they are not severity levels of the same condition. Jank concerns whether frames arrive at the expected cadence; responsiveness concerns the delay from an action to its visible result; an ANR is triggered when the system detects a timeout in a particular situation. ANR types have different triggering conditions and timeout rules. Main-thread blocking can affect all three, but many dropped frames do not automatically imply an ANR, and slow responses need not be rendering problems. Here, “smoothness” is a broad organizing term. User reports still require a specific symptom and measurement definition. See the official guides to rendering performance and ANR diagnosis.

Here is my proposed chapter structure:

  1. Chapter 1: Overview of Android Smoothness: Concepts from the perspectives of users, developers, testers, AOSP, and hardware. It’s important not to limit your thinking to just one role.
  2. Chapter 2: Overview of Android Runtime Mechanisms: Essential knowledge for analyzing smoothness. Once you understand these, you can picture what is happening: what did the user do, how did the system respond, where has the app got to, what might be wrong, and which tool would help you check?
    • App Main Thread Principles (Main Thread vs. Render Thread)
    • Message, Handler, MessageQueue, and Looper mechanisms
    • Screen Refresh Mechanism and Vsync
    • Choreographer mechanism
    • Buffer and SurfaceFlinger workflows
    • Input handling flow
    • Design philosophy of ANRs
  3. Chapter 3: Performance Analysis Tools: A craftsman is only as good as his tools. This chapter would go beyond simple introductions, explaining regular performance analysis tools in the context of system mechanisms: Perfetto and the older Systrace tool, AS Profiler, Simpleperf, MAT, Log tools (analysis and principles), Command-line tools (dumpsys for meminfo, gfxinfo, cpuinfo, SurfaceFlinger, activity, input, window, etc.), and Third-party libraries (Koom, Matrix, Profilo, BlockCanary, LeakCanary, Tailor/Raphael, etc.).
  4. Chapter 4: Deep Dive into Android Jank: Practical strategies for identifying causes, workflows for analysis, case studies, and coding best practices.
  5. Chapter 5: Deep Dive into Android Responsiveness: Similar to the above, but focused on responsiveness issues.
  6. Chapter 6: Deep Dive into Android ANR: Understanding the design, types, causes, and analysis workflows for ANRs, along with case studies and best practices. (Likely a very detailed chapter).
  7. Chapter 7: Deep Dive into Android Memory Issues: Memory is a critical performance metric. This chapter would cover app memory footprint, analysis tools, memory leaks, and continuous growth analysis.
  8. Chapter 8: Performance Testing: Smoothness from a testing perspective: retrieving metrics (intrusive vs. non-intrusive), setting standards, competitor analysis, bug reporting flows, full-device testing, third-party specifications and platform metrics (the original examples include the Green Alliance, Master Lu, Umeng, and Bugly; distinguish specifications, scores, and monitoring services rather than treating them as one authoritative standard), and monitoring and test automation (components such as Matrix and KOOM, action drivers such as Fastbot and UI Automator, and scenarios such as memory growth). Also covers soft skills: distinguishing between system and app issues and arguing it out with PMs and developers (kidding!).
  9. Chapter 9: Online Performance Monitoring: Unlike offline testing, online monitoring must reflect real user experience with minimal impact while ensuring timely data reporting.
  10. Chapter 10: Introduction to System Performance Optimization: How do Android system developers (AOSP, Qualcomm, MTK, OEMs) optimize performance?
  11. Chapter 11: High-Efficiency Work Guide:
    • Necessity and process of compiling AOSP code.
    • Tips for reading AOSP code (cs.android.com, importing into AS/VS Code, flowcharts).
    • Recommended dev environments (Windows, Linux, Mac) and command-line configurations.
    • Work habits: writing, recording, summarizing, and sharing.

That’s my “armchair” outline. Everything is ready—just waiting for an expert to fill in the content!

Tools and validation update (October 2026): The chapter outline remains, with these distinctions for present-day use.

  • System tracing: Systrace and Perfetto are distinct tools. Android’s guidance recommends Perfetto for Android 10 and later. On supported Android 12 (API 31) and later systems, FrameTimeline also lets you compare expected and actual frame timelines. Check whether the capture covers the required data, windows, and frame types; an average FPS alone is insufficient.
  • App tools: Treat the book’s Profiler UI as historical. The current Network Inspector is under Android Studio’s View > Tool Windows > App Inspection. Maintenance differs across libraries: Profilo’s official repository is archived, so treat it as a historical implementation rather than a default integration for a new project. Check other libraries individually for version compatibility.
  • Reproducible tests: Macrobenchmark can measure startup and interactions such as scrolling, with traces for investigation. Control the scenario, device, build type, compilation state, and repetitions, and record factors such as thermal state. UI Automator and Fastbot drive actions; they do not automatically establish a universal smoothness pass criterion.
  • Development hosts: App development on Windows, Linux, or macOS is distinct from building the AOSP operating system. Current AOSP requirements specify a 64-bit x86 host running 64-bit Linux. Official macOS support for Android OS development ended with Android 11.

What Other Performance Books Are Available?

Many books on the market are a bit dated. However, the Juejin community has a wealth of articles on Android performance, and many large companies open-source their internal tools. Let’s keep moving forward on the shoulders of giants.

Here are a few books I’ve read:

  1. Evaluation and Optimization of Mobile App Performance by Tencent TMQ: Published in 2016, very professional and practical. (Available on WeChat Reading). Original book link.

  2. Understanding Android: Java Virtual Machine ART by Deng Fanping (邓凡平): A massive tome on the ART VM, helpful for understanding “black tech” involving the VM. (Available on WeChat Reading). Original book link.

  3. High-Performance Android Apps by Doug Sillars: Published in 2016, an early comprehensive guide. Original book link.

  4. Best Practices for Android App Performance Optimization by Tencent developers: Published in 2017. (Available on WeChat Reading). Original book link.

  5. BPF Performance Tools by Brendan Gregg: Chinese edition published in 2020. A fundamental tool for system performance. Original book link.

  6. Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud by Brendan Gregg: Chinese edition published in 2020. A must-have for anyone doing performance work. (Available on WeChat Reading). Original book link.

  7. Android Development Master Class by Zhang Shaowen (Geek Time column): Listening to it again recently, all I could think was: the man really knows his stuff.

    Original course link

  8. Linux Performance Optimization by Ni Pengfei.

Final Thoughts

  1. Feel free to share your own recommendations for Android performance books, blogs, videos, or tutorials.
  2. What do you think should be included in a book about Android smoothness?
  3. This article is for sharing only, with no promotional links.
  4. Feedback is welcome on my Zhihu or WeChat accounts, or via WeChat (553000664) with “Blog” in the request.
    • This article on Zhihu
    • This article on WeChat

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal introduction and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro: Includes personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Welcome to recommend projects/articles.
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Android System Development Series (1): Downloading, Compiling, and Flashing Android 12
entry.content:
Android 12 source was released in 2021. My test phone at the time was a Pixel 3 XL. This article keeps that hands-on record and pins the release-build example to android-12.0.0_r3. Verify version mappings in the AOSP tags/build numbers table.

Compiling the code locally offers several advantages:

  1. Direct Debugging: You can flash the build onto a physical device for local debugging and import the code into Android Studio.
  2. Userdebug Builds: These provide additional debugging capabilities. adb root/remount still depends on adbd, AVB/verity, partition layout, and build configuration. A userdebug build does not make every directory writable or replace an app’s own debugging permissions.
  3. Studying the System: You can enable more system debug logs, add your own, and change the code to see how it works.

Historical version note (reviewed 2026-10-14): Android 12 r3, Pixel 3 XL, and the 2021 screenshots are references for studying an old release, not recommendations for current devices or production firmware. The r3 security patch level is 2021-10-05. Some original screenshots instead show the master development branch: Tiramisu/AOSP.MASTER does not prove an Android 12 r3 build. They are retained with explanations below.

For current AOSP, use the download and build guides. In a separate checkout, the documented android-latest-release branch follows current releases; it does not pin Android 12:

This is the current guide’s Cuttlefish virtual-device example, not a Pixel 3 XL flashing target. Its product-release_config-variant format differs from Android 12’s product-variant. Check availability in the actual checkout and save repo manifest -r output to identify revisions. Do not mix vendor files across releases. The USTC mirror limits concurrency to four, so do not copy the official-server -j8 setting there.

For source browsing alone, use cs.android.com. Reproducing this article requires:

  1. A matching Pixel 3 XL (crosshatch) whose bootloader can be unlocked. Pixel 3 is blueline and is a different target. SIM unlocking does not imply bootloader unlocking; “Pixel 3 or newer” does not mean all later models can run Android 12.
  2. An x86-64 Linux host with a case-sensitive filesystem and sufficient storage/RAM. The historical host screenshot shows Ubuntu 18.04.6. The old 32GB suggestion was contemporary experience, not a current guarantee; swap is not equivalent RAM. Current official requirements specify at least 400GB free storage and 64GB RAM. Old-branch resource needs still depend on target and parallelism.

1. Downloading the Code

At the time, downloading from Google’s servers in China could be painfully slow; even .repo could get stuck. That is why I used the USTC AOSP mirror as an alternative here; the official download guide remains the reference. Follow mirror protocol and concurrency rules. Its current documentation uses HTTPS, replacing the old git:// URLs in this article.

Download into the Linux filesystem you will build from. Running Git/Repo commands on WSL2 or macOS does not establish a validated Android 12 build/USB-flashing environment. Do not assume Windows-mounted or case-insensitive directories meet source-tree requirements.

1.1 Step 1: Download the Repo Tool

On Ubuntu repositories that provide the package, install the launcher using the official setup instructions:

If your distribution lacks the package, use the official manual download/signature-verification procedure. Do not install an HTTP error page as an executable or edit the launcher’s internal REPO_URL. The launcher and downloaded Repo tool can have different versions; retain the actual repo version output.

1.2 Step 2: Configure Personal Information

If you haven’t installed Git yet, do so first. Then configure your identity:

1.3 Step 3: Create a Working Directory

1.4 Step 4: Initialize the Repository

Choose the version first. For this article, use the pinned Android 12 r3 tag in section 1.4.2. Keep current-branch experiments in a separate checkout. -b selects a manifest branch or tag; device/build-matched binaries are required regardless of whether the option appears.

1.4.1 Original Default-Branch Workflow (Historical)

The original unpinned workflow used the then-current master branch. It did not download every Android release or guarantee Android 12. Repo defaults and remote settings can change; select the version explicitly.

If access to the Repo tool’s own repository fails, the mirror documents this exported variable:

This setting is separate from the manifest’s -u URL; do not edit the launcher. Continue with the pinned tag below for this example, and run the shell setup in section 3.2 for either workflow.

1.4.2 Option B: Download a Specific Tag

Use the build numbers table to select a version for the device. This original 2021 list is a historical snapshot, not a claim that Android 12 has only two tags:

This example pins android-12.0.0_r3, mapped to SP1A.210812.016.A1, with Pixel 3 XL in its supported-device list. Selecting a tag pins the manifest; it does not automatically make a shallow clone, retain only one commit, or guarantee a smaller download.

For the official server, change -u to https://android.googlesource.com/platform/manifest and retain the tag. Recheck manifest, device configuration, and binaries when changing versions; do not reuse a vendor directory from an unrelated tag.

1.5 Step 5: Sync the Code

repo init configures the Repo client and manifest; project content still needs synchronization. USTC limits concurrency to four:

-c focuses on the manifest-required branch; it does not turn every repository into a shallow clone. Inspect the failing project and error before retrying. Transient network failures can be retried; insufficient disk space, missing refs, permissions, and local changes need specific fixes. Avoid indefinite three-second retries that obscure persistent failures. Proceed only after sync exits successfully.

2. Downloading Drivers (Proprietary Binaries)

Physical-device builds need matching proprietary binaries. These can include HALs, userspace libraries, vendor images, and firmware; they are not all driver source code. Match the device, source Build ID, and vendor instructions regardless of the presence of -b. These files are also distinct from Google Apps or Pixel Launcher.

2.1 Drivers for the Master Branch

Preview binaries apply only to listed device/development-build combinations, not arbitrary master/main commits. The original image’s build number 7798681 is historical and does not replace the r3 binaries:

If matching binaries are unavailable, do not infer compatibility from the Pixel model alone. Select a supported combination or a corresponding virtual-device target.

2.2 Drivers for a Specific Tag

On the Google driver binaries page, select Pixel 3 XL / Android 12.0.0 / SP1A.210812.016.A1. The r3 mapping is also confirmed by build_id.mk.

The image also includes SP1A.210812.015; select the correct row. Download both the matching Google vendor image and Qualcomm package, checking each SHA-256 against the page. Do not mix versions.

2.3 Extracting Drivers

Unpack the matching archives and run their extraction scripts from the source root. Read the license and confirm only if you accept it; do not treat typing I ACCEPT as a substitute for review. These filenames are specific to the example:

Check the generated files under vendor/google_devices/crosshatch and vendor/qcom/crosshatch. Extraction success means files were written, not that the combination is compatible or bootable.

3. Compiling the Code

This target uses an x86-64 Linux build host. macOS platform-build support ended in 2021; browsing the source on a Mac does not establish that this Android 12 target can be built there.

3.1 Initializing the Build Environment

Install host dependencies using the official setup guide. This is its general Ubuntu package list. Older extras such as libncurses5 from the original article are not necessarily available under the same names on newer distributions.

Android 12’s old prebuilt tools can still require older host libraries. Diagnose the failing tool and use a matching Linux environment; do not treat arbitrary old-library downloads or system-library replacement as a universal fix. Use the toolchain selected by the checked-out branch rather than applying a current Android branch’s JDK requirements.

3.2 Setting Up the Shell Environment

Every time you open a new terminal, you must run:

3.3 Selecting a Target

The Android 12 r3 AndroidProducts.mk lists aosp_crosshatch-userdebug. Pixel 3 XL is crosshatch; select the name rather than a historical menu number:

The original menu numbered it 25; numbering can change:

The next configuration image belongs to the historical master build. It shows PLATFORM_VERSION=Tiramisu and BUILD_ID=AOSP.MASTER, not the expected r3 output. Check product, version, and Build ID, not merely the userdebug variant.

3.4 Starting the Build

The first full build means a long wait, especially if CPU or memory is limited. Run m for the selected product’s default build. -jN controls parallelism; otherwise the build system selects it. More jobs do not guarantee a faster build and can increase memory pressure.

Interpret helper commands using Android 12 envsetup.sh:

CommandScope
m / m droidNormal selected-product build, not all products at once
m <module>An existing module target; not proof that every flashable image was updated
mma / mmma <dir>Modules in the current/specified directory and their dependencies
crootReturn to the source-tree root
m help / hmmBuild-target/environment-command help
m cleanClear the configured output directory’s contents; check OUT_DIR first, rather than assuming the current directory’s out/

The branch defines what m all includes; it is not a promise to compile every Android.mk independently. Android 12 Soong’s clean implementation clears the actual output location and preserves its directory. Routine incremental builds do not need a clean each time.

This is another original master-build image with contemporary deprecation warnings, not a new r3 validation:

The recorded successful build took 03:40:47. That duration does not generalize across hardware, branches, or cache states. Confirm a successful exit and matching target artifacts for your own build before flashing.

4. Flashing the Device

Use a dedicated test device and match its Pixel 3 XL target, binaries, and artifacts. Bootloader unlocking and the -w option below erase user data; back up first. Enabling OEM unlocking is not itself unlocking. If needed, follow the official procedure: run fastboot flashing unlock in bootloader mode and confirm on the device. Do not casually relock a device running an unverified custom image.

Check adb/fastboot versions and the connected target. Keep the configured envsetup/lunch shell so ANDROID_PRODUCT_OUT points to this build’s crosshatch output. With multiple devices, select the intended serial using -s.

The original adb reboot fastboot enters userspace fastbootd on supported devices, unlike adb reboot bootloader. The flashing tool may change modes for dynamic partitions; see the fastbootd documentation. Do not bypass partition or compatibility checks with --force.

The Android 12 fastboot implementation reads flashall images from ANDROID_PRODUCT_OUT and normally reboots on completion. A second fastboot reboot is not mandatory. flashall is not a universal replacement for matching bootloader/radio firmware; resolve firmware mismatches using the device-specific official procedure.

The top of the old image contains an earlier command error; the later flashall shows OKAY/Finished. That is historical tool output, not current r3 device acceptance. After booting, compare ro.build.id, ro.product.device, and ro.build.type with the built artifacts, then check required USB/display/network functions. Reaching a home screen does not validate all hardware.

I found the AOSP Launcher I had just built pretty ugly and bare-bones. Without Google’s closed-source extras, it looked rather sparse. I much preferred the official Pixel Launcher. That was my reaction to those 2021 builds, not a review of their current versions.

For restoration, select the matching device in Google Factory Images and follow its version/anti-rollback instructions. Restoration can erase data and is not guaranteed to fix every flashing or hardware failure.

5. What’s Next?

This guide focused on downloading, compiling, and flashing. I will cover how to import code into an IDE, modify modules, and debug in a follow-up article.

About Me && Blog

Below are my personal details and links. I look forward to connecting and sharing knowledge with fellow developers!

  1. About Me: Includes my WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Navigation: A guide to the content on this blog.
  3. Curated Android Performance Articles: A collection of must-read performance optimization articles. Self-nominations/recommendations are welcome!
  4. Android Performance Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

“If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”

entry.title: Android Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3 - Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
entry.content:
Jank, slow response, and ANRs can share causes or occur together, but they are not three severity levels of the same problem. When a user says an app feels slow, first distinguish uneven animation, a long delay after an action, and a system-detected failure to respond.

Animation and scrolling stutter is usually called jank. Long startup, screen wake-up, or navigation delays are slow response / high latency. An ANR depends on a specific system timeout condition. Frame-drop rate, startup duration, and ANR rate measure different things.

This is the third article in the Responsiveness series, focusing on extended knowledge when using Systrace to analyze app responsiveness, including startup speed testing, log interpretation, state analysis, and third-party startup libraries.

Versions and historical context (reviewed 2026-10-14): The 2021 figures and chapter structure are retained. Traceview is deprecated; the text uses Android Studio CPU Profiler terminology and corrects the sampling unit. Thread/component examples are checked against AOSP Android 10/11, command units against Android 16, and dependency/lazy initialization behavior against App Startup 1.2.0. Figures from different tools are not one experiment; corrected text takes precedence over old state, component, and readiness annotations.

Table of Contents

  • 1. Interpretation of the Three Process States in Systrace
  • 2. Using TraceView for Responsiveness Analysis
  • 3. Using SimplePerf for Startup Speed Analysis
  • 4. Locating Other Component Startups in Systrace
  • 5. Can AppStartup Optimize Startup Speed?
  • 6. Using IdleHandler in App Startup Scenarios
  • Series Articles
  • References
  • About Me && Blog

If you are not familiar with the basic use of Systrace (Perfetto), please catch up on the Systrace Basics Series first. This article assumes you are already familiar with using Systrace (Perfetto).

Systrace Series Articles:

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

1. Interpretation of the Three Process States in Systrace

These are thread scheduling states, not one state for an entire process. A main thread can wait while a worker runs. Older Systrace viewers commonly show Running in green, Runnable in blue, and Sleep as blank space. Colors depend on the viewer; function-slice colors do not identify scheduling state.

Select the thread-state track and inspect its label and scheduling events. Other states, including uninterruptible waits, also exist. Blank or missing data is not automatically Sleep.

1.1 Analyzing the Sleep State

Sleep means the thread is neither running nor waiting to be scheduled on a CPU. It does not by itself distinguish “active/passive” waiting or establish that the wait is harmless. Common causes include Looper polling, synchronous Binder replies, locks/conditions, and explicit sleeps. nativePollOnce waiting with no due message can be normal, but a missing startup task, delayed message, or synchronization barrier may still need investigation.

The figure contains an IWindowSession.remove Binder call. Correlate its interval with thread-state intervals. Synchronous calls can wait for the remote side; oneway calls have different semantics. Call count alone does not establish a bottleneck: inspect accumulated critical-path waits and remote work.

Select binder transaction to follow request and reply flows:

The selected transaction has a 34.216 ms wall duration, not necessarily 34.216 ms of Sleep or remote CPU work. This figure’s outgoing flow is 29928→1515 and incoming return is 1515→29928. Its bottom annotation mistakenly calls the outgoing flow “incoming.” Verify transaction identity and receiving thread rather than treating any incoming flow as a reply.

Wakeup information helps continue the dependency investigation:

Here, wakeup from tid: 1515 identifies the observed waker, not automatically a lock owner, complete wait object, or root cause. Inspect the preceding stack, remote work, and subsequent scheduling. A method named invokeSuspend also does not mean that its OS thread slept throughout the method slice.

1.2 Analyzing the Running State

Running means the thread is scheduled on a CPU. If an interval grows, compare workload and inputs before examining CPU capacity, frequency, cache/memory behavior, and context switches. A function’s wall interval may include multiple Running and waiting intervals; it is not the same as CPU time.

The selected execution is on CPU 0; the second image shows a 5.112 ms selection. Neither establishes the CPU topology or numeric frequency. It therefore cannot prove “the wrong little core” or insufficient frequency. Foreground UI/RenderThread work is not guaranteed to stay on big cores: scheduling also depends on energy, thermal limits, affinity, and available capacity.

1.3 Analyzing the Runnable State

A sleeping thread becomes eligible to run when woken, then executes when scheduled. A preempted Running thread can return to Runnable as well. Runnable does not guarantee immediate execution, and very short intervals may be hard to see at the current zoom level.

This older figure primarily illustrates Java thread states, not the Linux scheduler state machine. Java Thread.State RUNNABLE can include waiting for CPU time; RUNNING and READY are not separate enum constants. VM BLOCKED is also different from a kernel uninterruptible wait. A waiter notified by Object.notify must reacquire the monitor; notification does not mean it immediately enters Running.

For long Runnable intervals, examine allowed CPUs, priority, cpuset/affinity, competing work, and available capacity. System-wide saturation is one possible cause. Restricted placement or higher-priority work on eligible CPUs can also delay a thread while other CPUs are idle.

2. Using TraceView for Responsiveness Analysis

The historical heading says TraceView, but the screenshot is Android Studio CPU Profiler. Standalone Traceview is deprecated; for Android Studio 3.2 and later, the official guide recommends CPU Profiler. Distinguish method sampling/instrumentation, system tracing, and the viewer used to inspect them.

2.1 Capturing TraceView During Startup

This is an ART Java/Kotlin method-sampling diagnostic, not a general native-stack capture or end-to-end startup benchmark. Check the device’s am start --help, target debugging permissions, and writable output path first. --sampling is in microseconds: 1000 microseconds equals 1 ms. The original --sampling 1 did not mean one sample per millisecond. See the AOSP Android 16 command help.

-S stops the target package to avoid reusing its process; it does not clear file caches/app data or reproduce the Launcher touch path. Resolve launch failures, permission errors, or Activity reuse before interpreting results. An empty trace is not a fast startup. Stop after the agreed scenario completes, rather than assuming ten seconds means fully loaded. Import steps and format compatibility depend on your Studio version.

2.2 Interpreting TraceView

After importing the method trace, confirm process/thread, selected interval, sampling versus instrumentation mode, and timing basis. Green regions in these older figures include bundled third-party libraries, not only the app author’s code. Interpret colors using method names and the viewer’s legend.

In Top Down/Bottom Up views, distinguish inclusive time from self time; do not add parent and child totals twice. Sampling can miss short calls, so its timeline and counts are not a complete invocation log.

Application.onCreate

Activity.onCreate

doFrame

WebView Initialization

This WebView figure includes Tencent TBS/X5 classes. It illustrates that sample’s third-party implementation, not a universal system WebView initialization stack.

2.3 Pros and Cons

Method sampling has statistical error; instrumentation records more method boundaries but can introduce greater runtime overhead. They are different capture modes, not one “TraceView high-frequency sampling” mode. A requested short interval does not guarantee samples arrive at that rate, especially for a one-microsecond request.

Use profiles to find hotspots and call relationships, and compare them with explicit timing definitions, sample counts, and overhead controls. Recheck final startup latency with lower-overhead system tracing/benchmarks; a profiling-perturbed method duration is not automatically the user’s real delay.

3. Using SimplePerf for Startup Speed Analysis

simpleperf can sample Java/Kotlin and native call stacks, subject to Android version, permissions, symbols, and unwind information. The official guide documents interpreted/JIT/AOT Java support from Android 9 and profileable release-app support from Android 10. It does not promise complete stacks from any production APK.

Run from your installed NDK/simpleperf scripts directory and check that version’s --help. This example follows the official application profiling guide, specifying the Activity and recording parameters:

The current script’s -a path attempts to stop an existing process before starting recording and the Activity. Keep the script/NDK version and logs and confirm the resulting startup state. With only -p, ensure the target is not running, wait for the recorder to be ready, then launch manually. Finish recording; do not kill the app just to end the capture. Process discovery/attachment has timing limits and need not cover every earliest instruction. The original historical log below explicitly uses a ten-second recording duration:

After a successful capture, report_html.py reads perf.data to generate the report. Keep matching unstripped native libraries, binary_cache, and any required obfuscation mapping. Unknown stacks do not mean no cost.

Flamegraph width represents sampled event weight; horizontal position is not startup chronology. The example’s task-clock:u covers user-space on-CPU work, not a direct explanation of Binder/lock waits or kernel cost. Check device support before using off-CPU features, or combine profiles with a system trace. Distinguish missing samples, lost samples, and missing symbols.

Further documentation:

  1. simpleperf README
  2. Android Application Profiling
  3. Android Platform Profiling
  4. Executable Commands Reference
  5. Scripts Reference

4. Locating Other Component Startups in Systrace

4.1 Service Startup

This excerpt is from AOSP android-11.0.0_r1 ActivityThread, with debug logging omitted. It is framework source, not code to paste directly into an app.

The system schedules Service creation/binding through ApplicationThread, which posts work to H on the app main thread. A returned startService call does not mean Service.onCreate has run; system scheduling or process creation may still intervene. MessageQueue considers due times, synchronization barriers, and async status, not just submission order.

These callbacks follow a doFrame in this sample; this is not a guarantee that Services run after the first frame, nor proof that the frame has been physically presented. The image’s “register receiver” annotation also needs correction: broadcastReceiveComp identifies component broadcast delivery, not receiver registration.

4.2 Custom Messages

This is a Handler callback interval with an AndroidX LiveData class in its label. Inspect the Handler/Runnable and nested calls before attributing all such work to custom app logic.

4.3 Service Startup Visualized

The label is LoadedApk$ServiceDispatcher$RunConnection: client-side connection-state dispatch, which can invoke ServiceConnection.onServiceConnected and related callbacks. It is not Service.onCreate itself. See Android 11 LoadedApk; locate creation/binding/argument delivery in the service process as well.

4.4 BroadcastReceiver Execution

broadcastReceiveComp is the execution interval for delivery to a manifest component. Handler message numbers alone are not stable cross-version identifiers.

The next image shows registration called from Activity.onStart. The registration call’s thread and a later onReceive callback’s thread are separate matters. Dynamic receivers normally receive callbacks on the main thread; overloads with a scheduler Handler can change delivery. Registration does not automatically choose its calling thread for future callbacks. Match registration lifetime with unregistration.

4.5 ContentProvider Startup Timing

In the normal Android 11 process-binding path, initial providers for that process are installed after Application creation/attachment and before Application.onCreate. Every Activity launch does not initialize every provider in the APK, and each query does not rerun onCreate. The publishContentProviders marker reports installed providers to the system; that Binder interval is not the total provider initialization cost.

5. Can AppStartup Optimize Startup Speed?

Third-Party Library Initialization

Some libraries quietly initialize themselves even though you never called their initialization method in Application.onCreate. A common way to do that is through a manifest ContentProvider. This depends on process assignment, enabled state, and process binding; it does not mean every provider declared anywhere in the APK is initialized on every launch.

SDK behavior changes across versions. For example, WorkManager uses App Startup from 2.6; instructions for removing its old standalone provider cannot be applied unchanged to newer versions. Inspect current dependencies and the final merged manifest rather than inferring behavior from an SDK name.

This figure summarizes normal process-initialization ordering. Separate automatic initializers can add startup work and obscure dependencies. Developers are not categorically unable to control them: disabling, replacing, or deferring initialization depends on each SDK’s documented contract.

AppStartup Library

App Startup lets participating Initializers share InitializationProvider and declare prerequisites through dependencies(). It does not automatically convert arbitrary SDK providers or promise a fixed global order among unrelated initializers. AppInitializer in 1.2.0 recursively initializes dependencies, caches results, and detects cycles. Automatic initialization normally runs on the main thread; a manual call does not automatically move work to a worker thread.

The original “50+ providers” threshold and “less than 20 ms for 20–30 libraries” lack reproducible device/version/baseline and repeated-sample evidence. They are not general performance limits. Gains depend on critical-path work removed or deferred; merging entry points does not erase SDK initialization work.

To defer an existing Initializer, remove its automatic-discovery metadata within the app manifest’s <application>. Declare xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools" on the root manifest element:

Removing this metadata alone does not defer the initializer if another automatic initializer still depends on it. Inspect the dependency graph, then initialize before first use on the thread required by the SDK:

ExampleLoggerInitializer is a placeholder for your existing Initializer implementation; import androidx.startup.AppInitializer. Do not remove metadata without providing initialization, or delete the shared provider merely to defer one component. The app/SDK must still handle asynchronous completion and multiple processes.

Summary

  1. Consolidate participating components under one entry point with explicit dependencies.
  2. Move nonessential initialization off the startup critical path, checking TTID, TTFD, and first-use latency for shifted cost.
  3. Ordering does not automatically reduce work or make it asynchronous; measure repeatedly under matched conditions.

Action Items for App Developers:

  1. Inspect the target build’s merged manifest/final APK for providers, processes, and initializer metadata, not just source-manifest counts.
  2. Record initialization threads, wall/CPU time, and dependencies to identify the critical path.
  3. Check SDK requirements: what can be deferred, who triggers it, and how readiness is guaranteed before use.
  4. Verify cold launch, background entry points, multiple processes, and first use after changes. Keep failed/missing samples distinct and compare matching compilation/data conditions.

6. Using IdleHandler in App Startup Scenarios

IdleHandler runs on the Looper thread owning its MessageQueue. In AOSP Android 10 MessageQueue.next, idle handlers can run when the queue is empty or its head message is not yet due. All future messages need not have completed. An already-due synchronization barrier also affects this condition.

The original “all messages completed” annotation is too strong. Network work, background tasks, GPU work, or the next draw may remain unfinished while the main queue is momentarily idle. A continuously busy queue can also postpone an idle handler indefinitely.

  1. Defer short, nonessential work. Registering a main-queue IdleHandler in Activity.onCreate does not guarantee execution after the first frame or on a background thread. A long callback delays subsequent input/frame work. Returning false from queueIdle removes it; true retains it for future idle opportunities, not a separate loop or guaranteed timer. Remove handlers that are no longer needed when their owner’s lifecycle ends.

  1. Report full display from a business readiness condition. Activity.reportFullyDrawn() is available from API 19 to report critical content/usability; IdleHandler is not required. The old example below waits for a data-loaded signal and then one idle opportunity. Neither data arrival nor an idle queue proves the list and images have appeared.

The Android M (API 23) guard relates to using Looper.getQueue(), not the introduction of reportFullyDrawn. Define readiness for success, empty data, and error states, and avoid duplicate registration, destroyed Activities, or stale request callbacks reporting readiness. AndroidX readiness-reporting helpers still need the same explicit business conditions.

The overview image’s onWindowFocusChange should be onWindowFocusChanged. Focus does not establish initial display or content readiness, and am start -W does not measure the same event as the focus callback. Accounting across Splash→Main depends on the actual launch sequence and OS implementation. Retain separate initial/full-display definitions using the official TTID/TTFD guide.

This historical output shows SplashActivity Displayed +968 ms, MainActivity Displayed +475 ms, and Fully drawn +3s221ms; am start -W reports TotalTime 968 and WaitTime 975. These fields have different boundaries and Activity associations. Do not add/subtract them to derive a stage, or assume +3s221ms begins with physical contact on the Launcher icon. The screenshot command also sleeps five seconds before reading an existing logcat buffer, which can include older records. Correlate logs by time, package/Activity, and the specific launch.

Correct TTFD reporting complements TTID; it does not make TTID an incorrect measurement. Missing reports, data failures, and incomplete captures are distinct outcomes, not zeros.
