entry.title: Android Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2 - Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
entry.content:
Jank, slow response, and ANRs can share causes or occur together, but they are not three severity levels of the same problem. When a user says an app feels slow, first distinguish uneven animation, a long delay after an action, and a system-detected failure to respond.

Animation and scrolling stutter is usually called jank. Long startup, screen wake-up, or navigation delays are slow response / high latency. An ANR depends on a specific system timeout condition. Frame-drop rate, startup duration, and ANR rate measure different things.

This is the second article in the Responsiveness series, using Android App Cold Start as an example to explain how to use Systrace for analysis.

Historical case and versions (reviewed 2026-10-14): This article retains the 2021 WanAndroid startup example. Its figures include separate OPPO, Launcher3, and Meizu captures, without a complete matching device, firmware, APK version, and raw trace set. They cannot be joined into one precise startup timeline. AOSP Android 9/10/11 sources explain the older paths below; Android 12 splash screens and Android 16 startup accounting are identified separately. Where old image annotations conflict with the text, use the corrected explanation.

Table of Contents

  • 1. Preparation
  • 2. Analysis of Android App Cold Start Flow
  • End
  • Series Articles
  • References
  • About Me && Blog

If you are not familiar with the basic use of Systrace (Perfetto), please catch up on the Systrace Basics Series first. This article assumes you are already familiar with using Systrace (Perfetto).

Systrace Series Articles:

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

1. Preparation

This case study and the corresponding Systrace are engineering-focused and omit many details, as App startup involves a vast range of knowledge. For an extremely detailed breakdown, I recommend: Complete Analysis of Android App Startup Flow.

We will follow the system trace through the major startup modules. This figure maps trace regions to phone screens. Systrace and Perfetto are different capture/analysis tools; Perfetto UI can also open older Systrace files, but their commands are not interchangeable.

Before recording, identify the launch entry point, app version, system build, cold/warm/hot state, compilation and cache state, account/network conditions, display mode, and thermal conditions. Confirm that the target app process did not exist before a cold launch. Swiping a task away does not guarantee process termination, and a cold process does not imply cold file caches or fresh app data.

  1. Capture a basic system trace first. System Tracing is available in developer options from Android 9 (API 28); it saves Perfetto format from Android 10. See the on-device capture guide. Enable available scheduling, frequency, Input, Activity/Window Manager, View/graphics, and Binder events. Cover the interval before the tap through critical content readiness. A missing track requires checking configuration, permissions, and data loss; it does not mean zero latency.
  2. Add IRQ events when needed. Availability of the legacy Systrace irq category depends on the device and permissions. Check the installed systrace.py --help and --list-categories before selecting categories. Category lists vary by device, so avoid copying an entire list without checking support. For new captures, follow the Perfetto system tracing tutorial, and examine IRQ handlers alongside scheduling of threaded interrupts.
  3. Use IPC debugging as an optional addition. am trace-ipc enables Binder tracking; it does not recover names for every native or Java IPC call. AOSP Android 11 checks caller permissions and filters non-debuggable apps on non-debuggable systems. “Requires root” and “root reveals everything” are both incomplete descriptions. Android 9 Java Binder tracking can add call stacks and some method/transaction names, with additional overhead. Start tracking before reproducing, then stop and export:

The exported file contains IPC debugging information, not a replacement system trace. If the command fails or the target process is ineligible, use the basic Binder events; missing method names do not prove no call occurred. See Android 11 ActivityManagerService and Android 9 Binder.

If you can rebuild the app, add manual Trace sections around key initialization work or use TraceFix for bytecode instrumentation. It covers selected, instrumentable methods, not system Framework or native methods, and does not guarantee a section for every function. Check the plugin’s AGP/Gradle/JDK compatibility matrix. Limit instrumentation when investigating, and control its overhead in final timing comparisons.

Without this plugin, existing Framework, system, and custom app trace points can still be visible:

Instrumentation exposes more app method sections. These figures compare visibility; they do not establish that instrumentation has no timing cost:

2. Analysis of Android App Cold Start Flow

This case follows a cold launch from the Launcher, from touch input through the launch request and process initialization to critical UI content readiness. These are participating modules, not six serial durations to add together; animations and app initialization often overlap:

  1. Touchscreen interrupt handling.
  2. InputReader and InputDispatcher event processing.
  3. Launcher input handling.
  4. SystemServer startup event processing.
  5. Startup animations.
  6. App internal startup and logic.

Choose the start explicitly: physical contact, Input Down, Input Up, the Launcher request, or system receipt of the launch Intent. Choose the end separately: initial feedback, the destination Activity’s first frame, or critical content becoming usable. TTID and TTFD cover different intervals and are not automatically physical touch-to-photon measurements. This article examines the software path; physical input-to-display timing needs separately synchronized measurement.

We’ll trace this through Systrace’s key stages:

2.1 Touchscreen Interrupt Handling

This historical figure shows a threaded interrupt named irq/382-sec_ts. It is an early software observation point, not the exact time of finger contact. Interrupt names, numbers, and touch reporting paths are device-dependent:

The corresponding CPU scheduling and IRQ tracks follow. Scheduling exposes the interrupt thread’s execution; IRQ events expose handler intervals. They are related but distinct records:

The driver reports through Linux input/evdev; EventHub reads events, InputReader interprets them, and InputDispatcher dispatches them. Interrupt counts do not map one-to-one to Java MotionEvents. The displayed 2.427 ms is a selected interval, not a measured sensor latency or the summed CPU execution time of IRQ handlers. Attribution requires wakeup, scheduling, and driver evidence.

2.2 InputReader and InputDispatcher Stage

These Native threads in SystemServer handle input events. See Input Explained for details.

The example annotates Down, several Move events, and Up as a tap. A tap need not contain Move events, and Cancel, movement thresholds, or long-press handling may prevent a click. Verify action types in event details rather than inferring them from similar-looking slices.

After a Launcher window establishes its input channel, InputDispatcher selects targets using touch coordinates, touchable regions, window ordering, and input policy. Process creation or foreground visibility alone does not guarantee delivery of every event. The flow through SystemServer and the app is detailed in Input Explained; here are the core visualizations:

2.2.1 Event Flow in SystemServer

2.2.2 Event Flow in Launcher

These two older figures come from a Meizu Launcher capture, not the same recording as the WanAndroid example above. A falling wq generally indicates Dispatcher has received an event-finished acknowledgment, not that a frame was presented. The second image’s aq annotation also needs correction: Android 10 ViewRootImpl decrements the pending count when removing the event, before calling deliverInputEvent. Zero pending events does not prove processing has finished.

2.3 Launcher Input Handling Stage

Inspect two intervals in Launcher handling:

  1. Down to the pressed-feedback frame: for example, dimming or shrinking the icon. Updating its state and presenting that frame are different moments.
  2. Up/click recognition to the launch request: useful for examining Launcher delay. Measuring from Down or the first feedback frame also includes the user’s hold time, which is not all Launcher processing.

Desktop swipe response time is another useful measure: physical finger movement to the first visible screen movement can be examined with synchronized high-speed footage. Cross-device comparisons require matched refresh rates, gesture speeds, content, and boundaries; software traces alone do not measure that entire physical interval.

A normal icon tap passes click recognition after Up, then requests Activity launch. From Android 10, ActivityTaskManagerService (ATMS) handles Activity/Task management in SystemServer, while AMS and related modules participate in process management. The proxy in this figure is IActivityTaskManager. Notification and deep-link launches need not pass through Launcher.

This stage helps separate pre-app system/Launcher delays from app initialization. Animation coordination depends on the OS version and Launcher implementation. Icon animation, window transitions, and app preparation can overlap; slow-motion footage helps inspect continuity but cannot identify a code bottleneck by itself.

2.4 SystemServer StartActivity Stage

Focus on three kinds of work: handling the request and task/window state, coordinating existing Activity lifecycles, and requesting a target process when needed. They can interleave across threads rather than form three fixed, consecutive intervals. Multi-window and launch modes can change the path.

Processing the Launch Command

The Binder call in SystemServer is triggered by Launcher via ActivityTaskManager.getService().startActivity.

When the target process is absent, it must be created before its Activity can run. In a common path, SystemServer sends a socket request to the Zygote matching the app ABI; SystemServer does not itself execute that fork. Devices need not offer both 32-bit and 64-bit Zygotes. Android 10 ZygoteProcess already includes an optional USAP process-pool path, so not every launch has an identical on-demand fork interval.

The code image calls appZygote.getProcess().start(...), an App Zygote-related branch, not a universal implementation of ordinary Activity cold starts. The 7.343 ms Start proc selection is not pure fork CPU time; it can include request construction, communication, and waiting for a result.

Zygote 64 Executing Fork

This Java method writes to the Zygote socket and reads the PID/status on the caller side; it is not the function executing fork inside Zygote. Compare the ordinary request and USAP paths in Android 10 ZygoteProcess, then identify the actual path using process, thread, and scheduling evidence.

App Process Appearance

The old ActivityThread.main screenshot shows main Looper preparation, ActivityThread construction, attachment to the system, and entry into Looper.loop. Its source points to the then-current master without a fixed commit; it illustrates the entry path but does not identify the Android version of every capture.

The launching: com.aboback.wanandroidjetpack selection below is 904.966 ms. It is a system startup interval, excluding the preceding full icon press, and does not establish full content readiness. Check the recorded boundaries and destination Activity for that version. A SplashActivity → MainActivity flow does not universally stop accounting at SplashActivity: Android 16 ActivityMetricsLogger, for example, supports coalescing consecutive launches. Inspect the associated Activity and window-drawn events.

2.5 App Process Startup Stage

This example has a separate SplashActivity, so the following milestones help divide its startup. They are not a required architecture for every app. “UI stable” is too vague as an end condition: specify which content must be visible, which actions must work, and how errors or empty data are handled.

  1. Process Start to SplashActivity First Frame (or directly to MainActivity if no Splash).
  2. SplashActivity First Frame to MainActivity First Frame.
  3. MainActivity First Frame to Fully Loaded.

Analysis details for each:

Process Start to SplashActivity First Frame

The new process passes through runtime entry, ActivityThread.main, and attachment to the system before the system schedules work such as bindApplication. It does not jump directly from fork to app onCreate. Binding initializes a process, not every Activity launch. A process previously started for a service or broadcast may be reused when opening an Activity.

In the normal binding path in AOSP android-11.0.0_r1 ActivityThread, Application creation/attachment precedes installation of the process’s initial ContentProviders, followed by Application.onCreate. Provider initialization can therefore run before Application.onCreate, rather than all belonging to a later component phase.

A common foreground Activity creation sequence is onCreate → onStart → onResume. In this older View/HWUI example, subsequent work includes traversal measure/layout/draw, RenderThread activity, and the graphics pipeline. It is not a guarantee of one doFrame followed by one fixed Vsync interval until display: GPU, buffers, SurfaceFlinger, HWC, and the display still have their own work.

The finishDrawing marker is an app-to-WindowManager drawing notification, not a physical presentation timestamp. Android 10 ViewRootImpl sends it through WindowSession; Android 11 WindowStateAnimator can then be in COMMIT_DRAW_PENDING before later committing/showing the window. The image’s onStart/onCreate ordering should also be corrected as described above. See MainThread and RenderThread Explained for the broader pipeline.

SplashActivity to MainActivity

This sample transitions from SplashActivity to the main Activity. Follow its lifecycle, app initialization, WebView work, and dependencies to the destination window’s first-frame milestone. A separate SplashActivity is neither necessarily an ad nor a required launch step. From Android 12 (API 31), distinguish the system SplashScreen from an app Activity; retaining a dedicated splash Activity can produce duplicate splash screens. See the migration guide.

The 829.966 ms selection below spans the illustrated drawing-notification boundaries, not independently verified physical presentation timestamps. Whether WebView or other work delays startup depends on dependencies and waits; slice colors or lengths alone do not establish a cause.

MainActivity First Frame to Fully Loaded

The main Activity’s first frame may contain only a shell, with images or list data arriving later. Define critical content readiness, mark that business event, and correlate it with subsequent drawing/presentation. An onDraw call, itemCount greater than zero, or a completed network request alone does not guarantee the user can see or interact with the finished UI.

The 1.648 s selection marks the later loading interval chosen in the original example. Without the synchronized source recording, readiness marker, and complete trace, the final doFrame alone cannot establish full readiness. Do not add this duration to illustrative intervals from different devices.

For new measurements, retain both system TTID (initial display) and app-reported TTFD (full display). Activity.reportFullyDrawn() is available from API 19; report after the agreed critical-content/usability condition is met, not early to improve the number. Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric supports repeated measurements of timeToInitialDisplayMs and timeToFullDisplayMs. The latter uses the fully-drawn signal and related frame completion; it is not an arbitrary business Trace section with a different label. Missing reports or incomplete captures are separate outcomes, not zeros.

Keep the launch entry point, cold/warm/hot mode, compilation policy, and data conditions consistent. Retain each iteration’s trace and compare typical and slow samples. A faster first frame with later usable content is not an improvement in both measures.

I put together this demonstration using Systrace and phone screenshots, so you can see where each startup stage appears in the trace. The app is an open-source WanAndroid client:

End

This article focuses on visualizing the complete cold start flow in Systrace to help you locate bottlenecks and perform competitive analysis.

  1. For “How to Analyze,” see the routine in Understanding Responsiveness Principles.
  2. For “How to Optimize,” see Complete Record of Android App Startup Optimization. Optimization techniques evolve; I’ll maintain that article. If you find new techniques, leave a comment or contact me via WeChat (553000664).

entry.title: Android Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1 - Understanding Responsiveness Principles
entry.content:
Jank, Responsiveness, and ANR often appear together and can share contributing causes, but they are not severity levels of one mechanism. Uneven visual progress, delayed feedback, and an ANR triggered by a particular timeout need separate evidence. Treat a user’s “the app is slow/stuttering” as an experience report first, then establish which action and outcome are delayed.

Uneven animation or scrolling is usually called Jank. Long startup, screen-wake, or transition delays are slow response / high latency; ANR means Application Not Responding. These categories can overlap. High latency can coexist with jank, while ANRs must be diagnosed by their specific trigger.

Furthermore, within Apps or manufacturers, Jank, Responsiveness, and ANR have individual metrics like Frame Drop Rate, Startup Speed, and ANR Rate. Mastering the analysis and optimization of these issues is crucial for developers.

This is the first article in the Responsiveness series, focusing on theoretical knowledge, including an overview of performance engineering, key responsiveness concepts, and analysis methodologies.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-14): Originally published in 2021, this article retains its methodology, book passage, and figure. It corrects the assumptions that thread states identify app/system responsibility and that Message completion means response completion. Startup initialization references AOSP android-11.0.0_r1, with added TTID/TTFD, Android 12 (API 31) SplashScreen, and current-tool boundaries.

Table of Contents

  • Performance Engineering
  • Responsiveness Overview
  • Methodology for Analyzing Responsiveness Issues
  • Series Articles
  • References
  • About Me && Blog

For articles on Jank, refer to Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles. ANR articles will follow. This article focuses on the basic principles of responsiveness.

If you are not familiar with the basic use of Systrace (Perfetto), please catch up on the Systrace Basics Series first. This article assumes you are already familiar with using Systrace (Perfetto).

Performance Engineering

Before introducing responsiveness principles, here is a passage from the book “Systems Performance” regarding performance. It fits the questions we’re discussing here. If you work on performance, I recommend keeping it close at hand and returning to its methods:

Performance is Challenging

Systems performance engineering is a challenging field for many reasons, including the facts that system performance is subjective, complex, and often characterized by multiple concurrent issues.

Performance is Subjective

  1. Technical disciplines are often objective; many in the industry view problems as black or white. In software troubleshooting, deciding whether a bug exists or is fixed is usually clear-cut. Bugs are accompanied by error messages that are often easy to interpret, leading you to understand why the error occurred.
  2. In contrast, performance is often subjective. When starting on a performance issue, judging whether a problem even exists can be ambiguous, and the same applies when it is fixed. What one user considers “poor” performance, another might consider “good.”

Systems are Complex

  1. Besides subjectivity, performance engineering is challenging because systems are complex and often lack a clear starting point for analysis. We often begin with guesses—blaming the network, for example—and performance analysis must determine if that is a correct direction.
  2. Performance issues can arise from complex interconnections between subsystems, even when those subsystems perform well in isolation. They can also result from cascading failures, where one failing component causes performance issues in others. To understand these, you must untangle component relationships and how they collaborate.
  3. Bottlenecks are often complex and interconnected in unexpected ways. Fixing one issue might simply push the bottleneck elsewhere, resulting in no overall performance gain.
  4. Additionally, the complexity of production workloads can cause issues that are difficult to reproduce in a lab or occur only intermittently.
  5. Solving complex performance problems often requires a holistic approach. The entire system—including internal and external interactions—may need investigation. This work demands a broad skill set, rarely found in one person, making performance engineering a dynamic and intellectually challenging endeavor.

Multiple Issues May Coexist

  1. Finding a single performance issue is often not the end; complex software usually has multiple problems.
  2. Another difficulty: the real task isn’t just finding problems, but identifying which ones are the most significant.
  3. To do this, performance analysis must quantify the importance of issues. Some problems may not apply to your workload or only to a small degree. Ideally, you should not only quantify the problem but also estimate the speedup expected after fixing it. This information is especially useful when management reviews engineering or operations resource allocation.
  4. One metric is particularly well-suited for quantifying performance: latency.

– Excerpts from “Systems Performance: Enterprise and the Cloud” (paraphrased)

The retained passage motivates attention to perception and system complexity; it does not mean latency cannot be measured objectively. Bugs can also occur without error logs. Defined boundaries, workload, and measurement procedures make performance comparisons repeatable. See the author’s book page.

Systrace Series Articles:

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness

Responsiveness Overview

Responsiveness is a critical metric for App performance. Poor responsiveness typically manifests as delayed click effects, operation wait times, or prolonged white screens. Primary scenarios include:

  • App startup scenarios: Cold start, hot start, warm start, etc.
  • Interface transition scenarios: Page jumps within an App, or between different Apps.
  • Non-transition click scenarios: Toggles, pop-ups, long presses, control selections, single/double clicks, etc.
  • Screen wake/sleep, power on/off, unlocking, facial recognition, camera, video loading, etc.

Define response time as the interval from an agreed trigger to an agreed outcome. Triggers can be touch, notifications/Intents, system actions, or app events. Touch input enters through InputChannel/native Looper processing, not a direct Java Message for every hardware event. Long presses are typically recognized by gesture logic; fingerprint recognition uses separate hardware/service callbacks.

The endpoint can be initial button feedback, the first page frame, significant content becoming usable, a captured photo, or actual screen illumination. Name each metric explicitly. Worker, network, GPU, composition, and display waits may remain after a main-thread Message finishes. The figure shows app events interleaved with UI drawing, not a complete response path.

Expectations vary, but latency within agreed boundaries is objectively measurable. Smoothness also needs a defined target cadence and presentation criterion. “Subjective response versus purely objective jank” is too simple. Roles can choose different scopes, provided they name them:

ScopePossible boundariesWhat it can miss
System/end-to-endDefined input event or launch request → result/presentationPhysical contact, interrupt, and InputReader timestamps differ; logs may not cover optical display
App-stageattachBaseContext / Application.onCreate → app readinessEarlier scheduling/process creation; starting at onCreate can also miss Provider initialization
Experience testAutomated/physical trigger → agreed visual or usable outcomeIcon highlighting is already feedback, so starting there excludes prior delay; camera/recognition adds sampling error

These are choices, not mandatory role-specific procedures. Cameras, automation, app markers, and system evidence can complement one another; no single equipment setup is a universal industry standard.

Startup metrics: Android distinguishes TTID and TTFD. TTID covers framework-defined startup through first display, observable through Displayed; TTFD adds app-reported readiness of significant content. Neither automatically represents the entire physical-touch-to-result path.

Activity.reportFullyDrawn(), available since API 19, should reflect agreed readiness of significant data and UI. Early/late calls change its meaning; no report means missing data. Android 12 (API 31) SplashScreen adds a system launch surface and exit transition. Distinguish that surface, the app’s first frame, significant content, and interactivity. Faster placeholder feedback does not mean the underlying work finished sooner.

Methodology for Analyzing Responsiveness Issues

Define the Start and End Points

Agree on start/end events, clock source, and detection rules first. Record cold/warm/hot state, compilation/warmup, account/data state, network, display mode, temperature, and background load. Compare distributions and tails under matched boundaries rather than ranking numbers measured from different starts.

  1. Competitor Analysis: Use a baseline competitor device or App. Under identical conditions, how long does the competitor take from click to response?
  2. Regression Analysis: Compare against previous system or App versions to ensure no regression.

Take a complex app such as Taobao: at exactly what point should we call startup complete? That endpoint is not easy to settle on. Starts can also be ambiguous: physical contact, ACTION_DOWN, ACTION_UP, click callbacks, and launch requests occur at different times. Displayed is useful for its TTID definition, but does not mean all content is loaded. onWindowFocusChanged() reports focus changes, not completion. For user-required content, define a verifiable ready condition and corroborate it with markers, automation, or optical measurements.

Common Responsiveness Issues

Android System Issues Causing Slowness

These are possible resource or cross-process dependencies. Thread states guide investigation; they do not assign responsibility. The same symptom can originate in the app, a service, or shared-resource contention.

ObservationPossible contributorsFurther evidence
Long RunningMore work, frequency/core capacity, cache/memory behavior, driver executionComparable-work stacks, topology/residency, frequency/limits, available hardware counters
Long RunnableCPU waiting, priority/affinity/cpuset constraints, competing worksched_switch/wakeup, allowed CPUs, priority and per-core activity; not necessarily system-wide saturation
Synchronous Binder waitRemote queueing, execution, locks, nested callsMatching transaction and server thread; the server need not be system_server
Sleep/lock waitConditions, worker/remote work, network callbacks, locksWaiting stack, owner, and wakeup chain; the waker need not be the root cause or lock owner
D/Uninterruptible SleepKernel waits including some I/O and other uninterruptible waitsBlocked reason, kernel stack, block/file I/O; not synonymous with low memory
Reduced frequency ceilingThermal, power, or other policy constraintsThermal state, policy/limits, matched comparisons; low frequency alone is not an error
Long buffer operationsSlot availability, slow consumption, fences, drivers, BinderSpecific producer/consumer path and dependencies, not SurfaceFlinger alone

Low memory can affect latency through reclamation, faults, compression/swap, process restarts, and I/O. Correlate memory/pressure, reclaim, fault, and lmkd events. ART’s HeapTaskDaemon and kernel kswapd perform different work, not one GC mechanism; frequent activity alone does not prove low memory. Use PSI where supported and captured; missing data is not zero pressure.

If SystemServer delays a launch, the target process may not yet exist, so this is not always an app-main-thread Binder sleep. Graphics paths also change: AOSP android-16.0.0_r1 BLASTBufferQueue manages a client-side queue and submits transactions. Not every dequeue/queue executes in an SF Binder thread.

App-Specific Issues

Inspect necessary initialization and dependencies, asking which work lies on the current response’s critical path:

  1. Application.attachBaseContext(), onCreate(), class/static initialization, and SDK work. Measuring only onCreate misses earlier work.
  2. Activity onCreate → onStart → onResume and restoration paths. Callback completion is not presentation. Default main-thread Service/BroadcastReceiver callbacks can compete with UI work, but a long callback is not automatically a system timeout.
  3. ContentProvider initialization. In the normal AOSP android-11.0.0_r1 ActivityThread binding path, providers are installed before Application.onCreate. Initialization usually runs on main; remote data operations require analysis of their actual Binder/calling threads.
  4. View inflation, measure/layout/draw, or initial Compose composition/layout; not every response runs all phases. Distinguish graphics initialization and texture uploads from per-frame queue/dequeue or Surface/fence waits.
  5. Extra SplashActivity → MainActivity hops, repeated loading, and async data dependencies. On Android 12+, account for system SplashScreen behavior instead of adding an Activity solely for launch animation.
  6. Long UI Messages and waits for workers, other processes, networks, or synchronous Binder replies. Separate waiting from computation; making work asynchronous does not automatically shorten time to the user’s required result.
  7. WebView creation, resource access, class loading, JIT/AOT, and compilation configuration. First-run cost is not all JIT; record installation, compilation, and warmup state.

AndroidX App Startup manages initialization dependencies and supports manual initialization after disabling automatic startup for the component. It does not eliminate the underlying work. Before deferring nonessential initialization, check thread contracts, dependencies, and first-use latency so that delay is not merely shifted to the next interaction.

Analysis Routine (Mainly Systrace)

  1. Fix the scenario and measurement definition: Record device/system/app versions, data/account, startup state, cache/compilation, network, and thermal conditions. Define trigger, endpoint, clock, and success. Count failed/incomplete samples separately, never as zero duration.
  2. Capture the critical path: Use Perfetto/Systrace, relevant logs, and app trace markers. Check coverage and lost/missing events. A main-thread call chart is not whole-system evidence. Correlate cross-process IDs and align different clocks before comparing timestamps.
  3. Separate stages by dependency: Follow launch request, process creation, Provider/Application, Activity, first frame, and significant-content readiness. Do not sum overlapping work; improving one critical-path stage may reveal another bottleneck.
  4. Use states to form hypotheses: For long Running, inspect execution and resources; for Runnable, allowed CPU capacity and competition; for Sleep, dependencies; for D, the actual kernel wait. A state alone does not establish app/system responsibility. See Main Thread I/O Latency.
  5. Follow relevant areas:
    • Kernel: Verify topology/capacity rather than assuming CPUs 0–3 are small. Below-maximum frequency is not inherently wrong, and one saturated thread does not saturate a multicore device. Use capacity-aware scheduling concepts alongside actual policy and allowed CPUs.
    • SystemServer: Correlate input, launch requests, Binder, and locks. Investigate the server even before the app exists. Identify lock owners instead of labeling every sleeping Binder thread AM/WM contention.
    • SurfaceFlinger: Establish the graphics path, then connect submissions, fences, composition, and presentation. Long queue/dequeue can originate in the client or driver.
    • Launcher: Inspect click handling, pause, and transitions when launch comes from the home screen. Notification/deep-link launches need not involve Launcher. Animation and content preparation can overlap; do not simply add their full durations.
  6. Add function-level evidence when needed: Traceview is deprecated; Android Studio CPU Profiler is a replacement, not the same tool renamed. simpleperf depends on system support, symbols, and debug/profileable permissions; Android 10+ supports the documented profileable-release route. The original TraceFix link is an instrumentation example whose build-tool compatibility must be checked. Sampling and instrumentation have different coverage and overhead.
  7. Repeat with the same definitions and coordinate fixes: Prioritize the largest critical-path contributors, reporting sample size, percentiles, and incomplete-run rate. Vendor/app interfaces require explicit version/contract checks, not assumptions of universally available private SDKs. Some limitations may remain unresolved, or have only a small effect. Talk those through with the testers, including the evidence and the impact. Previous bug reports suggest leads, but recheck whether the current version has the same cause.

This article provides a foundation for responsiveness knowledge. It involves significant system-level details; please review the Systrace Basics Series for depth.

entry.title: Android Systrace Smoothness in Action 3 - FAQs During Jank Analysis
entry.content:
Different people have different understandings of smoothness (jank/dropped frames) and different perceptions of jitter thresholds. Therefore, before starting this series, it is necessary to clarify the content to avoid misunderstandings. Here are some basic explanations:

  1. For mobile users, jank encompasses many scenarios: dropped frames when scrolling lists, excessive white screen during app startup, slow screen wake-up when pressing the power button, unresponsive interface followed by a crash, no response when clicking an icon, incoherent window animations, lagging touch response, or stuttering when entering the desktop after a reboot. These scenarios differ slightly from what developers understand as “jank.” Developers categorize these more finely, which is a cognitive gap between developers and users that must be noted when handling feedback from users or testers.
  2. Developers can initially classify feedback as Smoothness (uneven visual progress), Responsiveness (long waits after an action), or Stability (crashes and ANRs). These can overlap. An icon that appears unresponsive is not necessarily a stability failure; input, application state, and logs determine the diagnosis.
  3. These are not one Message-timeout mechanism with different thresholds. Long main-thread tasks can delay both input and rendering, but GPU work, SurfaceFlinger, the display stack, scheduling, or remote services can also cause delays. ANRs depend on specific input or component timeout rules; crashes have separate causes such as exceptions or signals. A long Message alone establishes neither.
  4. This series primarily analyzes smoothness-related issues. Responsiveness and stability will be covered in dedicated articles. Understanding smoothness first will make analyzing responsiveness and stability much easier.
  5. This series focuses on using Systrace (Perfetto) for analysis. Systrace is our entry point because many factors affect smoothness—some within the app itself and others within the system. Systrace (Perfetto) provides a holistic view of the system’s operation during the problem, helping us initially pinpoint the root cause.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-14): This FAQ accompanies the 2021 MIUI case and retains the original images. Color rules below are verified in the attachments’ embedded legacy viewer, not a universal Systrace/Perfetto contract. HWUI synchronization and statistics are checked against AOSP android-11.0.0_r1; the screenshots’ full firmware/viewer versions were not recorded. New captures on Android 12 (API 31) or later can use FrameTimeline and supported benchmark metrics. Legacy dot colors are not modern presentation results.

Table of Contents

  • What Do the Frame Colors in Systrace Mean?
  • No Red Frame Means No Dropped Frame?
  • Why Does the Main Thread Wait for the Render Thread?
  • Why Doesn’t It Jank When Swiping Without Releasing?
  • If It Doesn’t Jank, How Do We Measure Performance?
  • Why Can’t I See Jank in Screen Recordings?
  • Series Articles
  • Attachments
  • About Me && Blog

  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace

If you are not familiar with the basic use of Systrace (Perfetto), please catch up on the Systrace Basics Series first. This article assumes you are already familiar with using Systrace (Perfetto).

What Do the Frame Colors in Systrace Mean?

These are F dots in the legacy Frames track, not function-slice colors. Selecting one highlights the UI/RenderThread intervals associated by the viewer, subject to its implementation and available trace events.

The original explanation in terms of one/two periods of the current display is inaccurate. The embedded AndroidAuditor in xiaomi_launcher.html uses a fixed 16.67 ms threshold (EXPECTED_FRAME_TIME_MS), applying these rules in order:

Dot classCondition in the embedded viewer
Red (TERRIBLE)frame.totalDuration > 33.34 ms
Yellow (BAD)Not red, and either totalDuration > 16.67 ms or an estimated deadline exists and frame.end is later
Green (GOOD)Neither condition above

totalDuration sums viewer-constructed thread intervals; it is neither a single doFrame’s duration nor Running CPU time. The RenderThread endpoint can be the end of queueBuffer/buffer swapping, not GPU completion or presentation. The viewer estimates deadlines from Vsync information rather than measuring physical display timing. On a 90 Hz display, its red threshold therefore cannot simply be read as about 22.22 ms.

Green Frame

Green means neither BAD nor TERRIBLE was triggered by this viewer. It guarantees neither completion within one actual Vsync period nor smooth on-screen output; read the original image annotation with that correction.

Yellow Frame

Yellow can result from a duration above the fixed 16.67 ms threshold or from missing the estimated deadline. It does not imply a duration between one and two periods of this device’s refresh cycle; investigate the underlying events.

Red Frame

In this embedded viewer, red means a constructed totalDuration greater than 33.34 ms. This flags a long app-side work/wait interval, still requiring composition and presentation correlation. No red dots does not imply that 90/120 Hz deadlines were met.

No Red Frame Means No Dropped Frame?

No. Correlate app submission, GPU completion, SurfaceFlinger selection/composition, and presentation rather than replacing app analysis with SurfaceFlinger alone. Either activity or inactivity in SurfaceFlinger is insufficient to classify a target window. See Triple Buffer and, for Android 12+ captures containing the data, FrameTimeline. Separate app completion deadlines from presentation.

Yellow Frame Without Jank

Previously submitted content that is ready in time may sustain display updates during a long app interval. That depends on queue and presentation timing, not an automatic triple-buffer guarantee. Extra queueing can increase input latency, and buffer count is not determined by refresh rate alone. “Without jank” requires presentation evidence, not a yellow dot or continuous SurfaceFlinger activity.

Yellow Frame With Jank

The image marks two consecutive yellow dots. Its 28.432 ms ruler spans the selection, not 28.432 ms for each frame. The original “first janked, second did not” classification is not established by this image or a complete per-frame presentation mapping. The attachment does show a long first RenderThread interval and a later main-thread wait, with dependencies between them. See the next section and Part 2’s event checks.

Why Does the Main Thread Wait for the Render Thread?

The UI thread hands frame state to RenderThread, whose drawing tasks execute serially. If earlier work is unfinished, the next synchronization task can queue and keep the UI thread waiting. Sleep indicates a wait for some event or condition; identify the dependency using call intervals, wakeups, and source, not state alone.

In AOSP android-11.0.0_r1 DrawFrameTask, postAndWait() posts work and waits on a condition variable. After syncFrameState(), run() unblocks UI early only if canUnblockUiThread is true; otherwise it unblocks after the subsequent draw/wait branch. Synchronization ending therefore does not always mean immediate unblocking, and unblocking is not GPU or display completion.

The attachment contains these intervals, in trace seconds:

EventStart/endWall time
Previous RT DrawFrame28306.209230 → 28306.22574916.519 ms
Next UI doFrame28306.217610 → 28306.22964212.032 ms
Next RT DrawFrame28306.225780 → 28306.2349509.170 ms
Next RT syncFrameState28306.226040 → 28306.2295603.520 ms

This is consistent with earlier RT work delaying the next synchronization and UI completing afterward. Without complete waiting stacks, do not label all 12.032 ms as waiting or infer every wakeup dependency from proximity alone. Background: MainThread and RenderThread.

Why Doesn’t It Jank When Swiping Without Releasing?

On this version, I found scrolling smoother while holding my finger down, with more noticeable stutter after release. That is an observation from the time, not a rule that holding prevents jank. Input-related policies, velocity, and rendering work can differ between phases.

The selected CPU 4 policy in the image has upper/lower limits around 2,419,200 / 1,056,000 kHz. This alone proves neither continuous operation of every boost mechanism nor exclusive RenderThread execution on CPUs 4–6, and says nothing conclusive about presentation.

Rechecking PID 3553/TID 3690 in xiaomi_launcher_scroll_all_the_time.html yields 110 complete DrawFrame slices, 19 of which include Running intervals on CPUs 0–2. The attachment includes gesture boundaries, so its filename does not establish that every frame belongs to the holding phase. It does refute an all-file claim that RT never uses the presumed small cores. First identify input phases, then compare topology, workload, deadlines, and presentation.

The 120 ms boost timeout I noted at the time lacks supporting PerfLock requests, configuration, or expiry events. It cannot be derived from this frequency-limit image and is not an Android-wide constant. Treat it as an unverified historical parameter. Repeated input may renew requests, but confirming that requires vendor implementation/event evidence.

If It Doesn’t Jank, How Do We Measure Performance?

If a scenario feels smooth on both devices, how do we compare performance?

Start with dumpsys gfxinfo for the target process’s HWUI statistics. It is not a complete score for all display layers, custom game renderers, or perceived smoothness. Fields and definitions vary by OS version and rendering path.

  1. Fix the package, display mode, gesture distance/speed, content, warmup, and thermal conditions. Warm up first, then reset once immediately before measurement; repeating reset two or three times is unnecessary.
  2. Using the original Mi Launcher package as an example, reset its statistics (replace the package for another app):
  1. Perform the defined interaction, then capture promptly to avoid later animations contaminating the sample:
  1. Check process/window identity, Stats since, total frames, reset behavior, and coverage. Missing output is not zero. AOSP android-11.0.0_r1 ThreadedRenderer recognizes reset/framestats, but vendor behavior needs device verification. These commands were not run on a device in this review.

Interpret the fields as follows:

  • Janky frames: HWUI’s count/rate under that implementation, not a count of perceived stutters. AOSP 11 compares an adjusted duration with the frame interval, with flag/dequeue handling. Frame deadline missed is a separate classification count.
  • 95th percentile: An estimate of the P95 frame duration, not “95% smooth.” This implementation derives it from histogram buckets, so consider resolution and sample size.
  • HISTOGRAM: Duration buckets and counts; 5ms=11 means eleven frames in that bucket, not an ordered per-frame sequence. GPU HISTOGRAM is separate.
  • PROFILEDATA: Stage data for retained recent frames, not necessarily every frame since reset. Read column names, units, and Flags instead of hardcoding column numbers; distinguish timestamps from durations.

See AOSP 11 JankTracker and ProfileData. For repeatable modern testing, Macrobenchmark’s FrameTimingMetric includes frameOverrunMs on Android 12 (API 31) and later. Also consider tail durations, presentation cadence, input latency, and power.

Here are the two screenshots I used for comparison at the time. “90 fps” is the target, not a verified per-frame result. The text inconsistently named Reno 5 and Reno 5 Pro; the screenshot identifies only com.oppo.launcher, PID 3434, not an exact model/SoC. It therefore cannot support a chipset ranking.

Mi 10 Pro - 90 fps

Oppo Reno 5 - 90 fps

Transcribing the screenshot values under their original definitions:

MetricMi screenshotOPPO screenshot
Total frames rendered7690
Janky frames27 (35.53%)1 (1.11%)
P50 / P90 / P95 / P998 / 16 / 18 / 22 ms5 / 5 / 5 / 13 ms
Number Frame deadline missed71
Number High input latency6944
GPU P50 / P90 / P95 / P992 / 3 / 3 / 8 ms4 / 5 / 5 / 5 ms

The Mi sample has a higher HWUI Janky rate and longer tail durations. Frame counts, implementations, content/wallpaper, interaction duration, and thermal conditions were not fully matched, and repeated trials are missing. These samples do not establish an overall device ranking. High input latency is a count, not 69/44 milliseconds; classification counts should not simply be summed into a total jank count.

The GPU comparison is mixed: Mi GPU P95 is lower (3 versus 5 ms), but P99 is higher (8 versus 5 ms). Percentiles are not paired measurements from the same frame: subtracting GPU P95 from total P95 does not yield CPU duration. These summaries cannot exclude GPU/fence problems or prove a CPU bottleneck without corresponding per-frame evidence.

Why Can’t I See Jank in Screen Recordings?

Recording and direct observation can differ, but recording 90 fps content at 60 fps does not guarantee that jank becomes invisible:

  1. Different sampling cadence: A 90 Hz display refreshes about every 11.11 ms, while 60 fps video samples about every 16.67 ms. Short stalls can be missed or transformed; longer stalls can remain visible. Sampling can also introduce uneven pacing.
  2. A recording is not optical scanout: Android MediaProjection, for example, outputs through a virtual display and Surface. It does not capture the full physical-panel scanout. Recording/encoding can also alter workload; compare recording-on and recording-off behavior.
  3. Playback changes observation: Actual video timestamps, variable frame rate, player drops/repeats, and display refresh rate all matter. My observation that the Mi device switched to 60 during playback lacks the recording and mode logs; it is not a universal phone behavior.

Keep the original video and frame timestamps, aligning them with the same capture’s trace, display mode, and input timeline. An external high-speed camera is closer to observing the physical screen, but exposure, sampling rate, rolling shutter, and clock alignment still matter. A smooth-looking recording alone does not establish absence of jank.

Attachments

Attachments are on GitHub: https://github.com/Gracker/SystraceForBlog/tree/master/Android_Systrace_Smooth_In_Action

  2. xiaomi_launcher_scroll_all_the_time.zip: Continuous scrolling trace.
  3. oppo_launcher_scroll.zip: Comparison trace.

On 2026-10-14, the three ZIPs were downloadable, passed CRC checks, and contained readable ftrace. Embedded viewer rules were inspected as text without executing its JavaScript. New timings come from historical attachments, not rerun device/recording/PerfLock experiments. The gfxinfo images lack full per-frame source output, limiting further comparison.

The screenshots and original experience remain, while technical conclusions are narrowed using the attached trace and supplemented with event-level checks. The introductory Bilibili images are a separate example. If you are not familiar with the basic use of Systrace (Perfetto), please catch up on the Systrace Basics Series first. This article assumes you are already familiar with using Systrace (Perfetto).

The Routine for Analyzing Jank with Systrace

Use the following sequence to collect evidence:

  1. Reproduce with recorded conditions: Capture the steps, frequency of reproduction, system/app versions, display mode, thermal state, and battery state. Keep content, input, and cache conditions comparable across devices.
  2. Open with a compatible tool: First try Open trace file in Perfetto UI. Embedded legacy HTML viewers, chrome://tracing, and “Open With Legacy UI” are not stable instructions across browser versions. If import fails, preserve the original and use a viewer supporting that format. Compatibility of the embedded UI was not retested here.
  3. Establish context: Locate the interaction, process, and window/layer. Establish whether continuous updates were expected; static content or intentional frame-rate limits are not automatically jank.
  4. Check system evidence: Correlate scheduling, CPU frequency/limits, thermal state, memory pressure, and I/O. Low frequency alone does not prove thermal throttling; dense tracks do not prove sustained high utilization. lmkd, HeapTaskDaemon, or Block I/O activity alone does not prove low memory. Keep missing evidence unknown.
  5. Locate app work: Inspect the UI thread, RenderThread, and available GPU data, separating wall time into Running, Runnable, and blocked intervals. The Bilibili selection below is about 110.05 ms, with repeated inflation and drawing. It warrants investigation but does not identify a particular View to fix, and is separate from the MIUI case.

The next selection is 23.526 ms. Function-slice colors are not jank grades; F markers in the legacy Frames track are viewer-generated clues. Green/yellow/red cannot be mapped directly to actual presentation outcomes.

Target intervals for 60/90/120 fps are about 16.67/11.11/8.33 ms. Actual deadlines also depend on scheduling, pipelining, and display mode.

  1. Connect composition and presentation: The next images show SurfaceFlinger work gaps and a BufferTX counter. Investigate the target window: no composition can mean no update, while composition can update another layer. Check the counter’s implementation; blank space or zero alone does not establish a missed presentation.

  1. Follow dependencies and validate: Long Runnable intervals mean waiting for CPU. Follow long Binder calls into the remote execution/wait chain rather than labeling everything slow app execution. On Android 12+ with the relevant data, use FrameTimeline to relate expected and actual presentation, then inspect CPU/GPU work and dependencies. Validate changes with repeated comparable captures, checking deadlines, latency, and side effects.

App frame drops have many causes. Refer to these articles; different causes have distinct Systrace signatures:

  1. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - Methodology
  2. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - System Side
  3. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - App Side
  4. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - Low Memory Side

Case Study: Analyzing Jank with Systrace

Systrace / Perfetto exposes timing across processes, threads, and the system, helping form hypotheses. App and system effects can overlap rather than fit a binary classification. Missing source-level stacks or hardware data remain limitations.

For deeper analysis, combine source code with Android Studio CPU Profiler or sampling/custom tracing supported by the target version. Traceview is deprecated; official guidance recommends CPU Profiler from Android Studio 3.2 onward. Method instrumentation changes overhead, so timings from different recording modes are not directly comparable optimization results.

This article focuses on discovery and analysis. Solutions (like optimizing logic, scheduling, or layout) must be tailored to findings.

Case Description

On my Mi 10 Pro, I often felt a stutter during the common gesture of swiping the desktop. With the Mi 10 Pro’s 90Hz mode and a 90 fps target (not a guarantee of actual throughput), I noticed the stutter quite clearly—I’m fairly sensitive to this. After upgrading to MIUI 12.5, the issue remained, so I decided to investigate.

After capturing and studying the Systrace, I thought it would make a good practical example, so I decided to write it up.

I recommend downloading the attached Systrace and following along with the article.

  1. Because many factors affect jank, I’ll clarify the hardware and software versions first. Findings apply to the attached Systrace even if the scenario is optimized later.
  2. Hardware: Mi 10 Pro
  3. Software: MIUI 12.5.3 Stable
  4. Launcher Version: RELEASE-4.21.11.2922-03151646

These are the conditions I recorded at the time. The attachment lacks a full build fingerprint or APK identity, so it cannot independently verify the exact firmware/launcher version; the MIUI number alone does not establish the underlying Android version. Xiaomi’s FAQ confirms 90 Hz and Snapdragon 865 support. Current-device behavior needs fresh testing.

Starting with Input events

In the captured Systrace, I performed only one swipe, making it easy to locate. The input sequence consists of one Input Down, several Input Moves, and one Input Up.

In Systrace, we see InputDispatcher and InputReader threads in SystemServer, but we primarily focus on the App UI thread.

Down/Move/Up are my annotations for this gesture. deliverInputEvent marks an app input-processing interval; it does not by itself identify the action or represent pure CPU time. Correlate event details. In this case motion continues after release, called Fling below; an Up event does not guarantee fling in every gesture. Background:

  1. Input Explained
  2. Weibo Image Loading Optimization Case

Analyzing the UI Thread

Since this jank mostly occurred after releasing the finger, we focus on the segment after “Input Up.”

The legacy Frames track has green and yellow F markers. Does yellow necessarily mean jank? Does red? These reflect viewer rules and available data, not sufficient evidence of actual presentation. Do not confuse them with function-slice colors or modern FrameTimeline colors. The three marked points are starting points, not an exhaustive classification of anomalies.

Identifying three suspicious points, we move to the RenderThread.

Analyzing the Render Thread

The screenshot’s ruler spans about 19.103 ms; RenderThread’s DrawFrame takes about 16.519 ms. The ruler is not a measured presentation duration, and UI/RenderThread slices overlap rather than simply add.

Rechecking xiaomi_launcher.html using PID 3553, RenderThread TID 3690, B/E markers, and sched_switch gives:

ItemResult for this interval
DrawFrame start/end (trace seconds)28306.209230 → 28306.225749
Wall time16.519 ms
Running time15.517 ms
Running on CPU 2 / CPU 014.794 ms / 0.723 ms
Off CPU1.002 ms

“All green, always Running” is too strong. Execution dominates, but there are off-CPU intervals. Workload, core/frequency, cache/memory behavior, and driver work remain possible contributors.

Next correlate the target layer’s submissions and consumption with SurfaceFlinger work. Exceeding 11.11 ms alone does not determine the final presentation outcome.

Analyzing SurfaceFlinger

For basics on SF trace reading, see SurfaceFlinger Explained.

Inspect the target layer’s queue events and SurfaceFlinger work, then available GPU fences and presentation evidence. This counter is neither the app’s total buffer allocation nor a guarantee that every queued image is GPU-ready. The previous image can remain in use when the queue is empty.

The following three images offer clues, not universal jank tests:

Three cases to investigate:

  1. No new composition and an empty target queue: With expected ongoing updates, this suggests insufficient new content. Check target timing, window state, and presentation of retained content. Not every SurfaceFlinger gap is jank.
    (Matches the first suspicious point).

  2. Composition with an empty target queue: A separate com.miui.miwallpaper.snowmountain wallpaper layer is visible and may trigger composition. SurfaceFlinger activity does not prove Launcher updated; counters alone do not identify the sole trigger.

  3. Composition with queued target content: This is a useful intermediate state, but verify which buffer was selected, its fence, and presentation timing. “Normal” here describes the shown production/consumption pattern, not acceptance of the entire display path.
    (Provided for comparison).

Near the first point, Launcher’s queue counter reaches zero at 28306.212867 s and rises to one at 28306.224481 s; SurfaceFlinger refresh work also has a gap. This supports investigating production delay and stalled content, but does not independently establish an exact on-screen dropped-frame count or touch-to-display latency.

Back to the Render Thread

This DrawFrame lasts 16.519 ms versus 5.974 ms for the preceding one, about 2.77 times as long. A visually simple gesture or finger release does not prove identical work per frame. A live wallpaper is present, and Launcher/driver work is not fully resolved. Was this frame doing more work, or was the same work taking longer? Within the long slice, prepareTree is about 4.165 ms and flush commands about 4.656 ms of wall time; do not add these to their enclosing parent intervals. Stacks, content/command counts, cache state, and controlled comparisons are needed to separate increased work from slower execution.

Check the RenderThread CPU info:

Execution dominates this interval, so next inspect the actual CPU residency and switches in the Kernel area.

Analyzing CPU Info

See CPU Info Explained and Prerequisites for Systrace.

The trace confirms execution on CPUs 2 and 0. Device documentation describes four small, three big, and one prime core in Snapdragon 865. Mapping Linux CPU IDs to those types still requires device topology/capacity data; low IDs do not universally mean small cores. The discussion below retains my CPU 0–3 mapping from the time as an explicit premise.

The recorded value is 1,804,800 kHz = 1.8048 GHz. It is also the last CPU 0/2 frequency event before the target slice, with no new frequency event recorded during it. This is recorded frequency state, not a direct measurement of instantaneous hardware speed or utilization. Establishing a maximum requires the device’s frequency table and limits.

Clock Frequency Limits shows constraint changes. The selected minimum of 1,075,200 kHz and maximum of 1,804,800 kHz do not prove that every CPU boost mechanism has ended. Power HAL, cpuset, utilization constraints, or vendor policies may be unrecorded; “Boost ended” remains the original image’s inference.

My hypothesis at the time was that small-core capacity was insufficient for these long frames. The attachment supports an association between long slices and CPU 0/2 residency, not a controlled demonstration that the scheduler caused the problem.

The immediately following DrawFrame lasts 9.170 ms, running 3.890 ms on CPU 0 and 4.554 ms on CPU 5; it did not instantly run entirely on a big core. Other short DrawFrames last 3.843 ms and 5.809 ms, with their Running intervals entirely on CPU 0. “Short” describes RenderThread duration, not proven on-time presentation. These observations contradict a blanket “normal frames never use small cores” claim, while a fast small-core slice also cannot disprove every capacity problem.

Compare equivalent work, frequency, core residency, runnable delay, and thermal conditions, then change a supported policy under controlled conditions and measure deadlines and latency. See Linux CPUFreq and Capacity Aware Scheduling for the distinction between frequency and scheduling capacity; they do not document MIUI’s full kernel implementation.

What we can establish here is: Long RenderThread slices on cores I identified as small at the time are an evidence-backed investigation target. Establishing a particular scheduling policy as the root cause still requires controlled validation.

Vendors with source access, permissions, and regression coverage can investigate migration, frequency constraints, and power policies, measuring latency, temperature, battery cost, and fairness to other tasks. App developers should first investigate their own rendering work and supported performance interfaces; changing migration thresholds is not a general app-level fix. Competitor traces suggest hypotheses, not proof of private scheduling algorithms.

What Role Does Triple Buffer Play in This Scenario?

Triple Buffer Explained describes extra production/consumption overlap and tolerance of some short variations. More buffers do not shorten GPU work or remove sustained bottlenecks; they cost memory and may add queueing latency. Keeping every older frame for the next refresh is not necessarily desirable.

The following image comes from a Matrix sample (SurfaceFlinger PID 510), not this MIUI attachment (PID 990). Its “already composited but not consumed” annotation should mean submitted content awaiting selection, and the counter does not represent all fully rendered buffers.

While looking through this MIUI trace, I also noticed the target queue count sometimes going from 2→0. The step alone cannot identify a discarded image, but nested queue/acquire events provide more evidence:

Trace time (seconds)Launcher queue event
28306.212859Acquire label 4:617, then count 0
28306.224466Queue label 3:618, then count 1
28306.234435Queue label 0:619, then count 2
28306.235906Acquire label 0:619, then count 0

These are vendor trace labels. Interpreted as slots/sequential frame numbers, they support 618 being skipped and 619 being acquired. The full vendor source is unavailable, so these markers alone do not identify the exact code branch or each image’s final presentation.

As a mechanism reference, AOSP android-11.0.0_r1 BufferQueueConsumer::acquireBuffer can skip older entries according to expected presentation time, buffer timestamps, and frame-number conditions, acquire a later entry, then record the remaining queue length. A 2→0 step can therefore reflect skipping one and acquiring another in a single operation; it does not establish a bug.

A shallower queue can expose later production variation, but this does not prove that retaining the old image would prevent the next jank. Its intended presentation time, position, or input freshness may already be unsuitable, and retaining it can increase latency. Compare pacing and responsiveness under controlled conditions.

The next image retains the original annotations. It shows another long RenderThread slice and queue/SF gaps; “keeping the earlier buffer would prevent this drop” is an untested counterfactual.

Fling positions are not necessarily precomputed fixed increments for every future frame. Common animations evaluate position from frame/elapsed time, so the next image can reflect a later point after a missed presentation. Retaining an old position can reduce one visible displacement while increasing latency. Assess position, timing, and presentation together rather than declaring triple buffering harmful from queue counts alone.

For an illustration with fixed display intervals, let offset be an element’s horizontal position. These values are not measurements from the attachment:

  1. Regular progress: 2→4→6→8→10→12.
  2. Repeat old content, then show older positions in sequence: 2→4→6→6→8→10→12. The sequence is longer and may accumulate latency; it is not guaranteed smoother.
  3. Repeat, then catch up to a newer position: 2→4→6→6→10→12. The adjacent displacement is larger, but the state is fresher.

The appropriate strategy depends on animation timing, intended presentation times, and latency requirements. This illustrates a possible stall-then-jump sensation; it does not establish the positions actually displayed in this MIUI trace or justify disabling buffer-discard policies.

Series Articles

  1. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  2. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  3. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis

Attachments

Attachments are on GitHub: https://github.com/Gracker/SystraceForBlog/tree/master/Android_Systrace_Smooth_In_Action

  1. xiaomi_launcher.zip: Main analysis trace.
  2. xiaomi_launcher_scroll_all_the_time.zip: Continuous scrolling trace.
  3. oppo_launcher_scroll.zip: Comparison trace.

On 2026-10-14, all three ZIPs were downloadable, passed CRC checks, and contained readable ftrace data. New numbers above come from local event analysis of the first attachment, not a device reproduction or a complete frame-rate test. Device topology, full vendor scheduling source, complete fence/presentation correlation, and equivalent-work A/B tests are unavailable. The Bilibili example’s trace is not one of these three attachments.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”
