entry.title: Android Systrace Smoothness in Action 1 - Understanding Jank Principles
entry.content:
Different people have different understandings of smoothness (jank/dropped frames) and different perceptions of jitter thresholds. Therefore, before starting this series, it is necessary to clarify the content to avoid misunderstandings and help everyone approach these articles with the right questions. Here are some basic explanations:

  1. For mobile users, jank encompasses many scenarios: dropped frames when scrolling lists, excessive white screen during app startup, slow screen wake-up when pressing the power button, unresponsive interface followed by a crash, no response when clicking an icon, incoherent window animations, lagging touch response, or stuttering when entering the desktop after a reboot. These scenarios differ slightly from what developers understand as “jank.” Developers categorize these more finely, which is a cognitive gap between developers and users that must be noted when handling feedback from users or testers.
  2. Developers can initially classify feedback as Smoothness (uneven visual progress), Responsiveness (long waits after an action), or Stability (crashes and ANRs). These can overlap. An icon that appears unresponsive is not necessarily a stability failure; input, application state, and logs determine the diagnosis.
  3. These are not one Message-timeout mechanism with different thresholds. Long main-thread tasks can delay both input and rendering, but GPU work, SurfaceFlinger, the display stack, scheduling, or remote services can also cause delays. ANRs depend on specific input or component timeout rules; crashes have separate causes such as exceptions or signals. A long Message alone establishes neither.
  4. This series primarily analyzes smoothness-related issues. Responsiveness and stability will be covered in dedicated articles. Understanding smoothness first will make analyzing responsiveness and stability much easier.
  5. This series focuses on using Systrace (Perfetto) for analysis. Systrace is our entry point because many factors affect smoothness—some within the app itself and others within the system. Systrace (Perfetto) provides a holistic view of the system’s operation during the problem, helping us initially pinpoint the root cause.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-14): First published in 2021, this article retains its historical Systrace screenshots and attachments. Framework snippets are checked against AOSP android-10.0.0_r1, not the complete vendor implementations shown in the images. 60 Hz / 16.67 ms is an example; frame budgets and buffer paths depend on the system version and captured evidence. Prefer Perfetto for new captures and use FrameTimeline on Android 12 (API 31) or later when available; missing data cannot establish modern frame metrics.

Table of Contents

  • Understanding Jank Principles
  • System Operation Mechanism Overview
  • Series Articles
  • Attachments
  • About Me && Blog

Systrace Series Articles:

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

If you are not familiar with the basic use of Systrace (Perfetto), please catch up on the Systrace Basics Series first. This article assumes you are already familiar with using Systrace (Perfetto).

Understanding Jank Principles

Jank Phenomena and Impact

This article focuses on visual pacing during continuous animation and scrolling. fps (frames per second) counts frames over an interval; specify whether these were generated, submitted, or presented. If the intended cadence is 120 new presented frames per second and only 110 appear, the target throughput was not sustained. Average fps alone does not locate late frames, describe the distribution of pauses, or establish perceptibility. Evenly paced 60 fps differs from an average of 60 fps with irregular intervals.

Dropped frames have many causes: app-specific issues, system-driven jank, hardware bottlenecks, or overall system lag. Refer to these four articles:

  1. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - Methodology
  2. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - System Side
  3. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - App Side
  4. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - Low Memory Side

Jank is what users notice first:

  1. Occasional minor jank degrades user experience, like a stutter when scrolling Weibo or returning to the desktop.
  2. Severe system-wide jank makes the phone unusable.
  3. In the high-refresh-rate era, if users are accustomed to 120 fps and the system suddenly switches to 60 fps in an easily perceptible scenario, they will immediately notice and feel it as jank.

Therefore, both apps and systems should aim to avoid jank. Identified jank issues should be prioritized for resolution.

Jank Definition

Overall App Frame Rendering Flow

To understand why jank occurs, we must know how the app’s main thread processes a frame.

From the Perspective of Execution Order

For a hardware-accelerated View/HWUI window, follow the Choreographer callback through the UI thread, RenderThread, GPU, SurfaceFlinger/HWC, and finally presentation. CPU submission, GPU completion, composition completion, and presentation are distinct events. Pipeline stages can overlap across frames; the whole path need not fit inside the figure’s single 16.6 ms interval.

The “GPU” label inside the RenderThread box is misleading: RenderThread runs on the CPU and prepares/submits graphics commands; the GPU executes asynchronously. “Issue” means issuing commands, and swapping a buffer proves neither GPU completion nor presentation. Measure and layout run when required.

From the Perspective of Systrace

The flow is more intuitive when visualized in Systrace (Perfetto):

This historical OPPO Launcher trace illustrates the pipeline. Arrow order alone does not establish a causal chain for one frame: check the window/layer, buffer identity, and fences. A queue-count increase does not prove GPU completion, and an HWC call returning does not prove scanout. Follow actual dependencies across the main thread, RenderThread, GPU, SystemServer, SurfaceFlinger, and scheduling states.

Jank Definition

Here, jank means visual progress that misses the intended cadence during an ongoing update, producing late, stalled, or uneven presentation. A missing draw is only a possible intermediate symptom. Static pages, intentional frame-rate limits, and lower-rate content need not produce a new buffer on every display refresh.

The UI-thread gap below is a point to investigate. First establish that an update was expected, then follow the relevant window through submission and presentation. Queued frames, RenderThread animations, or SurfaceFlinger layer-property animations can decouple a missing main-thread draw from visible motion. The image’s Jank arrow alone is not proof.

Collect evidence at three levels; these are not equivalent detection rules:

  1. Visual output: Repeated content is a clue when a new image was expected on each refresh. Repeating each frame of 30 fps video twice on a 60 Hz display can be correct. Separate average fps, display refreshes, and content changes.
  2. SurfaceFlinger/display stack: Check the target layer’s content, acquire fence, composition deadline, and presentation. A layer without a new buffer can reuse its previous buffer or change properties. SurfaceFlinger may also sleep when nothing needs updating.
  3. Application: Compare frame start, UI work, RenderThread submission, and GPU completion against that frame’s plan. Missing queueBuffer in one Vsync period is insufficient evidence; timely queueing does not ensure timely GPU completion or presentation.

Long main-thread tasks are a common starting point, not a predetermined diagnosis. Short CPU slices can coexist with runnable delays, lock/Binder waits, GPU delays, or display-stack problems.

The original term Logical Jank describes content or animation that fails to advance despite continued buffer submissions. It is not a universal FrameTimeline category. Exclude static content, video cadence, and intentional repetition before investigating application state and animation timing; identical screenshots alone do not identify the root cause.

Android 12 and Later: Use FrameTimeline

When a Perfetto trace contains android.surfaceflinger.frametimeline, correlate Expected/Actual Timeline by window/layer and token. Check predicted versus actual presentation, jank_type, and on_time_finish. The app Actual endpoint accounts for GPU completion and posting, not just CPU time in doFrame. Buffer Stuffing can preserve smooth motion while increasing input latency. Coverage and fields depend on the system and capture; an absent track is not zero jank. See the Perfetto FrameTimeline documentation.

With legacy Systrace, connect thread, queue, and available fence evidence, explicitly leaving unknown presentation times unresolved. Diagnose ANRs separately using the official guide. An asynchronous broadcast, for example, may await PendingResult.finish() even while the main thread is idle.

System Operation Mechanism Overview

Because there are many causes for jank, analyzing it requires an understanding of Android’s system mechanisms. Here is a brief introduction:

  1. App Main Thread Operation Principles
  2. Message, Handler, MessageQueue, and Looper Mechanisms
  3. Screen Refresh Mechanism and Vsync
  4. Choreographer Mechanism
  5. Buffer Flow and TripleBuffer
  6. Input Flow

System Mechanism - App Main Thread Operation Principles

A normal app process is forked from Zygote and enters ActivityThread.main after runtime initialization. The following excerpts are checked against AOSP android-10.0.0_r1; omission comments represent unshown framework code, not a standalone app example. prepareMainLooper() creates the Looper and MessageQueue. ActivityThread’s instance-field initialization creates its Handler; prepare does not create all three.

After initialization, the Looper dispatches eligible Messages serially to their target Handlers. Application, Activity, Service, and ordinary BroadcastReceiver callbacks generally run on the main thread, but not every component method does. ContentProvider.onCreate runs there; remote data operations typically use Binder threads and must support concurrency. Broadcast delivery can also use a specified Handler. Below are selected H constants and the BIND_APPLICATION branch only.

For more, see Android Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained.

System Mechanism - Message Mechanism

Looper.loop dispatches currently eligible Messages and waits when none can run; it need not sleep immediately on entry. Delayed messages may not yet be due, and synchronization barriers may block synchronous messages. Input and display events also arrive through native Looper file-descriptor callbacks, so a wakeup need not correspond to an ordinary Java Message.

The core of the Android Message mechanism consists of: Handler, Looper, MessageQueue, and Message.

Many code-level analyses exist, so here is a brief overview of the components:

  1. Handler: Sends Messages/Runnables to a particular Looper’s thread; constructing one creates no thread. Implicit-current-Looper constructors are deprecated and can throw when no Looper exists. Explicitly choose a target, for example new Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()).
  2. Looper: Dispatches an eligible Message through its target’s dispatchMessage(), with separate paths for a Runnable, Handler.Callback, and handleMessage(). Traditional APM can observe dispatch boundaries through setMessageLogging(). That wall-clock duration can include waits and does not cover queue latency, GPU work, or presentation; logging also has overhead.
  3. MessageQueue: This Android 10 implementation manages due times, barriers, and asynchronous messages. nativePollOnce waits through the native Looper until an event, wakeup, or timeout. Waiting does not require an empty queue, and enqueueing does not guarantee immediate execution. An asynchronous Message still runs on the same Looper thread.
  4. Message: Carries fields such as what, arg1, arg2, obj, or a Runnable callback; its target Handler determines dispatch.

See the Handler API and ContentProvider threading contract. Check internal framework structures against the relevant OS version.

System Mechanism - Screen Refresh and Vsync

First, understand Screen Refresh Rate. A hardware concept, it refers to how often the screen hardware refreshes the image. E.g., a 60Hz rate means the screen refreshes its display 60 times per second; 90Hz means 90 times.

FPS counts frames at a stated stage: generation, submission, or presentation. A 60 Hz display can show 30 fps content; an app can also produce frames that never reach the screen. Android 11’s multiple-refresh-rate support lets display modes, policy, and content requirements influence the chosen rate. App fps and display refresh rate need not match.

Vsync (Vertical Synchronization) provides timing references for display updates and the graphics pipeline. It coordinates submission and presentation but does not guarantee enough application frames or eliminate jank by itself.

Target cadenceInterval between target frames
60 fpsAbout 16.67 ms
90 fpsAbout 11.11 ms
120 fpsAbout 8.33 ms

These are periods, not universal per-thread timeout thresholds. Available budgets depend on frame start, scheduling predictions, pipeline depth, GPU work, and composition deadlines. CPU slices shorter than 16.67 ms do not by themselves prove on-time presentation.

Further reading:

  1. A New Smooth Experience: A Talk on 90Hz
  2. Android Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained

System Mechanism - Choreographer

Choreographer coordinates application frame callbacks. When animation or traversal work requires a frame, it requests timing and runs due callbacks in phases. Static UI need not redraw on every physical refresh. Do not hardcode 16.6 ms: 60 Hz is only an example. The supplied frame time supports animation timing and is not a guarantee of callback execution or final presentation time.

It connects both sides of the pipeline:

  1. Callbacks: Android 10 includes Input, Animation, Insets Animation, Traversal, and Commit, while the figure shows only the main phases. Not all input waits for the Input phase, and measure/layout need not run every frame. Late-execution logs are clues, not final on-screen jank counts.
  2. Display timing: FrameDisplayEventReceiver requests/receives Vsync and schedules an asynchronous doFrame message on its Looper. This can bypass synchronization barriers, but cannot preempt a running main-thread task. The public Choreographer.postFrameCallback API (API 16 onward) runs its callback once; ongoing animation must request subsequent callbacks according to its lifecycle.

The following image shows Choreographer‘s frame drawing workflow via the Message mechanism when Vsync arrives. Details: Detailed Explanation of Android Rendering Mechanism Based on Choreographer.

System Mechanism - Buffer Flow and TripleBuffer

BufferQueue connects graphics-buffer producers and consumers, passing ownership, metadata, and synchronization information rather than copying the whole image on every queue operation. The endpoints can live in different processes or in one process. Start with the legacy app-Surface-to-SurfaceFlinger queue model below.

In the legacy window-Surface path, the app produces buffers and SurfaceFlinger consumes their graphical content:

  1. dequeueBuffer() obtains a writable slot/buffer, rather than freeing it. Respect the returned synchronization fence before safely reusing its memory.
  2. The app produces content through CPU or GPU work and calls queueBuffer() with a readiness fence. GPU execution may still be in progress; queue completion does not mean all pixels are ready to read.
  3. The consumer uses acquireBuffer() to obtain the content and fence, then respects the synchronization dependency. SurfaceFlinger selects suitable content for its schedule; it need not acquire a new image on every Vsync.
  4. Once the consumer no longer needs an old buffer, release and its fence communicate reuse conditions. A CPU-side release returning does not guarantee that display/GPU access has finished.

See BufferQueue and the synchronization framework. An app can have several surfaces/queues; capacity and actual allocations depend on the path and endpoint configuration, not a universal three-buffers-per-app rule.

Modern path: In AOSP android-16.0.0_r1, client-side BLASTBufferQueue acquires a buffer and passes it with its fence to SurfaceFlinger through a SurfaceControl Transaction’s setBuffer. The legacy diagram’s queue-consumer location is not universal for modern windows.

Comparison of double vs. triple buffering:

An additional buffer can increase overlap between production and consumption:

  1. Less waiting for a free buffer: If one buffer is being consumed and another produced, a spare may let production continue. Dequeue waits often occur on RenderThread or another producer thread and can indirectly block the main thread.
  2. Absorbing short variations: Queued content that is ready in time can sustain some display updates. The diagram’s reduction from two repeats to one applies only to its illustrated timing, not a universal benefit. It still shows the first repeated frame.
  3. Limits: More buffers do not shorten GPU execution or fix sustained production/composition overruns. App and SurfaceFlinger Vsync can have different phases. The app graphics stack submits GPU commands; BufferQueue is not a job queue waiting for SurfaceFlinger to start the GPU.

Costs include memory and potentially greater queueing latency. A deeper queue can delay the image reflecting the latest input, so evaluate responsiveness as well as smoothness. Details: Android Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained.

System Mechanism - Input Flow

Input is one common event source. The historical image places the native InputReader and InputDispatcher threads in system_server; verify thread locations and trace labels for the particular build. A long press is generally recognized by gesture logic using elapsed time and events, not read from EventHub as a distinct hardware “long press.”

  1. InputReader reads device events from EventHub and interprets/transforms them for dispatch.
  2. InputDispatcher selects targets based on focus, touch targeting, and policy, then publishes to the relevant window/monitor InputChannel. This is not a broadcast to every app.
  3. OutboundQueue contains events awaiting publication for one Connection, not necessarily all input for an app.
  4. WaitQueue contains published events awaiting completion acknowledgements. handled=false can also complete an event; queue length is not duration.
  5. PendingInputEventQueue is ViewRootImpl’s app-side queue. Android 10 decrements its count before deliverInputEvent, so zero does not mean processing or visual feedback is complete.
  6. deliverInputEvent is an asynchronous trace interval for app input-stage delivery, ending at finishInputEvent. It is not the thread wakeup time, and its duration need not be entirely CPU execution.
  7. The legacy viewer’s Input Response / Rendering Response interaction groupings do not directly measure physical touch-to-light latency.
  8. Handling input can request a visual update. Fling after release depends on velocity, boundaries, and gesture logic; UP does not guarantee fling. An input completion ACK also does not prove presentation.

Systrace representation:

This image is from Meizu Launcher; earlier images include OPPO Launcher and a Matrix sample. They cannot be joined into one device/capture’s causal chain. Green F markers are legacy-viewer frame analysis, not independent evidence of GPU completion or correct final presentation.

Details: Android Systrace Basics - Input Explained.

Series Articles

  1. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  2. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  3. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis

Attachments

Attachments are on GitHub: https://github.com/Gracker/SystraceForBlog/tree/master/Android_Systrace_Smooth_In_Action

  1. xiaomi_launcher.zip: Systrace for launcher scroll jank (main analysis case).
  2. xiaomi_launcher_scroll_all_the_time.zip: Systrace for continuous launcher scrolling.
  3. oppo_launcher_scroll.zip: Comparison trace.

On 2026-10-14, all three ZIPs were downloadable, passed CRC checks, and contained legacy Systrace HTML and ftrace data. These are historical captures, not a current-device reproduction. The interactions were not rerun, and the embedded viewer’s compatibility with current browsers was not tested. Use a tool that supports the format; FrameTimeline information absent from these captures cannot be reconstructed as if it had been recorded.

Source references, all android-10.0.0_r1: ActivityThread, Looper, MessageQueue, Choreographer, and ViewRootImpl.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.

entry.title: Why is the Weibo Experience Better on Huawei? A Technical Analysis and Reflection
entry.content:
A fellow developer shared a Weibo post (https://weibo.com/1808884742/IApbpEVQr) where blogger @王波粒 noticed a peculiar phenomenon on the Mate 30 Pro. I highly recommend watching the video first.

The question concerns a difference observed in 2020: some Huawei samples displayed feed images during scrolling, while some other samples waited until the list stopped. This is not a claim about every current device; configuration, caches, and system behavior can differ even with the same client version.

The same version of Weibo behaving differently on different phones was something I wanted to understand as a system performance engineer. Had Weibo made a specific adaptation? What had changed? Let’s look at the code and see what we can learn.

Historical version note (reviewed 2026-10-14): This is a 2020 case, labelled in the original as Weibo 10.8.1. The old images and impressions remain, but the original APK hash, complete Huawei firmware/PerfSDK versions, runtime trace, and controlled measurements are unavailable. Image work, vendor scrolling physics, and subjective feel require separate verification; this is not a ranking of current devices.

What makes this so special?

  1. Deferring some image work during fast scrolling is a trade-off, not a universal default. Downloading, decoding, transforming, caching, and displaying are separate stages; pausing one need not stop all of them.
  2. Images appearing mid-scroll need not be downloading at that moment; they may come from cache or earlier requests. Displaying images mid-scroll can reduce placeholder time while adding CPU, GPU, memory, or network work. The benefit depends on visible content and frame timing.
  3. I felt that the Huawei sample decelerated more gently at the time. Without matched initial velocity, content, refresh mode, and firmware, this is an impression rather than proof of universally longer or more iOS-like motion.

This was my view of the collaboration at the time, not a new benchmark result:

As an Android developer, I really admired the attention Huawei paid to this small part of the experience. I thought its work with Weibo was a useful example for cooperation with other major apps.

Contextual Notes

  1. Around June 2020, I saw some non-Huawei samples wait until scrolling stopped before showing images. When I looked again in August, images appeared during scrolling too. This is historical observation, not today’s server configuration.
  2. The code includes feed_scroll_loadimage_enable and gray-release configuration access. Without server responses, it cannot establish rollout dates, account/device coverage, or immediate propagation.
  3. Identical APKs can take different paths due to configuration, cache, OS version, and hot patches. PatchProxy checks appear in the images; an APK version alone does not identify executed code.
  4. The sample label is Weibo 10.8.1. Obfuscated method numbers vary across screenshots and are not stable APIs or proof of one exact build.

The Verdict

The images supply two clues: Weibo registers threshold callbacks controlling ImageLoader, and vendor Framework snippets calculate scrolling distance and velocity differently. The callback actions are visible; automatically enabling a new curve whenever the SDK is present, or guaranteeing smoother rendering, requires more evidence.

  1. HwPerfVelocityCallback reports the relationship to a threshold; the shown callbacks do not deliver numeric velocity every frame.
  2. The downward callback calls resume, and the upward callback calls pause. Which jobs pause, and whether in-flight work continues, depends on this ImageLoader implementation, which is not shown.
  3. The Framework fragment uses a SmartSlideOverScroller branch. Its complete activation conditions and connection to this SDK require the matching firmware or trace.

I tried this in AOSP myself and got a demo running. If you’re interested in the details, feel free to contact me. That demo is not attached to this repository and was not reproduced in this review.

How the Optimization Works

Phenomenon Analysis

For a typical AbsListView gesture:

  1. SCROLL_STATE_TOUCH_SCROLL = 1: the finger drags the list. Merely pressing down need not enter this state before the touch threshold is crossed.
  2. SCROLL_STATE_FLING = 2: an eligible release starts inertial motion. Minimum fling velocity, boundaries, and nested-scroll consumption also matter.
  3. SCROLL_STATE_IDLE = 0: no scrolling.

Dragging also has velocity and can be fast. Neither “velocity exists only during fling” nor “a finger on the screen guarantees slow scrolling” is correct.

Phase 1 Optimization

With the pictured optimization flag false, non-IDLE states call pause. With it true, non-FLING states call resume. That allows loading during TOUCH_SCROLL; it does not guarantee jank-free frames or immediate network requests.

Phase 2 Optimization (Fling)

The callbacks aim to pause during fast fling and resume as it slows. Request reduction and frame improvements depend on caching, cancellation, and the actual branch; two function calls cannot quantify them.

Curve tuning is separate. AOSP already uses a nonlinear spline, not constant-speed linear motion. A longer or gentler fling does not by itself make rendering faster.

Technical Deep Dive (Reverse Engineering)

These are partial decompiler and Framework views, without the complete SDK conditions, ImageLoader implementation, or firmware version.

Phase 1 State Callback

Optimization flagStateDirect action shown
trueIDLE / TOUCH_SCROLLresume
trueFLINGNo direct pause/resume in this branch
falseTOUCH_SCROLL / FLINGpause
falseIDLEresume

Thus state 2 does not itself pause loading in the enabled path; earlier state remains relevant until other code, such as a threshold callback, acts. The image also handles async_card and video preloading, so its whole performance effect cannot be assigned to images. A PatchProxy override can bypass the visible ordinary path.

Monitoring Velocity

The screenshot passes HwPerfSpeedLoader.HwPerfVelocityCallback to the list helper:

  1. HwPerfonVelocityDownToThreshold() calls ImageLoader.getInstance().resume().
  2. HwPerfonVelocityUpToThreshold() calls ImageLoader.getInstance().pause().

The threshold value, units, initial notification behavior, and hysteresis are not shown. Do not invent one universal value for all densities and refresh rates.

The Fling Curve (Framework Layer)

The supplied Huawei update fragment invokes getUpdateDistance/getUpdateVelocity on SmartSlideOverScroller and applies a distance cutoff:

Distance calculation:

Velocity calculation:

The velocity expression uses an exponential and normalized time, but the images omit full parameter sources, entry conditions, and the firmware tag. They show a different implementation, not proof of a longer total duration, universal activation, or equivalence to iPhone behavior. Distance correction and cutoff logic also matter.

The original discussion of iOS transitions remains background reading, not a replacement for measurements on these devices.

Handling Other Manufacturers

The boolean a is the helper’s registration result. False can reflect lack of support, initialization failure, or other conditions; it does not uniquely identify a non-Huawei phone. The ordinary fallback requires Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 28 (Android 9) AND the FeedAbManager feature flag:

FeedAbManager exposes several feature readers:

The corresponding method reads feed_scroll_loadimage_enable:

The configuration fragment distinguishes SYNC_WITH_SERVER, REMAIN_UNCHANGE_INAPPLIFECYCLE, and NOTCACHED policies. Names alone do not establish a fresh server request on every callback.

This fallback can permit mid-scroll loading, but the images do not show that it gains the same velocity callbacks or vendor curve. Measure the paths separately; an image appearing is not proof that PerfSDK is active.

The “Scroll-to-Click” Challenge

In Android 10 AbsListView, ACTION_DOWN during fling can be intercepted and treated as stopping or taking over scrolling rather than an ordinary item click. This explains some stop-then-tap interactions, not a rule that every Android list always requires two taps.

A longer fling can extend the interval in which it can be interrupted. Click behavior also depends on event dispatch, target stability, touch slop, and the widget. The comparisons below describe how it felt to me at the time, not measurements that apply to every device.

A short, abrupt fling feels like sliding a stone across rough concrete: it barely travels before stopping. Whether you’re the one throwing it or I’m standing nearby watching, neither of us is likely to admire how gracefully it moves. That was how the stock Android curve felt to me.

A longer, gentler fling is more like sending a block of ice across a smooth frozen surface. It keeps going. iOS took that too far for my taste: it felt painfully slow to settle, and I often had to tap once to stop the list before tapping the item I actually wanted. I preferred MIUI 12’s adjustment at the time. Pairing that kind of tuning with app cooperation, as Huawei and Weibo had done, seemed worth exploring.

I proposed allowing a click after 95% or 98% of the distance, borrowing the idea from Launcher; this was a design suggestion, not a verified MIUI 12/Huawei feature. Distance progress is not remaining time or instantaneous speed. Check target stability, finger movement, and accidental activations, preserve click/accessibility semantics, and do not simply pass touches through to moving items.

Extended Reading

Performance Considerations

Image work spans scheduling, network transfer, decoding, transforms, caches, texture upload, and View updates. Prioritize visible content, bound prefetch, and cancel or deprioritize obsolete off-screen requests when appropriate. Prefetching is legitimate; loading unseen content is not inherently a mistake.

Queues are not necessarily FIFO. The fiftieth image need not wait for all forty-nine predecessors: concurrency, priorities, cancellation, and cache hits matter. List reuse is normal; wrong images often involve stale request-to-item bindings. Resuming paused work may create a burst and needs measurement too.

Modern apps can start with public scroll callbacks and image-library request/lifecycle management instead of a vendor-private SDK. Define units, absolute-speed handling, initial state, hysteresis, and off-screen cleanup. Avoid reflecting into ListView’s private Scroller. If the app owns an OverScroller it can use its public API; VelocityTracker can estimate gesture velocity.

For validation, combine Macrobenchmark frame metrics and Perfetto with fixed content, cache state, network, account/rollout, refresh mode, and input. Compare frame overruns, visible-image timing, requests/bytes, and memory rather than video impressions or mean fps alone. No new benchmark gains are claimed here.

Scroll State Cheat Sheet

For AbsListView.OnScrollListener, the following is an interface summary with explanatory comments:

onScrollStateChanged reports state changes, not per-frame velocity. onScroll can run repeatedly during scrolling or layout updates; the API phrase “after the scroll has completed” must not be read as “only at final idle.” AOSP’s invokeOnItemScrollListener call sites confirm this.

AndroidX comparison: RecyclerView.OnScrollListener (since 1.0.0) uses IDLE, DRAGGING, and SETTLING. SETTLING also covers programmatic smooth scrolling. onScrolled dx/dy are displacement, not velocity; layout changes can trigger a zero/zero callback. Estimating speed requires valid time intervals and samples, not just translating AbsListView state names.

Scroll State Transitions

Typical gestures include:

  1. Release after a slow drag: IDLE → TOUCH_SCROLL → IDLE.
  2. Release satisfying fling conditions: IDLE → TOUCH_SCROLL → FLING → IDLE.

These are not exhaustive. New touches, boundaries, nested scrolling, or programmatic motion can change the path. VelocityTracker also estimates speed before the finger leaves the screen.

Computing the Fling Curve

The following restores the zero-time/end checks from AOSP android-10.0.0_r1 OverScroller.SplineOverScroller.update(). It is a Framework-internal method requiring surrounding fields, not a standalone app class or the Huawei-modified implementation above:

SPLINE interpolates sampled curve values. In that branch, multiplying distance/duration by 1000 converts pixels per millisecond to pixels per second. BALLISTIC models deceleration beyond an edge, while CUBIC returns to the valid range; neither should be equated directly with newer EdgeEffect stretch rendering.

The scrolling call chain drives updates; FlingRunnable schedules further work, but that does not guarantee one execution per display refresh. Elapsed-time position calculations can advance after scheduling delays. Internal axis mCurrVelocity values are not a uniform physical-speed contract across every branch; public getCurrVelocity returns the X/Y vector magnitude without direction.

Conclusion

I’d like to see more cooperation like this between manufacturers and apps such as WeChat, Kuaishou, and Douyin. When the two sides spend their time working around each other, users pay for it. Working together on these details looks like a better direction to me.

I included the Pinduoduo job description below because it specifically mentioned working with manufacturers on optimization. It was a 2020 example of that direction, not a current vacancy listing.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

entry.title: An Incident Caused by a 'Leap' Month - Analysis of Samsung System Reboots
entry.content:
Around 1:30 AM on May 23, 2020, a large number of Samsung phone users in China experienced severe issues including freezes, infinite reboots, and forced entries into Recovery Mode. Improper handling by users led to data loss, and the incident quickly became a trending topic on social media platforms like Zhihu, with service centers overwhelmed.

Social media responses ranged from frustration to anger, with some comparing the incident to the Note 7 battery disaster, “charging-gate,” or “green-screen-gate.” Some predicted Samsung would be forced out of the Chinese market. People lost job offers due to missed calls, others lost valuable data, and some even resorted to smashing their devices in frustration.

As an Android developer, I am not here to pile on Samsung. My goal is to uncover the root cause of this incident and see what we can learn from it. Since it’s a technical failure in the Android system, it’s essential to analyze it from a technical perspective.

Historical case note (reviewed 2026-10-14): This analysis uses screenshots and decompiled fragments retained from 2020. AOD version numbers identify old samples, not current update recommendations. Original APK hashes, complete firmware, and Samsung’s build records are unavailable here, so this review separates directly observed errors, version-comparison clues, and build-cause hypotheses.

The circulated shop photo also shows display units in recovery. It does not by itself prove hardware damage or complete data loss.

Conclusion

The retained log directly shows com.android.systemui’s main thread failing to resolve an integer field in R$string while inflating an AOD-related date view, producing NoSuchFieldError. It does not establish that strings.xml simply lacked the “leap” character, or identify a particular Maven dependency error in Samsung’s build.

AOD means Always On Display, showing information such as time while the screen is otherwise off. Availability depends on the model and settings, not a universal high-end-only rule. This stack runs through a SystemUI lock-screen plugin path, not an independently crashing AOD process.

The Hong Kong Observatory’s 2020 conversion table places 2020-05-23 on the first day of the leap fourth month. The old method accesses common_date_leap_month when isLeapMonth() is true, supporting a date-triggered explanation. The branch applies to leap months generally, not only a leap fourth month. The Chinese original’s common_data_leap_month spelling should be common_date_leap_month, matching the log and code.

Repeated SystemUI failures may trigger recovery policies. A recovery image alone does not establish the escalation sequence on every device, or prove that every device with a listed version must enter recovery. Firmware, plugin versions, locale/region configuration, and the executed path determine exposure; the user’s country is not itself the code’s condition.

Analysis

If you were just here for the drama, you can stop at the conclusion above. For Android developers who are curious, let’s keep going. The investigation isn’t complicated, but I think it is worth walking through.

External analysis can locate clues from logs and version samples. Without build configuration, runtime class-loading evidence, and regression results, it is not a complete vendor root-cause report. I’ll go through the steps and tools I used at the time, along with what the retained material can actually tell us.

1. Starting from the Symptoms

The recovery photo shows an Android 9 / PPR1-based build. Recovery entry, a SystemUI process restart, and a whole-device reboot are separate events to verify.

AOSP Rescue Party, introduced in Android 8.0, escalates recovery actions. In android-9.0.0_r1, persistent-app crashes are counted by UID with a threshold of five within a 30-second window. Escalation resets settings before the final level requests recovery with a user prompt to wipe data. It is not a rule that any repeatedly crashing system process automatically erases the phone. Enablement and OEM implementations vary; the pictured Erase app data/Safe mode flow cannot be equated item by item with AOSP.

The next photograph supplies the error itself. I guessed at the time that Samsung had added its own diagnostic screen. The photo alone can’t confirm that; if you know what it is, please let me know.

The readable fields identify com.android.systemui, PID 2388, java.lang.NoSuchFieldError, common_date_leap_month, type I (int), and declaring class com.samsung.android.uniform.R$string. The stack includes LocalDateView.getLunarCalendarInChina, updateLocalDate, onFinishInflate, and SystemUI lock-screen clock views. LocalDataView in the old explanation was a typo.

The investigation therefore asks why this branch accesses the field and why the loaded class cannot resolve it. FATAL EXCEPTION is the log heading; NoSuchFieldError is the specific error type.

2. Code Analysis

I used TTDeDroid. At this review, its latest published release is v1.8.0 (2024-06-12); bundled tools are not necessarily their upstreams’ current versions. JADX can also be used directly, but reconstructed Java is not a guarantee of complete or exact source recovery.

I found several AOD versions on APKMirror to compare. A reproducible comparison needs source, SHA-256, versionName/versionCode, signing identity, firmware build, and installed path. A named version may have variants, and a downloaded APK need not equal the device’s system package. The labels below belong to the original investigation; these are not newly unpacked or device-tested samples.

Normal Version (V5.2.05)

“Normal” is the original comparison label, not today’s latest version or an acceptance result across models. The shown branch is:

It accesses the field when shouldShowLeapMonth(locale) is true. The screenshot does not show that helper’s implementation, so its full conditions cannot be inferred from its name. The older method directly calls isLeapMonth(); the two should not silently be treated as identical. The retained samples do not establish how frequently the branch executes.

The next screenshot shows the field in com.samsung.android.app.aodservice.R, with value 2131689531. This is not the failing com.samsung.android.uniform.R$string class. A field in one namespace does not prove its presence in the other, and resource IDs should not be hardcoded across packages or versions.

The decoded resource image shows common_date_leap_month with text “闰.” A resource-table entry and a runtime class field are separate evidence.

Affected Version (V4.1.70)

I treated v4.1.70 as a suspect sample: the search window shows a reference but no definition.

That warrants inspecting the missing field, but does not prove that every DEX, resource table, and dynamically loaded class was examined. The method name matches the stack; decompiler line numbers do not establish exact build identity.

The original fragment follows. SECCalendarFeatures, the converter, and Time depend on the sample; this is not a standalone standard-Android example to compile:

Only the leap-month branch accesses the field. Array bounds checks cannot prevent field-resolution failure. Inspect DEX field references and the runtime ClassLoader to identify the actual R class, rather than relying solely on the Java view.

3. When did the bug appear?

The retained materials support this evidence table:

SampleRetained materialSupported reading
v3.3.18Search lists app.aodservice and uniform fieldsBoth definitions appear in that decompilation
v4.0.57Search shows only a reference; original notes date it 2018-10-24Suspected introduction point, without complete artifact verification
v4.1.70Reference and method screenshotsConsistent with the failing path, not a device reproduction
v4.2.24 / v4.2.44APK listing dated 2019-05-03 / 2019-06-24Listing dates, not independent proof of the fix or OTA coverage
v5.2.05New branch, R field, and resource screenshotsLater comparison sample, not today’s latest release

The v3.3.18 search includes definitions in both namespaces:

The v4.0.57 search shows only the use:

From the samples I found at the time, I placed the fix at v4.2.44. A corresponding fix commit or complete binary comparison is unavailable here. The range must not include v4.2.44 as universally faulty while simultaneously naming it as fixed; listing dates also do not prove all models received an update. The Chinese caption’s 4.3.44 typo is corrected to the pictured 4.2.44.

The Chinese agricultural calendar is lunisolar, not purely lunar. Leap months are not a once-in-a-decade event. Test the general isLeapMonth branch across leap months, rather than waiting for another leap fourth month.

4. The Build Issue

The question that bothered me at this point was: if the field can’t be found, how did this compile in the first place?
NoSuchFieldError is a runtime linkage failure: a required field is incompatible with the actual loaded class definition. Separate three checks:

  1. Can compilation resolve the field in the required fully qualified R class?
  2. Does the final DEX/runtime-loaded class have the matching name and field type?
  3. Can the integer ID resolve an entry in the active Resources/resource table?

Failure at step 2 can occur before getString executes. Missing resources at step 3 usually involve Resources.NotFoundException. The following character entry therefore cannot, by itself, explain NoSuchFieldError.

Resources need not originate in the main module’s strings.xml: libraries and resource merging also supply R symbols. Java’s constant rules can resolve constant values into caller code during compilation; a decompiler’s R.string expression does not necessarily mean a named DEX field read remains. Modern builds also cannot assume all R fields are final: AGP 8.0 defaults to non-final, non-transitive R. This is modern context, not an explanation of Samsung’s 2018 build.

Mixed dependency versions, class/resource removal during packaging, host/plugin incompatibility, or a ClassLoader selecting another definition are candidates to inspect. The screenshots cannot choose among them or establish the original “second Maven case.” They identify the runtime failure and triggering branch, but not the internal build step responsible.

For a fresh investigation, preserve original packages, inspect Manifest/DEX with apkanalyzer, inspect resource tables with AAPT2, and correlate runtime class origins with the system/plugin combination. Regress the actual release artifacts rather than checking only that the IDE shows the field.

Modern update: Android 16 introduced the Crash Recovery module, including PackageWatchdog and RescueParty. Trace source locations and recovery policy for the actual OS version; the old article is not a current universal recovery contract.

Summary

The reasoning wasn’t especially complicated, but finding versions, decompiling them, and checking the code took some tedious work. The direct clue is a calendar branch triggering runtime field-resolution failure. The date and error type can be checked; the exact build mismatch, complete affected-version range, and each device’s recovery sequence require more original evidence.

Lessons Learned:

  1. Feature Testing: Cover ordinary/leap months, month/year boundaries, time zones, locale, lock-screen view recreation, and plugin updates. Control time in tests instead of waiting for the real date.

  2. Dependency Management: Check compile-time inputs, final DEX, resources, runtime class origins, and host/plugin combinations. Compilation alone does not establish release compatibility.

  3. UI Stability: SystemUI and Launcher failures can affect essential interaction. Test plugin compatibility and isolate recoverable failures where appropriate; engineers must balance feature work with stability. They also sit between system development and app development, with dependencies on both sides. It isn’t easy. My wife had been doing this work for over six years when I wrote this—she deserved an extra chicken drumstick that evening…

  4. Updates: Use official updates matching the model, region, and system, read release notes, and back up important data. Updates may fix defects or introduce regressions; do not assume system-app updates are risk-free or install arbitrary mismatched system APKs.

  5. Curiosity and Humility: Curiosity helps me look past the symptoms and learn something new. Humility reminds me how little I know in an Android system this large.

  6. This was a serious incident for Samsung, and a case worth learning from. Samsung was already struggling in China, and the S20 series had only just shown signs of recovery when this happened. Own the mistake and apologize. There’s no shame in that.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Analysis of Android App Chain Wakeups
entry.content:
The release of MIUI 12 brought a long-standing battle between App developers and ROM developers into the public eye, revealing the intricate details of this technical tug-of-war. As the saying goes, “While the demon rises a foot, the path rises ten feet.” ROM developers, with their higher system-level permissions, generally hold the upper hand. App developers, however, are not easily deterred, employing various “black technologies” for background persistence and cross-app wakeups. Even Google has stepped in to mediate, establishing rules to regulate behavior for both parties. This competition is arguably healthy; a total victory by either side would inevitably lead to stagnation or the loss of useful functionality.

However, the victims of this struggle are undoubtedly the consumers. If App developers succeed, phones become cluttered with persistent background processes that hog CPU and memory. Conversely, if ROM developers are too aggressive, the app experience suffers—a pain well-known to many Android developers.

As discussed later in this article, most smartphone manufacturers have developed their own strategies to handle auto-starts and associated starts. Beyond the technical struggle, there’s the issue of privacy. Baidu’s Robin Li once remarked that “Chinese people are more open about privacy and relatively less sensitive. If they can trade privacy for convenience, safety, or efficiency, they are willing to do so in many cases.” Consider the convenience of copying a phrase in WeChat and having Taobao automatically open to the corresponding item. It’s helpful, isn’t it? But do we really want every app peering into our clipboards?

Privacy should not be dismissed lightly. Technology is a double-edged sword. If privacy falls into the wrong hands, the consequences can be severe. This is exactly why the EU implemented the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). For example, many domestic manufacturers now differentiate their products for the EU market, disabling various data collection features to avoid massive fines. In other markets, data collection often remains unchecked.

This article does not delve into the ethics of privacy—I unconditionally support privacy protection. Instead, I will analyze the technical aspects of “Auto-start” and “Chain Wakeup” as highlighted by MIUI 12.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-14): The personal discussion and AOSP Android 10 cases retain their 2020 context. App/SDK versions were not fully recorded; these observations do not establish current behavior. This review separates receiver declarations, actual process starts, and evidence of the caller. Old OEM settings and SDK snippets are historical, with relevant Android 7–15 restrictions added below.

Technical Terminology Explained

Distinguish processes, components, and launch causes before treating a component record as another app startup.

Process Startup

Android’s four app component types are Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver, and ContentProvider. A process hosts components; it is not an additional component category. Apps normally use a default process but can assign components to other processes created by the system, rather than child processes forked by the app’s main process. See Application fundamentals.

For an allowed request, the system reuses the required process or creates it when absent. Tapping a launcher icon can reuse an existing process and Activity. A context-registered receiver requires a running process; it is not equivalent to a manifest receiver that can trigger a cold start. A file observer cannot execute after its hosting process is gone.

This article focuses on Receiver, Service, and Provider paths without a new visible screen. Background Activity launches also face platform restrictions since Android 10. Starting a process or component does not mean an app UI has appeared.

Auto-start (Self-starting)

Here, “auto-start” means a process launch triggered by a system event or scheduled task without the user opening the app at that moment. It is an analysis term, not one Android API; the system still determines eligibility and timing.

Associated Start (Link-starting / Chain Wakeup)

Here, an associated start means one app’s cross-app component request causes another process to launch. A shared SDK can participate, but sharing an SDK alone is insufficient: visibility, exported status, permissions, target state, and background restrictions still apply.

Startup Blocking

ROM policy can act during resolution, requests, or process creation; AOSP already applies permission, background-execution, and state checks. A request may be rejected, deferred, or fail with an exception, rather than simply returning silently.

Imagine tapping Alipay to pay inside another app, only for the system to block the payment component. User-initiated payment and sharing flows need different treatment from background maintenance. Incorrect blocking breaks legitimate behavior; allowing one request does not grant permanent process residency.

Analysis Methods

Monkey

Monkey generates activity launches and input pressure, but is not required to establish a launch cause. For a single chain wakeup, record the build, app versions/targetSdk, initial process state, and one controlled action. For my original experiment, I installed plenty of apps, started the Monkey command below, and went to bed while it kept generating activity switches. That is the background to this long-running stress test, not a default reproduction command:

--pct-appswitch 90 controls the share of Activity-launch events, not a guarantee of switching to different apps 90% of the time. --throttle 10000 sets a 10-second delay, while 100000000 is an event count. A rough count-times-delay estimate is 31.7 years; event combinations and termination conditions affect actual duration. It is not an overnight completion setting, and ignored failures remain failures.

Using the official options, start with bounded sampling on a dedicated test setup, replacing the package with the app under test:

-p constrains Activities visited by Monkey, not system broadcasts or other processes requested by the app. A seed does not freeze networking, scheduling, or background jobs. These commands were not executed during this review.

EventLog

Process events are useful clues, but buffers can wrap and captures can be incomplete. Preserve raw context before filtering:

For a quick live view:

Android 10 EventLogTags defines the fields. am_proc_bound records binding the app process to system work; it does not establish a successful service bindService call or visible Activity. Correlate timestamps, user, and UID because PIDs are reused.

Dumpsys

The original used dumpsys activity. Narrower snapshots help inspect broadcasts and the target service:

Connections identifies binding clients at capture time, not a complete call history. Align snapshots with launch events, caller logs, or system tracing from the same interval. Record the build, app version, targetSdk, user ID, and capture time.

Technical Analysis of Auto-starts

The boot, network, and media cases below are historical. The existence of a broadcast does not mean every targetSdk can receive it through a manifest and cold-start a process; eligibility and delivery still require checking.

Boot Completed

BOOT_COMPLETED requires RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED and is not delivered in every state, including an ordinary never-launched installation or a force-stopped package. It differs from LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED during Direct Boot, which requires appropriate directBootAware and device-encrypted storage handling.

Boot broadcasts are exceptions to Android 8.0’s implicit-broadcast restrictions, but receiving one does not allow unlimited background execution. Finish onReceive promptly; deferrable backup/sync work can use WorkManager, which follows system scheduling and does not guarantee immediate execution or permanent residency.

Case Study: Tencent News

The original record describes a boot broadcast. The cropped image identifies com.tencent.news.system.BootBroadcastReceiver with process com.tencent.news:PushService, not the default process named in the old explanation.

Deliver +7s128ms does not directly mean seven seconds executing onReceive. Android 10 BroadcastRecord prints duration[i], assigned by BroadcastQueue.finishReceiverLocked from finishTime minus receiverTime. For a manifest receiver this interval can include process startup, dispatch, and waiting. It is approximately 7.128 seconds of system-tracked handling, not CPU time. The crop omits the action and matching am_proc_start, so it cannot independently establish a new process creation.

Network Changes

Suppose you’re watching a live stream and Wi-Fi drops, switching you to mobile data. The app can ask whether you want to keep watching; streaming uses a lot of data. Network changes can inform app behavior. However, CONNECTIVITY_ACTION was deprecated in API 28. On Android 7.0 (API 24) and later, apps targeting 24+ cannot receive it through a manifest receiver; context registration works while that context remains valid, not as a replacement for cold-starting a dead process.

Use registerDefaultNetworkCallback/registerNetworkCallback for network observation, or WorkManager network constraints for deferrable sync. A connected network does not guarantee that the destination server is reachable.

Examples

I listed these receivers in my notes at the time:

  1. DingTalk (com.alibaba.android.rimet): com.xiaomi.push.service.receivers.NetworkStatusReceiver
  2. Learning Strong Nation (cn.xuexi.android): com.xiaomi.push.service.receivers.NetworkStatusReceiver
  3. Weibo (com.sina.weibo): com.xiaomi.push.service.receivers.NetworkStatusReceiver
  4. DiDi (com.sdu.didi.psnger): com.didi.sdk.push.PushNetReceiver
  5. Inke (com.meelive.ingkee): com.network_optimization.NetWorkStateReceiver

The crop actually shows Learning Strong Nation and DingTalk as Pending, with maxManifestReceiverApiLevel=23. Android 10’s dispatch code checks targetSdk against that limit and can skip candidates. This is not evidence that every listed process started. The original “over 200” count cannot be verified from the retained crop.

This is another Pending list, including Tencent Mobile Manager and UC receivers. The Wi-Fi action differs from CONNECTIVITY_CHANGE; ordinary apps targeting 26+ also face Android 8.0’s manifest implicit-broadcast restrictions. These images are not current universal auto-start recipes.

Media Library Scanning

The first two describe the beginning/end of a directory scan; the third concerns a request to eject external storage. They are not a broadcast to every app for every new file. The implicit-broadcast exemption list includes MEDIA_EJECT and other storage-state events, not a blanket exemption for scanner broadcasts. Media access still requires applicable permissions and storage rules.

Case Study: JD Finance

The original presented this as an auto-start case. The image shows com.jd.jrapp.library.longconnection.receiver.BootReceiver as Pending #0 for MEDIA_SCANNER_STARTED, with data file:///storage/emulated/0:

It establishes inclusion in the broadcast record, not successful delivery or process creation. Those conclusions require subsequent delivery results and a matching am_proc_start.

Third-Party SDKs (e.g., GeTui)

Push SDKs may declare background components, but a process suffix cannot identify the SDK. Multiple libraries can use :pushservice. Inspect actual APK dependencies, the merged manifest, and runtime evidence.

The following 2020 snippet has no recorded SDK version and is retained to identify historical components, not as a current integration template:

The receiver has an intent-filter without an explicit exported value. Components with intent filters targeting API 31+ must declare exported explicitly; choose the value according to purpose and permissions, not by making everything public. GeTui’s current integration guide says it applies to SDK 3.1.2.0 and later and uses Maven/AAR configuration with matching dependencies. Follow the version in use instead of adding this old XML on top.

Although the process is com.ss.android.ugc.aweme:pushservice, the receiver is com.taobao.accs.EventReceiver, still Pending. The image does not establish a GeTui-triggered Douyin startup, or whether other SDKs are present in that APK.

Technical Analysis of Associated Starts (Chain Wakeups)

Shared SDKs may contact accessible services or providers, subject to platform checks. The old experiment does not support a general claim that most chain wakeups come from JPush. Here we examine only the retained JPush component records.

The Android 10 schema gives six fields: user 0, new process PID 19428, UID 10195, process com.qq.reader, type service, and component cn.jpush.android.service.DaemonService. UID is not the caller PID; this entry does not identify the requester.

Case Study: Qidian Launching QQ Reader via JPush

In that experiment, I ran adb shell am force-stop com.qq.reader, then watched EventLog for a start. Force-stop changes package stopped state; it is not equivalent to LMK reclaiming a process, normal process exit, or swiping away a recent task. The image alone cannot reconstruct every action between the stop and the next request.

The screenshot records 05-06 08:48:35.337, PID 4302, followed by am_proc_bound for the same PID. The textual example above has PID 19428 and must not be treated as this same launch record.

EventLog had not told me who made the request, so I next looked at QQ Reader’s ServiceRecord. It hosts PID 4302 and lists client 2808:com.qidian.QDReader:pushcore/u0a174. This establishes a binding relationship at capture time and a lead for caller analysis, not proof that this connection first created the process. started=false reflects startRequested at that moment; it does not mean the service never ran.

ActiveServices’ compact dump prints the binding Intent before the client, so flg=0x20 is Intent.FLAG_INCLUDE_STOPPED_PACKAGES, not bindService flags. It cannot determine whether BIND_AUTO_CREATE was used. Android 10’s service launch path also clears package stopped state; that explains an old platform mechanism, not the complete sequence behind the screenshot.

To establish causality, align the service request’s caller UID/PID, component, bind/start flags, and process creation, then compare runs changing only the triggering action. The original experiment had no MIUI 12 device screenshot, so the claim that its UI displayed “Qidian launched QQ Reader at 8:48” was an illustration, not a verified UI result.

Newer boundary: Android 15’s stopped-state changes require direct or indirect user action to leave stopped state and cancel PendingIntents on force-stop. The Android 10 observation is not a general method for bypassing current force-stop behavior.

JPush Wakeup Configuration

This historical callback document lists startService, bindService, and ContentProvider types. SDK callback reporting does not replace system evidence about the caller and timing.

JPush Associated-start Documentation

The old documents mention service wakeups in JPush 1.8.0 and shared channels in 3.1.6. Their component switches and VIP terms should not be presented as today’s product rules.

The current Android API documentation separately lists JCollectionAuth.enableAutoWakeup for auto-start and JPushInterface.setLinkMergeEnable for link merging; false disables the corresponding feature. These sections do not identify their earliest supported versions, so check the actual JPush/JCore dependencies. Do not assume an old APK supports them or that one switch disables every background entry point. Vendor power/delivery claims are not new measurements from this review.

OEM Responses

This was my experience with the test phone I had in 2020:

Process management is the most contested area in Android. MIUI chose to show this battle to users, but other manufacturers do the same quietly behind the scenes. Without these controls, phones would be unusable. On my test Pixel, processes are constantly killed by the Low Memory Killer (LMK) due to low RAM, only to be immediately restarted, draining the battery and making the phone so painfully slow I could barely recognize it.

The old settings list is outdated and retained only as historical context. Menus and behavior vary by vendor, OS version, region, and model; no current per-device testing is available here. Notification controls, background restrictions, and force-stop are distinct. Allowlisting does not guarantee survival.

JPush White-list Configurations

This original vendor-settings image includes legacy entries such as MIUI 7’s hidden mode; it is not a current universal menu guide:

GeTui White-list Configurations

EMUI OS (Huawei)

The old document lists auto-start, background protection, and notification controls. These govern different behavior; “manual launch is the only way to recover” is not a cross-version guarantee.

Flyme OS (Meizu)

The old list includes auto-start and notification switches. Blocking notification display does not stop a process; background scheduling follows the actual system policy.

Funtouch OS (VIVO)

The old path uses iManager. Cleanup, force-stop, and system reclaim are different operations; allowlist membership alone cannot predict a later start.

Color OS (OPPO)

The old document mentions Pure Background and locking a process. These are not universal current menu paths, and a recent-task lock is not Android’s promise of permanent residency.

MIUI OS (Xiaomi)

The old list includes auto-start management, battery policy, and MIUI 7 hidden mode. Retain these names for interpreting old records. Background network availability and message timing require testing the actual version; there is no universal “disconnected after a few minutes” rule.

Across ROMs, also check platform limits: background services and implicit broadcasts for targetSdk 26+; background foreground-service launch limits and exceptions for targetSdk 31+; and deferred boot broadcasts on Android 13+ for restricted apps targeting 33+. Android 14/15 impose additional limits on certain FGS types launched from boot receivers. Notification permission is separate from permission to execute in the background.

About Me && Blog

Below are my personal details and links. I look forward to connecting and sharing knowledge with fellow developers!

  1. About Me: Includes my WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Navigation: A guide to the content on this blog.
  3. Curated Android Performance Articles: A collection of must-read performance optimization articles. Self-nominations/recommendations are welcome!
  4. Android Performance Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

“If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
entry.content:
This is the fifth article in the Systrace series, primarily providing a brief introduction to the workflow of SurfaceFlinger. It covers several important threads within SurfaceFlinger, including Vsync signal interpretation, app buffer display, and jank detection. Since Vsync has already been covered in Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained and Detailed Explanation of Android Rendering Mechanism Based on Choreographer, it won’t be discussed in detail here.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Table of Contents

  • Series Article Index
  • Main Content
  • App Section
  • BufferQueue Section
  • SurfaceFlinger Section
  • HWComposer Section
  • References
  • About Me && Blog

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

Main Content

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-14): This article retains its 2020 Systrace images and analysis order. The two complete functions below match AOSP android-10.0.0_r1; the old Binder/BufferQueue path and HIDL track names are historical. Updates cover BLAST and commit/composite in android-16.0.0_r1, plus FrameTimeline on Android 12 (API 31) and later. The screenshots do not identify a system build, so similar method names cannot establish their exact source version.

Read this article together with Perfetto 8: Vsync and performance analysis. SurfaceFlinger’s main thread, BufferQueue, HWC, and app buffers still matter; combine them with FrameTimeline, buffer and Display/HWC tracks, and CPU scheduling.

Identify the frame and its expected presentation time, then follow app submission, GPU readiness, SurfaceFlinger latching, composition, and display submission. Neither exceeding 16.6 ms nor having a long slice alone establishes a jank cause.

The official SurfaceFlinger overview describes receiving layer content and state, coordinating composition, and passing the result to the display stack. Keep these qualifications in mind when reading the old diagram:

  1. Status bar, navigation bar, and app content are examples, not a fixed layer count. An app can use several surfaces; windows and layers are not simply one-to-one, and transactions can coordinate state changes.
  2. Display refresh rate is measured in Hz, content frame rate in fps. Neither 58–62 Hz nor a fixed 16.6 ms budget describes every device. App/SF scheduling involves prediction and phase offsets; a scheduled callback is not necessarily a hardware interrupt at that instant.
  3. Without a new buffer, a layer can retain old content. That differs from never having submitted a buffer; non-buffer layers such as solid-color layers also need separate treatment.
  4. Submission, GPU completion, and presentation are distinct events. Frames overlap in a pipeline. Producing faster than consumption can introduce backpressure, latency, or dropped buffers, depending on queue mode and scheduling.

The diagram includes both GPU composition and paths into display hardware. Repeated GPU boxes do not imply separate GPUs or that every layer passes through SurfaceFlinger’s GPU composition. We will follow App, BufferQueue, SurfaceFlinger, and HWComposer as dependencies, not as a strictly serial timeline across all threads and hardware.

App Section

See MainThread and RenderThread Explained for the app side. These screenshots use a traditional View/HWUI path:

The app submits image buffers through producer interfaces such as Surface. It does not store drawcalls in an image buffer for SurfaceFlinger to execute. Recording drawing operations, submitting GPU work, and writing image pixels are separate stages. “Finished drawing” in annotation 8 should mean buffer submission with synchronization dependencies, not guaranteed GPU completion.

Follow three interactions: the Vsync callback, dequeueBuffer, and queueBuffer.

Vsync Signal Reception and Processing

Choreographer rendering explains frame requests and callbacks. The callback starts input, animation, and traversal work; its timestamp can differ from when the thread actually gets CPU time.

The green F symbols are the old viewer’s frame-analysis markers, not proof of on-time presentation. Correlate the buffer and display frame as well.

RenderThread’s dequeueBuffer

dequeueBuffer gives the producer a writable buffer slot and synchronization information. In the old images, the consumer side resides in SurfaceFlinger and the app requests it through Binder. Buffers may be reused; each call need not allocate or copy an entire image.

App-side Systrace:

SurfaceFlinger-side Systrace:

An SF Binder thread handles the request separately from main-thread composition. Obtaining or writing the buffer may depend on available slots and release fences; inspect thread states to understand waits.

Modern path: Android 16 BLASTBufferQueue creates a local BufferQueue, acquires its buffers, and passes buffers, fences, and layer state to SurfaceFlinger through SurfaceControl transactions. On this path, a dequeueBuffer call need not make an App→SF Binder transaction. BufferQueues do not all live inside the SF process.

RenderThread’s queueBuffer

queueBuffer submits the producer’s buffer with metadata such as fences and timestamps. The pictured eglSwapBuffersWithDamageKHR → queueBuffer chain is an OpenGL ES path, not a universal chain for Vulkan, software Canvas, or every producer.

App-side Systrace:

The image also shows a waiting for GPU completion track after submission. Explicit synchronization allows buffers and fences to move ahead of unfinished GPU work. A queueBuffer return proves neither GPU completion nor presentation; a waiting interval is not continuous GPU execution time either.

SurfaceFlinger-side Systrace:

The layer counter represents queued items awaiting consumption, not all allocated buffers or a count of GPU-ready images. Acquisition decreases it and queuing increases it. The acquisition on the left and subsequent submission on the right are different events; the latter buffer was not consumed before it was submitted.

These steps correspond to the producer side of the diagram:

BufferQueue Section

Triple Buffer Explained covers queues and slot states. A BufferQueue connects a producer and consumer. One process may use several queues, and both ends may reside in the same process; there is no one-queue-per-visible-process rule.

The old path uses the app as producer and SF as consumer. BLAST places the consumer differently, but these four operations still explain the responsibilities:

  1. dequeueBuffer(): obtain a slot and a buffer matching dimensions, format, and usage, allocating or reusing as needed. Satisfy the returned synchronization dependency before writing.
  2. queueBuffer(): submit the buffer and acquire fence. Asynchronous writing may still be in progress.
  3. acquireBuffer(): acquire a queued item. Satisfy its acquire fence before reading, or pass the dependency to downstream hardware.
  4. releaseBuffer(): return the slot with a release fence. The next writer must still wait for earlier readers to finish.

These operations pass references/handles and synchronization information, not four pixel copies. The diagram does not determine buffer limits or whether a queue can replace older items.

SurfaceFlinger Section

Workflow

On the old path, SF processes transactions and candidate buffers, then decides whether composition is needed. Unchanged content does not require work on every Vsync. The image shows handlePageFlip → latchBuffer, followed by handleMessageRefresh:

The code below matches AOSP android-10.0.0_r1 SurfaceFlinger.cpp. onMessageReceived is shortened: it omits backpressure, display-mode changes, refreshNeeded checks, and signalRefresh, among other logic. It is not a complete implementation to copy. The next two functions retain the implementation from that tag.

  1. MessageQueue::INVALIDATE: process transactions, attempt layer updates, and conditionally schedule REFRESH.
  2. MessageQueue::REFRESH: enter handleMessageRefresh.

Read handleMessageRefresh by responsibility:

  1. Preparation: preComposition(), rebuildLayerStacks(), and calculateWorkingSet().
  2. Per-display work: beginFrame(), prepareFrame(), debug flashing, and doComposition().
  3. Follow-up: logLayerStats(), postFrame(), postComposition(), and composition-type, Vsync modulation, and queue-state updates.

The final group includes synchronization and accounting after submission; returning from these methods does not establish completed presentation. Their CPU slice durations are not direct GPU timings.

Android 16 entry points: In android-16.0.0_r1, commit() updates layer snapshots, processes transactions, and decides whether composition is needed. composite() prepares arguments and invokes CompositionEngine::present, which prepares and presents outputs. Some HWC present calls can be offloaded to other threads, with results awaited afterward. Follow these entry points and the device’s actual tracks/source instead of requiring the two old Message names. This outline omits display-mode, backpressure, and multi-display branches.
