There are far too many display-system details to cover them all here. If you’re just getting familiar with the flow, start with SurfaceFlinger’s main responsibilities. If this is the part of the system you work on, follow the matching source version and work through those branches and dependencies.

Dropped Frames (Jank)

First identify which frame of which layer missed its expected presentation time, then trace its dependencies:

  1. Check the refresh mode, target frame rate, and frame identity. Static content or content running below the display rate need not be recomposed on every Vsync.
  2. When an expected update is delayed, inspect SF scheduling, transactions, latch conditions, and backpressure from earlier frames. Follow CPU scheduling, Binder, and GPU/HWC fences to establish the actual wait.
  3. SF may compose while retaining this app’s old buffer or updating only other layers. A queue count of zero can mean an item was just acquired or has not been submitted yet. It does not assign blame to the app; downstream backpressure may delay production too.
  4. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, where captured data supports it, use FrameTimeline to connect app SurfaceFrames with SF DisplayFrames. Compare Expected/Actual timelines, present type, and jank type, then inspect thread/hardware evidence. Actual Timeline is not CPU Running time, and absent tracks do not prove an absence of jank.

See Triple Buffer: Jank Detection for the legacy Systrace view. These cropped screenshots cannot establish a complete jank rate.

HWComposer Section

The Hardware Composer HAL negotiates composition using layer state and device capabilities:

  1. Client composition: SurfaceFlinger uses RenderEngine and sends the client target to HWC. Android 16 RenderEngine supports GL/Vulkan backend selection; client does not universally mean GLES.
  2. Device composition: the device HWC implementation handles the layers. Overlays are common, but plane counts, scaling, rotation, blending, and formats depend on hardware and drivers. Android 4.4 and later do not guarantee four planes.
  3. Hardware composition may save GPU work, while static-content reuse, bandwidth, and blending costs also affect the choice. Client composition is not itself a performance fault; layer counts cannot directly predict dropped frames.

Interface version: The image below shows the historical HIDL android.hardware.graphics.composer@2.1-service. Android 13 introduced AIDL composer3, and HIDL 2.1–2.4 are deprecated. Android 13 did not require every vendor to switch immediately, so verify the actual device HAL.

SF’s executeCommands call crosses Binder into HWC, with Present/Commit/ATOMIC work visible below. The selected 642 μs is the marked interval, not an established GPU execution time or presentation-completion time. Hardware may continue processing or waiting on fences after HWC returns.

This is the latter part of the original diagram:

Distinguish acquire fences (dependencies before reading), release fences (safe reuse of earlier buffers), and display present fences (presentation synchronization). For example, NDK API 29 transaction stats expose separate present and previous-release fences. Devices without present-fence support can return an invalid value; that is not zero latency. A HAL return or SF latch timestamp is not the present fence’s signal time.

HWC waits can affect later frames; see System-side Jank Causes. Read Android P Hardware Composition HWC2 and its series as Android 9/P historical material, not as the current interface layout.

References

  1. Android P Hardware Composition HWC2 (historical)
  2. Android P Graphics Display System (historical series)
  3. SurfaceFlinger and WindowManager
  4. SurfaceFlinger Analysis Document (historical)

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro: Includes personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Welcome to recommend projects/articles.
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Android Developer Learning Path (2020 Edition)
entry.content:
On Medium, @MindOrks published a 2020 Android Developer Learning Path. Given that some readers may have difficulty accessing the original content, I am sharing it here combined with my own 2020 learning plan for your reference.

The original article is quite simple, mostly listing knowledge points without much explanation. I have added brief introductions for each point and included some additional topics based on my own understanding. This is for your reference only.

This article is primarily for Android developers. If you are a beginner, it will help you find a learning path. If you are an experienced developer, it can help you identify gaps in your knowledge. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to leave a message.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): The title and personal plan retain their 2020 context. Foundations remain useful; outdated tools, retired services, and learning links are updated below. New learners can start with Android Basics with Compose, build a small working and testable app, then add topics as needed. This is not a list of libraries every project must install.

A current path covers Kotlin, Compose/Material 3, lifecycle and state, Coroutines/Flow, a data layer, and testing. Maintaining existing projects still requires Java, View/XML, and Fragments. Check build tools, performance tooling, and distribution requirements against current versions rather than copying 2020 configuration.

Programming

Java

Java remains important for reading existing Android apps and Framework code, but should no longer be described as the default first choice for a new app. Android follows a Kotlin-first approach while continuing Java support; Framework code also includes Kotlin, C++, and other languages.

For those who want to dive deeper into the Java Virtual Machine, I recommend:

  1. Zhou Zhiming’s “Understanding the Java Virtual Machine (3rd Edition)”
  2. Deng Fanping’s “Understanding Android Java VM: ART”

Separate general Java/JVM concepts from ART implementation details. HotSpot collectors, flags, and tuning conclusions do not transfer directly to ART, and old source references need matching OS versions.

Kotlin

Focus on null safety, collections, generics, Java interoperability, and coroutine cancellation and exception propagation. IDE conversion assists migration but does not replace review of nullability and lifecycle behavior.

The previously recommended Converting to Kotlin Codelab is officially Deprecated. Keep it as a historical migration example; use the Compose course above and Android’s Kotlin documentation for current learning.

Flutter

As Google’s “favorite son,” Flutter receives significant official support. The version discussed here was v1.12.13+hotfix.7 in 2020, not a current release. Its commit record includes reportFullyDrawn API-level, Skia-extension, and text-affinity changes. The old hotfix discussion is historical context, not evidence of compatibility with every device today. The original Roadmap URL is a changing page, not a fixed 2020 snapshot.

The following retains my observations and plan from that time:

For the development of Flutter, you can refer to Gityuan’s Flutter Cross-Platform Evolution and Architecture. Currently, several Bytedance apps have integrated Flutter for hybrid development. Personally, I believe it’s no longer a time to wait and see on Flutter in 2020; readers can decide whether to start learning based on their own technical plans.

Updated entry point: At review time, the official stable-release notes include Flutter 3.47.0; check the SDK archive for patch versions. Learn Dart, widgets/state, platform integration, and DevTools. Dart 3 enforces sound null safety, so 1.x tutorials and dependencies cannot be copied unchanged. Flutter is an optional cross-platform direction rather than a requirement for every native Android project.

Android Studio

Android Studio IDE Overview

This was my experience in 2020:

As the default Android development tool, recent updates have resolved many performance issues. It still asks a lot of your hardware, but once you make peace with that, you may find yourself admitting: this is actually pretty great.

Key areas to master:

  1. AS Shortcuts
  2. AS Plugins
  3. AS Profiler: CPU, memory, and supported network/system-tracing capabilities. Not every version has a separate generic “I/O Profiler.”
  4. Layout Inspector, Compose debugging, Logcat, APK Analyzer, and emulators; entry points vary by Studio version.

Project Structure — Java/Kotlin/Flutter, XML, .gradle files

Understand source/resources, manifests, module boundaries, the Gradle Wrapper, build.gradle / build.gradle.kts, and version catalogs. Java/Kotlin and Flutter have different build layers; Gradle, AGP, Kotlin, and JDK versions are not interchangeable.

Android Basics

Core Components

These remain the component-model foundations; Compose does not replace them:

  1. Activity — lifecycle, tasks/back stack, configuration changes, and state restoration after process recreation.
  2. Service — a background component is not a background thread. Services normally run on their hosting process’s main thread; learn background-start and foreground-service restrictions too.
  3. Broadcast Receiver — registration, export/permission boundaries, and callback execution limits.
  4. Content Provider — data sharing, URI grants, and cross-process calls.

Intents

  1. Types of Intent - Implicit, Explicit
  2. Intent Filter
  3. Component exports, PendingIntent mutability, and permissions; learn verified Android App Links for web-to-app navigation.

Static User Interface

  1. View — Button, ImageView, TextView, EditText, and other widgets remain essential for maintenance and interoperability.
  2. ViewGroup — LinearLayout, RelativeLayout, and FrameLayout are common containers, not an exhaustive set.
  3. ConstraintLayout — useful for some complex constraints, not a universal replacement or default layout. Use the AndroidX reference.
  4. For new UI, learn Compose/Material 3, state hoisting, recomposition, View interoperability, accessibility, and resizable windows. Migration need not rewrite all existing screens at once.

Dynamic User Interface

  1. RecyclerView — recycling, DiffUtil, paging, and binding cost. Its capabilities do not guarantee better performance than ListView in every case. Learn LazyColumn/LazyRow for Compose.
  2. ViewPager — useful for old code. ViewPager2 1.1.0 is in maintenance mode for critical fixes; new Compose screens can use Pager.
  3. Spinner — a traditional selection widget; choose controls for the actual interaction and the corresponding Material approach in Compose.

CustomView

When default layouts don’t meet design requirements, you need to customize Views. Master the following:

  1. Canvas
  2. Bitmap
  3. Paint

Also study measurement, layout, touch handling, and accessibility semantics. Compose drawing/layout uses its own Canvas, Modifier, and lifecycle model rather than directly reusing View lifecycle assumptions.

UI Resources

Using resource files instead of hardcoding improves maintainability.

  1. Drawables
  2. Strings
  3. Styles
  4. Localization, plurals, dark themes, font scaling, and adaptive sizes; Compose still needs resources and themes.

Fragments

Many advocate for a Single Activity + Multiple Fragments architecture. Managing Fragments is an art in itself, and you’ll encounter various “gotchas” in practice.

  1. Fragment Lifecycle
  2. Fragment Manager

Distinguish the Fragment lifecycle from its View lifecycle when binding observers, coroutines, and ViewBinding. Single-activity architecture does not require Fragments; Compose screens can use their own navigation/back-stack approach.

Support User Interface

Common functional components:

  1. ProgressBar
  2. Dialogs
  3. Toast & Snackbar

Model loading, empty, failure, retry, and cancellation states. Unknown or not-yet-loaded data should not appear as zero.

Storage

App development inevitably involves file handling.

  1. SharedPreferences — maintain existing key/value storage; consider DataStore for new needs, without treating it as a relational database replacement.
  2. File Systems — distinguish private files, shared media, MediaStore, SAF, and Photo Picker. Scoped storage and permissions depend on OS/API and targetSdk; arbitrary external-path access is not a current default.
  3. Database — Room abstracts SQLite. Learn schemas, queries, transactions, migrations, and migration tests. RoomDatabase is its base class, not a separate database product.

Build

Gradle and AGP build most Android projects. Learn dependencies, variants, signing, and caching alongside Debug/Release. Channel packaging and bytecode manipulation are optional advanced topics.

  1. Gradle / AGP — the official release page at review time is AGP 9.4.0. Match Gradle, JDK, Studio, and SDK to its compatibility table rather than immediately upgrading every old project.
  2. Debug / Release Configuration — verify optimization, obfuscation, resources, and dependencies under the actual release setup.
  3. Multi-channel Packaging — distinguish product flavors, distribution channels, and backend environments; do not embed secrets in artifacts.
  4. ASM — understand bytecode and build APIs first. AGP 8.0 removed Transform API; choose Instrumentation/Artifacts replacements for the use case.
  5. Baseline Profiles / Startup Profiles — the former helps ART optimize execution; the latter shapes DEX layout at build time. They are distinct and need reproducible startup/interaction measurements.

Threading

Components normally execute on their hosting process’s main thread; a multi-process app can have multiple process main threads. Learn pools, communication, lifecycle, and cancellation rather than just starting workers.

  1. Threads
  2. Handler / Looper / Message / MessageQueue
  3. AIDL / Binder — remote synchronous calls can block callers; Binder does not remove thread-safety requirements.
  4. Coroutines / Flow — coroutines are not one thread each, and suspend does not automatically move blocking work off the main thread. Learn dispatchers, structured concurrency, cancellation, and lifecycle-aware collection.
  5. WorkManager — persistent scheduling, not a universal mechanism for long-running or exact-time work.

Debugging

These are some basic debugging tools you’ll reach for when problems come up. A few take more time to get comfortable with, and this is far from the whole list:

  1. Memory profiling — Studio Memory Profiler, heap dumps, and reference paths. MAT can still analyze compatible dumps, but does not cover all native/graphics memory.
  2. Logging — correlate threads, timestamps, and identifiers without exposing sensitive data. An absent log is not proof that an event never happened.
  3. System tracing — keep the Systrace series for old traces and mechanisms; learn Perfetto for newer captures. Tool migration does not invalidate every older analysis method.
  4. Exceptions / Error Handling — distinguish recoverable failures, uncaught exceptions, ANRs, and native crashes; catching every Throwable is not a substitute for fixing errors.
  5. Macrobenchmark, JankStats, and Android vitals — distinguish benchmark measurements, frame observations, and production aggregates rather than treating one metric as a complete assessment.

Memory Leak

Leaks include retained Java/Kotlin objects, native allocations, and unreleased resources. RSS growth alone is insufficient evidence, and Java leaks are not guaranteed to be easier than native ones.

  1. Detecting and Fixing Memory Leaks — learn LeakCanary, Matrix, and platform tools while checking their coverage.
  2. Context — longer-lived objects retaining short-lived Activities/Views are a common cause; Application Context is not a universal fix.
  3. Native Memory Leaks — allocation ownership, resource cleanup, and native profiling/detection require evidence beyond a Java heap dump.

3rd Party Libraries

Classic libraries save development time, but the old names need current selection criteria:

  1. Image Loading — Glide remains an option for View projects. Picasso is deprecated with no more public Maven Central releases planned; plan migration for existing use and evaluate options such as Coil for new projects.
  2. Dependency Injection — Dagger/Hilt; understand constructor injection first rather than forcing a full container into a small project.
  3. Networking — Retrofit/OkHttp. Fast Android Networking is a wrapper from the original route; inspect its dependencies and maintenance rather than making it a new-project default solely because it appeared here.
  4. Async — Coroutines/Flow is a common Kotlin path. RxJava projects still require subscription disposal and scheduling knowledge. RxJava 1.x/2.x are end-of-life; keep tutorials aligned with the major version, and do not treat a development branch’s future release plan as an already released stable version.

Data Formats

Common serialization formats:

  1. JSON — Gson is in maintenance mode and its authors advise against it as a default for new Android work. Check reflection, Kotlin nullability, and R8 rules. Evaluate code-generation-capable kotlinx.serialization or appropriate Moshi configuration, with migration tests rather than blind substitution.
  2. FlatBuffers — learn schemas and direct access where useful; not every data format needs to become binary.
  3. Protocol Buffers — learn field-number and compatibility rules. Serialization is not encryption.

Android Jetpack

Jetpack combines libraries, tools, and guidance rather than one framework to install wholesale. AndroidX releases are independent of the OS but retain their own minimum API and compatibility requirements. The old four-category list mixed platform APIs, libraries, and form factors:

  1. Foundation/UI — AppCompat, KTX, Compose/Material 3. With minSdk >= 21, native multidex support means the old support library should not be added automatically.
  2. State/data — Lifecycle, ViewModel, Flow/LiveData, Room, Paging, DataStore. Data Binding remains relevant to existing Views; Compose has its own state model.
  3. Navigation/background work — match navigation to the UI stack (Navigation 3 for Compose is one learning path), and select WorkManager or other mechanisms by workload.
  4. Media, notifications, and devices — learn Media3 for media and platform rules for notifications, permissions, and sharing. Auto, TV, and Wear OS are device scenarios rather than ordinary widgets. Study old Slices only for a relevant host or existing project, not as a requirement for every new app.

Architecture

Understand the common architectural patterns and choose what fits your project:

  1. MVVM — Model-View-ViewModel connects UI to a state holder through observable state.
  2. MVI — Model-View-Intent commonly turns user actions into state changes that render the UI. Intent here is an architectural concept, not necessarily Android’s component-messaging Intent.
  3. MVP — Model-View-Presenter, where the Presenter coordinates the View and data/business logic.

Focus on responsibilities, unidirectional data flow, state restoration, and testability using the Android architecture recommendations. Adding ViewModel alone does not complete an architecture.

Testing

  1. Local Unit Testing — verify logic, state, and data on the local JVM; ordinary local tests do not provide a real Android Framework environment.
  2. Instrumentation Testing — verify Android integration, databases, lifecycle, and UI on devices/emulators; these tests are not limited to clicking screens.
  3. Compose/View UI, configuration changes, process restoration, and accessibility. Measure performance separately with suitable benchmark conditions, not Debug-test timings presented as release performance.

Firebase

Back in 2020, my advice to developers in China was to take a quick look at Firebase even if they couldn’t use much of it—maybe one day that would change. For current projects, check product-specific device, network, SDK, and data-collection requirements. Do not generalize availability across all Firebase services.

  1. FCM — verify Google Play services and other device prerequisites, particularly on devices without GMS; it is not guaranteed delivery to every Android device.
  2. Crashlytics
  3. Analytics
  4. Remote Config
  5. App Indexing — Google Search App no longer uses its indexed local content. Learn Android App Links for web-to-app navigation and AppSearch separately for on-device search.
  6. Dynamic Links — Obsolete: the official shutdown date was 2025-08-25. Do not add it to new projects. Follow the migration guidance; App Links alone does not replace deferred post-install linking, short-link analytics, and attribution services.

Security

Encryption, decryption, and obfuscation are probably the parts you’ll encounter most often. User data comes first. Ignore that, and the EU will teach you a lesson.

  1. Encryption / Decryption — standard cryptography, Android Keystore, key management, and transport security. Static strings in client artifacts are not secret storage.
  2. ProGuard / R8 — R8 became the default with AGP 3.4. Shrinking, optimization, obfuscation, and keep rules are not encryption or substitutes for authentication and access control.
  3. Permissions, exported components, URI grants, WebView/deep-link input, and logging. Follow Android security guidance and verify the actual release configuration.

App Release

  1. .keystore / signing — certificates/private keys, backups, and update-signing continuity. With Play App Signing, the upload key can differ from the app signing key.
  2. App Bundle — AAB is a publishing format, not a directly installable package. Generate/test the APK or split APKs delivered to devices.
  3. Play Store — the target API requirements checked here require ordinary phone/tablet new apps and updates to target Android 16/API 36 or higher from 2026-08-31. Wear/Automotive/TV/XR, existing-app availability, and approved extensions have separate rules. Recheck at release time.
  4. Multi-channel Packaging — learn it where distribution needs it. For native dependencies, also check ABIs, third-party .so files, and 16 KB page-size compatibility introduced with Android 15.
  5. Pluginization — optional, subject to platform/distribution constraints, not a prerequisite for release. Quality also includes crashes/ANRs, permissions/data declarations, device coverage, and rollback planning.

Keep Learning and Improving

If you want to keep growing as an Android developer, build your own technical strengths and give yourself a plan. The former helps you stay competitive; the latter gives you something specific to work toward. Uninstall Douyin, Weibo, Douyu, and those games for a while, and make a plan for 2020. Keep Learning and Improving! Let’s keep at it.

If time management is giving you trouble, this video is from someone I know and respect, sharing their approach to work and study: How I Make Weekly Plans | Productivity | My Method.

“Plan ahead, or fail.” Annual plans are too long, and daily plans are too short. Managing time by the week is often the most practical way to maintain consistency over the long term.

Other Links

For further discussion, you can also find this article on:
Zhihu - Android Developer Learning Path (2020 Edition)

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal introduction and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro: Includes personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Welcome to recommend projects/articles.
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: My 2020 Reading List
entry.content:
Below is my 2020 reading list. Everything recorded here has been finished - technical books are not included since it’s hard to define when they’re “finished.”

I prefer reading history-related books. Among them, The Siege of Kaifeng was painful to read—the idea that a weak country has no say in diplomacy felt horribly real; Bad Kids lives up to its name, personally I feel it’s much better than the TV series; Rework 2 and Rework 3 are work-related, covering remote work and work methods, consistent with the 2020 trend of working from home - recommended for white-collar programmers; My Last Diet Book systematically and professionally discusses weight loss knowledge, very useful for someone like me who’s trying to lose weight; finally, Blades of the Guardians is already a classic in Chinese comics - I’ll definitely buy a physical set for collection once it’s complete (same for Attack on Titan).

Didn’t read much in 2020. Need to invest more in this area in 2021. Read + Record + Summarize - reading notes will be added later.

Current Reading List:

  1. Lessons from Ming Dynasty History
  2. The Siege of Kaifeng: Diplomacy, War, and People in Late Northern Song
  3. Android Efficient Progress: From Data to AI
  4. A Turbulent Hundred Years
  5. Remote: More Simple and Efficient Remote Work
  6. Shark’s Fin and Sichuan Pepper
  7. Rework 2
  8. Born a Crime
  9. Low IQ Crime
  10. Rework 3
  11. The Long Night
  12. Bad Kids
  13. Fifteen Days Between Two Capitals
  14. Permanent Record
  15. My Last Diet Book
  16. Blades of the Guardians
  17. Journey Through the Middle East

Lessons from Ming Dynasty History

First, let me introduce the author, so readers can have some context:

Wu Han, original name Wu Chunhan, courtesy name Chenbo. Historian and educator. From Yiwu, Zhejiang. Joined the Communist Party of China in 1957. Graduated from Tsinghua University in 1934. Later served as professor at Yunnan University, Southwest Associated University, and Tsinghua University, where he was department head and dean of the School of Liberal Arts. In 1943, he joined the China Democratic League and was actively involved in the democracy movement. After the founding of the PRC, he successively served as Deputy Mayor of Beijing, Vice Chairman of the 1st through 4th Beijing CPPCC, and member of the Philosophy and Social Sciences Division of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Elected Vice Chairman of the Central Committee of the China Democratic League in 1958. Was a deputy to the 1st through 3rd National People’s Congress, member of the 1st National CPPCC, and standing committee member of the 2nd and 3rd National CPPCC. His life’s work was research on ancient Chinese history, with particular achievements in Ming Dynasty history. Authored “Biography of Zhu Yuanzhang” and the historical play “Hai Rui Dismissed from Office.” After the “Cultural Revolution” began, Wu Han was brutally persecuted both mentally and physically. He was arrested and imprisoned in March 1968 and persecuted to death on October 11, 1969. His unjust case was only vindicated after the “Cultural Revolution” ended.

This “Lessons from Ming Dynasty History” is a collection of essays covering Zhu Yuanzhang’s ruling methods, internal contradictions of the ruling class, the Eastern and Western Depots and Jinyiwei, civilian life, factional strife, peasants, slaves and mutinies, the official class, bandits, etc. If “Those Things in the Ming Dynasty” tells the stories of great figures throughout the dynasty, this book takes us from another angle to understand the various chaotic phenomena from the ruling class to the ruled class in the Ming Dynasty. Many chapters are independent yet interconnected. It can be said that the internal troubles and external threats of the late Ming period were not simply the Qing invasion and the rise of bandits - the dynasty had rotted from top to bottom, and one or two people couldn’t save it.

This book is available on WeRead, recommended.

The Siege of Kaifeng: Diplomacy, War, and People in Late Northern Song

You’ve surely heard of the “Shame of Jingkang.” This book details the causes and consequences of the Jingkang Incident. Honestly, I didn’t have a detailed understanding of this period of history before reading it. After reading, I felt that calling it the “Shame of Jingkang” is absolutely right - especially how the army collapsed at first contact, the treachery in negotiations, and the repeated plundering of the capital Kaifeng during the siege that lasted most of a year. Reading it made me both angry and helpless. Without strength, you will be bullied - this eternal truth has been proven repeatedly throughout history. It only took three years from prosperity to destruction… There’s a passage in the book I really like: “It reminds us to be vigilant in peacetime. At any moment, crisis and prosperity are just one step apart. Peace is not inevitable - it requires us to view the world with humility, learning from the world’s strengths while avoiding arrogance and pride. More importantly, we must consciously avoid war. Humility is not wrong - misjudging the situation is the most terrifying thing, because all situations are interconnected. Once you take the first step, you cannot turn back, nor can you control the future direction.“

This book traces the complete historical details of the Jingkang Incident at the end of Northern Song, narrating the peace and war among Song, Liao, and Jin, focusing on the critical moments of the great historical turning point of Northern Song, and the causes and consequences of the comprehensive eruption of crisis from within and without the empire. During the Xuanhe years of Northern Song, the empire appeared prosperous, but hidden dangers lurked beneath the prosperity. Internal crises such as fiscal difficulties, military ailments, and vicious factional strife, combined with external crises like military threats from Liao and Jin in the north, gradually put the empire in a precarious situation. To “recover” the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun as a strategic buffer, Emperor Huizong decided to ally with Jin to destroy Liao. Although the Song-Jin alliance gradually consumed Liao, Jin saw through Northern Song’s weakness, and combined with complex interest disputes between the two countries, Jin turned south to attack Song. In the first year of Jingkang (1126), Jin’s army besieged Kaifeng for the second time, and the city fell in November. Northern Song collapsed, taking only three years from prosperity to destruction. Based on historical records considering the positions of Song, Liao, and Jin, the author uses accessible narrative style to recreate the historical process of the Jingkang Incident, exploring the deep causes behind Northern Song’s rise and fall, and its timeless significance as a mirror.

This book is available on WeRead, recommended.

Android Efficient Progress: From Data to AI

“Android Efficient Progress: From Data to AI” is a book combining Android advanced technology with practical application, organized into 3 main areas. First, Android engineering system practice and advancement, including mobile data technology, tool infrastructure advancement, efficiency advancement, as well as tool application advancement and engineering construction advancement; second, exploration of emerging mobile technologies at the time of publication, including container technology, large frontend technology, and AI technology; third, mobile application security attack and defense technology and advanced design pattern practice. The book is comprehensive, focusing on practical experience and advanced skills. Through this book, you can not only learn about mobile technologies from the time of publication and knowledge combining advanced technology with practical applications, but more importantly, comprehend the author’s spirit of technical research and thinking methods, helping Android developers progress efficiently.

“Android Efficient Progress: From Data to AI” is suitable for mobile application developers, Android system developers, Android system security engineers, and mobile technology leaders in the Android field.

From the book’s content, the author is an experienced developer. Many topics have fairly detailed architecture implementations that readers can use to build their own systems. It’s a rare book of experience, available on WeRead.

Technical reading update (reviewed October 2026): The publisher’s catalog lists Hu Qiang as the author and September 2019 as the publication date. The comments above remain my impressions from 2020. Evaluate the designs against your OS versions and project configuration; “emerging” describes their original context, not a current integration guide.

  • Keeping work running in the background: Android 8.0 (API 26) introduced background-service and implicit-broadcast limits. By default, they apply to apps targeting API 26 or higher; users can also enable restrictions for apps with lower targets. Evaluate each task against the official background execution limits and subsequent changes on supported OS versions. A keep-alive technique does not guarantee indefinite execution.
  • MultiDex: The book covers Dalvik and multiple DEX files, but ART has supported loading multiple DEX files natively since Android 5.0 (API 21). The current build documentation says multidex is enabled by default when minSdk is 21 or higher, with no compatibility library required. This condition concerns the minimum supported version, not targetSdk or the version on a single test device. Projects supporting older devices still need the documented configuration and validation.

A Turbulent Hundred Years

Author Wu Xiaobo presents China’s development over the past hundred years from a commercial perspective. The author mentions three phenomena in development: first, the interference of ideological debates on modernization; second, the central authority concept’s catalysis of national commercialism; third, the influence of traditional anti-commerce and official-commerce culture on the emerging entrepreneur class. Sadly, in the multiple economic reform movements after the Westernization Movement, these three themes haunted like ghosts, impossible to shake off.

My personal feeling after reading: national stability is too important for commercial development. China’s political situation in modern times was very unstable, and commercial development always rose and fell with political changes; commerce before the Reform and Opening was basically stagnant. It can be said that China’s commercial and technological development started basically from zero after the Reform and Opening. The gap with the United States, which had over a hundred years of stable development, is enormous. This is my biggest takeaway from this book. Although technology sharing and technological explosion exist, our country still masters too few core technologies.

In these 100+ years, suffering has given us the opportunity to focus and reflect, learning many things. It has allowed the Chinese to carefully examine their experiences and more harshly observe their thousand-year history. Without humiliation, we might not have paid attention at all, still immersed in the illusion of being a great nation.
Since the Opium War of 1840, one phrase has covered all themes, becoming the lifelong ideal of countless patriotic Chinese: “Strong Nation.” The urgency of “Strong Nation” made the country incredibly anxious, sometimes even impatient, willing to take risks before thoroughly investigating a path. At many sensitive critical moments, gradualist thinking was often seen as “reactionary,” and revolutionary upheaval, even bloody violence, became the choice of the entire nation. A hundred years of spring and autumn, with farces, tragedies, and comedies interweaving on stage.
In this 100 years driven by the “Strong Nation Dream,” China’s revival began at a dark and desperate moment of awakening. Commercial evolution has always been an important direction for national progress and national redemption. It is precisely in this process that the emerging entrepreneur class rose as an independent force. Their tortuous fate intertwined with the political changes and national choices of this country, sometimes united, sometimes split, but mostly in a discordant state. Over the past century, China’s economic problems can ultimately be summarized as adjustments in three interest relationships: first, adjustment between government interests and public interests; second, adjustment between central government and local government interests; third, adjustment between wealthy public and poor public interests. As representatives of the wealthy public, the entrepreneur group has never reached principled and constructive consensus in relationships with the government (including central and local), intellectuals, and the poor public. This has become one of the important reasons why Chinese commercial progress is always interrupted by various events.

Remote: A More Simple and Efficient Way of Remote Work

The book is called Remote. Why on earth call it “Rework 2” in Chinese?

The authors are the two founders of 37Signals. The book covers all aspects of remote work, including the advantages of remote work, how to collaborate remotely, side effects of remote work, employee management in remote work, and self-management in remote work. The 2020 COVID-19 pandemic made most companies try remote work, and many things mentioned in this book were encountered in actual remote work.

Here are some excerpts to ponder:

What really matters is getting the work done well, not rigidly sticking to work hours.

The luxury of the new era is breaking free from the mental shackle of “enjoy life later” and doing what you love now, alongside work. Why waste time on daydreams like “how wonderful life will be when I retire”? Drawing a line between work and retirement is actually quite arbitrary. Your life no longer needs to follow such rules. You can mix the two together, having both fun and income - designing a better lifestyle that makes work enjoyable, because work isn’t the only thing in life. Those golden handcuffs prevent you from living the life you truly want to live. Break free from that resentment!

When you can’t watch someone all day, the only criterion for judgment is work results. A whole bunch of other trivial standards disappear. You just look at work results. Therefore, you don’t need to ask remote workers “what did you do today” - just say “show me today’s results.”

When meetings become the norm, become essential tools for discussion and debate, used to solve any problem, they’re being abused, and everyone becomes numb. Meetings should be like salt, carefully sprinkled on dishes for flavor, not poured on by the spoonful. Too much salt ruins the dish; too many meetings lower morale and enthusiasm.

If you don’t manage the balance between life and work well, the freedom of remote work becomes slavery. This is possible because when you break free from the 9-to-5 job, you can easily fall into the shackles of working all day.

Remote work lifts the veil, letting people see a fact that has always existed but isn’t always acknowledged or seen: excellent remote workers are simply excellent workers. It’s that simple.

Internal motivation: Programmers write open source software generally because they love doing it, not for money. Money often comes along, but it’s rarely the source of motivation. That is, when you’re solving a particularly interesting, exciting problem, you don’t need managers constantly peering over your shoulder to check if you’re working.
Everything public: Most open source software is coordinated through mailing lists and code tracking systems like GitHub. As long as someone wants to help, they can, because all information is public. You can volunteer to participate, and the person most expert in a particular area can easily jump in.

Shark’s Fin and Sichuan Pepper

Author Fuchsia Dunlop grew up in Oxford and earned a Bachelor’s degree in English Literature from Cambridge University, then obtained a Master’s degree in Chinese Studies with distinction from SOAS, University of London. In 1994, after receiving a British Council scholarship, Fuchsia went to study at Sichuan University for a year; she then received three months of professional chef training at the Sichuan Institute of Higher Cuisine, becoming the first foreign student there.

I picked up Shark’s Fin and Sichuan Pepper expecting a relaxing read, and the first half was just that. I followed the author through Chengdu’s streets and alleys in search of home cooking, with a recipe at the end of each section. Her descriptions made life there sound wonderfully comfortable:

The slow, languid feeling of this place also subtly influences you. In Chengdu, forget about realizing plans - even making plans is completely impossible. Since the Tang Dynasty, this place has been famous for its comfortable and leisurely life. The climate is suitable, and the soil is legendarily fertile. Chengdu people don’t have to work particularly hard to eat well and have fun. The city has a bit of a southern feel, even somewhat Mediterranean. Chengdu people walk slower than Beijing or Shanghai people. They sit in teahouses for an entire afternoon and evening, playing mahjong, playing cards, joking and bickering in the slow-paced, sweet-toned Sichuan dialect with drawn-out vowels and cute erhua endings. They call this “bai long men zhen” - Sichuan’s unique way of chatting about everything. And the most vivid Sichuan phrase is “hao shua” (particularly fun). They say it in a lazy voice, grinning, with bamboo chairs creaking in the background. “Those coastal people,” a taxi driver chatted with me about Cantonese and Fujianese people, “they have big ambitions and work hard, so they got rich first. We Sichuan people, as long as we make enough money to eat well and drink spicy food, that’s enough.”

The dishes described in the book include Chengdu home-cooked dishes, Hong Kong Cantonese cuisine, Hunan cuisine, and Yangzhou Jiangsu-Zhejiang cuisine. However, since the author stayed in Sichuan longer, Sichuan cuisine and Sichuan life appear more frequently. Each region’s cuisine has its own characteristics, and just reading the author’s descriptions, you can almost smell the fragrant aromas.

The second half took me somewhere heavier: food safety, eating wild and protected animals, and parts of Chinese official life. The more I read, the more weighed down I felt, and there was nothing I could do about it. Cities change, society changes, people change. When the author returned to a transformed Chengdu, she recorded what she saw:

On one hand, such demolition is truly a tragedy - my personal tragedy: falling in love with a place that is disappearing so rapidly. My research into cooking and food originally intended to record a vibrant city. Only later did I understand that from many perspectives, I was writing the “epitaph” of old Chengdu. I feel this is also a tragedy for Chengdu people, though they don’t realize it. This city was so charming, so unique, now being replaced by a city that exists everywhere in China - a terrible waste, sad and lamentable.

On the other hand, 1990s China seemed to overflow with vitality and optimism. The previous utilitarianism, asceticism, and monotonous blandness disappeared. The whole country was moving, 1.2 billion people united, moving forward together. In England, even demolishing a dilapidated old building would make us sad and distressed. But in Sichuan, they swung hammers all the way, flattening the entire city! This reckless confidence was admirable. They firmly believed the future would be better than the past.

So, even though my heart still ached passing through those leveled streets, I was also stirred and agitated by this vibrant optimism. I too was in an unstable state, my life was also changing. I was tapping into potential creativity, making great friends, slowly shedding skin like a snake.

Born a Crime

You don’t choose where you’re born, but you can choose your life

Because of the Daily Show, I started following Trevor Noah. This book is Trevor Noah’s autobiography. The title is confusing - what does “born a crime” mean? I hadn’t paid much attention to African history before. After reading this book, I learned that “born a crime” refers to the apartheid era in South Africa, when Black and white people could not be together, let alone have children. Trevor had a white father and a Black mother. That was what the title “born a crime” meant.

Two major themes run through the article: one is racial segregation, one is racial identity. Under white rule in South Africa, apartheid was enforced. This segregation wasn’t just segregation of people, but also included language segregation, cultural segregation, ideological segregation, and even segregation between black tribes. The other is racial identity. In local terms, Trevor was classified as “Coloured” under that system - the kind that wasn’t accepted by either the black community or the white community. Indians and Chinese would also group together. For a child at that time, who to hang out with (gaining acceptance from which group) was very important. From childhood, Trevor was isolated by various groups, but through his mother and knowledge, he found a way to survive among various races and groups, eventually becoming a successful comedian, talk show host, and TV/radio host.

Apartheid represented a police state, a system of laws and surveillance that kept black people under absolute control. If all the laws could be written down and stacked together, it would take over three thousand sheets of paper, weighing up to five kilograms. But the essence of South African apartheid is very easy for Americans to understand. Three things happened in American history: driving Native Americans to reservations, black slavery, and segregation. Imagine these three things happening to the same group of people at the same time - that’s apartheid.

I found my place. Since I didn’t belong to any small circle, I could move between different circles. I was still a chameleon, a cultural chameleon. I knew how to blend in. I could exercise with athletic kids, discuss computers with nerds. I could jump into crowds and dance with small-town boys. I could have brief intersections with everyone, studying together, chatting, telling jokes, delivering food.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal introduction and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with peers - when three people walk together, there must be a teacher among them!

  1. Blogger’s Personal Introduction: Contains my WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A navigation guide for my blog content.
  3. Personally Curated Excellent Blog Posts - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Recommendations and self-recommendations welcome (just WeChat message me)
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One person can walk faster, a group can walk further

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - CPU Info Interpretation
entry.content:
This is the twelfth article in the Systrace series, primarily providing a brief introduction to the CPU information area (Kernel) in Systrace. It covers how to view CPU-related information output by the Kernel module, including CPU frequency, scheduling, frequency locking, and core locking.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): This article retains its 2019 Systrace figures. SoC models, CPU numbering, cpuset paths, and power states depend on the device and OS; errors in the old specification table are marked nearby. Framework/tool examples were checked against AOSP android-10.0.0_r1 and android-16.0.0_r1, with kernel semantics referenced to Linux 6.6. Device inspection and affinity commands were not executed during this review.

Table of Contents

  • Series Article Index
  • CPU Area Legend
  • Core Architecture
  • Core Binding (Pinning)
  • Frequency Locking
  • CPU States
  • Detailed Information in Systrace
  • References
  • About Me && Blog

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

CPU Area Legend

Read this with Perfetto 9: CPU information. Locate the target thread’s Runnable, Running, and sleep intervals, then correlate actual CPU placement, frequency, idle state, and competing work. CPU/thread tracks show timing; data such as sched, thread_state, and counters supports aggregation. Table details depend on the Trace Processor version.

This is an eight-logical-CPU example from an older Android device. The original text called it a Snapdragon 845, but the image alone does not establish its SoC. The three-tier annotation in a later figure is not independent device-identification evidence either.

Four useful kinds of information are:

  1. CPU tracks reconstruct which thread occupied each logical CPU from scheduling events. Thread colors do not rank performance.
  2. Clock Frequency contains recorded events or samples. The selected 2419200, in kHz, means 2.4192 GHz, not utilization.
  3. Clock Frequency Limits describes allowed bounds, not instantaneous frequency or the identity of a boost requester.
  4. C-State/idle describes CPU idleness. The old viewer can renumber raw states, as explained below.

The top CPU usage view aggregates utilization; inspect its time window and normalization. Low overall utilization can coexist with one saturated CPU or a critical thread waiting Runnable. High frequency does not mean continuous execution, and an idle CPU’s track may retain its last recorded frequency.

When a task is slow, the first questions might be: did it run on a small core? Was the frequency too low? For something like fingerprint unlock, could it run on a big core? Use those questions to start reading the trace, then separate scheduling delay, lock/Binder/I/O waits, CPU execution, and critical-path dependencies. Small-core placement or low frequency is a clue, not proof of a scheduling error. More frequency cannot remove a blocking dependency. Frequency events are often emitted only on changes, so missing initial data is not 0 Hz; supported sysfs polling can supplement the capture. See Perfetto frequency and idle data.

For basic thread-state interpretation, see Systrace Prerequisites.

Core Architecture

This article retains homogeneous, big/little, and big/medium/little as ways to discuss the old figures, not an exhaustive classification of modern SoCs. Microarchitecture, performance tier, shared cache, frequency policy, and Linux CPU numbering are distinct. Cores with the same architecture can belong to different frequency tiers.

The 0–3, 4–6, and 7 groups are annotations for a particular sample. They are not a universal numbering rule. Restricting background work to small cores is a policy choice involving cpusets, affinity, and scheduling, not a hardware rule.

Non-big.LITTLE Architecture

Homogeneous cores share a core design; they need not always run at the same frequency or power, or switch on and off together. For example, Helio A22 uses four Cortex-A53 cores. Shared frequency control and independent idle/online behavior still depend on the platform.

Snapdragon 636 was an incorrect homogeneous example. Its official brief specifies four performance and four efficiency cores: an eight-core Kryo 260 CPU, not the original text’s other description of “four small plus two large.”

big.LITTLE Architecture

Different performance/efficiency tiers let the scheduler place work according to load, allowed CPUs, and power constraints. CPU 0–3 need not be small cores or CPU 4–7 large cores. Clock speed alone is also insufficient for comparing different microarchitectures.

Snapdragon 845’s official specifications describe Kryo 385 with four performance and four efficiency cores, clocked up to 2.8 GHz. The old diagram below is retained as an illustration. Its peak rates and performance-uplift percentages are not measurements made in this review, and a Kryo product name should not be treated as an unchanged stock Cortex implementation.

The ratio varies: Snapdragon 670, for example, uses 2+6 cores. Whether it feels like enough also comes down to how much you’re willing to spend. You get what you pay for; Qualcomm isn’t running a charity. Engineering analysis needs the particular workload and device.

The following old table is outdated and contains errors; it is not a reliable specification reference. Corrections follow the retained image:

ModelVerified official informationCorrection to old image
Snapdragon 670Kryo 360, 2 performance + 6 efficiency; Adreno 615Not 4+4 or Adreno 620
Snapdragon 460Eight-core Kryo 240; Adreno 610Not Kryo 360 Silver or Adreno 605
Snapdragon 640 columnNo official specification supporting this column was verifiedDo not cite it as a released-product specification

Sources: 670 brief, 460 brief. Check the actual device’s policies and frequency tables for operating points.

Big-Medium-Small Core Architecture

Historical examples include:

  • Snapdragon 855’s Kryo 485 has 1 Prime + 3 performance + 4 efficiency cores. Its official technical presentation lists 2.84, 2.42, and 1.80 GHz, respectively.
  • Helio X30 has 2 Cortex-A73 + 4 Cortex-A53 + 4 Cortex-A35 cores.
  • Kirin 980 has 2 Cortex-A76 at 2.6 GHz, 2 Cortex-A76 at 1.92 GHz, and 4 Cortex-A55 at 1.8 GHz. The same A76 design can serve different tiers.

“Prime” and “medium” are descriptive tiers, not fixed core counts or Linux scheduling classes. Some numbers in the old comparison, including 855’s 2.41/1.78 GHz, differ from the official nominal figures. Without measurement conditions, they should not be used to compare peaks or infer performance.

Snapdragon 865, introduced in 2019, retained a 1+3+4 arrangement; the diagram labels its Prime core at 2.84 GHz. At the time, I wondered whether the 865 Plus would make it to 3 GHz. The 865 Plus announced in 2020 answered that question with a Prime specification of up to 3.1 GHz.

Newer designs need not retain traditional A5x efficiency cores. The 2025 Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 brief lists custom Oryon cores: 2 Prime up to 4.6 GHz and 6 Performance up to 3.62 GHz. Re-establish the SoC, topology, capacity, and frequency policies when reading a new trace instead of reusing the old numbering diagram.

Core Binding (Pinning)

Pinning restricts the CPUs on which a thread may run. It can reduce migration or constrain background work, but a smaller allowed set can also increase queueing. Pinning does not reserve a CPU, prevent preemption, or guarantee faster execution.

Configuring CPUsets

cpusets constrain CPUs and memory nodes for groups of tasks. Older Android systems commonly have top-app, foreground, background, and system-background, but their names do not specify fixed CPU masks. foreground/boost belongs to some older implementations, not every release.

The original 0-7 / 0-3 masks were not a universal Google default. Android 10 init.rc initially copies available sets from the root group and leaves device configuration to select appropriate CPUs. This is an init-language excerpt, not shell syntax:

The old cgroup-v1 path is lowercase /dev/cpuset/.../cpus. On a device exposing these nodes, read-only inspection can look like this:

These outputs are historical examples. tasks lists task/thread TIDs, not necessarily four application processes. Membership and allowed CPUs can change. Also inspect /proc/<TID>/cgroup and Cpus_allowed_list in /proc/<TID>/status, substituting a real thread ID.

cgroup v2 uses nodes such as cpuset.cpus and cpuset.cpus.effective; distinguish process membership in cgroup.procs from thread membership in cgroup.threads. Do not append v1’s tasks to arbitrary v2 paths. Android can combine v1/v2 controllers; use the device’s actual mounts and configuration. See Linux 6.6 cgroup v2.

A service can also select a group at startup. This is the complete service declaration from Android 10 lmkd.rc:

Android 12 introduced init’s task_profiles replacement for deprecated writepid usage. Android 16 lmkd.rc uses task_profiles ServiceCapacityLow; the default profile joins cpuset/system-background. Device/API/vendor configuration can override profiles, so the name alone does not identify the CPU set. See AOSP task profiles.

App scheduling groups can change with process state. These Android 10 Process.java constants belong to a hidden Framework contract, not a general app pinning API:

They are not CPU numbers, and not every constant implies a same-named cpuset directory. THREAD_GROUP_RT_APP alone does not select SCHED_FIFO. Android 10 OomAdjuster computes scheduling groups and uses a handler to perform operations such as setProcessGroup. Follow the native implementation and device configuration too; oom_adj is not a CPU priority value.

Configuring Affinity

taskset is a command-line tool using sched_getaffinity / sched_setaffinity. Linux affinity is per thread: changing the main thread does not automatically update every existing thread. Effective placement is further restricted by cpusets and online CPUs, and permission requirements apply. See sched_setaffinity.

Usage of taskset

Android 10/16 Toybox taskset uses hexadecimal masks and supports -p and -a, not util-linux’s -c CPU-list option. These are device-shell command forms; replace TID, PID, and COMMAND. Mutation forms belong in authorized, controlled experiments:

PurposeAndroid Toybox form
Inspect one thread’s allowed CPUstaskset -p TID
Inspect a process’s current threadstaskset -ap PID
Restrict one thread to CPU 3taskset -p 8 TID
Start a command with CPU 3 affinitytaskset 8 COMMAND

The least significant bit is CPU 0. Hexadecimal 5, binary 0101, therefore selects CPU 0 and CPU 2. CPU 3 uses hexadecimal mask 8. This is an allowed set, not the thread’s current executing CPU; use scheduling tracks for actual placement. Desktop util-linux versions supporting -c can use taskset -pc 3 PID, but that syntax does not transfer to these Android Toybox versions.

Scheduling Algorithms

The allowed set determines where a task may run; the scheduler chooses where and when it runs. Linux 6.6 EAS can use CPU capacity, load, and an energy model, while vendors may apply other policies. Seeing a thread remain on one core does not prove affinity pinning. Check affinity/cpusets and the available choices before judging placement.

Frequency Locking

Frequency scaling, task placement, and performance hints interact, but there is no universal sequence of maximizing a small core before trying medium and then large cores. Latency-sensitive work such as app launch may request a boost. Whether that raises a frequency floor, adjusts uclamp, changes placement, and for how long depends on OS, driver, and vendor policy.

Launch, installation, rotation, window animation, list flinging, and games are possible optimization scenarios, not a promise that Android maximizes every CPU/GPU/I/O/BUS resource in each case. Thermal, power-mode, and platform limits still apply. Linux 6.6 uclamp changes a performance-demand signal and can influence schedutil frequency selection; it does not promise a fixed MHz value or exclusive use of a large core.

Here is an older Qualcomm frequency-limit example:

The selected bounds are 768000–2016000 kHz: 768 MHz–2.016 GHz. Since the minimum and maximum differ, this is an allowed range rather than a single locked frequency. It also does not identify the requester, temperature, or actual execution rate.

Linux CPUFreq often manages multiple CPUs through a shared policy. related_cpus helps identify its membership. For many drivers, scaling_cur_freq reflects the most recent requested frequency rather than precise instantaneous hardware frequency. Correlate frequency events, idle, workload, and thermal evidence; see CPUFreq.

From Android 12/API 31, apps on supported devices can use PerformanceHintManager to report work-duration targets and completion data for associated threads. This is a performance-hint mechanism, not an app-controlled core or frequency lock.

CPU States

These are the old viewer’s C-State tracks. Values 0, 1, 2, and 3 belong to this sample, not a fixed four-state model for every Android CPU:

Separate raw events from viewer transformations. The Catapult power_parser already present before the 2019 article displays raw cpu_idle value 4294967295 (0xffffffff, idle exit) as 0 and adds 1 to other raw states. On that parsing path, displayed 1 means raw state 0, and displayed 3 means raw state 2.

Perfetto SQL’s cpuidle counter retains raw values: 0 means entry into idle state 0; 4294967295 means idle exit. Do not reuse the old viewer’s meaning of zero. Missing entry/exit events leave boundary state unknown.

These are indices into the platform’s cpuidle driver states. Where permissions allow, inspect name, desc, latency, and residency under /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpuN/cpuidle/stateN/ for the relevant CPU/state and units; latency and residency are normally expressed in microseconds. Deeper states often trade wakeup delay for savings, but a recorded request does not always establish the state that hardware actually reached. See Linux 6.6 CPUIdle.

Idle and offline/hotplug are different mechanisms. Modern kernels still support CPU hotplug; availability and policy depend on the device. CPU idle is also distinct from whole-device suspend. The original cross-platform HLT description, fixed 10 ns/100 ns wakeup claims, and “70% savings” do not explain these ARM tracks and have been removed from this interpretation.

Detailed Information in Systrace

Old Systrace HTML embeds trace data that can be inspected as text; compatibility of the old interactive viewer with current Chrome needs separate verification. Perfetto protobuf data requires appropriate decoding and is not the same plain-text format.

Here is the original scheduling record:

FieldMeaning in this record
appEventThread-8193Current task name and Linux TID; 8193 need not be the process TGID
[001]The event occurred on logical CPU 1, not CPU 0
d..2Four character fields, not four bits: IRQs disabled, no resched flag shown, ordinary context, preempt depth 2
1638545.400415Trace timestamp in seconds, in the selected trace-clock/format domain; not scheduling latency or calendar time
prev_* / next_*Outgoing and incoming tasks; this switches to CPU 1’s idle task swapper/1, TID 0
prev_state=SThe outgoing thread enters interruptible sleep; this is not evidence that it remained Runnable and was preempted
prev_prio=97 / next_prio=120Kernel scheduling-priority values, not direct nice values or enough information to distinguish every policy

d..2 describes context at event time, not an entire app interval spent with interrupts or preemption disabled. Other kernel versions can add flag fields. See the Linux ftrace format.

Other original samples and their interpretation:

  1. sched_waking: comm=kworker/u16:4 pid=17373 prio=120 target_cpu=003: waking TID 17373 toward CPU 3; it is not already Running and can migrate later.
  2. sched_blocked_reason: pid=17373 iowait=0 caller=rpmh_write_batch+0x638/0x7d0: this extension reports a blocking location and iowait flag. Zero does not exclude all I/O/hardware waits, and symbol offsets are not source lines. Not every kernel emits this event.
  3. cpu_idle: state=0 cpu_id=3: CPU 3 enters raw idle state 0, not an active C0 state.
  4. softirq_raise: vec=6 [action=TASKLET]: raises the softirq; inspect entry/exit for execution rather than treating the raise as completion.
  5. cpu_frequency_limits: min=1555200 max=1785600 cpu_id=0
  6. cpu_frequency_limits: min=710400 max=2419200 cpu_id=4
  7. cpu_frequency_limits: min=825600 max=2841600 cpu_id=7

The last three events report frequency limits in kHz. cpu_id can identify a policy’s representative CPU, so the limit need not affect only one core. These records do not replace actual frequency samples. The visual trace, raw events, and matching-version source should explain the same behavior.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro: Includes personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Welcome to recommend projects/articles.
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

References

  1. Linux sched_setaffinity: thread affinity
  2. AOSP cgroups and task profiles
  3. Linux 6.6 CPUFreq
  4. Linux 6.6 CPUIdle
  5. Perfetto CPU frequency and idle

Spring Bamboo Shoots

I took a photo and thought it was quite nice, sharing it with everyone.

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
entry.content:
This is the eleventh article in the Systrace series, providing a brief introduction to Triple Buffer within Systrace. It covers how to identify jank in Systrace, perform preliminary localization and analysis, and explains the impact of Triple Buffer on performance.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): This article retains its 2019 Systrace screenshots and 60 Hz timing diagrams. Buffering can still reduce pipeline waits, but the old topology and scheduling do not describe every newer system. Historical switches were checked against AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 / android-10.0.0_r1, and newer paths against android-16.0.0_r1. Historical properties describe those implementations rather than a universal runtime switch.

Table of Contents

  • Series Article Index
  • How to Define Dropped Frames (Jank)?
  • BufferQueue and Triple Buffer
  • The Role of Triple Buffer
  • Debugging Triple Buffer
  • References
  • Attachments
  • About Me && Blog

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

How to Define Dropped Frames (Jank)?

Read this alongside Perfetto 8: Vsync and performance analysis. Distinguish a missed app deadline, a buffer that was never presented, uneven visual updates, and increased input-to-display latency. They do not always describe the same event.

Display periods are about 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 11.11 ms at 90 Hz, and 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. Those numbers alone do not define the budget for a main-thread slice: target frame rate, scheduled deadlines, CPU/GPU pipelining, and target presentation time also matter. FrameTimeline, available from Android 12, provides related evidence when captured. Start with Expected/Actual Timeline, jank type, and presentation status, then follow app, RenderThread, SurfaceFlinger, fence, and scheduling tracks. Older traces without this data support narrower conclusions.

Judging Jank on the App Side

At first glance, you might think: the main thread took more than 16.6 ms, so surely that is a dropped frame? Let’s look a little further. The selected interval below is 30.891 ms, with a long main-thread Choreographer#doFrame. This indicates delayed production, but does not by itself prove that a particular display refresh repeated old content. Previously produced, not-yet-presented buffers might temporarily sustain output, or there might be none.

Correlate old app-side method timings with downstream presentation evidence. This does not mean that all app-side frame metrics are incapable of identifying jank.

Judging Jank on the SurfaceFlinger Side

In this old example, the layer has no newly queued item in the relevant interval, and SurfaceFlinger has no corresponding new work. If the scene was expected to update every period, this is consistent with retaining old content for an extra period. No new buffer does not mean that the app’s layer disappears or is omitted from composition. Its latched content can remain, including when other layers update. Reusing content for a static scene or a lower-rate source is not inherently jank.

Here is the SurfaceFlinger side of the first example, where previously produced items remain available as latch candidates:

The layer counter measures queued items, not the total allocation count or GPU completion. A positive value and visible SurfaceFlinger work do not independently establish on-time presentation or unchanged input latency. Follow frame numbers/tokens, acquire fences, and actual presentation. Values 0/1/2 are the range seen in this sample, not a universal limit.

Logical Jank

Content can also advance incorrectly despite timely output. Here, “logical jank” describes cases such as a flinging list unexpectedly moving 20, 10, then 30 pixels when its animation curve calls for a different progression. Users can see discontinuity even when rendering and presentation meet their deadlines.

Generic frame tracks may not reveal the cause. Add animation-progress, position, or input-timestamp instrumentation and compare with video. Acceleration, deceleration, and spring motion can be intentional; uneven steps alone are not proof of a bug.

Android 10’s AnimationUtils contains these related methods (signatures only):

In the Android 10 source, the first two are hidden test/Framework interfaces. Choreographer freezes a thread-local animation clock while processing a frame so animations use a consistent time. currentAnimationTimeMillis() uses the uptime time domain, not calendar wall time. Android 16 also has an internal overload carrying expected presentation time.

Apps normally use animation frameworks or Choreographer frame timestamps instead of calling those hidden methods. Actual callback execution can jitter with scheduling. A consistent frame-time basis helps coordinate animation updates, but cannot recover missed display updates or guarantee that system animations never have logic errors.

For other causes of jank, see:

  1. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - Methodology
  2. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - System Side
  3. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - App Side

BufferQueue and Triple Buffer

BufferQueue

BufferQueue connects a producer and a consumer using graphical-buffer handles and synchronization information; the queue does not copy the entire pixel image. The endpoints may share a process or cross a process boundary. The AOSP BufferQueue documentation introduces the model:

  1. The producer calls dequeueBuffer() to request a free slot, with dimensions, pixel format, and usage parameters. Before overwriting old content, it must respect the returned release fence. This requests an available buffer, not the release of an arbitrary one.
  2. After submitting CPU/GPU drawing work, the producer uses queueBuffer() to submit the buffer and fence. GPU work can still be pending; queued does not mean rendering is complete.
  3. The consumer uses acquireBuffer() to obtain an item and satisfies its acquire-fence dependency before reading the pixels. Obtaining the handle and accessing the content need not happen at the same time.
  4. The consumer returns the slot with releaseBuffer() and a release fence. Reuse must still wait for the relevant accesses to finish.

In ordinary, non-shared mode, slots commonly follow FREE → DEQUEUED → QUEUED → ACQUIRED → FREE. Ownership state does not replace fence completion. Cancellation, dropping, and other paths also change state; see Android 16 BufferSlot.h.

Vsync schedules rendering and presentation; ownership and fences synchronize access. The four queue operations are not all directly triggered by Vsync. Related articles:

  1. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  2. Android Rendering Based on Choreographer

Producer and consumer are still rather abstract. Let’s make that concrete with the app and SurfaceFlinger: in this old layer-BufferQueue path, the app produces buffers and SurfaceFlinger consumes them. The app dequeues, draws, and queues; SurfaceFlinger acquires during composition and releases old content when downstream use allows it. Returning from a SurfaceFlinger CPU composition function does not necessarily make the storage safe to overwrite: GPU/HWC dependencies can remain.

Newer systems have a different process boundary. Android 16 BLASTBufferQueue creates a queue and consumer in the client, then submits buffers to SurfaceFlinger through SurfaceControl transactions. Limits depend on producer/consumer constraints and modes, with refresh rate and work duration also involved. “Triple buffering” does not mean every window always allocates or occupies exactly three buffers.

So how many buffers does the queue need to keep things moving? The diagrams below use one, two, and three image buffers to illustrate overlap. Front/Back are roles, not fixed slots; A/B/C are reused storage, not permanent frame numbers. For hardware-accelerated rendering, the CPU work includes recording and submitting GPU commands. CPU, GPU, and SurfaceFlinger do not each permanently own a separate pixel buffer. The screen row denotes displayed content, which may pass through a composition target or HWC rather than directly scanning the app’s memory.

Single Buffer

With one image buffer, producer writes and consumer reads need coordination; they cannot freely overlap as in an ordinary multi-buffer pipeline.

This idealized diagram schedules CPU, GPU, composition, and display in sequence. A Vsync offset changes planned timing, but neither guarantees that work finishes within budget nor replaces synchronization:

Writing the same storage while it is being scanned can expose a mixture of old and new content, causing tearing. Merely missing a rendering deadline does not imply tearing: a correctly synchronized multi-buffer system generally delays presentation or retains old content.

Single/front-buffer rendering is not obsolete in every context. The low-latency front-buffer path, available from Android 10/API 29, supports small updates such as handwriting while managing tearing risk. It is not a general replacement for full-screen View rendering.

Double Buffer

Two buffers let the consumer use one while the producer works on another reusable allocation:

Here is the ideal A/B alternation. The fourth note at the bottom of the original diagram incorrectly says that the app produces A; its blue interval means produce B, consume A.

In the next example, production and release timing prevent timely preparation, and display periods two and four repeat old content. This is one particular schedule, not a universal outcome of two long app frames. The final clause of the fifth note should say reuse the released A for production.

Triple Buffer

An extra allocation can overlap some CPU submission work with earlier GPU/consumer work, reducing idle time spent waiting for a buffer’s return. If one buffer is being consumed and another is still being drawn by the GPU, the third may be available. There are not always two free buffers, and the extra allocation does not make unfinished GPU results ready.

In this example, C can be prepared during period two and displayed in period four. Period two still repeats B. The fourth note under the original diagram was copied from the double-buffer case: it should describe displaying C, not another missed update. The SurfaceFlinger row shows both B and A in period five; this simplified drawing does not establish that both are presented in one display refresh.

Together, the diagrams show two repeated-content periods becoming one in this model. More available storage can help under these conditions; it does not eliminate every source of jank.

The Role of Triple Buffer

Mitigating Jank
