Extra buffer capacity can absorb short production or consumption fluctuations. The benefit depends on which stage is waiting, when buffers are released, and whether useful not-yet-presented content already exists. A delay temporarily hidden by buffering is not necessarily a GPU problem.

This is the earlier sample again. Queue activity helps correlate production and consumption, but counters and composition slices alone do not establish on-time presentation. Sustained overload eventually exhausts the available capacity.

Reducing Wait Times

With two buffers, a producer may wait for an earlier allocation to be released before continuing. In the diagram, B becomes reusable only after downstream use and dependencies permit it. App and SurfaceFlinger Vsync phases can differ; simultaneous callbacks are not a prerequisite for this wait.

In the old HWUI path, a long RenderThread dequeueBuffer can also delay a later main-thread synchronization. The image illustrates that relationship; identify the actual blocking point with thread states and fence/Binder evidence:

A third buffer can shorten some waits. It can still block when all buffers are in use, consumption falls behind, or fences remain unsignaled. When HWUI releases the main thread also depends on its execution path; the entire DrawFrame duration is not necessarily a main-thread wait.

Lowering GPU and SurfaceFlinger Bottlenecks

The potential reduction is in additional waiting caused by buffer shortages, not in the computation required from the GPU or SurfaceFlinger. Submitted commands and dependencies drive GPU work; it does not simply start when SurfaceFlinger decides it wants a buffer. More overlap cannot remove sustained GPU overload, long composition, or scheduling delays.

These old images show SurfaceFlinger Binder-thread waits and long app RenderThread dequeueBuffer calls. They are clues for investigating consumer backpressure. The images and attachment filenames alone do not establish a controlled experiment proving that switching from double to triple buffering made the problem disappear.

Memory and Latency Costs

Extra buffers consume graphics memory; the size depends on stride, format, compression, and allocation. Producing too far ahead can queue not-yet-presented content and increase input-to-display latency, potentially appearing as Buffer Stuffing in FrameTimeline. Steady output can therefore still feel less responsive. Whether queued content is retained, replaced, or dropped depends on queue mode and presentation policy; not every produced buffer must reach the screen.

Evaluate frame intervals, target presentation, input latency, blocking points, and memory together, rather than relying only on FPS or allocation counts.

Debugging Triple Buffer

Dumpsys SurfaceFlinger

Start with read-only inspection of the build, property, and service state. These commands were not run on a device during this review; fields and permissions vary by system:

An empty getprop result means the property is unset or unavailable, not that its effective value is zero. Check both the source default and the branch that consumes it.

This is an old Buffering stats format. Android 9 SurfaceFlinger accumulates time over activity segments accepted by OccupancyTracker:

  • Active time: included activity time, in seconds, rather than the app’s full lifetime.
  • Two buffer: time share of segments with no recorded queue occupancy above 1.
  • Double buffered / Triple buffered: time shares of segments whose average queue occupancy is below 1, or at least 1 but below 2, respectively.

These are not instantaneous allocation counts or three mutually exclusive usage percentages. Two buffer can overlap the other classifications. A zero Triple buffered ratio does not prove that a third graphics allocation never existed. OccupancyTracker also filters segments, so an absent row must not be converted to zero use.

Disabling Triple Buffer

The following preserves the historical implementation, not a universal device switch. Follow the property’s use rather than inferring behavior from its disable name or log message.

Android Version <= Android P

Only Android 9, android-9.0.0_r1, is verified here; do not extrapolate to all earlier versions or vendor ROMs. SurfaceFlinger reads a default value of 1:

However, BufferLayer::onFirstRef uses a positive condition:

In this path, value 1 actually raises the producer’s maximum dequeued-buffer count from its default of 1 to 2; value 0 skips that expansion. The property’s name and logging do conflict with its use. It changes this queue’s parameter, not a guaranteed device-wide allocation count of exactly two or three.

Android Version > Android P

In Android 10, android-10.0.0_r1, the read default becomes 0:

BufferQueueLayer::onFirstRef also negates the condition:

Thus value 0 allows the expansion and value 1 skips it in this tag: both the default and the consuming condition changed. This does not describe every release after Android P. Android 16’s BLAST path obtains a maximum acquired-buffer count from SurfaceFlinger and combines it with other queue constraints. SurfaceFlinger’s calculation includes refresh rate and app/SF work duration.

The former adb root → setprop ro.sf.disable_triple_buffer → stop/start recipe is no longer provided as a general method. ro.* properties are write-once: ordinary setprop cannot overwrite an existing value even with root. First-setting an unset property is also permission-dependent; see property_service. System-level comparisons need a controlled test build, a verified configuration path and restart scope, and matched device, version, and workload evidence.

References

  1. AOSP BufferQueue and Gralloc
  2. Perfetto FrameTimeline and Buffer Stuffing

Attachments

The Systrace_Demo.zip archive contains five old HTML traces. This review checked the archive and embedded trace text without executing its scripts. Compatibility with current Chrome was not verified. Double/Triple filenames do not independently establish the active configuration; comparisons also need build details, actual queue parameters, and matching workloads.

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
entry.content:
This is the tenth article in the Systrace series, primarily providing a brief introduction to Binder and lock information in Systrace. It covers the basic situation of Binder, the representation of Binder communication in Systrace, how to view Binder information, and analysis of lock contention in SystemServer.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): This article retains its 2019 Systrace examples. The Binder and Java-lock analysis remains useful, but the old viewer, Framework line numbers, and device timings are version-specific. Code comparisons use AOSP Android 10, android-10.0.0_r1; ART waiter counting was also checked against Android 9 and Android 16. The screenshots come from vendor software and do not establish an exact AOSP build. Use the linked Perfetto workflow for newer traces.

Table of Contents

  • Series Article Index
  • Binder Overview
  • Binder Call Diagram
  • Lock Information in Systrace
  • Waiting for Lock Analysis
  • Related Code
  • References
  • Attachments
  • About Me && Blog

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

Binder Overview

This article maps to Perfetto 10: Binder scheduling and lock contention. In old Systrace, Binder analysis mainly used Flow Events, Binder slices, and lock-contention text to identify caller and callee. In Perfetto, the same relationship still matters, but the evidence is distributed across Binder slices, thread states, CPU scheduling, flow relationships, and SQL queries.

When analyzing Binder-related jank today, first use the old method to establish the call relationship: who called whom, how long the call took, and what the caller was waiting for. Then continue with the current Perfetto workflow: check whether the caller slept waiting for Binder return, whether the callee was running, whether it queued behind a SystemServer lock, whether the Binder thread pool was busy, and whether CPU was saturated at the same time. This separates “Binder is slow” into remote execution time, lock contention, Binder thread-pool queueing, and CPU scheduling delay.

Most inter-process communication in Android uses Binder. I won’t provide an over-explanation of Binder here. If you want a deep understanding of Binder’s implementation, I recommend reading these three articles:

  1. Understanding Android Binder Mechanism 1/3: Driver Layer
  2. Understanding Android Binder Mechanism 2/3: C++ Layer
  3. Understanding Android Binder Mechanism 3/3: Java Layer

I’m giving Binder and locks their own article because this is a path I often need to follow when investigating jank or slow responses. A synchronous remote call can pass a server-side delay back to its caller. If a SystemServer service is waiting for a Java lock, an app’s synchronous call may wait with it. The monitor contention events below describe Java object monitor contention recorded by ART, not a lock inside the Binder driver. Non-Binder threads such as android.display can contend for the same monitor.

A long dequeueBuffer can also involve unavailable buffers, GPU/fence dependencies, or consumer delays. Whether it crosses Binder and where the consumer lives depend on the OS version and BufferQueue topology. A long call alone does not establish that the SurfaceFlinger main thread caused the delay.

Remote synchronous calls wait for a reply, even with a void return type. Remote oneway calls do not wait for server completion, but still incur submission overhead and server-side queueing. Local AIDL calls can execute directly on the calling thread; oneway does not automatically move them to a pool. Nested synchronous Binder calls can also reenter an original thread in the call chain. See the AIDL calling rules and Binder threading model.

Here is a Binder architecture diagram from an article. This piece focuses on Systrace, so we’ll cover how Binder appears in Systrace without diving into its internal implementation.

Binder Call Diagram

This old-device example shows SystemServer communicating with Qualcomm’s vendor.qti.hardware.perf@2.0-service:

The annotated client and server intervals represent elapsed time, not necessarily CPU execution. Separate time before receipt, scheduling delay, lock waits, and execution using flows and thread states. The earlier Java/JNI architecture diagram does not cover every native/HIDL call path.

In the old viewer, ViewOptions → Flow Events displays relationships already captured in the trace. It cannot recover Binder events that were never collected.

Select a Binder slice for its details:

Here, Transaction Id=334303 correlates send and receive events. Calling PID=10661 is the sending thread’s TID; Calling tgid=1605 is its process ID. The attachment’s raw events contain both values. Dest Process=867 is the destination process. Dest Thread=0 at send time does not mean Linux thread 0 executes the call; follow the receive event to find the actual thread.

Flags=0x10 is TF_ACCEPT_FDS, allowing file descriptors in replies. It does not include TF_ONE_WAY=0x01, so this transaction is synchronous. Decode Code=0x6 against the correct interface and version; the viewer’s “Java Layer Dependent” label does not identify a Java method. Wall Duration=11.739 ms includes waits. Self Time=11.363 ms excludes child slices but is still elapsed time, not CPU time. See the Binder UAPI flag definitions.

The next sections examine Java lock information and waiting. After finding the threads, check the matching source to establish which object they actually contend for.

Lock Information in Systrace

monitor contention with owner Binder:1605_B (4667) at void com.android.server.wm.ActivityTaskManagerService.activityPaused(android.os.IBinder)(ActivityTaskManagerService.java:1733) waiters=2 blocking from android.app.ActivityManager$StackInfo com.android.server.wm.ActivityTaskManagerService.getFocusedStackInfo()(ActivityTaskManagerService.java:2064)

Let’s break the above message into two parts, using blocking as the dividing line.

Part 1 Interpretation

monitor contention with owner Binder:1605_B (4667) at void com.android.server.wm.ActivityTaskManagerService.activityPaused(android.os.IBinder)(ActivityTaskManagerService.java:1733) waiters=2

A monitor is the synchronization mechanism associated with a Java object. One thread holds it at a time, and that thread can reenter it. An instance synchronized method locks this; a static one locks the corresponding Class object; a synchronized block locks its expression’s object. “Two pools” is not a literal description of the mechanism. The Object.wait() wait set is distinct from contention when entering synchronized: wait() releases the monitor and must reacquire it before returning. See JLS 17.1–17.2.

Owner identifies the holding thread: Binder:1605_B, Linux TID 4667. The owner is a thread, not an object or a method.

at identifies ART’s recorded holder location. Android 10 records it on paths such as monitor acquisition or inflation; it is not a continuously updated stack trace. The holder might currently be waiting on another Binder call rather than executing that line on a CPU.

The screenshot names activityPaused at ActivityTaskManagerService.java:1733. The following AOSP Android 10 method provides a source comparison; its synchronized block is at line 1694, not the vendor screenshot’s line number:

The object is mGlobalLock. Other threads entering synchronized blocks on that same object must wait for its release and successfully acquire it. The owner can reenter. Exiting the synchronized block unlocks it, including an exceptional exit; the whole method need not have returned.

waiters is the monitor’s waiter counter sampled before registering this wait, excluding the current contender. Android 9/10 save num_waiters_ before incrementing it; Android 16 uses fetch_add, which returns the old value. In this example, waiters=2 corresponds to two earlier contenders plus android.bg, making three. This is neither a FIFO position nor a live count throughout the slice. ART’s Object.wait() path also uses the counter, so it cannot always be treated as the size of a pure monitor-entry queue.

Part 2 Interpretation

blocking from android.app.ActivityManager$StackInfo com.android.server.wm.ActivityTaskManagerService.getFocusedStackInfo()(ActivityTaskManagerService.java:2064)

This part identifies the blocked thread’s method: ActivityTaskManagerService.getFocusedStackInfo on android.bg. The AOSP Android 10 comparison is below. Its synchronized block is at line 2027; line 2064 belongs to the original device source:

This also locks mGlobalLock. Both methods contend for the same object; substituting ActivityManagerService.this would describe a different lock.

Summary

The record says that android.bg was blocked acquiring a monitor in getFocusedStackInfo. At recording time, its owner was Binder:1605_B, with the recorded holder location in activityPaused. The blocked thread can proceed only after the monitor becomes available and it successfully acquires it. The title is a snapshot; it does not establish that the same owner holds the monitor throughout the entire wait.

The original owner, holder location, counter, and blocked location are:

Waiting for Lock Analysis

Let’s stay with this trace and work through the order of events: first Binder:1605_B’s own wait, then the threads it blocks after acquiring the monitor:

The selected slice actually shows Binder:1605_B waiting for android.anim, whose recorded holder location is WindowAnimator.animate, for about 0.050 ms. It later acquires the monitor, and other threads wait for it. Nested Binder calls also mean its holding interval need not be continuous Running time.

Lock Waiting

These three records belong to different threads; the table corrects copied thread names in the old annotations. The attachment’s raw ATrace Begin/End intervals give:

Waiting threadBlocked methodwaiters in titleWait slice wall duration
android.display (1683)ActivityMetricsLogger.checkVisibility03.647 ms
android.anim (1684)WindowManagerService.relayoutWindow12.559 ms
android.bg (1692)ActivityTaskManagerService.getFocusedStackInfo23.835 ms

All three initially identify Binder:1605_B (4667) as the holder of mGlobalLock. The intervals overlap; their sum is not a single call’s latency. Waiting threads can sleep, become Runnable after a wakeup, and run again to attempt acquisition. Java blocking state and kernel scheduling state are different descriptions.

Lock Release

The annotated wakeup chain is present in the attachment: Binder:1605_B → android.display → android.anim → android.bg. A wakeup gives a thread an opportunity to run. By itself, it proves neither immediate acquisition nor a FIFO monitor policy.

The attachment also contains further contention visible in the figure. After its checkVisibility wait ends, android.display waits for android.anim in WindowProcessController.hasActivitiesOrRecentTasks for 3.808 ms. Later, android.anim waits for android.bg in Session.getInTouchMode for 3.148 ms. This is not a six-step sequence in which each thread waits once and then finishes. The original android.bg wait retains the Binder owner in its title, illustrating why that snapshot is not a complete ownership history.

Correlate slice boundaries, scheduling states, wakers, subsequent owners, and source code. The following is a separate example of longer SystemServer contention, with different process and owner IDs; it is not a continuation of the sequence above:

Seeing this many threads waiting on locks is pretty alarming. Concurrent lock waits can increase startup or interaction latency. This image does not establish that installing more apps or using a phone longer causes this problem, nor that all systems routinely have 7–10 waiters. Follow the holder to determine whether it is executing expensive work, waiting for remote Binder or I/O, or waiting for CPU time.

Reduce avoidable critical-section work and review cross-process calls made while holding locks, while preserving shared-state consistency. More Binder threads do not remove serialization on one monitor. Changing an interface to oneway changes completion and error semantics, so it is not a general fix.

For wakeup inspection, see Analyzing Thread Wakeup Information.

Related Code

Both excerpts come from AOSP android-10.0.0_r1, art/runtime/monitor.cc. They explain the old trace format and are not standalone compilable examples.

Monitor Info

PrettyContentionInfo assembles the owner, recorded holder location, and waiter count:

Block Info

This is a contiguous excerpt from Monitor::Lock. Note that the count is saved before incrementing it, and the event is emitted only when ATrace is enabled and an owner is available:

Android 16, android-16.0.0_r1, still emits monitor contention events, but uses atomic fetch_add and a different owner-information path. The Android 10 excerpt is not the current implementation. Missing events do not prove an absence of contention: check capture categories, instrumentation conditions, and data completeness.

For newer traces in Perfetto, associate the Binder endpoints, then align thread states and monitor contention in the same interval. The current standard library provides android.binder and android.monitor_contention. Tables and fields depend on the Trace Processor version, and relevant events must have been captured. Missing associations or parsed records remain unknown; do not turn them into zero latency or zero contention.

References

  1. Understanding Android Binder Mechanism 1/3: Driver Layer
  2. Understanding Android Binder Mechanism 2/3: C++ Layer
  3. Understanding Android Binder Mechanism 3/3: Java Layer

Attachments

The attachment is App_lunch.html.zip, containing an old Systrace HTML report. This review inspected its Binder, monitor contention, and scheduling events as text without executing embedded scripts. Interactive compatibility with current Chrome was not verified; use a viewer or import path that supports this format.
Click here to download the Systrace attachments related to the article

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.

entry.title: [Sticky] Blog Article Directory
entry.content:
The content of this blog mainly focuses on Android development and optimization-related topics, including the use of performance tools, Android App optimization knowledge, Android Framework explanations, and performance theory. Here is an organized directory for your reference. You can choose the parts you are interested in. This directory includes not only blog content but also some of my answers on Zhihu or historical discussions in The Performance, which has closed. This directory lists my original blog posts. Additionally, I have collected some excellent articles in Must-Knows for Android Performance Optimization, which I update periodically.

Articles come first; tools, Apps, and content projects are collected under Personal Projects. See also the AIW introduction and repository.

This directory will be updated with every blog post for easy reference. I will try my best to update weekly. Learning is endless; let’s encourage each other. If there is anything you want to know or if there are any inadequacies in the blog, please leave a message on the blog, Zhihu, Weibo, or WeChat. I will actively correct them.

Theoretical Knowledge

  2. Historical Introduction to The Performance (Closed)
  3. The Performance Planet Tea Party - Episode 1
  4. Performance Design in OS Design

Perfetto Series

Perfetto has become my main tool for everyday Android performance analysis. Readers new to performance work have told me that its busy interface and many features leave them overwhelmed. They asked me to revisit the Systrace articles using Perfetto, so that is what I’m doing in this series.

Tools and versions — updated October 13, 2026: Systrace belongs to the legacy workflow. Android’s System Tracing utility saves Perfetto-format data on Android 10 (API 29) and later; use Perfetto UI and Trace Processor as the primary analysis path. See Android system tracing. Supported legacy Systrace data can also be imported; legacy-viewer availability and compatibility depend on the viewer version. Older thread-state, Vsync, Input, SurfaceFlinger, and Binder articles remain useful learning references, but their functions, timing, and limits must be read against each article’s Android version.

  • Web edition and complete contents.
  • EPUB releases.
  • Contributing: include the Android version, source location, and reproducible observation when reporting an error.

SmartPerfetto

SmartPerfetto was the open-source project I was spending the most time on when I put this list together. It adds an AI Assistant to Perfetto. Questions about a loaded trace lead to evidence gathered through trace_processor_shell, SQL, YAML Skills, and scenario strategies. Results remain limited by the captured data; AI interpretation does not replace source inspection, queries, or reproduction.

  • Perfetto UI fork hosting the Assistant integration.
  • A TypeScript backend for agent execution, tools, Skills, reports, and streaming output.
  • YAML Skills and Markdown strategies for startup, scrolling, ANR, Binder, CPU, memory, and rendering.
  • Introduction, architecture, and architecture Q&A.

Android App Memory Analysis

Android-App-Memory-Analysis brings dumpsys meminfo, dumpsys gfxinfo, HPROF, and smaps into a common investigation.

  • Collect available data from connected devices. HPROF/smaps access depends on debuggability, permissions, and device policy.
  • Correlate Java heap, native, graphics, and process-level evidence, with readable reports.
  • The current README describes Android 17 / API 37 Demo and input-format adaptation, alongside Android 16 and 16 KB page-size notes. A build target or parser claim does not prove validation on every device.

TraceFix

TraceFix inserts paired android.os.Trace.beginSection/endSection calls into App bytecode at build time, reducing manual instrumentation work. Instrumentation also has a cost; bound its scope and compare equivalent runs.

As of October 13, 2026, Maven Central metadata and the POM confirm io.github.gracker:TraceFix:0.1.0. The repository README describes 0.2.x for Android 17 / AGP 9.1.x, but the 0.2.0 POM is not available at that repository endpoint. Distinguish source-branch documentation from published dependencies.

Perfetto Auto-Pin

Perfetto-AutoPin-For-Chrome pins frequently used tracks through presets such as Frame, Startup, Input, Memory, Binder, SurfaceFlinger, SystemUI, and CPU analysis, with custom track sets.

It relies on Perfetto UI internals, so compatibility can change with UI versions. Perfetto’s own commands and macros offer another way to reduce repeated track setup.

High Performance Friends Circle

Friends-Circle-Demo-Apks-For-Power-and-Performance-Test is a Moments-style Android workload suite for startup, scrolling, and App switching. Different UI implementations and loads support investigation of main/RenderThread work, SurfaceFlinger, CPU, frames, and power. A Flutter suite provides related workloads.

Systrace / Perfetto Utilities and Historical Demos

These projects retain older examples and tools. Build environments, private interfaces, and device permissions need their own checks before use on current Android.

  • SystraceForBlog: article traces and case materials.
  • SystraceAnalysis: legacy Systrace/ftrace analysis.
  • android_cpu_usage_calculation: CPU-usage calculation scripts.
  • FPSDump: an older system-permission/private-SurfaceFlinger-interface demo, not a universal current App-FPS meter.
  • GameBench: historical game-performance server/client tooling.
  • Android-FPS-Calculation: an FPS calculation demo.
  • Android_HardwareLayer_Example: hardware-layer animation examples.
  • DelayLoadSample: the startup DelayLoad article’s sample.
  • ListHeaderAnimationPerformance: list-header animation experiments.
  • AndroidLunchModeTest: launch-mode examples.
  • AndroidUML: Android diagrams written with PlantUML.

Historical Android / Java Projects

  • Cats: a personal App/practice project.
  • Girls: a Gank client built for practice.
  • Flutter-Gank: Flutter practice.
  • FriendsCircle_Flutter_Demo: a Flutter Moments demo.
  • SlideDelete-ListView: swipe-to-delete ListView example.
  • Android-NumberLimitEditText: input-length-limit feedback.
  • SystemMonitor: an Android monitoring example.
  • JavaReflect: Java reflection examples.
  • AndroidInterview-PrintAllViews: View-tree printing exercises.
  • MemoryAnalysisTools: an older Meizu-device memory tool.
  • Fragment-NetEase: an archived Fragment example.

Resources, Sites, and Translations

  • awesome-android-ai-dev-sources: developers, blogs, and technical sources I follow.
  • Gracker.github.io: the blog’s deployment repository.
  • hexo-theme-reading: an older Hexo theme.
  • claude-code-from-source-zh-cn: a Simplified Chinese translation of Claude Code from Source.

The GitHub profile has the full public repository list; this directory selects projects related to the blog and my longer-term work.

SmartProtobuf

SmartProtobuf is a Protobuf/trace-data-structure project. Its public repository and usage documentation will be linked when that information is ready; no unstable public entrypoint is listed here.

AI and Automation Projects

OpenClaw

OpenClaw has been part of my local automation practice, connecting Telegram, Obsidian, scheduled jobs, models, and engineering tools for research, knowledge management, notes, and collaboration.

  • Three Weeks of Running OpenClaw Locally.
  • OpenClaw FAQ.

AI Field Notes

awesome-ai-field-notes is an AI information directory. Its documented site, godofgpt.com, could not be reached during the October 13, 2026 check; use the GitHub repository for the material. Its documented OpenClaw pipeline collects, deduplicates, categorizes, scores, translates, and generates pages about models, agents, coding, infrastructure, and research. It is a long-term information archive and an example of my automation work.

Gracker Skills

I’ve turned some of my regular writing, research, and diagram workflows into public Skills:

  • gracker-writing: technical articles, retrospectives, FAQs, methods, and long-form writing.
  • gracker-deep-research-skill: local discovery, evidence collection, and offline drafting.
  • gracker-diagrams-skill: technical diagrams and infographics. It prepares prompt packs by default; rendering requires drawing capabilities in the host environment.

Open Design

Open Design is a design-tool project I previously forked and helped maintain, exploring local coding agents, design systems, Skills, export, and preview in one workflow. Its former public repository was unavailable on October 13, 2026, so no installation link is currently provided here.

Apps in Development

100Years

100Years is an iPhone / Apple Watch App for health trends and long-term health signals. It combines HealthKit, lifestyle, health records, workouts, and sleep data. Deterministic models produce estimates, with optional AI explanations. Lifespan, age-100, and healthy-lifespan outputs are product estimates without external clinical calibration, not personal survival probabilities or medical conclusions.

The source is not publicly linked here. Work continues on data import, health-data synchronization, SwiftUI, localization, and release readiness; this description does not establish a public release.

iBattery

iBattery is a cycling-device battery monitor for iOS, covering compatible Bluetooth sports devices such as power meters, heart-rate sensors, shifting systems, and cadence sensors.

  • Discovers and classifies nearby devices.
  • Updates battery state and alerts when the device exposes readable battery data; discovery alone does not guarantee access.
  • Shows recent readings in iOS Widgets. Widget refresh is not continuous Bluetooth sampling; reading age matters.
  • Includes localization, caching, notifications, and appearance settings.

The iOS repository is not publicly linked here; an Android version is also a local development direction.

Juju

Juju is an Android growth journal I’m making for my family, for recording a child’s age, milestones, and photos, with home-screen widgets. It is not presented as a public open-source release.

Content Projects

Android Performance Blog

AndroidPerformance.com is my longest-running public content project. It covers Perfetto, Systrace, system mechanisms, smoothness, responsiveness, ANR, memory, Framework, and App development, alongside reading notes and personal writing. This article directory is the main navigation page.

Android Weekly

Android Weekly is a free Chinese technical newsletter covering Android, Linux, iOS, Flutter, performance, and engineering tools.

  • Juejin column.
  • Zhihu column.

Personal Page

Below is my personal introduction and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  2. Blogger Intro: Includes personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
