  8. Juejin: https://juejin.cn/user/1816846860560749

Presentations and Training PPTs

This section will be released after some organization. As you know, PPTs don’t contain too much detail, mostly just an outline.

  1. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto Basics and Case Studies
  2. Video (Bilibili) - Android Perfetto: Trace Graph Types - AOSP, WebView, Flutter + OEM System Optimization

Knowledge Planet

The Performance closed in 2026 and no longer accepts new members. Its performance foundations, tooling guides, and case studies will gradually be organized into the blog and Android Internals Wiki.

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
entry.content:
This is the seventh article in the Systrace series, primarily introducing the Vsync mechanism in Android. This article examines the display of each frame in the Android system from the perspective of Systrace. Vsync is a critical mechanism in Systrace. Although invisible and intangible when operating a phone, we can see in Systrace how the Android system, guided by Vsync signals, orderly performs rendering and composition for each frame, ensuring stable frame rates.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Table of Contents

  • Series Article Index
  • Main Content
  • Android Graphics Data Flow
  • Graphic Data Flow in Systrace
  • Vsync Offset
  • HW_Vsync
  • Other Addresses for This Article
  • References
  • About Me && Blog

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

Main Content

Version note — reviewed October 13, 2026: The article and captures date from 2019; their full device builds were not recorded. Interpret DispSync, phase dumps, and old function names against AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 / android-10.0.0_r1. Android 16 uses a different prediction and callback-scheduling implementation. The 60 Hz and 0 / 4 ms offsets are example conditions, not universal device settings.

For newer captures, pair this article with Perfetto 8: Vsync Mechanism and Performance Analysis, following the same frame through the App, RenderThread, SurfaceFlinger, GPU, and Display/HWC. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, FrameTimeline can compare expected and actual timing when the required data was captured. Missing tracks are not zero duration, and adjacent slices do not alone establish frame identity.

Hardware timing and software scheduling work together. HWC reports display-related Vsync timestamps to SurfaceFlinger. Older DispSync builds a periodic model and uses software timing to issue App/SF callbacks at selected phases. That model can run while hardware callbacks are temporarily disabled. Thus “Vsync is now mostly hardware-generated” does not explain the origin of every App callback.

The old diagram’s retire fence provides display feedback; it is not each App’s GPU-completion notification. Retire/present fence terminology, meaning, and hardware timing offsets vary across implementations and should not be collapsed into one instant.

As described in Choreographer rendering, the App requests frame callbacks as needed and executes doFrame through its Looper. An unchanged screen need not redraw every display cycle. Common 60 / 90 / 120 Hz intervals are approximately 16.67 / 11.11 / 8.33 ms; App frame rate, display refresh rate, and callback rate need not match. See also Perfetto 6: Why 120Hz?.

SurfaceFlinger processes transactions, selects Buffers, and arranges composition according to scheduling and layer state. It does not unconditionally redraw every Surface on every signal. Here are the relevant legacy Systrace tracks:

Every 0/1 transition on these VSYNC-app / VSYNC-sf counters marks an event, not only rising edges. The high interval is not execution time. Software callbacks, delivery to the App, and actual CPU scheduling have distinct times, while a queued-Buffer counter does not prove GPU completion.

Android Graphics Data Flow

Use a conventional hardware-accelerated View’s older GL path to follow content toward the display. Games, software rendering, and other backends can have different functions and stages.

  1. doFrame processes due input, animation, and Traversal work, including necessary Measure, Layout, and Draw. A DisplayList records drawing operations; it is not a literal list of OpenGL commands.
  2. RenderThread synchronizes drawing state and drives the backend, potentially preparing resources, encoding, and submitting work. flush drawing commands is not simply a CPU-to-GPU upload. Shared memory does not eliminate cache coherency, lifetime, or synchronization requirements.
  3. GPU execution is usually asynchronous, but CPU threads may still wait for Buffers, driver queues, or fences. Submission is not guaranteed to return immediately on every physical device.
  4. The GL/EGL path uses operations such as eglSwapBuffersWithDamageKHR to hand off a Buffer and synchronization information. Swap / queueBuffer return is neither GPU completion nor presentation. A Vulkan path need not contain these EGL names.
  5. SurfaceFlinger arranges client/device composition using layer state and HWC negotiation. RenderEngine can use the GPU for client composition, while device composition can use display hardware. Fences constrain consumption and can be waited on by GPU/display hardware; SF’s main thread need not block on each layer before GPU-compositing everything. Legacy onMessageReceived, invalidate, and refresh names are not universal modern interfaces. See Hardware Composer.
  6. The display pipeline presents/scans out the result at an appropriate time. Buffer submission, a present fence signal, and every pixel finishing its visible update are different events. Every composition mode does not require one consolidated final frame buffer first.

This historical diagram includes both SF GPU composition and display-controller paths, illustrating why composition is not always entirely GPU work.

These diagrams introduce producers, Buffers, consumers, and display output rather than the entire Android 16 process/queue layout. Modern View paths can also involve BLASTBufferQueue.

Graphic Data Flow in Systrace

Follow the App, SurfaceFlinger, and composer service in this older capture:

  1. The App/SF markers here have nearly the same phase. That does not mean both threads run at the same nanosecond.
  2. SF selects a Buffer already eligible for that composition, labeled App frame N−1 in the image.
  3. The App processes frame N and submits a new Buffer through main-thread and RenderThread work. The queue counter changes; the image’s “rendering complete” annotation is shorthand for submission, not proof of GPU completion.
  4. Later SF work handles frame N while the App can prepare the next frame. This Buffer was submitted in step 3, not “rendered in step 2” as the original text stated.

This is one steady-pipeline sample. Old content may remain visible, and new frames may be delayed, replaced, or dropped. Use Buffer/frame identity, fences, and FrameTimeline where available instead of mechanically assigning N−1 / N to every capture.

Vsync Offset

Older DispSync maintains a model from hardware timestamps and display feedback, then schedules callbacks with App/SF phases:

phase-app and phase-sf are relative to the reference display timing. In this simplified diagram, the App starts earlier and SF works at a later phase.

For comparison, this article calls Δ = phase-sf − phase-app the offset between the two. That difference is not the entire Vsync configuration. Phases can be negative or span a cycle, and early/late configurations can change. They are not universally limited to 0–16.6 ms, and the article has no evidence that most manufacturers set the difference to zero. Equal planned phases do not guarantee simultaneous delivery or CPU execution.

adb shell dumpsys SurfaceFlinger can expose the device’s configuration, with version-dependent fields. These two historical dumps are retained as examples, not Android 16’s fixed output format.

Difference = 0: App and SF each have a phase of 1,000,000 ns, or 1 ms relative to the reference. Neither phase itself is zero.

Difference = 4 ms: 6,000,000 − 2,000,000 = 4,000,000 ns. The 16,666,666 ns period is approximately 60 Hz.

present offset is a separate display-feedback/timing setting, not the App/SF phase difference. Early and early-GL rows are candidate configurations; a static dump does not identify which one a particular frame used.

Offset = 0

Here is the original zero-difference example:

The planned callbacks approximately align, and the App’s new Buffer is used by the following SF work. The image’s roughly 16.6 ms label spans Vsync events. Waiting from Buffer submission to consumption is only the remaining part of that cycle, not invariably another full 16.6 ms.

At this point you may be wondering: if the App’s Buffer is ready, could SurfaceFlinger use it sooner and save some of that wait? A later SF phase can allow a new App frame to become eligible before that SF work. This is not an event-driven policy that immediately composites whenever queueBuffer completes. Latch/composition conditions still apply, with enough time needed for GPU and SF/HWC work before the target presentation.

Offset ≠ 0

The original labels this example as a 4 ms phase difference:

The red rectangle measures the gap between scheduling markers, not App rendering duration, GPU completion, or total touch-to-display latency. Follow that frame’s submission, synchronization, and display result to establish whether it presents earlier.

Pros and Cons of Offset

Phase tuning trades input freshness against App work time and composition headroom. Neither a larger nor a smaller value is universally better.

  1. With a short Δ, the new Buffer may miss that composition. Old content can usually remain visible; the App does not disappear. In an idealized periodic model, the next SF time might be T + Δ after App work starts, but that is not a complete input-to-display latency formula.
  2. A long Δ can reduce SF/HWC and related GPU headroom enough to miss the target presentation. It may still help under another workload; it does not simply become ineffective.

Android 16 update: Scheduler works with components including VSyncPredictor, VSyncReactor, and VSyncDispatchTimerQueue. The timer queue uses target Vsync, workDuration, and readyDuration to calculate wakeup times and handles scheduling updates. Old DispSync constants or one fixed phase pair cannot explain every frame. See VSyncDispatchTimerQueue.cpp, android-16.0.0_r1.

Android 15 ARR also requires compatible display hardware and HAL support. ARR can decouple display Vsync cadence from refresh intervals; the official example uses roughly 240 Hz Vsync steps with a maximum 120 Hz refresh rate. A Vsync period is therefore not automatically the App frame rate. See Adaptive refresh rate.

HW_Vsync

Disabling HWC Vsync event callbacks does not stop panel refresh or GPU execution. Software prediction can continue scheduling App/SF events without receiving every hardware callback; resynchronization, display changes, and other conditions can request new samples.

The original 500 ms claim needs correction. This is the complete method from Android 9 SurfaceFlinger:

It compares the current call with the previous call to this rate-limiting method, updating sLastResyncAttempted every time. It does not compare with the last composition, and this is not the only way to enable hardware callbacks. Android 10 Scheduler has a similar 500 ms condition; the corresponding limit in Android 16 Scheduler::resync() is 750 ms. Neither is a public API guarantee.

Distinguish transitions on HW_VSYNC_0 from the enabled interval on HW_VSYNC_ON_0. The latter is not a panel power switch. Missing transitions can reflect disabled callbacks or capture coverage, not a stopped display.

Without HW_VSYNC

The old diagram shows an established software model continuing to deliver events, without every App request waiting for a new HWC callback.

With HW_VSYNC

This diagram adds resynchronization, hardware timestamp reception, and model updates. Its arrow directly to the App is simplified: legacy EventThread distributes events through Connection / BitTube, followed by native reception and Looper/Choreographer processing. The server does not directly invoke Java onVsync.

For sample counts, use Android 9 DispSync.h and DispSync.cpp:

  • The resynchronization ring stores up to 32 timestamps. updateModelLocked() re-estimates the model at 6 or more. Six timestamps provide five intervals; removing the minimum and maximum leaves three intervals for the period average. That is not a minimum of three hardware events.
  • mPeriod is the period; mPhase is the model phase, used with a reference time and listener-specific phases. Initialization supplies a display period, and the first resync sample updates the reference. Six samples are not a prerequisite for any software callback to exist.
  • Valid present-fence timestamps provide feedback. mError is a mean squared error in ns²; the version’s 160000000000 threshold is (400 µs)². Model validity and half-threshold hysteresis affect continued sampling, while ignoring present fences takes a different branch. Missing valid samples or an error reset to zero does not establish measured zero error.

These are version-specific details, not permanent Android “6/32” rules. Android 16’s VSyncPredictor has its own sample parameters and prediction logic. The original SW-VSYNC article remains additional historical reading.

Other Addresses for This Article

The follow-up on this blog is Perfetto 8: Vsync Mechanism and Performance Analysis.

References

  1. VSYNC
  2. Sync and Vsync
  3. Android Graphics Architecture
  4. Generation and Transmission of SW-VSYNC
  5. DispSync Implementation Details

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro: Includes personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Welcome to recommend projects/articles.
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Complete Guide to Android App Startup Optimization
entry.content:
I’ve gathered the Android app startup optimization approaches I knew of when writing this article. Use them as a checklist: see what others have tried, then look for gaps in your own app. The details depend heavily on your business, so I won’t explain every implementation here. Once you find an approach that fits, follow up on that particular method.

I’ve also included some startup work done by system manufacturers, limited to the parts I know about. There are proprietary tricks I can’t cover here. Knowing what happens on the system side may still help, including when discussing whitelisting or SDK integration with a manufacturer.

Version note — reviewed October 13, 2026: This article was published in 2019. The original examples and categories remain, with updated startup definitions, measurement guidance, and splash-screen behavior. OEM whitelists, prediction, and restart strategies are historical leads rather than capabilities guaranteed on every device. Process-pool details use tagged Android 10 / 16 source.

First define the endpoint: the first frame, primary content, and interactivity are different milestones. Repeated Macrobenchmark journeys and Perfetto traces help locate main-thread, RenderThread, Binder, I/O, and GC costs; field monitoring should separate devices and versions. Baseline Profiles guide ART compilation, whereas Startup Profiles optimize DEX layout during the build.

App Startup Overview

General App Startup Flow

Launching from an icon can involve system scheduling, process and component initialization, UI construction, and content loading. This older diagram shows only some of those stages:

  • SystemServer coordinates process, Activity, and window management. It requests a normal App process through Zygote or an eligible USAP; SystemServer does not directly fork the App itself.
  • The App process handles binding, Provider initialization, Application.onCreate(), and Activity work after its main Looper exists. Not every launch initializes all four component types; Services and Receivers depend on the entrypoint and workload.

The diagram places Application.onCreate outside its MainThread box. That does not mean it runs on another thread or that the main thread is created afterward. Network content and interactivity may still be pending after the first frame.

Cold Start vs. Hot Start

The original two-way classification also needs warm starts. For common process/Activity states:

  • Cold: The App process needs to start, with application and UI initialization.
  • Warm: Typically, the process survives but the target Activity needs recreation, including onCreate().
  • Hot: An existing Activity and its UI state can be brought forward, though content restoration, layout, or drawing may still be needed.

Back and Home are not reliable switches between these categories. Activity behavior varies, background processes can be reclaimed, and a recent-task card does not prove that a process survives. Record process and Activity recreation, and use the measurement tool’s definitions. See startup states.

Measuring Startup Speed

Different teams have their own ways of measuring startup. What has always bothered me is deciding exactly when it ends. Complex screens need an observable completion condition, rather than whichever number looks smallest.

  • TTID: The destination screen’s first displayed frame. It may still contain placeholders or loading UI.
  • TTFD: The App signals primary-content readiness through reportFullyDrawn() or an appropriate ReportDrawn API. Its meaning depends on the App’s reporting condition; it does not automatically validate every interaction.
  • Interactivity or business completion: A usable list or completed login needs an explicit scenario and assertion. OCR can identify expected content, but visible text does not prove an image finished loading or a control is usable.

Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric reports timeToInitialDisplayMs and timeToFullDisplayMs. The latter ends with the relevant rendered frame containing or following the fully-drawn signal. Missing reporting is not a zero duration. Fix the release build, startup mode, compilation/Profile state, account and data state; repeat on physical devices, compare distributions, and keep traces. See Macrobenchmark setup.

adb shell am start -W remains useful for quick diagnosis, but its fields vary by version. Older output commonly has ThisTime/TotalTime/WaitTime; AOSP Android 16 prints LaunchState, TotalTime, and WaitTime, without ThisTime. WaitTime is neither content readiness nor pure App CPU time. A single command or screen recording does not replace a release benchmark.

The original Mobile Taobao case used automated, repeatable, CI-integrated measurement with OCR. Its OCR-service accuracy figure does not establish the accuracy of detecting this App’s startup endpoint.

App-Level Optimizations

Startup Window Optimization

A system StartingWindow, Android 12 SplashScreen, and an App’s own SplashActivity are different things. A splash improves waiting feedback; it does not remove initialization work.

  • For legacy preview windows, avoid unnecessary android:windowDisablePreview="true" settings that leave a blank wait. Keep the launch theme visually consistent with the destination.
  • Android 12 (API 31) introduces the standard system SplashScreen for cold and warm launches. Follow the migration guide; old background-image and preview-disable tricks are not universal modern solutions. An additional SplashActivity may produce two consecutive splashes.
  • Route directly to the destination where appropriate. Login, deep links, and advertising have their own constraints; measure them separately and preserve state restoration.

The original observations about WeChat, Zhihu, and TikTok did not provide reproducible versions or whitelist evidence. They cannot establish those apps’ current configuration or how often they start cold.

Thread Optimization

Control runnable work and dependency waits. Excess runnable threads can increase main-thread scheduling delay; Sleep may instead reflect locks, condition variables, Binder, or ordinary idle time.

  • Bound thread-pool concurrency and backlog according to task type. A pool alone does not prevent overload.
  • Follow locks to their owners. Moving a dependency to a worker and immediately waiting on the main thread can preserve the original blockage.
  • Distinguish main-thread-only initialization from work that can run elsewhere. mmkernel and Alpha are historical architecture references, not mandatory standard components.

System Scheduling Optimization

Reduce unnecessary work on the startup critical path:

  • Consolidate repeated synchronous Binder queries and investigate AMS/ATMS or WMS lock waits. Binder calls are not synonymous with all system calls, nor does every call compete for the same lock.
  • Defer extra processes not needed for the first screen. They add initialization and contention, but the cost does not simply double. Preserve required process isolation.
  • Inspect Provider and Service initialization on their process’s main thread, including Providers initialized before Application.onCreate(). Remote Provider requests and Service Binder methods can instead run on Binder pool threads.
  • Move suitable work off the main thread with an explicit readiness dependency. Main-thread-only essentials still need to be shortened.

The old CPU capture shows interleaved work. Colors alone do not establish saturation or identify a single App as its cause:

The SystemServer image shows monitor contention and lock-owner threads. Its 93.633 ms selection is an observation window, not the sum of every lock wait or the full launch time. Follow the owners:

GC Optimization

Reduce unnecessary startup allocations, then inspect allocation volume, GC pauses, and main-thread waits. Counting collections alone is insufficient.

  • Avoid repeated large strings, serialization, and parsing content not needed for the first screen.
  • Reuse objects only with clear ownership and size limits. Pools can increase retained memory or lock contention.
  • Native allocation still consumes process memory and adds JNI, lifetime, and leak concerns. Moving code to Native is not a general way to eliminate memory cost.

Historical example: Alipay startup garbage-collection optimization.

IO Optimization

File access, page faults, decompression, databases, and other processes’ I/O can interact during startup. Record the file, actual bytes transferred, call count, thread, and duration; distinguish parsing CPU time from waiting. File size is not the amount read or written by an operation.

Required first-screen network requests can start asynchronously; defer nonessential requests. A blanket ban on startup networking does not fit online-content screens. Move suitable disk operations off the main thread without immediately waiting for them there.

This is the original table of observation dimensions: the 500 MB chat.db file and the 800 KB write are separate fields. Its KB/MB labels do not specify decimal versus binary units, so they cannot establish exact throughput. The durations and Buffer sizes are examples, not recommended settings.

These captures involve the system screen recorder and another App, not a controlled comparison of one process. Identify I/O waits using the selected thread state, blocking stack, and related events. Orange/red method slices are not automatically I/O, and the partial images alone do not establish low memory as the root cause.

Resource Reordering

The historical approach rearranges APK resources to improve startup access locality, making better use of page cache and readahead. See the original Alipay package-layout case.

Page cache holds file content for ordinary buffered I/O and file mappings. Readahead benefits depend on access patterns and cache state. Adjacent file offsets do not guarantee contiguous physical storage, and page size, filesystem blocks, APK compression, and mapping behavior are separate concerns.

The diagram is labeled Linux 4.0 (2015); it is a historical illustration, not the complete modern Android storage stack. Modern packaging includes split APKs, compression, alignment, and signing. Reordering belongs inside the build/signing pipeline, followed by artifact validation. A warm cache may leave little benefit; compare equivalent device and cache conditions rather than assuming fewer disk reads.

Class Reordering

ReDex InterDex can use a startup class list to improve DEX layout; see the project documentation. DEX capacity, primary-DEX constraints, and other optimizations still apply. “Put every startup class in the primary DEX without considering constraints” is not an adequate implementation model. Measure the result with an equivalent A/B journey.

Consider Startup Profiles for current builds. They improve startup-code locality during the build; Baseline Profiles supply critical paths to ART for compilation. According to the configuration guide, DEX layout optimization is available from AGP 8.1 and enabled by default from 8.3. AGP 8.1–8.2 need explicit enablement, with R8 configured as documented. The recommended tool combination is Macrobenchmark 1.2.0+ and AGP 8.2+. Confirm that the release artifact consumes the generated rules, and test launcher and deep-link entries rather than adopting another app’s improvement percentage.

Main Page Layout Optimization

Inspect actual Measure, Layout, and Draw costs—or Compose composition and layout—on the target screen:

  • Reduce redundant hierarchy and repeated measurement; hierarchy depth is not the only cost.
  • Use ViewStub for Views not yet needed, while checking the first-expansion delay instead of moving jank to the first tap.
  • A custom View can reduce some stacking costs but brings interaction, accessibility, and drawing maintenance. It is not automatically faster than standard components.

Idle Calls

IdleHandler belongs to a MessageQueue and runs when its Looper’s queue meets idle conditions, not when a particular Handler is idle. Returning true retains it for a later idle callback; false removes it. Returning true does not create an immediate infinite loop.

The callback still executes on that Looper’s thread. A main-queue IdleHandler should not directly perform network requests, heavy I/O, or large View construction. It neither guarantees a deadline nor moves work to a worker thread. It can cheaply schedule nonessential work, but required first-screen tasks must not wait indefinitely for idle time. See IdleHandler and Android 10 MessageQueue.

Class Loading Optimization

A VerifyClass trace slice can identify verification work, but its wall duration can include scheduling waits. Every startup does not necessarily verify every method again. Inspect the ART version, compilation state, and loading path.

This dexopt / VERIFY_MODE_NONE diagram describes an old runtime model. It is not guidance for disabling modern ART verification. Since Android 7, ART combines interpretation, JIT, and AOT, with version-dependent artifacts and policy; see ART configuration. Reduce needless initialization and correctly generate, package, and validate Baseline Profiles. A packaged Profile alone does not prove that a particular device launch uses precompiled code.

App Thinning

Package size, installed storage, decoded-image memory, and startup duration are different metrics:

  • Use Android Lint and IDE inspections to find unused content, then check reflection, JNI, and dynamic-resource retention requirements.
  • Configure R8 and resource shrinking for release builds. Obfuscating names and removing unused content are different operations.
  • RGB_565 is a 2-byte-per-pixel Bitmap memory configuration without alpha, not an APK file format replacing PNG or JPEG. Consider transparency, color, and actual decode behavior; choose compression and decode dimensions separately.
  • Renaming resources or reducing DEX count does not guarantee a faster launch. Inspect real artifacts and startup work without breaking resource lookup or adding work merely to reduce a file count.

Choosing the Right Startup Framework

Model initialization and dependencies as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), then choose stages, threads, and concurrency bounds. The graph expresses ordering; it does not require multiple processes or automatically provide parallelism and congestion control. Define success and failure for required dependencies. Submitting a worker task is not the same as completing initialization.

These three images retain the original Taobao stages: core libraries, screen dependencies, optional preloading, and on-demand initialization. m-a, m-f-a, m-b-f, and m-idle are case-specific labels, not Android lifecycle states. The table’s guaranteed-execution column does not establish a guarantee for arbitrary IdleHandlers.

Jetpack App Startup can express Initializer.dependencies() and consolidate automatic initialization under one Provider. It synchronously calls create() in dependency order; it is not an automatic parallel scheduler. Default eager initialization usually runs on the main thread before Application.onCreate(). For manual/lazy initialization, inspect the merged manifest and remaining initializer dependencies to avoid early or missing initialization.

Historical case: Taobao full-link optimization.

Startup Network Optimization

These categories come from the historical Taobao case. Library names, threads, and durations describe that workload rather than default behavior in every App.

Problems and Optimization Points

  • Sending: library setup or bindService can delay requests; image tasks may wait in bounded queues.
  • Transfer: oversized or unnecessary resources compete with first-screen data.
  • Parsing: JSON, decoding, and callbacks occupy finite worker capacity.
  • Display: results may be available while main-thread queues or heavy callbacks still delay presentation.

The original 3-second parsing and 1-second/high-end versus 3-second/low-end delays lack reproducible conditions here. They are historical case descriptions, not device-tier thresholds.

Optimization Strategies

  • Deduplicate requests and defer nonessential data. Deduplication is not indiscriminately merging every network connection.
  • Bound download, parsing, and image-decode concurrency to avoid shifting the bottleneck to CPU, memory, or callback queues.
  • Parse on suitable workers, apply only necessary results on the main thread, and handle cancellation and stale callbacks.
  • Refresh intervals at 60 / 90 / 120 Hz are about 16.67 / 11.11 / 8.33 ms. One callback cannot consume the whole interval; staying under 16 ms is no guarantee against jank. Use the actual deadline and all main-thread work.

Preloading

When upcoming navigation is predictable, prepare data asynchronously and reuse it when the screen is ready. Handle cancellation, errors, account changes, expiration, and memory limits. Without an opportunity to run earlier, relocating the work need not reduce end-to-end waiting.

The original PreLoader project remains a historical implementation reference. Check maintenance and compatibility before integrating it.

Keep-Alive

Keeping a process can avoid some work on the next launch, but a destroyed Activity may still require a warm start. Process survival is not synonymous with a hot start and must not substitute for cold-start optimization.

The aim here is useful functionality and responsible resource use, not mutual wake-ups or notification flooding. Release background resources and stop unnecessary services and animations.

I know this can sound idealistic from an App developer’s side. You may release resources carefully and still have the process removed by a manufacturer’s background policy. Improving Android’s ecosystem takes work from both sides. Background limits, user settings, and OEM policies vary by version. Whitelisting is a specific cooperation arrangement, not a standard reward for reducing memory use. The App must still recover correctly after process death and cannot assume it always receives a low-memory callback first.

Business Organization

For each startup module, identify whether it is required, what it depends on, and which thread may execute it. The original four categories remain useful:

  • Required and expensive: Reduce the work first, then move allowed parts off the main thread. Define readiness for results needed by the first screen.
  • Required and inexpensive: Schedule it appropriately and account for cumulative cost.
  • Optional and expensive: Defer, load on demand, or cancel; avoid releasing a burst of all deferred work after the first frame.
  • Optional and inexpensive: Skip it during startup and load it when needed. This does not mean deleting useful functionality.

Staged, asynchronous, and deferred loading are different techniques; moving every expensive task to a worker does not finish the optimization.

Business Optimization

  1. Locate large bottlenecks and repeated work first, then check other entrypoints for regressions.
  2. Address technical debt within the scope of demonstrated startup problems.

The original business optimization case offers a checklist, but two claims need correction:

  • THREAD_PRIORITY_BACKGROUND = 10 is an Android thread-priority constant, not a maximum 10% CPU share. Scheduling groups, other runnable tasks, and device policy affect CPU allocation. Do not blindly lower the priority of a dependency the main thread urgently needs. See Process.
  • Each process in a multiprocess App has its own Application lifecycle. Gate particular SDK/business initialization by process; the system does not call Application.onCreate() only in the main process. Secondary processes still need their own required initialization.

Other transferable ideas include deferring nonessential updates and analytics; removing unused legacy, debug, duplicate, and SDK-demo work; bounding total concurrency; and caching repeated queries with expiration and account boundaries. After moving database or I/O work to a worker, verify that the UI no longer waits synchronously for it.

Reducing Activity Navigation Hierarchy

These are historical window-transition sketches. Whether and when a starting window appears depends on launch type and system version. A tap does not guarantee immediate display, and constructing an AppWindow object alone does not complete the handoff. Use the SplashScreen lifecycle when analyzing Android 12+.

Default App Startup Window Flow

Most Third-Party App Startup Flow

Worse Startup Flow

Even Worse: Disabled StartingWindow

Removing pointless intermediate Activities can shorten the path, while login, deep links, and restoration still need correct routing. The original “worse” labels describe an observed experience, not a platform ban on every SplashActivity.

Manufacturer Optimizations

The following categories retain the original system/OEM discussion. Except where tagged source is available, these are mostly observations from 2019 with unconfirmed coverage and current behavior. App acceptance must not depend on an undocumented vendor policy.

Startup Acceleration

Scheduling, performance hints, and frequency policy may help startup, subject to thermal limits, power, contention, and implementation. There is no cross-device guarantee of absolute resource preference.

The image contains CPU frequency, limits, and scheduling tracks without all values or policy settings. Dense colors do not prove that one App owns CPU, I/O, and GPU resources. Vendor SDKs need concrete device documentation; a performance request does not guarantee a big core.

PreFork

Android 10 (Q) introduced the USAP (Unspecialized App Process) pool. Processes are forked before being specialized for a particular App. This does not repeatedly recycle a process that previously ran another App.

Android 10 ZygoteProcess has a disabled default; device configuration determines enablement, and startup arguments must be eligible. Android 16 still checks policy and eligibility, with fallback to ordinary Zygote launch after a USAP communication failure. Ordinary Apps cannot require every Android 10+ device to use the pool.

The original process/memory snapshot follows verbatim, including its punctuation. It establishes those USAP entries in that capture, not a fixed pool size, fork duration, or universal memory cost.

Message Reordering

The original article lists this vendor direction without a public versioned implementation. Reordering must preserve lifecycle, synchronization-barrier, and dependency semantics. Posting arbitrary App messages to the front of the queue is not a general startup optimization.

Main Thread & Render Thread Acceleration

An OEM may adjust scheduling groups, CPU affinity, or performance hints during selected stages. Use traces and device policy to establish whether main/RenderThread work runs on big cores. Forced migration is not universal and can have thermal or contention costs.

Startup Prediction

A system may prewarm processes, code, or data based on usage history. The prediction policy is implementation-specific. A prewarmed process does not prove the target Activity exists or guarantee a hot launch. Separate prewarming hits and misses in measurements.

Background Keep-Alive

The system manages background processes according to importance and resource pressure, with additional OEM policies or user settings on some devices. Retention can avoid some initialization, but guarantees neither survival nor a hot next launch.

Background Restart

The original “seamless background restart” is an unversioned vendor observation, not a standard Android startup mechanism. Restarting can temporarily reclaim leaked memory without fixing the leak or repeated-crash cause. It guarantees neither preserved user state nor a hot next launch.

Memory Optimization

Memory-intensive launches may trigger reclaim, faults, and resource contention. The system can reclaim cache and, when necessary, low-priority processes; it does not always have to kill many Apps. Proactive vendor reclaim is one possible strategy whose benefit must be weighed against later restarts of reclaimed Apps.

Optimizing Startup Logic

System updates can shorten startup paths. The retained 2019 ViewRootImpl screenshot shows “Immediately start drawing when becoming visible”: removing an old new-Surface drawing delay, with a stated possible 5–10 ms first-draw delay at the time.

This is a particular system-branch change, not evidence that reducing any App’s doFrame count always improves startup. The commit-message estimate is not a current-device measurement.

OEM-Level Optimizations

The system and vendor categories above have different evidence and version boundaries; none substitutes for measuring the App on its supported devices.

References

  1. 都9102年了，Android 冷启动优化除了老三样还有哪些新招？
  2. App startup time
  3. 历时1年，上百万行代码！首次揭秘手淘全链路性能优化（上）
  4. 极客时间 ： Android 高手开发课
  5. Facebook-Redex
  6. 关于 Android 异步启动框架 alpha 的思考
  7. 支付宝 App 构建优化解析：通过安装包重排布优化 Android 端启动性能
  8. Redex 官网
  9. Redex 初探与 Interdex：Andorid 冷启动优化
  10. Android性能优化笔记（一）——启动优化

Other Locations for This Article

Since blog comments aren’t convenient for discussion, you can visit the Zhihu or Juejin versions of this article for likes and discussion:

知乎 - Android App 启动优化全记录

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal introduction and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Introduction : Contains personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation : A navigation guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows : Welcome self-recommendations and recommendations (WeChat private chat is fine).
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Comprehensive Record of Android App Startup Optimization
entry.content:
I’ve gathered the Android app startup optimization approaches I knew of when writing this article. Use them as a checklist: see what others have tried, then look for gaps in your own app. The details depend heavily on your business, so I won’t explain every implementation here. Once you find an approach that fits, follow up on that particular method.

I’ve also included some startup work done by system manufacturers, limited to the parts I know about. There are proprietary tricks I can’t cover here. Knowing what happens on the system side may still help, including when discussing whitelisting or SDK integration with a manufacturer.

Version note — reviewed October 13, 2026: This article was published in 2019. The original examples and categories remain, with updated startup definitions, measurement guidance, and splash-screen behavior. OEM whitelists, prediction, and restart strategies are historical leads rather than capabilities guaranteed on every device. Process-pool details use tagged Android 10 / 16 source.

First define the endpoint: the first frame, primary content, and interactivity are different milestones. Repeated Macrobenchmark journeys and Perfetto traces help locate main-thread, RenderThread, Binder, I/O, and GC costs; field monitoring should separate devices and versions. Baseline Profiles guide ART compilation, whereas Startup Profiles optimize DEX layout during the build.

Application Startup Overview

General Startup Workflow

Launching from an icon can involve system scheduling, process and component initialization, UI construction, and content loading. This older diagram shows only some of those stages:

  • SystemServer coordinates process, Activity, and window management. It requests a normal App process through Zygote or an eligible USAP; SystemServer does not directly fork the App itself.
  • The App process handles binding, Provider initialization, Application.onCreate(), and Activity work after its main Looper exists. Not every launch initializes all four component types; Services and Receivers depend on the entrypoint and workload.

The diagram places Application.onCreate outside its MainThread box. That does not mean it runs on another thread or that the main thread is created afterward. Network content and interactivity may still be pending after the first frame.

Cold vs. Hot Startup

The original two-way classification also needs warm starts. For common process/Activity states:

  • Cold: The App process needs to start, with application and UI initialization.
  • Warm: Typically, the process survives but the target Activity needs recreation, including onCreate().
  • Hot: An existing Activity and its UI state can be brought forward, though content restoration, layout, or drawing may still be needed.

Back and Home are not reliable switches between these categories. Activity behavior varies, background processes can be reclaimed, and a recent-task card does not prove that a process survives. Record process and Activity recreation, and use the measurement tool’s definitions. See startup states.

Measuring Startup Speed

Different teams have their own ways of measuring startup. What has always bothered me is deciding exactly when it ends. Complex screens need an observable completion condition, rather than whichever number looks smallest.

  • TTID: The destination screen’s first displayed frame. It may still contain placeholders or loading UI.
  • TTFD: The App signals primary-content readiness through reportFullyDrawn() or an appropriate ReportDrawn API. Its meaning depends on the App’s reporting condition; it does not automatically validate every interaction.
  • Interactivity or business completion: A usable list or completed login needs an explicit scenario and assertion. OCR can identify expected content, but visible text does not prove an image finished loading or a control is usable.

Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric reports timeToInitialDisplayMs and timeToFullDisplayMs. The latter ends with the relevant rendered frame containing or following the fully-drawn signal. Missing reporting is not a zero duration. Fix the release build, startup mode, compilation/Profile state, account and data state; repeat on physical devices, compare distributions, and keep traces. See Macrobenchmark setup.

adb shell am start -W remains useful for quick diagnosis, but its fields vary by version. Older output commonly has ThisTime/TotalTime/WaitTime; AOSP Android 16 prints LaunchState, TotalTime, and WaitTime, without ThisTime. WaitTime is neither content readiness nor pure App CPU time. A single command or screen recording does not replace a release benchmark.

The original Mobile Taobao case used automated, repeatable, CI-integrated measurement with OCR. Its OCR-service accuracy figure does not establish the accuracy of detecting this App’s startup endpoint.

App-Level Optimizations

1. Startup Window Optimization

A system StartingWindow, Android 12 SplashScreen, and an App’s own SplashActivity are different things. A splash improves waiting feedback; it does not remove initialization work.

  • For legacy preview windows, avoid unnecessary android:windowDisablePreview="true" settings that leave a blank wait. Keep the launch theme visually consistent with the destination.
  • Android 12 (API 31) introduces the standard system SplashScreen for cold and warm launches. Follow the migration guide; old background-image and preview-disable tricks are not universal modern solutions. An additional SplashActivity may produce two consecutive splashes.
  • Route directly to the destination where appropriate. Login, deep links, and advertising have their own constraints; measure them separately and preserve state restoration.

The original observations about WeChat, Zhihu, and TikTok did not provide reproducible versions or whitelist evidence. They cannot establish those apps’ current configuration or how often they start cold.

2. Thread Optimization

Control runnable work and dependency waits. Excess runnable threads can increase main-thread scheduling delay; Sleep may instead reflect locks, condition variables, Binder, or ordinary idle time.

  • Bound thread-pool concurrency and backlog according to task type. A pool alone does not prevent overload.
  • Follow locks to their owners. Moving a dependency to a worker and immediately waiting on the main thread can preserve the original blockage.
  • Distinguish main-thread-only initialization from work that can run elsewhere. mmkernel and Alpha are historical architecture references, not mandatory standard components.

3. System Schedule Optimization

Reduce unnecessary work on the startup critical path:

  • Consolidate repeated synchronous Binder queries and investigate AMS/ATMS or WMS lock waits. Binder calls are not synonymous with all system calls, nor does every call compete for the same lock.
  • Defer extra processes not needed for the first screen. They add initialization and contention, but the cost does not simply double. Preserve required process isolation.
  • Inspect Provider and Service initialization on their process’s main thread, including Providers initialized before Application.onCreate(). Remote Provider requests and Service Binder methods can instead run on Binder pool threads.
  • Move suitable work off the main thread with an explicit readiness dependency. Main-thread-only essentials still need to be shortened.

The old CPU capture shows interleaved work. Colors alone do not establish saturation or identify a single App as its cause:

The SystemServer image shows monitor contention and lock-owner threads. Its 93.633 ms selection is an observation window, not the sum of every lock wait or the full launch time. Follow the owners:

4. GC Optimization

Reduce unnecessary startup allocations, then inspect allocation volume, GC pauses, and main-thread waits. Counting collections alone is insufficient.

  • Avoid repeated large strings, serialization, and parsing content not needed for the first screen.
  • Reuse objects only with clear ownership and size limits. Pools can increase retained memory or lock contention.
  • Native allocation still consumes process memory and adds JNI, lifetime, and leak concerns. Moving code to Native is not a general way to eliminate memory cost.

Historical example: Alipay startup garbage-collection optimization.

5. IO Optimization

File access, page faults, decompression, databases, and other processes’ I/O can interact during startup. Record the file, actual bytes transferred, call count, thread, and duration; distinguish parsing CPU time from waiting. File size is not the amount read or written by an operation.

Required first-screen network requests can start asynchronously; defer nonessential requests. A blanket ban on startup networking does not fit online-content screens. Move suitable disk operations off the main thread without immediately waiting for them there.

This is the original table of observation dimensions: the 500 MB chat.db file and the 800 KB write are separate fields. Its KB/MB labels do not specify decimal versus binary units, so they cannot establish exact throughput. The durations and Buffer sizes are examples, not recommended settings.

These captures involve the system screen recorder and another App, not a controlled comparison of one process. Identify I/O waits using the selected thread state, blocking stack, and related events. Orange/red method slices are not automatically I/O, and the partial images alone do not establish low memory as the root cause.

Removing pointless intermediate Activities can shorten the path, while login, deep links, and restoration still need correct routing. The original “worse” labels describe an observed experience, not a platform ban on every SplashActivity.

OEM-Level Optimizations

The following categories retain the original system/OEM discussion. Except where tagged source is available, these are mostly observations from 2019 with unconfirmed coverage and current behavior. App acceptance must not depend on an undocumented vendor policy.

Startup Acceleration

Scheduling, performance hints, and frequency policy may help startup, subject to thermal limits, power, contention, and implementation. There is no cross-device guarantee of absolute resource preference.

The image contains CPU frequency, limits, and scheduling tracks without all values or policy settings. Dense colors do not prove that one App owns CPU, I/O, and GPU resources. Vendor SDKs need concrete device documentation; a performance request does not guarantee a big core.

PreFork

Android 10 (Q) introduced the USAP (Unspecialized App Process) pool. Processes are forked before being specialized for a particular App. This does not repeatedly recycle a process that previously ran another App.

Android 10 ZygoteProcess has a disabled default; device configuration determines enablement, and startup arguments must be eligible. Android 16 still checks policy and eligibility, with fallback to ordinary Zygote launch after a USAP communication failure. Ordinary Apps cannot require every Android 10+ device to use the pool.

The original process/memory snapshot follows verbatim, including its punctuation. It establishes those USAP entries in that capture, not a fixed pool size, fork duration, or universal memory cost.

Message Reordering

The original article lists this vendor direction without a public versioned implementation. Reordering must preserve lifecycle, synchronization-barrier, and dependency semantics. Posting arbitrary App messages to the front of the queue is not a general startup optimization.

Main Thread & Render Thread Acceleration

An OEM may adjust scheduling groups, CPU affinity, or performance hints during selected stages. Use traces and device policy to establish whether main/RenderThread work runs on big cores. Forced migration is not universal and can have thermal or contention costs.

Startup Prediction

A system may prewarm processes, code, or data based on usage history. The prediction policy is implementation-specific. A prewarmed process does not prove the target Activity exists or guarantee a hot launch. Separate prewarming hits and misses in measurements.

Background Keep-Alive

The system manages background processes according to importance and resource pressure, with additional OEM policies or user settings on some devices. Retention can avoid some initialization, but guarantees neither survival nor a hot next launch.

Background Restart

The original “seamless background restart” is an unversioned vendor observation, not a standard Android startup mechanism. Restarting can temporarily reclaim leaked memory without fixing the leak or repeated-crash cause. It guarantees neither preserved user state nor a hot next launch.

Memory Optimization

Memory-intensive launches may trigger reclaim, faults, and resource contention. The system can reclaim cache and, when necessary, low-priority processes; it does not always have to kill many Apps. Proactive vendor reclaim is one possible strategy whose benefit must be weighed against later restarts of reclaimed Apps.

Optimizing Startup Logic

System updates can shorten startup paths. The retained 2019 ViewRootImpl screenshot shows “Immediately start drawing when becoming visible”: removing an old new-Surface drawing delay, with a stated possible 5–10 ms first-draw delay at the time.

This is a particular system-branch change, not evidence that reducing any App’s doFrame count always improves startup. The commit-message estimate is not a current-device measurement.

References

  1. 都9102年了，Android 冷启动优化除了老三样还有哪些新招？
  2. App startup time
  3. 历时1年，上百万行代码！首次揭秘手淘全链路性能优化（上）
  4. 极客时间 ： Android 高手开发课
  5. Facebook-Redex
  6. 关于 Android 异步启动框架 alpha 的思考
  7. 支付宝 App 构建优化解析：通过安装包重排布优化 Android 端启动性能
  8. Redex 官网
  9. Redex 初探与 Interdex：Andorid 冷启动优化
  10. Android性能优化笔记（一）——启动优化

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
entry.content:
This is the ninth article in the Systrace series, primarily introducing the MainThread and RenderThread in Android Apps—commonly known as the Main Thread and Rendering Thread. This article examines their workflows from the perspective of Systrace and covers related topics: jank, software rendering, and dropped frame calculation.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Table of Contents

  • Series Article Index
  • Main Content
  • Creation of the Main Thread
  • Creation and Evolution of the Render Thread
  • Division of Labor: Main Thread vs. Render Thread
  • Main Thread and Render Thread in Games
  • Main Thread and Render Thread in Flutter
  • Performance
  • References
  • Attachments
  • Other Addresses
  • About Me && Blog

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness

Main Content

Version note — reviewed October 13, 2026: The original article and captures date from 2019; their exact device builds and Flutter SDK versions were not recorded. The View and process-entry explanations below use AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 / android-10.0.0_r1, with HWUI synchronization checked against android-16.0.0_r1. The old Flutter thread and Skia diagrams no longer describe all versions; that section includes the Flutter 3.27 and 3.29 changes.

The same topic continues in Choreographer Rendering in Perfetto and MainThread and RenderThread. The old captures show the relative positions of the UI thread, RenderThread, and SurfaceFlinger; the newer approach follows thread scheduling, FrameTimeline, and Buffer flow.

Start with the target frame rate, display refresh rate, and deadlines, then follow dependencies through the main thread, RenderThread, GPU, and presentation. Input, Animation, Insets Animation, Traversal, and Commit are separate doFrame phases; each need not have work on every frame. Scheduling, Binder, locks, and Buffer waits can also delay a frame.

Here is one hardware-accelerated View frame during list scrolling. Focus on the UI Thread and RenderThread rows. This is a concrete example, not a mandatory path for every View frame, game, or software-rendered window.

Read this capture in the following order:

  1. The main thread is waiting because it has no runnable work. Input and other events can also wake it; it does not wait exclusively for Vsync.
  2. After a frame has been requested, a Vsync event reaches FrameDisplayEventReceiver.onVsync. It posts an asynchronous message to its Looper, which later runs run() / doFrame(); receiving Vsync does not itself complete drawing.
  3. Due Input callbacks run. Not all input delivery goes through this batching phase.
  4. Due Animation callbacks run. Android 10/16 also have Insets Animation before Traversal, which this image does not separately show.
  5. Traversal performs Measure, Layout, and Draw as needed. Updating View drawing records can synchronize with RenderThread. Commit follows later in doFrame; this partial image does not establish whether it has callbacks.
  6. The main thread waits inside the synchronization call until RenderThread releases it. It can then overlap with later rendering when conditions permit. IdleHandler execution depends on queue-idle conditions, not merely on a frame ending.
  7. In this GL/EGL capture, RenderThread obtains a Buffer and submits rendering work. queueBuffer passes a Buffer and its associated fence; it does not prove GPU completion or display. SurfaceFlinger still handles the layer according to scheduling, readiness, and composition policy.

The old annotation about a “finished” Buffer is shorthand. Modern HWUI can use different graphics backends, and Android 16 View Surface paths also involve BLASTBufferQueue. CPU submission, GPU completion, composition, and presentation remain distinct stages.

For the Choreographer portion, see Android’s Choreographer Rendering Mechanism. This article focuses on thread creation and responsibilities, followed by games and Flutter.

Creation of the Main Thread

An ordinary Android App process is derived from Zygote through a path involving fork. A process and a thread are different objects: the initial execution thread in the child continues runtime initialization and enters the App entrypoint. The forked process is not itself a Java Thread object.

ActivityThread does not extend Thread. It manages framework transactions on the App’s main thread. ActivityThread.main() prepares the main Looper and creates ActivityThread and its Handler H. Other Handlers and native Looper callbacks also run there; H does not own every App message.

Creation of ActivityThread

In the ordinary App branch of Android 10 ZygoteConnection, the path is ZygoteInit.zygoteInit() → RuntimeInit.applicationInit() → findStaticMain(), followed by android.app.ActivityThread.main(). The original childZygoteInit() excerpt belongs to the child-Zygote branch, not ordinary App startup.

Here is the complete method from ZygoteInit.java, android-10.0.0_r1. findStaticMain() is in RuntimeInit.java at the same tag.

The corresponding ActivityThread.main() includes the startSeq parsing missing from the original excerpt. These are framework internals, not standalone code to paste into an App.

attach() registers the App-side interface through AMS’s attachApplication; application binding is handled afterward. The main thread is now up and running, processing work inside Looper.loop() rather than waiting for main() to return. The final exception makes an unexpected main-loop exit explicit.

Functions of ActivityThread

Activity lifecycle callbacks, common Service lifecycle callbacks, and default broadcast delivery usually run on their process’s main thread. Android 10’s H contains these internal message constants, among others; they are not stable SDK interfaces:

Activity client transactions also pass through EXECUTE_TRANSACTION / TransactionExecutor. The process already exists before these messages execute; H does not create it. Nor does this list mean every component method runs on the main thread: remote Service Binder calls and cross-process ContentProvider queries use Binder pool threads, and a receiver can be registered with a particular Handler. See Processes and threads.

Creation and Evolution of the Render Thread

HWUI introduced RenderThread in Android 5.0 (API 21) to move part of rendering work off the main thread. View GPU hardware acceleration already existed in Android 3.0 (API 11), however; pre-Lollipop does not mean CPU-only rendering.

Software Rendering

View hardware acceleration is enabled by default for targetSdkVersion >= 14, with configuration at several levels whose capabilities differ. This attribute fragment in <application> disables the application default; an Activity can override it:

Software View drawing rasterizes on the CPU and submits through the window Surface. That window need not use the usual HWUI RenderThread path, but other windows or embedded components may still use HWUI in the same process. A software layer on one View also does not disable acceleration for the entire window. To identify the current drawing Canvas, use Canvas.isHardwareAccelerated(). See the hardware acceleration controls.

This old capture shows lockAsync, drawing, and Buffer submission on the main thread. Its selected 21.064 ms interval also contains a fence wait; the entire wall duration is not CPU rasterization time. Two different captures cannot quantify a universal slowdown from disabling acceleration. Extra main-thread work or waiting does reduce time available for other messages.

Hardware-Accelerated Rendering

The Draw phase records or reuses DisplayLists and synchronizes with RenderThread. Recording, including View.onDraw(), still costs main-thread time. RenderThread can continue after the main thread is released, but that release is conditional, as described below.

Rendering Thread Initialization

Distinguish creating the thread from initializing a window Surface. Android 9 constructs a native RenderProxy from ThreadedRenderer, and that proxy obtains RenderThread::getInstance(). RenderThread can therefore exist before the first Draw. The initializeIfNeeded() call in ViewRootImpl concerns renderer / Surface initialization; it is not the unique point where the native thread is born.

This complete draw() method comes from ThreadedRenderer.java, android-9.0.0_r1. The original attributed it to android/graphics/HardwareRenderer.java and mixed signatures from different versions; the excerpt now uses one tag throughout.

It updates the DisplayList, registers animation nodes and callbacks, then reaches RenderProxy.cpp through JNI:

This is not a fire-and-forget notification. In Android 9 DrawFrameTask.cpp, postAndWait() posts to RenderThread and waits on a condition variable. syncFrameState() determines whether the UI thread may be released early. Otherwise, release occurs after later drawing or fence waiting. Android 16 retains this conditional structure. A long main-thread synchronization interval calls for inspecting what RenderThread is doing or waiting for.

dequeueBuffer, flush commands, and eglSwapBuffersWithDamageKHR label this GL/EGL path. They are not universal backend markers, and their end times do not directly identify GPU completion or presentation.

Division of Labor: Main Thread vs. Render Thread

For a typical hardware-accelerated View pipeline, the main thread handles messages, input, common animations, layout, and drawing-record updates. RenderThread synchronizes the RenderNode tree and drives backend rendering. Both are CPU threads; neither thread’s wall duration is itself GPU time. Window or SurfaceControl operations can also involve the main thread in system graphics interactions, so “the main thread never interacts with SurfaceFlinger” is too broad.

A DisplayList records drawing operations. RenderNode also carries properties such as transforms; the two are not interchangeable concepts. This division provides several benefits:

  1. Unchanged content can reuse drawing records without repeating the View recording work.
  2. Node properties such as translation and scale can reuse content when applicable; content changes may still require recording again.
  3. The backend can optimize while preserving ordering, clipping, and blending semantics. It cannot necessarily draw all text in one batch.
  4. RenderThread can handle rendering and supported animations, while business logic and ordinary View updates still need the main thread.
  5. When synchronization permits, the two threads can overlap. The main thread is not guaranteed never to wait for RenderThread.

The original RenderThread reference remains historical reading; use the tagged AOSP sources above for specific branches.

Main Thread and Render Thread in Games

Game engines often submit Buffers through their own Surface and rendering pipeline instead of the View HWUI path. The Android main thread still handles lifecycle, windows, input, and some plugin calls. Game logic, rendering submission, and worker tasks are divided according to the engine and its configuration.

The following Honor of Kings example was labeled 30 fps in the original article. It describes that historical capture, not the game’s current frame-rate options, the display refresh rate, or SurfaceFlinger’s execution frequency.

The Android UI thread and UnityMain are distinct in this image. A thread name alone does not establish that it only renders or that it runs almost all game logic. The method Trace below shows main-thread input dispatch entering the game’s View path. It does not show the full subsequent engine workload, GPU execution, or presentation; proximity alone cannot associate a particular input with a particular frame.

Main Thread and Render Thread in Flutter

This 2019 Flutter capture has separate .ui and .gpu threads alongside Android’s platform thread. The .gpu thread performs raster work on the CPU; it is not the hardware GPU. Flutter content follows its Engine pipeline rather than ordinary View HWUI drawing. This is not simply a consequence of using Skia—Android HWUI also uses Skia. An App embedding native Views can still have an HWUI RenderThread.

The thread diagram is outdated: Flutter 3.29 merges UI and platform threads by default on Android and iOS, running Dart UI work on the platform thread. Raster work remains a separate responsibility; the whole engine has not become single-threaded. Do not require a distinct old-style .ui track when reading a new capture. Slow platform-thread plugin calls can now delay Dart UI work on that same thread. See the Flutter architecture overview.

Flutter still uses Android for windows, input, and frame scheduling. The class in the old method capture is VsyncWaiter, not the original text’s VsyncView. Flutter 3.29.3 VsyncWaiter.java also uses Choreographer.postFrameCallback(); its callback forwards timing through flutterJNI.onVsync().

Shipping the rendering engine with the App permits SDK updates independently of Android OS updates. It does not automatically give every App the newest Skia or prove that a screen is faster than its native counterpart. This presentation slide explains the Skia architecture of its time, not a workload-specific benchmark.

The backend changed too: Flutter 3.27 made Impeller the default on Android API 29+. The official documentation describes fallback to the legacy OpenGL renderer on older Android versions or devices without Vulkan support. “Flutter always uses Skia → OpenGL” is therefore no longer an adequate model. Record the Flutter version, Android version, and actual backend. See Impeller.

The Framework / Engine division remains useful: the Dart framework builds and lays out the UI and records drawing work; the Engine rasterizes and submits the scene. The Engine box containing only Skia below is historical, not a complete diagram for newer versions.

When UI updates are needed, the framework requests a frame. Platform timing drives animation, build, layout, and paint work, then the scene reaches the raster pipeline. Not every Layer necessarily becomes a new texture. GPU submission still precedes Android Buffer, fence, and composition handling rather than directly displaying pixels.

This last diagram is also historical. “GPU Thread” means a raster CPU thread, and the top “GPU → Vsync” arrow should not be read as Flutter waiting directly for GPU completion to begin a frame. The bottom already says GL or Vulkan, not OpenGL alone. Account for both merged threads and Impeller when applying it to newer versions.

Performance

Slow queries, computation, or synchronous waits on the main thread delay input and drawing. Separate two kinds of failure:

  1. Jank: Refresh intervals at 60 / 90 / 120 Hz are about 16.67 / 11.11 / 8.33 ms, but lateness depends on the target frame rate and actual deadlines. Main-thread and RenderThread work includes synchronization and overlap; adding their wall durations is not a dropped-frame test. GPU work or system composition may also delay presentation. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, Perfetto FrameTimeline can compare expected and actual timing when the relevant data was captured.
  2. ANR: Input, broadcasts, Services, and other cases have their own timeout rules. An arbitrary message taking a few seconds does not always produce a dialog, and dialog display depends on context and policy. Inspect the ANR type, logs, and blocking dependencies; see Diagnose and fix ANRs.

Both harm the user experience and need continuing attention. ANR stacks help, but a late capture may miss the original blockage. Intermittent jank needs system Trace analysis and, where useful, method sampling. Instrumented tools such as TraceView perturb timing, so their durations are not automatically representative of an uninstrumented run. Understanding the two threads and their dependencies is a central motivation for this series.

These three articles cover further causes. System scheduling and resource contention can contribute too; first establish where the delay occurs.

  1. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - Methodology
  2. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - System Side
  3. Overview of Jank Causes in Android - App Side

References

  1. https://juejin.im/post/5a9e01c3f265da239d48ce32
  2. http://www.cocoachina.com/articles/35302
  3. https://juejin.im/post/5b7767fef265da43803bdc65
  4. http://gityuan.com/2019/06/15/flutter_ui_draw/
  5. https://developer.android.google.cn/guide/components/processes-and-threads

Attachments

The original repository still contains the Honor of Kings and Flutter Systrace HTML ZIPs and corresponding method Trace files. Both ZIPs can be extracted and read. Compatibility of the old HTML viewer with modern Chrome has not been verified; choose a tool supporting the actual legacy Systrace or ART method Trace format. A method .trace file is not automatically a Perfetto system Trace.

Download the article’s attachments

Other Addresses

Please visit the Zhihu or Juejin pages for this article for comments or likes:
Juejin - Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - Input Interpretation
entry.content:
This is the sixth article in the Systrace series, primarily providing a brief introduction to Input in Systrace. It covers the Input workflow, how Input information is represented in Systrace, and how to combine Input info to analyze related performance issues.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Version note — reviewed 2026-10-13: The 2019 screenshots and original dumpsys data are retained, with AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 as the historical reference and Android 16/Perfetto updates. Queue/trace names are not stable interfaces across every system. Both public attachment traces were inspected as text; no device experiment was rerun.

Table of Contents

  • Series Article Index
  • Main Content
  • Input in Systrace
  • InputDown Event Workflow in SystemServer
  • InputDown Event Workflow in App
  • Key Knowledge Points and Processes
  • Input Refresh and Vsync
  • Input Debug Information
  • References
  • Attachments
  • Other Addresses
  • About Me && Blog

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

Main Content

Read this with Perfetto 5: Choreographer and Perfetto 7: MainThread/RenderThread. Locate system entry, target selection, InputChannel publication, app receipt/handling, and completion acknowledgment, then correlate any required frame with presentation. Acknowledging input and displaying its result are different boundaries.

The Choreographer article distinguishes Looper message dispatch from native FD callbacks. Readable input channels can enter Java through the native Looper, so input is not always an ordinary Handler Message. This article focuses on touch MotionEvent; KeyEvent has different focus, interception, and fallback paths. Home/Back are not universally ordinary keys delivered to the current app.

A typical touch path is:

  1. The controller samples according to device policy and the driver reports kernel events. Sampling, reporting, and Reader scheduling frequencies need not match one-to-one.
  2. EventHub reads events; InputReader’s device mappers process coordinates/actions and notify the dispatch chain.
  3. InputDispatcher selects connections using event type, display, touch regions, gesture state, and policy. It does not broadcast to all apps registered for input.
  4. The app handles input immediately or in batches as appropriate. UI changes may schedule/coalesce frame work; one input does not guarantee one new frame.

Time runs left to right, but compare synchronized event/slice boundaries. Cross-thread order alone does not prove causality: check channels, sequences, stacks, and scheduling. I hope this graphical view helps you locate code execution in the larger flow.

Input in Systrace

This historical single-pointer Launcher scroll normally starts with DOWN, continues through MOVE, and ends with UP or CANCEL. Multi-pointer gestures also use POINTER_DOWN/POINTER_UP; Down-Move-Up is not every possible stream.

InputReader and InputDispatcher are native system_server threads in this capture. Interpret the other annotations separately:

  1. Reader processes EventHub data; touch uses Motion notifications and keys use Key notifications.
