  2. Dispatcher selects targets and maintains dispatch state. Names and trace points are version/vendor dependent.
  3. oq: counts outbound entries for a Connection, which may represent a window or monitor. An app can have multiple windows/connections.
  4. wq: tracks successfully published entries awaiting finished-protocol processing, not only events for which business code must return true.
  5. aq:pending counts queued ViewRootImpl input not yet taken for processing, not all in-flight input.
  6. deliverInputEvent tracks app delivery/processing, not the kernel wakeup instant. Inspect sched_wakeup/sched_switch separately.
  7. The old viewer’s Input Response / Rendering Response are interaction-analysis groupings, not direct universal hardware touch-to-display measurements.
  8. Release can continue into fling when gesture/velocity conditions allow; UP does not always cause fling.

DOWN comes first below. MOVE batching, history, and resampling materially affect timing and are not negligible differences.

InputDown Event Workflow in SystemServer

The image shows Reader work, Dispatcher scheduling, and connection-counter changes. Colors/counts guide investigation; select matching events and read timestamps for exact delays.

InputDown Event Workflow in App

An ordinary DOWN generally does not follow MOVE’s batching delay and can be delivered once its channel is readable. This is not determined by whether the system “has VSync.” A busy main thread, Runnable scheduling delay, or another input-stage wait can still postpone handling.

App’s Pending Queue

“Back to zero means finished” is too strong. Android 9 ViewRootImpl.doProcessInputEvents() decrements the count after dequeuing and before calling deliverInputEvent(). At zero, an event can still be processing, awaiting an asynchronous stage, or not yet acknowledged. A thread blocked before reading the native channel need not first build up this Java queue.

Main Thread Processing Input Events

The stack shows native poll → InputEventReceiver → ViewRootImpl stages → DecorView/Activity/View dispatch. Other event types can traverse different stages; instrumented method duration is not unqualified normal-runtime cost.

Key Knowledge Points and Processes

The normal path is Reader notification → Dispatcher inbound/pending → target selection and per-connection outbound → successful publication into wait → app handling → finished sequence/handled response over the input channel → Dispatcher completion policy and removal or continuation.

Events and acknowledgments primarily use the InputChannel socket protocol, not a per-touch Binder callback into Java InputManagerService. handled=false can be a valid result, and finished does not mean the UI has redrawn. Broken-connection cleanup can also reduce queues, so read connection state alongside counts.

InputReader

Using AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 as the reference, EventHub watches input-device FDs and device changes; mappers process RawEvents. Its 256-entry buffer stores RawEvents, not 256 gestures, a sampling rate, or a universal constant. Touch follows NotifyMotionArgs/MotionEntry; Key follows NotifyKeyArgs/KeyEntry.

The historical diagram includes key-specific policy such as interceptKeyBeforeQueueing, not a mandatory path for every touch:

Here is Android 9’s complete loopOnce() method. Notice that blocking reads and listener flush both happen outside the Reader lock. It remains system source, not a standalone app example:

InputDispatcher

Reader notifications may enqueue and wake Dispatcher; filtering and other wakeup sources also exist. The selected Runnable interval below records TID 25669, shown as InputReader, as its waker. That is evidence for this occurrence, not every Dispatcher wakeup.

Android 9 Dispatcher handles Key and Motion separately. Keys commonly involve focus and key policy; touch also involves hit testing, gesture targets, split/cancel behavior, and other conditions. The diagram below explicitly uses dispatchKeyLocked, findFocusedWindowTargetsLocked, and publishKeyEvent; it is not the exact touch path.

The following pseudocode describes the queue boundaries:

That version sets deliveryTime while attempting publication in startDispatchCycleLocked(). It is not the hardware sample time, nor should the first dispatchOnce entry time be treated as every later delivery time despite intervening waits. Backpressure such as WOULD_BLOCK and connection errors require separate handling. Policy commands can run from a command queue at appropriate lock boundaries.

InboundQueue

notifyKey and notifyMotion may enqueue after their respective checks. Removing an entry into mPendingEvent reduces iq, while that event may still wait for a target or continue dispatch. iq=0 does not mean all system input work is finished.

OutboundQueue

Each Connection has entries awaiting publication. One event can have multiple eligible targets or be filtered; an app can own multiple windows, and monitors have separate purposes. The selected counter below belongs to StatusBar, with value 1, not the entire Launcher input stream.

WaitQueue

After successful publication, Dispatcher moves the entry from outbound to wait. App finishInputEvent(event, handled) sends a native InputConsumer acknowledgment; Dispatcher processes it by connection/sequence and retires the matching entry, with fallback policy where applicable. See InputTransport and InputEventReceiver.

Sustained wait growth is a clue, with possible causes including scheduling, app work, MOVE batching, ACK transport/processing, and connection problems. Queue length is neither duration nor an ANR criterion. This next crop belongs to a separate sample.tencent.mat... list trace: the selection spans 32.276 ms, and one counter is 8. It is not the Launcher trace, nor proof that all eight entries have yet to enter the app.

Overall Logic

This Gityuan diagram includes KeyboardInputMapper/notifyKey. It is a historical reading aid, not the exact Android 16 path for every touch.

Input Refresh and Vsync

Does a higher touch sampling rate always help? First, separate touch sampling, reporting/dispatch cadence, display refresh rate, and actual app frame rate. 120Hz is about 8.33ms; 160Hz is 6.25ms. The original 8ms for 120Hz was approximate, and these are not universal current-device specifications.

I labeled this device 160Hz in the capture at the time, but Reader execution spacing is also affected by report batching and scheduling. Temporary WaitQueue accumulation does not mean the app never consumes input. Batched MOVE may be consumed in Choreographer’s INPUT phase against frame time; DOWN/UP cannot be generalized to the same rule.

Multiple samples are not simply reduced to the latest with all others discarded. The MotionEvent batching contract allows ACTION_MOVE to contain historical samples, read before current coordinates. Android 9 InputConsumer.consumeBatch/consumeSamples() selects the appropriate sample-time range, builds MotionEvent history, and maintains sequence chains for acknowledgment. Enabled resampling can also estimate positions relative to frame time.

A 60Hz display therefore does not prove 120Hz touch is sufficient, nor does 90Hz require exactly 180Hz touch. Higher sampling can reduce some waits or provide finer data, with processing/power costs. Alternating groups of two/three samples do not themselves prove visible jitter. Compare event times, history/resampling, presentation, and end-to-end latency rather than requiring an exact 2:1 ratio.

Input Debug Information

This command produces a lot of output. I picked out the Device, InputReader, and InputDispatcher sections below from the device snapshot I took at the time. Fields/formats depend on the system, and this is not a continuous record of an interaction. Interpret unknowns, empty fields, and sentinel values according to their meaning.

Device Info

Paths, descriptors, IDs, and mapping files belong to this snapshot. event6 is not every phone’s touch node, and these illustrative IDs alone do not identify a manufacturer.

Input Reader Status

Raw (660, 1338) and cooked (659.389, 1337.401) reflect coordinate mapping/calibration, not identical coordinate spaces. PhysicalWidth here is explicitly in px, not millimeters. unknown range is not a zero range. The external-stylus 9223372036854775807 values are old-state sentinels such as no active deadline, not real input times.

InputDispatcher Status

Distinguish focused application from focused window, per-display touch targets, window entries, monitors, and connections. MonitoringChannels is not the list of ordinary channels for every window, and this is an excerpt. DispatchFrozen describes input dispatch state, not the later cached-app freezer.

This snapshot has three waiting MOVE entries. age measures from event time to dump time; wait measures from that entry’s deliveryTime to dump time. Neither is total visual response latency. Its 5000.000ms is a reported dispatch timeout, not every device’s or every ANR type’s universal limit. The official input-dispatch ANR guide describes a default of 5 seconds and cases such as no focused window. Correlate timeout logs, targets, and blocking causes; three outstanding events do not themselves establish an ANR.

Continuing on Newer Versions

AOSP Android 16 InputDispatcher has a Perfetto input-event tracing backend, but that tag gates it on userdebug/eng builds and the relevant feature flag. Do not promise that ordinary user builds can obtain android.input.inputevent by toggling one setting.

With the required ATrace data, Perfetto’s android.input module can break down send, receive, handling, and ACK round trips. Structured android.input.inputevent is a separate source with its own fields; neither is guaranteed present. Frame associations may be missing or speculative. ACK round trip is not complete physical touch-to-display latency, and unavailable data is not zero latency.

References

Portions of this article reference Gityuan’s blog. These articles provide deep dives into code details for those interested after finishing this piece.

  1. http://gityuan.com/2016/12/11/input-reader/
  2. http://gityuan.com/2016/12/10/input-manager/
  3. http://gityuan.com/2016/12/17/input-dispatcher/
  4. https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/29386642

Attachments

The directory contains trace_input_blog_launcher_scroll.html.zip and trace_input_blog_list_jank.html.zip, respectively the Launcher and list-jank cases. Both readable archives contain HTML with an old viewer, process dumps, and ftrace data, targeting different apps. Current-browser compatibility of the embedded viewer was not tested here. A tool supporting legacy Systrace data can also be used to import and inspect the events:
Download Systrace attachments for this article

Other Addresses

For comments or likes, please visit the Zhihu or Juejin pages for this article:
Juejin - Systrace Basics - Input Interpretation

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro: Includes personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Welcome to recommend projects/articles.
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Analysis of 'Zombie Animations' in the Android Background
entry.content:
This article records a 2019 issue: animation work continued after the app’s UI was no longer visible. However, some apps continue to run “zombie animations”—animations that are completely invisible to the user yet consume precious CPU cycles and battery. When users discover this, the result is often a manual kill, an OS-level background restriction, or an outright uninstallation.

This issue can be easy to miss. In the original investigation, I used Systrace after opening apps and returning home, capturing traces while swiping between launcher pages. Some departed apps still fired callbacks. A reproduction should record versions, operations, and visibility; opening many apps is not itself a diagnostic requirement or proof.

Here, “zombie animations” means updates that continue when their UI is invisible and the feature no longer needs them. Many paths can schedule animation work through Choreographer. Investigate the actual stack, playback state, and library version. A live process is not necessarily free to consume CPU indefinitely; modern systems can freeze eligible cached processes.

Version note — technical review, 2026-10-13: These cases and screenshots are from 2019, not tests of current NetEase News, QQ Music, or Lottie versions. Updates below cover Lottie Android 6.7.1, lifecycle/window visibility, and the cached-app freezer supported from Android 11 / API 30. Complete original traces, app versions, and power measurements are unavailable; CPU screenshots are not battery measurements.

Let’s look at two real-world examples to understand the technical cause and the fix. If you are a developer, I highly recommend checking your app for this behavior—fix it if it’s there, celebrate if it’s not.

Case 1: NetEase News

At the time, I used NetEase News, returned home, and captured a Systrace while swiping the launcher. I could see that the app’s UI had left the foreground. The screenshot directly shows repeated doFrame activity in com.netease.newsreader.activity, PID 30962:

The selected frame contains animation work without visible input/traversal intervals. That alone does not establish background state: a foreground frame with no input or View updates can look similar. Chrome-related tracks are also present; not all process activity can be assigned to one animation library.

The CPU Slices selection spans about 3.636 s. Its reader.activity row totals 422.163 ms over 680 execution slices and appears first in the visible ranking. Those 680 occurrences are not animations, callback invocations, or dropped frames. A name-based grouping also needs thread/process attribution. CPU time is not a direct energy measurement, and the whole row cannot automatically be attributed to one animation callback.

I then checked MethodTrace and found ValueAnimator entering com.airbnb.lottie...onAnimationUpdate, updating layers and issuing invalidations. This identifies a Lottie update path to investigate. It supplies no exact library version, object identity, or visibility state, and cannot establish a defect in every Lottie version. Instrumentation also affects timing.

Case 2: QQ Music

Next I tried QQ Music: launch it, return home, and capture while swiping the launcher again. The historical com.tencent.qqmusic process, PID 19330, shows repeated frame activity:

The method trace contains three ValueAnimator/Lottie update branches within one AnimationHandler interval. Multiple updates merit investigation, but without object identities the branches do not prove exactly three distinct animation instances. They also do not establish a more severe battery impact than another app.

The zoomed 10.73 ms belongs to the selected obfuscated com.airbnb.lottie.aw.b method in this instrumented recording. It is not a power figure or an unqualified production-cost measurement.

Ordinary property animations can exhibit unwanted continued work too. The next stack includes ObjectAnimator, View.setRotation, invalidation, and later TraversalRunnable/performTraversals. It contradicts a universal rule that such animations never trigger traversal.

Root Cause

The investigation is about animation work still being requested and advanced after its UI may be invisible or its feature no longer needs it. Distinguish missing app stop intent, historical library visibility handling, ancestor/window changes, recycling, and late asynchronous loading that restarts work.

Choreographer runs registered callbacks; it does not uniformly delete all input/draw work while retaining animation merely because an app is backgrounded. No traversal slice only means no corresponding View work was observed there, not that every Surface, WebView, or native renderer has stopped. Background audio playback in QQ Music is a separate function: pausing decorative animation does not mean stopping all background work.

Modern system boundary: Android 11 / API 30 supports the cached-app freezer. On supported, enabled devices, eligible cached processes cannot perform CPU work while frozen. Not every background process immediately reaches that state, and freezing does not replace correct playback-state management. Record process state rather than equating existence, invisibility, and execution.

Development Recommendation

The original report was Lottie issue #987, opened 2018-10-31 and closed 2019-02-03. It described looping animations continuing while the View was hidden or the Activity paused, and questioned cleanup based only on detachment. This is a historical report; its closure alone does not prove every version or integration is fixed.

Do not copy the old onVisibilityChanged() subclass patch blindly. It omitted the state field and could clear a remembered resume flag on a second invisible notification. The visibility parameter alone also cannot represent host lifecycle, ancestor/window state, or a user’s explicit pause. Adding it over the library’s own state handling can duplicate control.

What Lottie 6.7.1 Already Handles

This review checked release 6.7.1, pinned to commit c8addcb776f6cd940abaf55ae6b471e55b626eb9:

  • LottieDrawable.setVisible() pauses a running animator when becoming invisible and remembers a later resume action. It explicitly avoids erasing that intent on repeated invisible notifications.
  • LottieAnimationView uses View/ImageView visibility propagation. Its pauseAnimation() delegates to the Drawable and disables autoplay; current handling is not limited to the old report’s detach cleanup.
  • LottieValueAnimator.pauseAnimation() removes its Choreographer callback. Drawable pause also clears deferred composition tasks and, while invisible, pending resume actions. Not currently running does not always mean no pending playback request.

These are implementation facts for the checked version, not a guarantee that upgrading makes every integration correct. Visibility propagation also depends on system and target-SDK compatibility paths; see Android 16 ImageView. Standalone Drawables, custom containers, Compose, and other versions require checking their own integration paths.

Separate Playback Intent from Temporary Suspension

Pausing an unneeded, invisible decorative animation is usually appropriate. Do not mechanically stop everything in onPause and restart everything in onResume: a paused Activity may remain visible in multi-window. Visibility-based work commonly follows onStart/onStop; Fragment work should follow its View lifecycle and release references/listeners when that View is destroyed.

Use one owner to decide whether animation should continue:

  1. Does the feature/user still request playback, or has the animation completed or been cancelled?
  2. Do the host lifecycle, View/ancestor/window visibility, and attachment state permit it? isShown() alone does not prove actual pixel visibility or detect every occlusion.
  3. Is the composition ready? Re-evaluate after loading, recycling, and navigation so obsolete load callbacks cannot revive unwanted playback.

This is a function that applies an existing decision, not a complete lifecycle component. Compute shouldAnimate from those states and update it when they change. Natural completion must also clear playback intent so a later update does not restart a finished one-shot animation:

pauseAnimation() retains the current position; resumeAnimation() continues from it. Starting over, completion, and cancellation are distinct product decisions. Do not use isAnimating() as the sole representation of intent or call resume unconditionally. Use the main thread and verify the installed Lottie version’s event semantics.

Verifying the Fix

Fix app/library/system versions and test Home, navigation, ancestor hiding, window invisibility, list recycling, and composition loading that completes in the background. Returning to visibility should resume only what is still requested; user-paused or completed animations must stay stopped. Test multi-window and picture-in-picture according to the product’s rules.

Compare the target thread’s scheduled CPU execution, animation stacks, and callback counts over equivalent operations and intervals. Confirm that unwanted self-reposting stops; evaluate energy separately with controlled power measurements. No animation slice, an uncaptured thread, or a frozen process alone does not prove that lifecycle handling is correct.

Article Discussion

Original Chinese discussion pages: Zhihu and Juejin.

About Me && Blog

I welcome discussion with fellow developers:

  1. About me: personal introduction and contact information.
  2. Blog navigation.
  3. Android performance resources: recommendations are welcome.
  4. Android performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One person can go faster; a group can go further.

entry.title: Detailed Explanation of Android Rendering Mechanism Based on Choreographer
entry.content:
This article introduces Choreographer, a class that app developers rarely encounter but is crucial in the Android Framework rendering pipeline. It covers the background of Choreographer‘s introduction, an overview, source code analysis, its relationship with MessageQueue, its use in APM, and optimization ideas from mobile manufacturers.

Choreographer coordinates animations, some input processing, and View updates with display timing. It requests frame callbacks when work is pending rather than unconditionally waking the app on every physical refresh. A 60Hz display, common in 2019, has an interval of about 16.67ms; 90Hz and 120Hz correspond to about 11.11ms and 8.33ms. Modern devices can also change refresh rates. A timely callback does not mean the image has been presented: RenderThread, GPU, composition, and display work remain. Understanding this flow helps explain Message, Handler, Looper, MessageQueue, Measure, Layout, and Draw.

Version note — reviewed 2026-10-13: Historical excerpts use AOSP android-10.0.0_r1 Choreographer as a reference and retain the 2019 screenshots. Updates cover Android 16 and API 24/31/33 observation interfaces. Source excerpts are not standalone compilable apps; vendor implementations and capture configurations are incomplete. Obsolete private interfaces are marked below.

This is the eighth article in the Systrace series, providing a brief introduction to Choreographer within Systrace.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  12. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  18. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

Essence of the Main Thread Mechanism

This article connects to Perfetto 5: Choreographer-based rendering flow. Looper dispatches Messages; MessageQueue does not itself execute app code. Native polling can also process file-descriptor events while obtaining the next message, including display events. “Every main-thread operation is a Message” is therefore an oversimplification.

In Perfetto, correlate the frame with the main thread, RenderThread, GPU, and SurfaceFlinger. On Android 12 / API 31 or later, with the relevant data captured, FrameTimeline expected/actual tracks help locate missed deadlines. Missing tracks do not mean zero jank. Investigate Sleeping, Runnable, and Running separately; a slice’s wall duration is not CPU time. These historical images show spaced dispatches, and method instrumentation itself affects timing.

MethodTrace Illustration

Systrace Illustration

Evolution

Choreographer arrived in Android 4.1 / API 16 to coordinate work with display timing. Both images below already contain Choreographer.doFrame and RenderThread. They cannot prove behavior before Choreographer existed. They show a different capture with denser rendering and waits; its precise configuration is unavailable.

MethodTrace Illustration

The crop includes RenderThread dequeueBuffer intervals, but does not establish the sole bottleneck or a fixed consumption rate. Buffer availability, consumer progress, and fences require investigation; SurfaceFlinger does not simply consume a “Front Buffer” at an invariant rate.

Consistent presentation matters, but stable 50fps is not universally smoother than fluctuating 40–60fps. On a fixed 60Hz display, 50fps itself cannot be presented uniformly in whole refresh intervals. VSync coordination and buffering improve pacing opportunities; they do not guarantee a stable rate or remove the workload.

Introducing Choreographer

Choreographer requests the next applicable VSync event and schedules callbacks on its Looper thread. It does not set the panel’s refresh rate, and app VSync callbacks are not hardware interrupt handlers. A normal View window with no pending work need not continuously produce new frames.

Read this as a simplified historical diagram. RenderThread is a CPU thread, so labeling its entire box “GPU” is inaccurate. Buffer acquisition, GPU submission, queuing, and composition are not always serialized as drawn. The 16.6ms interval approximates 60Hz, not every stage’s complete budget or end-to-end input latency. See the 90Hz discussion.

Choreographer Overview

Choreographer executes due frame callbacks in stages and requests display events when needed. Android 10 orders them INPUT → ANIMATION → INSETS_ANIMATION → TRAVERSAL → COMMIT. It does not collect every app Message, nor does every frame necessarily perform full measure/layout/draw.

Choreographer, SurfaceFlinger, and buffering participate in scheduling; they cannot guarantee 20, 60, or 90fps. Monitoring must distinguish public FrameCallback, hidden FrameInfo, Looper dispatch timing, and presentation data. IdleHandler runs under queue-idle conditions, not reliably at the end of every frame.

Diagrams are useful, but I don’t particularly enjoy drawing them. I spend more time looking at Systrace and MethodTrace in my day-to-day work: CPU, SurfaceFlinger, SystemServer, and App activity laid out from left to right. Once you know the code, it becomes easier to connect the trace with what is happening on the phone. So I’ll mainly use Systrace here.

Choreographer Workflow from a Systrace Perspective

This Launcher scroll is a historical example. A green F is an old Systrace frame-analysis marker, not independent proof of successful on-screen presentation. The alternating background represents that trace’s VSync reference; check the axis and configuration instead of assuming 16.6ms from its colors.

On a typical hardware-accelerated View path, the main thread updates drawing state and RenderThread prepares/submits rendering work. Buffer queuing must still be correlated with GPU completion, SurfaceFlinger composition, and presentation. UI and RenderThread work can overlap; adding their wall durations does not give display latency.

Zooming into one historical frame shows Choreographer’s callbacks and the handoff to RenderThread. The old annotations are qualified below:

Choreographer Workflow

  1. Create the thread’s Choreographer, bind Looper/FrameHandler, and initialize its display receiver and callback queues.
  2. When due work needs a frame and none is scheduled, request VSync. onVsync posts an asynchronous Runnable to that Looper; its later run() invokes doFrame().
  3. doFrame checks whether work remains scheduled, measures its start delay relative to frame time, and adjusts animation time when needed.
  4. Execute due INPUT, ANIMATION, INSETS_ANIMATION, TRAVERSAL, and COMMIT callbacks in order. Traversal may synchronize drawing state with RenderThread.
  5. RenderThread submits GPU work and a Buffer. Submission returning does not imply GPU completion; fences communicate completion/dependencies for subsequent composition and presentation.
  6. Schedule another frame only if work such as animation continues.

The old annotation above calls Traversal the third callback and omits Insets Animation; it is the fourth category in Android 10. Its “rendering complete, send Buffer” caption also needs the asynchronous GPU/fence qualification above.

Here is the corresponding MethodTrace (detailed view following):

Now, let’s examine the implementation via source code.

Source Code Analysis

These are Android 10 excerpts, with omitted checks and state maintenance marked in comments. They are not complete classes to assemble verbatim. Android 16 doFrame also receives VsyncEventData and uses its interval, vsync id, and deadline; see the versioned source.

Choreographer Initialization

Singleton Initialization

Choreographer Constructor

FrameHandler

Choreographer Initialization Chain

For a new Activity window, the resume/display path can add the window, create ViewRootImpl, and obtain the current thread’s Choreographer. Animation code may initialize it earlier, and resuming an existing root does not necessarily recreate it. This is an illustrative call chain:

FrameDisplayEventReceiver Overview

FrameDisplayEventReceiver handles Vsync registration, requests, and reception. It inherits from DisplayEventReceiver and has three key methods:

  1. onVsync – Vsync signal callback
  2. run – Executes doFrame
  3. scheduleVsync – Requests the Vsync signal

scheduleVsync() is implemented by the parent DisplayEventReceiver; code accessing its private mReceiverPtr does not belong inside the subclass. FrameHandler’s MSG_DO_FRAME is principally the timer fallback when VSync is disabled; the normal VSync path uses the Runnable above.

Vsync Registration in Choreographer

The FrameDisplayEventReceiver.onVsync inner class receives Vsync callbacks and notifies the UIThread. It achieves this by listening to file descriptors initialized as follows:

android/view/Choreographer.java

android/view/Choreographer.java

android/view/DisplayEventReceiver.java

Separate control requests from event delivery. DisplayEventReceiver::requestNextVsync() requests the next event through the Binder IDisplayEventConnection; events are read back over BitTube.

DisplayEventDispatcher::initialize() registers the receiving FD with the native Looper. A readable event is dispatched to Java onVsync(), which posts an asynchronous Runnable. onVsync and doFrame are distinct steps, not an app hardware-interrupt handler:

Logic for Processing One Frame

The core logic resides in Choreographer.doFrame. FrameDisplayEventReceiver.onVsync posts itself, and its run method calls doFrame:

android/view/Choreographer.java

doFrame performs three main tasks:

  1. Estimates dispatch-start delay relative to frame time.
  2. Records frame drawing information.
  3. Executes CALLBACK_INPUT, CALLBACK_ANIMATION, CALLBACK_INSETS_ANIMATION, CALLBACK_TRAVERSAL, and CALLBACK_COMMIT.

Dropped Frame Logic

The calculation is startNanos - frameTimeNanos: how late this doFrame starts relative to the supplied frame timestamp. Integer division estimates missed scheduling intervals, not this frame’s rendering duration or the full count of missed presentations. The surrounding source also adjusts animation frame time and handles backward time.

The diagram’s start_time should mean the timestamp carried by the event, not when Java happens to receive it. Its divisor must not be hardcoded to 16ms.

Earlier work can delay the next callback, but this is not simply a detector for “the previous frame.” GPU, composition, or presentation misses may produce no such warning. Runnable scheduling delays can contribute without the app continuously running on CPU. The final annotation also reverses the subtraction; the source subtracts the frame timestamp from dispatch-start time.

Recording Frame Drawing Info

Internal android.graphics.FrameInfo records some stage timestamps, and HWUI adds later fields. It is marked @hide, not a stable app SDK class. Stage boundaries are not per-business-callback timings. The following Android 10 indices must not be used blindly for newer output formats.

doFrame records times from Vsync to markPerformTraversalsStart:

Executing Callbacks

Input Callback Stack

input callback typically executes ViewRootImpl.ConsumeBatchedInputRunnable:

android/view/ViewRootImpl.java

This illustrates a batched-input path into DecorView/Activity/View dispatch. Not all input waits for the INPUT callback; keys, unbatched events, and other paths need separate analysis:

Animation Callback Stack

Commonly used via View.postOnAnimation:

Used for operations like startScroll and Fling:

The actual stack depends on the posted callback. This image shows AnimationHandler and ValueAnimator/AnimatorSet evaluation; it does not by itself establish an AbsListView FlingRunnable:

FrameCallback also uses CALLBACK_ANIMATION:

Traversal Stack

These ViewRootImpl excerpts retain a conditional outline, with local variables supplied by omitted surrounding code. Not every frame performs measure/layout/draw. A barrier does not raise CPU scheduling priority; its queue semantics are explained below.

doTraversal TraceView Example

Requesting the Next Frame’s Vsync

Continuous operations like animations or scrolling need a stable frame output. Further work may request another frame. invalidate and requestLayout can schedule traversal, but state checks and coalescing mean they do not each generate a separate VSync.

ObjectAnimator Animation Logic

android/animation/ObjectAnimator.java

android/animation/ValueAnimator.java

android/animation/AnimationHandler.java

The provider forwards to Choreographer; the internal path queues due work and schedules a frame, or posts a delayed scheduling message:

AnimationHandler reposts while animation callbacks remain. Public FrameCallback is one-shot; a continuous loop must explicitly repost and be cancelled when no longer needed:

Source Code Summary

  1. getInstance() returns the calling Looper thread’s instance, not a process-wide singleton; a missing Looper causes an exception.
  2. Requests go through the display connection, events through FD/Looper dispatch, and doFrame through an asynchronous Message. None is an app hardware-interrupt handler.
  3. FrameCallback is one-shot and runs in ANIMATION. One callback does not guarantee one new Buffer.
  4. Android 10/16 order due work as INPUT, ANIMATION, INSETS_ANIMATION, TRAVERSAL, COMMIT. Earlier updates can affect the later traversal.
  5. COMMIT runs after traversal, not after GPU/SF completion or presentation. ActivityThread.scheduleTrimMemory() uses it when the main Choreographer exists, but this is one use, not an onTrimMemory call every frame.
  6. ListView obtain/setup can be driven by input scrolling, continuing animation, or layout. Read the actual stack rather than inferring the cause from a stage name.

APM and Choreographer

These interfaces observe different stages; their numbers are not interchangeable FPS or dropped-frame counts:

  • FrameCallback observes callback pacing on its Looper, not Buffer/presentation counts.
  • gfxinfo ... framestats exposes window HWUI statistics with version-specific fields.
  • SurfaceFlinger --latency is a historical diagnostic whose target layer and implementation must match.
  • The private PageFlip query is historical and unavailable under its old code in Android 16.
  • Choreographer skip warnings indicate dispatch-start lateness, not complete presentation behavior.
  • Looper/BlockCanary measures message dispatch, not displayed frames.

Android 7 / API 24 provides Window.OnFrameMetricsAvailableListener. Its dropCountSinceLastInvocation counts dropped metric notifications, not dropped display frames. On Android 12 / API 31 and later, where captured, Perfetto FrameTimeline links expected/actual app and SF frames to help investigate CPU, GPU, and composition delays.

Using FrameCallback.doFrame

Use it on a thread with a Looper, normally the main thread for View apps:

postFrameCallback() is public from API 16 and one-shot. A continuous observer must repost and stop appropriately; the observer itself requests more frames, so callback counts are not necessarily app draw counts. frameTimeNanos is the animation frame time, possibly jitter-adjusted, not the instant execution starts.

TinyDancer was the historical callback-based pacing project referenced here. Its displayed rate is not automatically composited screen FPS. API 33 adds postVsyncCallback() with FrameData/FrameTimeline information such as candidate deadlines and expected presentation times. These are predictions, not measured presentation; use the data within the callback’s valid lifetime.

Using FrameInfo

Substitute the actual package. The preserved sample below says Window: StatusBar; it must not be presented as verified output of that Launcher command in the same run.

Keep and parse the CSV header: Android/HWUI versions change fields. Timestamps use the implementation’s monotonic clock in nanoseconds; Duration columns are durations, not timestamps. The old OldestInputEvent=9223372036854775807 and NewestInputEvent=0 combination indicates no valid input timestamps, not enormous input latency. FrameCompleted is not screen presentation. Slow-frame categories can overlap and must not be added as disjoint bad-frame counts.

Using SurfaceFlinger

These are Android 10-era diagnostic examples. List actual layers and query the relevant one; names change with windows, recreation, and versions:

In Android 10 SurfaceFlinger::dumpStatsLocked() and FrameTracker::dumpStats(), the first line is the refresh interval, followed by columns:

  1. A: desiredPresentTime, desired presentation time.
  2. B: actualPresentTime, recorded actual presentation time.
  3. C: frameReadyTime, when contents became ready for presentation, possibly obtained from a ready fence.

These are not app draw start, pre-submission VSync, and hardware acceptance. That implementation uses a 128-entry ring but dumps 127 slots per tracker. Zero and pending INT64_MAX entries are not valid frames. Check the target, time range, validity, monotonicity, gaps, and refresh changes rather than assuming 128 new frames per command.

The old ceil((C - A) / refresh_period) formula and “a change means jank” rule are not universal. Desired, ready, and actual times measure different things; even persistently high latency can leave that value unchanged. Analyze presentation intervals and expected deadlines according to the implementation, preferably correlating FrameTimeline where supported.

Using SurfaceFlinger PageFlip

Historical private interface, not a current app-monitoring recipe. Android 10’s private debug transaction 1013 returned the default display’s PageFlip count. Even with access, that was display-level activity, not one app’s frame count. The old command also omitted shell; correcting it to adb shell service call SurfaceFlinger 1013 does not make it public or remove permission restrictions.

Android 16 source explicitly contains:

The old example that read transact(1013) as a count and calculated app FPS is therefore removed. Use public window metrics or version-appropriate trace data. Never ignore transaction/return status or treat unsupported output as zero frames.

Choreographer Skip Warnings

Android 10 defaults SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT to 30 via debug.choreographer.skipwarning, read when the class initializes. This is a logging threshold, not proof that smaller delays are smooth or that every frame has been measured.

Frame time, dispatch start, work completion, and presentation remain separate. Changing the warning threshold does not fix latency.

BlockCanary

Tools such as BlockCanary time the boundaries of Looper message dispatch. This is an excerpt of the older dispatch path:

It measures dispatch wall time including waits, not pure CPU time or the complete RenderThread/GPU/SF chain. It also does not cover every native-poll callback outside dispatch. A backlog of individually short messages can delay work without one long-message warning. Logging, string construction, and sampling have overhead, and setMessageLogging must coexist with other observers. This is not zero-overhead, complete jank detection.

MessageQueue and Choreographer

In Android 10 MessageQueue.next(), a queue-head barrier with target == null makes the queue search forward for an asynchronous message, still respecting its when. Synchronous messages behind the barrier wait for removal. This neither preempts a running message nor raises CPU scheduling priority.

Message.setAsynchronous() is public from API 22, and Handler.createAsync() from API 28. “Asynchronous” means exempt from synchronization barriers, not automatically first, on another thread, or immediate. Without a barrier, normal queue timing/order still applies. The framework’s barrier insertion/removal APIs are not public app SDK contracts.

SyncBarrier Example in Choreographer

This ViewRootImpl outline omits other state management. scheduleTraversals() inserts the barrier and registers traversal work. An asynchronous VSync message can bypass the barrier and let doFrame run that callback:

doTraversal() removes the barrier before performTraversals(), not after GPU completion:

Asynchronous eligibility cannot bypass a long task already executing. Private barriers or arbitrary message reordering are not general app jank fixes.

Manufacturer Optimizations

Working on the system side gives us room to change source code and try scheduling policies. I can’t share the proprietary implementation here, but I can outline the ideas. If you’re interested, we can discuss them privately. The examples below do not include controlled results.

Input-event Optimization

AOSP already has CALLBACK_INPUT and batched-input consumption. The historical idea concerns changing input scheduling or responding earlier, not adding input support to a Choreographer that has none. Earlier work must be evaluated alongside batching, resampling, power, and presentation pacing. It is not automatically better.

Background Animation Optimization

An app’s self-reposting callbacks or animations can continue creating work when no longer useful. Decisions to stop them should account for lifecycle, window visibility, multi-window operation, and the actual feature; not every background callback is meaningless.

I recorded this historical com.netease.newsreader.activity capture as a background case. It shows dense frame activity but no independent visibility or power evidence, and makes no claim about the current app. Apps should cancel unneeded animations/callbacks; platform policies must also preserve legitimate visible-window and background behavior.

Frame Scheduling Optimization

“Compose without waiting for VSync” was an OEM exploration direction, not a public app switch. Scheduling still depends on buffers, fences, display hardware, and refresh constraints. Immediate scheduling can increase power or disrupt pacing without reducing end-to-end latency. No implementation or comparison is provided, so this is not a verified optimization result.

App Startup Optimization

First locate long work, locks, and queues on the launch critical path. System-level message reordering must preserve lifecycle and dependencies; moving arbitrary “important” messages to the front risks incorrect order and starvation. Apps should reduce critical-path work, defer unnecessary initialization, and measure first-frame and interactive readiness separately.

High-refresh-rate Optimization

60/90/120Hz correspond to about 16.67/11.11/8.33ms; the original 8.8ms for 120Hz was incorrect. Refresh intervals are not a full independent budget for every thread. Evaluate app/game load, rate transitions, thermals, power, and pacing together rather than requiring every app to render at maximum rate continuously.

References

Versioned primary sources are linked in the relevant sections. These are the original background references; they do not establish current platform behavior:

  1. Historical VSync explanation
  2. Gityuan’s Choreographer article
  3. Choreographer API reference
  4. Historical Jishuwen reference
  5. Historical Juejin entry
  6. Android development course

Article Discussion

Original Chinese discussion pages: Zhihu and Juejin.

About Me && Blog

I welcome discussion with fellow developers:

  1. About me: personal introduction and contact information.
  2. Blog navigation.
  3. Android performance resources: recommendations are welcome.
  4. Android performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One person can go faster; a group can go further.

entry.title: Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Low Memory
entry.content:
In the Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - System Layer article, we touched upon jank cases caused by low system memory. Since low memory has a significant impact on overall device performance, I’m dedicating this article to exploring those effects in depth.

As Android versions evolve and apps become more feature-heavy, their memory requirements increase. When this article was written in 2019, many devices had 4GB of RAM or less. These users are prone to low memory situations, especially after major system updates or as more apps and services run concurrently.

Memory pressure can contribute to slow responsiveness and jank. Examples include longer app launch times, more frame drops in scrolling, more frequent cold starts as background processes are killed, and extra reclaim/restart work that can increase power use. Heat alone does not diagnose memory pressure. Below, I’ll outline the causes, debugging methods, and potential optimizations for these issues.

Version note — technical review, 2026-10-13: This article retains 2019 logs and Systrace cases. Old kernel LMK logs, tuning interfaces, and function names have version limits. Updates below cover Android 10/11 PSI/lmkd, Android 16 framework code, and Linux 6.6 reclaim mechanisms. Complete original traces and controlled experimental conditions are unavailable; the review corrects visible evidence rather than presenting a new device benchmark.

  1. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Methodology
  2. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - System Layer
  3. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Application Layer
  4. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Low Memory

Identifying Low Memory

Meminfo Data

Start with Android’s system summary, then correlate processes and changes over time:

The original output is preserved below. 156,ba480K is corrupted text, not a valid number to reconstruct by guessing.

This is not a universal low-memory signature:

  • In Android 9 AMS, Free RAM combines cached-process PSS, some kernel caches, and actually free pages. It differs from both MemFree and MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo.
  • Used RAM and Lost RAM use different accounting involving PSS, swap PSS, kernel, and ZRAM values. Here, Used exceeds Total and Lost is negative. Check the system branch and original samples; do not interpret this as physically negative memory or proof of a leak. status moderate is also a framework state, not a per-frame pressure measurement.
  • 2,608K physical used, 301,256K in swap, and 4,247,544K total swap describe physical consumption, used swap space, and swap capacity. They are not interchangeable ZRAM utilization measures. These figures alone do not support the original claim of very high ZRAM use.

Caches are useful. Look for sustained loss of available memory, stalls from reclaim or swap-in, and foreground responsiveness in the same interval. A single low-free-memory snapshot is insufficient.

LMK and kswapd Activity

This is a historical in-kernel lowmemorykiller driver log, not the universal format of modern userspace lmkd:

It records selecting PID 15609, adj 906, in kswapd0‘s reclaim context, with cache 258652kB, threshold 261272kB, and other conditions. It does not establish a universal “adj 900 watermark.” -5540kB above reserved is a value after reserve accounting, not a negative physical free-page count. The exact selection policy requires that vendor’s kernel source.

kswapd performs background page reclaim. The old LMK driver and userspace lmkd are separate implementations; neither should be conflated with the Linux OOM killer or AMS cached/empty-process trimming. Active kswapd alone does not prove that a process was killed.

Version update: The AOSP lmkd guide describes PSI support in Android 10 and the Android 11 strategy’s additional consideration of memory use and page-cache thrashing. Actual operation depends on kernel support and product configuration. Use that version’s lmkd reasons and pressure data rather than searching only for the old lowmemorykiller: prefix.

/proc/meminfo

Read the kernel summary with the leading slash in the path:

This original sample has a different MemTotal from the dumpsys sample. Do not treat them as one synchronized device snapshot.

The Linux 6.6 /proc documentation distinguishes free RAM (MemFree) from an estimate of memory available to new applications without swapping (MemAvailable), accounting for reclaimable caches and reserves. The values here are 148928 kB and 864172 kB; they are not both almost zero. SwapFree of 42576 kB shows heavily used swap space, not necessarily active swap churn at this instant. Committed_AS is not physical residency.

Where the kernel provides the interfaces and permissions allow them, further read-only observations include:

Use deltas around a reproduction for reclaim scans/successes, allocstall*, pswpin/pswpout, and workingset_refault*; field names vary by kernel. Large lifetime totals do not date a stall. PSI some measures time with at least some tasks stalled; full measures simultaneous stalls of all non-idle tasks. avg10/60/300 are time percentages over those windows in seconds; total is cumulative microseconds. See the PSI documentation. Missing interfaces, denied access, or uncaptured data mean unavailable, not zero pressure.

System-wide Lag & Slow Response

Memory pressure can contribute to slow launches, dropped frames, and more cold starts, but CPU, storage, locks, and other loads can cause similar symptoms. Align the user-visible delay with pressure, reclaim, thread waits, and process-exit evidence before placing memory on the critical path.

Impact of Low Memory on Performance

Main Thread I/O Latency

Pressure adds reclaim work, may evict file pages needed soon afterward, and may cause swap-related work. Foreground latency grows if the thread then waits for pages or storage completion.

Distinguish plain Uninterruptible Sleep from subclasses tagged Block I/O, and inspect the blocking call site. D state or a yellow color alone does not establish disk I/O. wait_on_page_bit_killable indicates a page-state wait, not by itself low memory, a specific file, or saturated storage. Cached reads need not block this way; loading a View does not necessarily read storage.

The SystemUI screenshot shows io_schedule as its blocking call site. That supports investigating I/O waits, but supplies no simultaneous memory-pressure value:

The next screenshot shows OPScreenRecord in bindApplication, including APK/OAT loading. Its thread states suggest waits during startup; color alone does not identify every wait’s cause.

CPU Contention

Reclaim, compression/decompression, and reloading content consume CPU. They can increase foreground Runnable delays when competing for execution time; confirm that on scheduling tracks instead of inferring it from a thread name.

The crop below shows kswapd0 repeatedly running on CPU 7. The original article described a Snapdragon 855 device, but this crop lacks enough topology and numerical frequency data to prove “the prime core at maximum frequency.” It also does not measure power or a specific foreground thread’s delay.

HeapTaskDaemon processes ART heap tasks. Its activity is neither automatically all GC nor all stop-the-world time. Correlate actual heap/GC tasks and allocation activity before attributing it to system pressure.

Process Death-Restart Cycles

Repeated exits and restarts add allocation, code-loading, and I/O work. First identify both the kill and restart reasons. The original Monkey-test log is preserved:

All nine am_kill events say empty #3. Android 9 AMSuses empty # plus a count when trimming excess empty processes; Android 16 OomAdjusterstill has the corresponding too many empty path. This supports repeated framework trimming followed by restarts, not a direct LMK-killed-QQ conclusion. The restart label alone does not identify a parent process reviving the app; investigate component/service restarts and other launch requests.

The corresponding system_server screenshot shows repeated start and killProcessGroup activity. That shape is not exclusive to any one kill reason:

The CPU crop below shows dense execution slices, but lacks complete per-thread accounting. It cannot attribute all CPU work to QQ or LMK. These are historical observations, not judgments about current app versions.

Memory Reclamation and I/O Triggers

After a phone has been in use for a long time, opening an app you used earlier can feel slower than opening it for the first time: you have to wait for it to load again. That is one of the situations that led me to look into low-memory jank. The symptom alone does not tell us the cause, though. We need to separate these mechanisms:

  • The allocation fast path tries available free pages; it is not “fast-path reclaim.” On failure, the slow path may wake kswapd, reclaim directly, or compact memory depending on flags and conditions. Direct reclaim runs in the allocating thread’s context and can affect foreground latency. See Linux 6.6 page_alloc.c.
  • File-page reclaim does not always write storage. Eligible clean file-cache pages can be discarded and read again if needed; dirty pages generally involve writeback. Not every file-backed page must be written before eviction.
  • Anonymous memory and swap do not imply physical storage I/O. ZRAM compresses data in RAM, consuming memory and CPU; configured backing-device writeback can also involve storage. Inspect /proc/swaps and device configuration rather than assuming every phone uses RAM-only swap. See the Linux 6.6 ZRAM documentation.
  • A page fault need not read storage. Page/swap-cache hits and first mappings differ from faults requiring I/O. A slow return to an app may also be a cold start after process death, not merely swap-in.

Old names such as do_page_fault, lock_page_or_retry, and wait_on_page_bit_killable are investigation starting points, not a fixed chain on every architecture/version. Linux 6.6 file-cache paths use many folio interfaces. PG_locked and PG_writeback are separate states: folio_unlock() and folio_end_writeback()handle unlocking and writeback completion separately. The original statement that page locks clear only when writeback starts or read I/O finishes was incorrect; killable waits may also be interrupted by fatal signals.

Excessive readahead can create unused I/O and cache pressure; too little can hurt sequential access. Tune to access patterns, hits, and latency rather than assuming smaller is always better.

Case Study: App Startup Under Low Memory

I labeled these two captures low memory and normal memory at the time. Their arrows span bindApplication to around the first frame, not the full launch from the user’s tap or an independently verified presentation timestamp. Thermal, cache, and background-work conditions are incomplete, so they are not a controlled experiment varying memory alone.

Low Memory Startup

The arrow reads 2.044 s; the Thread Timeslices table spans 2053.451 ms, a slightly different interval. Running is 682.137 ms. The two Block I/O subclasses sum to 647.450 ms; all four Uninterruptible subclasses sum to 783.385 ms. The original “about 750ms” described only part of the classification.

The CPU Slices list includes HeapTaskDaemon, several kworker entries, and kswapd0. Grouping by name can combine same-named threads across processes; CPU time summed across cores is not foreground wait time or the interval’s wall duration.

Normal Memory Startup

The arrow reads 1.223 s; the thread-state selection spans 1227.232 ms. Running is 624.278 ms. All three Uninterruptible subclasses sum to 139.417 ms, of which the two Block I/O subclasses contribute 33.097 ms.

The thread-state tables compare as follows, in milliseconds. Do not mix their boundaries with the arrow selections:

MetricLow-memory sampleNormal sample
Selection extent2053.4511227.232
Running682.137624.278
Runnable63.06043.902
Sleeping524.869419.635
Uninterruptible, all subclasses783.385139.417
Of those, tagged Block I/O647.45033.097

The last row is included in the preceding row, not additional time. Uninterruptible states show the largest increase, but subclasses without a Block I/O tag cannot all be counted as disk I/O. The captures also cannot attribute every difference to memory pressure.

The normal sample still lists HeapTaskDaemon and other workers. kswapd0 is visible in the low-memory ranking and absent from the displayed normal ranking; absence from a cropped ranking is not zero reclaim activity. The unequal interval lengths also prevent comparing total CPU milliseconds as if they were rates.

Optimization Strategies

These directions come from my own experience and ideas shared by fellow engineers. Each problem still needs to be examined on its own. Platform tuning belongs to system/OEM work; ordinary apps should manage their own allocations, caches, and background tasks first. An ongoing notification does not prove high memory consumption or justify unconditional process killing. Retaining fewer processes can increase cold starts, lost work, and failed background functions. Optimize responsiveness and reliability, not the free-RAM number alone.

  1. Watermarks: extra_free_kbytes is a historical Android extension, not a universal kernel interface. The Android 16 adaptation script checks for it and otherwise calculates watermark_scale_factor. Their high-watermark effects differ; values are not interchangeable. Higher reserves can reduce burst-driven direct reclaim while increasing background work and reducing cache capacity.
  2. Storage: UFS 3.0 was a hardware-selection example in 2019, not a software fix or performance guarantee. Measure random I/O, queues, tail latency, and thermal state. A phone is not a desktop where replacing an SSD is a routine remedy.
  3. Readahead: Tune read_ahead_kb using access patterns and cache hits; no universal lower-is-better value applies.
  4. Background I/O: Match the device’s cgroup version and enabled controllers. v1 blkio differs from v2 interfaces such as io.max; excessive throttling can delay work the foreground depends on. See Linux 6.6 cgroup v2.
  5. Proactive reclaim: Experiment during verified idle periods while accounting for compression, writeback, CPU, and later refault costs. Periodically clearing caches is not capacity management.
  6. Exit/restart loops: Distinguish lmkd decisions, AMS count limits, crashes, and launch requests. Fix the actual loop; more kills do not imply better efficiency.
  7. kswapd: Tune around watermarks and allocation bursts, observing indicators such as allocstall*. “Periodically reclaim more to the high watermark” is not a universal scheduler policy.
  8. Swappiness: In Linux 6.6, its 0–200 range expresses relative swap versus filesystem paging I/O cost, not a percentage of RAM at which swapping starts. Do not mechanically set ZRAM devices to zero; measure the workload.
  9. Low-RAM products: Compare foreground tail latency, cold starts, exits, power use, and background-function success under comparable conditions. Do not copy a policy from another device based only on RAM size.
  10. Apps: Fix leaks, bound bitmap/object caches, reduce wasteful allocations and background tasks, and move suitable I/O off the main thread without blocking it for results. From Android 14 / API 34, ordinary apps cannot use killBackgroundProcesses() to clean other packages; see the updated Launcher case study.
  11. Unrecoverable incidents: A user-chosen restart can temporarily restore service; it does not fix the cause. Preserve relevant logs, pressure, and process data where possible and investigate the leak or abnormal load.

There are no universal best values. Validate changes with fixed device/build, workload, cache, and thermal conditions, repeated captures, and distributions rather than one improved screenshot.

References

Current mechanisms and versions are linked next to the relevant claims. The original historical references are retained below, not used as the sole authority for current behavior:

  1. Historical reference 1
  2. Historical reference 2

Article on Zhihu

For discussion, see the original Chinese low-memory case study on Zhihu.

About Me && Blog

Below are personal introductions and related links. Looking forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals - when three people walk together, one must be my teacher!

  1. Blogger’s Personal Introduction: Contains personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A navigation of personal blog content.
  3. Personally Organized and Collected Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Welcome self-recommendations and recommendations (private WeChat chat is fine)
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One person can walk faster, but a group of people can walk farther

entry.title: Case Study: Debugging the Android Launcher Kill Problem
entry.content:
This started with a bug I encountered at work. It was not a difficult one, but while writing my diary afterward, I thought the investigation was worth recording and sharing. I also learned some useful analysis and tool tricks from my clever colleague Mei Ming.

I’ve used a variety of tools mentioned in my Android Performance Optimization Methodology, including:

  • Reproduction Video
  • Event Log
  • AS Source/Debug
  • AS Profiler
  • Systrace
  • Dumpsys
  • Unix ps utility

You might wonder whether such a simple bug needs an article. I wanted to keep a record for myself, and the way we used the tools together may be useful in other investigations. If it helps you, all the better. If you have your own debugging tricks, please join our discussion group and share them!

Version note — technical review, 2026-10-13: This is a 2019 case from a specific Flyme/app environment, with AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 as a source reference. The old Studio workflow and cross-package cleanup behavior are not universal today. Updates below cover Android 14 / API 34 restrictions, Android 16 source, and API 30 exit records. The logs and screenshots are historical; the original app has not been retested and no claim is made about its current version.

The Phenomenon

Testing reported a classic performance bug: “Slow loading of icons when returning to the home screen.” They provided a video, logs, and a Systrace. We had the symptom and the records, so let’s start there.

The Analysis

1. Zeroing in on the Time

  1. Watch the reproduction video to find the approximate time.
  2. Align it with Event Log, then use Event and Main logs to reconstruct the actions.
  3. In this capture, Launcher was killed after com.jx.cmcc.ict.ibelieve came to the foreground. Returning home created a new Launcher process. The sequence alone does not yet identify the caller that requested the kill.

Launcher changed from PID 13509 to 14013, explaining the cold start on return. The 413,413 values are launch timing statistics. In AOSP Android 9’s ActivityRecord.reportLaunchTimeLocked(), they are written as thisTime and totalTime, from launch reporting paths including the window-drawn callback. They are neither CPU time nor a guarantee that all icons and asynchronous content have loaded. Match the device’s system branch when interpreting its fields.

In the original investigation, I observed roughly 2 seconds until the icons were fully visible. That was a video observation, not a value derived from the 413ms log. The complete video is not available here, so this is not a measurement of current Launcher versions or proof that all of that delay was database work.

2. Investigating the Kill Reason

Now we need to find out who killed Launcher. The app is a suspect, but the sequence alone is not enough. Let’s look at this event:

The Android 9 event definition lists user, victim PID, process name, OomAdj, and reason. 600 is not a memory size. The 1456/2269 prefix identifies the process/thread writing the log, not the original app caller. kill background points to a framework cleanup path; it does not by itself mean LMK under memory pressure.

Here is ActivityManagerService.killBackgroundProcesses() in android-9.0.0_r1. It checks permission and user scope before selecting processes by package, appId, user, and process-state criteria. It does not unconditionally kill every process belonging to the package.

Its client entry point is ActivityManager.killBackgroundProcesses():

This is a source reference for the historical path, not a claim that the Flyme branch was identical to AOSP. Killing background processes is also different from force-stopping an app; the system may restart processes later as needed. Android 14’s restriction on ordinary apps targeting other packages is covered below.

3. Debugging SystemServer

The next step was to identify the service caller, then inspect the app’s arguments and stack. Attaching to system services requires an authorized, debuggable test system and matching sources. Do not assume an ordinary retail device permits attaching to system_server. Pausing critical system threads also changes timing, so this is not a normal startup benchmark.

  1. In the historical Android Studio setup, select system_process and follow ActivityManagerService.killBackgroundProcesses() into its cleanup path.

  1. Reproduce candidate app launches. When I launched the suspected app, it hit the breakpoint. The stack shows a Binder transaction; the pictured stop is already inside killPackageProcessesLocked().

  1. The historical expression evaluator returned 29771 for getRealCallingPid().

This expression is not a portable AOSP instruction. No method with that name was found in the checked Android 9/16 Binder or AMS sources, and the screenshot does not supply its implementation. Treat it as a facility of that debugging environment.

The standard Binder.getCallingPid() / Binder.getCallingUid() can capture the incoming transaction identity at the service entry point, before Binder.clearCallingIdentity() and before any asynchronous handoff. The Android 9 method above clears identity before its internal cleanup call. Replacing the old expression with standard getCallingPid() at an arbitrary inner breakpoint would therefore not reliably identify the original client. See the Binder identity APIs.

  1. Correlate the PID, UID, and time with the process list from the same reproduction. The original screenshot uses adb shell ps | grep 29771:

Read the PID column: some rows match because 29771 is their PPID. They are not all the caller, and PIDs can be reused. This identifies a candidate process to check with app-side arguments and stacks.

4. Debugging the App

Matching framework sources can expose an SDK call even without business source code. The target must still be a debuggable build or accessible through the appropriate platform test environment; arbitrary installed release apps are not automatically attachable. profileable does not mean debuggable.

I put a breakpoint in the client android.app.ActivityManager.killBackgroundProcesses():

I reproduced it locally by logging in and then launching the app again. The screenshot shows the target package com.meizu.flyme.launcher and the path MainBasePresenter$2.loadComplete → IconUtil.useIcon → ActivityManager.killBackgroundProcesses. That is more direct evidence than a kill log appearing after an app launch.

This finding applies to the historical device, app version, and debugging setup. It says nothing about the app’s current behavior. The logs, debugger screenshots, and traces also come from different reproduction runs; their PIDs must not be combined into one execution.

5. Identifying the Root Code using AS Profiler

The following screenshots show the 2019 Android Studio interface: select the process and open CPU profiling.

I selected Trace Java Methods, recorded the operation, then stopped to inspect the result.

Method instrumentation shows captured Java/Kotlin call order, not every process or every native instruction. Instrumentation, debugging, and the test setup affect timing. The chart also contains a VAInstrumentation wrapper whose configuration is not supplied here; it does not establish an untouched release-build benchmark. I use this kind of recording to help follow framework and business code paths.

Searching for killBackgroundProcesses shows loadComplete → useIcon → the API:

The pictured 3.31ms is a wall-clock interval under instrumentation, not production CPU cost or the full reason icons appeared roughly 2 seconds late. The app developer now has a concrete call site to fix.

Current tooling update, checked 2026-10-13: Studio task names and layouts have changed. Follow the official Java/Kotlin method recording guide for instrumentation, and do not mistake sampling for an invocation-by-invocation record. The guide recommends keeping instrumented recordings to about 5 seconds or less around the operation; the old screenshot’s longer capture is not a current recommendation. See the Profiler documentation for debuggable/profileable build capabilities and overhead.

6. Permission Analysis

The historical API requires Manifest.permission.KILL_BACKGROUND_PROCESSES. @RequiresPermission documents that contract; the actual grant and service-side checks still matter. The original adb shell dumpsys package com.jx.cmcc.ict.ibelieve output included:

The permission protection level was normal:

A declared normal permission is generally granted at installation without a runtime prompt. This does not mean undeclared apps automatically hold it, or that a grant permanently authorizes killing another package’s processes.

The cross-package advice is outdated on Android 14 / API 34 and later. The official changes affecting all apps restrict ordinary third-party apps to killing their own background processes through this API. Passing another package name has no effect and produces an Invalid packageName log. This applies to all apps running on Android 14, regardless of target SDK.

The AOSP android-16.0.0_r1 implementation checks caller and target appIds, with an exception for the platform’s KILL_ALL_BACKGROUND_PROCESSES permission, protected as signature|privileged. Do not generalize ordinary-app restrictions to privileged system callers, or interpret the original permission still being normal as preservation of its historical cross-package behavior.

Android 11 and Later: Inspecting Exit Records

Android 11 / API 30 added ApplicationExitInfo. For an app you develop, a later launch can query retained records through ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons() and correlate time, PID, process name, reason, and status. Only limited recent history is retained. Reading another UID’s package requires additional permission; this is not an unrestricted way for third-party apps to investigate Launcher.

  • No matching record does not prove that a process was never killed.
  • REASON_SIGNALED with SIGKILL does not uniquely identify low-memory killing. Not all devices report REASON_LOW_MEMORY; check ActivityManager.isLowMemoryKillReportSupported().
  • Interpret reason names in their version and code-path context. The Android 16 background cleanup path above uses REASON_USER_REQUESTED with internal SUBREASON_KILL_BACKGROUND. The former alone does not prove a person tapped Force stop. The internal subreason is not presented here as a separate public SDK query interface.

7. Can Systrace find the Culprit?

Wakeup relationships can narrow the investigation, but a wakeup chain alone does not prove which app issued a particular kill request. See Systrace prerequisites for reading wakeups. The original investigation followed these steps:

  1. Find activity near killProcessGroup in system_server and inspect the relevant thread’s wakeup source. The screenshot points to thread 19688.

  1. Resolve the thread identity: 19688 is Binder:1295_1E in process 1295.

  1. Around the corresponding time, inspect that Binder thread’s wakeup source: thread 7289.

  1. This trace maps 7289 to the main thread of com.jx.cmcc.ict.ibelieve.

That chain points toward the app, but a waker is not automatically the kill caller. Correlate the same Binder transaction, timestamps, and thread handoffs in the complete trace, then use request arguments, service logs, or the client stack where needed. Some pictured selections only show thread identity at a different time; their durations cannot be joined into the kill’s execution time. Here, the client breakpoint and target package provide the more direct evidence. Low-level killProcessGroup is not exclusive to this API.

Conclusion

These observations are retained in the context of the 2019 case; the modern permission boundary is explained above.

In this case, the app had requested a permission and used the API incorrectly, seriously affecting the user’s experience. At this point our investigation was mostly done; the next step was to contact the app store and the app developers to get it fixed.

What surprised me then was how loosely Google allowed KILL_BACKGROUND_PROCESSES. I had assumed it needed special approval to stop apps abusing or misusing it. After all, it could decide whether another app lived or died.

Article on Zhihu

For comments and discussion, see the original Chinese case study on Zhihu.

About Me && Blog

I welcome discussion with fellow developers:

  1. About me: personal introduction and contact information.
  2. Blog navigation.
  3. Android performance resources: recommendations are welcome.
  4. Android performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One person can go faster; a group can go further.

entry.title: Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Application Layer
entry.content:
Technical review · 2026-10-13. The original 2019 images, thread listing, and author observations are retained. Technical checks use AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 and android-16.0.0_r1, with current entry points including API 31 frame timing and DataStore 1.2.1. The screenshots are not measurements of current app releases; no original-device or complete-trace reproduction was performed.

In the Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - System Layer article, we listed causes of jank originating from the system. In this article, we focus on causes stemming from the App itself. When you encounter lag, before blaming the phone manufacturer, consider if it’s the App’s own inefficiency.

OEM and app teams may use Matrix or their own monitoring. System access can reveal more evidence, but coverage still depends on build, capture configuration, and platform support.

Average FPS alone does not describe smoothness. Two periods averaging 55 FPS can have different frame intervals and pauses. Consider intended cadence, actual presentation, and input response rather than using a change from 60 to 55 as a diagnosis. This four-part series includes:

  • 0. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Methodology
  • 1. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - System Layer
  • 2. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Application Layer
  • 3. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Low Memory

Application-Side Performance Issues

Below are app cases I collected in 2019, shown in the Systrace images from then, mainly covering View/HWUI rendering. App names identify historical examples, not claims about current releases. Locate the critical frame and inspect thread states and dependencies before attributing a long slice entirely to app code.

The Systrace series explains the old views. Prefer Perfetto for current captures. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, where supported and captured, FrameTimeline relates deadlines, frame production, and presentation. Colors and average FPS are not substitutes for that evidence.

1. App Main Thread Execution Overhead

Input, animation, measure, layout, draw, and image decoding on the main thread can delay subsequent frames. Long intervals can contain computation, Runnable scheduling delay, locks, I/O, or synchronization waits. Separate elapsed duration from Running time before choosing an optimization. Not every frame executes every phase.

Measure / Layout Overhead

The image shows measure/layout within long traversal intervals. Hierarchy complexity, repeated requestLayout, and measurement logic are candidates, but first check whether the thread was running. The image alone does not prove an excessively deep hierarchy. Inspect measurement counts, callstacks, and update scope to identify unnecessary whole-tree work.

Draw Overhead

With hardware acceleration, main-thread Draw commonly includes recording or updating drawing commands, not complete GPU rendering. The first image has long Record View#draw work. The second selects about 17.746 ms; this is neither GPU time nor a universal diagnosis based on a fixed 16 ms line. Inspect custom drawing, repeated recording, resource access, and waits.

Animation Callback Overhead
