Business logic, allocations, or layout updates inside animation callbacks can add main-thread work. The image also shows Background concurrent copying GC overlapping animation/traversal. The whole concurrent-GC interval is not a main-thread pause, and overlap does not establish the callback as the sole cause. Inspect actual pauses, allocation pressure, and callstacks.

View Initialization Overhead (PlayStore Example)

In the historical PlayStore example, the 13.196 ms selection contains animation and multiple inflate slices. Initialization occurs on the critical path, but the selection is not one inflate call’s CPU time. Check repeated creation and opportunities for deferred work; construction that depends on View/UI-thread rules cannot simply move to an arbitrary worker thread.

List Item Initialization Overhead (WeChat Example)

The 91.972 ms interval includes input, obtainView, inflate, and layout/setupListItem. Inspect item reuse, data/image work during binding, and synchronous access rather than attributing the whole interval to inflation. This is a legacy list path; the image does not identify RecyclerView onBindViewHolder. Analyze the component actually in use.

decodeBitmap Overhead

The main thread repeatedly enters decodeBitmap. Decoding intervals may also include reads, allocation, and waits, so inspect thread state. Read/decode on an appropriate worker where possible, size images for their display use, and deliver results on the UI thread. Account for lifecycle, cancellation, and cache capacity so background work does not merely become resource contention.

2. uploadBitmap Overhead

Decoding a Bitmap into pixels and making those pixels available as a GPU texture are different stages. Large images, repeatedly modified content, or cache eviction can add upload work. Drawing the same Bitmap does not necessarily upload it again, and not every backend exposes a slice named uploadBitmap.

Inspect upload size/count, newly generated pixels, RenderThread execution, allocation, and synchronization waits. Reduce unnecessary pixels and repeated uploads, and reuse stable content with bounded caching. This fills the original explanatory gap; it does not introduce a new measured example.

3. BuildDrawingCache Overhead

Repeated buildDrawingCache/SW Layer work identifies the software-cache path, not necessarily explicit app calls on every frame or new Bitmap allocation each time. Content invalidation or a software layer can trigger it. Identify the invalidation source and size changes.

Android 9 View.java can reuse a matching-size Bitmap. The old drawing-cache API was deprecated in API 28 and is not a general modern acceleration strategy. The dynamic-sticker image is also a historical example, not a statement about current WeChat.

4. Software Rendering vs. Hardware Rendering

Disabling hardware acceleration for a View window changes rasterization and may add software drawing on the main thread, but does not almost always cause lag. Skia has both software and GPU backends; its use does not identify CPU-only drawing. System composition may still use the GPU/HWC afterward.

The image does not expose the configuration. Check window/View/Canvas acceleration state and API support. A local compatibility need may not require disabling acceleration for the whole Activity. See Hardware Layer details.

5. Main Thread Binder Latency

A synchronous Binder call waits for a reply; time can be spent in the receiver queue, locked work, nested calls, or scheduling waits. The long activityResume interval does not show the receiver stack or lock owner, so it alone cannot establish an AMS lock held by background work. Activity/task services and locking also vary by version.

Inspect redundant remote queries on critical frames where caching or asynchronous work is appropriate, and follow the matching transaction on the system side. Framework lifecycle calls required on the main thread cannot simply be moved elsewhere.

6. Uneven Game Content Drawing (SurfaceView)

Mismatch between game-engine frame production and SurfaceFlinger consumption/presentation can cause repeats or latency; actual buffer drops require queue and presentation evidence. The image shows different phases for GLThread onDrawFrame and SurfaceView updates. Its red box alone does not prove that the game computes too slowly.

Games may intentionally target fewer FPS than the display refresh rate. Inspect CPU, GPU, submission timing, and frame pacing. OpenGL/Vulkan games can use Android Frame Pacing (Swappy) to help schedule presentation, but it does not remove an over-budget workload.

7. WebView Inefficiency

JavaScript, style/layout, painting, images, network work, or host interaction can become bottlenecks in a WebView. This does not make WebView inherently slower than native UI. The image shows only partial Chrome_IOThread and glide-animation activity, without a page profile.

Record the WebView provider/version and use Chrome DevTools for WebViews in a development build (available since Android 4.4 / API 19). Inspect page tasks and rendering, then align them with the system trace. A Chrome thread name alone does not identify the responsible JavaScript.

8. Refresh Rate Mismatch

FPS describes content updates; Hz describes display refreshes. At a fixed 90 Hz, 60 FPS content can require uneven repetition unless a compatible cadence is selected. By contrast, 60 FPS at 120 Hz and 30 FPS at 90 Hz can hold each frame for two and three refreshes respectively. Lower FPS still affects motion detail, and an integer ratio does not imply zero input latency.

The old annotation below says “one frame every three Vsyncs at 90 Hz,” which corresponds to 30 FPS. It illustrates an integer match, not evidence of a 60 FPS / 90 Hz mismatch. Inspect actual presentation intervals and display mode rather than just nominal numbers.

9. Incompatibility with High Refresh Rates

Refresh intervals at 60, 90, and 120 Hz are about 16.67, 11.11, and 8.33 ms. Higher refresh rates generally demand a shorter critical path, but UI, RenderThread, GPU, and composition work are pipelined with distinct deadlines. A refresh interval is not the full budget for any one thread, and 14 ms does not guarantee meeting 60 Hz.

This historical image again shows buildDrawingCache/SW Layer work, not a controlled 60/90 Hz comparison of one app. Compare expected/actual frames, stage timing, and frame counts with workload and system conditions held comparable.

10. Main Thread I/O Operations

Database queries, file operations, serialization, or waiting for worker I/O can delay the main thread. Identify the call and wait site. Put storage work on an appropriate asynchronous path without immediately blocking the UI for its result, and combine unnecessary repeated writes.

SharedPreferences.Editor.commit() synchronously waits for persistence and returns success/failure. apply(), introduced in API 9, updates memory and schedules disk work asynchronously without a write-success result. It does not guarantee a nonblocking main thread: framework lifecycle transitions may wait for pending writes, and a later commit can wait for outstanding asynchronous work. Android 16 SharedPreferencesImpl registers a finisher from apply, while QueuedWork.waitToFinish processes/waits for that work. Initial reads can also wait for loading.

Replacing commit with apply mechanically is therefore insufficient. Where persistence completion or error reporting matters, handle commit and its result off the UI thread. For new settings storage, consider the asynchronous APIs in DataStore 1.2.1, preserving data semantics during migration and avoiding blocking waits on the main thread.

11. WebView/Main Thread Interaction

A WebView can involve host UI, renderer, compositor, and GPU-related threads/processes, depending on its provider and version. The first image identifies sandboxed_process0; the WeChat images separately show toolsmp and the main process. These are not one shared main-thread track.

Synchronous waits, heavy callback work, or message round trips can delay a page, but correlate the same request, callback, and rendering work. Scheduling gaps do not automatically identify a JS-bridge fault, and green host-UI frame markers do not guarantee fresh web content. Combine page profiling, scheduling, and host callstacks.

12. RenderThread Overhead

A long RenderThread DrawFrame interval can include tree preparation, texture work, driver submission, buffer/fence waits, or scheduling delay. It is not automatically excessive GPU commands or GPU execution time. Nor does the UI thread wait for GPU completion on every frame.

Both Android 9 DrawFrameTask and Android 16 DrawFrameTask use the syncFrameState result to decide whether to unblock the UI before drawing or release it later. The pictured syncFrameState/prepareTree work is an investigation lead. Identify exactly what the UI is waiting for and what RenderThread is doing.

13. Same-Named RenderThreads and Synchronization

Thread names can repeat. The HWUI RenderThread::getInstance paths in AOSP Android 9 and Android 16 each maintain one process-local instance. Multiple threads named RenderThread do not alone prove multiple HWUI instances or that the UI waits for all of them.

The screenshot shows PID 4439, while the following ps output is for PID 10300; these are not established as the same recording. Retain the old output as an example of duplicate thread names, then identify ownership through PID/TID, callstacks, creation source, and wait relationships.

Original capture command (historical PID; not executed in this review; grep matches substrings):

The S states and epoll/futex wait sites are snapshots, not proof of deadlock, continuous load, or what the UI is waiting for.

Summary

These were my observations about app versions and the market in 2019.

Android is an evolving platform, but its openness means app quality varies wildly. Unlike the tightly controlled App Store, Android apps come from many sources with varying levels of quality control.

Large companies cared about performance too, but the growing number of features could still hurt it. At the time, I complained about WeChat’s memory use and felt that the newer QQ was less smooth than its earlier versions.

Then there were the tricks for keeping processes alive, waking other apps, hot updates, and background tasks. I could understand why app developers wanted them. From the system side, though, we wanted foreground and background apps to behave well so the app the user was actually using stayed responsive. I hoped app developers would pay attention to that experience too.

When we find app-specific performance flaws that persist across different hardware, we often reach out to the developers to collaborate on a fix.

For more details on what OEMs do, see: What do phone manufacturers actually do when they say they are optimizing Android?

This series includes:

  • 0. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Methodology
  • 1. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - System Layer
  • 2. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Application Layer
  • 3. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Low Memory

Zhihu Article

Original Chinese article and discussion

About Me && Blog

For my introduction and related articles:

  1. About me
  2. Blog navigation
  3. Android performance optimization: skills and tools
  4. Android performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

entry.title: Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - System Layer
entry.content:
Technical review · 2026-10-13. These cases and screenshots date from 2019. The review uses relevant Android 8.1/9/16 source, Linux v6.6 documentation, and current Android documentation while preserving the images and the author’s experience. Long slices, CPU numbers, reclaim activity, and input pacing are no longer treated as standalone proof of root cause. No original-device rerun or complete trace replay was performed, and missing conditions are not invented.

The Application Layer article covers app-side problems. Here we organize cases around system services, display, scheduling, and memory. Hardware, kernels, and vendor implementations differ, so retain the actual system version and configuration.

OEM and app teams may use Matrix or their own monitoring. System privileges can expose more evidence, but capture scope still depends on build type, kernel configuration, and enabled sources.

Smoothness is not simply average FPS. An average of 55 FPS over one second on a 60 Hz display does not locate the delayed frames or determine every user’s perception. Examine intended pacing, actual presentation intervals, and input response. Static screens need not submit content on every refresh. The four-part series is:

  • 0. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Methodology
  • 1. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - System Layer
  • 2. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Application Layer
  • 3. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Low Memory

System-Level Performance Case Studies

These are real cases I collected in 2019. Some surfaced during development, with a chance to fix them before release. Others only appeared after long use and were harder to investigate. Some needed a particular scenario or piece of hardware to show up at all.

Some images establish waiting, composition, or reclaim activity; device-specific implementations and final causes require the original traces, logs, and source. The screenshots do not identify a complete system build, so their explanations are not universal Android behavior.

The images use legacy Systrace; see the Systrace series for background. Prefer Perfetto for current captures. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, when the relevant data is captured, use FrameTimeline to examine expected/actual frames, deadlines, and presentation. Old colors, long slices, and missing slices are starting points for investigation.

1. SurfaceFlinger Main Thread Overhead

SurfaceFlinger coordinates layers and composition. Critical work missing its frame deadline can delay presentation; there is no universal per-call threshold that always drops one frame. HWC, GPU, and display-driver work can be asynchronous, so inspect fences and presentation relationships.

dequeueBuffer may wait for a free buffer, allocation, or synchronization. queueBuffer submits through the producer interface; neither call is universally a Binder call blocked directly inside SurfaceFlinger. Older BufferQueues may cross processes, while Android 16’s BLASTBufferQueue can create a local queue and submit buffers through transactions. Inspect the actual call path.

The first two images show composition and queue timing. The third selects about 28.02 ms and also contains allocateBuffers work. The fourth shows delayed frame production after waiting. These screenshots alone identify neither the responsible layer nor GPU execution time for the whole selection.

2. Under-Screen Ambient Light Sensor Screenshots

The original account concerns one device’s under-display ambient-light implementation using screen content to help estimate ambient light. The Chinese text mixed this up with under-display fingerprint sensing; they are different features. This is not a claim that every under-display sensor takes frequent screenshots.

A vendor feature can interfere with frames if it synchronously occupies composition threads, locks, or GPU resources. The selected 211.867 ms below spans multiple frames and does not show an identifiable capture call or sensor request. Confirm the account through request timing, capture paths, and a controlled comparison with the feature enabled or disabled.

3. HWC Service Execution Overhead

HWC means Hardware Composer. These images show a historical HIDL path through android.hardware.graphics.composer@2.2-service, including PresentDisplay and DRM Commit/AtomicCommit. Long calls can contain driver or fence waits rather than continuous CPU execution.

Composition, submission, and scanout are dependent stages, so delays can propagate toward app queues. A slow HWC call does not automatically mean SurfaceFlinger skips the next composition. In the third image, overlapping CRTC and HWC work does not establish that CRTC is waiting for HWC; inspect wait sites and completion signals. The fourth image is a different process recording, not another view of the same measurement.

4. CRTC Execution Overhead

The crtc_commit track belongs to a display-driver-related kernel thread; its slices are not direct measurements of panel scanout time. The image also shows long dequeueBuffer and setTransactionState activity. Follow Binder, lock, fence, and driver-completion dependencies.

A display-commit delay may block upstream work, but concurrent tracks alone do not establish CRTC as the cause of every wait or guarantee that the next frame will not be composed. Vendor drivers and Android versions change these paths.

5. CPU Scheduling Issues

Analyze thread state, CPU topology, allowed CPUs, scheduling policy/priority, frequency, and frame deadlines together. A CPU number is not a core type. Small-core placement, low frequency, or migration is not inherently a fault; the question is whether critical work finishes in time.

Critical Tasks on Small Cores

Insufficient CPU capacity for critical work can cause missed deadlines. However, the 22.558 ms selection below is a RenderingResponse interval without full topology or thread-state details; it is not directly a single frame’s CPU duration on a small core.

The next image labels RenderThread intervals of about 1.66 ms at 2.4 GHz and 8.6 ms at 0.7 GHz. This motivates inspecting frequency and scheduling, but is not a controlled experiment with identical workload, caches, core type, and waits. The Linux v6.6 EAS documentation explains capacity/energy tradeoffs; check the device kernel before assuming that policy applies.

Low Priority and Slice Delays

A thread on the user-visible critical path may have modest scheduling priority. For a long Runnable interval, inspect competition on its allowed CPUs, policy/priority, cpuset/affinity, and resource limits. Also check dependencies on lower-priority threads. A name or priority value alone does not prove priority inversion.

Preemption by Real-Time Threads

RT here means real-time scheduling, such as SCHED_FIFO/SCHED_RR; it is not an abbreviation for RenderThread, nor a classification applied uniformly to a whole process. Real-time work on an allowed CPU can delay ordinary threads. Verify the policy, preemption, and running intervals.

Android 9 ActivityManagerService contains a sys.use_fifo_ui path, disabled by default, that changes scheduling for TOP_APP UI/RenderThreads. This does not establish that every version leaves it off because startup becomes slower, and is not a recommendation to make all app threads real-time.

Core Binding and Migration

An unsuitable affinity/cpuset or task placement can restrict available capacity. My diagnosis of the CTS case at the time was that the threads were constrained to CPU 7 and contention caused a timeout. The screenshot does not include the affinity mask, complete scheduling policy, or CTS report, so it cannot independently verify that cause.

A single allowed CPU also does not mean the UI thread must wait until RenderThread finishes all its work: ordinary threads can be preempted and time-shared. Inspect allowed CPUs, running competitors, wait duration, and the test deadline.

6. Thermal Throttling

Thermal management can limit CPU/GPU frequency, power, or sustained performance and affect demanding scenes. Heat or downclocking does not inevitably cause jank. Correlate thermal state, frequency limits, and frame timing rather than inferring the cause from surface warmth or one frequency trace.

Android 10 (API 29) added thermal-status APIs, and Android 11 (API 30) added getThermalHeadroom. Headroom is an estimate, not a thermometer; verify support and validity. Reduce sustained load and compare at similar temperatures. Clearing background tasks or rebooting alone does not establish a fix.

7. High Background Activity

Background work can compete with foreground work for CPU, I/O, memory, or shared locks. Process count itself is not a load metric. Inspect active work and its relationship to the critical path instead of treating every background process as a fault.

CPU Saturation

dumpsys cpuinfo reports a time window rather than a single frame’s scheduling. Process values above 100% can reflect accumulated multi-core use, not a percentage of total device capacity; establish the window and denominator. The lowmemorykiller log explicitly includes “no selected tsk,” which is not evidence that those scans killed a process.

Runnable Thread States

Runnable means eligible to run but not currently on a CPU. A long wait on the critical path may miss its deadline, but causes can include allowed CPUs, priority, or quotas rather than every CPU being busy. The pictured thread is UnityGfxDeviceW, not an established app main thread; inspect state details and scheduling records.

Irrelevant Active Processes

Determine relevance from dependencies in the current interaction, not merely a name or background status. The table contains Wall Duration, Average Wall Duration, and Occurrences: aggregated elapsed durations and counts, not CPU utilization percentages. UnityMain and RenderThread may be foreground work. Return to the timeline to see whether these tasks compete on CPUs available to the critical thread.

Memory Reclamation Overhead

Memory pressure can increase reclaim work. kswapd performs background kernel reclaim, while HeapTaskDaemon executes ART heap-maintenance tasks; they are not threads frantically requesting memory. The name alone also does not prove every HeapTaskDaemon interval is GC; inspect GC/trim events.

The image shows activity, not proof that these threads occupy every CPU. Correlate reclaim events, PSI, page faults, running time, and foreground waits before concluding resource contention.

System Lock Contention

The roughly 93.633 ms selection contains several monitor-contention slices involving AMS activityIdle and RecentsAnimation.finishAnimation, supporting the observation of lock contention. Follow the owner thread and nested waits to distinguish computation while holding a lock, preemption, and downstream waiting.

Not every Binder request uses the same AMS/WMS lock, and the full selection is not one lock-hold duration. Delay propagates through requests that depend on the blocked critical section. Check modern lock and animation implementations by version.

8. Excessive Layers

Layers that need traversal, updating, or visible-region computation can add composition-preparation work, but background-app count is not a sufficient measure. The image shows rebuildLayerStacks/visibility work without layer counts or a controlled comparison.

This did not first move into the SurfaceFlinger refresh path in Android P: Android 8.1 SurfaceFlinger already calls rebuildLayerStacks from handleMessageRefresh, as does Android 9. Android 16 uses newer layer/CompositionEngine machinery; the old function name is not a stable interface. Investigate layer lifecycle, leaks, and transaction updates instead of treating routine task clearing as a fix.

9. Uneven Input Reporting

Irregular touch delivery can affect responsiveness, but missing input does not prevent all drawing: animations, flings, timers, and invalidation can continue updates. InputReader/Dispatcher slices are not a one-to-one copy of raw touch reports; batching, coalescing, filtering, and capture loss must be distinguished.

Use this overview to locate an interval, not to prove that the touch device omitted events. Correlate raw timestamps, Reader/Dispatcher/filter stages, app delivery, and presentation to distinguish absent events, delayed dispatch, and delayed app response.

10. LMK Resource Competition

Distinguish the historical LMK from modern userspace lmkd. The AOSP lmkd documentation describes PSI-based pressure detection supported in Android 10 and an updated Android 11 strategy that also considers thrashing, subject to kernel support and device configuration. Active reclaim threads do not mean lmkd itself occupies all CPUs.

  1. CPU: repeated kills and restarts can add work, but a killed cached process is not guaranteed to restart immediately through its “main process.” Match actual kill/start records, PIDs, and timestamps to establish a cycle.
  2. Memory: ART GC, kernel reclaim, and lmkd process killing are different mechanisms. Global memory pressure does not establish simultaneous GC in all processes.
  3. I/O: revisiting reclaimed file pages may require storage reads; anonymous pages may be swapped. With zram, compressed pages primarily reside in RAM, so swap is not always disk I/O. Configured writeback requires separate inspection of storage activity.

The first image is an aggregate list, not a kill/restart count. The second is identical to the HeapTaskDaemon/kswapd image in section 7; it reuses the same historical interval rather than supplying an independent experiment.

11. Low Memory I/O Latency

Memory pressure may add waits through direct reclaim, reloading file pages, swapping, or writeback, but each needs evidence. Startup, GC, JIT, and D state are not interchangeable proof of slow storage caused by low memory. Linux v6.6 vmscan describes reclaim paths; the zram documentation distinguishes compressed memory from optional writeback.

The first image shows NativeAlloc concurrent copying GC, resource loading, and long traversal work. It alone does not identify disk I/O. Assess the following subcases separately.

Main-Thread I/O Waits

Here the SystemUI main thread explicitly shows Uninterruptible Sleep - Block I/O with io_schedule as the wait site, supporting an I/O-related wait in that interval. Identifying a file, device, reclaim path, or lock still needs callstacks and I/O events. D state alone does not always mean disk I/O or prove memory pressure.

Startup Loading and I/O

The first image contains screen-recorder process initialization, bindApplication, OpenDexFilesFromOat, and oat loading. The second includes Application.onCreate, VerifyClass, and JIT. Loading may involve reads, page faults, verification, CPU work, and waits; the entire startup interval is not pure I/O. Also distinguish process initialization, first frame, and user-interactive readiness.

Page Waits During Scrolling

The Launcher main-thread selection is about 57.994 ms and shows Uninterruptible Sleep | WakeKill - Block I/O at wait_on_page_bit_killable. This supports a page-related wait, but does not alone identify a file, establish memory pressure, or diagnose faulty storage. Correlate page faults, reclaim, and block-I/O timing.

12. GPU Composition Overhead

HWC can assign some layers to client composition, which SurfaceFlinger composites through the GPU. This is a normal path. Its impact depends on pixel workload, GPU load, buffers/fences, and display deadlines; GPU composition is not inherently slow. See SurfaceFlinger and HWC.

The images show hasClientComposition alongside FrameMissed. The second selects about 22.291 ms and also annotates an HWC issue. This does not independently establish a GPU cause, nor make the SurfaceFlinger CPU slice or entire selection a GPU execution measurement.

13. KSWAPD CPU Usage

The image shows frequent kswapd0 activity on CPU 7. Its core type requires the SoC topology, and no temperature or throttling evidence appears here. It does not directly prove that big-core reclaim caused thermal throttling. Measure reclaim running time on relevant CPUs, foreground Runnable delay, and sustained memory pressure to assess contention.

14. Uneven SurfaceFlinger Vsync

The legacy VSYNC-sf track represents scheduling signals, not every physical presentation. Uneven spacing merits investigation, but distinguish refresh-rate/display-mode changes, phase adjustments, capture loss, and implementation faults. Colored block widths alone do not implicate a SurfaceFlinger or HWC change.

Modern systems support multiple refresh rates. Correlate modes, target periods, app production, and actual presentation, using FrameTimeline where supported, to distinguish intended policy from missed deadlines.

15. Accessibility Services

Some accessibility features enable input filtering or transformations, with processing in system_server before forwarding. Android 9 AccessibilityManagerService enables InputFilter according to features such as magnification, touch exploration, key filtering, or gesture injection. Merely having an Accessibility service or listening for accessibility events does not imply that same path. Android 16’s AccessibilityInputFilter also handles events according to enabled features.

The image suggests a change in Reader-to-Dispatcher pacing, not that every non-immediate wakeup is a system fault. Correlate event times, filtering/forwarding, and Handler/Binder waits, then compare the specific feature under controlled conditions.

Summary

These were my thoughts on the work in 2019.

Android is a constantly evolving system. Each version solves many performance issues but might introduce new ones. OEMs add substantial custom code, which further impacts performance.

The cases above are just the tip of the iceberg. This is why manufacturers are investing heavily in optimization—from hardware and software to learning from usage and adjusting system policies. Those who neglect quality for pure design often lose their market share.

For more details on what OEMs do, see: What do phone manufacturers actually do when they say they are optimizing Android?

This series continues:

  • 0. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Methodology
  • 1. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - System Layer
  • 2. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Application Layer
  • 3. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Low Memory

Original Chinese article and discussion

About Me && Blog

  1. About me
  2. Blog navigation

  4. Android performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

entry.title: Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Methodology
entry.content:
Technical review · 2026-10-13. This article retains the manufacturer’s optimization-team experience and industry opinions from 2019. The technical sections now distinguish Android 12 (API 31) FrameTimeline, JankStats, and Macrobenchmark. Looper logging was checked against AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 / android-16.0.0_r1; Matrix v2.1.0 is the documented feature baseline. No new device measurements were performed.

Jank issues in Android matter to both smartphone manufacturers and app developers. Internal performance or platform teams often investigate and optimize them.

Tools such as Tencent’s Matrix provide app-side performance evidence. Manufacturers can add their own instrumentation and use system source access and suitable debugging privileges to collect deeper data. Actual visibility still depends on the OS version, kernel configuration, build type, and enabled data sources.

Smoothness is not just average FPS. Two intervals averaging 55 FPS can contain very different frame spacing: one might include a noticeable pause, while another is more evenly paced. Consider the intended update cadence, actual presentation intervals, and input response together. Refresh intervals at 60/90/120 Hz are about 16.67/11.11/8.33 ms, but they are not fixed CPU budgets summed across every thread. A static screen need not submit new content on every refresh.

Causes can lie in the app, system, kernel, or display pipeline. This series has four parts:

  • 0. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Methodology
  • 1. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - System Layer
  • 2. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Application Layer
  • 3. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Low Memory

Locating the scenario and following its critical path remains useful. Prefer Perfetto/System Trace for new captures. On Android 12+ with the relevant frame data captured, use FrameTimeline to compare expected/actual frames, deadlines, and presentation relationships. Legacy Systrace remains useful for historical records; changing viewers cannot add data that was never captured. The tools below answer different questions.

1. Overview of Smoothness Work

As a member of a manufacturer’s optimization group, I should briefly describe our workflow. Many factors can cause jank in Android, but testing and users experience it most directly as dropped frames in the foreground app. Since they often can’t pinpoint the root cause, they report it to us as a general bug. We are the first stop for jank reports. We investigate, then pass the bug to the responsible team: Framework, App, Multimedia, Display, BSP, etc.

We rarely solve the technical bug ourselves. Instead, we use specialized tools combined with source code to locate issues. Our primary tools include:

  1. Perfetto/System Trace and ftrace place frames, scheduling, Binder, and kernel events on a timeline when the device permits and captures those sources.
  2. strace inspects system calls and results for selected processes/threads. It is not a whole-system performance trace, and attaching has permission requirements and overhead.
  3. Android Studio Profiler uses callstack sampling to locate CPU hotspots and Java/Kotlin method instrumentation to inspect specific calls. Those are different measurement methods.
  4. MAT and memory tools answer different questions. MAT analyzes Java heap objects and references offline; native allocations, process footprint, and system pressure require their corresponding profiler, meminfo, reclaim, or LMK evidence.
  5. Logs and log reports can contain Main/System/Event/Kernel/Crash logs, vendor Power/Performance logs, screenshots, and videos. Preserve their clocks, time ranges, and missing fields.
  6. Videos and local reproduction establish the interaction and visual symptom, then align it with a trace from the same run.

This takes some understanding of app development, the Android Framework, display systems, and the Linux kernel, plus practice with the tools. Once we find the cause, we discuss the fix with the people responsible for that module.

For changes that affect the system as a whole, we work with those teams on the solution. Sometimes we also develop a feature to address the problem.

2. Analysis Tools and Workflows

Start with the visible symptom and its time range, then narrow down to the relevant frame or interaction. A trace supplies leads; callstacks, source code, or controlled comparisons help establish the cause.

  1. Locate the frame and critical path. Record app/OS versions, device, refresh rate, actions, and cold/warm state. Where FrameTimeline is supported and captured, connect app-surface frames to their SurfaceFlinger frames, then inspect the main thread, RenderThread, Binder peers, and available GPU/fence tracks. The app and SurfaceFlinger main threads are entry points, not sufficient evidence for every jank. Games, independent Surfaces, and missing frame tracks require attention to their actual rendering paths. Missing tracks do not mean no jank.
  2. Separate execution from waiting. A long slice can contain CPU execution, Runnable scheduling delay, or lock/Binder/I/O waits. Use scheduling events and dependencies to decide where to investigate: app, system_server, SurfaceFlinger, HWC/display drivers, or resource contention. App deadline missed is a useful classification, not proof that app code alone caused the delay. The Systrace series remains useful background.
  3. Verify hotspots against source. The current Android Studio callstack-sampling task requires API 26+. Samples reveal hotspots, not a complete record of every invocation. Java/Kotlin method recording adds instrumentation overhead; the guide recommends recordings of roughly five seconds or less. Custom trace sections cover selected business operations, not an automatic full call tree. Breakpoints can verify control flow, but pause execution and invalidate normal frame-timing comparisons. Framework debugging additionally needs suitable system builds, symbols, and privileges.
  4. Add log context. Screenshots identify the UI, not jank duration; EventLog does not cover every user action. Align clocks before examining errors, process state, memory, and CPU records. In AOSP Looper, Slow delivery measures delay from the message’s scheduled time, msg.when, to dispatch start. Slow dispatch measures dispatch start to finish and may include waits; it is not CPU execution time. Thresholds, enablement, and suppression affect reporting, so absent logs do not establish zero delay.
  5. Reproduce and compare. High-speed video helps inspect visible pacing, but camera frame rate, display refresh rate, and recording overhead affect the observation. Keep device, version, temperature/load, and actions comparable. Capture repeated normal and abnormal runs, then compare after the fix without selecting only the best result.

The original state commands remain useful supporting entry points, subject to device permissions and version. They expose snapshots or aggregation windows, not an automatic reconstruction of an earlier frame:

CommandEvidence and limits
adb shell dumpsys activity oomProcess importance/OOM adjustment information, not proof of an OOM or LMK event
adb shell dumpsys meminfoProcess/system memory statistics; one value alone establishes neither a leak nor the cause of jank
adb shell cat /proc/buddyinfoFree blocks by node, zone, and order; each block is 2^order × PAGE_SIZE. Useful for physical allocation/fragmentation, not total available memory or a jank score
adb shell dumpsys cpuinfoCPU usage over a reporting window, not instantaneous per-thread scheduling at the jank
adb shell dumpsys inputInput-system state; fields vary by version
adb shell dumpsys windowWindow/focus state to correlate with input and frames from the same interval

See the dumpsys guide and Linux v6.6 proc documentation. Unavailable permissions, disabled sources, and lost data are missing evidence, not zero load.

3. Data-Driven Analysis

User reports do not always give us the full picture, and our tests cannot cover everything. Performance data collected by the system or app gives us another way to investigate: users need not report each incident, and we can look for patterns across many samples.

Field data helps identify recurring scenarios, but device coverage, versions, sampling rates, and metric definitions affect the result. Jank rates from different measurement methods cannot simply be merged.

The 2019 Matrix feature diagram below is historical, not a current compatibility list. Matrix v2.1.0 includes Android tools such as Trace Canary, Resource Canary, IO Canary, SQLite Lint, and APK Checker. Applications still need to select/configure plugins and handle Issue callbacks and reporting. A historical “compatible with Android P” label does not establish compatibility with every newer release.

Manufacturers, with their source code access, collect even deeper data: CPU load, I/O load, Memory pressure, FSync times, Exception monitoring, Thermal monitoring, and Storage health. Each category might have dozens of sub-metrics. Someone with experience still has to decide which measurements are useful, what to collect, and how to interpret the results.

This was my view of manufacturers’ work in 2019, not a ranking of their current capabilities. The subsequent optimization work tests a company’s R&D strength. High-tier manufacturers optimize at the hardware-software boundary (resource allocation), while others focus on scenario-based resource policies.

Keep field trends and local regressions distinct. Android Vitals, JankStats, and custom APM differ in coverage and measurement. JankStats uses FrameMetrics on API 24+ and other mechanisms on earlier versions; its configurable jank heuristic is not SurfaceFlinger’s FrameTimeline presentation classification. Record scenario and version distributions so sample changes are not mistaken for improvements.

Turn a suspect interaction into a repeatable Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric journey and compare distributions and frame counts under matching conditions. Available since library version 1.1.0, frameOverrunMs requires API 31 and measures time relative to the frame deadline. frameDurationCpuMs covers the UI-thread/RenderThread CPU-side frame-production interval, not complete GPU/display latency. On older devices, keep unavailable frameOverrunMs data missing rather than reporting zero. A benchmark does not automatically replay a field user’s complete state, and one P99 result does not establish an improvement for the entire user population.

4. Summary

Those are the tools and approaches I wanted to outline. My work is mainly in Framework and apps, so much of this comes from that side. Kernel optimization teams will probably have useful angles I have not covered here.

The original article cited a 2019 discussion of Android system optimization. Its hardware/ecosystem grouping is retained as historical opinion, not a current product-performance ranking:

  1. Apple: Inhouse chips, OS, and ecosystem. They have the tightest control from hardware to app layers.
  2. Samsung & Huawei: Inhouse chips/core components but sharing the Android OS/ecosystem. They can perform Chip-to-OS integration.
  3. Other Top Android OEMs: Rely on different SoCs (Qualcomm, MediaTek). Their optimizations are often software-policy-based since they don’t always control the deepest chip layers.

The other articles in this series are listed below.

  • 0. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Methodology
  • 1. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - System Layer
  • 2. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Application Layer
  • 3. Overview of Jank and Frame Drops in Android - Low Memory

Zhihu Article

Original Chinese article and discussion

About Me && Blog

For my introduction and related articles:

  1. About me
  2. Blog navigation
  3. Android performance optimization: skills and tools
  4. Android performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

entry.title: A Detailed Guide to Activity Launch Modes in Android
entry.content:
Technical review · 2026-10-13. The 2019 sequences remain historical examples. Task selection, affinity, and Recents behavior were checked against AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 and android-16.0.0_r1; Android 12 (API 31) singleInstancePerTask is added below. The old records lack a complete device build identifier, and no device rerun was performed for this review.

Android Activities have several important launch modes: standard, singleTop, singleTask, and singleInstance. Plenty of articles explain these modes. I wrote a small demo to show how they change the arrangement of activities in tasks. The newer singleInstancePerTask mode is covered afterward.

Ordinary navigation within a task is commonly LIFO. Below, A -> B denotes the sequence of launch actions; task contents are listed top first. Keep an eye on the task contents after each action; following the changes makes the differences easier to see. Repeating a launch action does not necessarily create an instance. A Task is not a process or necessarily one visible Recents card.

I put the demo on GitHub too: AndroidLunchModeTest. The reviewed snapshot is eaa1f987e332e0f85187a911ad9ae01cd20fff05, using compile/target SDK 29 and min SDK 26. Its package is com.example.lunchmodetest, whereas the historical sequences below retain com.example.launchmodetest.

Check all navigation targets for each case. In the snapshot, MainActivity.startSingleTopActivity launches SingleTaskActivity, and StandardActivity launches SingleInstanceWithAffinityActivity by default. Changing one target does not implement every sequence. The WithAffinity classes actually use empty affinity; SingleTopWithAffinityActivity does not even declare singleTop. Class names are not configuration evidence. The sample code was inspected for this review; the project was not modified or compiled.

The explanations assume the same user, ordinary foreground Activity launches, and no extra Intent flags unless stated. Updating the old project to target SDK 31+ also requires explicit android:exported for components with intent filters; use true for the Launcher entry.

standard Mode

The default mode creates a new instance in these examples, which launch from an Activity without additional Intent flags that change reuse behavior. The manifest mode alone does not describe every possible launch.

singleTop Mode

If the selected task already has the target Activity instance at its top, that instance receives onNewIntent(). An instance lower in the same task is not reused by singleTop alone. “Top” means the selected task’s top, not a single global stack for the device.

Test 1: SingleTopActivity below the top

Test 2: SingleTopActivity at the top

singleTask Mode

  1. The system searches for a reusable task under the launch conditions, beyond just the caller’s current task. It creates a task if no suitable one is found.
  2. If the selected task contains the target instance, the system delivers the new intent to it and removes activities above it. Otherwise, a new instance may be added to the selected task with matching affinity.
  3. In the original example, omitting taskAffinity inherits the app’s default affinity, which can select an existing task. It does not mean “always stay in the current task,” nor does singleTask unconditionally require the target to be the root.

Android 9’s ActivityStarter.getReusableIntentActivity and ActivityStack.findTaskLocked consider the component, user, document intent, and rootAffinity. Android 16’s ActivityStarter also separates task selection, clearing, and instance reuse.

Test 1: singleTask with default affinity

The old “Without Affinity” label means no explicit attribute, so default affinity applies. The following preserves the original sequence and task contents.

Test 2: singleTask with empty affinity

Despite its name, SingleTaskWithAffinity declares android:taskAffinity="": no affinity. It cannot match an ordinary task through shared affinity, so the first launch creates a task when no reusable target task exists. Later launches can still match the target component and reuse its task; an empty affinity does not force a new task every time.

singleTask Summary

  1. These configurations select different Tasks in the example. A Task is not the old framework ActivityStack container, so this does not imply creation of a new ActivityStack.
  2. A normal launch of StandardActivity from SingleTaskWithAffinity can place it in the same task despite a different default affinity.
  3. Launching SingleTaskWithAffinity again from another task can reuse its task and instance, removing activities above it.
  4. A separate Recents card depends on Recents management, exclusion flags, and system behavior, not just the class name or empty affinity.

singleInstance Mode

The singleInstance task contains only that Activity. Other activities it starts must use another task. The system looks for an existing instance of the same target component for the same user; this is not a Java singleton shared across users, work profiles, or process death.

My notes about a task being absent or present in “multitasking” describe the Recents cards I saw, not whether the Task exists. They are historical UI observations, not guarantees of the launch mode.

Test 1: singleInstance with default affinity

No explicit taskAffinity is supplied, so the default applies. StandardActivity returning to Task 0 below is this example’s task-selection result; another launch can select a different existing task or create one.

singleInstance Summary

  1. singleInstance owns a dedicated task, but does not guarantee that its Recents card is hidden.
  2. Reuse matches the user and target component, allowing delivery of onNewIntent. Configuration changes or process recreation can still create a new client-side Activity object.
  3. Activities started from it use another task selected by the system, not necessarily “the previous task.”

For example, Android 9 RecentTasks.findRemoveIndexForAddTask and Android 16 RecentTasks compare nonempty affinity, base intents, and other conditions when deduplicating/trimming ordinary task entries. Shared affinity can therefore affect cards, but the old notes do not establish the precise cause of each device observation.

Test 2: singleInstance with empty affinity

Here too, the old “With Affinity” label refers to android:taskAffinity="", meaning no affinity. The separate Recents card is retained as a historical observation; empty affinity does not disable singleInstance reuse.

Since Android 12: singleInstancePerTask

Android 12 (API 31) added singleInstancePerTask. The Activity must be the task root, with one instance of that component per task; other activities can still join the task.

An ordinary repeat launch can reuse the task and clear activities above the target. Suitable MULTIPLE_TASK or NEW_DOCUMENT launches can create instances of the component in separate tasks. This differs from singleInstance, whose task contains only one Activity. Document modes and flags still interact, so one flag is not an unconditional guarantee of a new instance. The 2019 demo does not implement this mode.

Intent Flags and onNewIntent

Caller flags also affect the outcome. These combinations are particularly relevant to the examples:

Launch optionEffect
SINGLE_TOPReuse a target already at the selected task’s top; it does not automatically find it lower down and clear intervening pages
NEW_TASKSearch for or create a task; it does not always create one
CLEAR_TOPClear activities above the target; for a standard target without SINGLE_TOP or another reuse condition, the target itself can also be finished and recreated
NEW_TASK + CLEAR_TASKClear the selected task’s old contents and make the new Activity its root; this is not an alias for CLEAR_TOP

See Android 16 ActivityStarter and Task.clearTopActivities. Background launches must also satisfy the applicable platform restrictions; launchMode does not grant background-start permission.

Reuse does not automatically consume new parameters. The Activity API documents that getIntent() still returns the previous Intent unless updated with setIntent. Process the new parameters in the callback. For example, inside an existing Activity class:

This fragment illustrates Intent replacement, not a complete demo. Inspect onCreate/onNewIntent, getTaskId, and task contents before and after each operation to distinguish a new task, a new Activity, and a reused instance receiving another Intent. The original am_new_intent is a historical system event name, not a guaranteed current log tag.

Key Concepts

TaskAffinity

taskAffinity expresses an Activity’s affinity for a task. It participates in task selection and permitted reparenting; it does not force all activities with the same affinity into one task. A normal startActivity call can place activities with different affinities in the caller’s task, and one app can have several tasks.

ConfigurationMeaning
No activity taskAffinity attributeInherit <application> affinity; the app default is its package name
android:taskAffinity=""No affinity, commonly represented as null in dumps
android:taskAffinity="com.example.launchmodetest.detail"An explicit nonempty affinity, not a Task ID

NEW_TASK-related searches and allowTaskReparenting use affinity together with component, user, flags, and task state. Affinity grants no permissions and does not make apps share a process. See the activity manifest reference.

Relationships: ActivityRecord, TaskRecord, ActivityStack

These names describe the older AMS container model used by the historical diagrams. They are not unchanged across all Android versions.

  1. ActivityRecord is a server-side Activity record in system_server. One Activity class can have multiple records; a record does not imply that one Java Activity object remains alive forever in the app process.
  2. TaskRecord groups ActivityRecords in a task. Ordinary navigation commonly behaves as LIFO, while clearing, reordering, and cross-task launches change the sequence.
  3. ActivityStack manages TaskRecords; ActivityDisplay groups stacks for a display, coordinated by ActivityStackSupervisor. There is not always one display object, nor a fixed total of Home/App/Recents stacks.


The referenced Gityuan article was published in 2017. Its container relationships help explain the old model; the diagram is not a modern multi-window architecture map.

The next image preserves the original adb shell dumpsys activity containers output. It shows display 0 and numStacks=5, already contradicting a fixed “three stacks” rule. Task 671 contains several ActivityRecords. Task IDs, stack IDs, and PIDs identify different things.

In android-16.0.0_r1, containers include RootWindowContainer, DisplayContent, TaskDisplayArea, Task, and TaskFragment. Task itself extends TaskFragment. Root/leaf tasks, nested Tasks, and embedded activities prevent a mechanical three-level replacement of the old diagram. TaskRecord and ActivityStack are not stable cross-version APIs. Dump commands and formatting also vary; no new device dump was produced for this review.

Activity Types

These are Android 9 WindowConfiguration activity-type constants, not launch modes. For example, type=standard and android:launchMode=”standard” describe different dimensions.

Android 16 WindowConfiguration additionally defines ACTIVITY_TYPE_DREAM = 5. These framework role classifications are not a way to declare an app as Home, Recents, or Assistant through launchMode.

If you found this useful, please share it. I hope it helps others too.

About Me && Blog

For my introduction and related articles:

  1. About me
  2. Blog navigation
  3. Android performance optimization: skills and tools
  4. Android performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

entry.title: Detailed Explanation of Hardware Layer in Android
entry.content:
Technical review · 2026-10-13. The 2019 screenshots and logs remain historical evidence, not a current-device benchmark. Source checks use AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 and android-16.0.0_r1. Cache behavior still matters, but the original claims about reallocating every frame, fixed performance rankings, and CPU load inferred from gfxinfo have been corrected. Case 6 repeats Case 1’s entire log; its measurement provenance is unresolved.

Hardware Acceleration vs. Software Acceleration

Many people confuse hardware acceleration with Hardware Layer in Android. Enabling hardware acceleration does not automatically give every View an explicit hardware layer. Before discussing layers, let’s look at hardware acceleration.

The original background articles remain historical reading: Android Hardware Acceleration Principles and Implementation and Understanding Android Hardware Acceleration for Beginners. Check the official Android guide for API support.

For View drawing, the software path rasterizes primarily on the CPU; hardware acceleration lets HWUI use the GPU for drawing. The CPU still handles layout, records drawing commands, and submits work. Skia also has GPU backends, so its presence does not establish software rendering.

View hardware acceleration arrived in Android 3.0 (API 11) and is enabled by default for apps targeting API 14 or later. Application, Activity, and Window configuration, as well as software layers on individual Views, affect the actual path. The articles above cover the code and principles. Here I want to take another angle and walk through those differences in the traces I used at the time.

Hardware-Accelerated App Performance

Take home-screen scrolling as an example. In the typical HWUI path on Android 5.0 (API 21) and later, the main thread and RenderThread cooperate to prepare a frame.

Zooming in shows input, animation, and conditional traversal work on the main thread, followed by rendering work on RenderThread. The old annotations group some measure/layout work under “Draw”; distinguish these using the actual slices and call paths.

These are CPU-thread slices. RenderThread duration is not GPU execution time, and command submission or eglSwapBuffers returning does not prove that a frame has reached the screen. When the main thread is released from a wait also depends on the rendering path.

Software-Accelerated App Performance

For the software-drawing comparison, I used Cloud Flash Pay. Scrolling in that case was noticeably jerky and unpleasant. The screenshot shows drawing and buildDrawingCache on the main thread without visible RenderThread work. This does not prove that the entire process never has a RenderThread, or describe every version of this app. Download historical Trace

The selected interval in the enlarged image is about 20.878 ms. It shows a long interval, not that every frame misses its deadline. Even if the app draws window contents on the CPU, subsequent system composition may use the GPU or a hardware composer.

Summary

  1. Hardware acceleration changes the View drawing path; it does not remove CPU work. RenderThread visibility alone is not an app-wide acceleration test.
  2. Software Views or windows can coexist with hardware-accelerated windows. App drawing and system composition are separate stages.
  3. Hardware acceleration usually suits modern View UIs, but its benefit depends on workload, resources, and device. Two screenshots cannot establish that it is always faster.
  4. Check unsupported drawing operations against the Android API version. Where needed, use a software layer on the affected View instead of disabling acceleration for the whole app.

Software Layer vs. Hardware Layer

Software Layer and Hardware Layer refer to offscreen pixel caches for a View. They are distinct from SurfaceFlinger composition layers and from the hardware-acceleration setting for an entire window.

A View has three layer types:

  1. LAYER_TYPE_NONE: no extra explicit View pixel layer.
  2. LAYER_TYPE_SOFTWARE: draw View content through the software path into a Bitmap, including inside a hardware-accelerated window.
  3. LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE: use a GPU offscreen layer in a hardware-accelerated View hierarchy; otherwise behave as a software layer.

LAYER_TYPE_NONE

This is the default. It does not disable hardware acceleration or require all work to start from scratch: the hardware path can still reuse drawing commands recorded in RenderNodes/display lists.

LAYER_TYPE_SOFTWARE

How is a software layer implemented? In simple terms, it caches the View content in a Bitmap. This allocation fragment comes from Android 9 View.java; its variables belong to the surrounding framework code:

Invalid content requires a redraw. An existing Bitmap of the same dimensions can be reused; redraw does not necessarily mean destruction and reallocation.

The role of Software layer:

  1. In software rendering, a layer can apply opacity, color filtering, or blending to a View and its children as a group.
  2. In hardware rendering, it can handle local operations unsupported by that version’s hardware path; caching stable content may also reduce repeated drawing.
  3. Frequent updates incur software redraws and texture-upload work in the hardware path. A software layer is not a universal animation optimization.

LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE

A hardware layer draws View content into an offscreen GPU resource for later window drawing. FBO is a useful description for an OpenGL backend, not a universal implementation across Android versions and Skia GL/Vulkan backends. The View hierarchy must be hardware accelerated; otherwise the layer behaves as a software layer.

The role of Hardware layer:

Hardware layers can apply blending effects to a group and reduce repeated drawing of stable, complex content during translation, alpha, scale, or rotation animations. Caching also affects clipping and sampling in rotation or 3D transforms; it does not guarantee sharper or faster scaling.

Use the layer temporarily and restore its previous type. This example assumes UI-thread execution and exclusive control of the View’s layerType:

ObjectAnimator cancellation also invokes the end callback. Do not let overlapping animations manage the same View’s layerType. Since API 16, withLayer() lets ViewPropertyAnimator restore the type captured at the call when the animation ends or is canceled:

Transform-only changes may reuse cached content. Text changes, child additions/removals, or other content invalidation require redraws. Reallocation depends on dimensions, resource state, and backend; “the FBO is destroyed” is not a valid general description.

Summary

  1. Software and hardware layers use different pixel-caching paths. Choose based on supported drawing operations and measured cost.
  2. Hardware layers may benefit property animations of stable, complex content; compare against the default NONE path.
  3. Restore the previous type afterward instead of retaining an unnecessary layer. Graphics resources may be released later or reused internally; process memory need not drop immediately.

Performance Problem Cases Caused by Incorrect LayerType Usage

Performance Problems Caused by Incorrect Software Layer Usage

This historical WeChat Moments trace shows repeated buildDrawingCache/SW work on the main thread. Investigate content updates and invalidation that cause repeated software drawing; the slice alone does not prove allocation of a new Bitmap each time. Download historical Trace

Scrolling that large Moments image felt very jerky. Zooming into the trace shows long drawing work. Check whether repeated software drawing can be avoided, and inspect scheduling and other work before assigning the cause of jank.

Code Flow

Distinguish the two branches of buildLayer(). These excerpts from Android 9 View.java show that only LAYER_TYPE_SOFTWARE follows buildDrawingCache → buildDrawingCacheImpl; the hardware branch delegates to ThreadedRenderer. These framework fragments depend on class fields.

The trace covers cache drawing, not a dedicated allocation event. buildDrawingCacheImpl allocates when the Bitmap is absent or its dimensions differ; otherwise it can clear and redraw the existing Bitmap. The old drawing-cache API was deprecated in API 28 and is not a recommended modern optimization entry point for app code.

Performance Problems Caused by Incorrect Hardware Layer Usage

This historical folder-opening case has several icons using hardware layers and repeated layer drawing on RenderThread. Frequently changing content can offset caching benefits through extra offscreen work. These slices alone do not prove that a buffer is destroyed and reallocated every frame. Download historical Trace

The selected interval is about 21.68 ms, with one ShortcutIcon layer-drawing slice lasting about 4.783 ms. Keep a single slice, a whole frame, and GPU execution time separate.

For example, Android 9 SkiaPipeline::createOrUpdateLayer checks layer existence and dimensions and can reuse existing resources. Content redraw and resource allocation are different operations.

Debugging Tools

Some historical systems expose “Show hardware layers updates” in developer options. Its location and availability vary by version and vendor; it is not necessarily under Accessibility.

It highlights updated layer regions, not necessarily the entire interface. For a transform animation of stable content, reuse after initialization is desirable. Continuous highlighting is a reason to inspect update sources, but dynamic content legitimately needs updates. Absence of highlighting alone proves neither caching behavior nor performance. Inspect layer drawing, dimensions, and frame timing together.

Summary

  1. Check content stability and drawing complexity before adding a hardware layer to a property animation.
  2. Do not add layers indiscriminately. Cache creation, memory use, offscreen drawing, and subsequent window drawing all have costs.
  3. Additional offscreen work for alpha depends on overlapping content and rendering paths. Not every setAlpha call or opacity animation creates the same kind of buffer.
  4. Invalidation may require redraw, but not necessarily reallocation of an entire resource. Compare NONE with layer paths when content changes frequently instead of assuming a fixed ranking.
  5. Restore the prior layerType after temporary changes. Use software layers locally where compatibility or measured benefit justifies them.

Examples of LayerType’s Impact on Animation Performance

Example

Code

To compare the situations discussed above, I wrote a small example with just two TextViews: one starts the animation and one animates TRANSLATION_X, ALPHA, TRANSLATION_Y, SCALE_X, and SCALE_Y. Start/end listeners select a layer; the update listener controls text changes.

The example project at this source snapshot (0060782a6c32337641acc14af3f9b4e8818402a3) sets HARDWARE and then SOFTWARE consecutively in its start callback. SOFTWARE wins, and text updates are enabled. Running that snapshot unchanged does not produce six independent comparisons. It is a historical project with compile/target SDK 29 and min SDK 26.

The code retains the original 500 ms duration, 150 px translations, alpha target 0, and 150× scaleX/scaleY targets. These are not ordinary UI values. Dynamic cases append text every frame, adding string allocation, text measurement, and layout changes; differences cannot be attributed solely to layers.

These are syntax-corrected illustrative fragments, not newly measured code underlying the old logs. Install only one case’s listeners, replacing the default listeners below; do not accumulate all six. Use a fresh AnimatorSet and reset the View to layer NONE, original text, counter 0, alpha 1, scaleX/scaleY 1, and translationX/Y 0 before each run. Wait for layout and prevent overlapping runs. Resetting to NONE at the end is valid only under this explicit initial condition. Fields, View initialization, and imports still require the complete project.

Statistics Tool: GFXInfo

Alongside Systrace, I used adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo <package> to record HWUI frame statistics. Read the old annotations in this screenshot with the following corrections:

  1. Janky frames follow the system’s frame-interval/deadline rules, not a universal 16 ms threshold. Histograms and percentiles are bucketed; the 99th percentile is not the exact maximum.
  2. High input latency measures neither CPU load nor input-callback execution time. Android 9 JankTracker has a triple-buffering/deferred-deadline branch that can record high input latency without a missed deadline. Reason counters also cannot simply be added to obtain the janky-frame total.
  3. Android 16 JankTracker retains legacy and newer deadline accounting. For current comparisons, record the OS version, refresh rate, measurement interval, and original output. gfxinfo does not cover complete input-to-display latency.
  4. These historical samples contain only 29–31 frames each, with insufficient device, OS, and reset-condition records. Cases 1 and 6 have identical logs, including the histogram; they are not confirmed independent measurements. No device rerun or replacement data was produced for this review.

Case 1: Normal Layer + No Dynamic View Content Update

Code

Systrace Phenomenon

The screenshot contains yellow frame markers and a long flush commands slice on RenderThread. This is CPU-side work or waiting, not a direct GPU-duration measurement. Download historical Trace

gfxInfo Data

The preserved log reports 14/30 janky frames (46.67%), 99th percentile 32 ms, and High input latency 30. These are historical sample statistics, not a main-thread CPU-load measurement.

Case 2: Software Layer + No Dynamic View Content Update

Code

Systrace Phenomenon

The screenshot shows buildDrawingCache/SW initially, without the same cache-drawing work in the displayed later transform frames. This is consistent with reusing stable content. Green markers do not replace complete frame timing and repeated measurements. Download historical Trace

gfxInfo Data

The preserved log reports 1/31 janky frames (3.23%), 99th percentile 16 ms, and High input latency 0.

Case 3: Hardware Layer + No Dynamic View Content Update

Code

Systrace Phenomenon

The screenshot shows initial drawLayer work and green markers in the displayed frames. It supports investigating cache reuse, not a universal performance or input-latency claim. Download historical Trace

gfxInfo Data

The preserved log reports 0/31 janky frames (0.00%), 99th percentile 14 ms, and High input latency 0.

Case 4: Normal Layer + Dynamic View Content Update

Code

Systrace Phenomenon

Appending text introduces long Animation, measure, layout, and draw slices. Separate text updates, layout work, and scheduling waits. Download historical Trace

gfxInfo Data

The preserved log reports 12/31 janky frames (38.71%), 99th percentile 29 ms, and High input latency 31.

Case 5: Software Layer + Dynamic View Content Update

Code

Systrace Phenomenon

Repeated buildDrawingCache work shows software-cache redraws. It does not prove destruction of a Bitmap every frame or establish a single bottleneck for all elapsed time. Download historical Trace

gfxInfo Data

The preserved log reports 12/29 janky frames (41.38%), 99th percentile 32 ms, and High input latency 18.

Case 6: Hardware Layer + Dynamic View Content Update

Code

Systrace Phenomenon

Repeated drawLayer work appears while growing text changes content dimensions; the layer dimensions differ from the static case. Resizing can require allocation, but these slices do not establish buffer reallocation every frame. Download historical Trace

gfxInfo Data

The preserved log reports 14/30 janky frames (46.67%), 99th percentile 32 ms, and High input latency 30. These are historical sample statistics, not a main-thread CPU-load measurement. This entire block duplicates Case 1, including its histogram. Its independent provenance is unverified, so exclude it from quantitative comparisons.

Summary

The cases preserve a useful observation: caching may help stable content, while changing content needs redraws. They do not establish the original fixed performance rankings. Samples are small, Cases 1 and 6 duplicate data, and growing text changes the workload.

  1. For stable, expensive-to-draw Views, compare temporary hardware layers against NONE using frame timing, memory, and GPU cost.
  2. For dynamic content, inspect invalidation and size changes before assessing extra offscreen work. Do not assume that NONE or any layer type always wins.
  3. Repeated buildDrawingCache/drawLayer slices are investigation leads, not evidence of reallocation every frame or sufficient grounds to blame a system/vendor issue.
  4. Fix the version, refresh rate, initial state, and repetition count for current-device comparisons. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, Perfetto FrameTimeline can add expected/actual-frame evidence when that data is captured; missing data does not mean no jank.

For modern implementation details, compare Android 16 View, RenderNode, SkiaPipeline, and ViewPropertyAnimator. These source tags identify implementation boundaries; they do not imply that the historical experiment was reproduced on an Android 16 device.
