entry.title: A Deep Dive into Hardware Layers in Android
entry.content:
Technical review · 2026-10-13. The 2019 screenshots and logs remain historical evidence, not a current-device benchmark. Source checks use AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 and android-16.0.0_r1. Cache behavior still matters, but the original claims about reallocating every frame, fixed performance rankings, and CPU load inferred from gfxinfo have been corrected. Case 6 repeats Case 1’s entire log; its measurement provenance is unresolved.

Hardware Acceleration vs. Software Acceleration

Many people confuse hardware acceleration with Hardware Layer in Android. Enabling hardware acceleration does not automatically give every View an explicit hardware layer. Before discussing layers, let’s look at hardware acceleration.

The original background articles remain historical reading: Android Hardware Acceleration Principles and Implementation and Understanding Android Hardware Acceleration for Beginners. Check the official Android guide for API support.

For View drawing, the software path rasterizes primarily on the CPU; hardware acceleration lets HWUI use the GPU for drawing. The CPU still handles layout, records drawing commands, and submits work. Skia also has GPU backends, so its presence does not establish software rendering.

View hardware acceleration arrived in Android 3.0 (API 11) and is enabled by default for apps targeting API 14 or later. Application, Activity, and Window configuration, as well as software layers on individual Views, affect the actual path. The articles above cover the code and principles. Here I want to take another angle and walk through those differences in the traces I used at the time.

Hardware-Accelerated App Performance

Take home-screen scrolling as an example. In the typical HWUI path on Android 5.0 (API 21) and later, the main thread and RenderThread cooperate to prepare a frame.

Zooming in shows input, animation, and conditional traversal work on the main thread, followed by rendering work on RenderThread. The old annotations group some measure/layout work under “Draw”; distinguish these using the actual slices and call paths.

These are CPU-thread slices. RenderThread duration is not GPU execution time, and command submission or eglSwapBuffers returning does not prove that a frame has reached the screen. When the main thread is released from a wait also depends on the rendering path.

Software-Accelerated App Performance

For the software-drawing comparison, I used Cloud Flash Pay. Scrolling in that case was noticeably jerky and unpleasant. The screenshot shows drawing and buildDrawingCache on the main thread without visible RenderThread work. This does not prove that the entire process never has a RenderThread, or describe every version of this app. Download historical Trace

The selected interval in the enlarged image is about 20.878 ms. It shows a long interval, not that every frame misses its deadline. Even if the app draws window contents on the CPU, subsequent system composition may use the GPU or a hardware composer.

Summary

  1. Hardware acceleration changes the View drawing path; it does not remove CPU work. RenderThread visibility alone is not an app-wide acceleration test.
  2. Software Views or windows can coexist with hardware-accelerated windows. App drawing and system composition are separate stages.
  3. Hardware acceleration usually suits modern View UIs, but its benefit depends on workload, resources, and device. Two screenshots cannot establish that it is always faster.
  4. Check unsupported drawing operations against the Android API version. Where needed, use a software layer on the affected View instead of disabling acceleration for the whole app.

Software Layer vs. Hardware Layer

Software Layer and Hardware Layer refer to offscreen pixel caches for a View. They are distinct from SurfaceFlinger composition layers and from the hardware-acceleration setting for an entire window.

A View has three layer types:

  1. LAYER_TYPE_NONE: no extra explicit View pixel layer.
  2. LAYER_TYPE_SOFTWARE: draw View content through the software path into a Bitmap, including inside a hardware-accelerated window.
  3. LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE: use a GPU offscreen layer in a hardware-accelerated View hierarchy; otherwise behave as a software layer.

LAYER_TYPE_NONE

This is the default. It does not disable hardware acceleration or require all work to start from scratch: the hardware path can still reuse drawing commands recorded in RenderNodes/display lists.

LAYER_TYPE_SOFTWARE

How is a software layer implemented? In simple terms, it caches the View content in a Bitmap. This allocation fragment comes from Android 9 View.java; its variables belong to the surrounding framework code:

Invalid content requires a redraw. An existing Bitmap of the same dimensions can be reused; redraw does not necessarily mean destruction and reallocation.

The role of Software layer:

  1. In software rendering, a layer can apply opacity, color filtering, or blending to a View and its children as a group.
  2. In hardware rendering, it can handle local operations unsupported by that version’s hardware path; caching stable content may also reduce repeated drawing.
  3. Frequent updates incur software redraws and texture-upload work in the hardware path. A software layer is not a universal animation optimization.

LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE

A hardware layer draws View content into an offscreen GPU resource for later window drawing. FBO is a useful description for an OpenGL backend, not a universal implementation across Android versions and Skia GL/Vulkan backends. The View hierarchy must be hardware accelerated; otherwise the layer behaves as a software layer.

The role of Hardware layer:

Hardware layers can apply blending effects to a group and reduce repeated drawing of stable, complex content during translation, alpha, scale, or rotation animations. Caching also affects clipping and sampling in rotation or 3D transforms; it does not guarantee sharper or faster scaling.

Use the layer temporarily and restore its previous type. This example assumes UI-thread execution and exclusive control of the View’s layerType:

ObjectAnimator cancellation also invokes the end callback. Do not let overlapping animations manage the same View’s layerType. Since API 16, withLayer() lets ViewPropertyAnimator restore the type captured at the call when the animation ends or is canceled:

Transform-only changes may reuse cached content. Text changes, child additions/removals, or other content invalidation require redraws. Reallocation depends on dimensions, resource state, and backend; “the FBO is destroyed” is not a valid general description.

Summary

  1. Software and hardware layers use different pixel-caching paths. Choose based on supported drawing operations and measured cost.
  2. Hardware layers may benefit property animations of stable, complex content; compare against the default NONE path.
  3. Restore the previous type afterward instead of retaining an unnecessary layer. Graphics resources may be released later or reused internally; process memory need not drop immediately.

Performance Problem Cases Caused by Incorrect LayerType Usage

Performance Problems Caused by Incorrect Software Layer Usage

This historical WeChat Moments trace shows repeated buildDrawingCache/SW work on the main thread. Investigate content updates and invalidation that cause repeated software drawing; the slice alone does not prove allocation of a new Bitmap each time. Download historical Trace

Scrolling that large Moments image felt very jerky. Zooming into the trace shows long drawing work. Check whether repeated software drawing can be avoided, and inspect scheduling and other work before assigning the cause of jank.

Code Flow

Distinguish the two branches of buildLayer(). These excerpts from Android 9 View.java show that only LAYER_TYPE_SOFTWARE follows buildDrawingCache → buildDrawingCacheImpl; the hardware branch delegates to ThreadedRenderer. These framework fragments depend on class fields.

The trace covers cache drawing, not a dedicated allocation event. buildDrawingCacheImpl allocates when the Bitmap is absent or its dimensions differ; otherwise it can clear and redraw the existing Bitmap. The old drawing-cache API was deprecated in API 28 and is not a recommended modern optimization entry point for app code.

Performance Problems Caused by Incorrect Hardware Layer Usage

This historical folder-opening case has several icons using hardware layers and repeated layer drawing on RenderThread. Frequently changing content can offset caching benefits through extra offscreen work. These slices alone do not prove that a buffer is destroyed and reallocated every frame. Download historical Trace

The selected interval is about 21.68 ms, with one ShortcutIcon layer-drawing slice lasting about 4.783 ms. Keep a single slice, a whole frame, and GPU execution time separate.

For example, Android 9 SkiaPipeline::createOrUpdateLayer checks layer existence and dimensions and can reuse existing resources. Content redraw and resource allocation are different operations.

Debugging Tools

Some historical systems expose “Show hardware layers updates” in developer options. Its location and availability vary by version and vendor; it is not necessarily under Accessibility.

It highlights updated layer regions, not necessarily the entire interface. For a transform animation of stable content, reuse after initialization is desirable. Continuous highlighting is a reason to inspect update sources, but dynamic content legitimately needs updates. Absence of highlighting alone proves neither caching behavior nor performance. Inspect layer drawing, dimensions, and frame timing together.

Summary

  1. Check content stability and drawing complexity before adding a hardware layer to a property animation.
  2. Do not add layers indiscriminately. Cache creation, memory use, offscreen drawing, and subsequent window drawing all have costs.
  3. Additional offscreen work for alpha depends on overlapping content and rendering paths. Not every setAlpha call or opacity animation creates the same kind of buffer.
  4. Invalidation may require redraw, but not necessarily reallocation of an entire resource. Compare NONE with layer paths when content changes frequently instead of assuming a fixed ranking.
  5. Restore the prior layerType after temporary changes. Use software layers locally where compatibility or measured benefit justifies them.

Examples of LayerType’s Impact on Animation Performance

Example

Code

To compare the situations discussed above, I wrote a small example with just two TextViews: one starts the animation and one animates TRANSLATION_X, ALPHA, TRANSLATION_Y, SCALE_X, and SCALE_Y. Start/end listeners select a layer; the update listener controls text changes.

The example project at this source snapshot (0060782a6c32337641acc14af3f9b4e8818402a3) sets HARDWARE and then SOFTWARE consecutively in its start callback. SOFTWARE wins, and text updates are enabled. Running that snapshot unchanged does not produce six independent comparisons. It is a historical project with compile/target SDK 29 and min SDK 26.

The code retains the original 500 ms duration, 150 px translations, alpha target 0, and 150× scaleX/scaleY targets. These are not ordinary UI values. Dynamic cases append text every frame, adding string allocation, text measurement, and layout changes; differences cannot be attributed solely to layers.

These are syntax-corrected illustrative fragments, not newly measured code underlying the old logs. Install only one case’s listeners, replacing the default listeners below; do not accumulate all six. Use a fresh AnimatorSet and reset the View to layer NONE, original text, counter 0, alpha 1, scaleX/scaleY 1, and translationX/Y 0 before each run. Wait for layout and prevent overlapping runs. Resetting to NONE at the end is valid only under this explicit initial condition. Fields, View initialization, and imports still require the complete project.

Statistics Tool: GFXInfo

Alongside Systrace, I used adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo <package> to record HWUI frame statistics. Read the old annotations in this screenshot with the following corrections:

  1. Janky frames follow the system’s frame-interval/deadline rules, not a universal 16 ms threshold. Histograms and percentiles are bucketed; the 99th percentile is not the exact maximum.
  2. High input latency measures neither CPU load nor input-callback execution time. Android 9 JankTracker has a triple-buffering/deferred-deadline branch that can record high input latency without a missed deadline. Reason counters also cannot simply be added to obtain the janky-frame total.
  3. Android 16 JankTracker retains legacy and newer deadline accounting. For current comparisons, record the OS version, refresh rate, measurement interval, and original output. gfxinfo does not cover complete input-to-display latency.
  4. These historical samples contain only 29–31 frames each, with insufficient device, OS, and reset-condition records. Cases 1 and 6 have identical logs, including the histogram; they are not confirmed independent measurements. No device rerun or replacement data was produced for this review.

Case 1: Normal Layer + No Dynamic View Content Update

Code

Systrace Phenomenon

The screenshot contains yellow frame markers and a long flush commands slice on RenderThread. This is CPU-side work or waiting, not a direct GPU-duration measurement. Download historical Trace

gfxInfo Data

The preserved log reports 14/30 janky frames (46.67%), 99th percentile 32 ms, and High input latency 30. These are historical sample statistics, not a main-thread CPU-load measurement.

Case 2: Software Layer + No Dynamic View Content Update

The screenshot shows buildDrawingCache/SW initially, without the same cache-drawing work in the displayed later transform frames. This is consistent with reusing stable content. Green markers do not replace complete frame timing and repeated measurements. Download historical Trace

The preserved log reports 1/31 janky frames (3.23%), 99th percentile 16 ms, and High input latency 0.

Case 3: Hardware Layer + No Dynamic View Content Update

The screenshot shows initial drawLayer work and green markers in the displayed frames. It supports investigating cache reuse, not a universal performance or input-latency claim. Download historical Trace

The preserved log reports 0/31 janky frames (0.00%), 99th percentile 14 ms, and High input latency 0.

Appending text introduces long Animation, measure, layout, and draw slices. Separate text updates, layout work, and scheduling waits. Download historical Trace

Case 6: Hardware Layer + Dynamic View Content Update

The cases preserve a useful observation: caching may help stable content, while changing content needs redraws. They do not establish the original fixed performance rankings. Samples are small, Cases 1 and 6 duplicate data, and growing text changes the workload.

  1. For stable, expensive-to-draw Views, compare temporary hardware layers against NONE using frame timing, memory, and GPU cost.
  2. For dynamic content, inspect invalidation and size changes before assessing extra offscreen work. Do not assume that NONE or any layer type always wins.
  3. Repeated buildDrawingCache/drawLayer slices are investigation leads, not evidence of reallocation every frame or sufficient grounds to blame a system/vendor issue.
  4. Fix the version, refresh rate, initial state, and repetition count for current-device comparisons. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, Perfetto FrameTimeline can add expected/actual-frame evidence when that data is captured; missing data does not mean no jank.

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Analyzing Systrace
entry.content:
Technical update — 2026-10-13: Historical Systrace screenshots are retained, including cases added after the original 2019 article. Colors and shortcuts refer to the legacy UI. Linux state semantics are checked against v6.6 documentation; the modern UI reference is Perfetto v58.3 (11fbaed83). Inaccurate Self Time, wakeup and scheduling-state annotations in the images are corrected in the adjacent text. These are not new device measurements.

This is the second article in the Systrace series, primarily explaining the prerequisites for analyzing Systrace. With these prerequisites, analyzing Systrace will be more effective, allowing you to identify issues faster and more efficiently.

This article introduces how to view thread states in Systrace, how to analyze thread wakeup information, how to interpret data in the information panel, and common shortcuts. By studying this article, you will gain an understanding of process and thread-related information and know how to extract key information from complex Systrace traces.

Table of Contents

  • Series Article Index
  • Main Content
  • Reading This Article with Perfetto
  • Viewing Thread States
  • Analyzing Thread Wakeup Information
  • Data Parsing in Information Panel
  • Using Shortcuts
  • Zhihu Article Link
  • About Me && Blog

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

Main Content

Reading This Article with Perfetto

This article builds the basic skills needed before analyzing a trace: thread states, wakeup relationships, information-panel fields, and navigation shortcuts. The old Systrace UI and the current Perfetto UI look different, but these skills remain the same foundation.

In the old flow, Systrace HTML used colors to show thread states directly, and clicking a slice exposed fields such as duration, thread, process, and wakeup information in the lower panel. In the current flow, Perfetto spreads the same evidence across thread tracks, CPU scheduling tracks, the selection panel, search results, and SQL tables. The workflow changes from “read one HTML view” to “read tracks first, then narrow evidence with search or SQL.”

Use this mapping while reading:

Topic in this articlePerfetto entry point
Opening, zooming, searching, selecting slicesPerfetto 3: Perfetto View
Running, Runnable, Sleep, and similar thread statesPerfetto 9: CPU information
Main-thread waits, RenderThread waits, Binder waitsPerfetto 7: MainThread and RenderThread / Perfetto 10: Binder scheduling and lock contention

Viewing Thread States

When scheduling data is captured, legacy Systrace uses thread-state strips to help interpret slices. A slice is an instrumented interval, not necessarily an entire method. States narrow an investigation; they do not by themselves prove that Binder, a lock, I/O or CPU execution is the root cause. The colors below refer to the historical images. Read the State field and underlying events rather than relying on color alone.

When using Perfetto for the same problem today, do not look only for colors that match the old Systrace UI. A more reliable method is to read three signals together: slices on the thread track, actual running intervals on CPU tracks, and scheduling states such as Runnable, Sleep, and Uninterruptible Sleep. That is how you separate “the function itself is slow,” “the thread woke up but did not get CPU,” and “the thread is waiting for Binder, a lock, or I/O.”

Main thread states include:

Green: Running

The viewer shows a thread scheduled on a logical CPU during this interval, not merely ready and queued. Linux TASK_RUNNING and the R shown by ps include both executing and runnable tasks; the viewer distinguishes these using scheduling events. One thread cannot execute on two logical CPUs simultaneously, though it can migrate between intervals.

We often compare Running time for the same scenario: why is it faster here and slower there? Is the frequency different, is it running on another core, or is it repeatedly switching between Running, Runnable and Sleep? Read those clues alongside the CPU topology and scheduling events. A small core or lower frequency is not inherently a scheduling error; consider workload, power policy, thermals and the critical path. The image shows android.bg Running on CPU 0 for 41.743 ms. That describes this interval, not an entire method or the whole process.

Blue: Runnable

The thread is eligible to run but is not currently executing on a CPU. It may have been awakened or preempted. Delay depends on its allowed CPUs, priority, scheduling class, CPU quotas/throttling and competing work.

A long Runnable interval suggests scheduling latency, not necessarily that every CPU is busy, frequency is too low or too many background apps exist. Inspect the CPUs the thread may use, what they were running, and evidence of throttling, preemption or wakeup migration.

White: Sleep

This usually means interruptible sleep while awaiting an event, timer, Binder activity or synchronization condition. It can be healthy idleness or a critical-path wait for a result. Waiting does not imply there is no work left to complete.

The image shows audioserver’s Binder:1506_2 Sleeping at binder_thread_read. This is a clue about waiting for Binder-related events, not proof of mutex contention or a performance fault.

Orange: Uninterruptible Sleep - IO Block

The image’s State is Uninterruptible Sleep | WakeKill - Block I/O, and the displayed blocked function is wait_on_page_bit_killable, not the original text’s wait_on_page_locked_killable. Scheduling events and additional blocked-reason/I/O-wait data contribute to this interpretation. Availability depends on the kernel, permissions and recording configuration.

Investigate page-related waiting alongside faults, reclaim, storage requests and blocked stacks. Cold file reads, page locking or memory pressure may contribute; neither orange coloring nor this function name proves low memory or a busy disk. WakeKill also matters: “uninterruptible” does not mean every signal is always ineffective. Linux killable waits include wakeup by fatal signals.

Purple: Uninterruptible Sleep

This image explicitly says Uninterruptible Sleep. That does not mean “usually memory management,” nor simply that execution entered kernel mode. A thread executing a system call can still be Running. Uninterruptible waits may involve drivers, synchronization or other kernel resources; investigate the actual blocked location.

The pictured thread is [crtc_commit:127], with display-composition tracks nearby. Do not classify this as low memory from the color. Legacy viewers also reuse similar colors for other states, so inspect the State field.

Analyzing Thread Wakeup Information

Systrace identifies a very useful piece of information that helps us analyze thread calls and wait relationships.

A wakeup identifies a scheduling relationship: an execution context made the target runnable. It does not necessarily identify a lock owner, result producer or original root cause. Interrupt context, delegated wakeups, timeouts and missing events need separate investigation. After waking, the thread may still wait for CPU; separate sleeping time, wakeup-to-running delay and actual Running time.

For example, a synchronous Binder caller may wait for service execution, a lock or scheduling. This is a hypothesis to verify, not a general explanation for every slowdown after Monkey or with many background processes. Correlate the request/reply, peer thread and lock-owner evidence.

In the historical case below, the selection spans about 152.78 ms across Choreographer#doFrame / traversal, with substantial non-Running time visible in the state strip. That span merits investigation, but does not represent 152.78 ms of CPU execution or establish full input latency or a current device’s dropped-frame rate.

Zooming in, the selected Runnable interval shows wakeup from tid: 20424. Running instead is a different scheduling observation, not the waker or lock owner. In Perfetto, correlate thread_state fields such as state, waker_utid, io_wait and blocked_function with CPU scheduling. These fields can be absent; an IRQ-context wakeup should not simply be blamed on the interrupted userspace thread.

The original case identifies TID 20424 as RenderHeartbeat. The following crop shows that name but not its TID, so verify the mapping in the original trace, within the same process and time range, before inspecting app logic. One wakeup does not establish that RenderHeartbeat caused the entire long wait.

A sleeping thread becomes runnable before being scheduled, but preemption can also move a Running thread back to Runnable without a new wakeup. Zooming can hide short intervals, and lost events can leave gaps. The separate historical example below records wakeup from tid: 31388; do not combine it with the 20424 example into one call chain.

The CPU slice’s stateWhenDescheduled describes the thread when it is switched out at the end of that run interval. S below means it went to sleep when switched out, not its state “before wakeup.” The original red annotation is incorrect on this point:

Separate Linux states from ps display modifiers. The following follows the procps-ng ps manual. Android ps implementations/options can differ; a complete STAT string is not a Perfetto state name.

Main stateMeaning
RExecuting or runnable, not only queued
SInterruptible sleep awaiting a condition/event
DUninterruptible sleep, often I/O-related but not a disk diagnosis
IIdle kernel thread
T / tT: job-control stop; t: debugger tracing stop
Z / XZ: exited but not yet reaped; X: dead, normally not visible
WObsolete paging state, unused since Linux 2.6

BSD-style STAT modifiers include < / N for higher/lower priority, L for locked memory pages, s for session leader (not defined by having children), l for multithreading, and + for a foreground process group. This + is unrelated to the preemption marker in a scheduling trace’s R+. See also the Linux v6.6 proc documentation.

Data Parsing in Information Panel

Thread State Interpretation

The selected Weibo main-thread Running interval starts at about 1358.039 ms, lasts 5.360 ms and runs on CPU 4. It describes this scheduling interval, not all of bindApplication. PID and thread name identify the subject. CPU 4 alone does not tell you whether it is a big or small core; check the device topology.

Function Slice Interpretation

The bindApplication slice has 593.686 ms Wall Duration and 116.462 ms Self Time. Wall duration includes execution and waiting. Self time subtracts nested child slices and may still include waiting; the image’s “excludes waiting” annotation is wrong. Self Time is not CPU Duration. Uninstrumented child calls are not automatically subtracted, and Category is an event classification rather than a complete call stack. See the calculation in Catapult SliceGroup.

Counter Sample Interpretation

This selects a sample from a counter series at a particular timestamp. Value 3 is the metric’s sampled value, not the number of counters. Counter/Series identify the metric and series. Check the source for units, cumulative versus instantaneous meaning and sampling interval; one sample is not automatically a total over an interval.

Async Slice Interpretation

The animator event’s 199.579 ms Wall Duration spans its asynchronous start and end. It is not 199.579 ms of continuous execution by one thread, nor GPU time. Follow the event’s association identifiers; summing overlapping or cross-thread asynchronous intervals does not give CPU consumption.

CPU Slice Interpretation

The selected CPU run for android.bg (TID 1416) lasts 37.654 ms and reports prio 130. This is a kernel scheduling-priority representation, not MHz or Java Thread’s 1–10 priority. stateWhenDescheduled: R+ means the task remained runnable when switched out, with a preemption marker; it is not a pre-wakeup state or foreground-process-group marker. Active slices link instrumentation and need not list every function.

User Expectation Interpretation

The legacy Interactions area shows viewer-derived intervals such as Rendering Response and Input Response. The selected Input Response spans 48.993 ms according to that analysis; it is neither a human tolerance threshold nor a direct touch-to-photon measurement. Check its event boundaries. Modern frame diagnosis can additionally use FrameTimeline on Android 12 / API 31+, but that does not automatically cover the complete input pipeline.

Using Shortcuts

Reading a trace means switching often between selecting, panning and zooming. A few shortcuts save a lot of clicking. These are the common legacy Systrace/Catapult shortcuts. Letter keys below mean lowercase without Shift. Do not assume every binding carries over to Perfetto:

KeyLegacy UI action
w / sZoom in / out
a / dPan left / right
mSet the current selection as an interest range to compare boundaries
1Selection: click events
2Pan: drag to move
3Zoom: drag to zoom
4Timing: measure between selected endpoints

The default mouse mode may persist with viewer settings; press 1 explicitly for Selection. Keyboard focus also matters when editing a search field.

The Perfetto UI checked for this update is v58.3 (11fbaed83). Open Keyboard shortcuts under Support, or use ? to view its current help. Listed mouse controls include clicking events, dragging to select an area and Shift + drag to pan. On macOS the command palette uses Cmd + Shift + P; follow the modifier shown on other platforms. Legacy 1–4 mouse modes and m behavior are not a cross-version contract.

For current fields, see the PerfettoSQL Prelude: sched_slice describes CPU scheduling intervals, while thread_state describes thread states. utid is a trace-internal unique thread identifier, distinct from a reusable OS TID. Time fields are generally stored in nanoseconds and need conversion when read as milliseconds. Without the required scheduling/wakeup data, absent fields remain unknown, not zero waiting or proof that no waker existed.

Since blog comments are less convenient, feel free to visit the Zhihu or Juejin pages for this article to like or exchange ideas:

Juejin - Android Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Analyzing Systrace

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
entry.content:
Technical update — 2026-10-13: The historical screenshots and code are retained. Code excerpts were checked against AOSP android-10.0.0_r1; modern differences use android-16.0.0_r1 as an example. These tags do not identify the screenshot devices: the original traces, ROMs and build details were not supplied. The descriptions of animation ownership, StartingWindow and thread interactions are corrected below.

This is the fourth article in the Systrace series, primarily providing a brief introduction to SystemServer. It covers several important threads within SystemServer. Since Input and Binder are particularly critical, they are discussed separately and won’t be covered in detail here.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Table of Contents

  • Series Article Index
  • Main Content
  • Window Animations
  • ActivityManagerService
  • WindowManagerService
  • Input
  • Binder
  • HandlerThreads
  • ServiceThread
  • Modern Android Mapping
  • About Me && Blog

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

Main Content

Separate processes, services and threads first. system_server hosts services such as AMS, ATMS and WMS. One service can run work on Binder threads and several Handler threads; services do not map one-to-one to threads. Here, android.ui is a system-service thread, not an app’s main thread. SurfaceFlinger runs in a separate process.

Read this SystemServer article together with Perfetto 10: Binder scheduling and lock contention. In old Systrace, SystemServer analysis focused on long slices around window animation, Input, AMS/WMS, Binder calls, and lock contention. In Perfetto, the same problems should be read across SystemServer threads, Binder thread pools, caller app thread states, CPU scheduling, and lock-wait evidence.

If the symptom is an app waiting for a system call, locate the corresponding SystemServer request and check whether the server thread is Running (executing), Runnable (waiting for CPU), or sleeping/blocked. Lock waiting needs additional evidence. If it is a Binder call, also check whether the Binder thread pool is queueing, whether the caller is blocked by synchronous Binder, and whether CPU scheduling, wakeups and run queues contribute to the delay. This separates “SystemServer is slow” into window animation work, AMS/WMS lock holding, remote Binder execution, and CPU scheduling delay.

Window Animations

Window animations are a useful entry point into system_server, but window management, animation calculation, app drawing and final composition are separate responsibilities. Historical implementations commonly involve android.anim and android.anim.lf (lowercase l and f). Remote implementations such as Launcher can participate in some transitions; not all animations execute on these two threads.

For an icon launch, Launcher initiates the launch and may participate in its animation; system window management decides whether to show a StartingWindow. In AOSP Android 10, AppWindowToken makes the relevant decisions and schedules starting-surface creation. Launcher does not create the app’s StartingWindow itself. App frames, starting-surface removal and transition playback have synchronization conditions; they do not form one universal “Launcher animation ends, then the app window animation begins” sequence.

The historical case is retained below. The first two images show Launcher3 (PID 2089) and Contacts (PID 26196), both with a 253.986 ms selection for comparing Launcher animation and app startup work. That selection is not automatically the full launch duration or input-to-first-frame latency.

Launcher Animation:

Correspondingly, the App is starting:

The Contacts image shows activityStart, activityResume and Choreographer#doFrame. The next image shows activity on android.anim and android.anim.lf. Its embedded “startup complete/switch” labels are retained as the original case interpretation; these crops alone do not establish physical presentation of the first frame or a universal transition handoff.

ActivityManagerService

AMS and WMS are common investigation points, but which service is busiest depends on the workload. Activity/process-management instrumentation often uses TRACE_TAG_ACTIVITY_MANAGER, with atrace category am. An ActivityManager track does not imply one dedicated AMS thread. Android 10 already has a separate ActivityTaskManagerService for activities and task containers; do not attribute all modern Activity management to AMS.

The historical Start proc: sample.tencent.matrix slice reports 14.962 ms Wall Duration and 0.678 ms CPU Duration. These describe that slice, not the app’s complete cold start, and do not mean 14.962 ms of CPU execution:

Various scenarios for processes and the four components have corresponding Trace points, such as activityStart, activityResume, and activityStop. Some reside in the application process and others in SystemServer, so analyzing Activity logic requires toggling between both processes to understand state changes and SystemServer‘s role.

WindowManagerService

WMS instrumentation commonly uses TRACE_TAG_WINDOW_MANAGER, with atrace category wm. A Binder window request can enter a system_server Binder thread, while layout, animation and follow-up work may run on Handler threads. This image shows relayoutWindow on Binder:925_9; WMS should not be equated with the Binder thread pool:

Various Window scenarios have Trace points like relayoutWindow, performLayout, and prepareToDisplay.

Input

The input pipeline spans device reading, dispatch, window routing and app consumption. InputReader and InputDispatcher are two important native threads in system_server, but not the whole pipeline. This is detailed in Systrace Basics - Input Interpretation and won’t be repeated here.

Binder

Since SystemServer provides numerous base services, inter-process communication (IPC) is heavy, and most of it uses Binder. Synchronous Binder waits, thread-pool queueing and shared locks can increase latency, but background-app count alone is not root-cause evidence. A oneway call does not wait for a synchronous reply, yet still incurs queueing and execution work. Follow the specific call, peer and lock owner rather than diagnosing jank from the number of Binder threads. This is detailed in Binder and Lock Contention Explained.

HandlerThread

The constructors and two usage excerpts below were checked against AOSP android-10.0.0_r1. They are internal Framework implementations, not public app APIs. Search-result screenshots show the source at the time, rather than a complete call-site inventory for every release.

BackgroundThread

com/android/internal/os/BackgroundThread.java

BackgroundThread in Systrace:

BackgroundThread is a shared singleton HandlerThread within each process that uses it. It suits deferrable background work, not tasks with no performance requirements at all. A long task delays later work on the same queue. Check the PID as well as android.bg: this name alone does not identify system_server.

ServiceThread

ServiceThread inherits from HandlerThread. Several worker threads mentioned below inherit from ServiceThread, performing different functions with varying priorities: UiThread, IoThread, DisplayThread, AnimationThread, FgThread, and SurfaceAnimationThread.

Each started HandlerThread has its own Looper/MessageQueue and normally dispatches its queued work serially. Separate queues do not isolate shared locks, synchronous Binder calls, CPU contention or cross-thread waits. In this version, ServiceThread’s allowIo=false initializes a StrictMode thread policy; it is not a kernel prohibition on all I/O. Conversely, allowIo=true does not make work asynchronous or parallel.

The constructor priority is an Android/Linux nice priority, not java.lang.Thread’s 1–10 scale. In the Android 10 Process constants, smaller values generally have higher priority. Thread groups/cpusets, scheduler policy and later boosts also affect execution; the constructor does not freeze the runtime priority forever.

Thread nameConstructor priorityInterpretation
android.bgBACKGROUND = 10Deferrable work on a shared serial queue
android.uiFOREGROUND = -2System-service UI thread, not an app main thread
android.ioDEFAULT = 0I/O-related work, not a parallel pool
android.displayDISPLAY + 1 = -3One step below -4 animation priority; not SurfaceFlinger
android.animDISPLAY = -4Historical WindowAnimator and related work
android.fgDEFAULT = 0Its name does not imply the FOREGROUND nice value
android.anim.lfDISPLAY = -4Some Surface animation work, still subject to waits and contention

UiThread

com/android/server/UiThread.java

UiThread in Systrace: the UiHandler slice below has 39.383 ms Wall Duration and contains monitor-contention slices. Its 0.194 ms Self Time is not the total CPU time; the full span does not mean continuous execution.

UiThread is shared UI work infrastructure for system services, not system_server’s main thread or an app’s main thread. The search image includes AMS, PreBootBroadcaster and ATMS users. Their tasks still share a serial Looper; search UiThread.get() in the relevant version for exact responsibilities.

IoThread

com/android/server/IoThread.java

IoThread hosts I/O-related service work, but remains a serial HandlerThread rather than an unbounded parallel I/O pool. The image shows historical call sites; search IoThread.get() in the relevant revision.

DisplayThread

com/android/server/DisplayThread.java

DisplayThread in Systrace:

AnimationThread

com/android/server/AnimationThread.java

AnimationThread in Systrace:

Android 10 WindowAnimator initializes Choreographer on AnimationThread and schedules frame callbacks there; related paths still access the WMS global lock. SurfaceAnimationThread already exists in Android 9 / P and handles some Surface animation work separately. This does not guarantee lock-free or jank-free behavior for all window animations.

FgThread

com/android/server/FgThread.java

FgThread in Systrace:

FgThread serializes work that should not be subject to background scheduling restrictions. Its name does not imply THREAD_PRIORITY_FOREGROUND: the constructor uses DEFAULT. The following Android 10 UserController excerpt serializes credential-key eviction with related unlocking work to avoid data corruption. The mLock check finishes before lockUserKey is called:

SurfaceAnimationThread

com/android/server/wm/SurfaceAnimationThread.java

SurfaceAnimationThread in Systrace (named android.anim.lf):

The corresponding historical SurfaceAnimationThread call sites:

This thread handles some Surface animation work with less dependence on android.anim/WMS paths. “LockFreeAnimation” does not mean no locks exist: Android 10 SurfaceAnimationRunner still has mLock and mCancelLock, and posts completion callbacks back to AnimationThread. Historical further reading: Android P——LockFreeAnimation.

The SurfaceAnimationRunner constructor above obtains that thread’s Choreographer on android.anim.lf through runWithScissors. getSfInstance() selects the SF Vsync source; it does not move Java animation code into the SurfaceFlinger process. SurfaceControl transactions still have to be submitted and processed by the display pipeline.

Modern Android Mapping

In AOSP android-16.0.0_r1, these thread classes still exist with comparable constructor names/priorities. Their presence does not mean the whole window-animation architecture is unchanged. ServiceThread and FgThread source now resides under core/java/com/android/server/; locate the other classes by their respective paths.

  • Activity and window management: follow the specific AMS, ATMS and WMS entry points and executing threads. Confirm requests, waits and replies using PIDs/TIDs and Binder associations, rather than inferring a thread from a service name.
  • StartingWindow: Android 16 StartingSurfaceController requests starting windows through TaskOrganizerController. This does not support the old “Launcher creates it” explanation.
  • Transition animations: when Shell transitions are enabled, TransitionController cooperates with WM Shell Transitions, which may delegate to remote handlers. Inspect the actual Shell/Launcher/SystemUI processes and threads rather than only android.anim.lf in system_server.
  • Graphical state and timing: use Perfetto for scheduling, Binder and recorded frame data. Use Winscope when window/layer state, transactions or transition participants are needed. Configure the relevant sources and permissions separately; the historical screenshots cannot acquire this missing information retroactively.

Distinguish Wall Duration, CPU Duration and Self Time. Wall duration spans the slice; CPU time requires scheduling evidence; self time generally subtracts nested slices from the span. They are not interchangeable. After locating a waiter, identify the lock owner or Binder peer. A long slice, sleeping thread or collection of background apps alone does not establish the root cause.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - Introduction to Systrace
entry.content:
Technical update — 2026-10-13: First published in 2019, this article retains Systrace HTML and script workflows as historical references. Modern capture examples start from Android 11 / API 30+, with separate version requirements for app tracing APIs, permissions and data sources. Device-side atrace, host-side systrace.py and perfetto are different tools; their options are not interchangeable.

This is the first article in the Systrace series, primarily providing a brief introduction to Systrace, its basic usage, how to interpret Systrace traces, and how to analyze phenomena in Systrace in conjunction with other tools.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Table of Contents

  • Perfetto Series Article Index
  • Systrace Series Article Index
  • Main Content
  • Simple Usage of Systrace
  • Capturing Systrace with Command-Line Tools
  • Viewing Supported TAGs
  • What to Inspect First
  • About Me && Blog

Perfetto Series Article Index

How the Systrace workflow changed after Perfetto

When this article first described Systrace, the main workflow was systrace.py calling atrace, collecting ftrace and ATrace data, generating HTML, and opening it in Chrome. Today, split that flow into two layers:

  1. The underlying mechanisms are still useful: android.os.Trace, native ATrace macros, ATrace in system services, Linux ftrace, and CPU scheduling events remain core data sources for Android performance analysis.
  2. The tool workflow changed: current platform-tools no longer treats systrace.py as the main entry point. On Android 10 (API 29) and later, System Tracing saves .perfetto-trace files, and the default analysis tools are Perfetto UI and trace_processor.
  3. There are three common capture paths now: use the System Tracing Quick Settings tile for interactive issues; use adb shell perfetto ... --out /data/misc/perfetto-traces/xxx.perfetto-trace for reproducible issues; use a Perfetto config or the record_android_trace script when the configuration needs to be stable and repeatable.
  4. The Systrace concepts in this article map to Perfetto 1: Introduction, Perfetto 2: Capturing traces, and Perfetto 3: Perfetto View.

Perfetto combines protobuf traces, SQL, metrics, command-line processing and large-file analysis, supporting both short scenarios and long recordings. The old Systrace HTML flow is still good for quick visual inspection; the current Perfetto flow is better when the analysis needs search, filtering, SQL, metrics, or automation.

I will continue to update the Perfetto series, and all future illustrations will use Perfetto. Use both series as references, but prefer Perfetto for new work and check the OS version behind old functions, threads and captured data.

  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

Main Content

Systrace is a system event tracing and analysis tool introduced in the Android 4.1 era. It primarily records enabled events and instrumentation, rather than automatically sampling every method’s call stack. It helps developers collect execution information from key Android subsystems (such as SurfaceFlinger, SystemServer, kernel scheduling, input, display and the View system), allowing for a more intuitive analysis of system bottlenecks and performance improvements.

Systrace’s capabilities include tracking system I/O operations, kernel workqueues, CPU load, and the health of various Android subsystems. On the Android platform, it’s composed of three main parts:

  • Kernel Space: Systrace leverages the ftrace feature in the Linux Kernel. Therefore, to use Systrace, the relevant kernel tracing features, events and access permissions must be available; this is not simply a matter of installing an extra module.
  • Data Collection: The public synchronous android.os.Trace API is available from Android 4.3 / API 18 and lets applications mark custom code sections. Additionally, the atrace program in Android reads statistical info from ftrace and passes it to data analysis tools.
  • Data Analysis Tools: In the old flow, Android provided systrace.py (a Python script once located under Android SDK directory/platform-tools/systrace) to configure collection and generate HTML. In the current flow, perfetto records data into .perfetto-trace, while Perfetto UI and trace_processor open, query, and analyze it. Essentially, Systrace is a wrapper around Linux Kernel ftrace; Perfetto continues to support ATrace/ftrace while integrating more data sources, file formats, and analysis capabilities. Applications can still use Android’s Trace class to emit custom trace points.

Official documentation and usage for Systrace can be found here: system tracing and on-device capture

Design Philosophy of Systrace

Key flows in the system (such as Touch operations, Power button presses, scrolling), system mechanisms (input dispatching, View rendering, IPC, process management), and hardware/software status (CPU frequency, CPU scheduling, disk info, memory info) have Log-like info inserted, referred to here as TracePoints. Application/Framework ATrace markers and native kernel ftrace events come from different layers. These TracePoints demonstrate the execution time of core operations and the values of specific variables. The Android system then collects these TracePoints scattered across various processes and writes them into a file. After exporting this file, Systrace parses the enabled, permitted and successfully recorded events for that time range. It cannot fill in uninstrumented logic, disabled data sources or lost events.

Important modules in Android have TracePoints inserted by default, categorized by TraceTag:

  1. Framework Java-level TracePoints use the android.os.Trace class.
  2. Framework Native-level TracePoints use ATrace macros.
  3. App developers can define custom traces using the android.os.Trace class.

Placing process and kernel events on a shared timeline helps follow an operation across threads, waits and wakeups. This provides a view across layers, not all information about Android. Recording also has overhead; enabling every category or densely instrumenting a hot loop is not automatically useful.

Practical Applications

Because it contains a wealth of system info, parsed Systrace files are naturally suited for analyzing performance issues in both Android Apps and the system itself. App developers, system developers, and Kernel developers can all use Systrace for performance analysis.

Systrace can assist with responsiveness, jank/dropped frames and ANR investigations. Relevant user scenarios include:

  1. App startup speed (cold, hot, and warm start).
  2. Slow UI navigation or janky transitions.
  3. Sluggishness in non-navigation actions (toggles, popups, long-presses, selection, etc.).
  4. Slow screen on/off, power on/off, unlocking, or face recognition.
  5. List scrolling jank.
  6. Window animation jank.
  7. Content loading jank.
  8. System-wide sluggishness.
  9. App unresponsiveness or freezes; traces may help reconstruct the lead-up to a crash, but logs or tombstones are still needed to diagnose it.

ANR analysis also requires ANR records, thread stacks and system logs. Boot issues generally need a dedicated boot trace configuration; an ordinary interactive recording cannot cover a tracing service that has not started.

When encountering these issues, older systems can use compatible Systrace tools to generate HTML. On Android 10 and later, prefer System Tracing or perfetto to capture a .perfetto-trace file and analyze it in Perfetto UI. The methods in this series, such as reading threads, wakeups, CPU scheduling, and Binder waits, still apply; the entry point has moved from Chrome HTML to Perfetto tracks, search, the selection panel, and SQL.

Simple Usage of Systrace

Before using Systrace, understand how the usage changed across Android versions. Older articles mention Eclipse, Android Studio Device Monitor, and systrace.py; today, the recommended flow is System Tracing or Perfetto. The capture rhythm is similar, but the output file and analysis tool are different.

The old flow was:

  • Prepare the UI you want to trace on the phone.
  • Click to start capture, or run systrace.py from the command line.
  • Perform operations on the phone, keeping the reproduction short.
  • When the configured duration ends, open Trace.html in a viewer that supports that format. Directly opening old HTML in a current Chrome version may have compatibility problems.

The current flow, assuming Android 11+, is:

  • Start recording from the System Tracing developer option, or run adb shell perfetto.
  • Reproduce jank, slow response, slow launch, or another target issue.
  • Export the .perfetto-trace file.
  • Open it in Perfetto UI, then use search, SQL, metrics, or trace_processor_shell when visual inspection is not enough.

This historical Systrace UI example shows com.android.janktown PID 13409, SurfaceFlinger PID 118, CPU tracks, the main thread and RenderThread. It is neither a fresh capture from the current device nor the Perfetto UI:

Capturing Systrace / Perfetto with Command-Line Tools

I recommend the command line: set it up once, and capturing the same kind of scenario becomes convenient. It also makes the configuration easy to keep and reuse. The old systrace.py shipped with the SDK, but current Platform-Tools notes say it has been superseded. “Download version 33 or older” is not a reliable general installation instruction. Historical scripts are available in Catapult; match Python and dependencies to the chosen revision.

The following examples assume Android 11 / API 30+, an authorized ADB connection and device support for the selected categories. Perfetto platform services exist from Android 9 and are enabled by default from Android 11. For Android 9/10 setup and path restrictions, consult the official Android recording guide.

This is Perfetto’s simple mode, primarily configuring ftrace/ATrace. It does not automatically enable FrameTimeline, heapprofd or every other data source. The chosen -b 64mb ring buffer is an example, not a guarantee of preserving all ten seconds under high load. Use a full configuration for additional sources or long recordings; see the Perfetto CLI.

To capture app instrumentation, replace com.example.app with the actual app and check the instrumentation requirements below:

The following is a historical Systrace invocation. The path, Python interpreter and dependencies must match the script revision. Separate categories with spaces and specify an output filename:

Production user builds can provide substantial system tracing data. Visibility depends on Android/OEM version, categories, permissions and app configuration. Userdebug/eng may expose more debugging capabilities, but do not guarantee the same performance as production builds. Validate performance conclusions in the target production environment after investigating the mechanism.

Adding App Instrumentation

Trace.beginSection() / endSection() are available from API 18. Calls must be paired, properly nested and made on the same thread. This fragment belongs inside a synchronous app method; bindArticle() represents the actual work being measured:

Do not span synchronous begin/end calls across threads or asynchronous work that may resume on another thread. From API 29, beginAsyncSection() / endAsyncSection() pair events using the same name and cookie. See the Trace API.

-a selects the app; it does not add instrumentation or bypass permissions. On Android 10/11, release apps can allow shell profiling with <profileable android:shell="true" /> inside <application>, avoiding debuggable solely for timing measurements. Android 12 changed this gate: AOSP android-12.0.0_r1 allows app Trace when the app is debuggable or isProfileable(). The <profileable> android:enabled default is true, so the older shell restriction should not be generalized to all later releases. Check other profilers’ permissions separately. Profileable documentation

Keep the Three Command Interfaces Separate

The retained option list below belongs to device-side atrace, not systrace.py. It was checked against AOSP android-12.0.0_r1 atrace. Atrace writes raw tracing data; an .html filename does not turn it into an HTML report. Check the actual device with adb shell atrace --help.

For an interactive Bash/zsh session, the old script aliases can be written as follows. Replace the sample path and python with your actual environment. Use ordinary quotes, no spaces around =, and spaces between categories:

You do not need to memorize every option at once. Start with a simple capture; the options will become familiar as you use them. First make sure which tool you are using, then compare its common options here:

OptionDevice-side atrace, Android 12 revision abovePerfetto simple mode
-oRaw data output file on the devicePerfetto trace output file on the device
-tSeconds; help lists a five-second defaultExplicit durations such as 10s
-bKBExplicit 64mb in the example, not KB
-aComma-separated process command lines, with wildcard supportSelects app ATrace instrumentation

For old systrace.py, use that script’s own --help. Do not carry atrace’s -s (delay before starting) over to Perfetto, where simple-mode -s means maximum file size. A full ring buffer overwrites older events. Check data loss, shorten the capture window or adjust the full configuration instead of assuming the default buffer is sufficient.

Viewing Supported TAGs

The device’s currently available atrace categories can be listed with the following command. Different manufacturers may have various configurations; you can choose and configure TAGs based on your needs. Selecting fewer TAGs generally produces smaller Trace files but less content. Large Trace files can impact Chrome’s performance during analysis, so choose wisely.

Below is the output from the Android 12 phone I had on hand. The article does not record its vendor or build, so this is not a standard list for every Android 12 or current device. The HAL entries and repeated names belong to that device output. Names are on the left, descriptions on the right:

What to Inspect First

  1. Verify the reproduction window, target process and PID, enabled sources and evidence of data loss. A successfully created file does not prove that it fully records the problem window.
  2. Follow the operation through the main thread, RenderThread, Binder peers and CPU scheduling. Running means executing; Runnable means waiting for CPU. Follow wakeups, locks or Binder evidence to explain sleeping/waiting threads rather than assigning a root cause from one color.
  3. A synchronous slice can include waiting; its duration is not pure CPU time. Correlate threads and frames. Android 12 / API 31+ also supports FrameTimeline, which must be enabled separately and is not captured by the simple commands above.
  4. Cross-check with ANR stacks, crash logs or a specialized profiler. After a change, repeat the scenario on the same device/build under comparable load. Missing tracks or events remain unknown, rather than zero time.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.

entry.title: Android Systrace Basics - Why 60 FPS?
entry.content:
Technical update — 2026-10-13: First published in 2019, this article uses 60 Hz devices to explain frame pacing. 60 FPS is not a fixed standard for every Android device. The universal 16.67 ms budget, mismatched-rate examples and power claims are corrected below, with updated tools available from Android 11 / API 30 and Android 12 / API 31.

This is the third article in the Systrace series, explaining why 60 FPS is constantly emphasized. Here, FPS describes the app’s content frame rate, while Hz describes display refresh rate; they measure different things. For further context, refer to: A New Smooth Experience: A Talk on 90Hz.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

This article separates frame rate from refresh rate, then discusses pacing, power and response latency. On 90 Hz and 120 Hz devices, content updates still need to work with display timing, but 60 FPS and 16.67 ms are no longer universal targets.

Series Article Index

  1. Introduction to Systrace
  2. Systrace Basics - Prerequisites for Systrace
  3. Systrace Basics - Why 60 fps?
  4. Android Systrace Basics - SystemServer Explained
  5. Systrace Basics - SurfaceFlinger Explained
  6. Systrace Basics - Input Explained
  7. Systrace Basics - Vsync Explained
  8. Systrace Basics - Vsync-App: Detailed Explanation of Choreographer-Based Rendering Mechanism
  9. Systrace Basics - MainThread and RenderThread Explained
  10. Systrace Basics - Binder and Lock Contention Explained
  11. Systrace Basics - Triple Buffer Explained
  12. Systrace Basics - CPU Info Explained
  13. Systrace Smoothness in Action 1: Understanding Jank Principles
  14. Systrace Smoothness in Action 2: Case Analysis - MIUI Launcher Scroll Jank Analysis
  15. Systrace Smoothness in Action 3: FAQs During Jank Analysis
  16. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 1: Understanding Responsiveness Principles
  17. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 2: Responsiveness Analysis - Using App Startup as an Example
  18. Systrace Responsiveness in Action 3: Extended Knowledge on Responsiveness
  19. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Runnable
  20. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Running
  21. Systrace Thread CPU State Analysis Tips - Sleep and Uninterruptible Sleep

Main Content

Today, let’s discuss why we start with 60 FPS when talking about smoothness.

First, let’s clarify some basic concepts:

  1. 60 FPS means 60 frames per second, but specify whether you are counting frames generated, submitted or presented. Submitting 60 frames does not prove that the display showed 60 distinct content updates.
  2. The same average frame rate can produce different experiences. Continuous motion should be presented at reasonably even intervals; alternating short and long intervals creates an uneven cadence.
  3. If 60 frames are presented evenly each second, new content appears every 1000 / 60 = 16.67 ms. That is a target interval, not something an average of 60 FPS automatically guarantees.

Early Android explanations often targeted 60 FPS because a common display mode was 60 Hz: ideally, a new frame would be ready for every refresh. This explains continuous animation, but Android does not guarantee a new frame on every Vsync, and a static page need not keep redrawing to fill a 60 FPS quota.

Basic Concepts

FPS describes content frame rate; Hz describes display refresh frequency. In a fixed 60 Hz mode, the nominal period is 16.67 ms. A device may support several modes, with the active mode also depending on content, system policy and power conditions. A panel advertised as supporting “up to 120 Hz” need not currently be running at 120 Hz. Vsync coordinates rendering with display timing; it does not mean every software callback executes at the instant of physical refresh. AOSP multiple refresh rates

Fixed refresh modeNominal refresh intervalTarget for continuous animation updated on every refresh
60 Hz16.67 ms60 FPS
90 Hz11.11 ms90 FPS
120 Hz8.33 ms120 FPS
144 Hz6.94 ms144 FPS

These intervals are simply 1000 / Hz. Android does not forcibly run a full measure, layout and draw pass at each interval. Nor must all work on the main thread, RenderThread, GPU, SurfaceFlinger and display execute serially within one interval. Rendering can be pipelined. Assess a frame against its scheduling phase, deadline, GPU completion and presentation time; a main-thread slice shorter than 16.67 ms alone does not prove that the frame was free of jank.

Raising both refresh rate and content frame rate usually adds display and rendering work, but it does not establish a linear relationship between Hz and whole-device power. Workload, resolution, brightness, display mode and device implementation affect the result. Display constraints such as TFT write timing also depend on the specific panel. Measure power differences on the same device under comparable workloads.

Performance Gains

Different frame and refresh rates do not automatically cause jank. Steady 30 FPS content can hold each frame for two refresh cycles on a 60 Hz display; 60 FPS content can do the same at 120 Hz. The content frame count has not increased, but the cadence can remain even. Conversely, matching averages of 60 do not prevent stutter if submission and presentation intervals are uneven. Android Frame Pacing

For the same constant-speed motion, if both rates are presented steadily, 60 FPS shortens the interval between new images from about 33.33 ms to 16.67 ms compared with 30 FPS. The position change between adjacent frames is also smaller. Full response time still includes input, app processing, queueing and display, so doubling FPS does not guarantee halving touch latency.

The original two examples need qualification:

  • 60 FPS content on a fixed 75 Hz display: 75/60 is not an integer. If frames are repeated to match the display without a mode switch, each content frame cannot occupy the same number of refresh cycles, which can produce uneven cadence. “No benefit, only wasted power” is too broad a conclusion.
  • 60 FPS content on a fixed 30 Hz display: there are at most 30 display updates per second, so all 60 distinct updates cannot be presented. Whether excess frames are replaced, dropped or cause the producer to wait depends on the buffer queue and submission behavior. Exactly half being discarded is not a universal rule.

Higher refresh rates can also improve matching for lower-rate content. For example, 24 FPS video usually needs a 3:2 repeat cadence at fixed 60 Hz, whereas 120 Hz can hold every video frame for five refresh cycles. That reduces this source of judder without turning the video into 120 FPS content. It also does not make the latency requirements of film and interactive interfaces identical. Android frame rate API

This was my suggestion at the time, kept here as part of the original discussion, not as current buying advice:

If you want to experience a 120 Hz screen, I suggest trying an iPad Pro. You’ll notice that 60 Hz screens definitely have room for improvement.

The original videos remain as historical further reading. Distinguish content frame rate, display cadence and interaction latency; the titles do not establish a universal threshold for smoothness:

  1. Why 60 fps
  2. Why Games Need 60 FPS for Smoothness, but Movies Only Need 24

The original frame-stage chart is retained below. Its legend includes VSync, input, animation, Traversal, Draw, Sync and Frame Completed markers, which help illustrate the rendering stages discussed at the time:

The chart does not include its original trace, device or Android version. Colors and bar heights alone cannot establish the exact measurement definitions for every stage, independent GPU execution time or full input-to-display latency. Profile GPU/HWUI rendering in Developer options also changes its segments across system versions. Its 16.67 ms reference line targets 60 FPS; it is not a universal acceptance threshold for all refresh modes. Official rendering inspection guide

Checking Modern Android Devices

  1. Establish the intended cadence. Check the active display mode and target content frame rate. Static pages, video, games and continuous scrolling have different goals. A refresh-rate overlay is not an app FPS counter.
  2. Express frame-rate intent. From Android 11 / API 30, Surface.setFrameRate() lets a Surface express its intended frame rate. The system may choose another rate, and the call does not automatically change the app’s render loop. Games can use Frame Pacing (Swappy) to control submission timing and avoid extra latency from a backed-up buffer queue.
  3. Inspect actual frames and deadlines. From Android 12 / API 31, capture FrameTimeline and correlate App/SurfaceFlinger Expected/Actual Timelines, frame associations and thread scheduling. Missing data is not evidence of zero jank. FrameTimeline alone also does not replace a full input-to-display latency measurement.

Continue with the Perfetto series index or high refresh rate benefits and challenges.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro: Includes personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Welcome to recommend projects/articles.
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Android Systrace -- Series Article Index
entry.content:
Technical update — 2026-10-13: This page is dated 2019 and retains update records from earlier tutorials. The old Systrace tooling workflow is obsolete. Read historical screenshots, source code and experiments against the Android versions stated in each article; they do not describe every current implementation. Start with the Perfetto series below for current capture and analysis workflows.

As Systrace and Android changed, my earlier tutorials started to show their age. I had also learned to read more from a trace, which helped me solve performance problems. I wanted to write those things down and get better at explaining what I had learned. If the notes helped someone else too, all the better.

The purpose of this series is to view the overall operation of the Android system from a different perspective using Systrace, while also providing an alternative angle for learning the Framework. Perhaps you’ve read many articles about the Framework but can never remember the code, or you’re unclear about the execution flow. Maybe from Systrace’s graphical perspective, you can gain a deeper understanding.

Perfetto has essentially replaced Systrace in my daily work. Many newcomers to Android performance optimization find Perfetto’s busy interface and numerous features overwhelming. They have asked me to present the earlier Systrace articles using Perfetto. Android’s SDK Platform-Tools notes identify the old systrace tool as superseded. That does not mean ATrace instrumentation or kernel ftrace has been deprecated as well.

Read this index along two lines: the Systrace articles retain the Framework flows and case studies of their time; the Perfetto articles cover capture, viewing, search, SQL and large-trace analysis, alongside system mechanisms. Changing the viewer does not make the function names, thread relationships or timing in an old screenshot applicable to every newer system.

Getting Started Today: Tools and Versions

Entry point or capabilityVersion and scope
Legacy systrace.pyThe historical workflow typically produces an HTML report. Do not assume a current Platform-Tools installation still contains the script at the old tutorial’s path.
System Tracing in Developer optionsAvailable from Android 9 / API 28. Android 9 saves Systrace format (.ctrace); Android 10 / API 29 and later save Perfetto format (.perfetto-trace).
On-device perfetto and tracing servicesPlatform services exist from Android 9 and are enabled by default from Android 11 / API 30. Some Android 9 and 10 devices need an extra enabling step; check the official instructions and device support.
Perfetto UI and command-line analysisThe UI can display Perfetto and supported legacy Systrace formats; trace_processor supports local SQL analysis. A filename extension does not guarantee complete data.
FrameTimelineAvailable from Android 12 / API 31, with its data source actually recorded. Opening an old trace in a new UI cannot add frame data that was never captured.

Version references: on-device System Tracing, Perfetto Android capture guide, and FrameTimeline. The current graphical recording tutorial assumes Android 11+; for older devices, use its command-line branch. See Recording system traces.

Start with Perfetto 1–3 and capture a short scenario, then follow the particular problem into MainThread, RenderThread, CPU or Binder analysis. Record the device, Android/ROM version, refresh rate, app version and trace configuration. Before naming a bottleneck, confirm that the relevant time range, threads and data sources are present. A missing track may reflect configuration, permissions, device support or lost data; it does not mean zero time was spent there.

App developers can start with the system’s capture tools. Experiments that modify Framework code, change Buffer configuration or enable privileged data sources require the appropriate system build and permissions. You do not need to modify the OS before learning to read a trace, and not every experiment from a platform development environment applies to a retail device.
