entry.title: A New Era of Smoothness: Thoughts on 90Hz on Android
entry.content:
Version note — reviewed October 13, 2026: This article was written in 2019. Its device opinions, 90 Hz “sweet spot,” and buying outlook are historical, not current purchase advice. The technical explanations are corrected below, with Android 11/API 30 and Android 15 QPR1 updates. The old trace crops lack complete capture conditions and are not new device measurements.

High-refresh-rate screens have been common on PCs for years, but they’ve only recently made their way to Android. While the Razer Phone introduced a 120Hz screen in 2017 to a quiet reception, I believe the 90Hz screens on the Nubia Red Magic 3 and OnePlus 7 Pro represent the current “sweet spot” for Android. They offer a tangible, immediate boost to the user experience. If you’ve never used a high-refresh-rate mobile screen, I highly recommend visiting an Apple Store to try out the 120Hz ProMotion display on the iPad Pro.

The hardware timeline can be checked against vendor records: the original Razer Phone launched with 120 Hz in 2017, followed by the Razer Phone 2 in 2018. OnePlus 7 Pro and REDMAGIC 3 are the 2019 90 Hz examples discussed here. iPad Pro introduced up-to-120-Hz ProMotion in 2017. Specifications alone do not establish frame rates in a particular workload.

Terminology Explained

What is Screen Refresh Rate?

Refresh rate describes how frequently the display updates, measured in Hz. A fixed 60 Hz mode provides approximately 60 refresh opportunities per second; 90 Hz provides 90. The same image can be shown repeatedly, so a display refresh does not imply a newly generated app frame.

Hardware limits the available modes, while system policy selects how they are used. A phone advertised as “up to 120 Hz” need not run at 120 Hz all the time, and dynamic refresh cannot be described by one permanently fixed interval.

What is FPS?

FPS means Frames Per Second. State whether the measurement counts frames generated, submitted, or actually presented; these can differ. Frame rate depends on hardware, software, workload, and scheduling, not software alone.

An average of 90 FPS does not establish uniform frame intervals or low input-to-display latency. A static page need not continually generate new frames.

What is Vsync?

Vsync means Vertical Synchronization. It coordinates application rendering, SurfaceFlinger composition, and display updates; it does not automatically make app FPS equal the refresh rate.

For a fixed mode, the interval is 1000 / refresh rate:

Refresh rateRefresh interval
60 HzAbout 16.67 ms
90 HzAbout 11.11 ms
120 HzAbout 8.33 ms

These are refresh intervals, not guarantees that any CPU drawing task finishing below them avoids jank. App, GPU, composition, and display work can overlap across frames. Start times, phase offsets, queues, and deadlines all matter. See AOSP Vsync for app/composition timing relative to hardware Vsync.

What is the Input Scanning Cycle?

Touch scanning is hardware sampling; reading, dispatching, and consuming the events happen later. Sampling rate varies by device and mode, so the old “about 8 ms” assumption is not universal. An 8 ms period corresponds to about 125 Hz, not exactly 120 Hz.

Even with perfectly regular 8 ms sampling, phase alignment means a 16.67 ms window can contain two or three samples, while an 11.11 ms window can contain one or two. That difference alone does not prove uneven motion: timestamps, batching, resampling, and consumption matter.

For example, Android 9 InputTransport includes batching and touch resampling. Android 16 BatchedInputEventReceiver supports both CALLBACK_INPUT batching and direct consumption when batching is disabled. Not all input waits for Vsync.

The 90Hz User Experience

For scrolling and animation, a 90 Hz display presenting evenly paced 90 FPS content can provide finer updates than 60 FPS under comparable conditions. But the rates need not always be equal: 30 FPS on a 60 Hz display can have a stable two-refresh cadence.

Fixed 60 FPS content on a fixed 90 Hz display can alternate presentation durations because the rates are not integer multiples, causing judder. Switching to 60 Hz or a suitable multiple can improve the match. Conversely, 60 Hz cannot fully display 90 independent updates per second; excess frames may be replaced, discarded, or blocked by the queue, depending on buffering and presentation policy.

The original claim that Android architecture and hardware could not support 120 Hz/120 FPS was too broad. A 120 Hz Android phone already existed in 2017. Sustained 120 FPS depends on the workload and device implementation, not the platform name alone. The forecast about 2020 is now historical and should not remain future buying advice.

The original OnePlus 90 Hz versus 60 Hz comparison video remains a historical demonstration link. Capture, encoding, playback, and the viewer’s screen affect what can be seen; promotional video is not a controlled frame-time or latency benchmark.

How 90 FPS Works (Platform Perspective)

For a hardware-accelerated View/HWUI interface, the main steps are:

  1. Input, animation, or another state change creates work; updates are not limited to taps.
  2. Input is dispatched to the app, which handles logic or updates list state.
  3. Choreographer schedules the relevant callbacks. Traversal happens when needed, and a change does not necessarily require a complete measure/layout/draw pass.
  4. The main thread records or updates drawing state, while RenderThread performs rendering work and submits buffers. CPU completion is not GPU completion; synchronization determines buffer readiness.
  5. SurfaceFlinger accepts layer buffers and coordinates GPU client composition or HWC device composition before display presentation. Its CPU main thread does not necessarily draw every pixel of every layer.

See SurfaceFlinger and WindowManager. The broad workflow is similar at 60 and 90 FPS, but games, custom surfaces, and different OS versions can use different rendering paths.

App Rendering Flow at 90 FPS

The trace runs left to right. This crop labels android.contacts (PID 9952), and the selected interval is 10.891 ms. That cursor selection neither measures complete input-to-display latency nor replaces the nominal 90 Hz interval of 11.11 ms.

Two annotations need qualification: Input, Animation, and Traversal are separate Choreographer phases, not all children of performTraversals(). “DisplayPlayList” should read DisplayList; recording drawing state on the main thread is different from RenderThread/GPU execution.

SurfaceFlinger Flow at 90 FPS

This selection is about 11 ms, and a visible layer label is com.oppo.market/.... It is not a continuous trace of the same Contacts app shown above. StatusBar#0 is a layer name, not a SystemUI process row. App and SurfaceFlinger Vsync tracks can have different phases.

Composition submission does not establish completed screen presentation. These remain historical pipeline illustrations; without the full trace and device conditions, they cannot determine end-to-end latency or a system-wide jank rate.

Advantages and Challenges

Advantages

The following are the original 2019 impressions and buying outlook. “Irreversible” expresses a subjective preference, not an established physiological rule; the third point is outdated buying advice. Perception varies by person and scene, and advertised refresh rate alone does not establish better latency or frame pacing.

  1. To my eyes, 90 FPS looked smoother. After getting used to it, going back to 60 FPS could feel jerky and disconnected.
  2. I called high refresh rate a “one-way street”: once you were used to it, a lower-refresh screen could be hard to accept again.
  3. With people keeping their phones longer, my advice then was to choose a good screen, a large battery, a capable SoC, UFS storage, and enough RAM. I expected more such phones in the second half of 2019, so I suggested that anyone still undecided could wait a little.

Challenges

Performance. Higher refresh targets shorten update intervals, but bottlenecks can involve the main thread, RenderThread, GPU, memory bandwidth, composition, or resource waits. They cannot always be ranked CPU first, I/O second, GPU third. Snapdragon 855 and UFS 3.0 were OnePlus 7 Pro specifications, not universal prerequisites for 90 FPS. Storage can matter during loading without being a necessary operation on every frame. The Razer Phone’s experience also cannot be attributed entirely to its chip without matching tests.

Triple buffering can improve overlap while adding queuing latency; it does not guarantee that occasional deadline misses remain smooth. Inspect frame timing and presentation. Perfetto FrameTimeline, available from Android 12 (API 31), is more informative than checking whether one CPU bar is below 11.11 ms.

Power. With other conditions similar, more frequent rendering and display updates typically cost power, but the amount depends on panel, content, brightness, workload, and thermal state. Reducing rendering resolution can reduce some GPU/bandwidth costs without changing the physical panel or guaranteeing a fixed saving. Static or low-frame-rate content does not need the entire system to run at 90 FPS continuously.

Adaptation. Framework animation normally follows scheduled frame callbacks, but hard-coded 16 ms logic, custom rendering loops, and heavy workloads need attention. Games should pace production and submission for their target rate. WebView and SurfaceView host content; their names alone do not determine whether that content supports 90 FPS.

Modern Android Adaptation

  • Android 11 / API 30: Surface.setFrameRate() expresses the content’s intended rate. Display capability, other layers, and power policy influence the actual selection. The request is not guaranteed, and the API does not automatically speed up or throttle the rendering loop. Use FRAME_RATE_COMPATIBILITY_FIXED_SOURCE for fixed-rate video and DEFAULT for ordinary game content; avoid repeating the call every frame.
  • Game frame pacing: Android Frame Pacing, or Swappy, helps coordinate OpenGL/Vulkan submissions with display timing. Requesting a high refresh rate, producing frames on time, and sustaining performance are separate tasks to measure.
  • Android 15 QPR1 and later: Adaptive refresh rate (ARR) additionally requires the appropriate device HAL support. An OS update alone does not grant every panel the same capability, and static content need not be redrawn at 90/120 FPS continuously.

The developer-option refresh-rate overlay describes display mode information, not the app’s actual frame-production rate. Record the display mode, app frame intervals, input latency, power/thermal state, and workload when comparing high-refresh experiences.

Zhihu Article

The original discussion is available at Zhihu: A New Smooth Experience, Thoughts on 90 Hz.

entry.title: Sharp Tools - Efficient Tool Recommendations
entry.content:
I’ve been following the Sharp Tools Community Program for a long time. I’ve learned a lot from everyone’s sharing. As stated in the beginning: “Both tools and inspiration are sharp tools. When tools and inspiration from different fields and creators collide, more possibilities arise.“ Below are my simple answers to the six questions of the Sharp Tools Community Program. I hope some parts will be helpful to you.

Historical tool list (reviewed October 2026): This records my devices, software, and work experience in 2019. Those personal choices remain historical, rather than current buying recommendations. Significant service and technical changes are noted below.

Introduce yourself and the work you do.

I am an Android System Development Engineer working in the system R&D department of a smartphone manufacturer. My work mainly involves Android system-related tasks, such as performance, power consumption, stability, and framework maintenance. It’s a bit of everything—basically, I’m the odd-jobs person.

As for hobbies, I enjoy basketball, running, and gaming—essential skills for any programmer. I also appreciate more “artistic” pursuits like reading, raising cats, and drinking tea. In my spare time, I like browsing Bilibili and YouTube. When I have time, I try to finish pending articles for my blog. Currently, I’m obsessed with losing weight and fighting a life-and-death struggle against my belly.

What hardware are you using?

Computers: I primarily use three. A MacBook Pro for writing, developing my own small apps, and photo processing. A desktop provided by my company running Ubuntu, mainly for work and essential for compiling Android source code. A self-built desktop mainly for gaming and compiling AOSP code.

Phones: I also have three. My main device is an iPhone X—I’m satisfied with everything except the battery life. My backup is a OnePlus 6, an Android flagship; as an Android engineer, I must have a solid Android device. The third one is a Pixel, used mainly for running my own compiled AOSP code—a must-have for studying the framework.

Other Hardware: Apple ecosystem products like the Watch, iPad Pro, and AirPods. Sony wireless headphones—yes, I’m a fan (listed as MX-1000 in the original; the exact model is unconfirmed). A Kindle Voyage specifically for e-books.

AOSP version note: Writing apps on the Mac is separate from building the full OS. Current AOSP requirements use 64-bit x86 Linux; building the Android OS on macOS is unsupported from Android 11. My old Pixel used a matching historical branch. Check the exact device, build target, and vendor binaries before assuming a newer branch works.

What about software?

  • Things 3: Primarily for scheduling daily work and recording tasks.
  • MWeb: Dedicated to writing—this article was written using MWeb.
  • Keep: A great fitness helper. I just follow the courses; it’s great for tracking progress and setting goals, especially during HIIT sessions on the treadmill.
  • 海豚记账本 (Dolphin Ledger): A bookkeeping app for basic needs.
  • Kindle && WeChat Read: Reading apps; the two libraries complement each other. E-books are very convenient, especially on the iPad Pro.
  • YouTube && Bilibili: My main sources for learning and entertainment.
  • ShadowSocks && Wingy: At the time I used ShadowSocks on Android and Mac, and Wingy on my phone and iPad. The widget was handy for switching it back on if the app got killed.
  • Geek Time && Dedao: Knowledge-sharing platforms. I find that hearing what others are doing and how they do it is very helpful for self-improvement and avoiding pitfalls.
  • Google Photos: Almost all my photos are stored here. I’d be devastated if I ever lost access…
  • Reeder: I maintained a developer feed list and used Reeder 3 in 2019. October 2026: New Reeder syncs a timeline position; Reeder Classic keeps a traditional RSS approach. These are different models, not features to assume in Reeder 3.
  • Android Studio && VS Code: Productivity software; one for Framework Java code and the other for C/C++ code.
  • RescueTime: I used it to review computer time; seeing ten-plus hours could be discouraging. Usage time is not work output. October 2026: Official support no longer lists Linux. iOS 17+ tracking requires a paid plan and Screen Time permission; that activity stays on-device, separate from desktop statistics. The old view-only iOS description is outdated.
  • Shimo Docs: For daily/weekly reports and research notes. It synced conveniently between my devices and was useful for collaboration; I preferred the web version.
  • Nutstore (Jianguoyun): The sync drive I used at the time. Having an Ubuntu client felt like someone had remembered us programmers. Choose the Linux client for your distribution, architecture, and desktop environment. Uploading is not a guarantee against loss: deletions can propagate. Keep independent copies of important files.
  • Yinxiang Biji (印象笔记): Used to be for notes, but now it’s more of a collection center for interesting articles I find. I use Shimo Docs for daily work records.

Reading and photo services (October 2026): Amazon’s closure notice, reproduced in full by The Paper set June 30, 2023 for the Chinese Kindle store’s sales closure and June 30, 2024 for purchased-content downloads. Downloaded books remained readable; this was not a worldwide Kindle closure.

Keep independent photo copies: Google Photos deletions can propagate to devices with backup enabled. Google Takeout can export existing data for a separate, checked copy; it cannot recover permanently deleted photos.

What is your ideal working environment?

My ideal working environment is Work-Life Balance. As mentioned in the popular 996.ICU project, my current workload is similar to that. Therefore, I prefer the environment described in the 955.WLB project.

The biggest pressure of a 996 schedule is the lack of personal time for self-improvement. Working until 10 or 11 PM every day leaves no time for fitness, reading, or learning. As an article once said, “The most hidden way to ruin a person is to make them too busy to grow.”

If a person only learns from their work, this single way of learning will inevitably lead to a decreasing marginal contribution to growth. You must give yourself time to grow every day through diverse learning methods outside of work. Continuous growth is essential for a rising career path.

In summary, my ideal working environment includes like-minded colleagues, work I love, and the time/space for personal growth.

How do you usually get inspiration for your work?

One way is through reading—extracting the essence of others’ thoughts to see if I can apply, improve, or expand upon them. Another is thinking and recording—drawing flowcharts while thinking and capturing sparks of ideas.

Neither approach has worked all that well for me, though. When things get busy, I barely have time to read or think. If you’ve figured this out, I’d love some advice.

Recommend one “Sharp Tool” to everyone?

Instead of hardware or software, I want to recommend a learning method: Record - Summarize - Output. These three steps are closely linked:

Record: As the saying goes, “The palest ink is better than the best memory.” In today’s information explosion, having your own recording method is crucial. To-do lists, random ideas, problems encountered, solutions found, great articles, blog ideas, or YouTube tutorials—recording keeps you organized.

Summarize: Summarizing helps organize scattered thoughts or knowledge. A clear structure helps you see the big picture. Project summaries help avoid repeating mistakes, and knowledge summaries deepen your understanding of a specific topic.

Output: Output can be private notes, blogs, or videos. Output reinforces your own knowledge by explaining it to others. To explain something clearly, you must know it thoroughly. Discussions following your output further strengthen your understanding. It also helps others while building your reputation—if you’re good, you should let others know it too.

Conclusion

I recently visited Japan during the cherry blossom season. Let’s end with a photo of the blossoms.

entry.title: Case Analysis of System-wide Stutter Caused by Android Accessibility Service
entry.content:
Phenomenon

Version note — reviewed October 13, 2026: This is a historical 2019 case without the complete trace, ROM build, or app versions. The old call chain is checked against AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 as a reference, not an identification of the original ROM. An android-16.0.0_r1 comparison is added below. The findings concern the observed configuration, not every accessibility service or current versions of the named apps.

Some users reported that while scrolling on the phone, the list would jitter. This happens when scrolling on the desktop or settings (as long as it is scrollable), but this is not reproducible for everyone; it appears for some users, but not for others.

Onlookers can scroll directly to the bottom to see The Culprit and Self-Check. Those interested in analyzing the problem can read the analysis process.

Systrace Analysis

One of our test phones reproduced it. I took a look: dragging across the launcher or Settings caused stuttering every time on that device. Here is what the trace showed:

I marked the gaps in updates with red arrows. Launcher buffer supply appears intermittent, but this crop lacks complete frame and presentation timing. No new buffer does not mean SurfaceFlinger stopped working; it may keep displaying the previous frame.

The corresponding Launcher trace shows gaps in input-handling and drawing activity, making the input path worth investigating. This alone does not prove that a frame without a new input event cannot draw: animations, flings, and other updates do not require fresh touch input on every frame.

We were dragging continuously, so our first suspicion was a problem with touch sampling or event delivery. Sampling, batching, and display refresh are not one-to-one, however. Before investigating hardware, compare InputReader and InputDispatcher activity:

InputReader remains active, while InputDispatcher follows a different pattern from the comparison below. Thread activity alone does not prove that hardware sampling and every event are correct; event timestamps and wakeup details still need checking.

Looking back at the problematic trace, I noticed that some InputDispatcher activity aligned more closely with Vsync. This suggests a different delivery path for those events, not that every InputDispatcher wakeup became Vsync-driven.

I then opened the scheduling details and saw some wakeups from the system_server main thread rather than InputReader. The retained crop does not expose those scheduler details, so this remains a recorded observation requiring the full trace to verify. Aligned slices alone do not establish the waking thread.

Next, inspect the conditions that divert input from direct enqueueing.

Code Analysis

The following touch-Move path uses AOSP android-9.0.0_r1 as a reference. These are platform excerpts, not a standalone application; the first omits debug logging. The needWake condition means a new wakeup is not required for every event when work is already queued.

InputDispatcher.cpp

When filterInputEvent() returns false, this notifyMotion() call skips direct enqueueing and its wakeup. The filter has taken responsibility for the event; that does not mean the event is permanently lost or InputReader stopped running.

Continue with the JNI filterInputEvent implementation:

JNI calls InputManagerService.filterInputEvent. The object-creation failure and Java-exception paths above allow normal dispatch by returning true; these branches should not be omitted.

Here we examine mInputFilter as an AccessibilityInputFilter. AccessibilityManagerService.updateInputFilter combines enabled-feature flags and installs a filter when needed. Not every accessibility switch enables the same MotionEvent path.

InputFilter posts to its Handler. The second fragment below belongs inside H.handleMessage(). AccessibilityInputFilter uses context.getMainLooper(); the system_server main thread must not be confused with the separately named android.ui thread.

Continue with AccessibilityInputFilter.onInputEvent:

Continue to look at processMotionEvent

Continue to look at batchMotionEvent

Continue to look at scheduleProcessBatchedEvents

The task is scheduled for Choreographer’s CALLBACK_INPUT phase. Actual execution still depends on main-Looper scheduling, so delivery is not guaranteed exactly one Vsync later. The complete Runnable is:

processBatchedEvents() adds another timing condition: only entries older than frameNanos are processed; remaining entries at or after that time wait for a later callback.

Events forwarded after transformation reach AccessibilityInputFilter.onMotionEvent(), then InputFilter.sendInputEvent() and InputManagerService.InputFilterHost.sendInputEvent(), which asynchronously inject them into native dispatch with FLAG_FILTERED. A filter can also consume or transform events intentionally, so the earlier return alone does not establish event loss.

Main-thread queuing, the batch cutoff, and later dispatch can add latency on this Android 9 path. That is consistent with the recorded timing change, but does not prove every enabled service causes dropped frames or adds exactly 16 ms to every event. These remain the original case annotations:

Android 16 Path Change

In the same class at AOSP android-16.0.0_r1, processMotionEvent() calls handleMotionEvent() directly instead of the old batchMotionEvent()/Choreographer queue:

This comparison establishes a change between the checked implementations, not the first fixed release or the absence of accessibility-related delays on every modern device. Filtering, scheduling, service behavior, and OEM modifications still require investigation on the actual system.

The Culprit

We traced the symptom to certain enabled accessibility services, involving iFlytek Input Method and Yingyongbao, and saw similar behavior on Pixel and other vendors’ devices. Without the ROM/app versions and full comparison data, these remain 2019 case observations, not findings about current releases of those apps.

Accessibility services help users with visual, motor, and other access needs; some apps also use them for automation. Different capabilities enable different input-processing features. The historical settings page lists services, not proof that all were enabled or implicated:

The next permission dialog is for Voice Access, not a record of data accessed by iFlytek or Yingyongbao. It warns that these capabilities may expose sensitive UI information. The dialog does not prove that a service read all passwords, card numbers, or conversations. Access depends on declared capabilities, OS version, exposed accessibility nodes, and field protection.

Android 14 (API 34) added mechanisms such as accessibilityDataSensitive, restricting interactions with sensitive views by services not marked isAccessibilityTool. That declaration is not a certification of trustworthiness or a substitute for inspecting actual data exposure.

“Perform gestures” in the iFlytek dialog below is not merely gesture listening. The canPerformGestures capability permits gesture injection through dispatchGesture(), introduced in Android 7.0 (API 24).

In Android 9, updatePerformGesturesLocked() checks bound services for CAPABILITY_CAN_PERFORM_GESTURES, enabling FLAG_FEATURE_INJECT_MOTION_EVENTS, which belongs to FEATURES_AFFECTING_MOTION_EVENTS. That enabled capability can therefore route real touch input through the old filter path even without an active dispatchGesture() call. Magnification and touch exploration can also enable related paths; this is not one universal “gesture listener” switch.

Self-Check

Unused services can be disabled, but do not indiscriminately turn off screen reading, voice control, or other assistance you rely on. To investigate a suspected newly enabled service:

  1. Record the device, OS build, app version, enabled services, and reproducible scenario. Settings names and locations vary by vendor.
  2. If it does not prevent you from operating the device, change one suspected service at a time, repeat the same scrolling scenario, and restore needed functionality. One apparently smoother run does not establish causation or implicate all accessibility services.
  3. Developers should align input timestamps, main-Looper queuing, InputDispatcher delivery, and visible updates in Perfetto or equivalent traces. FrameTimeline on Android 12 and later can help, but is not a complete input-latency measurement: waiting that produces no new frame may not appear as a deadline miss for a generated frame.
  4. Service developers should declare only needed capabilities and measure the target system’s input path. Required gesture injection and touch exploration should be made responsive rather than removed from users who need them.

entry.title: 2018 Best Items Recommendations - A Reward for Your Hard Work
entry.content:
At the beginning of 2018, I wrote 2017 Best Items Recommendations. Recently, some people asked if I’d do one for 2018. Although 2018 was a tough year, there were still some great things worth recommending to everyone.

Just like in 2017, I’ll share things that I found helpful for work or life. The recommendations include apps, hardware, books, blogs, and columns. I hope they provide value to you in 2019.

Historical recommendations (reviewed October 2026): This is a record of my 2018 experience. Book lists, ratings, prices, course posters, and buying recommendations belong to that period. Updated platform support and membership limits are noted below; old QR codes are not current enrollment links.

Recommended Apps

RescueTime

RescueTime records app and website usage on supported devices, with the relevant client and permissions. It helps review time allocation; it does not capture all offline work or measure work output.

I used it to see where my computer time went. At the time, most of that time was in Android Studio, VS Code, and Terminator. Below are my screenshots from January 15th:

Detailed Programming Info:

The Productivity Pulse and programming duration in these screenshots depend on activity categories. They do not directly measure productivity or completed work, and unrecorded activity is not zero work.

October 2026 update: The current official support list includes Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, and a Firefox extension, but not Linux. This old article therefore cannot establish current official Linux support. The old view-only description of iOS is also outdated: the current iOS app supports iOS 17 or later, requires a paid plan, and tracks usage through Screen Time permission. That screen activity stays on the device, is not uploaded to RescueTime servers, and does not enter desktop statistics or goals.

Shimo Docs

In 2018, I switched my daily work logging from MWeb to Shimo Docs. The main reason is its multi-platform support (Mac, iOS, Android, WeChat Mini Programs). More importantly, the web version is excellent. I can record and view notes in real-time, and sharing is seamless with read-only or collaborative permissions.

There was another reason: to me, a web-based note editor shows its respect for programmers by handling Ctrl+S properly. In the versions and browser I used in 2018, Shimo handled it as a save action, while Yinxiang Biji (the separate Chinese service, not the international Evernote service) opened the browser’s save-page dialog. This describes my experience then, not the products’ current shortcut behavior.

Nutstore (Jianguoyun)

After looking around, I eventually settled on Nutstore for folder synchronization largely because it had a Linux client. While working on Linux, I could drop files into its sync folder and pick them up on another device once the upload and download finished. That was convenient. It still depended on network access, working clients, and storage or transfer limits.

October 2026 update: The official Linux download page still offers clients, with installation choices depending on distribution, CPU architecture, and desktop environment. File-manager integration is not identical across all Linux setups. Synchronization is not an independent backup: edits and deletions can propagate. Keep separate copies of important material; version history and deletion recovery have service limits.

These original feature and download-page screenshots show historical client versions and minimum OS requirements.


Recommended Technical Books

Understanding Android Kernel Design

A useful systems book, titled 《深入理解 Android 内核设计思想》 on the cover. The old heading named a different title and claimed a second edition; the supplied cover and description establish an Android 4.3-era baseline, not the exact edition or source tag. Check the ISBN, preface, and source baseline of your copy before comparing it with newer Android code.

The book discusses processes/threads, memory management, Binder, GUI, multimedia, and input systems. Its historical “Android 4.3 and above” description does not guarantee that the implementation details apply to every later release.

Douban: https://book.douban.com/subject/25921329/

Android Advanced Decryption

This book targets Android 8.0 source code combined with practical application knowledge. It covers system source code, JNI, ClassLoader, JVM, DVM/ART, Hook techniques, Hot-fixing, and performance optimizations (draw and memory). It builds a comprehensive knowledge system for developers.

JD: https://item.jd.com/12447229.html

Version note: This recommendation refers to the Android 8.0 (API 26) edition; the author also maintains system-learning material. Android 9 (API 28) introduced non-SDK interface restrictions, including access through reflection and JNI. Recheck Hook, hot-fix, and plugin examples against the target OS and targetSdkVersion before using them.

Running Linux Kernel

Essential for Android system engineers. Based on Linux 4.x, it covers memory management, process management, concurrency, and interrupts. Each section poses a problem to solve through source code analysis, making it highly practical for embedded and Android low-level developers.

Douban: https://book.douban.com/subject/27108677/

Version note: This is the Linux 4.x edition, useful for fundamentals rather than a complete description of current Android kernels. Match source code to the device’s kernel version, configuration, and vendor changes. See the AOSP kernel documentation for newer architecture.

Recommended Non-Technical Books

Blades of the Guardians (Biaoren)

A top-tier Chinese manhua (comic) set in the Sui and Tang dynasties with a 8.3 Douban rating. It follows a skilled escort, Dao Ma, across the Western deserts as he takes on a high-stakes mission to the capital, Chang’an. Available on WeChat Read.

Great Defeats 2 (Dabaiju 2)

After reading the first volume, I was hooked. As a Douban review states: “High-level reality. In the tide of the times, entrepreneurs and founders are no different from gamblers. Those with ambition get lost in the halo of success, only to see themselves clearly after a crushing defeat.” Volume 2 analyzes the downfall of nine famous Chinese enterprises.

How to Stop Sucking and Be Awesome Instead

Jeff Atwood’s How to Stop Sucking and Be Awesome Instead, published in Chinese as 《程序员的修炼——从优秀到卓越》, collects essays from Coding Horror. It covers time management, coding methods, testing, and technical reading. It is a useful guide to the human side of software development.

My reading notes:

  1. Part 1: How to Stop Sucking and Be Awesome Instead
  2. Part 2: The Way of Programming
  3. Part 3: Web Design Principles
  4. Part 4: Thoughts on Testing
  5. Part 5: Knowing Your Users

entry.title: Setting Up the Android System Development Environment
entry.content:
Whether you are an Android App developer or a System developer, having a foundational understanding of the Android system is extremely beneficial. I recently set up a development environment at home and decided to share the process for anyone interested.

The general steps involved are as follows:

  1. Installing Ubuntu
  2. Configuring Ubuntu
  3. Installing Essential Software
  4. Configuring Network Access (Optional)
  5. Downloading AOSP Code
  6. Setting Up the Build Environment and Compiling Pixel Code
  7. Flashing the Device
  8. Modifying and Compiling Framework, Services, and Res

Version note — reviewed October 13, 2026: The original is a 2018 environment record. Its screenshots show Ubuntu 18.04.1, PLATFORM_VERSION_CODENAME=Q, and aosp_sailfish-userdebug, but no complete manifest pins the original master checkout. The Pixel workflow remains historical. The new example uses Android 16 tag android-16.0.0_r1, Ubuntu 22.04 x86_64, and Cuttlefish x86_64. It is not presented as the latest release or as a way to flash Android 16 onto the original Pixel.

Recommended Hardware

The old “512 GB SSD and a Pixel” advice needs context. For a modern workstation, the current AOSP requirements list 64-bit x86 Linux, at least 400 GB of free disk space, and 64 GB RAM. A nominal 512 GB disk does not necessarily have that much free space; multiple checkouts and outputs require more. These are planning guidelines for modern builds, not universal limits for every old branch. Reading source needs less, and running this Cuttlefish example additionally requires usable KVM. A physical phone is optional.

1. Installing Ubuntu

Ubuntu 18.04’s standard security maintenance ended in May 2023; extended maintenance has separate conditions. See the Ubuntu release lifecycle. This update uses Ubuntu 22.04 LTS instead of the old 18.04.1 mirror ISO.

  1. Obtain an amd64 image from the official Ubuntu 22.04 release directory and verify it against the published checksums.
  2. Create a bootable USB drive and back up existing data before repartitioning.
  3. Install on a suitable Linux host. A VM can work with enough disk and memory, but running Cuttlefish also requires KVM/nested virtualization to be available inside it. Being able to compile in a VM does not prove it can run the virtual device.

This was my desktop at the time. Do not treat these Linux instructions as a native macOS or Apple Silicon build procedure.

2. Configuring Ubuntu

Choose an input method and editor to suit your workflow. Vim can be installed with sudo apt install vim. Obtain adb and fastboot through Android Studio’s SDK Manager or SDK Platform-Tools. AOSP builds also produce host tools; confirm which copy your shell uses before mixing installations:

Physical-device access on Linux also requires USB debugging authorization and suitable device permissions. Establish connectivity before deployment.

3. Installing Essential Software

I listed VS Code, Android Studio, and Meld for editing and comparing files. Wine, WPS Office, and the input method were my desktop preferences, not AOSP build dependencies. Install what you need; the build dependencies appear below.

4. Configuring Network Access (Optional)

Use a stable source-access path for your environment. The Repo tool’s own download location and the AOSP manifest/project mirrors are separate; changing only the manifest URL may not solve every connection problem.

5. Downloading AOSP Code

The official download guide supports selecting a branch or tag with -b. This example pins android-16.0.0_r1, listed in the Android version/build table. Omitting the branch, as the old article did, does not reproduce its historical checkout.

Download repo

First try the Repo launcher supplied by the Ubuntu repositories:

The official guide currently requires launcher 2.4 or later. If no suitable package is available, follow the official manual installation procedure, including signature verification. The original direct download into ~/bin/repo is not retained as a complete installation recipe.

Create Working Directory

Use a new directory with sufficient free space rather than changing the branch of an existing development tree:

Initialize the Repository

For Tsinghua’s mirror, its current instructions use https://mirrors.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/git/AOSP/platform/manifest. Substitute that URL for -u while keeping the same tag. Choose one initialization source; mirror lag can affect tag availability.

Sync the Code

-c narrows fetching to the manifest’s required branch/revision. The old --no-tags option affects tag fetching; it does not pin a release. Here, -j8 is an example sync concurrency level, which can be reduced for the host or network:

Export the manifest after a successful sync to record actual project commits. Resolve failed project syncs before building.

6. Setting Up the Build Environment and Compiling Pixel Code

The old Pixel sailfish screenshots and the new Cuttlefish example are different targets. Match the product, source, proprietary binaries, and outputs; do not combine their steps.

Install JDK

Installing openjdk-8-jdk is not a general requirement for modern AOSP. The pinned Android 16 build selects its Java toolchain, with envsetup.sh setting ANDROID_JAVA_HOME/JAVA_HOME; do not force it to use system JDK 8. Follow the relevant branch’s requirements for older versions. Building the AOSP tree is also different from building an app with Android Studio’s Gradle tooling.

Install Dependencies

For the selected Ubuntu 22.04 environment, use the official Linux package list:

This corrects the old lib32z-dev name and stops carrying forward obsolete package lists such as lib32ncurses5-dev. Other distributions and older Android branches need their own matching dependencies.

Download Pixel Drivers

Historical Pixel workflow: proprietary hardware binaries must match the device codename and Android build ID. The release driver page lists those combinations. Do not combine the latest preview binaries with arbitrary source. Follow the package instructions and license terms when extracting into the corresponding source root, normally under vendor/. The original article did not record complete archive versions, so the screenshots cannot establish a matching release tag.

The historical Qualcomm extraction output is shown below:

The Android 16 Cuttlefish target below does not use these sailfish binaries.

Compile the Pixel System Image

The historical interactive lunch menu and build configuration show aosp_sailfish-userdebug with the development codename Q:

For the new Android 16 Cuttlefish example, run in one Bash session at the root of the fully synchronized source tree:

The android-16.0.0_r1 envsetup source has removed the old interactive menu: argument-free lunch fails. The three-part selection specifies product, release configuration, and build variant. In this tag, aosp_current maps to bp2a; it does not move the checkout to today’s release. userdebug supports platform development, while production user builds do not provide the same debugging access by default.

m invokes the build, and -j8 allows up to eight parallel jobs rather than requiring exactly eight CPU threads. Reduce concurrency if memory is insufficient. A progress screenshot does not establish full build success.

Successful Compilation

After the build exits successfully, inspect the current target’s images in $ANDROID_PRODUCT_OUT. Existing files in out/ may be stale. The following screenshot remains the historical out/target/product/sailfish, not the Cuttlefish output:

Before running the local Cuttlefish build, complete the host preparation: usable KVM, installed host packages, and effective group/udev configuration. Then, in the terminal retaining the build’s envsetup/lunch configuration:

If using CI downloads instead, obtain the images and cvd-host_package.tar.gz from the same build. Verify actual startup, ADB connectivity, and changed behavior; compilation alone does not establish runtime success.

7. Flashing the Device

This section requires a physical-device target with matching source, proprietary binaries, and images. Do not flash the Cuttlefish images onto a Pixel. The original instructions omitted unlocking and data-loss prerequisites.

Back up data, confirm OEM unlocking is supported, authorize USB debugging, and verify the selected product matches the phone. Follow the official Fastboot procedure to enter the bootloader and unlock if required. Unlocking erases user data and normally needs confirmation on the device; the exact procedure is model-specific.

The original fastboot devices screenshot establishes tool visibility only:

In the correctly selected device build environment, the original command was:

The official first-flash example uses fastboot flashall -w; -w wipes /data. Omitting it does not guarantee cross-version data compatibility or prevent other steps such as unlocking from erasing data. Do not mix partition images from different devices or builds.

The screenshot records that command’s writes, not successful OS startup or functional tests. Dynamic partitions, fastbootd, AVB, and A/B slots on modern targets require their matching device procedure, not the old screenshot’s partition list.

8. Modifying and Compiling Framework, Services, and Res

Complete a full build of the same tree and target before incremental work. Directory names are not module names, and a module build does not necessarily regenerate a flashable image.

Recommended IDEs

  • Java/Kotlin: Android Studio can edit the source, but AOSP is not a normal Gradle project. Use the branch’s supported project-generation tooling, such as AIDEGen, for indexing and dependencies.
  • C/C++: use a familiar editor such as VS Code with matching compilation information. Source Insight and Eclipse were historical preferences, not build requirements.

Compiling Framework

The Chinese original’s mmm framework/base was missing an s; the old directory form was mmm frameworks/base. Do not assume that old entry point applies to Android 16. The pinned tag’s installable non-APEX framework module is:

Its module definition uses the installed stem framework. A separate module named framework is build-only; its name does not make it the deployable jar. Code owned by an APEX must be built through the appropriate module.

Compiling Services

The old directory command was mmm frameworks/base/services. Android 16 provides the installable services module:

Compiling Res

The old directory command was mmm frameworks/base/core/res. The modern module example is:

API, resource-ID, bootclasspath, APEX, or cross-partition interface changes can require dependent modules and complete images to be rebuilt. Replacing one file does not establish a correct deployment.

Root and Remount

The old successful output came from a debug build. It does not apply automatically to a production user build, and bootloader unlocking does not guarantee adb root:

Android 16 debugging may use OverlayFS for a writable layer. Follow the same-tag remount instructions on a test device or virtual device configured for system modification:

-R may arrange required verity-state changes and a reboot. These are debugging settings, not production-device recommendations. Resolve failures before assuming partitions are writable.

Push Changes

adb sync system updates system files from the current build output. It does not guarantee that other partitions, APEX packages, boot images, or preoptimized artifacts are updated. For a compatible, small system-file change on the same build, use separate steps:

Check each result. If synchronization fails, restore stopped Android services with adb shell start and resolve the error. Here, stop/start controls Android services, not the terminal shell. Changes involving initialization, the bootclasspath, or other partitions need the appropriate full rebuild/deployment procedure.

After reboot, verify the actual file or version marker and test the changed function. OverlayFS overrides have OTA limitations and can remain relevant after image flashing, so confirm the effective content. Command success is only part of validation.

About Me && Blog

Below are my personal details and links. I look forward to connecting and sharing knowledge with fellow developers!

  1. About Me: Includes my WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Navigation: A guide to the content on this blog.
  3. Curated Android Performance Articles: A collection of must-read performance optimization articles. Self-nominations/recommendations are welcome!
  4. Android Performance Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

“If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.”

entry.title: Lu Qi: Besides Good Code, What Makes an Engineer Excellent?
entry.content:
Reposted from: Baidu Family, based on Lu Qi’s internal sharing at Baidu in July 2017. It is highly worth learning and pondering for technical personnel.

Historical reprint (reviewed October 2026): The speech text and personal appreciation below are preserved. Roles, schedules, and patent counts in the introduction belong to the historical material. The interdisciplinary advice and entropy metaphor should also be read in their 2017 context. Separate technical notes follow the speech.

I personally admire Lu Qi. “Lu Qi is known for his incredible energy. He typically wakes up at 4 AM, checks emails, and then runs 4 miles on a treadmill while listening to classical music or watching news. He arrives at the office between 5 AM and 6 AM, using that time to prepare for the day undisturbed, and usually works until 10 PM, sometimes sending emails to colleagues at midnight. LinkedIn CEO Jeff Weiner, who worked with Lu Qi at Yahoo for years, initially thought this schedule was unsustainable but eventually said: ‘Lu Qi is indeed the most driven person I have ever met.’ Former Yahoo engineer Amit Kumar also praised Lu’s popularity. Lu says: ‘I don’t feel tired; I love my job every day.’ Lu Qi holds 20 US patents.”

The core ideas of Lu Qi’s speech can be summarized into the following five points. I have posted them on my study wall to remind myself constantly.

  1. “We must have an unwavering and profound belief that the entire world is ultimately driven by technology.”
  2. “Has anyone else already solved this problem? If so, put your time into better innovation.”
  3. “Whatever you do, aim to be the best, to be the strongest in the industry.”
  4. “I imagine myself as a piece of software, a piece of code. Today’s version must be better than yesterday’s, and tomorrow’s will surely be better than today’s.”
  5. “If you see a problem, don’t just ask others—Fix it.”

Believe in Technology

First, believe in technology. As I mentioned, for our industry, and especially for companies like Baidu, a steady and unwavering belief in technology is vital.

I’d also like to share that Bill Gates mentioned Microsoft’s mission as: writing software represents the future of the world.

Why? Because any industry in the future will become a software industry. Gates was right because the degree of automation in any industry will keep increasing, and ultimately, what you process is information and knowledge.

But the way software works has moved forward again. In the age of AI, it’s not just about writing code; you must understand algorithms, hardware, and data. The entire AI development process has advanced significantly. However, technology—especially the technology represented by our industry—will always be at the forefront of any future industry.

Therefore, we must have an unwavering and profound belief that the entire world is ultimately driven by technology.

Innovate on the Shoulders of Giants

If we look at Silicon Valley in the US or China, whether it’s an internet startup or a large corporation, the starting point for everyone is getting higher. Why is the speed of innovation so fast now? Mainly because the starting point is high. The code modules and service capabilities we can use have greatly improved.

Internally, I want to emphasize this. Many large companies, including Microsoft, have rewritten internal code countless times.

My requirement now is: Every time you write a new line of code, the first thing to do is think about whether that line is worth writing. Has someone else already done the same work, perhaps even better? Has anyone else already solved this problem? Then you can put your time into better innovation.

Especially in large companies, there is too much repeated or nearly repeated code, wasting too many resources. This isn’t good for anyone’s career.

Again, within a large company, think before you write code: Do I need to write this? Does someone else already have it? Stand on the shoulders of others to do this.

Pursue Engineering Excellence

Another thing I want to emphasize is Engineering Excellence—the technical excellence and capability in engineering.

Competition in any market is like war. It depends on the physical strength and quality of your troops, the level of training for each soldier, and the weapons you give them—machine guns, tanks, or something else.

Engineering Excellence is analogous to this. We want to build the world’s strongest force. Every soldier, every leader, everyone’s capability and training are top-notch, and the tools and weapons we provide are first-class.

Therefore, Engineering Excellence is a collective pursuit of individual and team capability, alongside innovation in tool platforms. Combined, they bring us long-term core competitiveness and create value for society—ultimately for every user, enterprise, and society as a whole.

I also want to emphasize here: Relentless pursuit of excellence—a never-ending, continuous pursuit.

We either don’t do it, or we do it best. This is my requirement for everyone. Whether it’s a database, a large platform, or big data, whatever we decide to do, we must be determined. Aim to be the best, to be the strongest in the industry.

Learn Every Day

Learning every day is perhaps the most important thing for everyone.

Today, I’ll share how I think about myself. It’s a simple concept: I imagine myself as a piece of software, a piece of code. Today’s version must be better than yesterday’s, and tomorrow’s will surely be better than today’s, because even if I make a mistake, I have an if statement inside that says: If I see this error again, never repeat it.

In English, there is a saying: “Life is too short, don’t live the same day twice.” Every day should be different, and every day should be better. Today’s version must be better than yesterday’s. Every outstanding engineer and technical leader must maintain the ability to learn, especially the scope of their learning.

To expand on this, if you only study Computer Science, it’s certainly not enough. For example, you must study Economics. Why? Computer Science has a major limitation: it assumes that once you have an input, you get an output. This problem-solving approach has its benefits but also its limitations.

Take map navigation as an example. If you use a purely technical approach, you just move people from one congested area to another. Economics models problems differently. It starts by assuming an overall ecosystem where one person’s input is another person’s output. To describe a navigation problem through economics, you calculate an Equilibrium. Markets work the same way.

If you want to truly understand Deep Learning, you must relearn Physics, look at Biology, and study Evolutionary Theory. Because Deep Learning is closely related to these fields. You can’t figure it out on your own; to understand it thoroughly, you must study.

Also, study Product. I’ve always told engineers: if you don’t understand the product, you can’t be a top engineer. To truly be a world-class engineer, you need to understand not just the product but also the entire business and ecosystem. Your responsibility is to see the future—to project technology into future needs and prepare your platform, development flow, and team for that future. So, learning is incredibly important.

Ownership

Finally, it starts with me.

Our company has a grand mission: to simplify a complex world with technology. The world is very, very complex. Essentially, what humans do is “Reduce entropy.”

According to the Second Law of Thermodynamics, the world tends to become more chaotic. What we want to do is make it simpler and make our lives better.

Specifically, we can use AI technology to “awaken all things.” But all of this is built on the accumulated actions of every individual—starting with me. Then there is Ownership: if you see an opportunity, don’t ask others—just do it. If you see a problem, don’t ask others—Fix it.

Treat our mission and our company as your own personal career. I can tell you honestly: if you treat the company’s mission and business as your own and “Own everything,” your career will certainly move the fastest. Start with yourself, start with everything around you.

Technical Notes (October 2026)

These notes distinguish the speech’s metaphors from technical conclusions.

  1. Computer science and equilibrium: Computer science also studies interacting participants. Tim Roughgarden’s algorithmic game theory notes (2013) examine congestion, selfish routing, and equilibrium. Individually preferred routes need not produce a system-wide optimum; computing an equilibrium does not itself solve congestion.
  2. Prerequisites for deep learning: The call to study physics, biology, and evolution is interdisciplinary advice, not a universal prerequisite list. Goodfellow, Bengio, and Courville’s Deep Learning (2016), for example, introduces linear algebra, probability and information theory, numerical computation, and machine-learning fundamentals before deep networks.
  3. Thermodynamic entropy and management: The nondecreasing-entropy statement of the second law concerns an isolated system. It does not mean every local, open system must become more disordered. Local entropy can fall through exchanges of energy or matter with the surroundings while the combined system respects the second law. Organizational “entropy reduction” is a metaphor; code complexity and team organization are not thermodynamic entropy.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal introduction and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro: Includes personal WeChat and WeChat group links.
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows: Welcome to recommend projects/articles.
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: Historical project; paid operations ended in 2026 and new paid members are no longer accepted.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: The Programmer's Apprenticeship - 08: The Beauty of Reading
entry.content:
This is the eighth post in the reading notes series for The Programmer’s Apprenticeship: From Good to Great. The author, Jeff Atwood, is one of the founders of Stack Overflow. His articles cover a wide range of topics. He is a seasoned programmer, manager, and entrepreneur. This book discusses many things beyond programming. Whether you are a junior engineer or a senior engineer, this book is worth reading. As your experience grows, every time you re-read this book, you will gain new insights. Just as the title “From Good to Great” suggests, the author points out the path for you, but whether you can succeed depends on your own cultivation.

I will excerpt some wonderful remarks from the book and sometimes add my own insights or experiences. The outline of the reading notes is consistent with the outline of the book itself. This is also a method I learned from another source and have been using: “How to Read a Book”. I record it for my own frequent review and for readers’ reference. Below is the The Programmer’s Apprenticeship reading note series:

  1. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 01: The Art of Fighting Back
  2. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 02: The Way of Programming
  3. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 03: Web Design Principles
  4. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 04: Reflections on Testing
  5. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 05: Know Your Users
  6. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 06: All About the Internet
  7. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 07: Games and Programming
  8. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 08: The Beauty of Reading

Source note (reviewed October 2026): These are reading notes and personal interpretations, not a verbatim translation. Links have been corrected to accessible original articles. The computer-crime section draws on 2012 writing and should be read as history, not as current threat statistics.

Not Reading, Whose Fault Is It?

(Based on Jeff Atwood’s Programmers Don’t Read Books – But You Should)

There’s a saying: “Programmers don’t read books.” Jeff explores why this might be true. Often, technical books are dry, outdated by the time they are printed, or just plain boring. The Internet has replaced the reference book for many of us.

However, Jeff argues that we are missing out. Deep knowledge often requires the long-form structure that only a book (or a very long series of articles) can provide. Reading code is important, but reading about code—the philosophy, the architecture, the “why”—is equally vital.

We can’t just blame the industry or the medium. If we don’t read, it’s our own fault. We stagnate. We miss the wisdom of the “giants” upon whose shoulders we stand. Books like The Pragmatic Programmer, Code Complete, and The Mythical Man-Month are timeless for a reason.

Heaven Helps Those Who Help Themselves

Related original article: Jeff Atwood’s Rubber Duck Problem Solving (2012).

This section echoes the core philosophy of Stack Overflow: Self-reliance.

Before you ask for help, you must demonstrate that you have tried to help yourself. “Heaven helps those who help themselves” implies that you shouldn’t expect others to solve your problems if you haven’t put in the effort first.

Start by asking yourself: “What have I tried?”

If you encounter a bug, don’t just post the error message. Tell us:

  1. What you expected to happen.
  2. What actually happened.
  3. What you have already done to try to fix it.

Writing out the problem and what you have tried often helps you find the answer before you even ask. That is the point of rubber duck debugging.

2026 update: For debugging questions, follow Stack Overflow’s minimal reproducible example guidance. Include necessary code and configuration as text, report the exact error, and rerun the reduced example before posting to confirm it still reproduces the issue. State the actual versions when version differences matter.

History and Status Quo of Computer Crime

(Based on Jeff Atwood’s Computer Crime, Then and Now and I Was a Teenage Hacker)

In the 2012 article “I Was a Teenage Hacker,” Jeff recalls writing an AppleBasic tool in the 1980s to try calling-card access codes for long-distance calls. This was calling-card code guessing, rather than wardialing to discover modems across telephone numbers.

In “Computer Crime, Then and Now,” Jeff contrasts earlier experiences with financially motivated crime and emphasizes the persistence of social engineering. The claim that techniques changed little belongs to that 2012 argument; it is not a survey of all attack methods in 2026.

These cases highlight risks in human behavior and account-recovery processes, beyond machine configuration. Historical examples help explain those risks, but assessing a system today still requires its current software versions, deployment, and actual threats. “Techniques have not changed” is not a substitute for that assessment.

How to Communicate with People

Related original article: Is Writing More Important Than Programming? (2006).

Ideally, code would speak for itself. In reality, communication is the most important skill for a programmer.

You can be the best coder in the world, but if you can’t explain your ideas to your team, persuade your manager, or understand your users, you will fail. Jeff emphasizes the importance of clear writing (blogging helps with this!) and communication.

Soft skills are hard. They require empathy, patience, and practice. But they are force multipliers for your technical skills.

Practice Basic Skills Diligently

Related original articles: The Ten Commandments of Egoless Programming (2006) concerns review and collaboration; The Ultimate Code Kata (2008) addresses deliberate practice more directly.

Finally, there are no shortcuts. To be awesome, you must practice.

But “practice” doesn’t just mean typing code for 10 hours a day. It means:

  • Deliberate Practice: Working on things you are bad at, not just things you are good at.
  • Code Katas: Small exercises to keep your skills sharp.
  • Reading Code: Reading other people’s code to learn new patterns.

Excellence is a habit. It comes from the daily discipline of trying to suck a little less than you did yesterday.

The Programmer’s Apprenticeship (or Building a Career in Software) is a compilation of the best articles from the Coding Horror blog. The book is divided into 8 chapters, covering topics such as time management, programming methods, web design, testing, user needs, the Internet, game programming, and technical reading. The topics selected by the author are all pain points in a programmer’s career. Many articles have high click-through rates and reply rates on blogs and the Internet. —— from Douban

Jeff Atwood founded the Coding Horror blog (codinghorror.com) in 2004 to record his thoughts and bits and pieces of his software development experience. Today, the blog has nearly 100,000 visits per day. Readers participate in comments, and various views and wisdom collide passionately there. —— from Douban

entry.content:
This is the seventh post in the reading notes series for How to Stop Sucking and Be Awesome Instead, published in Chinese as 《程序员的修炼——从优秀到卓越》 (the series title here is The Programmer’s Apprenticeship).   5. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 05: Know Your Users
  6. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 06: All About the Internet
  7. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 07: Games and Programming
  8. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 08: The Beauty of Reading

Reading note (reviewed October 2026): This is primarily a reflection on games and learning to program. Hardware details and source links have been checked; the text distinguishes the author’s account from my own takeaways. Later projects are dated separately.

My Programming Career Started with BASIC

(Based on Jeff Atwood’s About Me and Please Don’t Learn to Code)

In About Me, Jeff says he started programming with BASIC and names the Texas Instruments TI-99/4A as his first microcomputer. It did not boot straight into the interpreter: the manufacturer’s guide, page II-4 shows a title screen, a keypress to open the menu, then 1 to select TI BASIC. Being able to type a few lines and see a result made for immediate feedback.

These accounts make me think of the invitation early computers seemed to offer: the machine was waiting for you to tell it what to do. Complex tooling can make a first step daunting, but that does not describe every learning environment today.

His 2012 essay Please Don’t Learn to Code argues against treating coding itself as the goal: understand the problem and seek a solution first. It is not a rejection of everyone learning to program. For those drawn to it, that initial creative spark still matters—the joy of building.

If You Want to Play a Game, Write It Yourself

(The previously listed Coding Horror: The Game link is unavailable. A related source is Programming Games, Analyzing Games (August 22, 2007); the learning reflections below are my takeaways.)

There is no better way to understand how software works than to try to build a game. Games are complex systems that require mastering loops, logic, graphics, and user interaction.

My takeaway is that interested beginners can try making a small game, even without aiming for a game-development career. It offers a way to explore engagement, user experience, and performance, though those lessons do not automatically cover every software domain.

For me, the appeal of learning by doing is that the learning itself can be enjoyable.

Metamorphosis from Gamer to Programmer

(The previously listed The Gamer / Programmer and The PC Weenies links are unavailable. Compare the early experiences in Programming Games, Analyzing Games; the points below are reflections, not a list of findings from that essay.)

There is a huge overlap between gamers and programmers. Many of us got into this field because we wanted to understand how our favorite games worked—or because we wanted to mod them.

I see several habits that this background might encourage:

  1. Problem Solving: Every game is a series of puzzles to be solved.
  2. Perseverance: We are used to failing (dying) and trying again until we succeed.
  3. Optimization: We are always looking for the “min-max” strategy to get the best result with the least effort.

Transformation comes when we stop just consuming the content and start creating it. We peek behind the curtain. We realize that the “magic” is just code, and that we can wield that magic ourselves. The passion that drives a gamer to master a level is the same passion that drives a programmer to master a new language or framework.

Later material: In a December 31, 2021 essay, Jeff introduced a project to rewrite classic BASIC games in modern languages. The repository keeps original BASIC code alongside language-specific ports; its README also links to JavaScript versions in a browser. Check the requirements and completeness of each port before using it.

entry.title: The Programmer's Apprenticeship - 06: All About the Internet
entry.content:
This is the sixth post in the reading notes series for How to Stop Sucking and Be Awesome Instead, published in Chinese as 《程序员的修炼——从优秀到卓越》 (the series title here is The Programmer’s Apprenticeship). The author, Jeff Atwood, is one of the founders of Stack Overflow. His articles cover a wide range of topics. He is a seasoned programmer, manager, and entrepreneur. This book discusses many things beyond programming. Whether you are a junior engineer or a senior engineer, this book is worth reading. As your experience grows, every time you re-read this book, you will gain new insights. Just as the Chinese subtitle “From Good to Great” suggests, the author points out the path for you, but whether you can succeed depends on your own cultivation.

I will excerpt some wonderful remarks from the book and sometimes add my own insights or experiences. The outline of the reading notes is consistent with the outline of the book itself. This is also a method I learned from another source and have been using: “How to Read a Book”. I record it for my own frequent review and for readers’ reference. Below is the The Programmer’s Apprenticeship reading note series:

  1. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 01: The Art of Fighting Back
  2. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 02: The Way of Programming
  3. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 03: Web Design Principles
  4. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 04: Reflections on Testing
  5. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 05: Know Your Users
  6. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 06: All About the Internet
  7. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 07: Games and Programming
  8. The Programmer’s Apprenticeship - 08: The Beauty of Reading

Reading note (reviewed October 2026): The source essays date from 2007–2012. Their opinions and my reading impressions remain historical; current archiving and platform limits are noted separately. Net-neutrality and copyright rules vary by jurisdiction and date. The summaries below are not verbatim quotations.

Saving the Internet, Preserving All Memories

(Based on Jeff Atwood’s April 1, 2012 essay Preserving The Internet… and Everything Else)

In “Preserving Our Digital Pre-History”, Jeff nominated Jason Scott to be our generation’s digital historian in residence. It looks like a few people must have agreed, because in March 2011, he officially became an archivist at the Internet Archive.

In the 2012 essay, Jeff described Jason’s invitation to visit the Internet Archive. He quoted Stewart Brand’s view of it as the beginning of a remedy for society’s fading memory. That describes the mission, not a claim that a complete record of the Internet already exists.

One immediate benefit is reducing linkrot. We all know the frustration of clicking a dead link. If the Wayback Machine captured the page, its snapshot may help us find the information again.

The Archive also preserves books, audio, video, and software. Archiving everything is an ambition, not a coverage guarantee.

My takeaway: preserving the Internet’s history is worth supporting because it is part of our shared history.

October 2026 update: The Wayback Machine help page does not guarantee that a site has been archived. Images, dynamic scripts, and features depending on the original server may be missing. Save Page Now captures a page, not an entire site or an ongoing crawl. When repairing a dead link, inspect the snapshot’s text, resources, and date in its URL. Keep independent backups of important material.

The Importance of Net Neutrality

(Based on Jeff Atwood’s February 14, 2011 essay The Importance of Net Neutrality)

The essay introduces net neutrality through Lawrence Lessig’s argument: access networks should not discriminate against comparable lawful traffic to favor their own services or disadvantage competitors. This is a policy principle, not a promise of identical speed for every packet or a law applied uniformly worldwide.

Jeff admits he didn’t fully understand its importance until reading Lawrence Lessig and Tim Wu. The core argument is simple: innovation depends on a neutral network.

If the network owners can pick winners and losers (by throttling traffic or charging extra for fast lanes), then the next Google, Netflix, or Facebook might never get off the ground. The Internet was designed to be a dumb network that moves bits without prejudice. Keeping it that way is essential for the future of free speech and innovation.

My takeaway: concentrating control over communication networks can constrain ordinary people’s expression and opportunities to innovate.

Policy timeline update: On January 2, 2025, the US Sixth Circuit set aside the FCC’s 2024 Safeguarding and Securing the Open Internet order (FCC 24-52). That is a specific US federal ruling, not a statement of every jurisdiction’s rules. The legal situation described in the 2011 essay should not be read as current.

Copyright Protection on YouTube

(Based on Jeff Atwood’s YouTube vs. Fair Use (September 17, 2010) and YouTube: The Big Copyright Lie (October 7, 2007))

YouTube holds a vast range of creative work and copyright disputes. In 2007, Jeff criticized the gap between its upload rules and the movie or television clips available on the site. His essay was not a statistical survey, and it cannot establish that most popular videos today are unoriginal or infringing. Original work can itself be copyright-protected.

This raises fair use. The US Copyright Office explains four factors: the purpose and character of the use, the nature of the original work, the amount and substantiality used, and the effect on the work’s potential market or value. Commentary, teaching, or research can qualify, but the assessment is case-specific. A short clip, attribution, or noncommercial purpose alone does not settle it; copyright exceptions differ elsewhere.

In 2010, Jeff described uploading a roughly 90-second movie clip. A match led to blocking under the rights holder’s policy, and the rights holder rejected his fair-use dispute. He admired the matching technology while questioning how context could be handled. His account describes a claim and a dispute, not a court ruling that his clip was lawful.

My takeaway: protecting copyright and allowing new creative work require a balance; detecting matching material does not complete that judgment.

October 2026 mechanism update: Content ID matches uploads against audio and video reference files supplied by rights holders, not every copyrighted work in existence. Policies can block, monetize, or track, and can vary by territory. A Content ID claim differs from a removal request or copyright strike. One-to-three-minute Shorts with an active claim are blocked, so do not assume the handling of ordinary longer videos applies.

YouTube’s fair-use guidance states that automated systems cannot decide fair use. A dispute process exists, but filing a dispute is not permission or a successful legal judgment.
