entry.title: Some Thoughts on Android System Fluency
entry.content:
Version note — reviewed October 13, 2026: This article was written in 2018. Device examples, app experiences, and vendor opinions describe that period; the old hardware rankings and buying advice are outdated. Technical corrections and updates identify their Android versions. These are not new measurements of the named products.

I’ve long wanted to write about Android system fluency because it’s the most direct aspect of the user experience. The long-standing criticism that Android “gets laggier over time” still casts a shadow over the platform, and it’s a primary reason many users default to iPhone.

Because Google keeps Android open, different manufacturers produce devices with vastly different hardware, and app quality varies wildly. Consequently, fluency is affected by countless factors. It’s rarely just “the system isn’t optimized.” Often, two devices with the same OS but different SOCs offer completely different experiences.

I want to talk through some of the reasons Android can feel slow, so that the next time it happens, we don’t immediately blame the system. Perhaps uninstalling one app will turn out to be enough. Here are the areas I want to cover:

  1. Hardware
  2. System
  3. Applications
  4. The Optimization Loop

Ready? Let’s get started, and please join the discussion.

1. Hardware Level

CPU

The CPU handles much of an app’s business logic and layout work, but the phone’s overall experience also depends on its GPU, storage, memory, cooling, and software workload. The original Qualcomm > Huawei > Samsung > MediaTek ranking did not specify chips or test conditions and should not be used as a buying guide. Compare specific SoCs and devices, including sustained performance rather than just short bursts.

GPU

The GPU is normally part of the SoC: for example, Snapdragon 845 includes Adreno 630. Graphics-heavy games can put substantial pressure on it. However, a game’s name alone does not establish whether it is CPU- or GPU-bound. That applies to Honor of Kings too: version, scene, quality settings, and target frame rate all matter.

RAM

When I wrote this in 2018, 4 GB was common, and a phone almost needed 6 or 8 GB before it could call itself a flagship. That was a comment on the market then, not a current Android minimum or buying recommendation. More RAM can retain cached processes and files, reducing reloads, but capacity is different from bandwidth. Heap limits, rendering caches, and preloading still need bounds; more memory does not guarantee faster execution.

Keeping more background processes also has a cost if they continue running and competing for CPU or power.

Storage (UFS vs. EMMC)

The original comparison concerned eMMC 5.1 and UFS 2.1, common in the 2018 discussion. Storage affects file reads, installation, and resource loading, but interface names and sequential copy speeds do not determine every launch or interaction. Random I/O latency, implementation, and concurrent load also matter.

The Chinese original incorrectly stated that Snapdragon 660 did not support UFS. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 660 product brief lists both eMMC and UFS. Platform support does not tell us which storage a particular phone actually uses.

Screen Resolution

1920 × 1080 describes one 16:9 resolution; phones with other aspect ratios do not all use those dimensions. Higher actual rendering resolution can increase pixel processing and bandwidth costs in rendering, composition, screenshots, or recording. The impact depends on the rendering path and its bottleneck.

Physical display resolution, app rendering resolution, and recording output resolution can differ. I used the Meizu MX4 Pro as an example because users had reported lag and battery drain. Those reports alone do not establish its 2K panel as the sole cause.

Battery Capacity

Battery capacity affects runtime and device design, but workload, efficiency, display power, and temperature also matter. Comparing mAh alone can mislead when battery voltages differ, and a larger battery does not guarantee better sustained performance.

The Chinese article’s recommendations of Oppo Find X, Vivo NEX, and Huawei Mate 10 were 2018 buying advice and are now outdated. The broader point was to consider usable runtime and cooling alongside the SoC.

SoC Platform

The SoC (System-on-a-Chip) and its vendor software form a foundation for the device. OEMs integrate that platform with their hardware and Android customizations.

In my 2018 development experience, Qualcomm’s platform was comfortable to work with: plenty of optimization code and configuration options, good documentation, and quick support. This is a historical engineering opinion, not a controlled comparison or a ranking of today’s vendor platforms.

As for the patent fees, pay what needs paying. We used to joke that if Meizu had adopted Qualcomm SoCs earlier, it would have gone public ages ago.

2. System Level

App Management Policies

Back in 2018, app developers had plenty of reasons to resent Chinese OEMs’ aggressive background controls. But those controls had a reason too: apps from the same vendor kept waking one another up. In some of the cases we investigated, apps were busy in the background or too many processes were occupying memory, and ordinary users had no idea what to do about it. That does not establish the cause of most Android lag.

Examples of vendor policies included restricting apps from silently launching other apps, unnecessary background residency, and prolonged CPU work during screen-off. Their behavior depends on ROM, permissions, and user settings; they are not universal Android prohibitions.

Remote message delivery, posting a notification, and opening its destination are separate steps. An OEM Push SDK is not a universal prerequisite for notifications. For example, on devices with the required services and connectivity, FCM notification messages received in the background can appear in the system tray. OEM push services have their own requirements.

From Android 13 (API 33), non-exempt notifications also require the POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission; channels and user settings affect display too. Tapping a notification may require a cold start if the process has been reclaimed. The resulting delay depends on initialization and the destination screen, not just the push provider.

Memory Strategy

OEMs tune cached processes, memory-pressure handling, and rendering caches for their products. The original LowMemoryKiller threshold discussion reflects older implementations. Android 9 and later use userspace lmkd when no kernel LMK driver is present; Android 10 added PSI-based pressure monitoring, and Android 11 revised the killing strategy to account for thrashing. Kernel support and device configuration still matter. See AOSP lmkd.

Some low-memory cases we investigated involved repeated process kills, reloads, and high CPU use. Reclaim is not all disk swapping: clean file-backed pages can be discarded and read again on demand, while some anonymous pages can be compressed in RAM through zRAM. Devices may also configure zRAM writeback. See Android memory allocation.

Block I/O in a trace is a clue, not proof that memory pressure caused a missed frame. Correlate reclaim, page faults, I/O waits, and process restarts with the affected work. The old advice to buy 8 GB because memory needs only grow is no longer a useful general rule.

Process Scheduling

A rendering dependency that cannot get CPU time may miss its deadline. A Runnable interval in a trace means the thread is eligible to run but waiting for a CPU; it can also follow preemption. It does not by itself prove a scheduler defect.

Check competing runnable work, priority, CPU affinity or cpuset restrictions, and wakeup/migration behavior. Frequency limits and big/little-core placement can change completion time, but running on a little core does not automatically mean jank.

WMS/AMS lock contention and Binder waits require a separate dependency analysis: a blocked thread may be sleeping rather than Runnable. Distinguish slow execution, waiting for CPU, and waiting for another thread or resource. See Perfetto CPU Scheduling. System tuning must also account for the kernel, SoC, and power policy.

Main Thread & Render Thread

For hardware-accelerated View/HWUI rendering, the main thread and RenderThread are useful starting points. RenderThread is created on demand through the renderer path, not necessarily alongside the main thread at process startup. Games with their own rendering paths may use a different structure. See the Android 5.0 RenderThread walkthrough.

Profile GPU Rendering bars can identify slow stages, but they do not fully measure GPU execution, SurfaceFlinger, or screen presentation. Follow up in a trace. Possible causes include:

  • Long input handlers.
  • Heavy animation or list-update work, including item creation and binding.
  • Expensive Measure/Layout/Draw passes.
  • Frequent large bitmap uploads.
  • Rendering commands, GPU work, or buffer waits.

Not all jank originates in these two app threads. Composition, display scheduling, and resource contention also matter. The goal is to finish critical work on time while accommodating input, audio, other necessary work, and power limits; assigning the whole foreground rendering path the highest priority cannot guarantee that.

Triple Buffering

Android 4.1’s Project Butter introduced improvements including synchronized timing and triple buffering. Extra buffering can improve producer/consumer overlap, but queuing may add input-to-display latency. It does not guarantee that an over-budget frame will avoid jank.

Refresh intervals are approximately 16.67 ms at 60 Hz, 11.11 ms at 90 Hz, and 8.33 ms at 120 Hz. These are not universal per-thread budgets. Crossing a 16 ms bar alone does not fully establish presentation jank, and triple buffering cannot be used to dismiss it.

On Android 12 (API 31) and later, Perfetto FrameTimeline can help compare expected and actual timelines and identify late presentation, alongside CPU/GPU and SurfaceFlinger work. Availability depends on version, capture configuration, and rendering-path coverage. Missing data does not mean zero jank.

Virtual Machine (ART vs. Dalvik)

ART improved execution and memory management, but GC can still pause the main thread. Android 8.0’s default Concurrent Copying collector moves much of the work concurrently while retaining a pause phase; allocation pressure and the time needed to suspend threads also matter. See AOSP’s ART GC debugging guide.

Inspect allocation rate, GC frequency, pause duration, and their overlap with slow frames. Neither “Dalvik jank is all GC” nor “ART eliminates GC pauses” is a sound diagnosis.

Thermal and Low-Battery Limits

Thermal throttling, battery saver, and device-idle restrictions are different mechanisms. Depending on the device and state, they can affect frequencies, background work, or networking; overheating does not universally trigger core shutdowns, process kills, disabled effects, and network disconnection together.

A game slowing down after sustained play may be thermally limited, but workload, memory, and network changes need checking too. Android 10 (API 29) added PowerManager thermal-status callbacks. Observe them alongside frame times; ADPF thermal guidance also describes adapting workload for sustainable performance. A larger battery cannot substitute for cooling.

3. Application Level

Complex Layouts

Complex layouts can increase Measure/Layout/Draw work, especially during scrolling when items are created or bound. Hierarchy depth alone is not a diagnosis: inspect actual traversal counts, time spent, and missed deadlines.

Excessive Business Logic

Here is my complaint about Taobao’s cold start in 2018. The home screen would appear, but trying to use it felt like crap: tap a button, nothing; try to scroll, nothing. Some versions had improved, but on a low-end phone it was the same old story. This describes my experience then, not a test of the current release.

Heavy initialization, synchronous module loading, or competing CPU work can make an already visible home screen slow to respond.

The article did not include a complete trace proving substantial dex2oat work on every such launch. ART uses interpretation, JIT, and profile-guided AOT compilation, with behavior depending on installation, existing artifacts, usage, and system policy. A cold start does not mean recompiling the entire app. Modern apps can use Baseline Profiles for common paths, while still measuring initial display and business readiness separately.

Memory Churn

Rapid temporary-object allocation can increase GC frequency and CPU work. A sawtooth memory graph also occurs in normal apps; it does not alone prove a bug or leak. Examine allocation hotspots, GC pauses, and frame timing. If objects remain after their work is finished and collection has occurred, investigate why they are still referenced.

Slow Networking

Users may describe a long wait for content as lag, but network waiting and rendering jank are different metrics. An asynchronous request can be pending while the UI remains smooth. If network work, parsing, or updates block the main thread, investigate that execution path.

Suboptimal Design

Complex, nested animations can be a programmer’s nightmare. A flagship user might love the effect while someone with a low-end phone curses the stuttering. We need enough knowledge and measurements to talk through the tradeoffs with designers. Users of cheaper phones care about performance too, so the design needs to account for them, or provide an appropriate alternative.

Implementation Bugs

Performance bugs can be an unattractive job. At my company, the time spent investigating one could have fixed a dozen visible UI bugs, and we still might not have solved it. Even so, my view was that confirmed performance problems caused by implementation errors deserved top priority.

4. The Optimization Loop

Laboratory Monitoring

Use data to monitor performance during development, simulating user environments to catch problems early. Record device, OS/app versions, refresh rate, temperature, and compilation state so comparisons are meaningful. Separate startup waiting, interaction response, and rendering jank.

Real-World Data Collection

Collect performance metrics from users to identify the most common issues. Be careful to avoid the “observer effect” where monitoring itself causes lag. Focus on indicators such as CPU waiting, memory pressure, and thermal state, tied to the affected scenario. Correlation is a starting point, not causation; verify the explanation against the timeline and a reproducible case.

Targeted Optimization

Rank issues by frequency and impact. Often, this requires collaboration between OEMs and app developers. Incorporate these scenarios back into the lab environment to create a continuous improvement loop: Lab Monitor -> User Simulation -> Big Data Collection -> Targeted Fix -> Lab Update.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: Zhihu: Save Your StartingWindow
entry.content:
It’s often said that the overall iOS experience is superior to Android. This is partly due to third-party software quality (iOS versions are often more polished) and partly due to Apple’s tight control over its ecosystem. To get on the App Store, you must pass rigorous reviews.

Today we look at the system-provided transition before app content is ready: Android’s StartingWindow and iOS’s Launch Screen. Neither is the same as an advertising Activity or business home screen rendered by the app.

I originally wrote that iOS required a single image. I was wrong about that. Xcode 6 release notes document XIB/Storyboard launch screens from iOS 8. They provide early feedback, not a guaranteed zero-delay timestamp. Older Android theme paths allowed customization, disabled previews, and translucent windows; behavior depends on the OS version.

Historical case (reviewed 2026-10-13): The observations, screenshots, and logs concern Zhihu 5.17.2 in 2018, Xiaomi Mix 2S, and Meizu Pro 7. App lists and criticism describe that period, not current-version tests. AOSP android-8.1.0_r1 is a mechanism reference, not an identification of either device’s ROM. Android 12 / API 31 migration guidance is added below.

How StartingWindow Affects User Experience

Because the StartingWindow is the first thing a user sees, its misuse can lead to a terrible first impression. Let’s look at three scenarios:

  1. Theme-provided StartingWindow: The system can show a preview during a qualifying launch and transition to the app window. Its color depends on the theme; it need not be white, appear on every launch, or transition directly to a usable home screen. The examples I saw then included system apps, Jike, and Autohome.
  2. Lightweight custom starting theme: Background colors and drawables can visually match the first frame. The system creates this window; it does not pre-run the app’s setContentView or arbitrary custom layouts. Large resources can still add cost. My examples at the time included Taobao, JD, Weibo, Toutiao, and Meituan.
  3. Disabled preview or translucent theme: An older theme path may leave users looking at the launcher without clear progress. The visible symptom alone does not prove the exact attribute used. WeChat, WeChat Read, UC Browser, Alipay, ICBC, and Mi Home were my examples at the time.

I really could not understand why so many apps chose the third approach. Many users had only one phone to compare against, blamed the system, and sent us high-severity bug reports. It was enough to make me want to cry. Developers and product managers using this approach needed to give it some thought. Reusing a live process can hide the difference. I suggested trying adb shell am force-stop com.tencent.mm before relaunching. That forcibly stops the app; it is not identical to every natural process-death state, nor evidence that an OEM never kills WeChat.

Case Study: Zhihu’s UX Data

As a heavy Zhihu user, I’ve been frustrated by its deteriorating launch experience. In the original observation (v5.17.2), Zhihu uses the first approach (default window), but its startup is so slow that the user is stuck staring at a white screen for a significant amount of time.

I used a Xiaomi Mix 2S (Snapdragon 845) for the traces below; the log is from a Pro 7. White was the observed preview appearance, not a universal Android default. A long wait needs further investigation before assigning it to initialization, scheduling, or I/O.

  1. Selected startup interval in SurfaceFlinger-related tracks (1.933s) — the cropped image does not independently establish physical presentation timestamps:

  2. App process view of the same-length selection — showing bindApplication, Activity startup, and traversal work:

  3. Log Perspective (am_activity_launch_time):
    The Pro 7 event ends in 1078,2684 milliseconds. I also recorded 1552ms for Mix 2S at the time, but did not include that log line. These are not interchangeable measurements.

In the checked AOSP 8.1 ActivityRecord.reportLaunchTimeLocked() implementation, 1078 is the current Activity’s thisTime and 2684 is totalTime for the still-open stack launch interval. They overlap and must not be added; neither says that the advertisement has finished.

Both cropped traces select 1.933s; the Pro 7 log comes from another device. Without the original trace, complete conditions, or repeated samples, they cannot form one precise timeline or prove how much slower another device will be. Below is what I recorded then: roughly 2s of blank screen, followed by about 3s of ads. After waiting through the blank screen, we still had an ad to get past. So much for user experience. A prettier preview would not remove the waiting that followed.

The Visual Journey

Here are the three stages I saw on the Pro 7. The approximate 2s/3s durations are my observations from then, not timings recoverable from individual screenshots. The ad image includes a “skip ad 3” control, so it does not establish a wholly unskippable wait.

  1. Icon Tap -> Blank White StartingWindow (2s)

  2. White Screen -> Ad Page (3s)

  3. Ad Page -> Main UI

My suggestion was for Zhihu to use a lightweight starting theme, like the one in this iOS screenshot from the time. It improves feedback and visual continuity without automatically reducing initialization or advertisement time. Use the migration approach below for current Android implementations.

2026 Update: StartingWindow and SplashScreen

In AOSP android-8.1.0_r1, AppWindowContainerController selects a splash, snapshot, or no starting window based on launch/task/snapshot state. The older splash-theme path excludes translucent, floating, or windowDisablePreview cases. PhoneWindowManager creates a TYPE_APPLICATION_STARTING window from theme resources; its windowSplashscreenContent path wraps a Drawable, not an arbitrary app layout.

Android 12 / API 31 introduced SplashScreen for the relevant cold/warm launch paths; a hot start reusing an Activity does not show it. For migration:

  1. Use androidx.core:core-splashscreen; its 1.0.0 release supports API 23+. Configure Theme.SplashScreen, windowSplashScreenBackground, windowSplashScreenAnimatedIcon, and postSplashScreenTheme, and assign the starting theme to the launch Activity in the manifest.
  2. Call installSplashScreen() before super.onCreate(), then create app content. Remove a separate branding-only SplashActivity to avoid showing two splash screens. See the migration guide.
  3. If retention is needed, make setKeepOnScreenCondition a fast readiness check; do not do I/O or sleep there. A custom exit-animation listener must eventually call SplashScreenViewProvider.remove(). Icon-animation duration does not force the window to remain visible. See the API reference.
  4. Measure TTID and business readiness separately, reporting reportFullyDrawn() at the right ready state for TTFD. Use Macrobenchmark and Perfetto to investigate actual work. Better animation is not evidence of faster startup; see startup timing boundaries.

Historical source references: AppWindowContainerController, PhoneWindowManager, and ActivityRecord. They explain this AOSP version, not an exact reconstruction of either vendor ROM.

Parting Thoughts

Android’s user experience depends heavily on third-party developers. While OEMs can optimize the hardware and OS, the moment a user enters an app, the developer is in the driver’s seat.

StartingWindow is a small detail, but it is the entrance to your app. If even that feels bad, why would users want to come back? Zhihu was just one example; I hoped it would get developers to try their own startup flow and feel the wait for themselves. As the saying goes, speed wins. Better apps make the system feel better too, and users get the benefit.

The following list is retained as a 2018 observation, not a new test of these apps.

The Hall of Shame (Apps using disabled/transparent StartingWindows):

  1. WeChat
  2. WeChat Read
  3. UC Browser
  4. Alipay
  5. ICBC
  6. Mi Home
  7. … (Feel free to suggest more)

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

entry.title: [Sticky] Android Performance Optimization: Must-Know Skills and Tools
entry.content:
This article records the essential knowledge for Android performance optimization (mainly including outstanding articles, WeChat accounts, blogs, and technical teams), covering all aspects of performance optimization. This post will be continuously updated; personal recommendations are welcome.

Having worked on performance for a long time and touched many modules, I must say that doing a good job in performance isn’t easy. Why? Because the amount of knowledge required is immense. Android is a complex system; a single change can affect everything. You can’t excel by only knowing one module.

Alongside reading source code, I’ve learned a lot from other developers sharing their work online. Their articles saved me many wrong turns, and I collected quite a few in my notes. I’m putting that collection here in the hope that it helps others get started with Android system development and optimization. Sorting it out also helps me find gaps in what I know and keep learning.

This article lists the must-know skills and tools for Android performance optimization (if you have your own favorites, feel free to suggest them). Some articles may require specific access methods. Additionally, here is the Android Developer Learning Path (2020 Edition).

Version and reading notes (reviewed 2026-10-13): This evolving resource index includes historical Android, kernel, and tool versions. Original article titles are retained: claims such as “latest,” “ultimate,” and percentage gains belong to their original context, not a universal current guarantee. Login or access restrictions do not establish that content is gone. Confirmed migrations are repaired; unrecovered addresses are marked separately.

Choose evidence for the question. Capture tools, regression metrics, release optimizations, and field monitoring serve different purposes.

GoalCurrent entry pointsScope
StartupMacrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric, Perfetto, Android VitalsSeparate first display (TTID) from app readiness (TTFD); control launch and compilation state
JankPerfetto FrameTimeline, FrameTimingMetric, JankStatsUse frame deadlines and refresh rates; CPU frame duration is not presentation time
MemoryStudio heap dumps, LeakCanary, dumpsys meminfo, heapprofdJava objects, native allocations, and resident memory differ; MAT still analyzes compatible offline HPROF files
ANRAndroid Vitals, ApplicationExitInfo, bugreports, tracesCorrelate incident timing and threads; ordinary apps cannot read all system ANR files
Layout/renderingLayout Inspector, Studio Profiler, PerfettoInspect layout, method execution, and scheduling separately; old tool screenshots are historical

Version boundaries that affect interpretation:

  • StartupTimingMetric was added in Macrobenchmark 1.1.0. TTFD requires correct reportFullyDrawn() reporting and may be unavailable before API 29; missing is not zero. am start -W remains a rough check, not physical-tap-to-readiness measurement.
  • FrameTimingMetric was also added in 1.1.0; frameOverrunMs requires API 31. FrameTimeline provides Android 12+ frame evidence. A fixed 16.67ms is not every device’s deadline.
  • heapprofd requires Android 10+. On production user builds, the target must be debuggable or profileable. Sampled allocations are neither total RSS nor a Java reference graph.
  • ApplicationExitInfo and ANR diagnosis provide exit-record information from Android 11 / API 30. Access to /data/anr/anr_* is privileged; absent records or traces do not prove absence of problems.
  • Baseline Profiles guide ART compilation; Startup Profiles guide build-time DEX layout optimization, available from AGP 8.1 and enabled by default from 8.3. Neither replaces measurement or removing unnecessary startup work.

Read DDMS/Device Monitor, Hierarchy Viewer, and TraceView tutorials in their original environment; start with Android Studio Profiler for current IDE workflows. Age alone does not invalidate Systrace, MAT, or shell measurements: check formats, versions, and permissions.

entry.title: 2017 Best Recommendations - A Reward for Hard-Working Self
entry.content:
2017 slipped by before I knew it, and I haven’t updated the blog in ages. Partly, the more I learn, the less I feel I know, and I worry about misleading readers with a technical post. Partly, I’m just lazy. So I’ve decided this blog doesn’t have to be all technical articles. I’ll also write about things that matter to me and thoughts I want to keep. It’s a record for myself; if someone else finds it useful, even better. (Not that there are many readers…)

With 2017 just behind us, I wanted to share the things I enjoyed using or found helpful at work and at home. Maybe some will be useful to you in 2018. There are apps, hardware, books, and exercise equipment here. These are my picks; what worked for me may not work for you. Right, on to the list.

Historical note (reviewed October 2026): These are my 2017 experiences and recommendations. Models, features, and quoted promotional material retain their historical context and are not current buying or installation advice. Notes below clarify version and feature limits.

2017 Best iOS Apps

Keywords: Weight Loss Learning Knowledge

Keep

If you’re a fitness enthusiast, a weight-loss planner looking for an app to record your workouts, then I recommend Keep to you. Keep has a very famous slogan, I don’t know if you’ve heard it: “Discipline gives me freedom!” I also like another quote: “Don’t let work ruin your life—there’s always someone busier than you who’s exercising.”

The software is just an assistant—the most important thing is self-discipline. Life needs self-discipline, exercise needs self-discipline, diet needs self-discipline. Self-discipline doesn’t mean losing the fun in life; on the contrary, self-discipline brings freedom and confidence. People always long for a perfect version of themselves. Keep at it!

In 2017, with Keep’s help, my weight went from 78kg at my heaviest to my current 70kg. In terms of numbers, it might not seem significant, but looking back at photo comparisons, I really have much more confidence now.

Dedao

As my wife—the boss at home—puts it: you know some people are impressive, and that’s about all you know about them.

The Dedao app gives us a path to get close to those really amazing people, to know their learning methods and ways of thinking. You’ll discover that people smarter than you work even harder than you do—so what reason do you have to be lazy?

In 2017, I listened to Wu Jun’s “Letters from Silicon Valley,” listened to Xue Zhaofeng’s “Peking University Economics Course,” listened to Wan Weigang’s “Elite Daily Class,” spent a year listening to Luo Pang on “Logical Thinking,” and listened to plenty of books.

In terms of both broadened horizons and thinking, I already gained far more than the subscription fees for these columns.

WeChat Reading

There are many reading platforms; choosing one and sticking with it is most important. I have books on all three platforms: WeChat Reading, Duokan Reading, and Kindle—neither is better or worse, what’s important is actually acquiring knowledge.

People are always complaining about how much time we spend staring at our phones. Instead of swiping Weibo, Zhihu, Jike on the subway, it’s better to open a book, calm down, and read carefully.

2017 Best Mac Apps

Keywords: Work Arrangement Work Recording

Things 3

This thing is a bit expensive, but it’s truly useful. Various functions are complete, and data across all platform versions (iPhone, iPad, Mac) is synced.

Things handles the first part of my work routine: planning tasks. With a lot going on, I sometimes forget something important. Now I put everything I need to do in Things and choose the day’s priorities each morning. Anything unexpected goes in there too, so I don’t lose track.

Additionally, Things’ repeating tasks, task priorities, task timing, etc., are quite easy to use. I was previously using the web version of Tower, but I decisively migrated all data to Things.

Update: Things 3 prioritizes through Today ordering and custom tags, rather than a built-in P1/P2 field. Sync requires the same Things Cloud account. With Things 3.23, updating one device requires the others to run 3.22 or 3.23 to keep syncing; cross-platform support does not mean every old version remains compatible.

MWeb

MWeb is a Markdown editor. I tried several others before settling on it. It has the features I need, looks good, feels comfortable to write in, and handles images well.

MWeb handles the second part of my routine: recording what I did, including my daily work log. Things tells me what needs doing; afterward, I use MWeb to write down what happened and what I learned. Things keeps the list, MWeb keeps the thinking.

I also use MWeb to write blogs, company documents, summaries, etc. In short, it’s a Markdown editor I enjoy using.

Evernote

I don’t need to introduce Evernote much. Its browser clipping plugin helped me save many excellent technical articles; the team sharing function helped me share notes in the team.

Evernote handles the third part of my routine: archiving. Technical articles, meeting notes, project plans, PDFs—anything I want to keep long term goes there. Sometimes I even use its presentation mode in meetings instead of making slides.

Version note: This describes the older experience. Evernote and Yinxiang Biji are separate services, with separate accounts and feature sets. International Evernote decommissioned pre-v10 Mac, Windows, and Android clients on March 26, 2024. The old presentation workflow is not a promise about current versions; follow the documentation for the service you use when migrating or exporting.

2017 Best Android Apps

Keywords: Android Tools

Android Network and Resource Access Tools

As a long-time user of Google’s apps and services, I relied on Shadowsocks for the Android experience I wanted at the time. As an Android developer, I couldn’t imagine how many sources of knowledge I’d lose without it.

Crossing the Great Firewall took some care. Thankfully, the government hadn’t shut every route down. Don’t ask me how I set it up—keeping a low profile was how you got by.

Greenify

This was my 2017 recommendation for controlling background apps, not a universal must-install recommendation today. Android 6.0 (API 23) introduced system-level Doze and App Standby; later systems and vendors have their own policies. Check actual battery use and background behavior on the device before adding another tool.

I had the privilege to discuss issues with Greenify’s author Feng in the WeChat group. The depth of Feng’s knowledge and passion for technology—we can only look up to him with admiration. We all owe Feng a donation version.

The promotional description below is historical. The developer’s listing warns that hibernation interrupts background functions, including push messages, alarms, scheduled work, and widget updates. Foreground functionality does not imply unaffected background behavior or permanently new-device performance.

No need to envy friends’ iPhones anymore—even if they install many apps, their phones won’t become laggy or drain battery. With “Greenify,” your Android device can also maintain the smoothness and battery life it had on day one!

Highest user-rated Android power-saving app on Zhihu: http://www.zhihu.com/question/21007772

“Greenify” helps you identify and prevent app programs that have negative impacts on overall system performance and power consumption. Through unique “greenification” technology, it prevents these apps from consuming your battery power and occupying your precious memory. Apps processed by “greenification” technology cannot “secretly” run when you don’t actively launch them, while still having complete functions and experience when you normally launch them—just like iPhone apps!

2017 Best Non-Technical Books

Keywords: Self-Improvement Elevation

Deep Work

I strongly recommend this book, especially to programmers who expect to keep learning throughout their careers. Everyone will take something different from it. I tried some of its methods in my own work and found they helped. For me, it was the best book I read in 2017. Consuming lots of short snippets of information can make me feel as if I know a great deal. Without taking time to think them through, though, they remain fragments and soon fade.

Checking emails at any time and place, participating nonstop in large and small meetings, busy hands and feet in the scream of instant messaging software, constantly switching attention in the cluttered multi-thread work… You appear very busy, perhaps even unconsciously enjoying this busyness—but can your busyness really be converted into productivity?

This book’s author, Cal Newport, PhD in Computer Science at MIT, sharply reveals the shocking truth of the information economy era—more than 60% of knowledge workers’ working hours are spent handling such shallow tasks, and these tasks not only produce limited value but also permanently damage people’s ability to do deep work!

The author founded the concept of “deep work,” with its meaning being to engage in focused professional activities in an undisturbed state, maximizing personal cognitive capabilities. And precisely because deep work capabilities are increasingly scarce in today’s society, their relationship with economic success is becoming increasingly tight. All discussions in the book revolve around “deep work,” and the book is divided into two parts: in the first part, the author objectively analyzes from neuroscience, psychology, philosophy, and other angles the importance of implementing deep work in the new economic situation. The second part systematically teaches specific strategies for practicing deep work in daily life, such as incorporating deep work into daily work processes, improving brain’s deep thinking ability, staying away from social networks, etc.

The author also emphasizes that deep work is not an outdated skill, but a good medicine that rescues people from the mental alienation state caused by technology monopoly. In today’s shallow information era centered on the internet, advocating for deep work is no different from calling for a return to craftsman spirit.

Douban: https://book.douban.com/subject/27056409/

Deliberate Practice - From Novice to Master

This book already has quite a reputation. Actually, this book tells us a very simple truth: if you want to become an expert in any industry or field, you need to do a large amount of deliberate practice, not simply piling up time.

For anyone hoping to improve themselves in any industry or field, deliberate practice is the golden standard—the most powerful learning method discovered to date.

Douban: https://book.douban.com/subject/26895993/

2017 Best Technical Books

Keywords:

To be honest, in 2017 I didn’t seriously finish reading even one technical book. But out of so many technical books I’ve read, there are still two I can recommend to everyone—though the technical books I read are more related to my own work, not necessarily suitable for you.

Deep Understanding of Android Kernel Design Thoughts (Second Edition)

Edition note: The heading names the second edition, while the retained cover and description refer to Android 4.3 and 22 chapters. They do not establish the second edition’s exact source baseline. Check your copy’s edition, ISBN, and source version rather than extending the old compatibility claim indefinitely.

It can be considered a classic book for system development. This book had its second edition this year, adding some new content. Whether you’re an application development engineer or a system development engineer, knowing more about Android system’s architecture and design is very helpful for the depth of your knowledge.

Read source-oriented books against the Android version used by that edition first, then compare with your target system. Jumping straight to the latest branch can introduce path and architecture mismatches. The old description’s “Android 4.3 and above” does not establish compatibility with every subsequent version.

“Deep Understanding of Android Kernel Design Thoughts” applies to Android 4.3 and above versions. The book starts with basic operating system knowledge, comprehensively analyzes implementation principles of core technologies in Android such as processes/threads, memory management, Binder mechanism, GUI display system, multimedia management, input system, etc. Most knowledge points in the book come from engineering project R&D, thus having strong practicality, hoping to let readers “know what is and why it’s so.” The book is divided into four parts: compilation chapter, system principles chapter, application principles chapter, and system tools chapter, with a total of 22 chapters, basically covering all knowledge required to participate in Android development, and guiding readers’ learning through many illustrations and examples, in order to provide readers with more easily understandable thinking methods beyond source code analysis.

“Deep Understanding of Android Kernel Design Thoughts” is suitable for both Android system engineers and application development engineers to read to improve Android development capabilities. Readers can more deeply understand the Android system in the subtle learning process of “Deep Understanding of Android Kernel Design Thoughts,” and naturally apply learned knowledge to actual development problem-solving.

Douban: https://book.douban.com/subject/25921329/

Running Linux Kernel

I’m still reading this book, and due to lack of relevant knowledge, the progress is a bit slow. Essential for Android system engineers.

This book’s content is based on Linux 4.x kernel, mainly selecting relatively basic and commonly used memory management, process management, concurrency and synchronization, and interrupt management these four kernel modules to explain. The book is divided into 6 chapters, sequentially introducing ARM system architecture, Linux memory management, process scheduling management, concurrency and synchronization, interrupt management, kernel debugging techniques, etc. Each section’s content is a Linux kernel topic or technical point, and readers can think based on questions before each small section, then conduct kernel source code analysis around the questions.

This book has rich content and clear thorough explanations, not only suitable for personnel with certain Linux-related foundations, including personnel engaged in Linux-related development, operating system researchers, embedded development personnel, and Android bottom-layer development personnel to learn and use, but also suitable as a learning book for programmers interested in Linux and as a teaching material and training textbook for related majors in colleges and universities.

Douban: https://book.douban.com/subject/27108677/

Version note: This is a Linux 4.x-era book. For a current Android device, check its kernel version, configuration, and vendor changes. The Android kernel overview helps compare architectures; generic Linux mainline and book examples are not necessarily the device kernel.

2017 Best Phone – Meizu Pro 7 Plus

Keywords: Flagship

It’s not that I don’t want to recommend the iPhone X. I just can’t afford it…

The Meizu Pro 7 Plus gets plenty of criticism online, but I still think it’s an excellent flagship. I like Flyme, the hardware is decent, and that little secondary display looks cool. Whether it deserves both “Pro” and “Plus” is up to you.

2017 Best Router – Xiaomi Router Pro

Keywords: Drama

Xiaomi Router + Xiaomi Home Theater was convenient for me in 2017. Some sites offered a “Download to Xiaomi Router” link. One click, and the download would go to my router at home, ready to watch when I got back. That convenience was the whole point. The feature depended on the firmware and third-party services of the time; the old integration’s availability has not been verified for current use.

2017 Best Tablet – iPad Pro

Keywords: Perfect

In my eyes, iPad Pro has both iPhone’s advantages and Mac’s advantages. From usage scenarios, attending meetings, sending/receiving emails, reading e-books, reading technical documents, reading PDFs, etc.—it can handle all.

iPad Pro with a keyboard (don’t buy a pen, it’s useless) is essentially a shrunken version of Mac. Except for writing code, it can satisfy all my other needs. Since I got this good thing, my usage rate of that Mac I’ve been using for several good years has been lower.

Those apps I mentioned earlier: Keep, Dedao, WeChat Reading, Things, MWeb, Evernote all have iPad versions, much better than the iOS versions.

Apple knows how to make good products. My word for the iPad Pro: perfect!

Technical note: “A smaller Mac” describes my use cases, not macOS or native Mac-app compatibility. “Except coding” is also not a current platform limit: supported iPads can build Swift/SwiftUI apps with Swift Playground, subject to its device and OS requirements.

2017 Best Wearable Device – iWatch

Keywords: Recording

Of my four Apple devices, the Watch is the one I notice least. Battery life is my biggest gripe: charging the first generation every day and the second every two days gets old. After I switched my main phone from iOS to Android, I stopped using its calls, texts, and alarm reminders. But it still solved one problem for me: tracking exercise.

Feature note: “iWatch” means Apple Watch here. My phone-switching experience does not mean alarms stop without an iPhone: alarms, timers, and workout tracking remain available offline. Setup still requires a compatible iPhone rather than Android pairing; calls and messages have separate model, network, and carrier requirements.

The treadmill and iWatch make a useful pair for my weight-loss efforts. Seeing the details of each workout pushes me not to slack off. The watch has become something I wouldn’t want to do without.

2017 Best Headphones – MDR-1000X

Keywords: Noise Cancellation

Wireless noise-canceling headphones make a big difference in a noisy office. Whether I’m thinking, coding, or reading, it feels good to get some quiet. And without a cable, I don’t have to worry about it getting tangled around my chair.

I’ve used MDR-1000X for so long, and I’m satisfied with all three aspects: noise cancellation, usability, and sound quality. The original post provides no test source for the claim of 50% fewer interruptions, so it should not be treated as a measured benefit. The effect depends on the environment and how you use the headphones.

2017 Best Weight Loss Companion – Treadmill

Keywords: Persistence

It’s easy to put off a run. I know it helps with weight loss, but sticking with it is another matter. Outside, there’s always the weather: too cold, too hot, rain, snow.

I squeezed a treadmill into my already crowded home. I can run whenever I want, and starting feels like less of a struggle. After work, I open Keep and get going. Five kilometers a day isn’t so hard; keeping it up is the hard part.

Others

Of course, there are still some things that can significantly improve happiness, but I won’t list them one by one. I think I’ll update them below as I think of them.

  1. Rouqilin’s beef sauce—look for 三观正的牛 (roughly, “a cow with its values in the right place”). Give it a try; I think you’ll love it
  2. Dishwasher—once you use one, cooking at home feels less daunting
  3. Floor-sweeping robot, who doesn’t want the floor at home to be clean every day? Especially when you have a long-haired monster and two cats at home

entry.title: 2017 Annual Best Recommendations - Reward Yourself for Hard Work
entry.content:
2017 has passed before we knew it. The blog hasn’t been updated for a while - one reason is that I increasingly realize how shallow my knowledge is and fear that writing about technical topics might mislead readers, and another reason is simply that I’ve been too lazy. Given these two reasons, I’ve decided that blog updates no longer need to be limited to technical articles - things I find meaningful, thoughts, and reflections will also be shared here. On one hand, it serves as my own record, and if it happens to help readers along the way, that would be even better (though there aren’t many readers anyway…).

Since 2017 has just passed, I feel it’s necessary to recommend to everyone the things that I found to be great experiences or very helpful for work and life in 2017 - perhaps you’ll need them in 2018. The recommendations include Apps, hardware, books, equipment, etc. It should be noted that these are things that brought me great help in 2017 - what works for me may not work for you. Without further ado, let’s get into it!

Historical note (reviewed October 2026): These are my 2017 experiences and recommendations. Models, features, and quoted promotional material retain their historical context and are not current buying or installation advice. Notes below clarify version and feature limits.

2017 Best iOS App Recommendation

Keywords: Weight Loss, Learning, Knowledge

Keep

If you’re a fitness enthusiast, planning to lose weight, or looking for an app to track your exercise, I recommend Keep. You may have heard Keep’s famous slogan: Self-discipline gives me freedom! I also love another quote: Don’t let work ruin your life - there’s always someone busier than you who’s still exercising.

The software is just an aid - the most important thing is self-discipline. Life requires self-discipline, exercise requires self-discipline, diet requires self-discipline. Self-discipline doesn’t mean life loses its fun - on the contrary, self-discipline gives me freedom and confidence. People always aspire to be their best selves. Keep It!

In 2017, with Keep’s help, my weight went from a peak of 78 kg to 70 kg. The numbers might not seem like a big deal, but looking back at photo comparisons, I’m really much more confident now.

Dedao (iGet)

As my wife—the boss at home—says, some people you know are impressive - and that’s about it.

Dedao actually gives us a way to get closer to those impressive people and understand their learning methods and ways of thinking. You’ll find that people smarter than you work even harder - so what excuse do you have to slack off?

In 2017, I listened to Wu Jun’s “Letters from Silicon Valley,” Xue Zhaofeng’s “PKU Economics Course,” Wan Weigang’s “Elite Daily Lesson,” Luo Pang’s year-long “Logical Thinking,” and many audiobooks.

In terms of expanding horizons and stimulating thought, what I gained far exceeded the subscription price of these columns.

WeRead

There are many reading platforms - the most important thing is to pick one and stick with it. I read on WeRead, Duokan, and Kindle. There’s no absolute better or worse - what matters is actually gaining knowledge.

People who constantly look at their phones are often criticized nowadays. Instead of scrolling through Weibo, Zhihu, or Jike on the subway, why not open a book and read quietly?

2017 Best Mac App Recommendation

Keywords: Work Planning, Work Recording

Things 3

It’s a bit pricey, but it’s really useful. All the features are complete, and data syncs across all platform versions (iPhone, iPad, Mac).

Things mainly handles the first part of my work routine: task planning. Often there are many tasks, and sometimes important things get forgotten. Now I record everything I need to do in Things, and every morning I filter out what to do today based on priority. If other urgent matters come up, they also get recorded, so nothing gets overlooked.

Things’ recurring tasks, task priorities, and task timing are all quite useful. After using the web-based Tower, I decisively migrated all my data to Things.

Update: Things 3 prioritizes through Today ordering and custom tags, rather than a built-in P1/P2 field. Sync requires the same Things Cloud account. With Things 3.23, updating one device requires the others to run 3.22 or 3.23 to keep syncing; cross-platform support does not mean every old version remains compatible.

MWeb

MWeb is a Markdown editor. I tried several before settling on this one. It’s feature-complete, has a beautiful interface, makes Markdown writing comfortable, and has excellent image support.

MWeb handles the second part of my work routine: task recording, including daily task completion records. Things is for planning tasks, but after completing tasks, you need to record and summarize - that’s the daily task record. Things records the workflow, while MWeb records the thoughts.

I also use MWeb to write blog posts, company documents, summaries, etc. In short, it’s a Markdown editor I enjoy using.

Evernote

No need to introduce Evernote much. Its powerful browser clipping plugin has helped me store many excellent technical articles; team sharing features help me share notes within the team.

Evernote handles the third part of my work routine: archiving. Whether it’s technical articles, meeting minutes, project plans, or PDFs - if you need a place for long-term storage, Evernote is a very reliable choice. Sometimes during meetings without making PPTs, Evernote’s presentation feature can also do the job.

Version note: This describes the older experience. Evernote and Yinxiang Biji are separate services, with separate accounts and feature sets. International Evernote decommissioned pre-v10 Mac, Windows, and Android clients on March 26, 2024. The old presentation workflow is not a promise about current versions; follow the documentation for the service you use when migrating or exporting.

2017 Best Android App Recommendation

Keywords: Android Tools

Android Network and Resource Access Tools

As a long-time user of Google’s apps and services, I relied on Shadowsocks for the Android experience I wanted at the time. As an Android developer, I couldn’t imagine how many sources of knowledge I’d lose without it.

Crossing the Great Firewall took some care. Thankfully, the government hadn’t shut every route down. Don’t ask me how I set it up—keeping a low profile was how you got by.

Greenify

This was my 2017 recommendation for controlling background apps, not a universal must-install recommendation today. Android 6.0 (API 23) introduced system-level Doze and App Standby; later systems and vendors have their own policies. Check actual battery use and background behavior on the device before adding another tool.

I had the privilege of discussing issues with Mr. Feng, the author of Greenify, in a WeChat group. Mr. Feng’s depth and passion for technology is something I can only aspire to. We all owe Mr. Feng a donation for the paid version.

The promotional description below is historical. The developer’s listing warns that hibernation interrupts background functions, including push messages, alarms, scheduled work, and widget updates. Foreground functionality does not imply unaffected background behavior or permanently new-device performance.

No more need to envy friends with iPhones - even with many apps installed, your phone won’t become slow and battery-draining. With ‘Greenify’, your Android device can stay as smooth and long-lasting as the first day you got it!

The most endorsed Android battery-saving software on Zhihu: http://www.zhihu.com/question/21007772

‘Greenify’ helps you identify apps that negatively impact overall system performance and battery consumption, and uses unique ‘hibernation’ technology to prevent them from draining your battery and occupying precious memory. Apps processed with ‘hibernation’ cannot ‘secretly’ run when you haven’t actively launched them, yet retain full functionality and experience when you do launch them normally - just like iPhone apps!

entry.title: Reflections on Work and Growth (2017)
entry.content:
In the blink of an eye, it’s 2017. I’ve been working for nearly four years. I went to school in Weihai in 2009, started my internship in Shanghai in 2012, stayed in Shanghai after graduating in 2013, joined Meizu in Zhuhai in 2014, and have been here ever since.

I’ve been writing on this blog since graduation—writing, deleting, and rewriting—recording my journey from App development to System App development, and finally to System Framework development. Looking back after a few years is a great way to appreciate how far I’ve come.

This post records my thoughts on my blog, my job, my work habits, and my expectations for 2017. It’s a mix of confusion and ambition.

We are already 30% through 2017. I hope it’s not too late to share this.

About the Blog

Looking at the timestamp of my last post, it’s been exactly a year. I’m quite ashamed. Every time I intended to start writing again, something always got in the way.

When I first graduated, I loved writing. Study notes, tutorials, everything went up on the blog. But as my career progressed and I learned more, I wrote less. One reason is that as my technical level improved, I realized my depth was still lacking. I knew the “how” but often not the “why.” In that state, I worried my writing might mislead others.

Now that I’ve had a little more time to learn, I want to share some of the experience and tips I’ve picked up. I also want a record for myself. If I don’t write down an idea, it’s easy to forget it.

About Work

From my internship at HTC, a short stay at Firefly Lewa, to Meizu, I’ve worked for several years now—all in Android. Moving from App to System development has taught me that software engineering is fascinating, especially when your features are used by millions. That excitement and responsibility drive me to be better. I believe Android’s dominance in the smartphone world won’t be shaken for at least another five years, so it’s worth investing time here.

Beyond specific technical points, learning Android’s design philosophy, software architecture, and cultivating the ability to solve general problems is even more important. That is my current focus.

I haven’t decided which technical area to go deeper into yet. Right now, Android and Linux process management and CPU scheduling interest me. On the performance side, I’m leaning toward responsiveness, smoothness analysis, and tuning. These areas alone are enough to keep me busy for a long time.

Visiting the headquarters a few days ago, I saw that our company released 15 phones in 2016. Each one required performance tuning. Between the massive list of performance features and the unique performance bugs on every model, the team barely had time for deep, meaningful work. It felt like we were standing still. I hope to change this in 2017—starting with myself.

About Work Scope

My work mainly involves system-level optimization. I cover a lot of ground without going very deep. This year, I want to pick one area and really work on it:

  1. System-level performance optimization (Framework and App layers).
  2. Optimizing responsiveness, smoothness, memory, startup speed, overdraw, HWUI, and SurfaceFlinger.
  3. Defining performance test cases and standards.
  4. Identifying and implementing new performance optimization points.
  5. Developing key system projects like the Intelligent System Tuner and process priority optimization.
  6. Analyzing performance issues for both legacy and new devices.
  7. Training new employees and hosting internal tech sharing sessions.
  8. Competitive analysis.
  9. Documentation and summaries.

About Habits

Since 2016, I’ve developed a set of work habits, but I haven’t always followed them strictly. In 2017, I need to be more disciplined.

Daily Schedule

Every morning, I plan out my day based on yesterday’s records and emails:

  • Priority: Identifying the priority of each task and doing the most important ones first.
  • Time Estimation: Estimating the time for each task, down to 30-minute blocks.

I also leave a buffer for emergencies—like someone needing an urgent analysis that disrupts my plan. Managing time is a skill. Based on my experience at the company, my schedule usually looks like this:

  • Morning: Fewer interruptions. I focus on developing important features or researching new technologies.
  • Afternoon: Handling bugs, emails, and less critical features.
  • Evening: Technical research.

Of course, reality often gets in the way of the ideal. Software development is unpredictable. Someone suggested using a Pomodoro timer to avoid interruptions, but my personal tip is: just wear headphones!

I use Tower to manage my personal tasks. I tried to get the team to use it for a while, but it never quite fit, and they gave up. So here I am, using a team tool on my own. Priorities and times are displayed as tags:

Work Logging

After arriving home, I record the day’s work. While Tower is great for planning, it’s not ideal for logging. It’s hard to review, and personal logic or ideas get lost in it.

I use MWeb for logging. I record every task completed, no matter how small. For important tasks, I record my logic and solution. I also do weekly summaries, pulling from Redmine, email, and Tower. This ensures I don’t miss important data.

Article Clipping

I use Evernote to clip good articles or important findings, which I organize and review periodically.

About 2017

The company has been quite turbulent lately. Several colleagues have left, and we are in a painful transition phase. I’ve had my hesitations, but I’m not spending too much time overthinking it. I’ll just do every task at hand well. Opportunity favors the prepared.

As a software engineer, coding ability must always come first. I need to learn from my idol, 百万 (the screenshot below shows a week with 51 hours of coding)!

entry.title: Android Bottom Navigation Spec Part 2: Style, Behavior, and Dimensions
entry.content:
In March 2016, Google added Bottom Navigation to its design guidelines. This release was quite surprising to many, as Bottom Navigation hadn’t been mentioned in previous Material Design iterations. Bottom tab bars were common in iOS apps, while older Android guidance discouraged them. These were design recommendations, not platform limitations or a requirement for every iOS app.

This is the second article in a series on Android Bottom Navigation, covering style, behavior, and dimensions.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): The main sections preserve 2016 Material Design 1 (M1) illustrations, not current Material 3 (M3) implementation requirements. Some values in the surviving M1 archive differ from the original images; those differences are identified below. Section 5 uses Compose Material3 1.3.0 as an explicit source reference, not an Android OS version.

See Part 1 for usage and window adaptation.

1. Style

1.1. Icons and Text

Use icons that communicate their destination. These are historical M1 label rules; “focused” here means the selected destination, not keyboard or accessibility focus:

  • Show the icon and text label for the focused (active) item.
  • If there are only three items, show icons and text labels for all items.
  • If there are four or five items, show only the icon for inactive items.

1.2. Color

M1 recommended the primary color for the selected destination, as illustrated below. M3 uses theme color roles and an active indicator; this primary/black/white recipe is not its universal styling rule.

If the bottom navigation bar is colored, use black or white for the icons and text labels.

1.3. Text Labels

The M1 examples favor concise labels over confusing wrapping, truncation, or shrinking. Modern implementations must also accommodate translated labels, larger system fonts, and accessible names; do not shrink text merely to reproduce an old image.

2. Behavior

Read the M1 behavior advice within its scope:

  • Each icon represents a top-level destination, not a menu or dialog command. The original translation’s ban on a “separate window” was broader than the source.
  • Reselecting an item may return to its top or refresh, according to the product’s convention; the component does not perform that business logic automatically.
  • The whole bar can be configured to hide or show during scrolling. Individual icons need not independently disappear, and scroll handling is not automatically wired up.
  • M1 discouraged switching bottom-bar destinations by swiping content and recommended cross-fades. It did not prohibit carousels or other horizontal gestures within a destination.
  • M1 also advised against cycling through bottom destinations with Back. Modern Back behavior must follow the actual navigation stack; do not simply intercept system Back or destroy the Android task on each switch. See Part 1 for Navigation 2.4.0 state restoration.

3. Dimensions

3.1. Fixed Bottom Navigation Bar

“Fixed” describes equal-width items, not an always-visible bar. Dividing available width by item count gives the entire item’s width, not the icon size; minimum and maximum constraints still apply on wider layouts.

Width constraints (including padding):

  • Maximum: 168dp
  • Minimum: 80dp in the surviving M1 archive. The original text gave 120dp/104dp for large/small layouts, and the retained image below explicitly says 104dp. These sources represent different revisions, not one combined specification.

Height: 56dp
Icon size: 24x24dp

Alignment: The icon sits above its label, horizontally centered; they are not a side-by-side pair.

Padding:

  • 6dp above icon (active view), 8dp above icon (inactive view)
  • 10dp below text label
  • 12dp left and right of text label

Text Labels:

  • Roboto Regular: 14sp (active view)
  • Roboto Regular: 12sp (inactive view)

3.2. Shifting Bottom Navigation Bar

“Shifting” is the historical layout with different selected and unselected widths, not horizontal scrolling. The equal-width formula does not apply to every item here.

Width constraints (including padding):
Active Item:

  • Maximum: 168dp
  • Minimum: 96dp

Inactive Item:

  • Maximum: 96dp
  • Minimum: 64dp in the original image; the surviving M1 archive specifies 56dp. The image is retained as historical evidence.

Height: 56dp
Icon size: 24x24dp
Alignment: A selected icon sits above its label, horizontally centered. An icon-only inactive item is centered according to the old layout.

Padding:

  • 6dp above icon (active view), 16dp above and below icon (inactive view)
  • 10dp below text label

Text Labels:

  • Roboto Regular: 14sp (active view)

4. Elevation and Hierarchy

M1 assigned conceptual elevations of 6dp to Snackbar and 8dp to bottom navigation. “Behind” describes layering, not a requirement to obscure the message: the image below keeps it readable above the bar. Modern placement cannot be inferred from those two numbers alone.

Drawers, modal sheets, and keyboards interact through their layouts, windows, and inset handling. The IME is a system window, not simply a higher-elevation View in the app, and does not invariably cover the entire navigation bar.

5. 2026 Update: Check the Component Version

The reference here is the Google Maven Compose Material3 1.3.0 source archive, specifically NavigationBar.kt, NavigationBarTokens.kt, and Scaffold.kt. These are versioned implementation details, not fixed values for every M3 implementation.

  • Labels and width. With a label supplied, NavigationBarItem defaults alwaysShowLabel to true; four or five items do not automatically hide inactive labels. Items receive equal weight. Historical shifting behavior is not this component’s default.
  • Size and color. Its ordinary NavigationBar uses an 80dp container minimum-height token and a 24dp icon token. Constraints, content, and insets affect measured height; do not replace a hardcoded 56dp total with a hardcoded 80dp total. Default selected-icon, indicator, and label colors come from onSecondaryContainer, secondaryContainer, and onSurface, respectively.
  • Insets. The bar handles bottom and horizontal system-bar insets by default, not the entire page or IME. Content must apply the innerPadding supplied by Scaffold and consume insets appropriately, avoiding duplicate manual padding. See Material inset responsibilities and IME/inset handling.
  • Snackbar. In Scaffold.snackbarHost, this version positions it using the actual bottomBar/FAB dimensions. Raising elevation to cover the bar is unnecessary. Custom layouts still need to keep messages and actions visible and reachable.
  • Accessibility. A 24dp icon is not a touch target. Check at least 48dp targets, meaningful names, selection state, font scaling, and RTL. Avoid duplicate announcements where a text label already supplies the name. See Compose accessibility defaults.

In-app navigation, system navigation, and the keyboard are separate surfaces with separate sizing and inset responsibilities.

entry.title: Android Bottom Navigation Spec Part 1: Usage
entry.content:
In March 2016, Google added Bottom Navigation to its design guidelines. This release was quite surprising to many, as Bottom Navigation hadn’t been mentioned in previous Material Design iterations. Bottom tab bars were common in iOS apps, while older Android guidance discouraged them. These were design recommendations, not platform limitations or a requirement for every iOS app.

This is the first article in a series on Android Bottom Navigation, covering its usage and historical evolution.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): The images and Do/Don’t guidance below belong to historical Material Design 1 (M1), not a complete specification for Material 3 (M3). The official change log records bottom navigation in March 2016. Section 6 adds current implementation guidance. Material design versions are not Android OS versions.

1. Previous Android Bottom Bar Design Specs

2. WeChat’s Redesign

WeChat’s navigation redesign caused a stir before Google’s official guidance. The original article associated it with version 5.2. The two historical screenshots below show different tab placements, but do not establish exact releases, test scope, or how quickly a change was reversed.

3. Google+’s Redesign

Google+ was another prominent example discussed at the time. Google announced its redesign on November 17, 2015; the original screenshot is retained below:

Well, so much for that rule. WeChat hadn’t followed it and seemed to be doing a lot better than Google+ anyway.

4. Bottom Navigation Design Specs

Enough gossip; let’s look at the official Bottom Navigation Design Guidelines. Most of us programmers aren’t as good at design as the designers. Some guidelines can at least help us avoid making something too ugly.

4.1. Usage

M1 bottom navigation primarily targeted mobile layouts; side navigation was an alternative on larger displays. This is an in-app component, distinct from Android’s system Back/Home buttons or gesture-navigation area.


4.1.1. When to Use

Use Bottom Navigation when:

  • There are three to five top-level destinations of equal importance.
  • These destinations need frequent, direct access.

This does not require a visible bottom bar on every login, editing, or full-screen task. M1 itself excluded focused tasks such as composing an email.

[Do and Don’t] 1. Number of Items

M1 suggested considering tabs below three destinations. Choose by content hierarchy, not count alone: two categories within one content area may fit tabs, while independent top-level destinations need a broader navigation decision.


[Do and Don’t] 2. No Horizontal Scrolling

The M1 page mentions alternative access above six destinations in one paragraph, but explicitly limits the bar to five elsewhere. Six is not an endorsed bar size. Regroup additional destinations or provide another entry, such as a drawer, instead of scrolling the bar horizontally.


[Do and Don’t] 3. Optimal Item Count

Keep three to five primary destinations; excessive items compromise tap targets as well as appearance. These M1 illustrations are historical examples, not current M3 color or label templates.


5. Bottom Navigation vs. Tabs

Bottom navigation and tabs can coexist when their hierarchy is clear. For example, a bar can switch between Home, Favorites, and Profile, while tabs inside Favorites group related content. Avoid having both controls compete for the same pages or silently change the bar’s destinations.

Tabs support tapping; swipeable pages require an additional implementation such as a pager. Swiping is not an automatic feature of a Tab or the defining distinction between the controls. See the current Compose tabs guide.

6. 2026 Update: Implementation Choices

  • Components. Use M3 NavigationBar / NavigationBarItem in Compose, or Material Components BottomNavigationView in View projects. Three to five consistent top-level destinations of similar importance remain the recommendation. Keep M2/M3 imports distinct; library versions are not OS API levels.
  • Windows. Adapt to the app’s current window, not a device or orientation label. NavigationSuiteScaffold belongs to material3-adaptive-navigation-suite. From 1.0.0-alpha07, its version line moved to Material3 1.3.0, released September 4, 2024; consult the release notes for project compatibility. The current adaptive guide describes a default bar for compact width or height, or tabletop posture, and a rail otherwise. A drawer requires customization, not merely a tablet device.
  • State. Displaying a selected item does not manage the back stack. Keep selection aligned with the actual destination and decide how each flow resumes. Jetpack Navigation 2.4.0 added multiple-back-stack support. The relevant View setupWithNavController() integration differs from configuring Compose navigation. Saving an index with rememberSaveable is not a substitute for stack management.

Continue with Part 2: Style and interaction, again distinguishing historical M1 illustrations from modern components.
