entry.title: How to Calculate App Startup Time in Android?
entry.content:
Someone recently asked on Zhihu: “How to calculate APK startup time?”

“How can I use Python or direct ADB commands to calculate APK startup time? I want to measure the time from clicking the icon to the APK being fully started. For example, in a game, this would be from the icon tap to entering the login screen. Existing methods like adb shell am start -W provide ThisTime and TotalTime, but I’m unsure of the difference and they don’t seem to match visual reality.”

My colleague Guo Qifa and I answered different parts of the question. With his permission, I put our answers together here: partly so I could find them again, and partly to make them easier for other developers to find outside Zhihu.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): The original three-column output is explained against AOSP android-5.1.1_r1. The command in android-4.4.4_r2 did not print WaitTime, while android-16.0.0_r1 no longer prints ThisTime. Interpret results using the OS version, launch state, and measurement boundaries. The historical example remains, with TTID, TTFD, and current guidance added; its numbers are not a new device measurement.

1. Startup Scenarios

Startup can be measured once its boundaries are defined: a system launch request to initial display differs from an icon tap to an interactive login screen. Both games and ordinary apps can keep loading after the first frame, so the distinction is not simply “game versus app.”

1.1 App Startup

The launcher normally resolves a MAIN/LAUNCHER entry, which need not be named MainActivity and may route through an existing task. Creating a new instance involves onCreate/onStart/onResume; reusing an instance need not repeat every callback.

Returning from onResume() does not guarantee drawing or presentation. The View path may perform later traversals with measurement, layout, and drawing as needed; there is no fixed requirement for two traversals. The first frame may contain only a background, placeholder, or loading state, not all usable business content.

Distinguish time to initial display (TTID) from time to full display (TTFD), which depends on the app declaring its usable state. Timing lifecycle callbacks alone does not cover the whole launch path.

adb shell am start -W issues a shell launch request. The option is uppercase -W; it does not automatically include the physical tap, launcher processing, or all host-side adb startup overhead.

1.2 Cold Startup: Target Process Not Running

A cold start means the target process is not running, not necessarily the first launch after installation or reboot. Reentering after process death can be cold again. Installation/login state, data caches, and code compilation state are separate variables to record.

The original output is retained below, in milliseconds. Its 355/365 values are historical, not targets or new device results:

There is no universal rule to choose WaitTime, and the three numbers must not be added. They have different boundaries in android-5.1.1_r1.

The waiting branch in frameworks/base/cmds/am/src/com/android/commands/am/Am.java calls AMS startActivityAndWait(). The unreadable first source image is replaced by the relevant timing excerpt:

The command later prints WaitTime = endTime - startTime. This is the command’s internal waiting interval, covering the launch call and its return wait, not time since a physical tap. It usually covers an outer interval, but its difference from the other values is not exclusively the previous app’s pause time.

ActivityRecord.reportLaunchTimeLocked(curTime) computes the other two values:

  • curTime: SystemClock.uptimeMillis() supplied here by windowsDrawn().
  • displayStartTime: the current Activity’s display-launch accounting start, maintained through paths such as ActivityStack.setLaunchTime(), not necessarily the start of onCreate().
  • stack.mLaunchStartTime: the beginning of this stack’s still-open launch accounting interval. If zero, TotalTime falls back to ThisTime.

The values match when a single Activity has identical start points. They can differ when an earlier Activity has not reported drawing complete and a later Activity is part of the same still-open interval. This is not a universal first-to-last-Activity stopwatch: a completed report clears mLaunchStartTime, and an intermediate visible splash Activity may already have ended an earlier interval.

The old diagram misspells TotalTime as TotolTime. Its aligned endpoints do not mean that the window-drawn report and command return happen simultaneously. The numbered segments are a schematic of one old launch path:

  1. ① can include task selection, pausing the foreground Activity, and scheduling/preparation.
  2. ② can include process creation, an earlier Activity’s initialization, and a transition.
  3. ③ extends beyond onCreate/onResume to the window-drawn report; it does not guarantee that business content such as a login screen is ready.

ThisTime and TotalTime overlap, and WaitTime is not another stage to add. TotalTime can describe the application’s window-launch interval; WaitTime describes the command’s wait. Neither directly measures tap-to-business-readiness end to end.

In this tag, am_activity_launch_time and the Displayed log are written by the same reportLaunchTimeLocked() method. They can correspond to the same successful wait result, but field names and meanings should not be forced across separate launches, timeout paths, or OS versions. Bringing an existing task forward also has paths returning 0 or waiting for visibility, rather than using the first-draw formula above.

The end point is the report in ActivityRecord.windowsDrawn(). WMS calculates drawn and visible states separately and excludes the StartingWindow from application-window drawing counts. This is a system window-drawing signal, not an optical timestamp proving visible pixels, and not proof that asynchronous content is fully loaded.

1.3 Warm and Hot Startup

Reusing the process while recreating an Activity is normally a warm start. Bringing an existing Activity forward while its process and instance remain alive is the usual hot-start case. “Opening it a second time” or “pressing Back earlier” is not sufficient classification: Back behavior, task state, and OS version affect whether the instance survives.

Android 16 WaitResult also distinguishes internal RELAUNCH (process reused but an existing Activity must be destroyed and recreated, for example after an unhandled configuration change) and UNKNOWN states. Do not silently mix all results into one cold/warm/hot sample group. Define the preparation steps and record the observed state.

2. Game Startup

Command-line tools can launch a game Activity and observe system window-startup accounting. They cannot automatically know when game content becomes usable. Ordinary apps with network content, session restoration, or database loading have the same limitation.

2.1 System Phase

A game commonly has an Activity hosting its window. System traces can cover process creation, the Activity, and initial window drawing. A shell-originated launch should not be labelled as starting at the user’s launcher tap.

2.2 Game Phase

After the Activity appears, the game may load assets, update data, read configuration, or initialize its engine. The first Surface/window frame can be a loading screen. The game must define a verifiable condition for an interactive login screen or menu.

Logs are not the only option. Combine monotonic-clock markers, Trace events, and reportFullyDrawn() when the app reaches its fully usable state. A game engine must distinguish resource readiness from rendered, usable content; download completion alone is insufficient. Use the same clock basis at both ends. Timing from onCreate cannot recover earlier tap or process-creation time.

3. Conclusion

What fascinates me about computers is their precision. A launch may take a different amount of time on each run, but each measurement records that particular run.

Companies have different priorities. When I wrote this, ROM makers wanted their built-in apps to open quickly, while many Internet apps put ads or feature introductions before the main screen. I can understand the different needs. As a user, though, I would rather reach the main screen sooner. Startup time deserves a place among an app’s performance metrics.

As they say:

“In the world of Kung Fu, speed defines the winner!”

4. 2026 Update: Making Measurements Comparable

Fix the launch entry and state first. For a local rough check, replace the package/component below with the app’s real launch entry. -S force-stops the target package before starting its Activity. It does not reset installation, login, or disk caches to a first-install state, nor does it simulate a physical tap.

Check Status, the returned Activity, timeouts, and messages about bringing an existing task forward before interpreting timing. The checked Android 16 ActivityManagerShellCommand prints LaunchState, nonnegative TotalTime, and WaitTime, but no ThisTime. Do not replace a missing column with zero. Its force-stop and following wait occur before startTime; the host-side wall-clock duration of the entire adb command is not WaitTime either.

Use Macrobenchmark to compare versions. In a separate benchmark module, use StartupTimingMetric (since 1.1.0) and explicitly select StartupMode.COLD/WARM/HOT, CompilationMode, data/login state, and repetition count. Use a release-like non-debuggable target, a physical device, and consistent conditions; configure profileable as required by the version in use. Inspect the median and distribution plus the generated traces, not just one fastest run. Do not mix uncompiled and Baseline-Profile-precompiled results.

Keep the metrics separate:

  • timeToInitialDisplayMs measures from the system receiving the launch Intent to the destination Activity’s first-frame rendering. It does not mean all business content is ready.
  • timeToFullDisplayMs depends on the fully-drawn signal and ends when the frame containing or following that signal finishes rendering. Missing app reporting, an early-ended recording, or unavailability before API 29 must not become a zero or a passing result. The benchmark measureBlock must wait for the real ready condition to observe asynchronous content.
  • To measure a physical tap through an interactive login screen, define the input event, ready condition, and clock, then correlate system/display evidence. Adding command-output columns does not produce that interval.

Start from the official Macrobenchmark examples and configuration guide. Android 12 / API 31 onward supports correlating app, GPU, and SurfaceFlinger work with Perfetto FrameTimeline; a DrawFrame CPU slice ending does not prove presentation. Field metrics from Android Vitals have their own sampling and definitions and should be interpreted separately from application-specific readiness.

Sources

  • AOSP 5.1.1 Am.java, ActivityRecord.java, ActivityStack.java, ActivityStackSupervisor.java, AppWindowToken.java
  • AOSP 4.4.4 Am.java
  • AOSP 16 ActivityManagerShellCommand.java, WaitResult.java, ActivityMetricsLogger.java
  • App startup time, StartupTimingMetric, Macrobenchmark configuration, Perfetto FrameTimeline

entry.title: Android App Launch Optimization: Implementation and Principles of DelayLoad (Part 2)
entry.content:
In the previous article, we tried the third DelayLoad approach. That article showed the code; here I want to follow what happens when it runs.

That takes us through several Android framework classes and Activity lifecycle methods.

I found tracing it quite fun: use the tools, add some debug code, and follow it one step at a time. Doing that helped me understand Activity startup better. I hope walking through it helps you too.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): This preserves the historical startup path, using AOSP android-5.1.1_r1 for platform code. The two support-v7 methods are checked against the support repository’s android-6.0.1_r1 tag, not an assertion about the app’s original Maven dependency version. The final section covers Android 16, Android 12 SplashScreen, and current tools. Nested posts can alter ordering under particular queue conditions; they do not guarantee that the first frame is visible. Framework excerpts below are not standalone app examples.

In the previous article, the core method of DelayLoad we ultimately used was to add the following method in the Activity’s onCreate function:

Here myHandler should be an ordinary synchronous Handler explicitly bound to the main thread, such as new Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()). Both Runnables still execute on the UI thread; the completed cancellable example is in Part 1. Now follow the relevant classes and methods.

1. Activity.getWindow and PhoneWindow Initialization Timing

In this platform implementation, an ordinary Activity’s getWindow() returns its Window, implemented by PhoneWindow:

mWindow is created in Activity.attach(). This excerpt shows window creation only; the factory method belongs to a different class:

PolicyManager.makeNewWindow() delegates to Policy.makeNewWindow():

ActivityThread calls activity.attach() before Instrumentation invokes onCreate(). This connects the Activity object to framework state; it does not mean its DecorView is attached to a window.

Summary:

  • An ordinary Activity owns its application window. Dialog and system starting windows are separate, so there is no universal one-to-one mapping between every PhoneWindow and Activity in the system.
  • Android describes PhoneWindow as an “Android-specific Window.”
  • PhoneWindow has many methods that everyone is relatively familiar with, such as setContentView/addContentView, etc.; it also has several important internal classes, such as: DecorView;

2. PhoneWindow.getDecorView and DecorView Initialization Timing

Earlier we said that DecorView is an internal class of PhoneWindow, and its definition is as follows:

DecorView is created on demand in this version. The first getDecorView(), setContentView(), or another install path can trigger installDecor(). The old android.support.v7.app.AppCompatActivity in the example accesses decor through its delegate during super.onCreate(), producing the chain below. This is not a universal creation point for every Activity subclass or release:

In the checked support tag, AppCompatDelegateImplV7.onCreate() obtains decor directly. It does not include the super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) call shown in the original excerpt:

That is, here’s mWindow.getDecorView(), which instantiates the DecorView:

installDecor() creates the root View through generateDecor() and builds the application window’s decor/content container through theme-driven generateLayout(). It does not insert the system StartingWindow into this app DecorView. The old PhoneWindowManager.addStartingWindow() creates a separate Window with TYPE_APPLICATION_STARTING. They can use the same app theme without being the same window.

Summary

  • Decor has the meaning of decoration. DecorView’s official comment is “This is the top-level view of the window, containing the window decor.” We can understand that DecorView is the layout at the very bottom of our current Activity. So when we open DDMS to view the Tree Overview, we can discover that the rootmost View is the DecorView:
  • Legacy starting previews depend on theme properties such as android:windowBackground; an unspecified background is not guaranteed to be white. A suitable background can improve the blank-screen appearance but does not reduce initialization work. Whether a starting window appears also depends on system policy and window attributes. (Of course, I can understand the widespread SplashActivity + ads approach.) Android 12 system splash screens are covered at the end.

3. Post

When we call DecorView’s Post method, it will ultimately call View’s Post method because DecorView ultimately inherits from View:

For the ordinary newly created Activity path here, decor has not yet been added to the window during onCreate(), so this View’s mAttachInfo is null. Do not infer the same state for every View from a lifecycle callback name: an already attached View posts directly to its associated Handler.

What do the Activity callbacks actually do? When writing an app, it can feel as though everything happens in onCreate. onStart? onResume? We may barely touch them. But the framework still has work to do there.

PhoneWindow was created earlier in Activity.attach(). Decor and content Views can be created during onCreate(), but construction is not window attachment, layout, or presentation. In this old ActivityThread’s ordinary visible-start path, handleResumeActivity() calls the resume logic and then adds decor through WindowManager. Creating ViewRootImpl and a hardware renderer also depends on window and acceleration conditions; onResume() itself is not a completion guarantee.

ActivityThread.handleResumeActivity:

wm.addView(decor, l) reaches WindowManagerGlobal.addView() through WindowManagerImpl. These excerpts show root creation, registration, and the later setView call; lock and exception-handling scopes are in the full source:

We know that ViewRootImpl is a core class in the View system, and its definition is as follows:

ViewRootImpl creates its View.AttachInfo in its constructor, but that does not immediately assign it to every View. During the first traversal, host.dispatchAttachedToWindow(mAttachInfo, 0) propagates it through the tree; View.dispatchAttachedToWindow() assigns the View’s mAttachInfo. Root state existing and a particular View being attached are different events.

Continuing with addView’s root.setView(view, wparams, panelParentView); the view passed in is decorView, and root is ViewRootImpl. This function sets ViewRootImpl’s mView variable to the passed-in view—that is, the decorView. So now the relationship between ViewRootImpl and DecorView is also clear.

Returning to post, this old unattached-View path uses ViewRootImpl.getRunQueue(). It is neither the Looper MessageQueue nor a private queue per ViewRootImpl instance: static sRunQueues is a ThreadLocal<RunQueue>, reused by calls on the same thread. This discussion assumes calls on the UI thread, not arbitrary background-thread access to Views.

The following excerpts show RunQueue posting and forwarding members; its HandlerAction type and cancellation methods are in the full source:

This branch stores the Runnable and relative delay in HandlerAction. executeActions(handler) later forwards each item with handler.postDelayed and clears the temporary list; it does not execute the Runnables inline. In this old unattached-View postDelayed path, the delay starts again when forwarded to the Handler, rather than forming a precise timer from the original call.

So when is the executeActions method executed? And which Handler is the passed-in Handler?

4. PerformTraversals

performTraversals() measures, lays out, and draws as required by state. Every frame need not perform all three, and RenderThread-driven animation frames need not rerun UI traversal. The old RunQueue forwarding occurs here:

The executeActions we discussed in the previous section is executed within performTraversals:

We can see that the Handler passed in here is mAttachInfo.mHandler. In the previous section, we mentioned that mAttachInfo is initialized together when ViewRootImpl is initialized:

The mHandler here is a ViewRootHandler object:

ViewRootHandler extends Handler without explicitly supplying a Looper in this tag. A default Handler binds to the creating thread’s Looper, not automatically to mainLooper. This ordinary Activity path creates ViewRootImpl on the main thread, so it uses the main Looper. A thread without a Looper would cause that constructor to throw.

On this old UI-thread/first-attachment path, the next performTraversals() forwards the outer Runnable to the main queue. It can run only after the current call stack returns. That explains the first post, but not yet why the second post sometimes lands after another traversal.

After that detour, we’ve finally explained the line at the start. I did ramble a bit, and I suspect few people will have the patience to get this far. If you’re still here, add an index++ in the comments. Let’s start at index = 0 and see how many people made it.

5. UpdateText

A reader asked in the comments on Part 1: why post again inside run() instead of calling updateText directly? We need to follow the sequence a little further to answer that.

Part 1 observed updateText after a later traversal when using two posts. Old source contains conditions that explain such ordering, but “EGL initialization always causes two traversals” is too broad.

In android-5.1.1_r1, acquiring a valid Surface during relayout when there was none sets newSurface = true. The source explains that drawing is deferred and another traversal scheduled so WindowManager can learn about the windows to display; hardware-renderer initialization also occurs in that branch. Pre-draw cancellation, visibility, skipDraw, and other state still affect drawing. Two is not a universal startup count.

Synchronization barriers are the other condition. scheduleTraversals() inserts a barrier when arranging traversal:

doTraversal() removes its barrier before entering performTraversals():

When the queue head is a barrier with a null target, MessageQueue looks for an asynchronous message instead of dispatching ordinary synchronous messages behind it. Choreographer marks its VSYNC message asynchronous, so it can pass. Asynchronous messages can still run on the same main thread; this does not mean background execution.

For one source-supported ordering consistent with the observation, label the outer task A and the updateText task C:

  1. The first traversal forwards pending A to the main queue.
  2. That traversal schedules another traversal because of newSurface or related conditions and inserts barrier B. A is already before B.
  3. A runs and posts C through an ordinary Handler. C lands behind B and cannot yet be dispatched.
  4. An asynchronous frame message runs. The next doTraversal() removes B and performs traversal.
  5. C can run after that main-thread call stack returns. GPU, SurfaceFlinger, and display work may still be in progress.

This requires the relevant implementation, an unattached-View posting path, the A/B/C ordering, a synchronous Handler, and a subsequent traversal actually being scheduled. The original image lacks complete queue logs, so it does not prove this arrangement for every launch. An attached View, asynchronous Handler, or other scheduling state changes the outcome. Apps should not use internal barrier APIs to manufacture a post-first-frame callback.

6. Summary

DelayLoad is a small example. What I wanted to show is how to investigate an implementation or optimization you don’t yet understand. Here we used Systrace and Method Trace, along with building and debugging the source.

Regarding the use of Systrace and Method Trace, there will be detailed articles introducing them later. These two tools are very helpful for understanding source code and some technical implementations.

Systrace

Method Trace

Source Code Compilation and Debugging

Code

The code involved in this article has been uploaded to GitHub:
https://github.com/Gracker/DelayLoadSample

The project’s 62e03ae snapshot now uses one image and an IdleHandler example, with getWidth() incorrectly used for height. Part 1 explains the differences and provides the corrected three-pair example.

7. 2026 Update

  • Android 16 / android-16.0.0_r1: DecorView is now the separate com.android.internal.policy.DecorView class. An unattached View keeps actions in its own HandlerActionQueue, forwarding them during dispatchAttachedToWindow. The old ThreadLocal RunQueue reasoning does not transfer unchanged. Handler.createAsync, available from API 28, bypasses synchronization barriers; it is not a background executor for startup delays.
  • Android 12 / API 31 onward: The system SplashScreen adds new API boundaries to the old starting-window/theme-preview discussion. Follow the official migration guidance and the appropriate windowSplashScreenBackground, postSplashScreenTheme, and related attributes. Changing old windowBackground alone is not the whole configuration, and a separate SplashActivity can produce duplicate splash screens. Keeping a splash visible does not reduce initialization time.
  • Tools: Android Device Monitor was deprecated in Android Studio 3.1 and removed in 3.2. Use Layout Inspector for hierarchy inspection, Perfetto/System Trace for system timing, and the current Profiler for method analysis. The original screenshots are historical, not current tool UI. Instrumented method tracing and debug logging add overhead and should not be treated as an unperturbed startup benchmark.
  • Choose the right condition: Use layout callbacks for dimensions; even API 29 frame-commit callbacks do not guarantee visible pixels. See Part 1 for examples. Validate initial display, full usability, and subsequent frames instead of substituting traversal counts or Runnable completion for presentation evidence.

Sources

  • AOSP 5.1.1 Activity.java, ActivityThread.java, PhoneWindow.java, PhoneWindowManager.java
  • ViewRootImpl.java, View.java, WindowManagerGlobal.java, Handler.java, MessageQueue.java, Choreographer.java
  • support android-6.0.1_r1 AppCompatActivity.java, AppCompatDelegateImplV7.java
  • AOSP 16 View.java, HandlerActionQueue.java, DecorView.java
  • SplashScreen migration, Handler API, Device Monitor migration, Layout Inspector, Java/Kotlin method tracing

entry.title: Android App Startup Optimization - DelayLoad Implementation and Principles (Part 1)
entry.content:
To make an Android app start faster, the main idea is to do less during startup. In practice, we usually reach for:

  1. Asynchronous Loading
  2. Delayed Loading (DelayLoad)
  3. Lazy Loading

If you have worked on startup optimization, you have probably used these already. Here I want to look at one DelayLoad implementation and why it behaves as it does. The code is simple, but following it takes us through Looper, Handler, MessageQueue, and VSYNC. I’ll also discuss the problems I ran into and some thoughts along the way.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): This is a historical 2015 experiment; its screenshots and three approaches are retained. Neither “two posts guarantee execution after the first frame is visible” nor “startup always needs two performTraversals calls” is a valid API guarantee. The discussion checks AOSP Android 6.0 and 16 queue behavior and adds layout callbacks, Android 10 / API 29 frame-commit callbacks, and current measurement guidance. The screenshots establish only the observed ordering in those samples, not universal presentation timing.

1. Implementation of Optimized DelayLoad

A common DelayLoad approach is Handler.postDelayed in onCreate. It sets an earliest eligible execution time, not a signal that the interface is ready. Queue contention, a busy main thread, and deep sleep can delay it further. The first question is therefore: how long should it wait?

The same fixed delay can behave differently across devices and startup states; fast hardware alone does not guarantee a particular initialization time.

Here is the original nested-post approach; its limits are discussed below:

  1. Create a Handler and a Runnable for UI updates.
  1. Add the following code to your main Activity’s onCreate:

This explicitly uses the main Looper (import android.os.Looper). Both Runnables still run on the UI thread; posting does not create a background worker. Expensive work can still block input and subsequent frames, even if it starts later. Now compare the three approaches.

2. Comparison of Three Approaches

To compare the three approaches, I wrote a small app with three differently sized images and a TextView under each to show its dimensions. getWidth() / getHeight() report View layout dimensions in pixels, not the intrinsic dimensions of a Drawable or Bitmap. The complete example below explicitly binds the main thread, balances tracing, and removes pending callbacks when destroyed. It has been edited and is not a verbatim copy of the linked repository.

Use an API 21+ project already configured with AndroidX AppCompat and an AppCompat theme. Adjust the package and declare this Activity in the manifest. Select one MODE per run and relaunch; 300ms and the later 50ms are comparison settings, not recommended production delays.

Use this matching res/layout/activity_main.xml and place the repository’s sample zhihu.png in res/drawable/. The sizes create three distinct layouts; they do not reproduce the historical screenshots’ pixel values. Enable DUMP_QUEUE only for debugging, and leave it off for performance comparisons.

Keep three questions separate:

  1. When is updateText executed?
  2. Have the ImageViews been laid out, and do the values reflect that layout?
  3. Has work left the initial-display critical path, and does it delay later usability?

2.1 Approach 1: Immediate Post

When is it executed?

In this capture, updateText follows the Activity startup callbacks and precedes the first traversal. That is this sample’s ordering: Handler.post() is not a dedicated “after onResume” or “after layout” API.

Are dimensions correct?

The screenshot shows 0 because these Views had not yet been laid out when read. Completion of onCreate/onStart/onResume does not guarantee measurement or layout; initial dimensions are normally established in a later traversal. A legitimate layout can also have zero dimensions, so 0 alone does not diagnose the same issue in every app.

Is there a DelayLoad effect?
Here the task still ran before the first traversal and could lengthen the initial-display path. There is no universal requirement for two traversals before the first frame. Traversal count depends on window state and other conditions, and finishing CPU drawing is not proof of GPU completion or presentation.

2.2 Approach 2: PostDelayed (300ms)

When is it executed?

In this sample, updateText follows the two early traversal sections, and setText causes another UI update. Those CPU sections alone do not precisely establish when the first frame was displayed.

Are dimensions correct?

Yes in this capture: the ImageViews had been laid out. These are their current layout dimensions, not the source image dimensions.

Is there a DelayLoad effect?
It depends on the delay and that run’s load. I recorded about 170ms of extra waiting at the time. The cropped image lacks a full time axis and presentation track, so that number remains a note from the experiment; it cannot be remeasured from this image.

Here we are only updating a TextView. With a large part of the first screen, the user may see blank space followed by content popping in, perhaps with a bonus flash. Expensive work may also stall later interactions. That is hardly the effect we want.

Why not just shorten the delay? The same 300ms behaves differently across devices, startup states, and scheduling loads. I changed it to 50ms and captured another trace:

Here updateText falls between the early traversal sections. Layout dimensions were available, but that does not establish that the first frame was already visible. Available dimensions, completed UI-thread work, and visible pixels are separate conditions.

2.3 Approach 3: Optimized DelayLoad

After trying the first two approaches, I wanted to move the task later without guessing a delay in milliseconds. This third approach was that attempt. It changed the ordering in this experiment, but nesting two posts does not mean “run after the first frame is visible.”

When is it executed?

In this historical trace, updateText follows the later traversal while RenderThread work is still in progress. The TextView change still needs scheduling and rendering; it is not guaranteed to appear at exactly the next VSYNC.

Are dimensions correct?
The dimensions had been established in this run:

Is there a DelayLoad effect?
It deferred the task in this sample without a fixed millisecond value. It does not guarantee post-presentation loading across Android versions, attachment states, or window lifecycles.

3. Reflections

The code is small, but understanding the observed order requires looking at Handler/MessageQueue/Looper, View attachment, and ViewRootImpl traversal scheduling. The next part follows those details. A successful delay in one capture is not a stable first-frame callback.

4. Code

The historical project is DelayLoadSample. The checked snapshot is 62e03ae (2020-02-25): it uses one image and defaults to an IdleHandler example, unlike the three pairs here. Its height label incorrectly calls getWidth(); use getHeight() instead, as in the completed example above. Its old Gradle, SDK, and dependency configuration is historical, not a promise of compatibility with current tools.

5. 2026 Update: Choose the Condition You Need

For layout dimensions, use a layout callback. This Kotlin helper uses AndroidX Core’s doOnLayout (available since 1.1.0). Call it on the UI thread for each bound ImageView/TextView pair. If layout is already complete with no pending layout request, it runs immediately; otherwise it runs once after the next layout and removes its listener. It does not wait for presentation and should not contain expensive initialization.

For pre-draw or frame submission, distinguish the signals. OnPreDrawListener runs before drawing. Android 10 / API 29 registerFrameCommitCallback reports rendered content submitted to the swap chain and only works with hardware rendering; the frame may still not be visible. Register before the target frame and remove unfired callbacks as required by the lifecycle. It is not an exact presentation-complete notification.

For deferring nonessential work, first identify dependencies. Keep only short UI-required work on the main thread. Handler posts and IdleHandler do not create background work; queue idleness does not mean the first frame is visible. Run CPU/IO work on an appropriate executor and manage cancellation. Primary-content loading still contributes to the user’s wait. AndroidX App Startup manages initialization dependencies and entry points, not post-frame scheduling. For manual lazy initialization, remove its automatic initialization configuration and check that another initializer does not initialize it early as a dependency.

The third approach is not a contract: in AOSP android-6.0.0_r1, an unattached View posts into ViewRootImpl.getRunQueue(), forwarded to a Handler during traversal. In android-16.0.0_r1, each View has its own queue, forwarded during attachment. Attached Views post directly to their associated Handler in both versions. Posting again creates another queued task; it does not wait for the GPU or display.

Measure initial display separately from full usability. Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric (since 1.1.0) exposes timeToInitialDisplayMs and timeToFullDisplayMs, the latter based on the fully-drawn signal. It ends when the frame containing or following that signal finishes rendering. This metric may be unavailable before API 29; a missing value is not zero. Report fully drawn when primary content has rendered and meets the product’s usable-state definition, not unconditionally in onCreate. Compare repeated cold/warm/hot starts with device, build, data, and compilation state held constant, and inspect subsequent frames. Moving work past the first frame alone does not establish a successful optimization.

Baseline Profiles guide ART precompilation; Startup Profiles improve DEX layout at build time. Neither schedules tasks. DEX layout optimization is available from AGP 8.1 and enabled by default from AGP 8.3, with the required configuration, R8, and generated profiles. No fixed speedup is promised. Android 12 / API 31 onward also supports correlating app, GPU, and display work through Perfetto FrameTimeline.

Sources

  • AOSP 6.0 View.java, ViewRootImpl.java
  • AOSP 16 View.java, Handler.java
  • ViewTreeObserver, doOnLayout
  • App Startup, StartupTimingMetric, App startup time
  • Baseline Profiles, Startup Profiles, FrameTimeline

entry.title: RenderThread Workflow in Android hwui
entry.content:
Preface

These are my notes from learning how hwui’s RenderThread works in Android 5.0. I haven’t covered every detail; I wanted to trace the main flow so that, next time I hit a problem, I would know where to look.

I captured the first RenderThread Draw during app startup with Systrace, as shown below. It helps show the execution order on that thread, but the end of a DrawFrame slice is not the moment pixels appear on screen: GPU work, buffer consumption, composition, and presentation still matter. A StartingWindow may appear during startup; this CPU slice alone does not establish when it disappears.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): This preserves the Android 5.0 workflow and uses AOSP android-5.0.0_r1 as its source baseline. The original screenshots include device-side instrumentation, so event names need not match AOSP exactly. Incomplete excerpts below have been filled in and aligned with this tag. The old OpenGLRenderer, DisplayListRenderer, and EGL details are historical; the final section covers Android 16 counterparts and FrameTimeline from Android 12. The scope is hardware-accelerated View rendering, not every custom Surface renderer.

Starting from the Java Layer

Choreographer normally schedules pending frame callbacks against VSYNC. Not every VSYNC necessarily redraws every View. Here we follow one scheduled traversal into the drawing path:

The entry point is Choreographer.doFrame(), not drawFrame(). Its CALLBACK_TRAVERSAL callbacks reach ViewRootImpl.TraversalRunnable.run() → doTraversal() → performTraversals(). When drawing is needed, this reaches performDraw() → draw(boolean fullRedrawNeeded). That last method is private to ViewRootImpl, not a custom View’s onDraw().

The following excerpt shows its hardware-rendering branch; the surrounding control flow is omitted:

If the hardware rendering path is taken, mHardwareRenderer.draw is called. Here, mHardwareRenderer refers to ThreadedRenderer, whose draw function is as follows:

updateRootDisplayList(view, callbacks) updates or reuses the View tree’s display lists and records the root node when needed; its trace section is named getDisplayList. Recording commands is not the same as the GPU drawing pixels. It then calls:

The UI thread waits in native postAndWait() until RenderThread signals it, then returns with syncResult. This wait can end before context->draw(); it does not necessarily last until GPU completion or presentation. The signal points are shown in DrawFrameTask::run() below.

The Native Layer

The Native code is located in android_view_ThreadedRenderer.cpp. The implementation is as follows:

The RenderProxy implementation can be found in frameworks/base/libs/hwui/renderthread/RenderProxy.cpp:

Here, mDrawFrameTask is a DrawFrameTask object, located in frameworks/base/libs/hwui/renderthread/DrawFrameTask.cpp. Its drawFrame code is:

The implementation of postAndWait() is:

This enqueues the current DrawFrameTask. The UI thread then waits on a condition variable, releasing mLock while waiting and reacquiring it on return. The RenderThread queue method is:

mQueue is a TaskQueue. It orders tasks by mRunAt and rejects queuing the same task object twice:

Going back to the queue method in RenderThread, the wake() function is called:

In this Android 5.0 tag, wake() writes W to the wake pipe so the listening Looper can leave its wait. Not every enqueue writes to the pipe: queue calls it only when the new task is earlier than the next scheduled wakeup.

HWUI RenderThread

Where do we go next? First, let’s get familiar with RenderThread. It inherits from Thread (defined in utils/Thread.h). Here is the RenderThread constructor:

The run method is documented in Thread:

This triggers the threadLoop function, which is critical:

The for loop is infinite. pollOnce(timeoutMillis) can return because of the wake pipe, another file-descriptor event, or a timeout; with a zero timeout it does not block. It does not depend solely on wake(). nextTask() then retrieves tasks that are due:

The queue can hold more than drawing tasks. For the enqueue traced here, the task is a DrawFrameTask, whose run method is:

unblockUiThread() pairs with the earlier mSignal.wait(mLock):

The signal allows the UI thread to resume; it does not guarantee immediate CPU scheduling. If early unblocking is unavailable, the signal follows the drawing branch, whether it called draw() or skipped drawing. Neither signal is a GPU-completion notification.

RenderThread.DrawFrame

The run method of DrawFrameTask coordinates the stages shown in the initial trace diagram. Let’s break down the DrawFrame process step by step, combining the code with the trace visualization.

1. syncFrameState

syncFrameState prepares frame state on RenderThread: it processes layer updates, synchronizes the node tree, prepares textures, and advances animations.

The UI thread and RenderThread use staged rendering state. This does not copy a complete Java View tree into a second tree: Java RenderNode holds a native node through mNativeRenderNode, and that native node contains both mStagingProperties / mProperties and mStagingDisplayListData / mDisplayListData.

prepareTree pushes staging state into the rendering state in MODE_FULL: dirty properties are updated, and display-list data can be transferred by pointer rather than deeply copied every frame. canUnblockUiThread comes from info.prepareTextures; it determines whether the UI thread may be released early, not whether synchronization or GPU rendering has universally “succeeded.” For example, this version’s prepareSubTree disables the flag when ownedBitmapResources are present, so false alone does not prove that the texture cache ran out of space.

First is makeCurrent. Here, mContext is a CanvasContext object:

mEglManager is an EglManager object:

isCurrent(surface) allows an early return. When switching surfaces, eglMakeCurrent binds the existing mEglContext and its read/draw surfaces to the current thread. It does not recreate the EGLContext; creation uses eglCreateContext. The branch using EGL_NO_CONTEXT releases the current binding.

After makeCurrent, mContext->prepareTree(info) is called:

Within this, mRootRenderNode->prepareTree(info) is the most important part. Back at the Java layer, the ThreadedRenderer initializes a pointer:

This is the native root node held by ThreadedRenderer. RenderNode.adopt() wraps that pointer in Java; it does not create a separate native root node.

Next, nCreate creates a RenderProxy using the root-node pointer. The RenderProxy constructor posts a task to create CanvasContext on RenderThread and waits for the result; CanvasContext receives the same root node. This is not all performed directly on the UI thread.

updateRootDisplayList first calls updateViewTreeDisplayList. It then records the renderer’s root display list when that root needs updating or is invalid. canvas.drawRenderNode(view.getDisplayList()) records a draw reference to the root View’s node; it does not render it immediately:

The final implementation is:

Returning to CanvasContext::prepareTree, the mRootRenderNode is the one passed during initialization. Its implementation is in RenderNode.cpp:

Further details on these operations can be explored in the source code.

2. draw

After synchronization, draw() is called only if canDrawThisFrame is true. This version checks whether the consumer is running behind and can skip this draw and schedule a later frame callback.

CanvasContext::draw() is in frameworks/base/libs/hwui/renderthread/CanvasContext.cpp. Below is the complete AOSP 5.0 method, including the previously omitted beginFrame, viewport, and dirty-region handling. The original vendor-specific overdraw debug additions are not part of this AOSP tag.

2.1 EglManager::beginFrame

As shown in the complete method above, CanvasContext::draw() calls mEglManager.beginFrame():

This method ensures the context/surface binding and queries dimensions before calling Android’s then-current eglBeginFrame entry point. In this tag’s frameworks/native/opengl/libs/EGL/eglApi.cpp, that entry mainly traces and validates the display and surface; it is not a standard EGL operation that waits for the GPU to begin a frame.

2.2 prepareDirty

Here, mCanvas is an OpenGLRenderer object. Its prepareDirty implementation is:

2.3 drawRenderNode

Next, OpenGLRenderer::drawRenderNode is called to perform the actual rendering:

Here, renderNode is the renderer’s root node. The default deferred path organizes drawing operations, processes pending layer updates, then starts the window-target frame and replays batches. These four lines summarize that path:

defer / flush batch and order operations while preserving drawing semantics; they do not arbitrarily reorder every command or create a new FBO for every View. They issue work to the graphics driver, and returning does not prove GPU completion. For the historical details, see Luo Shengyang’s Display List rendering analysis.

2.4 swapBuffers

CanvasContext::swapBuffers() calls EglManager::swapBuffers(), which invokes eglSwapBuffers(mEglDisplay, surface) and handles errors such as an invalid surface. The consumer still needs to acquire the buffer, and SurfaceFlinger/HWC must compose and present it. Buffer handoff also involves synchronization fences: returning from swap is neither proof of GPU completion nor proof that the pixels are already on screen.

2.5 FinishFrame

This ends the profiler’s frame accounting; it is not a GPU- or presentation-completion barrier.

Summary

Since I’m a bit lazy and my summarizing skills don’t quite match Luo’s, I’ll follow his outline here, with the technical boundaries clarified against AOSP 5.0:

  1. The UI thread records View drawing state, submits a DrawFrameTask, and waits. RenderThread synchronizes native RenderNode staging state and handles textures, layers, and animations.
  2. When info.prepareTextures permits early release, the UI thread is signaled before the drawing branch; otherwise it is signaled afterward. That branch may also skip drawing. Neither path is a notification of GPU completion or final presentation.
  3. The default deferred path processes offscreen layers that need updates and renders the window into a graphics buffer obtained through the Surface/BufferQueue producer interface. The buffer is submitted to its consumer; for this application window, SurfaceFlinger/HWC then compose and present the result.

Step 2 enables overlap: while RenderThread processes the current frame, the UI thread may begin preparing the next. The threads still have synchronization and resource dependencies, so early unblocking cannot guarantee that the next frame meets its deadline.

In the Android 4.x View/HWUI path discussed here, display-list recording and playback were mainly CPU work on the UI thread, rather than split across this RenderThread. The UI thread had to finish its current drawing call before handling subsequent work. GPU and SurfaceFlinger work could still be asynchronous; the whole graphics system did not run on the Main Thread alone. The historical trace below illustrates the UI-side work:

The following two historical Android 5.0 traces illustrate overlap between the threads:

The second trace shows the next UI traversal overlapping the previous frame’s RenderThread work, illustrating reduced serial waiting. It does not include complete GPU-fence, SurfaceFlinger, or presentation evidence, so it cannot establish that exactly one frame was dropped or that the second frame was unaffected. RenderThread queuing, GPU backlog, and BufferQueue backpressure can still affect later frames.

2026 Update: Following the Pipeline Today

  • Android 16 / AOSP android-16.0.0_r1: DrawFrameTask still posts work, synchronizes state, and conditionally releases the UI thread. Queue interfaces, frame metadata, and trace names have changed. This tag emits DrawFrames <vsyncId> and carries deadline and interval information; the 5.0 signatures and a fixed frame budget are not current contracts.
  • Rendering backends: CanvasContext dispatches through IRenderPipeline to SkiaOpenGLPipeline or SkiaVulkanPipeline, depending on configuration. Do not assume every device uses GLES. Even an internal method named swapBuffers in the Vulkan pipeline is not eglSwapBuffers. The old OpenGLRenderer/DeferredDisplayList analysis above remains historical.
  • Android 12 / API 31 onward: Perfetto FrameTimeline provides Expected/Actual tracks, jank types, and app-to-SurfaceFlinger frame relationships. An app Actual slice ends at the later of GPU completion and buffer posting, which still differs from final presentation; follow the corresponding SurfaceFlinger/DisplayFrame to inspect the display outcome. If those tracks were not captured, a DrawFrame CPU slice alone cannot establish full frame latency or a dropped-frame count.

The original sequence is still a useful way to investigate, provided the questions remain separate: is the UI thread recording display lists or waiting for synchronization? Is RenderThread waiting to be scheduled, preparing textures/drawing, or waiting for a buffer? Have the GPU and display stages completed their work? This identifies the stage to optimize instead of attributing every long slice to onDraw().

Source and Documentation Checks

  • AOSP 5.0 ThreadedRenderer.java, Choreographer.java, ViewRootImpl.java
  • AOSP 5.0 DrawFrameTask.cpp, RenderThread.cpp, RenderProxy.cpp
  • AOSP 5.0 RenderNode.cpp, RenderNode.java, CanvasContext.cpp, EglManager.cpp
  • AOSP 5.0 OpenGLRenderer.cpp, Looper.cpp, eglApi.cpp
  • AOSP 16 DrawFrameTask.cpp, CanvasContext.cpp, Properties.cpp, SkiaVulkanPipeline.cpp
  • Android graphics architecture, EGLSurfaces and OpenGL ES, BufferQueue and Gralloc
  • Perfetto FrameTimeline

About Me && Blog

Below are my personal details and links. I look forward to connecting and sharing knowledge with fellow developers!

  2. Blog Navigation: A guide to the content on this blog.
  3. Curated Android Performance Articles: A collection of must-read performance optimization articles. Self-nominations/recommendations are welcome!

entry.title: Java 7 HashMap Source Code Analysis
entry.content:
Finding a value in an unsorted array or linked list without an additional index can require scanning every element. A hash table uses a hash to locate a bucket and supports constant-time basic lookup when hashes are well distributed; it does not guarantee O(1) lookup for every input.

HashMap is an implementation of the Map interface based on a hash table. This implementation provides all optional mapping operations and permits null values and null keys. (The HashMap class is roughly equivalent to Hashtable, except that it is unsynchronized and permits nulls.) This class makes no guarantees as to the order of the map; in particular, it does not guarantee that the order will remain constant over time.

This article follows the source through the array-and-list structure, constructors, put and resizing, get, and the iterator checks using modCount. A final section covers changes in later JDKs.

Version note (reviewed 2026-10-13): This preserves the original 2015 source analysis, checked against OpenJDK jdk7u21-b11. Eager array allocation, Entry chains, and alternative hashing are historical implementation details, not descriptions of every later release—even Java 7 updates differ. These are JDK source excerpts, not standalone classes to copy and run. Android implementations must be checked against the relevant libcore version.

1. HashMap Data Structure

This version uses an array and linked lists: each array slot holds the head of a bucket chain, or null for an empty bucket. The excerpt below shows only the Entry fields; its methods are in the linked source.

Entry is a package-private static nested class implementing Map.Entry<K,V>. Its next reference points to the following node. A final key reference does not make the key object immutable: do not change state used by its hashCode() or equals() while it is stored as a key.

2. Constructors

HashMap has four constructors:

  1. HashMap(): Constructs an empty HashMap with the default initial capacity (16) and default load factor (0.75).
  2. HashMap(int initialCapacity): Constructs an empty HashMap with a specified initial capacity and the default load factor (0.75).
  3. HashMap(int initialCapacity, float loadFactor): Constructs an empty HashMap with a specified initial capacity and load factor.
  4. HashMap(Map<? extends K,? extends V> m): Constructs a new HashMap with the same mappings as the specified Map.

In essence, these boil down to two types: one where you specify initial capacity and load factor, and another that generates a new HashMap from an existing map. Let’s look at the first type:

initialCapacity requests an initial bucket count, not the number of mappings that fit without resizing. This version allocates the array in the constructor. Negative requests are rejected, requests above MAXIMUM_CAPACITY are clamped to 1 << 30, and the capacity is rounded up to a power of two; a request of 0 produces an array of length 1. The defaults are 16 buckets and a load factor of 0.75.

The constructor calculates threshold using capacity * loadFactor and the expression shown above. Do not treat (1 << 30) + 1 as a lifetime threshold limit: resize sets it to Integer.MAX_VALUE when maximum capacity is reached. The bucket limit of 1 << 30 does not guarantee enough heap memory to allocate that array.

As shown below, addEntry requests resizing only for a new key when the pre-insertion size >= threshold and the destination bucket is nonempty. Reaching the threshold alone does not immediately trigger a resize.

The constructor throws IllegalArgumentException if the load factor is nonpositive or NaN, the special floating-point “not a number” value.

3. put Operation

Since HashMap allows null keys, it first checks if the key is null and performs special handling.

A null key is always inserted at index 0 of the array. If an entry already exists at that position with a null key, its value is replaced; otherwise, a new entry is added. We’ll examine the addEntry function shortly.

Question: If a null key is always inserted into table[0], why do we still need to traverse the linked list?

For a non-null key, put calls hash(key). This mixes bits from the key’s hashCode(); when alternative hashing is enabled, it also uses a seed and a separate String path. Here is the complete method from this version:

useAltHashing, hashSeed, and sun.misc.Hashing are implementation details, not public APIs for application code. This tag defaults the alternative-hashing threshold to Integer.MAX_VALUE, so an ordinary map should not be assumed to use that path. indexFor then selects a bucket:

There is a neat trick in that one-line indexFor method. Remember the restriction on the array length? Because length is a positive power of two, length - 1 is a mask of low-order ones. The bitwise AND produces an index from 0 to length - 1. This is not unconditionally equivalent to Java’s h % length: a negative h can produce a negative remainder, whereas this index is nonnegative. For other lengths, the mask would not cover all buckets evenly. The operator alone does not establish a performance advantage on every runtime.

This also answers the previous question. Since indexFor returns values ranging from 0 to (length - 1), it’s possible for non-null keys to also map to table[0]. Thus, we must traverse the linked list to find the exact key.

The bucket chain is searched for a matching hash and a key matching by identity or equals(); equal hashes alone do not imply equal keys. Replacing an existing value returns before modCount++. The count is incremented only on the new-key path here, before addEntry; it tracks structural changes for fail-fast checks, not every value write.

addEntry takes the hash, key, value, and bucket index; the last comes from indexFor(hash, table.length). It attempts to double capacity only when size >= threshold and the destination bucket is nonempty. Inserting into an empty bucket does not lengthen an existing chain, so this version can defer resizing. After a resize, it recalculates the pending key’s hash and bucket index before calling createEntry.

resize first checks if the table has already reached its maximum capacity (1 << 30). If so, the threshold is set to Integer.MAX_VALUE to prevent further resizing. Otherwise, the addEntry call path shown here creates an array with double the previous length. Because capacities are powers of two up to MAXIMUM_CAPACITY, this doubling does not exceed that limit. The transfer function then migrates the elements.

transfer moves the existing nodes. It calls hash(key) again for non-null keys only when rehash is true, meaning that resizing switched alternative hashing on. Otherwise, it uses each node’s cached hash to calculate its new bucket index.

Doubling capacity does not move every node to a different index. With an unchanged hash, the new index is either the old index or that index plus the old capacity. Head insertion during migration can reverse node order within a chain. resize then replaces table and updates the threshold. Applications must not depend on HashMap iteration order, even without resizing.

Choosing capacity from an expected data size can reduce migration, but excessive capacity costs memory and traversal time: iteration scans both the bucket array and its nodes, not just size entries.

Back in addEntry, after potentially resizing, a new entry is created:

createEntry uses the same parameters as addEntry. Its logic is closely tied to the Entry constructor:

The constructor takes an Entry object (n) and sets it as the next value for the new entry. Effectively, createEntry takes the existing list at table[bucketIndex], attaches it to the end of the new entry, and then places the new entry at the head of table[bucketIndex].

This concludes the put function. If a new key-value pair is inserted, it returns null.

4. get Operation

Like put, it first handles null keys:

For non-null keys, it calls getEntry:

getEntry calculates the hash and bucket index, searches the chain, and returns a matching node or null. The outer get returns the node’s value. Thus, get(key) == null can mean either a missing key or a key mapped to null; use containsKey(key) when that distinction matters. The two calls do not form an atomic concurrent operation.

5. Fail-Fast Mechanism

HashMap is not thread-safe. Fail-fast checks detect structural changes during iteration, such as adding or removing mappings through the map. A modification outside the iterator in the same thread can also trigger the check; a second thread is not required. Merely replacing an existing key’s value is not a structural change here.

modCount is an ordinary int, not volatile, and supplies no synchronization. transient affects default serialization, not cross-thread visibility. The iterator saves expectedModCount at construction and compares the counts in nextEntry() and remove(). Here is the complete internal iterator class:

hasNext() only checks whether a node remains; it does not compare modification counts. The iterator’s own remove() updates expectedModCount after deletion, so that permitted operation does not invalidate the iterator because of its own change.

Note: Fail-fast is a best-effort bug detector. It cannot guarantee detection of unsynchronized concurrent modification, and correctness must not depend on ConcurrentModificationException. Shared reads and writes need suitable synchronization or a concurrent-container design. A value replacement that leaves the count unchanged is not automatically safe across threads.

6. Changes in Later JDKs (2026 Update)

  • OpenJDK jdk7u80-b15: An ordinary empty-map constructor no longer allocates the bucket array immediately. table starts as EMPTY_TABLE, and the first put calls inflateTable. The 7u21 allocation timing does not describe every Java 7 update.

  • OpenJDK jdk8-b132: Entries use Node, and collision chains can become red-black trees. TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8 and MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64, but the insertion path and capacity also matter: the eighth node does not unconditionally trigger treeification. A small table is resized first. Resizing ordinary chains splits them into low and high groups while preserving relative order within each group, unlike the old head-insertion transfer.

  • Java SE 19 onward: HashMap.newHashMap(expectedMappings) accepts an expected mapping count and uses the default load factor. This differs from the constructor’s initial bucket-capacity argument. Checked here against the Java SE 25 API documentation.

These changes do not make HashMap ordered or thread-safe. For modern JDK implementations, follow putVal, resize, and treeifyBin in the relevant release. For Android, check platform API availability and libcore as well: the JDK selected for compilation alone does not establish on-device behavior.

References

  • Original reference: Core Java (edition not specified in the original).
  • OpenJDK 7u21-b11 HashMap.java
  • OpenJDK 7u80-b15 HashMap.java
  • OpenJDK 8-b132 HashMap.java
  • Java SE 25 HashMap API
