entry.title: Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - OnTrimMemory
entry.content:
Android Memory Optimization Series:

  1. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Android (Official)
  2. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Java (Official)
  3. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Android Resources
  4. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - OnTrimMemory

onTrimMemory(int level), introduced in Android 4.0 (API 14), hints when an app should reduce unnecessary memory usage. Trimming caches can help the system retain more background processes, but does not guarantee process survival or a faster next return.

This article keeps the Q&A format to explain callback delivery, integration, and cleanup. Decide what to retain by resource purpose, and make sure the UI can recover what was released.

Technical review: October 13, 2026. Five old memory-pressure levels are no longer delivered from Android 14 (API 34), and their constants were deprecated in API 35. UI_HIDDEN and BACKGROUND remain useful for state-related memory management. The Launcher/Contacts examples below are checked against AOSP android-4.4.4_r2 and retained as historical code, followed by a current cache example.

0. What is the role of the onTrimMemory callback?

The level gives a cleanup hint. It does not report every change in free RAM and is not a guaranteed final opportunity to save data before process death. Release resources that are no longer needed without breaking active work.

The two levels still used today were both introduced in API 14:

LevelMeaning and response
TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDENThe current process no longer displays UI. Reduce rebuildable UI-only caches while preserving data needed by ongoing work.
TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUNDThe process has entered the background LRU state. Release more easily rebuilt resources; this alone does not establish critical device-wide memory pressure.

The following five describe historical behavior only: delivery stopped in API 34; the constants were deprecated in API 35.

While the App is Running:

Historical levelIntroducedHistorical meaning
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_MODERATEAPI 16Initial device memory-pressure hint to a running process.
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_LOWAPI 16Greater memory pressure while the process is running.
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_CRITICALAPI 16Severe memory pressure while the process is running.

While the App is Cached:

Historical levelIntroducedHistorical meaning
TRIM_MEMORY_MODERATEAPI 14Near the middle of the background LRU list.
TRIM_MEMORY_COMPLETEAPI 14Near the end of the background LRU list.

These hints never guaranteed that an app could not be killed. Use threshold comparisons appropriate to your policy, and do not expect every level in sequence. See ComponentCallbacks2 and its Android 16 source.

1. Which components can implement onTrimMemory?

Application, Activity, Service, and ContentProvider provide onTrimMemory(int level). Override it when needed and follow the superclass-call contract.

Distinguish the two Fragment APIs:

  • The old android.app.Fragment has this callback from API 14. The platform Fragment API was deprecated in API 28.
  • Current androidx.fragment.app.Fragment has no same-named callback to override directly. Let the host or a shared cache owner handle trimming, or explicitly register a separate callback and unregister it at the end of its scope. Do not apply the platform Fragment’s method list to AndroidX unchanged.

Implementing ComponentCallbacks2 on an ordinary class does not subscribe it automatically. Register it through Context.registerComponentCallbacks() and pair this with unregisterComponentCallbacks(). Application-level registration retains the callback, so avoid accidentally retaining an Activity or View through it. The API name starts with lowercase: onTrimMemory, not OnTrimMemory.

2. What resources should I release?

Define ownership, capacity budgets, and rebuild costs during design. Typical candidates include unused memory caches, rebuildable previews, and listeners or requests whose work has ended. Preserve unsaved user state and data needed by background work.

Disk and memory caches differ: deleting files mainly frees storage, not the Java heap, and large synchronous disk operations do not belong in this callback. Setting a View to GONE does not destroy it; inspect parent, listener, and queue references. Fragment View references also follow their own View lifecycle rather than waiting for a trim event.

The following two historical examples are followed by a current integration example.

2.1 Example: Releasing Views (Launcher)

These method excerpts come from AOSP Launcher2, android-4.4.4_r2, with field names matched to that tag. They depend on the rest of Launcher2 and are not standalone application code. The old MODERATE notification no longer arrives on Android 14+, so its trigger is not a current solution.

Launcher.java:

AppsCustomizeTabHost.java:

AppsCustomizePagedView.java:

PagedViewGridLayout.java:

This path does more than hide content: it cancels preview tasks, removes widget-page children, clears layout listeners and layer settings, and marks pages for reloading. GONE alone cannot do this, and dropping references does not guarantee an immediate GC or process-memory reduction. The reusable idea is to separate cleanup of rebuildable content from restoration, not to copy the old threshold or launcher internals.

2.2 Example: Clearing Caches (Contacts)

These excerpts are from ContactsCommon’s ContactPhotoManagerImpl (android-4.4.4_r2), with debug logging omitted:

The source clears a pending-request map and two memory-cache layers. Clearing the map does not interrupt I/O already in progress, and background results can refill a cache. Handle cancellation, stale results, and reloading together when adapting this pattern. MODERATE remains a historical trigger.

2.3 Current Example: A Budgeted UI Bitmap Cache

This complete API 19+ example caches rebuildable software Bitmaps associated with the UI configuration. The caller supplies a positive pixel budget based on measurement. getAllocationByteCount() is available from API 19; this budget counts allocated pixels, not every key, object header, or container, and is not a hard process-memory limit.

The example clears the same UI cache at UI_HIDDEN or higher levels, avoiding duplicate branches. The old RUNNING_* levels do not trigger this example. A null result from get() requires the image to be rebuilt or loaded again. The cache also clears on configuration changes so content can be rebuilt for the new configuration. onLowMemory() is included for older systems only and is not called on API 34+.

Create and manage this object on the main thread, normally under an application-level owner. If its scope ends before the process does, call dispose() and stop submitting work or data to it. Do not register a new object on every Activity transition. External owners must not arbitrarily call recycle() while a Bitmap is cached. evictAll() drops cache references without recycling Bitmaps still held elsewhere.

Clearing does not stop data production: cancel unnecessary prefetch or ignore stale results to prevent immediate refilling. A measured policy may retain selected entries or trim in stages for smoother recovery. Do not apply this UI-only cache policy wholesale to playback, uploads, or other business data. See LruCache.

3. onTrimMemory vs. onStop

onStop() concerns one Activity; UI_HIDDEN concerns UI visibility for the current process. Moving from Activity A to B can stop A while the process still has visible UI. Multi-process apps must also distinguish their processes rather than treating one callback as global visibility state.

Page-visible resources can follow paired onStart/onStop handling. Bounded caches shared across pages can have a longer-lived owner. Not every UI resource must wait for UI_HIDDEN before release.

Do not rely on UI_HIDDEN always occurring before onStop. These notifications have different scopes, and the public APIs do not provide a universal ordering contract for synchronizing application logic. Cleanup should be repeatable and recoverable, without relying on a trim callback before process termination.

4. onTrimMemory vs. onLowMemory

onLowMemory() is the older, coarse low-memory notification. Comparing it with COMPLETE in the old article described cleanup intensity, not identical triggering conditions.

It is no longer called from API 34 and was deprecated in API 35; see ComponentCallbacks. It is therefore not a replacement for old trim-pressure notifications that no longer arrive. Combine supported state callbacks, component lifecycles, and ordinary cache budgets instead.

5. Why bother?

The app should respond to this callback when appropriate. Passing a level manually executes local cleanup; it does not declare that process state to the system.

Reducing unused memory can help the system retain background processes, but reclamation also depends on component state, dependencies, and global pressure. It is not a fixed “walk LRU and kill the largest app first” rule. Nor does a surviving process guarantee a hot start or a fixed 2–3x speedup: an Activity that needs recreation can still undergo a warm start, and aggressive trimming can increase reload costs.

Distinguish cold, warm, and hot startup and measure the same device, version, and interaction path. See App startup time. Balance lower retained memory with the cost of restoring the experience.

6. Typical Use Cases

6.1 Long-lived Apps

Long-running apps such as a launcher can clear unused preview pages and UI caches while retaining the ability to rebuild them. Labels such as launcher, phone, or security center do not guarantee process survival; system roles and implementations determine priority. Respond to system notifications and the app’s lifecycle rather than repeatedly calling trim methods to keep a process alive.

6.2 Apps with Background Services

Music playback and downloads can continue to need data when the UI is hidden. Reduce display-only cover art or preview caches without releasing the player, transfer buffers, or connections still in use.

A Service is not a process-survival guarantee. Follow current background-execution and foreground-service rules, and manage each resource by purpose. Validate backgrounding, return to UI, internal Activity transitions, and configuration changes while recording the levels actually received. On Android 14+, do not wait for the five retired pressure levels to establish that cleanup works.

About Me && Blog

Here are my introduction and related links. I welcome conversations with fellow developers and opportunities to learn from one another.

  1. About me: contact details and WeChat groups.
  2. Blog navigation: a guide to this blog’s articles.
  3. Android Performance Optimization: Essential Skills and Tools: recommendations and contributions are welcome through WeChat.
  4. Android Performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.

entry.title: Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Android Resources
entry.content:
Android Memory Optimization Series:

  1. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Android (Official)
  2. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Java (Official)
  3. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Android Resources
  4. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - OnTrimMemory

I wrote this because understanding common memory problems before writing the code can save a lot of diagnosis later. We will look at Bitmaps, database queries, list reuse, and drawing: who creates each resource, what keeps it alive, and when it is no longer needed. Retention, repeated allocation, and leaks need different remedies.

Technical review: October 13, 2026. First published in 2015. Recycling every Bitmap manually is no longer sound general advice, and pixel visibility in MAT depends on the Android version. Cursor, Adapter, and Handler examples are completed below, with corrections to NinePatch, lifecycle, and ownership guidance. The eight sections and two illustrations are retained.

Android Resource Optimization

1. Bitmap Optimization

Bitmaps can dominate memory in image-heavy apps, but not every Android memory problem comes from them. Measure live objects, caches, and allocation sources before choosing an optimization.

Pixel storage has changed across versions, so not every HPROF contains a corresponding byte[]:

Android versionTypical pixel storage
Android 2.3.x and earlier (API 10 and below)Native memory; the Java Bitmap object is a wrapper.
3.0 / API 11 through 7.1 / API 25Managed heap alongside the Bitmap.
8.0 / API 26 and laterNative heap; the Java wrapper alone does not represent all pixel memory.

See Managing Bitmap Memory. Interpret the actual bitmap type, graphics allocations, and device implementation using the available tools. An uncollected object is not automatically a leak: bounded caches and images being displayed or processed have legitimate owners.

1.1 Manually Releasing Bitmap Resources

Do not treat recycle() as mandatory cleanup for every image. The old guide specifically recommended explicit recycling for API 10 and earlier. Current code should first address decode sizes, cache limits, and ownership.

The current Bitmap.recycle() contract describes immediate pixel-memory release for images certainly no longer needed, such as an exclusively owned intermediate transformation buffer. It also warns against recycling Bitmaps used by Views or potentially referenced elsewhere. GC still manages the Java wrapper. The old mBuffer and nativeRecycle() excerpt describes an older implementation, not every version.

isRecycled() == false only says the bitmap has not been marked recycled. It does not establish exclusive ownership or remove races. Dropping your reference, detaching an image, and cancelling a load are different operations; assigning null to a method parameter does not clear the caller’s field. Follow an image library’s target-cleanup and bitmap-pool ownership rules rather than recycling its images independently.

1.2 Releasing ImageView Images

getDrawable() can return a VectorDrawable, ColorDrawable, LayerDrawable, or another type, so a direct BitmapDrawable cast is unsafe. Even a BitmapDrawable can contain a bitmap shared with caches or other Views.

After cancelling relevant asynchronous loading, this helper removes the ImageView’s image reference on the UI thread:

It detaches this View’s image without promising immediate release of all pixel memory. Stop asynchronous requests from delivering into the old target too, or the image can be repopulated after clearing. Prefer the library’s clear/cancel interface for library-managed targets.

1.3 Releasing ImageView Backgrounds

The background and src hold separate references. A background can be any Drawable. This helper performs no cast and does not recycle a shared bitmap; setBackground() is available from API 16:

Clear only backgrounds that are no longer needed, preserving visual and state feedback. Other Views, caches, and drawing work may still retain the bitmap; one null assignment does not establish that all use has ended.

1.4 Use Nine-Patch for Suitable Stretchable Backgrounds

NinePatch is itself a PNG format. Its app-resource extension is .9.png, not .9.webp. Border markers define stretchable and content regions. It suits backgrounds such as bubbles and borders, not every photograph, and choosing the wrong stretch region can still distort an image.

A small source image can replace several larger backgrounds, but cost still depends on its dimensions, decoding, and use. Android Studio’s Draw 9-patch tool edits these markers and previews different sizes.

1.5 Decode Large Images for the Target Size

Reducing encoded file size and decoding fewer pixels are different optimizations. Lowering JPEG quality generally makes the compressed file smaller; with unchanged dimensions and pixel format, decoded pixel memory may remain similar. Decoding the full image and then scaling it has already incurred the larger peak allocation.

For thumbnails, determine the required size before decoding. Account for zooming or editing if needed. With BitmapFactory:

  1. Set inJustDecodeBounds = true to read dimensions and type without allocating the full pixels. Check that outWidth and outHeight are valid before using them.
  2. Compute inSampleSize for the target pixel dimensions, then disable bounds-only decoding and load the sampled image. Resource-density scaling can also affect output size, so inspect the actual result.

From Android 9 (API 28), ImageDecoder.setTargetSize() can specify output dimensions; preserve the aspect ratio required by the task. When using an existing loading library, pass the right target size and let it coordinate decoding, caching, and cancellation.

Avoid blocking the UI thread with decoding and large-image processing. See Loading Large Bitmaps Efficiently.

2. Unclosed Database Cursors

Code obtaining a Cursor directly is responsible for closing it on success and failure paths. Do not close only when moveToNext() succeeds, or treat a null query result as an empty result set.

This complete example uses Java 7+ try-with-resources on API 19 and later. Counting demonstrates the resource scope. Supply a URI the caller is authorized to access and the necessary projection, and run the query on an appropriate background thread:

Zero means that a valid Cursor contains no records; this example treats a null Cursor as an error. It does not copy all rows into a collection, but getCount() can still perform real query work and should not be assumed cheap. Explicit finally cleanup in older projects must also cover failures; do not silently swallow every close exception.

When ownership has been transferred to a Loader, adapter, or other manager, follow that component’s contract instead of closing its Cursor prematurely. See Cursor.close() and ContentResolver.query().

3. Not Recycling convertView in Adapters

ListView’s convertView is an old row available for reuse. It can be null initially or when no suitable row is available. Recreating a row every time adds allocation, layout, and GC pressure, but does not automatically cause a growing leak.

Check the View type and bind current data on both the creation and reuse paths.

This complete single-row-type adapter uses a standard layout. It copies the input list at construction and only demonstrates display, without a data-update API:

Complex rows must also reset visibility, selection, and old image requests so state from the previous item does not leak into the next one. Implement getItemViewType() and getViewTypeCount() correctly for multiple layouts. RecyclerView also requires complete binding and appropriate recycling; it cannot remove every application-owned reference automatically. See Adapter.getView().

4. Releasing Object References

To understand retention, follow strong references back to their owners and GC roots. Setting one variable to null removes only that reference; another cache, callback, or queue can still retain the object.

Scenario A: Handlers and Runnables

The original example copied obj to local variable o and set obj = null. That removes the Activity field’s reference, but the Runnable still captures o. Calling an Activity instance method can also capture the Activity itself. The queue can retain them until execution or cancellation. A Handler executes on its Looper’s thread; it does not automatically move work to a background thread.

This complete class demonstrates a delayed title update needed only by visible UI. Call showTitleLater() on the UI thread while the page is visible. New work replaces the previous request, and onStop() removes the pending callback:

Cleanup removes the specific Runnable owned by this page, without deleting unrelated work on a shared Handler. removeCallbacks() cannot interrupt work that has already started. Removal scans the queue; this example is intended for a small number of page-owned tasks. Persistent background work needs its own lifetime and cancellation policy. See the Handler API.

Scenario B: Listeners and Subscriptions

The old LockScreen/PhoneStateListener example illustrates a longer-lived owner retaining a shorter-lived object. That is a useful risk to examine, but forgetting to unregister does not establish an inevitable system_ui OOM. The Android version, listener implementation, and actual strong-reference chain require inspection.

PhoneStateListener was deprecated in Android 12 (API 31). New code uses TelephonyCallback with paired registerTelephonyCallback() and unregisterTelephonyCallback() calls. The current registration contract says the framework retains the callback weakly, so the caller must retain it during the subscription; the old listener’s ownership model cannot simply be carried forward. Meet the permissions for the chosen events, and unregister the same instance when its subscription ends. See PhoneStateListener and TelephonyManager.

5. Releasing Resources in Lifecycle Callbacks

Match release to acquisition and purpose. A listener needed only while visible can follow onStart()/onStop(), while interaction-only work can follow onResume()/onPause(). In multi-window scenarios from API 24, a paused Activity can remain visible.

onDestroy() is not guaranteed before the system terminates a process. Do not defer all persistent state saving until then or perform large synchronous I/O in lifecycle callbacks. Separate data retained across configuration changes from references to one particular Activity/View instance. See the Activity lifecycle and process lifecycle.

6. Eliminating Overdraw

Overdraw means drawing a pixel more than once in a frame. Text over a background can be necessary; remove redundant backgrounds and covering layers that contribute no visual result, rather than removing all backgrounds.

Extra drawing can increase GPU work and memory-bandwidth demand, but a deep View tree does not mean every layer covers the same pixels. Eliminating one draw does not promise a proportional reduction in Bitmap or process-heap usage. Evaluate clipping, transparency, actual frame timing, and GPU evidence.

See this blog’s Overdraw and Its Optimization and the official Reduce overdraw guide.

7. Using System Resources

Public system strings, drawables, styles, and layouts can replace duplicate app resources when their meaning and appearance fit. Their appearance can vary with system version, theme, or device, so inspect target devices and avoid hidden internal resources.

For example, this layout uses the public android:id/list identifier:

That ID is not a shared ListView object. The app still instantiates the View. Using a system ID alone does not establish a runtime memory saving. Check packaged resources, APK size, and runtime allocations separately. See Access platform resources.

8. Using Memory Profiling Tools

It is hard to get memory management right in one pass. At each stage of development, check screen entry/exit, scrolling, image loading, and foreground/background transitions. Look for objects surviving beyond their intended lifetime, not merely a high number at one instant.

Android Studio heap dumps expose Java/Kotlin objects and reference paths. MAT remains useful for compatible HPROF files, while native and graphics memory need additional tools. Lint gives static clues; it does not prove the absence of leaks.

For bitmap investigations, also consider the version limits in this blog’s Restoring Bitmap Objects from MAT. A native address alone cannot reconstruct pixel data. Recheck allocations, retention, and user experience through the original scenario after each fix.

About Me && Blog

Here are my introduction and related links. I welcome conversations with fellow developers and opportunities to learn from one another.

  1. About me: contact details and WeChat groups.
  2. Blog navigation: a guide to this blog’s articles.
  3. Android Performance Optimization: Essential Skills and Tools: recommendations and contributions are welcome through WeChat.
  4. Android Performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.

entry.title: Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Android (Official)
entry.content:
Android Memory Optimization Series:

  1. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Android (Official)
  2. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Java (Official)
  3. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Android Resources
  4. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - OnTrimMemory

For GC to reclaim unused objects, longer-lived owners must stop retaining references that are no longer needed. Reachability from GC roots matters, not whether another object holds a reference: a group of mutually referencing objects can still be collected when the whole group is unreachable. Becoming unreachable does not mean GC runs immediately or that the memory is immediately returned to the OS.

Memory management also includes bounded caches, resource ownership, and component lifecycles. Close files, connections, and native resources through their own APIs rather than waiting only for their Java wrappers to be collected.

Technical review: October 13, 2026. This article originated in Android’s memory guidance from around 2015. Advice about IntentService, some trim callbacks, nano protobuf, dependency injection, and APK packaging has changed. The original 16 topics are retained with version boundaries. Fixed object sizes and blanket prohibitions are no longer presented as general Android rules.

Introduction

The historical source is Managing Your App’s Memory in AOSP android-5.1.1_r1. Start with the current Android memory documentation for newer guidance. Distinguish the Java heap, native/graphics allocations, code mappings, and whole-process memory instead of treating them as one heap number.

1. Use Services Sparingly

Keep a Service active only while work requires it, and end its started work or bindings when appropriate. A Service is a component, not an automatic worker thread or a guarantee that its process cannot be killed. Unnecessary resident work consumes resources, but system process reclamation and Java memory leaks are different problems. Stopping a Service does not fix every leak.

The old recommendation to use IntentService is outdated. It stops after processing its queue, but is subject to Android 8.0 (API 26) background execution limits and was deprecated in Android 11 (API 30). See the IntentService API.

For persistent tasks that need scheduling across app exits or device reboots, evaluate WorkManager. Short tasks tied to a screen should be cancelled with that screen. User-visible ongoing work such as playback must follow the relevant foreground-service rules; replacing every Service with WorkManager is not the answer.

2. Release Memory When UI is Hidden

When UI is no longer visible, reduce caches retained only for that UI and which can be rebuilt. Do not also discard data needed for playback, uploads, or state restoration, or call recycle() on Bitmaps still used elsewhere.

TRIM_MEMORY_UI_HIDDEN, available since API 14, indicates that the current process no longer displays UI. It is different from one Activity’s onStop() and is not a unified notification covering every process of an app. onStop() can end work tied to that Activity’s visible lifetime. Release resources according to their ownership and acquisition lifecycle rather than waiting for UI_HIDDEN in every case.

This is a callback-method fragment for an existing Application or Activity class. Connect the comments to the app’s own cache-cleanup operations, and handle thresholds rather than only one exact value:

This callback is an opportunity to adjust caches, not a guaranteed notification before process death. Keep cache capacities bounded during normal use and persist user state promptly. See the current ComponentCallbacks2 contract.

3. Release Memory During Pressure

Version change: from Android 14 (API 34), apps no longer receive five old pressure levels: RUNNING_MODERATE, RUNNING_LOW, RUNNING_CRITICAL, MODERATE, and COMPLETE. The constants were deprecated in API 35. UI_HIDDEN and BACKGROUND remain useful for memory management during process-state changes. BACKGROUND alone does not prove that the device is critically short of memory.

3.1 While the App is Running

These are historical meanings for interpreting old code and logs, not a current sequence of callbacks:

Old level (all introduced in API 16)Historical meaning
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_MODERATEMemory pressure is beginning; consider reducing unnecessary caches.
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_LOWPressure is increasing; release unused resources.
TRIM_MEMORY_RUNNING_CRITICALPressure is severe; reduce non-essential usage as far as possible.

These hints never guaranteed that a running app could not be killed. A trim level also cannot establish whether an OOM, system process kill, or app crash has occurred.

3.2 While the App is Cached

TRIM_MEMORY_BACKGROUND (API 14) indicates entry into the background LRU list and offers a chance to release rebuildable caches. The old MODERATE and COMPLETE levels, introduced in API 14 and no longer delivered from API 34, indicated positions nearer the middle and end of the background list. Do not depend on them to trigger progressively stronger cleanup today.

onLowMemory() is not a current fallback: it is no longer called from API 34 and was deprecated in API 35. The original compatibility advice for devices below API 14 is historical. See ComponentCallbacks and the Android 16 ComponentCallbacks2 source annotations.

Reducing background usage can help the system retain more cached processes, but an app cannot guarantee a fixed order of process survival.

4. Check Your Memory Limits

getMemoryClass() reports an approximate normal application memory class in MB, useful for budgeting. It is neither remaining heap capacity nor a limit on total process RSS/PSS. Observe Java, native, and graphics allocations separately; subtracting current usage from this value cannot guarantee that the next allocation will succeed.

For a justified large-heap requirement, set android:largeHeap="true" on <application> and consult getLargeMemoryClass(). Available since API 11, it can equal the normal memory class on some devices. Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() reports the maximum Java heap memory the current runtime will attempt to use, in bytes, also not remaining capacity.

Do not use largeHeap as a general OOM or leak fix. Identify who allocates and retains memory, and why retention is necessary. A larger live set can increase GC and system pressure, but does not make every collection slower.

5. Avoid Bitmap Waste

Decode images at the size required for display, zooming, or editing. Loading a full-resolution image just for a small thumbnail usually adds no value, but zoom or crop requirements must be considered too.

Compressed file size is not decoded memory size. At four bytes per pixel, a 1500 × 1000 ARGB_8888 image requires an estimated 6,000,000 bytes, about 5.72 MiB, even if its file occupies only 100 KB. This does not include every object, reused allocation capacity, or additional graphics cost.

From API 19, getAllocationByteCount() reports allocated pixel capacity. After reuse or reconfiguration it can exceed getByteCount(). Account for where pixel storage lives rather than treating the Java wrapper’s size as the entire bitmap cost.

6. Use Optimized Data Collections

SparseArray<E> uses int keys, avoiding key boxing and a separate entry object for each mapping, but its values are still objects. Specialized containers such as SparseBooleanArray and SparseIntArray also use their corresponding primitive value types. LongSparseArray<E> supports long keys; the framework version is available from API 16. The old android.support.v4 link is no longer the current entry point.

These containers prioritize memory efficiency. Lookups generally use binary search, while insertion and removal involve array maintenance, so they are not guaranteed to outperform HashMap. Choose by key/value types, size, and access patterns.

7. Be Aware of Memory Overheads

The old figures—roughly 500 bytes per class, 12–16 bytes of instance overhead, and enums costing over twice as much—were rough descriptions of an older environment. They are not layout guarantees from Java or Android. The historical 500-byte figure described code size, not fixed RAM usage after loading a class. Object headers, field layout, alignment, runtime implementation, and optimization affect actual costs.

The historical 32-byte figure referred to a HashMap entry object, not a rule that boxing one int always allocates 32 bytes. A container’s footprint also includes its arrays, references, keys, values, and sharing relationships.

Enums offer type safety and clear semantics; an old ratio is not a reason to prohibit them throughout Android code. If many small objects form a bottleneck, inspect counts, retention paths, and actual usage on the current build and device before comparing representations.

8. Be Careful with Abstractions

Abstraction can introduce objects, indirection, and initialization. More source-level classes do not prove that all of them must occupy memory or impose a fixed runtime cost: optimization, class loading, and executed paths matter.

I would keep interfaces that support clear responsibilities, testing, and evolution. Once a hotspot is identified, compare implementations that preserve those contracts. Removing useful module boundaries usually does not fix a retention chain or an unbounded cache.

9. Use Nano ProtoBufs for Serialized Data

“Always use nano on Android” is outdated. Evaluate Protobuf Java Lite against the required features; its runtime artifact is com.google.protobuf:protobuf-javalite. It trades features for mobile binary-size and memory goals, does not offer the full Java runtime’s entire feature set, and is not always faster.

From Protobuf 3.8.0, lite generation is built into protoc’s Java output through the lite option. This is a migration boundary, not a recommendation to pin new projects to 3.8.0. See the official Gradle plugin documentation. Check the generator, generated code, runtime versions, data compatibility, and R8 rules together; changing one dependency name is not a complete migration.

The original DEX limitation concerns method and other symbol references, not string length. Generated code size is also different from the memory occupied by live objects at runtime.

10. Avoid Dependency Injection Frameworks

The blanket prohibition in this old heading is outdated. The original concern was runtime scanning in frameworks such as Guice/RoboGuice, not every form of dependency injection. Current Android guidance recommends Hilt, built on Dagger’s compile-time code generation. Avoiding findViewById() and injecting application dependencies are separate concerns.

Simple cases can construct dependencies manually. This complete Java class accepts its source of names from the caller without a framework or runtime annotation scan:

The caller supplies a Names implementation, which tests can replace. More complex object graphs can use Hilt/Dagger. For memory review, inspect creation timing, scope, and ownership: a long-lived container must not retain a short-lived Activity unintentionally. Compile-time generation does not mean zero initialization cost or freedom from leaks.

11. Be Cautious with External Libraries

Before adding a library, inspect its maintenance status, dependency graph, initialization, caches, and final output. R8 may remove unused code when safe, so source or download size alone does not establish the APK or RAM increase.

Watch for duplicate logging, image-loading, serialization, and cache implementations. If they are all used, a shrinker cannot decide which behavior to remove for you. Consider smaller modules while accounting for the correctness and maintenance benefits of established libraries; using only a few features is not automatically a reason to rewrite them yourself.

12. Optimize Overall Performance

Evaluate memory changes in user flows. Smaller caches may cause frequent reloads, and an allocation-saving change may add main-thread work.

Use Layout Inspector to inspect UI hierarchy and Android Lint for static findings. Confirm the resulting benefit during startup, scrolling, and screen transitions.

13. Use ProGuard

Modern Android builds primarily use R8, the default code shrinker since AGP 3.4.0. Check settings such as isMinifyEnabled for release code optimization and isShrinkResources for resource shrinking. Upgrading AGP does not enable optimization in every build.

R8 can remove unreachable code, optimize calls, and obfuscate names. Smaller code does not automatically reduce runtime caches, Bitmap allocations, or leaks. Maintain keep rules for the actual library, reflection, and JNI requirements rather than keeping entire packages to hide a problem. See app optimization setup.

14. Use zipalign

zipalign aligns uncompressed APK entries for direct memory mapping. Normal Android Studio/AGP builds perform alignment automatically, so manual modification of the final file is usually unnecessary.

With apksigner, align first and sign afterwards. Modifying the APK after signing invalidates its signature. The old jarsigner workflow has a different order; the original advice to realign after compilation cannot simply be applied to every modern workflow.

To inspect an existing APK without modifying it, use the tool from Android SDK Build-Tools 35.0.0 or later and replace the example filename with your artifact:

-P 16 checks 16 KiB page alignment for uncompressed .so files; the final 4 specifies four-byte alignment for other uncompressed entries. For 16 KB page-size devices, the official guidance recommends AGP 8.5.1 or later and NDK r28 or later, with compatible prebuilt dependencies. ELF alignment, native page-size assumptions, and runtime behavior still require checking; passing zipalign alone does not establish all of these. See 16 KB page-size support.

15. Analyze RAM Usage

Inspect memory throughout development. Exercise startup, repeated screen entry/exit, scrolling, rotation, and foreground/background transitions. Look for whether usage settles, caches remain bounded, and instance counts keep growing.

Android Studio heap dumps expose Java/Kotlin objects and retention paths. Native and graphics memory also require the relevant profiler or system data. Distinguish shallow size, retained size, process RSS, and PSS’s proportional accounting of shared pages instead of judging everything by one Java heap peak.

Heap dumps and allocation tracking perturb the observed app. After a fix, recheck user flows on physical devices with a configuration close to release, rather than treating one debugging measurement as stable performance.

16. Use Multiple Processes

A separate process can sometimes allow a heavy UI process to be reclaimed independently in the background, but adds runtime, initialization, cache, and IPC costs. Unreachable UI objects can already be collected within a shared process. Continued music playback does not imply that every UI allocation must remain alive.

This snippet shows only process isolation, not a complete background-playback configuration:

The colon prefix names an app-private process, not an independent permission sandbox. Processes have separate heaps, static state, and Application initialization; ordinary in-memory references do not share objects between them. Also inspect bindings and ContentProvider dependencies on the UI process, which may prevent the intended reclamation.

For background playback, start with Media3’s MediaSessionService and its notification, foreground-service declaration, and lifecycle requirements. A separate Service component does not require a separate process. Compare the total cost of all relevant processes and the restoration experience before splitting them.

About Me && Blog

Here are my introduction and related links. I welcome conversations with fellow developers and opportunities to learn from one another.

  1. About me: contact details and WeChat groups.
  2. Blog navigation: a guide to this blog’s articles.
  3. Android Performance Optimization: Essential Skills and Tools: recommendations and contributions are welcome through WeChat.
  4. Android Performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.

entry.title: Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Java (Official)
entry.content:
Android Memory Optimization Series:

  1. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Android (Official)
  2. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Java (Official)
  3. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - Android Resources
  4. Android Code Memory Optimization Suggestions - OnTrimMemory

This article covers micro-optimizations in Android Java code. Choosing suitable algorithms and data structures still comes first; these techniques are most useful for reducing repeated work and temporary allocations in hot paths.

The original source was Google’s Android Training article, Performance Tips. “Java (Official)” in the title refers to its Java coding advice for Android, not to an Oracle Java performance specification.

Technical review: October 13, 2026. The old fixed speed ratios, some string implementation details, and compiler limitations are outdated as general Android advice. The original 11 topics are retained below, with their historical context and current use separated. The historical source is available in AOSP android-5.1.1_r1.

Introduction

Efficient code should avoid two kinds of overhead:

  • Unnecessary repeated work.
  • Temporary allocations that can be removed from hot paths.

Saving one allocation does not justify breaking an interface or complicating state management. Performance also depends on the CPU, OS, runtime, and compilation state. Android 7.0 (API 24) introduced an ART JIT that works alongside AOT; a method may be interpreted, JIT-compiled, or AOT-compiled. The old rankings based simply on “with or without JIT” do not describe every current release build. See the Android 7.0 JIT/AOT notes and ART JIT documentation.

1) Avoid Creating Unnecessary Objects

GC can reclaim unused objects, but allocation and collection have costs. Start with short-lived objects in frequently executed code, rather than counting every new in the source.

  • If a method’s returned string is only ever appended to an existing StringBuffer, it can append directly to that buffer and avoid an intermediate string. StringBuilder is also suitable for single-threaded concatenation; do not introduce shared mutable buffers just for this optimization.
  • The old advice to use substring() relied on sharing the original char[]. This implementation is visible in Android 4.4.4’s Dalvik String source, but retaining a small substring could retain the entire backing array. The current String.substring() contract specifies the character range returned, without promising zero-copy behavior or shared storage. The old implementation is not a portable memory-saving technique.

Choose array layouts for the data being represented. An int[] avoids an object reference for each element and is generally more compact than boxed Integer[], but cannot represent null. The original discussion compared arrays of (int, int) or (Foo, Bar) tuple objects with two parallel arrays, which avoid the tuple objects. It did not establish that splitting any two-dimensional array makes it faster. Parallel arrays also require their indices to remain aligned; measured allocation or memory pressure should justify that maintenance cost.

Reducing temporary allocations can reduce GC pressure. One allocation does not imply one GC, and a smaller object count alone does not guarantee smoother UI.

2) Prefer Static Over Virtual

Declare a method static when it does not semantically belong to an instance and does not need instance-method overriding. The old “15%–20% faster” figure describes early runtime behavior; current results depend on inlining, the call site, and the compiled output.

static means there is no implicit this, not that the method has no side effects. It can still modify static fields or objects passed to it. Do not change a polymorphic interface just to chase that old ratio.

3) Use Static Final for Constants

Consider these field declarations:

These assignments become part of the class initializer, <clinit>. After initialization, ordinary field reads do not rerun <clinit> on every access.

For constants, use:

Both fields here are compile-time constants, so references can use their constant values directly. Under Java SE 25 JLS §4.12.4, a constant variable must be final, have a primitive or String type, and be initialized with a constant expression. An arbitrary static final object reference, or a value returned by a method call, does not meet that rule. A reference that cannot be reassigned can still point to a mutable object.

4) Avoid Internal Getters/Setters

This heading retains the historical advice, but calling getters “bad practice on Android” is no longer a useful rule. Direct access to a simple field within its class can be clear. Bypassing an accessor that performs validation, lazy initialization, or synchronization changes behavior.

The old 3x and 7x figures do not represent current ART in general. R8 at build time and runtime compilers can inline simple methods, but the result depends on the output and must be measured. R8 became the default code shrinker in Android Gradle Plugin 3.4.0; that does not mean shrinking and optimization are enabled for every build. Check the actual release configuration. See the AGP 3.4.0 release notes and app optimization setup.

Keep useful encapsulation and compare access patterns only in confirmed hot paths.

5) Use Enhanced For Loop Syntax

The three methods below calculate and return a sum using different loop forms. They illustrate syntax; this is not a microbenchmark that establishes a ranking:

The original ranking of zero(), one(), and two() depended on limitations of the JIT at the time. It does not prove that zero() is always slowest today or that manually caching the length always helps.

Enhanced for has two cases. Under JLS §14.14.2, array traversal is translated into an indexed loop, while traversal of an Iterable uses an iterator. An array for-each does not create an iterator just because it uses that syntax. For an Iterable, actual allocation and dispatch costs depend on its implementation and optimization.

For arrays, readability is usually a good starting point. An indexed loop over an ArrayList can be a candidate in a hot path, but this does not establish a faster pattern for all collections. It also does not remove the need to consider the semantics of modifying a collection during traversal.

6) Use Package Access Instead of Private Access for Inner Classes

This is another historical recommendation that needs a version boundary. In the following example, calling new Foo().run() prints Value is 27:

Java permits this inner class to access the outer class’s private members. Older compilation pipelines generated synthetic methods with names such as access$100 and access$200 to bridge the VM’s access rules at the time. These names are compiler details, not APIs to write by hand.

Java 11 introduced JVM nestmate access, allowing classes in the same nest to access each other’s private members; see JVMS 11 §5.4.4. Android APKs also pass through D8/R8 to produce DEX, so the desktop JDK version alone cannot prove whether helper methods survive in the final output.

Use private where encapsulation requires it. Package access exposes a member to other classes in the package. Consider changing it only after identifying meaningful overhead in the final output and evaluating that visibility change.

7) Avoid Float

This old recommendation is outdated. “Float is half as fast as int” is not an Android API guarantee or a fixed ratio for all floating-point operations and memory accesses. The outcome depends on the processor, instructions, data dependencies, and optimization.

Choose types for the required range, precision, and algorithm. Replacing fractional arithmetic with integers can change results through truncation or overflow. Compare alternatives that preserve the numerical requirements only after locating a bottleneck.

8) Use Library Functions

Prefer library operations whose semantics match the task, such as System.arraycopy(). Its contract defines type checks, bounds checks, and copying between overlapping regions; a manual implementation must handle those conditions too.

The old “over 9x faster” figure specifically referred to a Nexus One with JIT enabled. It is not a current performance guarantee. Results depend on array types, lengths, and the target device. Library calls should not be described as always executing through JNI, either.

The original reference to Effective Java, second edition, Item 47 (“Know and use the libraries”), corresponds to Item 59 in the third edition.

9) Use Native Methods Sparingly

JNI can be evaluated when porting an existing native library or addressing a measured compute hotspot. Include the costs of crossing the boundary, converting data, and copying it; timing only the native function’s body misses part of the work.

Reduce frequent small cross-boundary interactions and define ownership of native resources and JNI references. The current Android NDK guide is JNI Tips.

10) Performance Myth: Concrete vs. Interface

Map<K, V> map = new HashMap<>(); and a variable declared as HashMap<K, V> can refer to the same implementation. This comparison concerns the declared type and method dispatch at a call site, not the data-structure performance of two different containers.

The old “about 6%” and “almost no difference with JIT” figures also depended on their runtime environment. Choose types for the interface design, then inspect optimization in measured hot paths. An unmeasured dispatch difference is not a reason to replace every Map declaration with HashMap.

11) Measurement

The original Dalvik-era Traceview measurements were affected by method tracing’s interaction with JIT. That does not mean all profilers disable JIT, or that uninstrumented execution can be estimated as merely a little faster.

Traceview is deprecated; the official guidance recommends CPU Profiler for Android Studio 3.2 and later. Use Android Studio Profiler or Perfetto to locate hotspots, then choose the measurement scope:

  • Jetpack Microbenchmark compares identified methods or loops, handles warmup, and measures timing and allocations. Use representative inputs and consume results so unused computation cannot be optimized away.
  • Macrobenchmark and app performance measurement cover user flows such as startup and scrolling, showing whether a local optimization improves the experience.

Control the device, OS, build configuration, and compilation state. Measure on physical devices using a suitable non-debuggable build, and record warmup and sampling conditions. Debug builds, emulator results, and different compilation states should not be mixed into one ranking.

About Me && Blog

Here are my introduction and related links. I welcome conversations with fellow developers and opportunities to learn from one another.

  1. About me: contact details and WeChat groups.
  2. Blog navigation: a guide to this blog’s articles.
  3. Android Performance Optimization: Essential Skills and Tools: recommendations and contributions are welcome through WeChat.
  4. Android Performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.

entry.title: Enabling Multi-Window Mode on Nexus 6 with Android M
entry.content:
On May 28, 2015, Google announced the Android M Developer Preview for devices including Nexus 6. This records that experience; the images below show the home screen and Easter egg.

Obsolete experimental procedure · Technical review (2026-10-13): Changing system properties to expose this switch is retained only as history for Nexus 6 (shamu) and the 2015 Android M preview. Google’s later announcement identifies the initial preview as MPZ44Q, but this article retained no device build-number output to verify its exact image. Modern multi-window development uses the versioned APIs discussed at the end, without these system modifications.

The “Changes” and “Afterword” sections retain their 2015 perspective.

Changes

  1. The most noticeable change in Android M is the app drawer:

As shown, the apps in the drawer are indexed alphabetically. The top row shows frequently used apps, which currently cannot be customized.

  1. Another significant change is in the animations—both folder animations and app launch animations have been updated. It’s hard to describe in words, so you’ll have to experience it yourself.

  2. The preview’s Developer options Theme menu offered Light, Dark, and Automatic; Light is selected in the screenshot. This does not establish which options survived in later releases.

Multi-Window Mode

The user build in the original experiment did not display this switch. As a source reference from the same Android generation, Android 6.0.0_r1 DevelopmentSettings checks !"user".equals(Build.TYPE), rather than specifically requiring userdebug. Toggling the preference writes persist.sys.debug.multi_window. This release source explains the mechanism; it is not a reproduction of the exact preview binary.

Build.TYPE reads ro.build.type, whereas Build.IS_DEBUGGABLE reads ro.debuggable. Changing the former to userdebug does not rebuild the OS, install debug modules, or automatically set ro.debuggable to 1. A full userdebug build has other build settings.

Flashing a Third-Party Recovery

The historical steps below assume the old shamu partition layout, an already-unlocked bootloader, adb/fastboot on the computer, and backups of the device and data. Bootloader unlocking involves a user-data wipe; it is not a lossless setup step. See the official bootloader guidance.

Changing system can also affect subsequent OTAs, as TWRP’s system read-only explanation describes for block-based updates. Modern partition layouts, verification, and mounting differ; these are not generic commands for current devices.

1. Enter Bootloader Mode

2. Flash twrp.img

I used TWRP 2.8.6.0 for shamu. The official download was slow at the time, so I also put a copy on Baidu Netdisk for others. Use the official Nexus 6 device page and version archive, where that historical file is still listed. It is not a current-version recommendation or an image for other devices. After confirming the image and device match, the historical command was:

3. Mount System

After flashing, enter Recovery from the bootloader instead of starting Android first; the old system may restore stock recovery on a normal boot. In TWRP Mount, confirm system is mounted writable as expected by that old image. Checking a label alone does not verify the path or write access.

4. Modify /system/build.prop

On the computer, confirm the Recovery adb connection and copy the original file to a local backup. These paths assume /system/build.prop exists in the historical environment:

Inside the Recovery shell, I used vi with the absolute path. Availability of that editor depends on the Recovery image:

Find the line:

And change it to:

Preserve the file’s permissions, owner, and security labels when saving. Exit the Recovery shell, then run adb reboot on the computer. After rebooting, I saw the switch below. Other releases may behave differently. Use adb shell getprop ro.build.type to verify the changed string:

In that preview interface, tap Recents and select a task-position icon; modern interfaces may differ:

  • The first one places the window in the top half.
  • The second one places it in the bottom half.
  • The third one sets it to full screen.

And here was the result:

Multi-window development today

Public APIs have replaced the preview switch. The relevant behavior varies by version:

VersionRelevant change
Android 7.0 / API 24Public split-screen support, configured through multi-window APIs and manifest settings
Android 10 / API 29Multi-resume permits multiple visible activities to be RESUMED; onResume alone does not establish exclusive-resource ownership
Android 12 / API 31Broader multi-window support on large screens; resizeableActivity="false" may lead to compatibility mode rather than universally disabling multi-window
Android 16 / API 36, targetSdk 36+Orientation, aspect-ratio, and resizability restrictions are ignored by default on displays at least 600dp in smallest width; game and user-setting exceptions require attention

See the multi-window guide for version and lifecycle behavior, and Android 16 changes for exceptions and the temporary opt-out. The adaptive-app guidance states that targetSdk 37+ removes that temporary opt-out, so it is not a long-term substitute for adaptation.

Check layouts after window resizing, state restoration after activity recreation, and lifecycle behavior when visible without focus. Exclusive resources such as cameras can be reclaimed. Do not mechanically add a long configChanges list to avoid recreation. Test full-screen/split-screen transitions, divider dragging, rotation, and folding on supported devices or emulators.

Afterword

They called it “multi-window,” though at the time it only supported two. Even two windows didn’t make great use of the space; adding more didn’t sound very useful either. We would have to see what Google did with it.

Samsung had already done multi-window, with resizing too. But I didn’t find much use for it then. It felt more like something to show off than something I would use, and needed a few more iterations.

I wrote my posts on Jianshu first, then copied them elsewhere, so I also wanted to recommend it here. The Chinese version is on Jianshu: Nexus6-with-Android-M开启多窗口模式.

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

  1. Blogger Intro
  2. Blog Content Navigation: A guide for my blog content.
  3. Curated Excellent Blog Articles - Android Performance Optimization Must-Knows
  4. Android Performance Optimization Knowledge Planet: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

One walks faster alone, but a group walks further together.

entry.title: A Detailed Guide to Java Singleton Pattern
entry.content:
The Singleton pattern restricts how instances are created and accessed. This article follows eager initialization, double-checked locking, the holder idiom, and enums, explaining their initialization behavior and limits.

Technical review (2026-10-13): These patterns remain applicable. The discussion is checked against the Java 5+ memory model and Java SE 25 specifications. It corrects the loading/initialization distinction, runtime access checks, and the explanation of enum reflection. The code blocks named Singleton are alternatives, not declarations to combine in one source file.

What is the Singleton Pattern?

The Singleton pattern is a software design pattern that restricts the instantiation of a class to one “single” instance.

“One instance” needs a scope: the designated access path returns the same instance of the same runtime class. Different defining class loaders can create distinct classes with the same name, and separate processes do not share one static instance. Ordinary classes also need separate consideration of reflection and deserialization. See JVMS 5.3.

A singleton does not automatically make mutable state thread-safe or manage resource cleanup and lifetime.

Constructing the Singleton Pattern

Initialization timing gives us two broad approaches:

  1. Lazy initialization: defer creation until the instance is needed.
  2. Eager initialization: create the instance when the class holding the static field is initialized.

Loading, linking, and initialization are different phases. The static initializer below normally runs on the first active use of the class, such as calling getInstance(), not merely when its bytecode is loaded. See JLS 12.4.1.

Class initialization safely publishes this instance. If initialization is inexpensive and need not be deferred, this is already a simple solution.

For deferred creation, one option is double-checked locking (DCL):

The second check under the lock prevents duplicate concurrent creation. volatile safely publishes the reference together with preceding construction writes: a write to that volatile field happens-before subsequent reads of the same field. This is more precise than saying it freezes one instruction in place. The outer read holds no lock, so volatile must remain. See JLS 17.4.5.

This DCL form relies on the memory model in Java 5 / JDK 1.5 and later; adding volatile on an older JVM does not provide the same guarantee. See the JSR-133 authors’ FAQ. The example assumes the instance is never reset and this does not escape during construction. Subsequent mutations still need their own synchronization policy.

Another Singleton Pattern

The initialization-on-demand holder idiom is usually simpler than DCL:

Initializing the outer Singleton class does not automatically initialize LazyHolder. The first read of LazyHolder.INSTANCE triggers holder initialization; the runtime coordinates competing threads and visibility. No extra volatile field is required. This comes from class-initialization semantics, not an incidental compiler optimization. See JLS 12.4.2.

The field can be private: access to a nested class’s private members is permitted within the same top-level class. Package access is not required. See JLS 6.6.1. The original holder-idiom discussion could not be retrieved during this review and remains a historical reference.

If static initialization fails, the class enters an erroneous state; subsequent initialization attempts may throw NoClassDefFoundError. A holder is not an automatic retry mechanism. Objects requiring external configuration, explicit retries, or replaceable lifetimes may need a different ownership design.

Using Enum

When one fixed enum constant fits the object, I recommend this simpler form, available since Java 5:

Use Singleton.INSTANCE. The constant is created during enum-class initialization. An enum can implement interfaces but cannot extend another class, and mutable business fields are not automatically thread-safe.

Serialization of an ordinary singleton class

Adding serialization to a singleton can be a bit of a pain. The preceding ordinary classes do not implement Serializable, so Java object serialization cannot directly write them. If an ordinary singleton must support it, a readResolve() method can return the existing instance. Here is a separate complete example:

readResolve() is recognized by serialization; it does not override an Object method, so do not add @Override here. It supplies a replacement after the object has been read, rather than preventing every temporary object from being created. Complex object graphs can retain references established before replacement, so this is not an absolute instance-control guarantee. See Serialization Specification 3.7.

Use transient according to whether a field belongs in serialized state and the object graph, not mechanically on every field because the class is a singleton. The stateless example above has no such instance fields.

Why Constructor.newInstance cannot create enum constants

I hadn’t looked deeply into reflection when I first wrote this. Reflection performs runtime access checks; private access is not enforced only at compile time. Where permitted, setAccessible(true) can suppress some checks; Java 9+ module boundaries may prevent access from being enabled. See AccessibleObject.

Enums have an additional rule: JLS 8.9 prohibits reflective enum instantiation, and Constructor.newInstance throws IllegalArgumentException for an enum constructor. This is not because every enum is abstract. The simple enum above is implicitly final; the abstract modifier on its java.lang.Enum base class does not automatically apply to the subclass.

What enum serialization preserves

Enums support serialization; they do not prohibit it. ObjectOutputStream uses special handling with the enum type descriptor and constant name, without serializing the constant’s instance-field values. ObjectInputStream resolves the existing constant using Enum.valueOf(enumType, name) instead of creating a new enum instance. See Serialization Specification 1.12.

The following identity comparison uses the enum version of Singleton. The helper requires Java 7+ for try-with-resources. Put the public types in separate Singleton.java and SingletonSerializationDemo.java files:

Under that contract, identity is preserved for the same runtime enum type. The example reads back its own in-memory data; it is not a snapshot of business state. Enum serialization ignores custom readObject, writeObject, and readResolve hooks.

A friendly reminder: do not casually rename or remove constants when existing serialized data must remain readable. If an old name is absent from the receiving enum, Java object deserialization fails; a direct Enum.valueOf() lookup of a missing name throws IllegalArgumentException. Reordering constants does not change name-based matching.

Recommended Reading:

  1. Effective Java, second edition Item 71, “Use lazy initialization judiciously”; third edition Item 83 covers the same topic, with instance control in Item 89.
  2. Core Java, Volume I, volatile/concurrency chapters. The original “14.5.8” did not identify an edition and should not be assumed to match every edition.
  3. JLS 17.4.5: happens-before and JLS 12.4: initialization.
  4. JSR-133 authors’ FAQ on volatile and DCL across the Java 5 memory-model change. The old IBM developerWorks article URL now redirects to a Java category page and is obsolete as an article link.
  5. Double-Checked Locking and Lazy Initialization: historical translation, not retrievable during this review; use the specifications above for the technical guarantees.

entry.title: Android Performance Patterns: Profile GPU Rendering
entry.content:
Series Catalog:

  1. Overview of Android Performance Patterns
  2. Android Performance Patterns: Render Performance
  3. Android Performance Patterns: Understanding Overdraw
  4. Android Performance Patterns: Understanding VSYNC
  5. Android Performance Patterns: Profile GPU Rendering

Technical review (2026-10-13): The three-color diagrams are retained from the 2015 video. Their Update / Execute / Process stages can be compared with Android 4.4.4 source. Android 6.0 and Android 16 use finer breakdowns and different reference-line implementations; the old legend does not apply unchanged to every device.

Original video introduction:

“If you can measure it, you can optimize it” is a common term in the computing world, and for Android’s rendering system, the same thing holds true. In order to optimize your pipeline to be more efficient for rendering, you need a tool to give you feedback on where the current perf problems lie.

In this video, Colt McAnlis walks you through an on-device tool built for this exact reason. “Profile GPU Rendering” will help you understand the stages of the rendering pipeline, see which portions might be taking too long, and decide what to do about it in your application.

Profile GPU Rendering Tool

Profile GPU Rendering is a quick on-device tool for finding operations associated with high rendering-stage costs. Despite its name, the bars do not directly measure GPU hardware execution time, and cannot identify every cause of jank on their own. See the official explanation.

Use the bars to identify a suspicious operation, then examine its thread, scheduling, GPU, and composition evidence in a system trace. An app’s HWUI bars are not a complete SurfaceFlinger timeline and do not cover every custom OpenGL/Vulkan rendering path.

On Android 4.1 / API 16+, look for Profile GPU Rendering or Profile HWUI Rendering in Developer options and select On screen as bars. Names and locations vary by version and vendor:

The historical example shows blue, red, and orange/yellow segments with a green reference line:

This screenshot contains graphs for the app and System UI windows: one near the status bar, one near navigation, and one for the app. Their positions are not a universal rule that the top measures notifications and the bottom navigation. Identify the window each graph belongs to.

Using the GPU Profile Tool

Each bar represents a recorded frame for that window, with segment heights showing the measured stage durations. Only a limited history remains visible. These bars are neither FPS values nor full input-to-display latency measurements. A static page may produce no new drawing work, so the absence of new bars does not itself mean a freeze.

The Green Line

The historical figure labels the line 16ms. This matches getThreshold() returning 16 in Android 4.4.4 HardwareRenderer. Android 6.0 FrameInfoVisualizer also uses a fixed 16ms reference, whereas a 60Hz period is approximately 16.67ms.

Crossing the line warrants investigation, but does not prove the user saw a stutter; staying below it does not guarantee timely presentation. At 90Hz and 120Hz, periods are about 11.11ms and 8.33ms. Use the device’s actual reference-line implementation and frame deadlines for newer or high-refresh systems.

The Bar Colors

First, consider the old three-segment graph. The timing scopes below are checked against Android 4.4.4 Java HardwareRenderer; the exact system build used by the video is not established:

Blue: Update / Draw

The old implementation times display-list construction or updates inside buildDisplayList(). This includes drawing logic for Views that need updating; it does not rerun every View’s onDraw each frame, or measure the entire measure/layout pass. Unchanged display lists can be reused.

A tall blue segment is a reason to investigate frequent invalidation, expensive drawing code, or work that could leave the drawing path. Use a trace to locate the cost.

Red: Execute / Issue commands

The old timer wraps canvas.drawDisplayList(), including CPU-side replay and command submission. OpenGL ES in the illustration describes that version’s rendering path. Submitted commands do not mean the GPU has finished or the image is on screen.

Many drawing operations, complex paths, or waits during submission can increase this segment. A complex custom View is a candidate cause, not a conclusion established by red bars alone.

Transforms or animations can resubmit cached display lists without recording them again. Red can therefore increase without blue increasing, and this does not prove that every underlying View reran onDraw(). See the stage analysis.

Orange/yellow: Process / Swap buffers

Android 4.4.4 measures around eglSwapBuffers(). The old illustration says glSwapBuffers; the relevant API is EGL’s eglSwapBuffers. This is not simply the CPU waiting for the GPU to acknowledge a command. CPU and GPU work can run asynchronously; driver or buffer-queue backpressure, including waiting for a reusable buffer, can lengthen the call. A tall segment points to a wait/submission path, not proof of insufficient GPU compute power or a direct GPU execution-time measurement.

Reading Android 6.0 / Android 16 graphs

Android 6.0 / API 23 FrameInfoVisualizer and the Android 16 / API 36 implementation use seven segments. This table summarizes those source tags; vendor colors are not a fixed API contract.

ColorStageWhat the interval helps investigate
TealMisc / VSync delayIntendedVsync to HandleInputStart; may include a late start or other main-thread work
Dark greenInput / AnimationInput handling and animation-related work
Light greenMeasure / LayoutTraversal start to DrawStart; measurement and layout
BlueDrawDrawStart to SyncStart; drawing-command recording and related work
Light blueSync / UploadRendering synchronization and resource preparation
RedIssue commandsIssueDrawCommandsStart to SwapBuffers
OrangeSwap buffersSwapBuffers to FrameCompleted

The Android 16 source also draws green, lime, and red reference lines at 0.8, 1.0, and 1.5 times the supplied frameInterval, scaling the vertical axis. A green horizontal line no longer universally means 16ms. These are timing intervals, not guarantees that each contains only one kind of work; a color cannot represent all costs of one component in a mixed View/Compose page.

Record the system version, refresh rate, action, and most prominent stage. On Android 12 / API 31+, use Perfetto FrameTimeline to compare expected and actual frames; use available system-trace evidence on older systems. After a fix, disable on-screen debug overlays and run the same scenario/device with Macrobenchmark. FrameTimingMetric was added in AndroidX Benchmark 1.1.0; frameOverrunMs requires API 31+ and differs from frameDurationCpuMs. Follow the configuration requirements for a non-debuggable, profileable target app.

Summary

The GPU Profile tool is great for finding rendering issues, but fixing them requires deeper code analysis to find and optimize specific bottlenecks. Sometimes, you can use these metrics to convince designers to adjust their requirements for a better user experience.

Perf Matters

Keep calm, profile your code, and always remember, Perf Matters.
