entry.title: Android Performance Patterns: Understanding VSYNC
entry.content:
Series Catalog:

  1. Overview of Android Performance Patterns
  2. Android Performance Patterns: Render Performance
  3. Android Performance Patterns: Understanding Overdraw
  4. Android Performance Patterns: Understanding VSYNC
  5. Android Performance Patterns: Profile GPU Rendering

Technical review (2026-10-13): The introduction and nine diagrams are retained from the 2015 video. The text corrects the fixed-60Hz assumption, tearing explanation, and “VSync copies the back buffer” description, and adds modern frame-rate hints and analysis tools.

Original video introduction:

Unbeknownst to most developers, there’s a simple hardware design that defines everything about how fast your application can draw things to the screen.

You may have heard the term VSYNC - VSYNC stands for vertical synchronization and it’s an event that happens every time your screen starts to refresh the content it wants to show you.

Effectively, VSYNC is the product of two components: Refresh Rate (how fast the hardware can refresh the screen), and Frames Per Second (how fast the GPU can draw images). In this video, Colt McAnlis walks through each of these topics and discusses where VSYNC (and the 16ms rendering barrier) comes from, and why it’s critical to understand if you want a silky smooth application.

Basic Concepts

To understand smoothness and jank, distinguish app frame production, system composition, and display presentation. VSync (vertical synchronization) coordinates their timing. It is not the mathematical product of refresh rate and FPS, nor an operation that renders the app’s content for it. See the AOSP VSync explanation.

The original video mainly uses 60Hz, corresponding to refresh intervals of about 16.67ms. At 90Hz and 120Hz, the intervals are about 11.11ms and 8.33ms. These are not separate full budgets for every thread; actual deadlines depend on pipeline scheduling, discussed below.

Before diving into VSYNC, we need to understand two concepts:

Refresh Rate

Refresh rate, measured in Hz, describes the display’s refresh cadence. Hardware limits the supported modes, but the active rate need not be fixed: the system may choose it based on content, power policy, and other windows. Do not assume 60Hz is the default on every Android device. See Android’s frame-rate guidance.

Frame Rate (FPS)

Frame rate, measured in fps, counts frames per second, but the measurement point matters. Frames submitted by the app, completed by the GPU, and shown as distinct images to the user may produce different counts. FPS is also distinct from the GPU’s clock frequency in MHz.

A higher rate is not always the goal. Interactive motion benefits from consistent pacing and low latency; video has its own content frame rate. Unneeded work costs power. Showing each frame of a steady 30fps video twice on a 60Hz display can be normal playback, rather than a dropped app frame.

How It Works

The app produces images, SurfaceFlinger organizes composition, and the display system presents the result. Each column below is a simplified content-to-display illustration. CPU work, queues, composition, and synchronization are omitted; it is not a full Android timeline and does not mean a static page must redraw continuously.

Display and content rates may differ; how their timing is coordinated is what matters.

Production faster than refresh: distinguish skipped presentation from tearing

The 100fps / 75Hz diagram illustrates that not every produced frame is necessarily shown. Which frames are discarded or queued, and where the producer is throttled, depend on queueing and presentation policy. The rate mismatch alone does not establish tearing.

For example, take a photo, rotate by 5 degrees, take another, and join their upper and lower halves:

The halves depict different moments and do not line up. This illustrates tearing: without correct synchronization between scanout and updates, a scan can contain parts of different frames. For example, an image might be modified while it is being read, or the display source might switch too early. Different frame and refresh rates are not sufficient to cause tearing; incorrect synchronization can also tear at equal average rates.

Android coordinates reads and writes through buffer ownership, synchronization fences, and presentation scheduling. With BufferQueue, a producer dequeues an available buffer and submits it; the consumer acquires and eventually releases it. BufferQueue passes handles without copying pixel contents. Buffer counts depend on producer/consumer constraints and the rendering path, rather than one universal double-, triple-, or quadruple-buffer rule.

A queued buffer is not necessarily finished on the GPU. Synchronization fences express completion dependencies: a reader must respect outstanding writes, and a producer must respect outstanding reads before reuse. Composition may still produce a new output buffer; a queue that does not copy pixels does not imply that the entire pipeline never copies anything.

The Back Buffer / Frame Buffer illustration is a teaching model for avoiding concurrent overwrite of an image being displayed. It does not mean every VSync copies the back buffer into the front buffer. VSync coordinates app, SurfaceFlinger, and display timing. Those stages can overlap and wake at different offsets; the GPU does not simply finish each frame and wait for the same hardware interrupt.

Normal View animation and traversal are scheduled through the framework’s Choreographer, available since Android 4.1 / API 16. Apps typically use animation APIs or View.postOnAnimation() instead of simulating VSync with sleep(16).

Refresh faster than production: distinguish intended repetition from missed deadlines

Without an available new frame, the display system can keep presenting previous content. The original 58fps / 60Hz figure is only illustrative. How long each new image stays visible, and whether it misses its expected presentation time, tells us more about stutter than average FPS alone.

An intentionally lower content rate differs from an animation unexpectedly missing an intended update. The latter can cause stutter or latency, but should not generally be called flicker. GPU overload is not the only possible cause: main-thread blocking, scheduling delays, rendering, queueing, and composition can all affect the result.

Surface.setFrameRate(float, int), available since Android 11 / API 30, declares the content’s intended rate. It helps the system select a display mode, but does not guarantee a switch, produce frames for the app, or throttle the app to that rate. Normal UI still follows framework scheduling; video and custom renderers must also manage presentation timing.

On Android 12 / API 31+, use Perfetto FrameTimeline to compare expected and actual timelines and jank reasons, then correlate captured thread, GPU, and SurfaceFlinger evidence for the same frame. Detailed fence and scheduling tracks depend on the device and recording configuration. Choreographer callback counts are not counts of actually presented frames, and one code section exceeding 16ms is not a complete diagnosis.

Perf Matters

Keep calm, profile your code, and always remember, Perf Matters.

entry.title: Android Performance Patterns: Understanding Overdraw
entry.content:
Series Catalog:

  1. Overview of Android Performance Patterns
  2. Android Performance Patterns: Render Performance
  3. Android Performance Patterns: Understanding Overdraw
  4. Android Performance Patterns: Understanding VSYNC
  5. Android Performance Patterns: Profile GPU Rendering

Technical review (2026-10-13): The excerpts and diagrams are from the 2015 video. Overdraw remains a useful concept; the text now adds versioned color mappings, transparency exceptions, and conditions for removing backgrounds. Lighter overlay colors alone are not evidence of a performance gain.

Original video introduction:

One of the most problematic performance problems on Android is the easiest to create; thankfully, it’s also easy to fix.

OVERDRAW is a term used to describe how many times a pixel has been re-drawn in a single frame of rendering. It’s a troublesome issue, because in most cases, pixels that are overdrawn do not end up contributing to the final rendered image. As such, it amounts to wasted work for your GPU and CPU.

Fixing overdraw has everything to do with using the available on-device tools, like Show GPU Overdraw, and then adjusting your view hierarchy in order to reduce areas where it may be occurring.

What is Overdraw?

At the beginning of the video, the author uses a house painter as an analogy: painting a wall is hard work, and if you have to repaint it because you don’t like the color, the first layer was a waste of effort. Similarly, some drawing beneath a fully opaque region may make no contribution to the final image. When you try to balance high performance with perfect design, you often run into a common performance issue: Overdraw!

Overdraw means drawing the same pixel more than once within a frame. In the stacked-card example below, work beneath a fully opaque card may be unnecessary. Overlap is not always waste: translucent content, shadows, and antialiased edges still need the underlying color for blending. Removing that content would change the image. Clipping and renderer optimizations also affect the work performed. See the official explanation.

Overdraw is distinct from View inflation, measurement, and layout. A complex hierarchy may add CPU work, but a parent that draws no background does not necessarily increase pixel coverage. Compose recomposition counts cannot be converted into overdraw counts either.

Stacked layouts can be a double-edged sword: they look good, but may add repeated drawing. Start with redundant drawing that can be removed without changing the image, then measure whether it was a bottleneck.

Tracking Overdraw

In Developer options, find Debug GPU Overdraw and select the option that shows overdraw areas. The old screenshot calls it Show GPU Overdraw. Availability and labels vary by system and vendor. It mainly covers HWUI drawing paths; it is not a complete counter for every independent Surface or custom OpenGL/Vulkan renderer.

The default palette distinguishes extra draws from total draws, as shown in Android 4.4.4 OpenGLRenderer and Caches. The overlay blends with the original image, so its visible shade also depends on the underlying color:

  • Blue: 1x overdraw (pixel drawn 2 times)
  • Green: 2x overdraw (pixel drawn 3 times)
  • Light Red: 3x overdraw (pixel drawn 4 times)
  • Dark Red: 4x or more overdraw (pixel drawn 5 or more times)

Original colors mean no additional debug tint, not that the GPU did no work. Android 16 SkiaPipeline retains the default blue/green/light-red/dark-red mapping and provides an alternate palette for color-vision needs. It creates its count image by replaying drawing commands, rather than reading how many times GPU hardware actually shaded each pixel.

Reducing large, unnecessary red areas while preserving the image helps narrow the investigation. Blue is not a mandatory target, and red alone does not prove jank; transparency can legitimately require repeated drawing.

Root Causes of Overdraw

While overdraw often comes from overlapping views, developers should pay special attention to unnecessary backgrounds.

If the Window, root layout, and child layouts all draw the same background color, they may repeatedly cover large regions. The historical comparison below shows fewer green and red areas after redundant backgrounds were removed. The right-hand image still has tinted text and image regions; it is not zero overdraw, nor does it provide measured frame-time gains.

The original call replaces the Window background with a transparent color Drawable:

That does not remove the Drawable, and it is not a universal optimization switch. First use Layout Inspector to establish which elements draw backgrounds. Often you can retain one background for the page and remove redundant backgrounds that are fully covered. Do not remove every source of the page’s base color.

If the content fully and opaquely covers the Window’s background area in every relevant state, you can evaluate removing the Window background itself from the Activity. Window.setBackgroundDrawable has existed since API 1:

null does not configure a transparent window; it differs from a transparent ColorDrawable. See the Window API contract. Check the first frame, loading and empty states, transitions, resizing, and areas near system bars for exposed backgrounds, color changes, or flashes. On Android 12 / API 31+, the splash screen has its own configuration; this runtime call does not replace the launch theme.

Turn off overdraw tinting and other debug overlays before measuring again on the same device and scenario. On Android 12 / API 31+, compare affected frames with Perfetto FrameTimeline and correlate the captured thread, GPU, and SurfaceFlinger evidence. On older systems, use the trace data available. Less background drawing in the app does not automatically reduce SurfaceFlinger’s composition time.

Perf Matters

Keep calm, profile your code, and always remember, Perf Matters.

Appendix

For more in-depth reading on overdraw and its optimization, check out these two articles on my blog:

  • Android Overdraw Optimization: Basics
  • Android Overdraw Optimization: Practice

About Me && Blog

Below is my personal intro and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow professionals. “When three walk together, one can always be my teacher!”

entry.title: Android Performance Patterns: Render Performance
entry.content:
Series Catalog:

  1. Overview of Android Performance Patterns
  2. Android Performance Patterns: Render Performance
  3. Android Performance Patterns: Understanding Overdraw
  4. Android Performance Patterns: Understanding VSYNC
  5. Android Performance Patterns: Profile GPU Rendering

Technical review (2026-10-13): This is a study note from the 2015 video series. The Nexus 5 example and tool screenshots remain historical material. The original introduction uses 16ms as an approximation for 60Hz; the discussion below now clarifies refresh behavior, jank, and tool limitations.

Original video introduction:

Rendering performance is all about how fast you can draw your activity, and get it updated on the screen. Success here means your users feeling like your application is smooth and responsive, which means that you’ve got to get all your logic completed, and all your rendering done in 16ms or less, each and every frame. But that might be a bit more difficult than you think.

In this video, Colt McAnlis takes a look at what “rendering performance” means to developers, alongside some of the most common pitfalls that are ran into; and let’s not forget the important stuff: the tools that help you track down, and fix these issues before they become large problems.

Android Rendering Knowledge

When you think you’ve developed a world-changing app, your users might not agree. They might think your app is slow and laggy, failing to achieve the smoothness they expect, let alone changing the world. Straight into the bin! Hang on, it runs smoothly on my Nexus 5. How can it be slow? If you know anything about Android fragmentation, you’d know that many low-end phones don’t have the powerful processor and GPU of a Nexus 5, or the same clean stock Android installation.

If a large number of users complain that your app is laggy, don’t just blame their hardware. Sometimes the problem lies within the app itself, including rendering work or a blocked main thread. Measure first to identify the cause and choose a fix. Thus, knowing how Android rendering works is essential for any Android developer.

At 60Hz, display intervals are about 16.67ms. At 90Hz, 120Hz, and 144Hz, they are approximately 11.11ms, 8.33ms, and 6.94ms. Scheduling and the rendering pipeline also affect the app’s actual deadline. One function taking more or less than 16ms does not, by itself, prove that a frame missed its deadline or appeared smoothly.

Design vs Performance

Rendering issues come up often when building an app. Designers want something dazzling, but those animations and Views won’t run smoothly on every Android phone. That is the tradeoff we have to work with.

Drawing Principles

Android does not unconditionally redraw the entire Activity every 16ms. In the View system, invalidation, layout requests, and animations can drive another frame. ViewRootImpl schedules its traversal through Choreographer. A static interface with no pending update does not need to rerun drawing for the entire View tree simply because another refresh arrives. This demand-driven behavior already exists in Android 4.4.4 ViewRootImpl and Choreographer.

Hardware acceleration still needs CPU work for measurement, layout, and recording drawing commands; unchanged display lists can be reused. Android 5.0’s ThreadedRenderer delegates rendering to RenderThread. The GPU executes commands asynchronously, followed by SurfaceFlinger composition and presentation. The main thread finishing does not mean the frame is already on screen. See the hardware-accelerated drawing model.

The original diagram uses a simplified 60Hz model: a continuous animation appears smooth when successive frames meet their expected presentation times. Its 16ms labels are approximations, not universal thresholds.

If an update takes 24ms and misses its intended presentation opportunity, it may cause what we commonly call a dropped frame or jank.

When no new buffer is available, SurfaceFlinger can keep the previous buffer. The display has not necessarily stopped refreshing, and other layers may still update. See the SurfaceFlinger documentation.

In a simplified fixed-60Hz example that misses one presentation opportunity, old content remains for about 33.33ms instead of 16.67ms. Neither the diagram’s “34ms” nor the original text’s “32ms” is a precise measurement. Buffering, scheduling, GPU completion, and submission timing affect the actual outcome; “24ms” alone cannot tell you how many frames a particular device will miss.

Frame Drops

Frame drops are a core user experience issue. Users easily perceive the stuttering caused by dropped frames, especially during interactions like list scrolling or typing. Users will immediately complain, and the next step is often uninstalling your app. Understanding the causes of frame drops is critical.

Unfortunately, many things can cause frame drops, such as:

  • Triggering unnecessary measurement, layout, or drawing-command recording, adding CPU work.
  • Drawing pixels that will be covered by later content; the cost depends on clipping, transparency, and renderer optimizations.
  • Animations repeatedly triggering expensive layout or drawing. Animation count alone does not prove a CPU or GPU bottleneck.

Detection and Solution

Detecting and solving these issues depends heavily on your application architecture. Fortunately, we have many developer tools to help. Some tools can even trace down to specific lines of code or UI controls. These tools include but are not limited to:

Hierarchy Viewer

The old Hierarchy Viewer helps reveal unnecessary nesting in a View tree. Depth is a clue, not proof of jank or overdraw. The screenshot and Window → Open Perspective → Hierarchy View refer to historical tools. Their host, Android Device Monitor, was deprecated in Android Studio 3.1 and removed in 3.2; those launch instructions are obsolete.

Use Layout Inspector for debuggable View, Compose, or hybrid apps. It shows hierarchy, attributes, snapshots, and Compose recomposition/skip information. These explain structure; node counts and recomposition counts alone do not establish frame cost or missed deadlines.

On-Device Tools: Profile GPU Rendering, Show GPU Overdraw, GPU View Updates

These tools live in Developer options; their names and locations vary by Android version and vendor. From Android 4.2, enabling Developer options usually requires tapping Build number seven times in the device’s About screen. See the official instructions.

  • Profile GPU/HWUI Rendering displays rendering stages as bars, useful for spotting anomalies. Despite its name, it measures CPU-side stages and waits, not pure GPU execution time. It also does not cover every custom OpenGL/Vulkan rendering path. See the tool documentation.
  • Debug GPU Overdraw highlights repeated drawing of pixels in the rendering paths it covers. It does not directly measure frame latency or per-pixel execution cost; the next article covers it further.
  • Show GPU View Updates flashes updated regions in older versions. In Android 4.4.4 HardwareRenderer, debug.hwui.show_dirty_regions overlays a translucent red rectangle on dirty regions in some frames. No red flash does not mean software rendering on the CPU. The region might be unchanged, or the overlay might not be drawn in that frame. This is not a CPU/GPU classifier, and it is distinct from Show Surface Updates and Show Hardware Layer Updates.

TraceView

Traceview is a legacy method-trace viewer. The screenshot shows thread timelines and method statistics, not each frame’s presentation timeline. It can help find Java method hotspots, but does not describe the entire GPU workload, cross-process scheduling, or actual presentation, nor does it guarantee visibility into every native function.

Traceview is deprecated; Android Studio 3.2+ uses CPU Profiler for these .trace files. Method instrumentation adds overhead, while sampling can miss short-lived calls. Absolute timings from a recording are not automatically representative of an unprofiled run. See method tracing and profile types.

A practical workflow today is:

  1. Capture a system trace of a reproducible scrolling or animation scenario. On Android 12 / API 31+, Perfetto FrameTimeline compares expected and actual timelines and helps connect app frames, SurfaceFlinger, and jank reasons. Older systems and unsupported rendering paths do not automatically provide the same tracks.
  2. Examine the captured main-thread, RenderThread, scheduling, and GPU evidence for an affected frame. CPU work, lock waits, scheduling delays, and unfinished GPU work are different causes. A system trace does not automatically log every function.
  3. Re-run the same scenario and device with Macrobenchmark after the fix. FrameTimingMetric was added in AndroidX Benchmark 1.1.0, and frameOverrunMs requires API 31+. Follow the target-app configuration for a non-debuggable, profileable app; a Layout Inspector debugging session is not a performance baseline.

Perf Matters

Keep calm, profile your code, and always remember, Perf Matters.

Summary

The first video covers the basics of rendering performance, what can go wrong, and the tools for investigating it. It gets us through finding and locating a problem; fixing it is mostly left for practice. That is how this series works: learn to use the tools and understand what they show, then work out a fix for the app in front of you. There is no single fix for every app.

About Me && Blog

entry.title: Overview of Android Performance Patterns
entry.content:
Series Catalog:

  1. Overview of Android Performance Patterns
  2. Android Performance Patterns: Render Performance
  3. Android Performance Patterns: Understanding Overdraw
  4. Android Performance Patterns: Understanding VSYNC
  5. Android Performance Patterns: Profile GPU Rendering

In 2015, Google introduced the Android Performance Patterns short-video series. The original playlist is on YouTube; Google’s companion-course announcement also documents the series.

Technical review — 2026-10-13: The original 2015 motivation and viewing experience are retained. The videos remain useful background, while the old tools, Google+ resources, and fixed “16ms” guidance need the version context below.

Overdraw, VSYNC, and main-thread/RenderThread cooperation still matter, but the refresh interval is not always 16ms. It is about 16.67ms at 60Hz, 11.11ms at 90Hz, and 8.33ms at 120Hz. Use the system’s scheduling deadlines and trace data when judging actual frames instead of applying one fixed threshold to every device and scenario.

InvestigationCurrent entry point and conditions
View / Compose hierarchy and attributesUse Layout Inspector on debuggable apps. It can also show Compose recomposition/skipping; hierarchy inspection is not a frame-duration measurement
Quick rendering-stage and overdraw signalsDeveloper options provide Profile GPU/HWUI Rendering and Debug GPU Overdraw. The bars represent CPU-side rendering stages, not pure GPU execution time, and do not cover every custom rendering path. See the official guide
Frames missing their deadlinesPerfetto FrameTimeline requires Android 12 / API 31+. Relate frames to the thread, scheduling, and SurfaceFlinger tracks actually captured
Regressions during scrolling or transitionsMacrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric is available from AndroidX Benchmark 1.1.0. frameOverrunMs requires API 31+ and measures something different from frameDurationCpuMs

The old Android Device Monitor, which hosted Hierarchy Viewer and Traceview, was deprecated in Android Studio 3.1 and removed in 3.2. Use the current Profiler for method analysis and Layout Inspector for hierarchy inspection. For Macrobenchmark, follow the setup requirements: a release-like, non-debuggable, profileable target, with consistent device and scenario conditions.

Introduction quoted in the original 2015 article:

Android Performance Patterns is a collection of videos focused entirely on helping developers write faster, more performant Android Applications. On one side, it’s about peeling back the layers of the Android System, and exposing how things are working under the hood. On the other side, it’s about teaching you how the tools work, and what to look for in order to extract the right perf out of your app.

But at the end of the day, Android Performance Patterns is all about giving you the right resources at the right time to help make the fastest, smoothest, most awesome experience for your users. And that’s the whole point, right?

The videos explain Android performance in three to five minutes each. The speakers talk fast; before subtitles were available, they really tested my listening. Subtitles were available when this article was written; check each video’s current subtitle tracks rather than assuming complete coverage today.

While the videos are short, they are packed with information. A point the speaker passes over in one sentence can take a lot of reading to understand, or a while spent learning a debugging tool. This means the series doesn’t directly teach you “how to optimize your app” step-by-step; rather, it tells you what you need to know about Android performance so that you know which tools to use, what steps to take, and what goals to aim for.

I was studying Android performance at the time, so I watched the videos several times as soon as they came out. My first plan was to translate them into Chinese. After watching them again, I felt that a translation alone would leave too much unexplained: each topic could fill a blog post, sometimes several. That is what I decided to write.

In each article, I will first list the knowledge points covered in the video and then explain them one by one. Some debugging tools might be detailed in separate posts due to their complexity.

Another person who inspired me to write this series is Hu Kai. His blog http://hukai.me/android-performance-patterns was among the first to translate this content into Chinese. His beautiful layout and high-quality translation helped the content spread widely. He is also the initiator of the android-training-course-in-chinese project on GitHub. I highly respect his passion for sharing. If you are not an Android developer or are not interested in technical details, you can simply read his overview for a quick understanding.

Below are some resources related to the Android Performance Patterns series:

  • YouTube Playlist: Android Performance Patterns
  • The author’s Google+ profile and the series community are obsolete. Consumer Google+ closed on 2019-04-02. See the official shutdown notice.
  • Hu Kai’s blog URL is retained as a historical reference; it could not be reopened in this review. His Android Training translation repository remains accessible, but older translations are not current API contracts.

OK, let us start!!!

entry.title: Android Memory Optimization (3) - Viewing Original Bitmaps in MAT
entry.content:
This is the final article in our MAT series, detailing how to reconstruct original images from memory snapshots to debug leaks.

  1. Android Memory Optimization (1) - Introduction to MAT
  2. Android Memory Optimization (2) - Advanced MAT Usage
  3. Android Memory Optimization (3) - Viewing Original Bitmaps in MAT

Technical review — 2026-10-13: This historical technique depends on the Bitmap implementation. The original screenshots are retained. The field is checked against AOSP android-4.4.4_r2; Android 8.0 / API 26 explains the native-pixel change. Updated GIMP 3.2.6 import settings and a current debugging alternative follow.

When investigating image-related memory problems in MAT, knowing which image a Bitmap contains makes the object much easier to connect to an app feature. “Original image” here means the pixels held by the runtime Bitmap, not the downloaded JPEG/PNG, its compression settings, or EXIF. MAT can show what retains the object; a large Bitmap alone does not establish a leak.

This workflow requires the dump to contain the pixel array. A Java wrapper and a native address alone cannot reconstruct pixels missing from the dump.

1. Exporting Raw Bitmap Data

Select a Bitmap in MAT’s Dominator Tree and inspect its fields:

The original screenshot shows mWidth = 1536, mHeight = 2560, mBuffer, mNativeBitmap, and mIsPremultiplied. Width and height are pixel dimensions, not screen dp or the size of the displaying View.

AOSP android-4.4.4_r2 Bitmap.java contains this hidden implementation field:

It is not a stable SDK contract. Even that release supports native-backed Bitmaps with mBuffer == null. In android-8.0.0_r1, the implementation uses mNativePtr and NativeAllocationRegistry instead; the old export recipe is not universal.

If mBuffer references a byte[], follow the field to that array instance, then select Copy → Save Value to File. Do not export only the Bitmap wrapper, an address string, or the whole table. MAT’s copy/export rules write a single primitive array as binary, while other objects may produce only a printable value.

The .data extension helps GIMP choose its raw loader; it does not convert the pixel format. Saving as .raw likewise changes neither channel order nor bit depth. Keep the original export and record:

ParameterWhat to verify
Width and heightActual pixel dimensions: 1536×2560 in this screenshot
Config / bytes per pixelARGB_8888 uses four bytes per pixel and eight bits per channel; RGB_565 and other layouts need different settings
rowBytesFirst-pixel offset and bytes per row, including padding
Channels and byte orderRGBA, BGRA, or another arrangement; the ARGB_8888 name alone is insufficient
Alpha and color spaceWhether values are premultiplied and how the importer interprets them
Array length and valid rangeWhether export is complete and includes unused capacity after reuse

For tightly packed four-byte pixels with no spare allocation capacity, the pictured dimensions require 1536 × 2560 × 4 = 15,728,640 bytes (15 MiB). Retained Size in the Inspector is not the raw-file length. If data is missing or the layout is unknown, check the export and pixel metadata first; the image cannot be reliably reconstructed without them.

2. Opening the Raw Data

Linux

Here I used GIMP’s raw-data importer. This is the interface from that time:

The screenshot shows the old parameter dialog. Replace its 350×350 values with the earlier Bitmap’s actual dimensions. For data confirmed as tightly packed RGBA, eight bits per channel, and no header, choose File → Open, and manually select Raw image data under Select File Type if needed. See the GIMP 3.0 file dialog.

The GIMP 3.2.6 raw loader provides these settings:

  • Pixel format: RGBA 8-bit, corresponding to the older RGB Alpha choice.
  • Data type: Unsigned Integer. Java’s signed byte representation does not make the pixel channels signed values.
  • Planar configuration: Contiguous, for interleaved per-pixel channels.
  • Width / Height: the actual dimensions, 1536 / 2560 in this example.
  • Offset: 0 only when the first pixel starts at byte zero of the headerless export.

These settings apply only to that layout. BGRA data needs the appropriate channel reordering. If rowBytes exceeds width × 4, handle each row’s padding rather than reading it as pixels in the next row. Without the layout metadata, the reconstruction is underdetermined.

Premultiplied alpha also matters. Android’s copyPixelsToBuffer() copies stored pixels as-is, including premultiplication. Interpreting them as straight-alpha RGBA can darken translucent edges. For an eight-bit premultiplied channel and alpha above zero, round(premultipliedChannel × 255 / alpha), clamped to 0–255, approximately recovers the straight value. At zero alpha, the original color cannot be recovered. The screenshot’s mIsPremultiplied is a clue to investigate alongside Config and runtime version. When the running app can encode the Bitmap as PNG, the workflow below is usually more direct.

Mac & Windows

My recommendation at the time was to use GIMP across platforms, so there was only one set of steps to learn. It was free and had the features needed here.

GIMP also runs on macOS and Windows; the operating system does not determine the raw pixel layout. The official downloads page lists platform options and 3.2.6 (2026-09-10) as the stable release at this review.

In Photoshop, choose Photoshop Raw, not Camera Raw. For confirmed tightly packed RGBA8 data, specify the actual dimensions, four channels, eight bits per channel, interleaved channels, and Header = 0 when headerless. The earlier “32-bit depth” instruction was misleading: RGBA8 totals 32 bits per pixel, while Photoshop’s 32 Bits/Channel uses 32 bits for each channel, or 96 bits for RGB alone. See Photoshop bit depth and Raw parameters.

The fourth channel must also be applied appropriately as alpha/transparency. Photoshop does not eliminate the need to handle stride, channel order, or premultiplication.

Android 8.0+: When mBuffer Is Absent

From API 26, Bitmap pixels live in the native heap, and Config.HARDWARE involves graphics memory. See the official version history. Inspect Bitmap wrappers, BitmapDrawables, and cache ownership in Android Studio, then combine that with native-allocation or image-library cache evidence. An address cannot supply pixels absent from a Java HPROF.

If your own debug code holds a valid Bitmap, let Android encode it as PNG instead of guessing raw channel layout. This complete helper class targets an API 26+ debugging scenario. The caller provides a writable file and keeps the Bitmap from being recycled or modified during export:

Run it on a worker thread and handle failures. The compress() contract notes that encoding can take seconds. PNG ignores the quality argument, but the output is still a new encoding, not the original source file; it also does not promise a byte-exact recovery of wide-gamut or high-bit-depth content. With only an offline HPROF and no pixel data or accessible live Bitmap, report the actual limit: ownership can be analyzed, but the image cannot be reconstructed.

About Me && Blog

Below are personal introduction and related links. I hope to communicate more with everyone in the industry. If three people walk together, there must be one who can be my teacher!

entry.title: Android Memory Optimization (2) - Advanced MAT Usage
entry.content:
This is the second article in our MAT series, focusing on advanced techniques for analyzing memory issues in Java and Android applications.

  1. Android Memory Optimization (1) - Introduction to MAT
  2. Android Memory Optimization (2) - Advanced MAT Usage
  3. Android Memory Optimization (3) - Viewing Original Bitmaps in MAT

Technical review — 2026-10-13: The 2015 screenshots are retained; concepts and query descriptions were checked against MAT 1.17.0 documentation. The old Studio conversion/GC menus are historical. Reference directions, unreachable-object interpretation, and leak criteria are corrected below, with missing steps restored.

For capture, see the introductory article: obtain a heap dump in Android Studio Profiler with debuggable / complete data, then export to MAT as needed. LeakCanary can support automated tests, but the ordinary leakcanary-android dependency belongs in debug builds. The official 2.14 release-analysis workflow is still marked experimental; adding LeakCanary is not a generic production-capture strategy. See UI-test integration and LeakCanary for releases.

Characteristics of Java Memory Leaks

  • A typical Java memory leak is an object that is still reachable but no longer useful.
  • Compare its intended lifetime with the actual ownership path, rather than judging only its size or instance count.
  • Recreating reusable objects adds allocation and GC work. If old objects are collected normally, that is allocation waste, not necessarily a leak. An oversized legitimate allocation can also cause OOM.

Advanced MAT Techniques

Dumping Memory with Android Studio

The screenshot shows an early Android Studio capture UI:

Use the current heap-dump workflow: select Analyze Memory Usage (Heap Dump), inspect instances and references, then export .hprof from Past Recordings. Debug.dumpHprofData() can capture at a chosen point in app code, but dumping introduces pauses and overhead; it is not cost-free continuous sampling.

Convert Android-format HPROF with hprof-conv when the destination analyzer requires it, keeping input and output filenames different. The historical right-click conversion command is not a menu guaranteed in every Studio version.

Manual GC is neither mandatory nor a guarantee. Runtime.gc() requests a best-effort collection; it does not promise a snapshot with no unreachable objects afterward. Comparable post-GC snapshots can help examine lasting retention. For short-lived allocation churn, collecting first can remove useful evidence. The old button is shown below:

Unreachable Objects

An object with no path from ordinary GC Roots in the parsed graph is considered unreachable. It may no longer be needed but not yet collected. Dump format, parsing options, and configured object discarding also affect this result, so it does not prove that no GC previously ran.

By default, MAT removes these objects from its main parsed graph while retaining a summary of class names, counts, and shallow sizes. The Unreachable Objects Histogram has no complete per-object reference graph behind it. See the official explanation.

The old Calculate Retained Size menu distinguishes the quick lower-bound estimate, Minimum, from Precise calculation for an object set:

The zero Retained Heap values in this old summary table do not mean that the objects occupy no memory, or that every unreachable object must always have zero retained size. Parsing with the objects retained creates different analysis conditions.

To inspect their references, follow MAT’s reparse procedure:

  1. Close the snapshot.
  2. Use Heap Dump History → Delete Index Files for that snapshot, retaining the original HPROF.
  3. Enable Preferences → Memory Analyzer → Keep unreachable objects.
  4. Reopen the dump and let MAT reparse it.
  5. Run Java Basics → GC Roots, select Unreachable Objects, and run Show Retained Set.

MAT introduces special unreachable roots to keep those objects available for analysis. These are analyzer-created roots, not real strong-reference owners in the app.

Histogram Analysis

Histogram usually aggregates instance counts and shallow heap by class. It is a useful starting point for investigating large consumers or unexpected counts.

  • Sort by actual columns such as object count or Shallow Heap. A Percentage column in one view is not universal.
  • Group by class loader or package to narrow the investigation; Dominator Tree also offers grouping.
  • Repeat the same entry/exit scenario and capture comparable states. Growth may reflect cache warm-up, pending work, or a leak; inspect lifetimes and ownership paths.
  • Histogram shows classes and counts; Dominator Tree shows domination. A dominator-tree edge need not be an actual field reference. Use incoming/outgoing references for the object graph.

For a growing class, inspect concrete instances, determine which should have gone away, and find what retains them. Count growth alone does not prove a leak.

Thread Information

MAT shows thread information present in the snapshot. Stack and local-variable availability depends on the dump format and parser settings. See Thread Overview.

The original screenshots suggest two lines of investigation:

  1. Threads retaining substantial heap. Inspect their tasks, local references, and context. Retained heap is not the thread’s total native-stack allocation.

  2. An unexpected thread count. Check names, pool sizing, and task completion. Many threads alone are not sufficient evidence of a leak.

Context Menus and Help

Right-click a result item to find analysis options:

Use Search Queries or Query Browser to find a command and read its description and arguments; its fixed position in an old menu is unimportant.

These are MAT analysis queries, not necessarily configured SQL statements. MAT separately supports OQL, an SQL-like language for querying heap objects, classes, and fields.

Here are the options we use most often, with their meanings from the List Objects documentation:

  • List Objects → with incoming references: Objects that reference the selected object.
  • List Objects → with outgoing references: Objects referenced by the selected object.
  • Path to GC Roots → exclude all phantom/weak/soft etc. references: Apply the preset’s non-strong referent exclusions to find retaining root paths. A path establishes reachability; the object must also have outlived its usefulness to justify a leak diagnosis. It does not establish that OOM has occurred.
  • Other exclusion presets or custom exclusions: Inspect the actual fields/types excluded. Excluding weak/soft references alone does not remove every other non-strong path. See the query arguments.
  • Merge Shortest Paths to GC Roots: Merge shortest paths for one or more objects to expose shared owners. It does not enumerate all retaining paths; after removing a shortest path, other paths may remain. See Merge Shortest Paths.

Debugging Bitmaps

Bitmap memory depends on decoded pixel dimensions, configuration, and actual allocation, not just whether the screen is “2K.” A tightly packed 2560 × 1440 ARGB_8888 image needs 14,745,600 pixel bytes, about 14.06 MiB. Reused allocation capacity can also exceed the current image’s requirements. On API 19+, inspect getAllocationByteCount(). See the Bitmap API.

Exporting a Bitmap’s byte[] from MAT is a conditional historical technique: the snapshot must contain the pixels, and their layout must be understood. From Android 8.0 / API 26, pixels reside in the native heap, so not every Bitmap has a directly recoverable Java-heap array. The original process is retained in Viewing Original Bitmaps in MAT; check its version and data requirements before using it.

Debugging ArrayLists

For an ArrayList instance, List Objects → with outgoing references reveals its backing storage and fields:

Expanding the backing array exposes the internal storage, but reading it element by element is awkward. Its capacity can exceed the list’s logical element count, and field names or layout may change between runtimes. For recognized implementations, use Java Collections → Extract List Values:

The result presents the elements more directly:

The query depends on MAT recognizing that collection layout; it does not automatically support every custom container. When extraction is unsupported, inspect the actual class and fields. See collection queries.

Big Drops In Dominator Tree

Open Query Browser / Search Queries, find Big Drops in Dominator Tree, and run it on the current snapshot. See the query description.

The query looks for substantial drops in retained size across dominator-tree levels. It helps find an owner retaining many objects and may also show large arrays. Accumulation Point is a candidate concentration of memory; Dominator identifies the associated dominator, not necessarily a direct Java-field owner.

Inspect candidate contents and capacity, then follow incoming references and paths to GC Roots to find their owners. Judge them against the intended lifecycle: a large cache may be deliberate, while a small retained object can still leak. Big Drops provides a starting point rather than an automatic diagnosis.

entry.title: Android Memory Optimization (1) - Getting Started with MAT
entry.content:
This is the first article in the series on using the MAT tool. This series consists of three articles, detailing how to use MAT to analyze memory issues, whether they are Java application memory issues or Android application memory issues:

  1. Android Memory Optimization (1) - Getting Started with MAT
  2. Android Memory Optimization (2) - Advanced MAT Usage
  3. Android Memory Optimization (3) - Opening Original Bitmap Images in MAT

Technical review — 2026-10-13: The tutorial and historical screenshots are retained. MAT’s heap-analysis concepts remain useful, while the Eclipse/DDMS capture workflow is obsolete. Installation requirements now reference MAT 1.17.0 (2026-06-10; Java 21+ for the standalone tool). The ART, Bitmap, retained-size, and reference explanations have been corrected.

Start with a Java/Kotlin heap dump in Android Studio Profiler, then export to MAT when its analysis is useful. LeakCanary can help find Android memory leaks. MAT mainly explains why managed-heap objects remain reachable; process-wide memory and native allocations also require tools such as dumpsys meminfo, native allocation recording, or Perfetto heapprofd on Android 10+. On user builds, heapprofd requires a debuggable or profileable app; it cannot arbitrarily profile other apps.

Introduction to MAT

What is MAT?

MAT (Memory Analyzer Tool) is an Eclipse-based Java heap analyzer. It helps us find memory leaks and reduce memory use by showing how much space objects occupy and which references keep them alive. Its reports give us places to start investigating.

MAT is available as an Eclipse plugin or a standalone Eclipse RCP application. The standalone tool does not require a full Eclipse IDE, but it still needs a compatible Java runtime. Whether an Android HPROF needs conversion depends on its format and the analyzer’s support, not on which MAT installation method you chose.

Download and Installation of MAT Tool

The current entry point is Eclipse MAT Downloads. At this review, it offers 1.17.0, with Java 21 as the standalone runtime minimum and separate OS/CPU-architecture downloads. That is a requirement for running MAT, not for the Android app being analyzed.

The download and Eclipse installation screenshots below come from the MAT 1.4 era and illustrate the three installation choices:

  • Update Site: For MAT 1.17.0, enter https://download.eclipse.org/mat/1.17.0/update-site/ in Eclipse’s Install New Software dialog to install online.

  • Archived Update Site: Install an offline package through the same Eclipse dialog. Each update needs a new package download; the online Update Site can fetch updates directly.
  • Stand-alone Eclipse RCP Applications: Run MAT without installing the Eclipse IDE. This is useful when Android Studio is your main IDE. The Android HPROF conversion step is explained below.

After downloading and installing, you can use MAT for actual operations.

Common Memory and Resource-Management Problems in Android (Java)

Android Memory

Before opening MAT, it helps to know how Android allocates memory and what can keep an object alive. The following examples show what to watch for in code.

Android apps normally run in their own processes, and an app can configure multiple processes; one app does not necessarily mean one runtime instance. Dalvik describes the early runtime. ART is the default from Android 5.0 / API 21, as documented in the ART compatibility guide.

A process has a Java-heap capacity limit, and further allocations can fail with OutOfMemoryError. The system may also reclaim processes under memory pressure. Neither event means the system has diagnosed a memory leak: a legitimate but oversized allocation can cause OOM, while useless retained objects can leak well before that limit. Excess memory usage can pressure the whole system, so its effects are not necessarily confined to the allocating process. See Android memory management.

Common Cases of Improper Memory Usage

Cursor Not Closed After Querying Database

Close a Cursor that you own when finished, including on failure paths. A Cursor can hold resources such as CursorWindow; a small result set is not a reason to skip cleanup. Conversely, do not close a Cursor that another component still owns and uses.

This method demonstrates a query, a null-result policy, and cleanup in finally. The caller supplies resolver, uri, and the required column projection. Queries may involve I/O and should run in an appropriate background context:

Do not hide close failures in an empty catch block or silently interpret a null Cursor as a successful zero-row result. See the Cursor contract.

Not Using Cached convertView When Constructing Adapter

For a ListView backed by a BaseAdapter, rows come from this method:

ListView asks the adapter for enough Views to fill the visible area. As the list scrolls, a row that has moved off screen can be reused for one entering the screen. It reaches getView() as the second argument, convertView. When no recycled View is available, as during initial creation, this argument is null.
Creating a fresh View every time increases allocation, layout, and GC work. If those objects can be reclaimed, however, it is allocation churn rather than evidence of a leak or unlimited memory growth. A reused View must have its current data and state rebound to avoid showing a previous item’s content.

This BaseAdapter method fragment assumes one item type using simple_list_item_1, with getItem(position) supplying the displayed text:

Both new and reused rows are bound. Heterogeneous lists must implement getItemViewType() / getViewTypeCount() correctly instead of casting arbitrary recycled Views to one class. See Adapter.getView(). With RecyclerView, likewise distinguish ViewHolder creation from binding.

Bitmap Cleanup Depends on Version and Ownership

“Always recycle a Bitmap when done” is not a universal rule. Pixel storage changed across releases: native memory through Android 2.3.3 / API 10; the managed heap on Android 3.0–7.1 / API 11–25; native heap again from Android 8.0 / API 26. See Bitmap memory management.

The old recommendation to use recycle() carefully addressed API 10 and earlier. Manual recycling still requires clear ownership and certainty that no View, cache, or task will draw the Bitmap again. Drawing a recycled Bitmap fails. Follow the ownership rules of any image library or reuse pool managing it.

Assigning one variable to null removes only that reference. Other strong references may keep the Bitmap alive; becoming collectible does not guarantee immediate GC or an immediate drop in process RSS. On API 26+, the Java wrapper’s shallow size also does not represent the full pixel allocation.

Releasing References to Objects

These reference relationships are easier to follow with examples. Let’s look at two.

Example A: The old example stored work data in Activity.obj and posted a Handler callback to process it. If the Activity no longer needs that field, let the callback capture a local variable instead:

These are Activity method fragments; initObj() / useObj() stand for the example’s existing business methods. This Handler belongs exclusively to the Activity. post() does not create a background thread: this callback runs on the main thread and must not perform lengthy work there.

The callback retains its data until it finishes, and calling an Activity instance method also retains the Activity. Cleanup here removes pending work from the dedicated Handler. On a shared Handler, cancel by Runnable or token to avoid removing another owner’s tasks. Cancellation does not interrupt a callback already running. Moving data from a field to a local variable shortens one retention path; it is not a general Activity-leak fix. See Handler.

Example B:
Suppose we want to listen to the telephone service in the system to obtain some information (such as signal strength, etc.) on the lock screen (LockScreen), we can define a PhoneStateListener object in the LockScreen and register it to the TelephonyManager service. For the LockScreen object, a LockScreen object is created when the lock screen interface needs to be displayed, and we want the object to become collectible once the interface no longer needs it.

If the registration retains the listener, and the listener references LockScreen through a field or inner class, the screen can stay alive after it disappears. Whether that causes OOM, and which process is affected, depends on the actual reference graph and execution context; a system_process crash is not inevitable.

For the old API, unregister the same listener with listen(listener, PhoneStateListener.LISTEN_NONE). PhoneStateListener was deprecated in API 31; use TelephonyCallback for new code and pair registration with unregisterTelephonyCallback(callback). Individual callbacks have their own permission requirements. See PhoneStateListener and TelephonyManager.

When a longer-lived owner retains an object that is no longer useful, remove that ownership path or subscription. Nulling a variable inside the shorter-lived object alone does not remove incoming references.

Others

Pair cleanup with the lifecycle in which a resource is acquired. For a listener needed only while a screen is visible, onStart() / onStop() can be an appropriate pair; Activity-instance resources follow the instance lifetime. Process termination does not guarantee onDestroy(), so critical user data must not depend on that callback for persistence. See the Activity lifecycle.

Using MAT for Memory Debugging

Obtaining HPROF File

An HPROF snapshot records objects, classes, and references. An ordinary Android heap dump mainly answers which objects are alive at that moment; it usually does not provide the timestamp and full allocation stack for every allocation. Record allocation activity separately when investigating how memory was allocated.

Current Entry Point: Android Studio Profiler

Follow Capture a heap dump: select Analyze Memory Usage (Heap Dump) and run the target as debuggable / complete data, then reproduce and capture. Inspect instances, Retained Size, Fields, and References, and export .hprof from Past Recordings. A profileable app does not automatically provide the same complete heap-dump data.

Capture pauses the app and temporarily needs additional memory. Compare snapshots under consistent scenarios while accounting for GC timing. A large object or a reference path alone does not establish a leak.

Historical Entry Point: Eclipse / DDMS

The screenshot below shows the old workflow. Android Device Monitor was deprecated in Android Studio 3.1 and removed in 3.2; a new installation need not provide these DDMS buttons. Historically, select the process under Devices and click Dump HPROF file. An Eclipse setup with the corresponding integration could convert the file and open it in MAT:

Export Format and Conversion

When an analyzer does not support Android-format HPROF, use the documented hprof-conv workflow to produce Java SE HPROF. Input and output must be different files:

Replace the example tool path with an existing installation, retain the original, and open mat-converted.hprof in MAT. If the installed SDK lacks the tool, check available versions or continue in Android Studio. Renaming an extension does not convert the format, and an already-compatible dump needs no additional conversion.

Introduction to MAT Main Interface

The screenshots here show the Overview page after importing a dump.

  • Open the converted hprof file:

If the first one is selected, a report will be generated. This is fine.

  • Select OverView interface:

We need to pay attention to the Actions area below

  • Histogram: Lists objects in memory, the number of objects, and size

  • Dominator Tree: Organizes objects by domination, commonly using Retained Heap to locate major retainers. Its edges need not be actual field references.

  • Top Consumers: Lists the largest objects graphically

  • Duplicate Classes: Finds classes with the same name loaded multiple times, useful for investigating class loaders. It does not automatically diagnose all memory leaks. A Leak Suspects report also supplies leads rather than a definitive diagnosis. See Duplicate Classes.

Generally, Histogram and Dominator Tree are the most commonly used.

Introduction to Some Concepts in MAT

To understand MAT’s list information, the concepts of Shallow heap, Retained Heap, and GC Root must be understood.

3.3.1 Shallow heap

Shallow size measures an object’s own managed-heap footprint, excluding referenced objects. Headers, primitive fields, reference fields, runtime layout, and alignment affect it. Object arrays hold references; primitive arrays hold their elements. Java fields are not all references, and Java byte[] / char[] arrays are not native allocations.

A Histogram row’s Shallow Heap aggregates the instances of that class. Sorting is selectable, and the leading types depend on the snapshot rather than always being byte[] or char[]. See MAT’s size definitions.

3.3.2 Retained Heap

The retained set of X contains X and the objects reachable from GC Roots only through X. Retained heap sums the shallow sizes of that set. It describes retention in the current object graph, not all native memory or process RSS.

If A and B are independently reachable from GC Roots and both reference array D, removing A does not make D unreachable. D therefore does not belong to A’s individual retained set, or B’s. This is shared ownership rather than a failure of the metric. If D has no other root path, removing the set {A, B} makes it unreachable. Run a Retained Set query for selected objects; neither summing individual retained sizes nor choosing Group by package automatically gives the precise retained size of the group.

Dominator Tree has a specific rule: X dominates Y only when every path from the roots to Y passes through X. A tree parent is its children’s immediate dominator. In a diamond where only A connects the roots to B and C, and both B and C point to D, A dominates B, C, and D; all three can be its direct children. The graph’s actual references have not been changed, and tree edges are not Java field references. See the dominator definition.

For actual references, right-click and choose List Objects:

  • with outgoing references: objects referenced by the selected object.
  • with incoming references: objects that reference the selected object.

To better understand Retained Heap, an example is cited below for illustration:

Treat objects in memory as nodes in the figure below, and objects reference each other. There is a special node GC Roots here, which is the starting point of the reference chain:

Starting from obj1, the blue nodes in the above figure represent objects that can only be accessed directly or indirectly through obj1. Because obj3 can be accessed via GC Roots, obj3 in the left figure is not a blue node; while in the right figure it is blue because it is already included in the retained set.
So for the left figure, the retained size of obj1 is the sum of shallow sizes of obj1, obj2, obj4;
The retained size of the right figure is the sum of shallow sizes of obj1, obj2, obj3, obj4.
The retained size of obj2 can be calculated in the same way.

GC Root

GC Roots are starting points for reachability analysis, such as active-thread local references, JNI references, or runtime-retained classes. Their types depend on the runtime and dump format; “the JVM itself is a GC Root” is not a useful definition. MAT can also use special root types to retain otherwise-unreachable objects in its analysis, so inspect the reported root type. See MAT GC Roots.

An object without a retaining path may become collectible, but GC determines when collection happens. Unreachability does not mean the memory has immediately returned to the OS. Strong, soft, weak, and phantom references must also be distinguished when reading paths.

Some Useful Views in MAT

Thread Overview

Thread Overview shows thread information available in the snapshot. Stacks and local variables depend on the dump; this is not a live thread monitor:

Group

Histogram and Dominator Tree offer several grouping options, with different defaults. Group by package makes it easier to find your app’s classes and see which packages use the most memory.

Path to GC Root

On a certain entry in the Histogram or Dominator Tree, right-click to view its GC Root Path:

Reference types affect retention; their relative strengths do not establish a fixed collection schedule:

  • Strong Reference: An object strongly reachable from GC Roots is not garbage. Removing just one strong reference may not change that.
  • SoftReference: The collector decides when to clear it in response to memory demand. Sufficient free memory does not guarantee indefinite retention. Android recommends a capacity-controlled LruCache for most caches instead of relying on soft-reference timing.
  • WeakReference: The collector clears relevant weak references when it processes a weakly reachable object. This is not synchronous with losing a particular strong reference. An object that is still softly reachable is not yet weakly reachable.
  • PhantomReference: get() always returns null; a ReferenceQueue can support collection-related notification and cleanup. It does not replace explicit close() or guarantee timely work after finalize().

For a strong-reference leak, usually start by excluding weak/soft/phantom referent paths, then inspect the full graph as needed. with all references includes non-strong paths, so not every displayed path is evidence that GC is being prevented. See the Path to GC Roots arguments.

The historical screenshot below shows Path to GC Roots → with all references:

Reference Documents

  1. Eclipse MAT downloads and runtime requirements
  2. MAT: Shallow and Retained Heap
  3. MAT: Dominator Tree
  4. Android Studio: Capture a heap dump
  5. Android: Bitmap memory management

entry.title: Android Performance Case Study Follow-up
entry.content:
Introduction

This is an annotated edition of Android Performance Case Study Follow-up by Romain Guy. The first-person case narrative below belongs to the original author.

Technical review — 2026-10-13: The 2015 Falcon Pro 3 / Moto X 2014 case is retained. Android Device Monitor, which hosted Tracer for OpenGL ES and Hierarchy Viewer, was deprecated in Android Studio 3.1 and removed in 3.2. The old workflow is historical; an Android 12+ Perfetto workflow is added below. The original website could not be reopened during this review; the technical corrections use the linked official documentation and versioned source.

Case study

Two years ago, I published Android Performance Case Study to help Android developers understand the tools and techniques needed to identify, track, and optimize performance bottlenecks.

That article used the Twitter client Falcon Pro as a case study. Its developer, Joaquim Vergès, was kind enough to let me use his app as an example and quickly addressed the issues I found. Fast forward to recently: Joaquim was building Falcon Pro 3 from scratch. Before its release, he contacted me about a scrolling performance issue. Once again, I had to analyze it without access to the source code.

Joaquim had already exhausted most tools. He confirmed that Overdraw wasn’t the culprit and suspected that his use of ViewPager (the old Support Library version; see the current AndroidX reference) was the cause. He sent over these screenshots:

Joaquim used the built-in GPU profiling tool to identify dropped frames. The left screenshot shows the timeline scrolling without a ViewPager; the right shows it with one (captured on a 2014 Moto X). The problem was stark.

My first thought was to check if the ViewPager was abusing hardware layers, as it looked like the system was performing a layer update every frame during scrolling. However, the hardware layers updates debugging tool didn’t show much. I inspected the layout with Hierarchy Viewer, and to my surprise (or rather, disappointment for a quick fix), the ViewPager was behaving correctly.

Then I turned to another powerful but less-used tool, Tracer for OpenGL ES. It recorded application GLES calls and, with framebuffer readback enabled, could show the progressive frame images. This describes the old GLES rendering path, not a GPU timer covering every modern rendering backend. See the historical tool documentation.

Historical workflow — Android 4.3 onward: Reordering and merging drawing commands made grouping them by View harder. This switch is confirmed in AOSP android-4.4.4_r2 Properties.h; it disables the old HWUI draw deferral before the app starts:

Record the original value, then restore it and restart the app after inspection. If it was unset, false restores the normal path. Disabling an optimization changes the workload: do not use those timings as a performance baseline or assume the property applies to current Android releases.

Reading old GL traces: Click a blue draw call and the Details panel shows the framebuffer after that call. Clicking through them in order lets me watch the frame being built; that is usually how I analyze it. Uploads, state changes, and waits can also be expensive, so other calls cannot simply be ignored when investigating cost. The displayed Wall Time / Thread Time is not pure GPU execution time.

After scrolling through Falcon Pro for a bit, I examined the GL trace. I was surprised to find many SaveLayer/ComposeLayer groups. These describe drawing into an offscreen layer and compositing it back, not thread-blocking instructions named SaveLayer.

These groups indicate an offscreen drawing target. Canvas.saveLayer() redirects drawing there until a balancing restore() composites it back. That is different from a retained View hardware layer configured through setLayerType(LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE, ...). The saveFlags overloads were deprecated in API 26; the overloads without that argument have been available since API 21. See the Canvas reference.

For the old hardware-accelerated path discussed here, a typical combination was:

  • A translucent View alpha: 0 < alpha < 1.
  • onSetAlpha(int) returning false, leaving alpha handling to the framework.
  • No configured View layer: getLayerType() returning LAYER_TYPE_NONE.
  • hasOverlappingRendering() returning true.

The Android 4.4.4 View implementation provides the historical context. These conditions explain the example; they do not imply an identical temporary-layer path on every Android release.

Chet and I have discussed why to use alpha with care. Offscreen rendering can add render-target changes, storage, and compositing work. On the Moto X 2014 in this case, that made the layers worth investigating. Vendor names such as Adreno, SGX, or Nvidia alone do not predict the cost on a current GPU; the hardware, driver, rendering backend, and content all matter.

So, what was creating these layers? Tracer provided the answer. In the image above, the GL commands in the SaveLayer group were rendering a small circle. Let’s look at the app:

See the circles at the top? Those are ViewPager indicators. Joaquim was using a third-party library to draw them. Interestingly, the current page was indicated by a solid white circle, while others were a “grayish” white. The library was achieving this “gray” by drawing white circles and then calling setAlpha() on the View to make them semi-transparent.

Solutions

There are several ways to address this while preserving the intended appearance.

1. Draw the inactive color directly

Keep the View’s alpha at 1 and draw the dot with the appropriate Paint color or alpha. An opaque gray can replace translucent white only when the background and intended color make them equivalent. They are not interchangeable over a changing background.

2. Report non-overlapping drawing accurately

hasOverlappingRendering() is available from API 16. A View that draws only one dot, with no overlapping background or foreground, can override it as follows:

This lets the framework apply alpha to individual drawing operations instead of compositing the content as a group. It describes overlap within the View’s own drawing, not whether the View intersects a neighboring View. Returning false when content actually overlaps can change the color or opacity at intersections. See the API contract.

3. Handle alpha inside the custom View

The argument of onSetAlpha(int alpha) is already an integer from 0 to 255. This method fragment belongs in a custom dot View; indicatorPaint is the initialized Paint also used to draw its only dot in onDraw():

Returning true makes the View responsible for applying opacity to all its drawing. Do not omit other content or overwrite the alpha with a later setColor(). The Chinese edition’s paint.setAlpha((int) alpha * 255) was incorrect: a 0–1 float such as getAlpha() needs multiplication before conversion, (int) (alpha * 255). The integer received by onSetAlpha() needs no multiplication.

For this single-dot View, the second option is straightforward; pre-API-16 versions require another color or drawing approach. I suspect Joaquim may already have replaced the library with his own indicator.

I hope this post illustrates how seemingly “innocent” or “safe” operations can hide major performance pitfalls. Never assume—always verify, measure, and trace.

2026 update: investigating the same issue today

The useful lesson is tracing an abnormal frame back to the content being drawn. A current investigation does not require restoring the old SDK tools:

  1. Find the affected frames. On Android 12 / API 31 and later, capture Perfetto with FrameTimeline. Relate expected and actual frame times to the main thread, RenderThread, and SurfaceFlinger. A saveLayer marker alone does not establish the cause of jank.
  2. Inspect the content. From Android Studio 3.1, Layout Inspector replaces Hierarchy Viewer for hierarchy/property inspection, without reproducing its layout-timing results. For individual GPU commands, AGI requires a supported Android 11+ physical device and driver. Its GLES frame capture runs through ANGLE to Vulkan, so it is not an unchanged replay of the native GLES path. See the Device Monitor retirement notice.
  3. Change the confirmed issue and compare again. Keep the device, scenario, and build conditions comparable. Verify the appearance over different backgrounds, selection states, and alpha animations as well as the measured frame behavior.

The renderer has also changed. In android-16.0.0_r1 RenderNodeDrawable.cpp, effective layer type and overlap properties select different paths. The source even retains an alpha caused saveLayer trace label to flag risk on older releases. That label alone does not prove a fresh offscreen allocation, and the 2015 timing conclusions cannot be carried forward unchanged.

Appendix

Historical further reading: Android Tips: Best Practices for Using Alpha. It could not be reopened during this review; use the official references and versioned source above for the current contracts.

entry.title: Android Tips Round-Up, Part 5
entry.content:
In the original Chinese post, I translated Dan Lew’s fifth and final Android tips round-up, which he published in May 2014. As in the earlier parts, I added explanations and notes of my own rather than translating word for word. I hope a few of these tools save you some trouble. Technical corrections and version updates are noted below.

Technical review — 2026-10-13: Old Support Library links now point to AndroidX. Storage, thumbnail generation, and app languages have version-specific updates. The side effects of clearing app data and yielding a database transaction are explained in their entries.

ViewDragHelper — Helps custom ViewGroups implement child dragging and settling; use the androidx.customview.widget version. AndroidX DrawerLayout is a useful reference. The container must still connect touch handling and callbacks; constructing a helper alone does not make every View draggable. Flavien Laurent’s original article is retained as a historical link; it could not be reopened during this review.

PopupWindow — Displays temporary floating content above the current Activity. It attaches to an existing window; avoiding a new Activity does not turn it into a system overlay that may cover arbitrary apps. Configure focus, touch, and input-method behavior for the intended interaction.

ActionBar.getThemedContext() — Available since API 14, this provides the themed Context for custom Views placed in an ActionBar. Confirm that the page actually has an ActionBar before dereferencing getActionBar(); a no-action-bar theme does not supply one.

ThumbnailUtils — Available since API 8. The old createVideoThumbnail(String, int) was deprecated in API 29, which introduced createVideoThumbnail(File, Size, CancellationSignal). Use the File overload when direct file access is available; for provider-owned content Uris, consider ContentResolver.loadThumbnail(), also introduced in API 29. Run decoding and I/O off the UI thread and handle failure or cancellation.

Context.getExternalFilesDir() — Since API 8, this returns an app-specific external-storage directory whose contents are removed on uninstall. Access to your own directory needs no storage permission from Android 4.4 KitKat / API 19. External storage is not necessarily a removable SD card, and an unavailable volume can produce null. Android 10 introduced scoped storage; on Android 11 with target API 30+, WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE grants no additional access. The old claim that permission lets an app write anywhere is obsolete. See Android 11 storage changes.

SparseArray — Saves memory for int keys by avoiding Integer boxing and per-entry HashMap objects. It uses arrays and binary search, so it is not faster for every operation and does not implement the general Map interface. Consider collection size and insertion/deletion patterns. SparseBooleanArray, SparseIntArray, and SparseLongArray store the corresponding primitive value types.

PackageManager.setComponentEnabledSetting() — Changes a manifest component’s enabled state; it does not start the component. Explicit enabled/disabled states override the original setting, while COMPONENT_ENABLED_STATE_DEFAULT restores the manifest setting. DONT_KILL_APP requests that the containing app not be killed, but component changes still affect behavior. Disabling a receiver does not necessarily stop all associated business work already in progress.

SQLiteDatabase.yieldIfContendedSafely() — When contention causes an actual yield, it ends the work so far as a successful transaction, then starts a new transaction that is not yet marked successful. It is not a pause that preserves one transaction’s atomicity. Do not use it arbitrarily inside a group of operations that must roll back together. Do not call setTransactionSuccessful() first, and do not use nested transactions here. The return value indicates whether a yield occurred.

Environment.getExternalStoragePublicDirectory() — Returns a File path for a public directory such as Pictures or Music, not permission to access it. The path API remains available in Android 16 source, but the old unrestricted-write assumptions do not apply to scoped storage. Prefer MediaStore for shared media, or the Storage Access Framework, available from API 19, for user-selected document locations. Keep internal app data in app-specific storage.

View.generateViewId() — From API 17, generates a runtime value suitable for setId() without colliding with build-generated R.id values. It does not detect manually duplicated assignments or provide a stable cross-process business identifier. Preserve the appropriate identity mapping when restoring View state across recreation.

ActivityManager.clearApplicationUserData() — From API 19, requests the equivalent of clearing the app’s storage in system settings. It removes private and app-specific external data, revokes related runtime permissions, and stops the app, while retaining the APK. See the Android 16 server implementation. A true return means the request was accepted. Ordinary logout should revoke sessions and remove the relevant tokens/account data according to product requirements, rather than indiscriminately deleting all local user content.

Context.createConfigurationContext() — From API 17, returns a new Context with resource configuration overrides, such as a locale used for selected resources. It does not change the entire app’s language in place. For app-level language preferences, Android 13 / API 33 provides LocaleManager; AppCompat 1.6.0+ offers AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales() for older versions, with its documented Activity and persistence requirements. See the app-language guide.

ActivityOptions — From API 16, supplies Activity launch options such as custom animations; pass toBundle() to an appropriate launch overload. Use AndroidX ActivityOptionsCompat for compatibility, but not every new option has equivalent behavior on older systems. setLaunchDisplayId() was added in API 26 and remains subject to device capabilities and target-display access rules.

AdapterViewFlipper.fyiWillBeAdvancedByHostKThx() — This one earns a mention for the name alone. From API 11, AppWidgetHost uses it to announce that the host will call advance(), allowing the flipper to stop advancing itself. AOSP has other playful names such as GRAVITY_DEATH_STAR_I.

ViewParent.requestDisallowInterceptTouchEvent() — Requests that the parent and ancestors avoid onInterceptTouchEvent() for the current touch sequence. Parents should propagate and honor the request until UP / CANCEL. It cannot recover events already intercepted or bypass system gestures. The original touch-system talk is retained as a historical link; its contents could not be retrieved during this review.
