entry.title: Android Tips Round-Up, Part 4
entry.content:
In the original Chinese post, I translated Dan Lew’s fourth Android tips round-up, which he published in May 2014. These are small tools worth sharing, and I added my own notes where I had something to contribute. The version updates are noted below.

Technical review — 2026-10-13: Most of these View/XML APIs remain usable, but the explanations of configuration changes, clipping, and atomic files needed correction. The Gradle Daemon has been enabled by default since 3.0. AtomicFile behavior is illustrated using Android 4.4.4 and Android 16 source versions below.

Activity.isChangingConfigurations() — Available since API 11, this identifies an Activity being destroyed because its configuration is changing. It does not save state or replace appropriate saved-instance-state, ViewModel, or persistent storage handling. A false result at an arbitrary moment does not rule out later recreation; an already stopped Activity can still be recreated after a configuration change.

SearchRecentSuggestionsProvider — Supplies recent-query suggestions for the system search framework. Subclass it, call setupSuggestions() from the constructor, and keep the authority consistent with the manifest and searchable XML. The app also needs to save queries with SearchRecentSuggestions.saveRecentQuery(); the provider does not automatically capture all input or create the search interface.

ViewTreeObserver — Dan Lew often used this to wait for Views to be measured before starting animations. It observes global layout, pre-draw, and related events, letting you read dimensions after layout. It does not actively measure a View. Callbacks can repeat, so remove a listener when only one notification is needed. Check isAlive() before using a long-lived observer reference; a dead observer cannot be operated on.

org.gradle.daemon=true — Reusing a JVM can reduce command-line build startup overhead. However, the Daemon is enabled by default from Gradle 3.0, so modern projects generally do not need this extra line to enable it. Daemons, incremental builds, and the build cache are separate mechanisms; repeating a setting is not a new optimization.

DatabaseUtils — Provides helpers for Cursor inspection, queries, and ContentValues conversion. For example, cursorRowToContentValues() works on the current row, while dumpCursor() helps with debugging. The caller still owns resource-lifetime decisions and must close Cursors as appropriate.

android:weightSum (LinearLayout) — Sets the total weight used to distribute remaining space; otherwise LinearLayout sums its children’s layout_weight values. A larger explicit total can leave some space unallocated. Base child sizes and parent measurement constraints still affect the result, so a weight is not automatically a percentage of the screen.

android:duplicateParentState (View) — Uses the direct parent’s drawable state, such as pressed or focused. It does not copy every parent property or install click listeners.

android:clipChildren (ViewGroup) — Defaults to true and clips each child to that child’s own bounds. Setting it to false permits drawing beyond those bounds, but ancestors may still clip the result. clipToPadding is a separate setting. Drawing outside a View does not automatically enlarge its layout or touch target.

android:fillViewport (ScrollView) — Stretches a short direct child to fill the ScrollView’s available viewport height, not necessarily the entire screen. Taller content still scrolls. A ScrollView permits only one direct child; use a container when several controls are needed.

android:tileMode (BitmapDrawable) — Chooses bitmap tiling: repeat repeats the image, mirror alternates mirrored copies, and clamp extends edge colors. The default is disabled. Enabling tiling ignores gravity; this is separate from ImageView scaling.

android:enterFadeDuration / android:exitFadeDuration — From API 11, these control the fade durations when a DrawableContainer switches child Drawables, such as state-list transitions. Values are milliseconds of fading, not a delay before displaying content or an automatic entrance animation for the whole View.

android:scaleType (ImageView) — Controls Drawable scaling and cropping inside the content area. centerCrop preserves aspect ratio and covers the area, potentially cropping edges; centerInside preserves the ratio while fitting the whole image inside. This affects presentation, not automatic downsampling of a large source bitmap during decoding.

<merge> — As a layout root, it inserts children directly into an existing parent, avoiding an unnecessary ViewGroup. <include> performs layout-file inclusion; <merge> itself is not a View. Inflating it requires a valid parent and immediate attachment. Preserve any required background, padding, or interaction role before removing a container.

AtomicFile — Dan Lew had written similar functionality himself and was glad to find an official implementation. The framework class, available since API 17, updates a single file. Android 4.4.4 used a .bak backup; Android 16 writes a .new file before replacement and handles legacy backups. Complete startWrite() with finishWrite() or failWrite() instead of merely closing its stream. It provides no inter-thread or interprocess file locking: the caller must enforce mutual exclusion for access.

entry.title: Android Tips Round-Up, Part 3
entry.content:
In the original Chinese post, I translated Dan Lew’s third Android tips round-up, which he published in April 2014. As with the earlier parts, I added my own notes and explanations where I thought they would help. Some of these are tools I use myself; if a few are new to you, I hope they come in handy. The API corrections and version limits are noted below.

Technical review — 2026-10-13: Platform android.app.Fragment was deprecated in API 28; the Fragment entries below use AndroidX. LocalBroadcastManager and Otto are no longer maintained. Other tips remain useful within the API and behavior limits stated below.

UrlQuerySanitizer — Parses URL query parameters and processes values using configured ValueSanitizer rules. It does not validate an entire URL or establish that its destination is safe. Check the scheme, host, and business fields for the intended use, and decide how unregistered and repeated parameters should be handled.

Fragment.setArguments() — Put saveable initialization parameters in a Bundle, usually after constructing the Fragment instance and before adding it to FragmentManager. Arguments can be restored across destruction and recreation. The default restoration path uses a no-argument constructor; AndroidX Fragment 1.1.0 introduced FragmentFactory for custom instantiation. Parameterized constructors are therefore not categorically forbidden, but the factory must also handle restoration.

DialogFragment.setShowsDialog() — A DialogFragment can appear as a dialog or embedded content. Setting this to false suppresses the Dialog; configure it before the UI is created and provide embedded content through onCreateView(). A layout created only inside onCreateDialog() does not automatically become the embedded Fragment’s View.

FragmentManager.enableDebugLogging() — This logging switch was deprecated in AndroidX Fragment 1.2.0. For debugging, the documented replacement is adb shell setprop log.tag.FragmentManager VERBOSE, followed by inspecting Logcat.

LocalBroadcastManager — The old process-local Intent dispatcher was fully deprecated in 1.1.0 (2022), with no further releases planned. Choose LiveData or reactive streams according to data ownership and observer lifetimes. The original alternative, Otto 1.3.8, is also deprecated and archived. A process-local event bus does not provide interprocess communication.

PhoneNumberUtils.formatNumber() — Formats telephone numbers, not general numeric values. The single-String overload was deprecated in API 21, which added formatNumber(phoneNumber, defaultCountryIso) for a default country/region such as CN. Handle a possible null result with an appropriate display fallback. Formatting does not prove that a number exists.

Region.op() — Performs region intersection, union, difference, and related operations. For overlap, compute INTERSECT into a result Region and inspect whether it is empty. Paths must first be converted with a clip via setPath(), which produces a non-antialiased pixel region rather than an exact floating-point path intersection. op() mutates the result receiver.

Application.registerActivityLifecycleCallbacks() — Available since API 14 for observing Activity lifecycle events within the app process, not for monitoring every app on the device. Unregister short-lived observers when finished and avoid retaining destroyed Activities in callbacks.

versionNameSuffix — Android Gradle Plugin can append a version-name suffix by build type or product flavor, such as -SNAPSHOT for debug builds. It does not change versionCode or installation identity. To install debug and release variants alongside each other, use distinct application IDs, for example through applicationIdSuffix.

CursorJoiner — A SQL join works when the data is in one database. What if it comes from two separate ContentProviders? CursorJoiner can compare the two Cursors. Both must already be sorted by the specified key columns in ascending order, with unique key tuples on each side. Results are LEFT, RIGHT, or BOTH; this does not create a new SQL result table or implement an arbitrary many-to-many join.

Genymotion — Dan Lew wrote that he used it all day and found it much faster. It still offers desktop and cloud products, but that was his experience at the time, not a fixed comparison with today’s Android Emulator. Compare under equivalent host, virtualization, image-architecture, and workload conditions.

-nodpi — Bitmaps in a directory such as res/drawable-nodpi/ are not automatically scaled to match device density. This does not control assets/, disable dp / sp conversion, or fix the entire layout to pixel dimensions. ImageView sizing and scaleType can still scale the displayed image; nodpi does not guarantee equal visual size across devices.

BroadcastReceiver.setDebugUnregister() — Enable it before registering a receiver to retain a later unregister call’s stack for diagnosing an incorrect subsequent unregister. It retains that information for the process lifetime and causes a leak itself, so it is a debugging aid rather than a production leak-prevention mechanism.

Activity.recreate() — Available since API 11, this requests a new Activity instance and is useful for checking restoration. It does not restart the process or automatically preserve all business state. Follow the lifecycle state-saving contract.

PackageManager.checkSignatures() — Compares package signing identities; check specifically for SIGNATURE_MATCH. This is not merely an installed-app query. A package name alone does not establish trust, and Android also checks signing compatibility during installation and updates. The original warning should not be read as allowing differently signed apps with the same package name to coexist or overwrite each other freely. Authorization still needs a trusted identity as the comparison baseline and must handle unknown packages and mismatches.

entry.title: Compiling Android Lollipop Firmware for Nexus 5
entry.content:
Technical review — 2026-10-13: This is a historical Nexus 5 / Android Lollipop tutorial with an obsolete device and toolchain. Its LRX22C binaries correspond to Android 5.0.1 / AOSP android-5.0.1_r1. The source, binary, and flashing requirements below are tied to that combination. An Android 16 Cuttlefish example is added separately; do not mix it with the old phone firmware.

Following my previous article, Using Android Studio to View Android Lollipop Source Code, we know that simply reading code has its limits—understanding can remain superficial and easily forgotten. In contrast, code you’ve personally written or modified tends to leave a much deeper impression, and the process becomes easier to grasp during the implementation phase. While studying the source code, being able to modify it, run it on a phone, and see the results firsthand significantly boosts both learning efficiency and enthusiasm. This article explains how to compile the Android Lollipop source code yourself and run it on a Nexus 5.

Why compile your own firmware instead of using Google’s factory images?
The goal here is a userdebug build suitable for platform debugging. User builds restrict facilities such as ADB root. Userdebug enables more debugging operations, but does not make every partition freely writable under all conditions.

This guide assumes a consistent Lollipop source tree and a Nexus 5. See the historical AOSP environment guide and source download instructions. Android 5.x uses OpenJDK 7 on Linux. Keep its old OS and dependencies in a dedicated historical build environment rather than using it as the setup for a current workstation.

AOSP means Android Open Source Project. It includes the platform and open-source apps, but not the proprietary Google Mobile Services (GMS) suite. Hardware binaries, GMS licensing, and Android compatibility are separate matters. Meeting the CDD and passing CTS establishes compatibility; it does not automatically grant GMS. For the requirements, see the Android compatibility overview.

A Current Learning Path: Android 16 Cuttlefish

For changing system code and observing its behavior, start with a Cuttlefish virtual device. This example pins the source to android-16.0.0_r1. Use a separate new directory on a host meeting the Linux build requirements:

The product is defined in that tag’s Cuttlefish configuration, and its release map maps aosp_current to bp2a. Launching also requires the host packages, KVM, and group setup described in the Cuttlefish launch instructions; a successful m does not start the virtual device.

The official getting-started guide uses the moving android-latest-release branch. Record the actual manifest for reproducibility. For a physical device, verify the device tree, vendor binaries, bootloader, and baseband for each release. An old Pixel or Nexus entry on the download page does not imply support for every new Android version.

1. Initializing the Build Environment — Android 5.0.1

Return to the legacy Nexus 5 workspace. The AOSP build table maps LRX22C to android-5.0.1_r1. Confirm that the source tree consistently uses this version, then run from the source root:

2. Choosing the Target

The old branch supports the interactive lunch menu. Selecting the target directly avoids depending on a menu number:

3. Checking the Device and Build Variant

3.1 The Target Used Here

DeviceDevice codenameAndroid 5.0.1 build target
Nexus 5 (GSM/LTE)hammerheadaosp_hammerhead-userdebug

The original multi-device table mixed product names and targets from different eras. Check product definitions in the selected source tree for other devices instead of merely replacing hammerhead with another codename.

3.2 Build Variants

VariantPurpose
userProduction configuration with restricted debugging access
userdebugSimilar to user, with additional facilities such as root debugging for platform development
engEngineering configuration with more debugging behavior; not a direct proxy for production performance

The relevant configuration values for this example are:

Use the version defined by the selected source tag. TARGET_BUILD_TYPE=release can coexist with TARGET_BUILD_VARIANT=userdebug; they are different settings.

4. Setting Up Proprietary Binaries

Use the hammerhead / LRX22C section of Google’s binary download page. These packages provide hardware support missing from the open-source tree; they are not workstation USB drivers. The SHA-256 values below are published by Google.

Hardware componentCompanyDownload
NFC, Bluetooth, Wi-FiBroadcomLRX22C
Camera, Sensors, AudioLGLRX22C
Graphics, GSM, Camera, GPS, Sensors, Media, DSP, USBQualcommLRX22C

Official SHA-256 values:

Check downloaded files against the official checksums. Extract each archive, read its license and instructions, then run its extraction script from the source root and complete the license prompts. The files go under vendor/. Each supplier’s package has a distinct role; duplicating the LG package does not replace Qualcomm’s, and binaries from different build IDs should not be mixed.

5. Starting the Build

-j8 is the original concurrency example; adjust it for CPU, memory, and observed build behavior. The full build must exit successfully and produce the required files under out/target/product/hammerhead/. A message saying system.img was generated does not prove the whole build succeeded.

The build takes a while. These lines come from my build log at the time and show the system-image stage:

6. Flashing the Firmware

Unlocking the bootloader and flashing with -w both erase user data. Back up first, confirm the device is a Nexus 5 / hammerhead, and verify that the build artifacts, bootloader, and baseband match the intended build.

If Android is running and ADB is authorized, use adb reboot bootloader to enter bootloader / fastboot mode. For powered-off devices, consult the official key-combination table; it lists both volume buttons and Power for Nexus 5. This is fastboot mode, not recovery.

Check the connection and product name:

If still locked, a pre-2015 device such as Nexus 5 uses fastboot oem unlock, followed by on-device confirmation to erase data and unlock. Do not substitute the later fastboot flashing unlock workflow. See the official Fastboot instructions.

In the same terminal where envsetup and lunch aosp_hammerhead-userdebug were run, confirm that ANDROID_PRODUCT_OUT points to this build’s hammerhead artifacts, then use the original flashing command:

The historical fastboot implementation reads android-info.txt and images from the product output directory. Merely changing to the source root does not initialize that environment. With multiple devices connected, use -s DEVICE_SERIAL consistently for all fastboot operations.

My flash log from that run ended with rebooting... and finished. total time: 70.095s. After flashing, check normal boot and the required Wi-Fi, camera, audio, and other functions. Fastboot success or a visible launcher alone does not prove all vendor components match.

7. The Original Desktop Screenshot

And here was the desktop, finally.

entry.title: Android Performance Optimization - Introduction to Systrace (Part 1)
entry.content:
Technical review — 2026-10-13: This article was written in 2015. Its event-timeline concepts remain useful, while the Eclipse / Device Monitor entry points are obsolete. Historical script options below are checked against AOSP android-5.0.0_r1. The added Perfetto commands target Android 11 / API 30 and later, with older-system differences noted separately. Continue with the Android Perfetto series catalog.

Old workflowCurrent counterpart
Systrace button in Eclipse / Device MonitorOn-device System Tracing from Android 9 / API 28, or capture through ADB
systrace.py calls atrace and produces HTMLPerfetto records a binary trace, with events selected by categories or a config file
Open the old HTML directly in a browserImport the trace into Perfetto UI, or analyze it with Trace Processor SQL
Assume user builds cannot traceUser builds can record system traces; available data depends on the OS, data source, app configuration, and vendor policy

This is the first article in the Android Performance Optimization Tools series. This series mainly introduces the tools used during the Android performance optimization process, how to use these tools to discover problems, and how to solve them. In terms of performance optimization, Android provides many performance tools for everyone to use. Following our consistent “discover problem - solve problem” thinking, discovering the problem is the most important part. Trying to solve a problem without first identifying it properly often leads to twice the effort for half the result.

In this article, we’ll start with a brief introduction to the Systrace tool.

Introduction to Systrace

Systrace arrived with Android 4.1 / SDK Tools R20 as a system-event tracing and visualization tool. It places enabled CPU scheduling, SurfaceFlinger, WindowManager, View, and other events on a shared timeline. It does not automatically sample every Java method or provide complete call stacks. See the original SDK Tools R20 announcement.

The historical workflow has three parts:

  • Kernel events: These depend on enabled ftrace support and accessible kernel events. Scheduling, I/O, frequency, and other categories must be checked on the device.
  • Userspace annotations and collection: System components emit ATrace markers, while atrace configures categories and reads tracing data. Apps can add their own sections with android.os.Trace.beginSection() / endSection(); these public APIs were added in Android 4.3 / API 18, not Android 4.1.
  • Host-side reporting: The old systrace.py invokes atrace over ADB, processes the data, and builds an HTML report with a viewer. Existing system events can be captured without changing app code; custom business-operation sections require instrumentation.

Perfetto supports additional data sources, so describing all of it as an ftrace wrapper would be incomplete. It still reads android.os.Trace markers. See the Trace API and Perfetto ATrace documentation.

Simple Usage of Systrace

The basic sequence is the same with either tool: prepare the page, start recording, reproduce the interaction, stop and save the trace, then confirm that the required events and time range were captured. A successfully created file alone does not establish that it contains the problem.

Historical GUI Entry Points — Obsolete

These locations are retained for reading older instructions. Android Device Monitor was deprecated in Android Studio 3.1 and removed in 3.2.

  • Eclipse: Open the DDMS perspective, select a device in Devices, then use its Systrace button.
  • Early Android Studio: Open Tools → Android → Monitor, select a device, and click Systrace.
  • Standalone Device Monitor: Run monitor from an old SDK tools directory and follow the same process. These buttons are not part of current Android Studio.

Today, open System Tracing in the device’s Developer options. Android 9 produces Systrace .ctrace files; Android 10 / API 29 and later produce Perfetto traces. Select the needed categories, record the interaction, stop, and retrieve the file.

Command Line: Perfetto

I recommend the command line: set it up once, and repeating a capture is much easier. This example assumes an Android 11 / API 30 or later device connected and authorized through ADB. Inspect available categories before choosing what to record:

Perform the interaction during the 10-second recording, then pull the file after the command finishes. Adjust unsupported categories using the device’s list. -b 64mb configures the Perfetto ring buffer; it is not the old script’s KB value or a guarantee of the final file size. With multiple devices connected, use the same adb -s DEVICE_SERIAL selection for every command.

This is Perfetto’s simple mode, primarily configuring ftrace / atrace. It does not enable every data source; FrameTimeline, for example, requires its own data-source configuration. See the Perfetto CLI reference.

Perfetto was included in Android 9, but some Android 9 / 10 devices require tracing services to be enabled first, and Android 9 has different file-pull permission constraints. Consult the Android capture compatibility notes before applying this entire workflow to an older device.

App Custom Events

To include app ATrace markers, specify the app process name. The default main process usually matches the package name; check actual names for a multiprocess app. For example:

-a enables selected app markers; it does not insert method instrumentation. The app must already contain Trace calls in framework, library, or business code and satisfy that OS version’s tracing requirements. For example, on Android 10 / 11 user builds, an app generally needs to be debuggable or declare <profileable android:shell="true" /> inside <application>, an option introduced in API 29. Prefer an appropriate profileable release build for timing comparisons so debug overhead is not mistaken for production behavior. See the profileable version and access rules.

Synchronous beginSection() / endSection() calls must be paired on the same thread and correctly nested; use try/finally to ensure the end is recorded. A section’s elapsed duration can include waiting and preemption, so it is not necessarily CPU execution time.

Historical Systrace Commands — Android 5.0 Source Version

The following options are checked against systrace.py at AOSP android-5.0.0_r1. It uses Python 2 syntax and adjacent report resources; the script alone is insufficient. Historical SDK packages placed it under locations such as platform-tools/systrace, but do not assume that directory exists in a current installation.

From a matching old tool directory containing the script and its assets:

Python 2 describes the historical environment here; do not restore an obsolete interpreter just to capture a current device. Existing HTML traces can be imported directly into Perfetto UI rather than relying on the old embedded viewer to work in a current Chrome release. See supported external trace formats.

These options belong to that script version, not to perfetto:

OptionPurpose
-h, --helpDisplay script help
-o FILEWrite HTML; the default filename is trace.html
-t N, --time=NRecord for N seconds; this Android 5.0 combination inherits atrace’s five-second default when omitted; check help for other versions
-b N, --buf-size=NPass a KB buffer setting to atrace, corresponding to per-CPU kernel buffers; CPU count, events, and compression also affect report size
-k FUNCTIONS, --ktrace=FUNCTIONSSelect comma-separated kernel functions, subject to kernel support and permissions
-l, --list-categoriesList categories available on the connected device
-a NAMES, --app=NAMESEnable markers for comma-separated app process names
--from-file=FILEBuild a report from an existing compressed trace, not from an arbitrary renamed file
--link-assets, --asset-dir=DIRControl the historical report’s CSS / JavaScript resource references and directory
-e SERIAL, --serial=SERIALSelect an ADB device

See the Linux ftrace documentation for per-CPU buffers, and Android 5.0 atrace.cpp for the five-second default.

Common categories include gfx, view, wm, am, input, sched, freq, and idle. The original list also included membus, load, sync, and workq; these are not available on every version. The historical dalvik category name does not establish that a device runs Dalvik rather than ART. Query the actual category list before copying a long set of tags.

Saving Historical Aliases

If you maintain a matching legacy environment, Bash / Zsh aliases can shorten the commands. Replace the example path before loading this configuration:

There must be no spaces around = in an alias assignment, and the quotes must be straight shell quotes. The categories still need device support. Use .html for an identifiable output name; changing the extension to .Trace does not change the format. You don’t need to memorize every option now. Start by capturing the events you need; the options will become familiar as you use them to analyze traces.

entry.title: Viewing Android Lollipop Source Code with Android Studio
entry.content:
Technical review — 2026-10-13: The original article targets Android 5.0 Lollipop and Android Studio 1.x. The historical IDEGen workflow below has been checked against AOSP android-5.0.0_r1; the added AIDEGen example uses the documentation at android-16.0.0_r1.

Android Studio

Google has always looked after its own. The Nexus 5 got Android 5.0 right away, and Android Studio was getting plenty of attention too. I switched from Eclipse early on and followed Android Studio from the betas through to 1.0.

Reading Source Today

For browsing, use Android Code Search and check the selected branch. For an exact release, use its tag in AOSP Gitiles.

For local navigation and editing, sync the intended branch, run source build/envsetup.sh, and select a valid lunch target using that branch’s instructions. With the environment configured, the Android 16 AIDEGen documentation supports this example from the source root:

Paths also work: aidegen packages/apps/Settings frameworks/base -i s. The default example launches IntelliJ; -i s explicitly selects Android Studio. -s skips building, so do not use it to work around missing generated sources or dependencies. Check your branch’s language and IDE options for C/C++ or Rust instead of assuming one Java project covers every language.

Modern AOSP builds require Linux; official macOS support for Android OS development ended in the Android 11 era. This is separate from developing ordinary Android apps with Android Studio on macOS. See the AOSP environment requirements. Start with the modules you need. Regenerating projects overwrites generated IDE configurations, so preserve any manual customizations first.

Why I Chose Android Studio Then

I don’t need to elaborate on the benefits of Android Studio; the following two points should be enough to convince you to switch:

  • Android Studio is Google’s official Android IDE; version 1.0 was released in December 2014.
  • ADT retirement came later: in June 2015, Google announced that development and official support for Eclipse ADT and the Android Ant build system would end that year. That change should not be dated to this article’s January 2015 timestamp.

The later 1.1 stable release was in February 2015, a month after the first version of this post. For the release and ADT timelines, see the Studio 1.0 announcement and the ADT announcement.

Switching to Android Studio is the general trend. There are countless posts online about how to use Android Studio, so I won’t waste words praising it. The screenshot below might tempt you too. For more details, you can view the Android Studio Official Documentation.

Android 5.0: Lollipop

Android 5.0 Lollipop brought new interface and platform capabilities. You can check the Official Lollipop Introduction for detailed information. As developers, we shouldn’t just stay on the surface (like Lollipop’s fancy interface and the new Material Design language); we need to understand the underlying principles.

Preparation

These are historical Android 5.0 requirements, not instructions for every AOSP version:

  • Download a complete, consistent Lollipop source tree and configure the JDK and build environment required by that branch.
  • The IDEGen README at this version recommends running make to produce generated Java sources. The script itself needs a built idegen.jar; a full build is not an absolute prerequisite for generating project files, but missing generated sources and dependencies can leave the index incomplete.

If the docs or source downloads won’t load, sort out the network connection first. My view was: if spending a little money solves it, don’t spend all your time on it.

Steps — Historical Android 5.0 Workflow

From the source root, initialize the environment, choose the target, and compile IDEGen:

The interactive lunch menu is the old branch’s behavior. Choose a target matching the downloaded device sources. After compilation succeeds, run:

This version of the script finds idegen.jar under out and runs the generator. Its IntelliJ generator writes android.ipr and android.iml, not all three files originally listed; .iws is an IDE workspace file.

Open android.ipr in the historical Android Studio version, wait for indexing, and configure the branch’s JDK, sources, and dependencies. Opening the project does not turn the whole Android platform into a normal Gradle app project.

And that’s it. Once indexing and configuration are done, you can read the source. There isn’t another step.

Troubleshooting

IDEGen Fails to Compile

Inspect the first actual compiler error. Check source completeness, environment initialization, target selection, and the branch’s JDK requirements. A failed compilation alone does not establish that a full platform build is missing. Search the error with Google or Stack Overflow.

A Directory Is Parsed as a Java File

When generating the project, I ran into this error:

Here, res.java is a directory. In Configuration.java at android-5.0.0_r1, the .java suffix check runs before directory traversal, so the directory is passed to FileReader.

My workaround at the time was to rename res.java to res.j. That can disrupt later builds by changing a generated directory under out, so I wouldn’t carry that workaround over. For this version, the appropriate repair is to check the file type in traverse():

Directories then reach the later traversal branch. Rebuild IDEGen and regenerate the project after applying the change. On other branches, inspect the actual source instead of applying a patch solely by an old stack trace’s line numbers.

Conclusion

Using Android Studio to view Android source code is a great experience. These were my impressions of Android Studio 1.x at the time, not an assessment of current releases:

Pros

  • Perfect integration with Android.
  • Comprehensive code completion.
  • Powerful code navigation.
  • Better looking IDE than Eclipse (I’m talking about the dark theme).
  • Powerful plugins (based on IntelliJ IDEA).
  • Free (SourceInsight gets a negative score here. What? You use a cracked version? Pretend I didn’t say anything).

Cons

  • Support for C++ code is not very good.
  • Has a certain learning curve.

entry.title: Android Performance Optimization: Overdraw - Practical Application
entry.content:
Introduction

The previous article covered the theory of overdraw and tools to detect it. While iOS users rely on Apple’s curation, Android users rely on developers’ discipline. Unfortunately, many market-leading Android apps still suffer from significant overdraw issues. As a developer, I want to see Android bridge and eventually surpass the experience gap with iOS.

This post follows one overdraw optimization case. It uses only a few of the available techniques; apps differ, and so will the changes they need. Treat it as an example. Getting this right still takes work.

If you missed the theory part, check it here: Android Performance Optimization: Overdraw (Part 1)

Technical review — 2026-10-13: This is a 2015 File Manager case study. The exact OS and app versions were not recorded. The Monitor, Hierarchy Viewer, and Tracer for OpenGL ES instructions are obsolete: Android Device Monitor was deprecated in Android Studio 3.1 and removed in 3.2. The screenshots remain useful, but fewer overdraw colors do not establish a frame-rate or power improvement; the original article contains no frame-time measurements.

For View-based pages today, use Android Studio Layout Inspector to inspect the runtime hierarchy and backgrounds, and Debug GPU Overdraw to locate repeated drawing. Compare the same interaction on the same device and OS, with debug coloring disabled during System Trace collection. Perfetto FrameTimeline is available on Android 12 / API 31 and later; it currently does not support SurfaceView, so it is not a measurement path for every type of content.

Identifying Overdraw Regions

1. Enable Overdraw Visualization

Find Debug GPU Overdraw → Show overdraw areas in Developer options. The original device placed this under Settings → Accessibility → Developer tools → Hardware-accelerated rendering; menu locations vary by system.

2. Open the Page Under Test

Enabling the overlay does not normally require killing the app. The original screenshots below were taken after reopening File Manager and Settings. For a before-and-after comparison, keep the launch state, list contents, and menu position consistent.

In the default scheme shown here, blue, green, light red, and red indicate one, two, three, and at least four extra draws respectively. File Manager has large green and red regions worth investigating. Settings helps illustrate the colors, but a different app is not a controlled performance baseline or an acceptance threshold.

3. Analyze Suspicious Regions

  • The blue ActionBar and bottom SmartBar suggest an extra draw. A theme background is one possibility, but the color alone cannot identify the responsible View or Drawable.
  • The green content area has two extra draws. A background fully covered by opaque content might be redundant; a color difference from Settings does not prove that it is safe to remove.
  • Start with these large regions, then inspect icons, list items, and the sliding menu.

Step-by-Step Optimization

The original workflow opened Monitor and switched to Hierarchy View. The screenshot below preserves that workflow; use Layout Inspector for a current project.

The screenshot shows PhoneWindow$DecorView as the root, followed by ActionBarOverlayLayout. This is the hierarchy on the original device and theme, not a universal Android layout. The parent-child relationship alone does not establish that the window background belongs to ActionBarOverlayLayout.

1. Remove a Fully Covered Background

Distinguish the Window background from each View’s own background. In this case, I added the following line to File Manager’s main Activity in onCreate():

This replaces the window background with a transparent color Drawable; it does not remove the Drawable object. If the page’s content always covers the window completely and opaquely, another option to evaluate is getWindow().setBackgroundDrawable(null), available since API 1. Setting a null background does not make the window transparent. Check loading, empty-list, menu-sliding, and transition states for exposed areas or flashes before adopting either change.

These are the original screenshots after applying the transparent background:

Compared with the earlier screenshots, the blue overlay on the ActionBar is gone, and the content has shifted from green to blue. Those regions have one fewer repeated draw in these frames.

2. Eliminate a Redundant Container Background

The original investigation identified DragRelativeLayout, derived from the project’s SlidingMenu. Its CustomViewAbove held the movable content, while CustomViewBehind held the menu behind it.

In the CustomViewBehind constructor, I found this line setting the background color:

The finding was that the menu content added by SlidingMenu.setMenu() completely covered this background. The change therefore removed the container’s background drawing, not the CustomViewBehind View. It also did not rely on CustomViewAbove always covering the menu. This was a finding about that project’s implementation, not a guarantee for other libraries or versions with the same class names. Exposed areas must still be checked with the menu open.

Repeated drawing is reduced in several regions. The intended appearance still needs checking with the menu both open and closed.

3. Inspect List-Item Drawing

Looking further under CustomViewAbove, I found a ListView with ID FilesList. I tried removing a setBounds() call from PartitionItemLayout.onDraw(). The overdraw colors decreased, but the list items also became lighter. These are the screenshots from that attempt:

The lighter list items matter: this step doesn’t yet count as a successful optimization. Drawable.setBounds() defines the rectangle used by a subsequent draw() call; it doesn’t draw anything itself. Removing it can leave stale bounds or stop a background that should still be visible from being drawn.

The next step is to find the call that draws the background, check whether that drawing is redundant, then remove or reduce it while preserving the intended appearance. Blue still means one extra draw; fewer colors don’t prove an optimal rendering path.

Improving Code Quality

Using Lint

Lint and IDE inspections can identify redundant layouts, unused resources, and potential errors. In the example below, a FrameLayout or its parent may be unnecessary. Remove it only after checking that it has no required background, padding, layout-parameter, or event-handling role.

The original article also listed unused variables, possible null dereferences, empty branches, redundant return / continue, and simpler loop forms. Some are general IDE inspections rather than Android Lint performance rules. An enhanced for loop is not automatically faster. Removing a container primarily affects inflation, measurement, and layout; it reduces pixel overdraw only if it also eliminates actual repeated drawing.

Tracer for OpenGL ES — Historical Tool

These steps describe the old Device Monitor and do not apply to Android Studio 3.2 or later. Open the Tracer for OpenGL ES perspective, create a GLTrace, select the app and Activity, click Trace to start, and Stop to finish.

I replayed the frames to check whether the default and CustomViewBehind backgrounds were still being drawn. The screenshot below remains, but the original GLTrace files aren’t available here for another analysis.

Avoiding fully covered backgrounds across multiple frames removes that drawing work. How much GPU time it saves, and whether it improves missed frames, requires a separate measurement. The historical screenshots do not provide those results.

References

  1. Android: Reduce overdraw
  2. Android Device Monitor deprecation and replacement tools
  3. Layout Inspector
  4. Window.setBackgroundDrawable()
  5. Drawable.setBounds()
  6. Optimize View layouts
  7. Perfetto FrameTimeline
  8. Original reference: Android Performance Case Study — a historical link that could not be reopened during this review; it does not support the newly added conclusions.

About Me && Blog

Below are my introduction and related links. I look forward to exchanging ideas with fellow developers.

  1. About the author
  2. Blog content navigation
  3. Android performance optimization: skills and tools
  4. Android Performance community: The paid community stopped operating in 2026 and no longer accepts new members; this link preserves its history.

entry.title: Android Performance Optimization: Overdraw - Theory
entry.content:
Updated 2026-10-13: This article was written in 2014. Its source excerpts have been checked against AOSP android-4.4.4_r2. Overdraw remains relevant, but ADT, monitor, Hierarchy Viewer, and the old OpenGL tracing workflow are outdated. Android Studio 3.1 and later use Layout Inspector for hierarchy inspection; use Perfetto for frame timing. The historical source is retained below, with Android 12 and Android 16 boundaries added.

It’s been a while since my last update. After joining a new company, things have been busy, but I’ve been spending a lot of time researching Android performance. I’ve realized there’s so much I still don’t know, so I’m starting from the application level and working my way down. This series will document my learnings on Android performance optimization.

First, we’ll discuss GPU Overdraw, which is often the most direct point of contact for developers. This topic is split into two parts: Part 1 covers the theory and optimization suggestions, and Part 2 will walk through a practical optimization example.

What is Overdraw?

GPU overdraw means drawing the same pixel more than once within a frame. For example, drawing a TextView background and then its text can draw the pixels under the characters twice. Extra shading, blending, and memory accesses cost resources, but whether they cause missed frames depends on area, transparency, GPU capabilities, and the rest of the frame’s work. A color overlay alone cannot establish the performance impact. See Android’s overdraw guide.

Start with Debug GPU Overdraw to locate repeatedly drawn regions, then inspect their backgrounds and hierarchy in Layout Inspector. Compose recomposition counts and pixel overdraw measure different things and cannot substitute for each other.

After making a change, turn off debug coloring and compare frame timing on the same device, refresh rate, and interaction. On Android 12 (API 31) and later, Perfetto FrameTimeline can relate application and SurfaceFlinger frames; the data source currently does not support SurfaceView. Removing an app background does not by itself prove that SurfaceFlinger composition became faster.

Causes of Overdraw

  1. Multiple backgrounds or custom drawing operations cover the same area, with some pixels completely hidden by opaque content.
  2. Translucent content needs to blend with underlying pixels, so those pixels cannot simply be skipped.
  3. A drawing sequence repeatedly submits graphics that add nothing visible.

View count, nesting depth, and inflation time are separate concerns. A parent that draws no background or content can add layout work without adding pixel overdraw. A flat custom View can still draw the same pixel many times.

Impact of Poor XML Layouts

  1. Inflation reads compiled layout resources, constructs Views, and applies attributes. This is primarily CPU work; node count, constructors, and attribute handling affect its cost, not the number of GPU drawing layers directly.
  2. Layout changes can trigger measurement and placement, while visual updates require recording and executing draw commands. Every frame does not necessarily repeat inflation or a complete layout pass. Use a trace to determine whether the cost is creation, measurement, layout, drawing, or waiting.

Basic Tools for Detecting Overdraw

On supported devices, enable Developer Options → Debug GPU Overdraw → Show overdraw areas. The original Meizu dialer code and menu path were specific to the historical device, not general instructions for current devices. The overlay primarily describes the app window drawn by HWUI; it is not a complete GPU counter for every Surface on the device.

Distinguish total draws from extra draws. The default colors in the Android 4.4.4 implementation checked for this article correspond to:

ColorTotal draws of the pixelDraws beyond the first
Original color, no debug tint10
Blue21
Green32
Light red43
Red5 or more4 or more

Blue still means overdraw. My checks at the time were at most 2x, no 4x, and 3x covering less than a quarter of the screen. These were project guidelines, not universal Android acceptance criteria. The colors help locate areas to investigate; whether a change is worthwhile also depends on frame cost and visual requirements. Text, rounded corners, shadows, and translucent effects can legitimately require overlapping draws.

Optimization Tools

1. Lint

Android Studio lint checks layout and code issues, and projects can run their Gradle lint tasks. Editor hints do not prove that the full lint task has run. Rules and severity depend on the project’s Android Gradle Plugin / lint version and configuration. See the lint guide.

The following historical screenshot is retained; it is not the current Android Studio interface:

2. Common Lint Suggestions and Their Limits

  • Compound drawables: A TextView compound drawable can replace separate image/text nodes when they do not need independent layout, interaction, or accessibility semantics.
  • Merge root frame: Consider <merge> only when the root has no required background, padding, layout, or interaction behavior and an appropriate host parent exists. It is not a standalone View.
  • Useless leaf / parent: Check custom drawing, foregrounds, interaction, animation, and accessibility before removing a node. An absent background alone does not establish that it is useless.
  • Deep layouts: Nesting can increase measurement and layout work. The official layout guide lists a default depth-warning threshold of 10, subject to tool version and configuration. That is a static-analysis clue, not a rule that every hierarchy deeper than 10 drops frames.

These suggestions primarily concern View/XML layouts. Preserve layout behavior and semantics when resolving warnings. See layout hierarchy optimization.

3. Hierarchy Viewer and Layout Inspector

Hierarchy Viewer is no longer maintained. It displayed view trees and relative measure/layout/draw costs through Android Device Monitor. Connectivity depended on system builds, debugging capabilities, and protocol support, not disk encryption. Adding ViewServer for that old workflow is historical advice.

Use Layout Inspector in Android Studio 3.1 or later to inspect runtime hierarchy and attributes. It does not replace frame profiling: use system traces, frame metrics, or application measurements to establish timing costs.

Layout Optimization Principles

  • LinearLayout suits simple rows and columns; compare ConstraintLayout or other options for complex View layouts. Container names alone do not rank performance, and View/XML measurement rules do not directly apply to Compose.
  • Reuse layouts through <include>. Where host requirements are satisfied, use <merge> to remove a behaviorless intermediate container.
  • Use ViewStub to postpone creation of content not needed initially. Changing visibility on an existing View does not create the objects again, so dynamic inflation is not inherently faster than setVisibility(). ViewStub moves work to first expansion rather than eliminating it.
  • Remove backgrounds only when they make no visible contribution. The covering content must remain fully opaque over the affected area. Check empty lists, scrolling edges, loading, errors, pressed states, and transitions.
  • A selector’s normal state can omit drawing when the design allows it. Do not blindly replace every normal background with transparency or remove selection, press, and accessibility feedback.
  • Nested weighted LinearLayouts can require additional measurement passes. This is a measure-stage cost, not a guarantee that every child draws twice. Consider MeasureSpec conditions and actual traces.
  • Remove unnecessary nodes and repeated measurements while preserving semantics. Optimize measured cost rather than the appearance of the hierarchy diagram.

Source Code References

If you’d like to follow this into the source, take a look at OpenGLRenderer.cpp in AOSP android-4.4.4_r2. These excerpts depend on HWUI internal state: renderOverdraw() maps stencil counts to debug colors, and countOverdraw() reads the debug result and calculates an average.

glReadPixels() belongs to that historical diagnostic implementation. Adding a readback to every application frame is not an optimization, and the returned average is not GPU time in milliseconds.

The numerical overlay comes from frameworks/base/core/java/android/view/HardwareRenderer.java at the same tag. These are excerpts of debugOverdraw() and drawOverdrawCounter(). The corresponding file at AOSP android-5.0.0_r1 no longer contains these methods, so this is not a current-system entry point:

These excerpts describe Android 4.4.4, not modern HWUI source organization. For example, AOSP Android 16 tag android-16.0.0_r1 calls renderOverdraw() from a Properties::debugOverdraw branch in SkiaPipeline.cpp. Pin the source tag for the target device before tracing its rendering backend.

Reference Articles

  1. Original optimization case study (historical reference; not accessible during this review)
  2. Decompiling and Adding GPU Display
  3. Optimizing Layouts
  4. Reusing Layouts
  5. Loading Layouts On-Demand
  6. RecyclerView guide (the old Smooth Scrolling URL now redirects here)
  7. Hierarchy Viewer Documentation

entry.title: Android Tips: How to Prevent EditText from Automatically Getting Focus
entry.content:
Reviewed 2026-10-13: This technique applies to traditional Android View layouts. The focus attributes have been available since API 1 and remain supported. Input focus and keyboard visibility are separate states, so adding the attributes does not guarantee that the keyboard stays hidden in every situation.

In Android development, using EditText is very common. However, sometimes EditText automatically grabs focus when entering a page, causing the soft keyboard to pop up immediately. While this is convenient in some cases, most of the time we prefer the keyboard to appear only when the user explicitly clicks on the EditText.

Set these attributes on the parent layout to make it eligible for input focus in touch mode and give it priority during focus search:

These are attribute fragments for the parent layout’s opening tag. If the container takes initial focus, EditText is no longer the default input target; the user can still tap EditText to edit. See ViewGroup’s focus rules. An explicit <requestFocus />, a code call to requestFocus(), or restored focus can change the result, so inspect those sources as well.

If the requirement is only to hide the keyboard when entering an Activity while allowing EditText to retain focus, set this attribute on the existing Activity declaration:

stateHidden controls the initial keyboard state when the user navigates forward to the Activity. It does not prevent a later explicit request to show the keyboard, and returning to an existing screen can behave differently. See windowSoftInputMode. Choose focus handling and keyboard visibility according to the actual requirement.

entry.title: Android Tips Round-Up, Part 2
entry.content:
For the second Chinese post in this series, I translated Dan Lew’s Android Tips Round-Up. As in the first part, I’ve added notes from using some of these tools and filled in explanations where I thought they would help. If a few of the APIs are new to you, I hope the list comes in handy. The API updates are noted below.

Reviewed 2026-10-13: This 2014 list covers View and system utility APIs. Activity.onBackPressed() was deprecated in API 33, and text layout has a Builder API from API 23. The notes below add replacements and correct the explanations of alarms, application memory, and screen density.

DateUtils.formatDateTime() formats an epoch-millisecond timestamp using local date/time conventions. Flags choose which date, weekday, or time components to display. Use it for user-facing text rather than a fixed data-exchange format.

AlarmManager.setInexactRepeating() lets Android adjust repeating-alarm delivery times to batch wakeups. It does not automatically call cancel(); the app cancels alarms when no longer needed. From Android 4.4 (API 19), repeating alarms for apps targeting API 19 or later are inexact. RTC does not wake a sleeping device, while RTC_WAKEUP requests a wakeup; power-management policies still apply. An eight-hour sleep does not establish a guaranteed sixteen-to-one delivery rule or a fixed energy saving. Use a one-shot alarm for a single event. See the alarm scheduling guide for task-scheduling and exact-alarm boundaries.

Formatter.formatFileSize() converts a byte count into localized display text. Android 8.0 (API 26) and later use SI units, such as 1000 bytes per kB; older releases use powers of 1024. Do not parse the formatted result back into an exact byte count.

ActionBar.hide() / show() hide or show the application’s ActionBar. They do not hide the system status and navigation bars and therefore do not by themselves enable immersive fullscreen. A standalone Toolbar also needs handling appropriate to that component.

Linkify.addLinks() adds URLSpans to text matching a type mask or regular expression. When using the Spannable overload and displaying the result in a TextView, configure an appropriate MovementMethod for link clicks.

StaticLayout lays out, measures, and draws multiline text in a custom View. From Android 6.0 (API 23), prefer StaticLayout.Builder: supply the text, TextPaint, and width, set optional properties, then call build(). Rebuild the layout when the text or width changes.

Activity.onBackPressed() is the legacy back-event hook and was deprecated in Android 13 (API 33). Use OnBackPressedDispatcher / OnBackPressedCallback with AndroidX Activity 1.6.0 or later, or the platform’s API 33 OnBackInvokedCallback. The original advice to simply override onBackPressed() needs migration; see the predictive back guide.

GestureDetector recognizes taps, long presses, scrolling, and flings from MotionEvents. Feed events into onTouchEvent(). With SimpleOnGestureListener, onDown() normally needs to return true for the rest of the gesture to be handled. See common gesture detection.

DrawFilter can temporarily modify Paint properties used by drawing operations on the Canvas where it is installed, including antialiasing flags. It does not replace onDraw() or let a child View automatically change every ancestor and descendant’s rendering. For custom drawing, configure the Paint you own directly where possible.

ActivityManager.getMemoryClass() reports an approximate per-application memory class in MB, useful for budgeting the managed heap and caches. It is neither available device RAM nor the process’s current memory use. Native allocations and graphics buffers need separate observation.

ViewStub defers layout inflation. Calling inflate() or setting visibility to VISIBLE/INVISIBLE replaces the stub with the inflated hierarchy; keep the returned root View for subsequent operations. A <merge> root is not supported for the inflated layout. See loading views on demand.

SystemClock.sleep() blocks the current thread for the requested number of uptime milliseconds while preserving its interrupted state. Deep sleep is excluded from that clock, and scheduling can delay the return further. It can simulate a delay in a background debugging task, but it does not make work asynchronous and should not block the UI thread or a task that must promptly respond to cancellation.

DisplayMetrics.density is the logical dp-to-px scale factor, not physical screen dpi; typically px = dp × density. It is a field, not a method. Use resources from the current UI Context instead of fixing the value to one device.

Pair.create() constructs a Pair<A, B> whose values are available through first and second. It is a two-value container factory; a named type is usually clearer when the data has specific business meaning.

More

  4. Part 4

entry.title: Android Tips Round-Up, Part 1
entry.content:
Reviewed 2026-10-13: This 2014 list focuses on Android’s View system. Most APIs remain valid. The old Html.fromHtml(String) overload was deprecated in API 24; the notes below add its replacement and correct the descriptions of cache directories, layout inflation, and reverse playback.

For the first Chinese post in this series, I translated Dan Lew’s Android Tips Round-Up. You may already know some of these small SDK tools; I’m writing them down in case a few are new to you. It isn’t a word-for-word translation. I use some of these classes myself, so I’ve added my own notes and explanations where I thought they would help. This English edition includes the API updates below.

Activity.startActivities() builds a launch path in the order specified by an Intent array, useful when entering the middle of a flow while retaining a back path. Usually only the final Activity is created immediately; earlier ones are created when visited by navigating back. Launch modes and Intent flags still affect task behavior.

TextUtils.isEmpty() returns true for null or a zero-length character sequence. A string containing only spaces is not empty by this test.

Html.fromHtml() parses HTML into styled Spanned text for widgets such as TextView. It neither generates HTML nor implements a full browser. From Android 7.0 (API 24), use fromHtml(source, flags); HtmlCompat.fromHtml, added in AndroidX Core 1.1.0, provides a compatibility option, but ignores flags below API 24. For a simple bold span, constructing a Spannable directly avoids HTML parsing. Whether parsing is a bottleneck depends on text size and call frequency.

TextView.setError() displays an error icon and message after input validation fails. Pass null to clear it. The application still supplies the validation rules.

Build.VERSION_CODES defines named API-level constants. Read Build.VERSION.SDK_INT for the device’s running API level, then compare it with a constant such as Build.VERSION_CODES.N before calling an API 24 method. The constant table itself is not the current OS version.

Log.getStackTraceString() converts a throwable’s stack trace to a string for custom logging. It returns an empty string if an UnknownHostException appears in the cause chain, so an empty result does not establish that no exception occurred.

LayoutInflater.from() will be familiar if you write Adapters often. It takes a Context and returns its LayoutInflater; the subsequent inflate(layoutId, parent, attachToRoot) call creates the View. Supplying the actual parent in an Adapter gives the inflated View appropriate LayoutParams.

ViewConfiguration.getScaledTouchSlop() returns the movement distance, in pixels, tolerated before a touch is considered a scroll. Obtain the configuration through ViewConfiguration.get(context) instead of hard-coding one threshold across display densities. Gesture code still performs the displacement comparison.

PhoneNumberUtils.convertKeypadLettersToDigits() maps letters in a phone number to telephone-keypad digits: 1-800-GOOG-411 becomes 1-800-4664-411. It does not provide T9 word prediction or validate whether a number is usable.

Context.getCacheDir() returns the app’s internal cache directory. The external Android/data/<package>/cache/ directory comes from getExternalCacheDir(), which can return null. Cached files may be removed under storage pressure and are removed on uninstall. Handle cache misses and keep persistent data elsewhere; obtain paths from the API instead of constructing them manually.

ArgbEvaluator, available from API 11, interpolates ARGB colors. I hadn’t used this class when I translated the post, so I made a note to come back to it. Its evaluate() interface uses object arguments and returns an object. The original concern about boxing is worth measuring before deciding to write an implementation yourself. From API 21, ValueAnimator.ofArgb() provides a direct color-animation factory; it does not promise boxing-free execution.

ContextThemeWrapper supplies a different theme when creating a View or Dialog. Set the theme before constructing those objects; wrapping a Context does not automatically restyle an existing View tree.

Space, introduced in Android 4.0 (API 14), is a lightweight layout placeholder. Its draw() produces no content, but it still participates in measurement and layout.

ValueAnimator.reverse() plays an animation backward, from its current position if running or from the end if stopped. It does not cancel the animation. Use cancel() for an immediate stop, on the thread running the animation.

entry.title: Android Tools - Log2File
entry.content:
Updated 2026-10-13: The 2014 implementation wrote directly under the external-storage root, which is outdated. Android 10 (API 29) introduced scoped storage; Android 11 (API 30) ignores requestLegacyExternalStorage for apps targeting API 30 or higher. The replacement below uses app-internal storage, requires Android 4.4 (API 19) or later, and needs no storage permission. See Android 11 storage changes.

Log2File records logs explicitly supplied by an Android application to a file. It is useful when:

  1. A computer cannot be connected for debugging, for example because USB OTG occupies the port.
  2. Logs are difficult to capture in real time.
  3. An intermittent bug requires a record of the operations preceding it.
  4. I’ll leave the other uses to your imagination.

It saves only the content passed to w(); it does not automatically capture system logcat. Use the Logcat tools for system logging.

0. Introduction

This article originally appeared on my CSDN blog before moving here. The original GitHub source URL returned 404 during this update, so the replacement implementation is included below.

1. Log2File Source Code

The original static writer and separate logInit flag could race during concurrent writes and closure. This version gives one object ownership of a logging session and uses the same lock for writing and closing. Initialization, write, and close failures propagate as IOException for the caller to handle.

Files live under context.getFilesDir()/log2file/. This is app-internal storage, needs no storage permission, and is removed when the app is uninstalled. Use temporary read access through FileProvider or a similar sharing mechanism to export a log. See app-specific files.

The implementation uses UTF-8 and Unix epoch milliseconds instead of the deprecated, locale-dependent Date.toLocaleString(). StandardCharsets is available from API 19:

Use a single Log2File object per file within a process. synchronized does not coordinate different logger objects or different processes. Writing after close() throws an exception; resource ownership must make it clear who closes the object and when.

This example flushes each line, which is suitable for short, low-frequency diagnostic sessions but adds I/O. flush() forwards Java-buffered data to the underlying stream; it does not guarantee recovery after power loss. Long-running or high-frequency capture needs file-size limits, retention rules, and bounded write queues, with batching and rotation as appropriate. Those policies are outside this minimal example. See BufferedWriter.

2. Usage

The constructor replaces the original static init() call. Open a logger in a background task, write the relevant events, and close it when the task finishes:

try-with-resources calls close() on both normal and exceptional exit. If capture spans several callbacks, let one task or component own the instance and close it only after all writes finish. Do not reopen the file for every log message.

Record only the information required for diagnosis; avoid passwords, tokens, and complete user input. App-internal storage controls file ownership and access, but does not replace redaction or retention limits.

entry.title: Android Service: Building Your Own Notification Center (2) - Accessibility Service in Practice
entry.content:
Updated 2026-10-13: This article records the historical approach of observing notifications through accessibility events before Android 4.3. That approach is outdated for a general notification center. Android 4.3 (API 18) introduced NotificationListenerService; section 4 adds a minimal listener for Android 7.0 (API 24) and later. The legacy examples explain the earlier implementation and do not provide a complete notification list.

1. Accessibility Service in Practice

The previous article introduced accessibility services and their basic configuration. This article follows the original implementation of a simple notification center. Android’s system notification UI displays notifications from apps and system components, such as missed calls, screenshots, weather, and news updates. Before Android 4.3, ordinary third-party apps did not have a public API to query the active notification list. Accessibility events offered a limited way to observe notifications; Android 4.3 added the dedicated NotificationListenerService.getActiveNotifications() API.

The following sections preserve the accessibility-based implementation. Layout resources came from the original project, so these excerpts are not a complete Android project. New notification centers should use the dedicated API in section 4.

2. Building a Third-Party Notification Center

2.1 Extending AccessibilityService

Following the previous article, create a service extending AccessibilityService. Check the event and payload types before forwarding the notification to this application’s interface:

The callbacks have distinct purposes:

  1. onServiceConnected() runs when the system connects the service, not when an Activity binds to it. This implementation handles only notifications, so it subscribes only to TYPE_NOTIFICATION_STATE_CHANGED.
  2. onInterrupt() asks the service to interrupt accessibility feedback; it is not a disconnection callback.
  3. onAccessibilityEvent() receives matching events. Check the type of getParcelableData() before casting it to Notification. See the AccessibilityEvent reference.

Once I had the Notification, I sent it to the Activity through a broadcast. The updated example restricts delivery to the app’s package and uses a signature permission on both sender and receiver. Package targeting limits where the broadcast goes; the receiver’s permission limits who can send data to it.

I also ran into the broadcast payload-size limit with large notifications, including screenshots and missed calls. A full Notification can contain large RemoteViews, images, or extras and trigger TransactionTooLargeException. The original post suggested keeping contentView temporarily in Application, but that doesn’t handle cross-process access, process restarts, or other large fields. For a current implementation, keep the fields you need in the app’s data layer and let the UI read snapshots instead of repeatedly broadcasting whole notification objects.

2.2 Registering the Service in Manifest

This example assumes an applicationId of com.example.notificationcenter. Change the custom permission prefix if using another package. Permission declarations belong under <manifest>, while the service belongs under <application>:

BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE restricts service binding to the system. The metadata refers to res/xml/accessibilityserviceconfig.xml; XML service configuration is available from Android 4.0 (API 14):

This selects the notification events handled by the service.

2.3 Receiving and Displaying Notifications

The Activity excerpt below reads the notification and attempts to display its legacy custom RemoteViews. The activity_main layout must contain a TextView named notify_test_textview and a LinearLayout named root_layout. Compile against SDK 33 or higher and declare this Activity in the manifest.

The receiver is registered in onStart() and unregistered in onStop(), so it stops receiving notifications when the Activity stops. A signature permission protects both ends. Android 13 (API 33) and later also use RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED. See the context-registered receiver lifecycle.

The user must enable the service in Settings → Accessibility. The manifest declaration alone does not grant access.

RemoteViews is a description of a remote layout, not a View that can be passed directly to addView(). Call apply() to obtain a View first. Notification.contentView was deprecated in API 24 and may be absent for modern template notifications, so this cannot reproduce every notification. The excerpt preserves the original display approach with failure handling.

A complete notification center still takes some work: updates, removals, ordering, user interaction, and process restarts all need handling. I couldn’t share the full implementation because it was a company project. If you’re interested, feel free to get in touch privately.

3. Summary and Limitations

This post took me a while to finish. It also gave me a chance to wrap up the work from that project. These were the problems left in the implementation at the time:

  1. Accessibility events do not supply the complete current notification list or reconstruct notifications that have already been dismissed.
  2. I kept the data only in memory, so it was lost when the service was killed. I tried saving whole notification objects with an object database, db4o, but couldn’t get it working. An app can persist the text, package names, timestamps, and other fields it needs in its own database; whole Notification or RemoteViews objects aren’t a stable persistence format.
  3. Not every system change produces an observable notification event. USB state, for example, should be observed through the relevant system API rather than inferred entirely from notifications.

4. Notification Listening After Android 4.3

NotificationListenerService has supplied posted/removed callbacks and active-notification queries since API 18. The following example uses both onListenerConnected() from API 21 and onListenerDisconnected() from API 24, so its minimum runtime version is Android 7.0. From API 24, these callbacks run on the main thread.

Declare the dedicated service inside <application>. This approach does not need the accessibility service or internal broadcast shown earlier:

The user must also grant notification access in system settings. This is separate from accessibility authorization and Android 13’s POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission to post notifications.

This listener retains only notification keys to demonstrate synchronization on connection, updates, and removals. It does not read or log notification bodies:

Call getActiveNotifications() only after connection. It synchronizes notifications that are still active and visible to this listener, not a history of dismissed notifications. After disconnection, an empty local set represents unavailable state, not proof that the device has no notifications. A real UI should observe data-layer snapshots that include connection status and move persistence work out of callbacks.

From Android 15 (API 35), untrusted notification listeners cannot read unredacted content from notifications in which an OTP is detected. Notification access therefore does not guarantee access to every field. See Android 15 notification-content protections.

entry.title: Ubuntu: Adb Command Cannot Find Device
entry.content:
This post dates from 2014, when I was using a Nokia X and an old Android SDK. The udev and user-group instructions were updated for Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on 2026-10-13. The old SYSFS rule and Upstart restart procedure no longer apply; the adb_usb.ini workaround remains at the end as a historical note.

1. Problem Overview

Recently, while developing for a Nokia project, I encountered the following issue:

When I plugged in a Nokia X, the computer did not respond at all—it wasn’t recognized. My colleague’s Windows machine also failed to detect it. After searching Google for a long time, I finally found a solution. Since I didn’t record it originally and later forgot how to configure it when helping someone else, I decided to document it here for everyone.

2. Solution

Enable USB debugging on the device and use a cable that supports data transfer. Check the selected Platform-Tools version with adb version, then inspect the connection using adb devices -l.

  • Empty list: check the cable, port, USB debugging setting, and whether the host enumerates the device.
  • no permissions: check Linux udev rules and the current user’s groups.
  • unauthorized: ADB has found the device; unlock it and accept the RSA debugging prompt.
  • offline: the device is not responding normally to ADB; reconnect it or restart the ADB server and inspect the state again.

USB enumeration, host permissions, and device authorization are separate checks. See the ADB reference and hardware-device setup guide.

2.1. Run lsusb

Run lsusb and identify the entry added when the device is connected. The original Nokia X appeared as follows; use the IDs actually reported for other devices:

0421 is the vendor ID and 06e8 is the product ID. Neither is a Linux permission mode. USB enumeration alone does not establish ADB authorization.

2.2. Configure udev Rules and User Groups

On Ubuntu, start with the distribution’s rules package. Android’s official setup guide specifies the following package and group; the Ubuntu 24.04 package is in the universe repository:

Log out and back in after changing group membership. Check id for plugdev, then reconnect the device. This package supplies common files and USB rules; continue using the ADB binary from the selected SDK’s Platform-Tools installation.

Add a custom rule only if the distribution’s rules do not cover the device. For the Nokia X above, the rule in /etc/udev/rules.d/51-android-local.rules would be:

ATTR{} matches device attributes, MODE sets device-node permissions, and GROUP selects the owning group. This example grants read/write access to root and plugdev, not every user. The rule file itself does not need executable permission. Reload the rules, then unplug and reconnect the device:

Reloading does not retroactively change an existing device node; reconnecting generates device events that apply the rules. See systemd’s udev and udevadm manuals for the syntax and reload behavior.

2.3. Restart ADB as the Regular User

Check that the commands refer to the same Platform-Tools installation, then restart the server as the logged-in user:

Routine development does not require sudo adb start-server to bypass USB permissions. If a server was previously started as root, stop that process before returning to the regular user. Also check SDK paths so the terminal and Android Studio do not use different ADB versions. Restarting the server interrupts existing ADB connections.

2.4. Historical adb_usb.ini Configuration

My Nokia X needed one more step back then. It still wasn’t recognized after the earlier setup, so I had to add its vendor ID to the old SDK’s ~/.android/adb_usb.ini. I’ve kept that entry below as a record of the workaround; it isn’t needed for the Ubuntu 24.04 procedure above:

For current devices, start with the documented USB debugging, udev, and authorization checks. Windows uses ADB USB drivers rather than Linux udev rules; follow the OEM USB driver instructions.
